question: After the rebellion of Korah in the wilderness, the tribes murmur again against Moses and against the priesthood. To settle the matter once and for all, Moses gathers a rod from each tribal chief and lays them up in the Tabernacle before the testimony overnight (Numbers 17). How many rods does he lay before the testimony?
context: One rod for each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Numbers 17:2 -- 'Speak unto the children of Israel, and take of every one of them a rod according to the house of their fathers, of all their princes... twelve rods.' Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Numbers 17.

question: When Moses goes into the Tent of the Testimony in the morning, only one of the tribal rods is alive -- it has budded, put forth blossoms, and even yielded ripe fruit overnight. The rod belongs to Aaron, Moses's brother. Which tribe of Israel does Aaron represent?
context: Aaron is of the tribe of Levi (Numbers 17:8: 'the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded'). The rod-test settles that the Levites, and not any other tribe, are the chosen priestly line. Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Numbers 17.

question: The dead wooden staff of Aaron does not merely bud overnight in the Tabernacle -- it goes the whole way from bud to blossom to ripe fruit in one night. What fruit does Numbers 17:8 say the rod actually yields by morning?
context: Numbers 17:8 -- 'the rod of Aaron... was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.' The almond tree is the earliest to bloom in the Holy Land, a fitting image of a first-fruits sign. Source: Bible Hub, Numbers 17:8.

question: According to the Epistle to the Hebrews (9:4), the budded rod of Aaron was afterwards kept as a sacred relic inside the Ark of the Covenant, alongside two other objects preserved from the wilderness years. What are the two other objects?
answer: the pot of manna and the tables of stone
choices: the pot of manna and the tables of stone
the seven-branched menorah and the ephod
the incense censer and the breastplate
the scroll of the Law and the shewbread
context: Hebrews 9:4 lists 'the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant' inside the Ark. Later Jewish tradition disagrees on whether the pot and rod were literally in the Ark or beside it, but Hebrews puts them in. Source: Wikipedia, Aaron's rod; Hebrews 9:4.

question: Further along the wilderness journey, the people speak against God and Moses -- 'wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?' (Numbers 21:5). In response, God sends a plague of biting creatures into the camp, and many die. What kind of creatures does God send?
context: Numbers 21:6 -- 'the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.' 'Fiery' probably refers to the burning venom of the bite. The people repent; Moses is told to make a bronze serpent on a pole, and any bitten man who looks at it lives. Source: Wikipedia, Nehushtan; Numbers 21.

question: Centuries after Moses set the bronze serpent on the pole in the wilderness, King Hezekiah of Judah walks into the temple and breaks the healing-relic in pieces, because the people had begun burning incense to it as an idol (2 Kings 18:4). Hezekiah gives the shattered thing a contemptuous nickname. What does he call it?
context: 2 Kings 18:4 -- 'he brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan.' The name puns on the Hebrew nehoshet (brass) -- a merciless nickname meant to strip the object of the sacred aura Israel had wrongly given it. Baal-zebub, Dagon, and Molech are all real gods Israel encountered but were never nicknames for the serpent-pole. Source: Wikipedia, Nehushtan; 2 Kings 18.

question: An old man named Abram, his wife Sarai, and his nephew Lot were told by God to leave their home and walk toward a land they had never seen. From what city did Abram set out on that journey?
context: KJV Genesis 11:31: 'Terah took Abram his son ... and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan.' Nineveh is Jonah's Assyrian city; Haran was a way-station Abram stopped at on the road out of Ur; Babylon rose to power much later.

question: Abram and Sarai reached the land God had promised, and at the great tree of Moreh in Shechem, God appeared to him again and swore the land to his descendants. What did Abram do on that spot to mark the promise?
answer: built an altar unto the LORD
choices: built an altar unto the LORD
cut down the tree for firewood
set up a pillar of twelve stones
planted a vineyard and a grove
context: KJV Genesis 12:7: 'Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.' Twelve-stone pillars belong to Jacob and Joshua later; the vineyard is Noah's after the flood.

question: Abram grieved that he was rich but childless, with only his servant to inherit. One night God brought him out of his tent and told him to look up at something impossible to count, saying 'so shall thy seed be.' What did God tell him to look at and try to number?
choices: the grains of sand on the shore
the leaves of the terebinth trees
the flocks on the surrounding hills
context: KJV Genesis 15:5: 'And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.' Sand on the shore is the promise given to Isaac and Jacob later; the other two never appear as the count.

question: God changed the name of Abraham's wife on the same day he changed her husband's. What was her new name?
context: KJV Genesis 17:15: 'As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be.' Hagar was the Egyptian handmaid who bore Ishmael, Rebekah married Isaac a generation later, Rachel married Jacob two generations later.

question: Abraham was sitting in the door of his tent at the oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day when three visitors appeared. He ran to fetch a tender calf and cakes, and after they ate, one of them announced that in the coming year Sarah would bear a son. Sarah, listening from inside the tent, did something Isaac was later named after. What did she do?
choices: she wept quietly in her veil
she sang a song of Miriam
she poured out a jar of oil
context: KJV Genesis 18:12: 'Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' The son's name Isaac (Yitzhak) means 'he laughs' -- Genesis 21:6, 'God hath made me to laugh.' Miriam's song and the pouring of oil belong to Moses's sister and to the anointing scenes.

question: When Abram returned from rescuing his nephew Lot from four raiding kings, a mysterious king of Salem came out to meet him. This king was also a priest of the most high God, and he brought out two things and blessed Abram. What did he bring?
context: KJV Genesis 14:18: 'And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.' The name Melchizedek means 'king of righteousness' and later became one of the most argued-over figures in Jewish and Christian tradition. Gold and myrrh belong to the visit of the Magi much later.

question: The three visitors left Mamre and walked toward Sodom, where the cities of the plain were destroyed by fire and brimstone. As Lot and his family fled the burning city, one of them broke the angels' warning and looked back at what she was leaving. What became of Lot's wife in that moment?
context: KJV Genesis 19:26: 'But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.' Ancient travelers pointed to salt formations near the Dead Sea as her supposed remains; the moral of the story in the biblical text is about looking back at what one has been told to leave behind.

question: The sea-nymph Thetis was warned that her son Achilles would die young at Troy. To hide him from the war she sent him to the palace of King Lycomedes on a small Aegean island, told to live there in a disguise nobody would suspect on the son of Peleus. What disguise did she give him?
answer: A girl among the king's daughters
choices: A girl among the king's daughters
A shepherd boy tending the palace flock
A kitchen slave serving the king's table
context: From Statius, Achilleid Book 1 (1st c. CE). The disguise runs deep: Achilles takes a girl-name, lives among the princesses, and fathers a son on one of them (Deidameia) before he is ever unmasked.  (Legend.)

question: Hidden among the daughters of King Lycomedes on his Aegean island, the boy Achilles took a girl-name to match his disguise. The name he chose meant 'red-haired' in Greek -- and it stuck so hard that his own son, born on the island, would grow up called by a male form of it. What girl-name did Achilles take?
context: Pyrrha means 'red-haired'. Their son Neoptolemus ('new to war') was also called Pyrrhus, the male form of his father's alias -- a joke the Greeks did not forget. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles on Skyros; Neoptolemus.  (Legend.)

question: The seer Calchas told the Greek chieftains gathered at Aulis that Troy could not fall unless one specific warrior sailed with them -- and that warrior was hidden somewhere in the world, dressed as a girl. The chieftains chose one man to go find him. Whom did they send?
context: The errand needed a trick, and Odysseus's tricks are why the assignment fell to him. Source: Apollodorus, Epitome 3.13-14; Statius, Achilleid.  (Legend.)

question: In the palace courtyard on the island, Odysseus spread his merchant's wares in front of King Lycomedes's daughters: bright cloths, jewels, mirrors, ribbons. Hidden among the finery he placed two objects that had nothing to do with a girl's wardrobe. What were the two hidden objects that would betray Achilles?
context: In the Apollodorus version, one 'daughter' ignored the pretty things and reached for these two -- and Odysseus had his man. Source: Apollodorus, Epitome 3.13-14.  (Legend.)

question: In a second version of the unmasking, Odysseus did not just wait for the shield-grab. As the 'daughters' fingered the wares in the courtyard, his men stationed outside sounded one specific battle-signal to see which 'daughter' would flinch toward the weapons. What signal did they sound?
choices: A clash of shield on shield
context: Some vase paintings show the trumpet version rather than the shield-reach; either way, only Achilles reacts as a fighter. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles on Skyros.  (Legend.)

question: The island where Thetis hid Achilles was ruled by King Lycomedes -- and in another Greek legend that same king turned host-turned-killer to a far more famous guest. The Athenian hero Theseus, slayer of the Minotaur, came to Lycomedes in his old age and was murdered by him on the island. How did Lycomedes kill Theseus?
answer: He hurled him from a cliff into the sea
choices: He hurled him from a cliff into the sea
He poisoned his cup at the welcome feast
He set his hounds on him in the hunting field
He drowned him in the palace bath
context: The same court that sheltered young Achilles had already thrown Theseus to his death from a Skyrian cliff. Source: Wikipedia, Skyros; Lycomedes.  (Legend.)

question: The Iliad's greatest fighter on the Trojan side was the eldest son of Troy's aged king, and Troy's chief defender. When the Greek army came against the city he led every sortie and killed many Greek captains. What was this Trojan prince's name?
context: Hector is the moral centre of the Iliad's Trojan side -- husband to Andromache, father to baby Astyanax. Source: Homer, Iliad; Wikipedia, Hector.  (Legend.)

question: In Iliad Book 6, Hector comes home from battle. His wife meets him at the gate with their baby son. When Hector reaches for the child, the baby screams -- not at his father, but at the horsehair crest on his father's war-helmet. What does Hector do?
answer: Takes the helmet off and laughs
choices: Takes the helmet off and laughs
Sings the baby a battle hymn
Presses the baby to the helmet plume
Hands the baby back and leaves at once
context: Iliad 6.466-473. One of the tenderest scenes in Homer; the emotional weight the death-scene later cashes in. Source: Wikipedia, Andromache.  (Legend.)

question: Alone outside the Scaean Gate, Hector waited for Achilles. His father and mother on the wall begged him to come inside. When Achilles finally came on him in the new god-forged armour, Hector's nerve broke and he bolted. What happened next?
answer: Achilles chased him around the walls of Troy
choices: Achilles chased him around the walls of Troy
Achilles cornered him against the city gate
Achilles caught him within a single spear-cast
Achilles let him go and turned back to the ships
context: Iliad 22.136-207. The chase went three full laps of the city; Homer compares it to a hawk swooping on a trembling dove. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22; Wikipedia, Hector.  (Legend.)

question: Hector finally turned to fight only because a figure appeared beside him promising to stand at his side -- his own brother, come out from the city to help. Except it was not his brother at all. A goddess had taken that shape to trick him into stopping. Which goddess wore the disguise?
context: Athena took the shape of Hector's brother Deiphobus. When Hector reached for a second spear from his 'brother' after the duel began, no one was there. Iliad 22.226-247.  (Legend.)

question: In the duel outside the walls, Hector was wearing Achilles's own old armour -- stripped from Patroclus's body earlier in the war. Achilles knew the armour better than anyone alive: he knew every joint of it and every gap in it. He drove his spear into the single unguarded place. Where did the spear go in?
context: Iliad 22.324-329. The spear-point kept Hector alive just long enough to speak -- and to prophesy Achilles's own death. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Dying at Achilles's feet, Hector spent his last breath not begging for himself but making a prophecy. He named two figures -- one mortal, one god -- who would together kill Achilles at that same gate before Troy fell. Who did he name?
context: Iliad 22.359-360. The prophecy is fulfilled: Paris later shoots Achilles with a bow, Apollo guiding the arrow. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Hector had begged with his dying words that his body be given back to his family for a proper burial. Achilles refused. He pierced the tendons behind Hector's heels, ran oxhide thongs through the holes, and tied the corpse to a moving vehicle so it would be dragged face-down through the dust. To what did he tie the body?
answer: The back of his own chariot
choices: The back of his own chariot
A litter borne by two horses
The mast of a beached ship
context: Iliad 22.395-405. The horses dragged Hector in circuits within full view of the walls -- and of Priam, Hecuba, and Andromache watching from the ramparts. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 22.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles did not stop after one day. Every morning for a stretch of days after Hector's death, he hitched the body up again and dragged it round the burial mound of his own dead friend Patroclus. Homer gives the exact number of days he kept doing this. How many days?
context: Iliad 24.14-18. The gods on Olympus were sickened by the excess and finally forced Zeus to intervene. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 24.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus finally lost patience with Achilles's excess and decided the body must go back. That decision sets up the last book of the Iliad, in which an old man crosses the Greek lines alone at night, unarmed, into the tent of the man who killed his son -- and asks for the body. Who is the old man?
context: Iliad Book 24. Guided by Hermes, King Priam kisses the hands 'that have killed my sons' -- and Achilles weeps with him. The two eat together, and Hector goes home for burial. Source: Homer, Iliad Book 24.  (Legend.)

question: The mother of the Greek hero Achilles was not a mortal queen but a divine being of the sea, one of the fifty Nereids -- daughters of the sea-god Nereus. She had married a mortal king and Achilles was their only son. What was her name?
context: Thetis is the sea-nymph mother; her wedding to the mortal Peleus is where the golden apple 'to the fairest' rolls in, and starts the chain of events that leads to the Trojan War. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: To make her baby son Achilles proof against weapons, his sea-nymph mother dipped him in the black waters of an underworld river. There was only one problem with her method: her own hand. She held the child by one part of his body as she lowered him, and that one part -- gripped in her fingers -- was the only patch of skin the water never touched. Which body part did she hold him by?
context: The heel became the single un-dipped spot. Every language in the West now has the phrase 'an Achilles heel' for the single vulnerable spot in something otherwise proof. Source: Wikipedia, Achilles heel.  (Legend.)

question: When Paris drew back the bow to shoot Achilles, the arrow did not fly true on its own. A god stood at the archer's shoulder and steered the shaft. Homer names the same god in Hector's earlier dying prophecy: he had warned Achilles that this same god, with Paris, would bring him down at the great gate. Which god guided the arrow?
context: Iliad 22.359-360. Apollo, patron of Troy and of the bow, is the god Hector names in his last breath. Source: Homer, Iliad; Wikipedia, Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: Hector, dying at Achilles's feet earlier in the war, had prophesied that Achilles would fall in one specific place -- the same great gate of Troy where Hector himself had made his last stand. Homer names this gate several times in the Iliad. Which gate was it?
context: The Scaean Gate is the western gate of Troy, facing the Greek camp on the beach. Hector waits there for Achilles in Iliad 22; Achilles falls there later. Source: Homer, Iliad 22.359-360.  (Legend.)

question: On the last night of Troy, a young Trojan warrior named Aeneas fights all night to hold the citadel until his own mother -- a goddess -- appears to him and tells him to get out, that staying to die will change nothing. Which goddess was Aeneas's mother?
context: Called Venus in Latin. She warns him that the city's fate is sealed and the future of Troy must be carried out by him. Source: Virgil, Aeneid Book 2; Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas runs home through the burning streets of Troy to fetch his family, but his old father refuses to leave -- he cannot walk on his own and would rather die in the city. What is Aeneas's father named?
context: Once Aphrodite's mortal lover; struck lame by Zeus for boasting about her. Priam is the king of Troy; Laocoon warns of the wooden horse; Antenor is another Trojan elder. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: Anchises refuses to leave the burning city, and Aeneas cannot carry him against his will. Then the family sees something amazing: a tongue of fire plays harmlessly around the head of Aeneas's small son, without burning him or his hair. What is that son named?
context: Also called Iulus, the name Roman tradition uses to link him to the family of Julius Caesar. Astyanax is Hector's baby son, killed in the sack; Telemachus is Odysseus's son; Orestes is Agamemnon's son. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2 (Theoi); Wikipedia, Ascanius.  (Legend.)

question: Anchises finally agrees to leave. Aeneas is a strong young warrior; his father is old and lame; his small son cannot keep up in the smoke. How does Aeneas get his father out of the burning city?
answer: He hoists Anchises onto his own shoulders
choices: He hoists Anchises onto his own shoulders
He carries him in a litter with three servants
He puts him on a horse and leads it by the reins
He drags him on a shield across the flagstones
context: This is the founding image of Roman piety. The small son Ascanius walks beside them, holding his father's hand. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius; Virgil, Aeneid Book 2.  (Legend.)

question: Bernini as a young man of about twenty carved the escape from Troy in marble around 1618: a single upright column of three living generations -- the old grandfather on the shoulders of his son, and the grandson walking beside them. In which Roman museum does that statue stand today?
context: The sculpture is titled 'Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius' and is about 220 cm tall. Anchises holds a vessel of ashes topped by two tiny Penates. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius.

question: As Aeneas walks out of Troy carrying his father and leading his son, his wife follows a little way behind them. In the smoke and the dark and the crowds she is separated from the family and lost. What is Aeneas's wife named?
context: Andromache is Hector's widow; Hecuba is Priam's queen; Cassandra is the prophetess daughter of Priam who is dragged from Athena's altar in the sack. Source: Wikipedia, Creusa of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas gets his father and son safely out of Troy, realizes his wife is missing, and rushes back into the burning city alone to look for her. What does he find?
answer: Her ghost, which speaks to him and then fades from his arms
choices: Her ghost, which speaks to him and then fades from his arms
Her body pinned under a burning beam in the courtyard
The Greek soldier who killed her, whom he cuts down at the well
Nothing at all -- he searches the smoke until dawn and gives up
context: She tells him a new wife and a new kingdom in a western land await him, and to care for their son; three times he tries to embrace her and three times his arms pass through her. Aeneid Book 2, from about line 650. Source: Wikipedia, Creusa of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Aeneas gathers other Trojan survivors on Mount Ida and sails west on a long wandering that echoes the Odyssey -- Delos, Crete, Sicily, and Carthage, where queen Dido falls in love with him. He finally lands at the mouth of a river in Latium, in central Italy. At the mouth of which river does he land?
context: The river Rome will be built on, generations later, by Aeneas's distant descendant Romulus. The Rubicon is the small stream Julius Caesar later crosses; the Po and the Arno are further north. Source: Wikipedia, Aeneas.  (Legend.)

question: A young god of the Tuatha De Danann falls asleep and dreams of the most beautiful woman he has ever seen, standing at the foot of his bed. He reaches for her -- and she vanishes. She comes back every night for a full year. He is the love-and-youth god of the Irish, son of the Dagda and the river-goddess Boann, and his name means 'the Young Son'. Who is he?
context: Aengus (also spelled Oengus), often called Aengus Og ('Young Aengus'), is the Tuatha De god of love and youth. Lugh is the sun-and-craft god; Nuada the Silver-Arm was king of the Tuatha De; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god. Wikipedia: Aengus; Aislinge Oenguso.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus's home in Ireland is a great mound on the River Boyne -- the oldest surviving monument in the country, older than the Egyptian pyramids by five hundred years. Modern archaeologists call the site Newgrange. What did the ancient Irish call it?
context: Bru na Boinne means 'the Dwelling of the Boyne'. Emain Macha is the Ulster capital; Tara is the seat of the High King; Dun Aengus is a cliff-fort on Inishmore (unrelated despite the name). Wikipedia: Bru na Boinne.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus falls so sick from the nightly dream of the vanishing woman that he cannot eat and will not speak. His mother Boann searches every hill and glen of Ireland for a year and cannot find the girl. His father the Dagda searches for another year -- nothing. In desperation they send for a third searcher, the king of the sidhe of Munster, and HE finds her after a third year. Who is this king?
context: Bodb Derg ('Bodb the Red') is king of the sidhe of Munster and later chosen king over all the Tuatha De after the Milesian conquest. Midir and Elcmar are other sidhe-lords; Manannan rules the sea-realm. Mythical Ireland: Aislinge Oengusso.  (Legend.)

question: Wherever Aengus goes, four small creatures circle his head. The Irish poets say they are his kisses, turned by his own love-power into living things. What creatures follow him?
context: The Dindsenchas records the four kiss-birds; a druid later traps them out of a tree. This is the root of a long strand in Irish poetry about love-as-birds. Wikipedia: Aengus.  (Legend.)

question: Bodb Derg finds the woman of the dream at last, on a lake in the west of Ireland where a strange company of women is gathered. She stands among one hundred and fifty of them, all chained in pairs by chains of the same metal. Only she -- the fairest -- wears a chain of a different metal, single around her neck. What metal marks her out?
context: The hundred-and-fifty are paired by silver; the fairest, Caer, is marked out by a single gold chain. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: The name of the woman Aengus has been dreaming of turns out to mean 'Yew-Berry' -- the yew being the Irish tree of eternity, since it grew in graveyards and lived for centuries. Her father is Ethal Anbuail of Connacht. What is her name?
context: Ibormeith = 'yew-berry'. Deirdre, Grainne, and Emer are other named heroines of Irish myth (Ulster Cycle and Fenian Cycle), all adjacent-real distractors. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: When Aengus reaches Loch Bel Dracon to claim Caer, he finds she is not simply a woman. Every alternate year, on one day of the calendar, she and her one-hundred-and-fifty companions change shape -- for a full year they are neither girls nor human at all, but a company of chained birds on the water. On which day does the change come?
context: Samhain is the Irish threshold between summer and winter and the classic moment for the veil between worlds to thin -- the natural day for a shape-change. Beltane, Imbolc, and Lughnasa are the other three great Irish quarter-days. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: On Samhain morning Aengus stands at the edge of Loch Bel Dracon and calls to Caer among the flock on the water. She answers that she will come to him only on ONE condition -- something HE must do first, before she will leave the lake with him. What is the condition?
answer: he must turn himself into a swan too
choices: he must turn himself into a swan too
he must strike off her silver chain with his own sword
he must fast for three days and three nights
he must give up his home at Bru na Boinne
context: The condition is transformation, not payment or oath -- Aengus must MEET her in her other shape. He does, and joins her on the water. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith; Mythical Ireland: Aislinge Oengusso.  (Legend.)

question: The two swans lift off the water together, circle back to Bru na Boinne, and sing as they fly. The song is so sweet that everyone in Ireland who hears it is overcome. What does the singing do?
answer: it puts all of Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights
choices: it puts all of Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights
it heals every wound in Ireland at once
it silences every other bird in Ireland for a year
it turns every lake in Ireland to gold at sunrise
context: This is the closing image of Aislinge Oenguso: the swan-song lays the whole island under a three-day sleep. Wikipedia: Caer Ibormeith.  (Legend.)

question: Aengus does not INHERIT Bru na Boinne -- he TRICKS his father the Dagda out of it. The trick turns on the Old Irish phrase 'laa ocus aidche'. Aengus asks the Dagda if he can have the Bru for laa ocus aidche and the Dagda agrees. What does Aengus then argue the phrase actually means, and so keep the Bru forever?
answer: 'day and night' -- meaning all of time, forever
choices: 'day and night' -- meaning all of time, forever
'a hundred summers' -- the span of an old man's life
'until the salmon return' -- the never-arriving day
'while the yew stands' -- meaning as long as the tree lives
context: Old Irish has no indefinite article, so 'a day and a night' and 'day and night' are the same phrase. Aengus takes the second meaning and keeps the Bru. The trick is preserved in the Tochmarc Etaine, where the elder version has the Dagda helping Aengus play it on Elcmar. Wikipedia: Aengus.  (Legend.)

question: Agatha is a young Christian noblewoman of a great Sicilian city, martyred by tradition in 251 CE. Her city keeps her white silk veil to this day and honors her every February with round pastries baked in her name. In which Sicilian city was Agatha martyred?
context: Catania sits on the east coast of Sicily at the foot of Mount Etna. Syracuse is Sicily's other famous martyr-city (its own martyr is Lucia); Palermo and Messina are the western and northeastern great cities and are the home cities of other saints (Rosalia of Palermo, for instance) -- but Agatha is Catania's own.

question: Agatha is caught up in one of the great empire-wide crackdowns on Christians -- ordered by an emperor whose edict of 250 CE required every citizen to sacrifice publicly to the Roman gods and receive a certificate to prove it. Under which emperor was she killed?
context: The Decian persecution of 250-251 CE was the first empire-wide required sacrifice -- refusing meant death. Nero's persecution (60s CE) was earlier and confined to Rome after the great fire; Diocletian's (303 CE) was later and worse; Trajan's early-second-century policy was much milder and case-by-case (see Pliny's famous letter).

question: The Roman official who prosecutes Agatha wants her both for her family's wealth and for herself. When she refuses him, he becomes the villain of her whole Passio. What is the prefect's name?
context: Quintianus is the prefect of Sicily in the Passio Agathae. The three distractors are all real Roman officials who prosecuted OTHER famous early martyrs: Aspasius prosecuted Vincent of Saragossa, Rusticus was the prefect of Rome who condemned Justin Martyr, and Anullinus prosecuted Felix of Thibiuca in North Africa. Real names, wrong martyr.  (Legend.)

question: Wanting Agatha broken before he tries her, Quintianus sends her not to a prison but to a house of ill fame run by a woman with nine equally corrupt daughters. For a whole month they fail to bend her. What is the name of the brothel-keeper?
context: Aphrodisia -- her name openly evokes Aphrodite, the goddess of the trade -- is the madam in the Legenda Aurea's version. Herodias is the wife of Herod Antipas who calls for John the Baptist's head; Salome her daughter dances for it; Livia is the empress-wife of Augustus. Real ancient women, all wrong for a third-century Sicilian brothel.

question: The night after her worst torture, Agatha lies alone in her cell in agony. An old man appears at the door followed by a small boy carrying one object; the old man will not leave until he has healed Agatha's wounds. What is the boy carrying?
context: Legenda Aurea, 'Saint Agatha': the old man is followed 'by a young man carrying a lamp'. The lamp is the classic hagiographic image for a night visitor in a martyr's cell. A torch would suit an outdoor procession; a candle would suit a liturgy; a brazier is a fire-basin for warmth or incense. The lamp is the object named in the Passio.

question: The old man in the cell speaks to Agatha, refuses to leave until he has healed her wounds, and finally tells her exactly who he is -- one of the apostles, come to her in prison the night before her death. Which apostle does he say he is?
context: In the Passio the old man reveals himself as Saint Peter the apostle and heals her wounds so completely that when the jailers open the cell in the morning she is untouched. Andrew is Peter's own brother and was crucified on the X-cross of Patras; John lived to old age on Patmos; James son of Zebedee was the first apostle martyred, beheaded under Herod Agrippa. Real apostles all, but Peter is the visitor named in Agatha's Passio.  (Legend.)

question: Bakers in Catania celebrate Agatha's feast on 5 February by making small round pastries called minni di Sant'Agata -- white-iced, each topped with a single candied cherry, and famous throughout Sicily. What creamy filling do the bakers pipe inside each pastry?
context: Sweetened ricotta cheese is the classic Sicilian pastry filling (the same filling used in cannoli and cassata), and the minni di Sant'Agata are stuffed with it, iced snow-white, and finished with the cherry. Custard is the French/English standard; marzipan is another Sicilian classic but is usually shaped as fruit (frutta martorana); chocolate is not the traditional filling.

question: On 1 February 1886 a lava flow from Etna crawled down the mountain's south flank toward a village whose walls it had almost reached. The archbishop of Catania carried Agatha's veil out to meet the flow, and by tradition the lava halted at the village's outer walls. Which village did the veil save?
context: Nicolosi sits high on Etna's south slope and has been threatened by lava many times; the 1886 procession is the most famous of all the veil-against-Etna stories. Zafferana Etnea on the east flank was saved from a 1992 flow (by lava barriers and dynamite, not the veil); Mascali on the northeast coast was destroyed by the 1928 eruption; Belpasso to the southwest was destroyed by the 1669 eruption (the same flow that reached Catania itself) and rebuilt.  (Legend.)

question: Many young men of high rank in Rome ask for the child Agnes's hand. She refuses every one. Slighted, one of these rejected suitors takes a step that changes her fate. What does he do?
answer: Denounces her to the Roman authorities as a Christian
choices: Denounces her to the Roman authorities as a Christian
Challenges her father to a duel in the Forum
Kidnaps her from her family's estate
Buys her family's estates out from under them
context: Wikipedia: 'Slighted by her resolute devotion to religious purity, they submitted her name to the authorities.' The suitors expose her faith as a way of forcing her submission; it backfires into her execution. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: The prefect Sempronius, hoping to break the girl's resolve, orders that Agnes be stripped and dragged naked through the streets of Rome to a place of public shame. To what place is she sent?
context: Wikipedia: 'The Prefect Sempronius condemned Agnes to be dragged naked through the streets to a brothel.' The Passio then reports that her hair miraculously grew long enough to cover her, and any customer who tried to approach her was struck blind. Legend, preserved in the medieval Passio and the Golden Legend. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: Brought back before the prefect, Agnes is sentenced to die. In one version they try to burn her at a stake; the wood will not catch fire or the flames part around her. So a Roman officer steps forward to finish her with a sword. In the version the bishop Ambrose preserves in De Virginibus, what does the executioner himself do as he takes his stroke?
answer: Trembles, as if he were the one condemned
choices: Trembles, as if he were the one condemned
Weeps and begs her forgiveness before the crowd
Turns his back so as not to see her face
Kneels and asks to be baptised on the spot
context: Ambrose of Milan, De Virginibus (c. 377 CE), gives the earliest full narrative of her death and describes the executioner as trembling to strike a girl so composed. Ambrose's account is a generation after Damasus's tomb epigram. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: Eight days after Agnes's death in 304, her grieving parents came to keep vigil at her tomb on the Via Nomentana. According to the legend that gave rise to the second feast called Agnes-secundo, what did they see there?
answer: Agnes standing among a flock of white lambs
choices: Agnes standing among a flock of white lambs
A single lamb at the tomb with a wound at its throat
A dove descending onto the tomb with a crown in its beak
A hand writing her name in Latin on the tomb wall
context: The legend behind Agnes-secundo ('Agnes second') held that eight days after her death Agnes appeared to her parents at her tomb surrounded by a flock of white lambs. The second feast was kept on 28 January until Pope John XXIII revised the Roman calendar in the 1960s. Source: Wikipedia, Agnes of Rome.

question: The Roman governor of Milan is halfway through his speech to the crowded church, telling both sides to keep the peace during the bishop's election, when a single voice cries out from the assembly, 'Ambrose for bishop!' -- and the whole packed church takes up the shout as one. Whose voice, in the traditional story, started it?
choices: a soldier of the governor's guard
the widow of the dead bishop
context: Paulinus's Vita Ambrosii records that a child's voice began the acclamation and the packed church took it up at once. The detail has been told the same way since Paulinus, Ambrose's own secretary, wrote the Life around 412. Source: blog.oup.com/2011/12/ambrose.  (Legend.)

question: Horrified at being acclaimed bishop, Ambrose tries to slip out of Milan by night rather than accept the office. He rides for the country estate of a personal friend, hoping to be hidden there until the crowd forgets him. According to Paulinus, what did the friend do?
answer: refused to hide him and gave him back
choices: refused to hide him and gave him back
hid him for a month in a wine cellar
took him on horseback into the Alps
smuggled him aboard a ship for North Africa
context: Paulinus's Vita Ambrosii records that Ambrose fled at night to the country house of a friend, but the friend, once he learned what had happened, refused to conceal him and turned him back over. Source: blog.oup.com/2011/12/ambrose.  (Legend.)

question: After Ambrose's attempted escape fails, he is still trying to refuse the bishopric -- he is a lawyer and a governor, not a churchman, and he has never even been baptised. He finally submits only when a letter arrives from a higher authority approving the crowd's acclamation. Whose letter forced him to accept?
context: Gratian was the Western Roman emperor in 374 and Ambrose's civil superior; his letter approving the acclamation ended Ambrose's resistance. Julian had died in Persia in 363; Damasus was the bishop of Rome but had no authority to command a Milanese governor; Valens ruled the East. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose.

question: In John's gospel Andrew is one of the very first people to follow Jesus. What does he do straight away after meeting him?
answer: Goes and fetches his brother Peter
choices: Goes and fetches his brother Peter
Rushes home to tell his father
Sells his fishing boat that day
Runs to the synagogue in Capernaum
context: John 1:40-42. Andrew was already a disciple of John the Baptist; he attaches himself to Jesus, then goes to find his brother -- who will later be renamed Peter.

question: When Andrew finds his brother after meeting Jesus, he says one short line that is preserved in John's gospel. What does he tell his brother?
context: John 1:41, King James Version. It is Andrew, not Peter, who first uses the word 'Messias' in the gospel of John.

question: In Greek Orthodox tradition Andrew carries a special one-word Greek epithet that no other apostle shares. Which Greek epithet is Andrew's alone?
context: Petros is Peter's nickname ('rock'); Boanerges is the epithet Jesus gives James and John ('sons of thunder'); Didymos is Thomas's nickname ('twin'). Andrew alone is Protokletos in the Eastern churches -- a title that stuck because John's gospel has him attach himself to Jesus before any of the other Twelve.

question: At the miracle of the feeding of the five thousand, one of the Twelve is the one who spots a boy in the crowd carrying a small meal and brings him forward to Jesus. Which apostle plays this small practical role?
context: John 6:8-9. Andrew points out a boy with five barley loaves and two small fishes -- 'but what are they among so many?' The whole miracle turns on his small act of bringing forward what looks like nothing.

question: Andrew is not crucified on the shape of cross Jesus died on. Instead tradition says he is bound to a cross of a very different shape, which became known ever after by his own name. What shape is Saint Andrew's Cross?
context: The saltire tradition (Andrew asking not to die on the same shape as Jesus) is later Western hagiography, not first-century record. But the X-cross is the shape that stuck.  (Legend.)

question: Andrew's X-shaped cross ended up as the national flag of a country that took him as its patron saint and whose national day is his feast day, 30 November. Which country?
context: Scotland's flag is a white saltire on a blue field. Medieval legend says a monk named Saint Regulus brought some of Andrew's bones -- an arm bone, three fingers, a kneecap and a tooth -- shipwrecked to Fife, founding the town later called Saint Andrews. Spain claims James, Ireland claims Patrick, Portugal claims James as well through Compostela pilgrimage tradition.

question: Flying home from the Gorgon's cave with Medusa's head in his bag, Perseus passed over the Ethiopian coast and saw a princess chained naked to a sea-cliff rock, waiting to be devoured. What was her name?
context: Andromeda, daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia of Ethiopia. Persephone (dragged to the underworld), Ariadne (Minos's daughter with the thread), and Antigone (Oedipus's daughter) are all real Greek princesses in famous tales, but none were chained to a sea-cliff.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus asked how Andromeda had come to be chained on the rock. He was told that her mother, Queen Cassiopeia, had bragged that Andromeda was more beautiful than the Nereids, and the great god those nymphs served took the boast as an insult. Which god took offense?
context: The Nereids were the fifty sea-nymphs of Poseidon's court; the insult to them was an insult to him, and he sent the monster Cetus in punishment. Zeus and Hera were famously jealous of mortal beauties (Semele, Io) but the Nereids were not their attendants; Dionysus punished many boasts (Pentheus, the pirates) but the Nereids were not his either.  (Legend.)

question: The offended sea-god sent a monster to ravage the Ethiopian coast, and the local oracle said only chaining Andromeda to the rock as a sacrifice would satisfy it. What was the sea-monster called?
context: Cetus was the sea-monster (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.3). Scylla and Charybdis are real Greek sea-monsters but belong to the Odyssey and threaten Odysseus. Typhon was a monstrous storm-giant Zeus battled, not a sea-monster in this story.  (Legend.)

question: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, when the monster rose from the water Perseus dived at it from above on his winged sandals and killed it by stabbing it in the side. What weapon did he stab with?
answer: The harpe, the sickle-sword from Hermes
choices: The harpe, the sickle-sword from Hermes
A spear made from Cetus's earlier victim
A trident borrowed from Poseidon's temple
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.717-740: Perseus killed Cetus by driving his sickle-shaped sword (the harpe) into the monster's side. The harpe was the same divine sword Hermes had given him for beheading Medusa. Later Roman art sometimes shows him using the Gorgon head on Cetus, but Ovid's is the standard version.  (Legend.)

question: At the wedding feast for Perseus and Andromeda, an armed band burst in led by a man who claimed Andromeda had been promised to him first. Who was this rival fiance?
context: Phineus, Andromeda's earlier suitor, burst in with armed men to reclaim her. Acrisius was Perseus's grandfather. Cepheus was Andromeda's father (and gave her willingly). Polydectes was the king back on Serifos who had sent Perseus for the head in the first place.  (Legend.)

question: The stone bodies of Phineus and his men had barely cooled before Perseus and Andromeda sailed back to the island where Perseus had grown up. There he found his mother Danae hiding in a temple, taking refuge from the king who wanted her. On which island had Perseus grown up?
context: Serifos in the Cyclades: the fisherman Dictys had found the chest with Danae and baby Perseus, and Dictys's brother King Polydectes later coveted Danae. Delos (Apollo's birthplace), Aegina (Aeacus), and Ithaca (Odysseus) are famous Greek islands but not Perseus's.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus walked straight into the great hall where the king sat at feast with his nobles, told them what he had brought, and lifted the head from the bag one more time. The whole court turned to stone where they sat. Which king was petrified at his own dinner?
context: Polydectes of Serifos and his court were petrified at feast (Apollodorus 2.4.3). Cepheus (Andromeda's father) was spared. Acrisius (Perseus's grandfather) died later at Larissa by a badly-thrown discus. Proetus was the twin brother of Acrisius and Perseus's great-uncle, a real Argive king but not petrified.  (Legend.)

question: With Polydectes turned to stone, Perseus made his stepfather Dictys the new king of Serifos. Long before, when the wooden chest holding the infant Perseus and his mother Danae washed up on the island, what had Dictys done?
answer: Pulled the chest from the sea in his fishing net
choices: Pulled the chest from the sea in his fishing net
Hidden the pair in a cave from Acrisius's soldiers
Carried the pair to the temple of Athena for sanctuary
Traded the pair to King Polydectes for a share of the catch
context: Dictys the fisherman drew the sealed chest out of his nets, opened it, and raised the boy Perseus as his own; his brother Polydectes was the king who later coveted Danae. The other three options are plausible-sounding but not the story told by Apollodorus and the Perseus tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Finished with his hero-work, Perseus returned each borrowed gift to the gods: the winged sandals and the cap of invisibility to the nymphs, the harpe to Hermes, the polished shield and the terrible head itself to one goddess. To which goddess did Perseus return the shield and the Gorgon's head?
context: Athena had guided Perseus from the start; she took the Gorgoneion and set it at the centre of her aegis, the goatskin storm-shield she wears on the chest. Hera was Heracles's enemy, not Perseus's helper; Artemis (hunt) and Demeter (harvest) had no part in Perseus's story.  (Legend.)

question: The Ethiopian royal family and Perseus and even the sea-monster were later placed together as a group in the northern night sky, one constellation for each of them. Which member of the family was set into her chair upside-down for half the year as her punishment?
context: Cassiopeia sits in her starry chair; the constellation rotates so that she hangs upside-down for half of each year, a punishment for her original boast about Andromeda's beauty. Andromeda, Cepheus, Perseus, and Cetus are also constellations, all near each other; Danae has no constellation.  (Legend.)

question: Long before the hero Sigurd was born, three Norse gods were travelling together through Midgard when they stopped to rest at a waterfall. One of the three was Odin himself. Another was Honir. Who was the third god of the travelling company, the one who would throw the stone at the otter?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14 and Reginsmal prose: the three travellers are Odin, Honir, and Loki. Thor is off in Jotunheim in most of Snorri's tales; Tyr belongs to the Fenrir story; Freyr is a Vanir god who rarely walks with Odin. Loki is the one who throws the stone -- and the trouble that follows fills the rest of the Volsung cycle.  (Legend.)

question: At the foot of the waterfall Odin, Loki, and Honir spotted a small brown animal on the bank eating a salmon it had just caught. Loki picked up a stone and killed the creature with a single throw. What kind of animal did Loki kill at the waterfall?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the animal is an otter. Herons, beavers, and foxes were all known creatures of Norse country, but the specific animal in this story is the otter -- because it was really a man in otter-shape, as the gods will discover that night.  (Legend.)

question: The three gods skinned the otter, took the pelt with them, and stopped for the night at the house of a wizard. The wizard took one look at the pelt and burst into grief -- the animal Loki had killed was actually his own son, who fished in that river in otter-shape by day. What is the name of the wizard whose son Loki had killed?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the wizard is Hreidmar. His shape-shifting son is named Otr. Andvari is a different dwarf altogether, whose ring will enter the story soon. Mimir is the guardian of the well of wisdom. Volund is the smith-hero of his own Eddic poem.  (Legend.)

question: Hreidmar's TWO SURVIVING SONS seized Odin, Loki, and Honir at the door and held them prisoner until a blood-price could be paid for their dead brother. Name the two brothers who seized the gods -- the pair whose names run through the whole Volsung cycle to come.
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Hreidmar's surviving sons are Fafnir and Regin. Sindri and Brokkr are the dwarves who forged Mjolnir; Fjalar and Galar murdered Kvasir for the Mead of Poetry; Baldr and Hodr are Odin's own sons in Asgard, not Hreidmar's.  (Legend.)

question: The gods sent Loki -- who had thrown the stone in the first place -- to find that much gold. Loki went to a waterfall where a dwarf lived alone in the pool below. He caught the dwarf and made him give up his whole treasure. What is the name of the dwarf whose gold Loki took?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: the dwarf is Andvari, and his hoard is the treasure of the whole Volsung cycle. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf whom Thor talks to death at dawn. Alberich is the name Wagner GAVE this same dwarf in Das Rheingold seven centuries later, but Andvari is his Norse name. Sindri forged Mjolnir with his brother Brokkr.  (Legend.)

question: When Loki came for the dwarf's gold, the dwarf tried to hide from him inside his own pool by turning himself into another animal that could disappear in the water. What form was Andvari in when Loki caught him at the waterfall?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Andvari was in the shape of a fish (a pike, in most tellings). Loki caught him in a net borrowed from the goddess Ran, who used the same net to drown drowning sailors. Frogs and eels and swans do not appear in the story.  (Legend.)

question: Andvari surrendered his whole hoard to Loki, but he tried to keep back a single small band of gold, hoping Loki would not notice. Loki spotted it and took it too. This one ring has its own name in the Volsung cycle, and it is the ring that will destroy every person who ever owns it. By what name is that ring known?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14 and Reginsmal prose: the ring is Andvaranaut, which means 'Andvari's gift.' Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring, which drips eight new rings every ninth night. Sviagris is the boar-ring of the Swedish king Adils in Snorri's Skaldskaparmal. Hnitudr is a ring named in Gudrunarkvida II. Wagner later renamed Andvaranaut 'the Ring of the Nibelung' and Tolkien built the One Ring on the same model -- but Andvaranaut is the Norse original.  (Legend.)

question: As the ring left his hand, Andvari SPOKE ALOUD over it -- one of the most-quoted curse-lines in all Norse poetry (Reginsmal 4). He did not curse only the ring; he cursed the ring AND the whole hoard together. What did Andvari's curse promise would happen to whoever owned the ring?
answer: it would be the death of whoever owned it
choices: it would be the death of whoever owned it
it would blind whoever looked at it
it would turn whoever wore it into a slave
it would burn whoever touched it to ashes
context: Reginsmal 4: 'This ring, and all this gold with it, shall be the death of whoever owns it.' Andvari's curse-line is one of the most-quoted in Norse poetry. It is close enough to Tolkien's curse-language on the One Ring that scholars flag the influence -- Andvari's ring is a direct ancestor of Sauron's ring.  (Legend.)

question: Loki brought the treasure back to Hreidmar and helped cover the otter-pelt with gold. Odin tried to keep Andvaranaut for himself, hidden in his fist. But Hreidmar walked around the pelt inspecting the payment and refused to accept the ransom because of ONE thing he could still see. What did Hreidmar see on the pelt that made him demand more gold?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: a single whisker of the otter-pelt was still visible above the gold. Hreidmar refused to release the gods until it was covered. Odin was forced to give up Andvaranaut to cover the last whisker -- and so the ring, and the curse, passed to Hreidmar.  (Legend.)

question: The curse began working before the gods had even ridden out of the yard. That very same night the wizard Hreidmar was stabbed to death in his sleep, and one figure took the whole hoard alone and drove the surviving kin off empty-handed. Who killed Hreidmar the first night the cursed gold sat in his hall?
answer: his own son Fafnir in a rage
choices: his own son Fafnir in a rage
his own son Regin in a rage
the dwarf Andvari come for revenge
the god Loki come back for the ring
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14 and Reginsmal prose: Fafnir murdered his own father in the night, drove Regin off, and took the whole treasure to himself. Regin will later plot twenty years of revenge. Andvari never leaves his waterfall. Loki does not come back for the ring -- he is out of the story once the ransom is paid. The curse claims its first life within a day of leaving Andvari's hand.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir carried the entire hoard -- ring included -- to a lonely heath called Gnitaheid and settled down there alone. Over years of guarding the treasure, gold-greed slowly changed him into something no god or man could kill without a plan. What did Fafnir gradually turn himself INTO to guard the cursed gold on Gnitaheid?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 14: Fafnir became a dragon (in Old Norse ormr, sometimes translated 'serpent' or 'worm'). Wolves belong to Fenrir; stone giants to Hrungnir; the eagle at Gnitaheid is a different figure. Regin will spend twenty years plotting revenge and eventually foster the boy Sigurd, who will kill the dragon Fafnir with the sword Gram -- and take the cursed ring for himself, and die of it too.  (Legend.)

question: Loki the trickster is married to the goddess Sigyn in Asgard, but secretly he keeps a lover in Jotunheim, the land of the giants. She is a giantess whose very name is a warning -- it means 'she who brings grief'. What is her name?
context: Snorri names her Angrboda in Gylfaginning 34 of the Prose Edda. Skadi is the giantess-bride of the sea-god Njord; Gerd is the giantess Freyr wins in Skirnismal; Hyrrokkin is the giantess who later launches Baldr's funeral ship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angrboda  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth the trickster Loki fathers three monstrous children by the giantess Angrboda. Two are beasts -- a wolf and a huge serpent. The third is a GIRL, born in Jotunheim among the giants. What is the girl's name?
context: Snorri lists the three siblings in Gylfaginning 34: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the serpent, and Hel the girl. Gerd is the shining giantess Freyr wins as bride in Skirnismal; Skadi is the giantess who marries the sea-god Njord; Nott is the giantess of night whose son is Day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: Snorri describes Loki's daughter Hel with a shocking body: one whole side of her face and body is the healthy pink of a living woman, and the OTHER side is something else entirely. What is the other side of Hel like, in Snorri's Gylfaginning 34?
context: Snorri writes that Hel is 'half black and half flesh-coloured' -- the corpse-side and the living-side joined in one body. Ice belongs to the giant Ymir's origin; fire to the fire-giant Surt of Muspelheim; the raven is Odin's bird. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth the giant wolf Fenrir is raised inside Asgard, right among the gods, because Odin thinks he can be controlled if kept close. But the wolf grows so fast and fierce that only ONE god will still walk up to feed him. Which god has the nerve?
context: Snorri says only Tyr had the courage to give Fenrir food. Tyr later loses his hand when the gods trick the wolf into being bound. Thor is the thunderer; Heimdall is the watchman of the rainbow bridge; Bragi is the god of poetry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenrir  (Legend.)

question: The middle child of Loki and Angrboda is a serpent. Odin throws him into the great ocean that goes all the way round the world of men. In that sea the serpent grows so long that he eventually wraps the whole world -- and does one memorable thing with his own body. What does he do?
choices: swallows the sunken sun each night
sleeps with one eye always open
context: In Gylfaginning the serpent grew so vast in the ocean around Midgard that he encircled the entire world and grasped his tail in his mouth. Because he lies in the sea round Midgard he is called the Midgard-Serpent or World-Serpent, Jormungandr. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jormungandr  (Legend.)

question: Odin casts Loki's daughter Hel down into the misty world of Niflheim and gives her rule over one specific category of the dead. She does NOT receive the warriors slain in battle -- those go to Valhalla. Which dead does Hel receive instead?
answer: those who die of sickness or old age
choices: those who die of sickness or old age
those killed by their own kin
those who die without a name
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Odin gives Hel authority over all who die of sickness or old age. Warriors killed in battle are chosen by the valkyries for Odin's Valhalla and Freyja's Folkvangr. The drowned in later folklore belong to the sea-giantess Ran. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: Snorri gives Hel's underworld hall a full grim inventory in Gylfaginning 34: a dish called Hunger, a knife called Famine, a bed called Sick-Bed, and a threshold called Stumbling-Block. The HALL itself is also named, from a word meaning 'sprayed with damp'. What is Hel's hall called?
context: Snorri names the hall Eljudnir ('sprayed with damp / rain-damp'). Bilskirnir is Thor's own hall in Thrudheim; Valaskjalf is Odin's silver-roofed hall; Sessrumnir is Freyja's hall in Folkvangr. Every object in Eljudnir is a grim pun on death. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: In Snorri's description of Hel's dreary underworld hall Eljudnir, even the household servants have punning names built around slowness. The manservant's name means 'slow-mover' and the maidservant's name means 'slow-goer'. What are the two servants called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the servant is Ganglati and the maidservant Ganglot -- everything in Hel's hall moves as slowly as death itself. Huginn and Muninn are Odin's two ravens; Geri and Freki his two wolves; Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's OWN two wolf-sons who chase the sun and moon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hel_(mythological_being)  (Legend.)

question: At Ragnarok all three of Loki and Angrboda's children turn on the gods who tried to control them. The wolf Fenrir gets the biggest kill of all -- swallowing one god whole. Which god does Fenrir swallow at Ragnarok?
context: In Gylfaginning and Voluspa, Fenrir breaks loose at Ragnarok and swallows Odin the All-Father. Odin's son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart. Thor dies fighting Jormungandr; Frey falls to the fire-giant Surt; Heimdall and Loki kill each other. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenrir  (Legend.)

question: At Ragnarok, Loki's serpent-son Jormungandr faces Thor in the final battle. Thor swings Mjolnir and kills the world-serpent -- but he does not walk away. Snorri gives an exact count of the paces Thor takes before he falls dead of the serpent's venom. How many steps?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning: Thor kills the Midgard-Serpent, then walks nine paces from the body before the venom brings him down. The number nine runs everywhere in Norse myth -- nine worlds of Yggdrasil, Odin's nine nights on the tree, Draupnir's nine-night cycle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jormungandr  (Legend.)

question: A wealthy young Coptic Egyptian named Anthony, around age twenty, hears one gospel verse in church one Sunday, takes it as spoken to him, and by week's end has sold his family's estates and walked out of the village for good. Where does he go?
context: The verse was Matthew 19:21: 'If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.' Anthony (c. 251-356 CE) becomes the most famous of the Desert Fathers and the founding figure of Christian monasticism. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: The word 'monasticism,' for the way of life Anthony pioneers, comes from a Greek root that names what makes his choice extreme. What does the Greek MONOS mean?
context: MONOS is Greek for 'alone'; a MONACHOS is 'one who lives alone.' Anthony is the model for the whole tradition of hermits and (later) monasteries, though the word originally meant strict solitude, not community. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: For his first years in the desert Anthony shuts himself inside an abandoned structure carved into the cliffs. Athanasius's biography says it is here that the demons attack him and beat him unconscious. What kind of place has Anthony chosen?
context: Athanasius's Vita Antonii (c. 360 CE) says a friend brought bread one morning, found Anthony unconscious on the floor of the tomb, and thought he was dead. Anthony revived, insisted on being carried back, and shouted at the demons, 'Here I am, Anthony; I do not flee from your blows!' Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Anthony then moves deeper into the desert to an abandoned Roman fort at Pispir, on the east bank of the Nile, and seals himself inside behind a bricked-up door with only a small hole for bread. He remains shut in there for how long?
context: When pilgrims finally break down the door after twenty years, they expect a wraith, and find Anthony 'the same as before,' in perfect physical health. He emerges to teach and quickly becomes the most famous man in Christian Egypt. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: As an old man Anthony sets out across the desert to find an even older hermit, Paul of Thebes. On the road, according to Jerome's Life of Paul, he meets a creature straight out of Greek myth. What creature points out his way and then vanishes?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 7. The creature, which Jerome calls a HIPPOCENTAUR (half-horse, half-man), makes 'a sort of guttural noise,' then extends its right hand to indicate the direction Anthony seeks. A little further on Anthony meets a satyr who asks him to pray for its kind. Legend from Jerome's romantic Life. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: When Anthony finally reaches Paul of Thebes in his cave, they sit down to talk. A bird arrives, as it has arrived every day for sixty years, carrying bread for Paul. This time, because there are two of them, the bird brings a whole loaf instead of half a loaf. What bird?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 10. Paul says, 'For the last sixty years I have always received half a loaf; but now Christ has doubled his soldier's rations.' The raven-feeding-a-hermit motif echoes 1 Kings 17, where ravens feed the prophet Elijah at the brook Cherith. Legend. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: Paul dies. Anthony wants to bury him but has no spade and is too old to dig with his hands. Two animals come out of the desert, mourn beside the body, then paw a grave into the sand. What animals?
context: Jerome, Vita Pauli 16. Two lions come, whimper over Paul's corpse, then dig a hole 'just large enough to hold a man.' Anthony wraps Paul in a tunic that had been given to him by the bishop Athanasius of Alexandria. Legend. Source: New Advent, Jerome Vita Pauli.

question: In his hundred-plus years in the desert Anthony leaves it for a city TWICE only. Both times he goes to the same great Mediterranean city: once during Diocletian's persecution around 311 to encourage imprisoned Christians, and once around 338 to help his friend the bishop Athanasius against the followers of Arius. Which city?
context: Alexandria is the great see of Coptic Egypt and the seat of Athanasius. The Arian controversy (which denied the full divinity of Christ) was the theological fight of the 4th century, culminating in the Council of Nicaea (325). Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Anthony dies at over a hundred years old. His last instruction to his few disciples is a specific request about his body. What does he ask them to do?
answer: Keep his burial place a secret
choices: Keep his burial place a secret
Send his cloak to the emperor at Constantinople
Burn his body on a pyre
Bury him with the pagan hermits he had known
context: Anthony feared the growing cult of relics and asked to disappear from the world as he had lived in it. His grave was in fact unknown for centuries; relics later claimed as his were moved to Constantinople in the 6th century and to France in the 11th. Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: In the Middle Ages the disease ergotism, caused by moldy rye bread and marked by gangrene of the limbs, was popularly named for Anthony because the Hospitallers of the Order of Saint Anthony cared for its sufferers in their hospices. By what name was the disease known?
context: Ergot poisoning produced a burning sensation and gangrene in the limbs. The Hospitallers of Saint Anthony ran hospices for its sufferers from the 11th century onward. (Distinct from 'Saint Anthony's Bread,' a modern charitable custom of Anthony of Padua, a different, later saint.) Source: Wikipedia, Anthony the Great.

question: Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, has one bird sacred to her -- a bird that flutters through her stories and around the shoulders of her Roman statues. What bird is sacred to Aphrodite?
context: The dove was Aphrodite's own bird; the peacock belonged to Hera (its eyes are the eyes of Argus); the owl to Athena; the eagle to Zeus. Doves drew her chariot in later art, and pairs of doves were often shown at her feet.  (Legend.)

question: The Romans borrowed the Greek gods and gave them Latin names. When they told Aphrodite's stories -- her love-affairs, her marriage to the smith-god, her son Cupid -- they called her by their own name for the goddess of love. What did the Romans call her?
context: Aphrodite = Venus. Hera = Juno. Athena = Minerva. Artemis = Diana. Venus's name lives on in the planet Venus and in the word 'venereal.'  (Legend.)

question: At the very beginning of things, the Titan Cronus took a jagged sickle of adamant to his father the sky-god Ouranos and hurled the severed part into the sea. Where it fell, a white foam began to spread across the water -- and out of that foam rose a full-grown goddess. Which Olympian was born like this?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 176-206. Hesiod explicitly derives Aphrodite's name from the Greek word 'aphros' (foam). Athena was born from Zeus's head; Artemis on Delos to Leto; Hera is Cronus's daughter. This is the oldest and strangest birth-story of any Olympian.  (Legend.)

question: The foam-born goddess did not stay in the open sea. The west wind Zephyr blew her over the water, and she came to shore first on a small Aegean island called Cythera, then on a larger island whose name became one of her most-used titles. On which larger island did she land?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 192-200. From this landing come her epithets Cypris (Lady of Cyprus) and Cyprogenes (Cyprus-born). Cythera also gave her the epithet Cytherea. The temple of Aphrodite at Paphos on Cyprus was one of the great cult centres of the ancient world.  (Legend.)

question: When Aphrodite comes ashore in ancient and later art, she is almost always shown standing on a specific kind of seashell -- an emblem so bound up with her that pilgrims to her shrines wore one as a badge. What kind of shell?
context: The scallop shell became the signature emblem of the goddess in art from antiquity onward, and later of pilgrims to her shrine at Cyprus. The same scallop shell also became the badge of Christian pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela -- an odd echo across the traditions.  (Legend.)

question: As the foam-born goddess stepped onto the shore of Cyprus, something remarkable happened to the earth wherever her bare feet touched it. What did the earth do beneath her feet?
answer: Fresh grass and flowers grew up out of the soil
choices: Fresh grass and flowers grew up out of the soil
Salt crystals hardened out of the sea-spray
Wet footprints appeared that would never fade
Silver coins bubbled up struck with her likeness
context: Hesiod, Theogony 194-195: 'grass grew up about her beneath her shapely feet.' The scene is the origin of the tradition, in painters from Botticelli to the modern age, of scattering roses and myrtles around her feet.  (Legend.)

question: In defiance of her marriage, Aphrodite took as her lover another Olympian -- a fierce and bright one, a scandal her cuckolded husband Hephaestus once trapped them in with an invisible net of golden mesh cast over their bed for all Olympus to laugh at. Which Olympian was her lover?
context: Homer, Odyssey 8.266-366 (the song of the bard Demodocus at Alcinous's court). Hephaestus made a net of gold-thread finer than a spider's web, dropped it over the sleeping lovers, and called the other gods in to see. Ares is the war-god; the pairing of Love and War produced Harmonia and, in some accounts, Eros.  (Legend.)

question: Aphrodite owned a magical embroidered belt -- a girdle -- with the power to make anyone who saw its wearer fall helplessly into love. In Book 14 of Homer's Iliad, another goddess borrows this girdle to seduce Zeus on Mount Ida and distract him from the Trojan War. Who borrows it?
context: Homer, Iliad 14.214-217. Hera wanted to draw Zeus's attention away from the battlefield so the Greeks could regain ground; she borrowed the kestos himas (embroidered girdle) from Aphrodite, and Zeus was undone. Hera and Zeus made love hidden in a golden cloud on the summit of Ida. Leto, Demeter, and Thetis all have their own stories with Zeus but none borrow the girdle.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod tells one story of Aphrodite's birth -- the sea-foam one. But Homer in the Iliad tells a completely different story: when Aphrodite is wounded on the battlefield by the mortal Diomedes and flees crying up to Olympus, she is comforted by her mother -- a Titaness who is NOT Gaia. According to Homer, who was Aphrodite's mother?
context: Homer, Iliad 5.370-430. In Homer's genealogy, Aphrodite is simply the daughter of Zeus and Dione -- one of the older Titanesses, in some traditions the wife of the oracle at Dodona. So the ancient world had two Aphrodites side by side: Hesiod's foam-born Heavenly one (Urania), and Homer's Zeus-daughter Common one (Pandemos). Plato in the Symposium makes both of them serious.  (Legend.)

question: About 1485, the Italian painter Sandro Botticelli finished a picture that now hangs in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence -- an image so famous it has become what Western art means when it says Aphrodite. What is the painting called?
context: Now in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence. Primavera is another Botticelli of the same period, showing Venus in a spring grove but not her birth. Venus Anadyomene ('Venus Rising from the Sea') is the ancient Greek term for the type-scene, most famously painted in antiquity by Apelles. The Judgment of Paris is a different Aphrodite story painted by many hands. But Botticelli's Birth of Venus is THE picture.

question: Apollo, the bright Olympian of music and prophecy, was born as one of a pair of twins -- his twin sister the archer-goddess Artemis was born the same day. Who was the mother of the twins Apollo and Artemis?
context: Leto was a Titaness, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, and one of Zeus's early lovers. Maia is the mother of Hermes; Metis is the mother of Athena; Demeter is the mother of Persephone. All four are divine mothers of Olympian children -- easy to confuse.  (Legend.)

question: Hera in her jealousy had forbidden every place on earth to receive Leto in her labour, and Leto wandered from country to country finding no shelter. In the end only one place accepted her -- a small floating island that finally anchored itself to the sea-bed to let her give birth under a palm tree. On what island were Apollo and Artemis born?
context: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 25-88. Delos was a bare rocky island in the Cyclades; because it had been drifting, Hera's command against 'land' had not bound it. Delphi -- deliberately named as a distractor here -- is where Apollo will later plant his oracle, not where he is born.  (Legend.)

question: As a young god, Apollo went hunting a great female serpent that Hera had sent to torment his mother Leto. The beast lived in a rocky chasm on the slopes of Mount Parnassus. Apollo shot her dead with his silver bow. What was the serpent called?
context: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300-374. The name Python comes from the Greek verb 'pytho,' 'to rot' -- for the serpent's body rotting inside the chasm after Apollo buried her there. The Hydra was killed by Heracles; the Chimaera by Bellerophon; Typhon by Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo took over the place where he had killed the serpent as his own -- a rocky sanctuary on the slopes of Mount Parnassus that became the most famous and powerful oracle in the whole Greek world. Every Greek city and many foreign kings would send messengers there to ask about war, marriage, and colony-founding. What is that place called?
context: Delphi sat in a great natural amphitheatre of rock high above the Gulf of Corinth. Dodona in Epirus was the oracle of Zeus, delivered by the rustling of an oak; Olympia was the shrine of Zeus with the games; Eleusis was the sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone. Delphi was considered the omphalos, the navel of the world.  (Legend.)

question: The priestess of Delphi did not sit on an ordinary chair. She sat on a specific bronze seat set directly over the chasm from which the sacred vapour rose -- a seat that became one of the most famous symbols of Apollo across the Greek world, cast in bronze and set up as trophies at every important sanctuary. What was the seat called?
context: Plutarch, De Pythiae oraculis; Diodorus 16.26. Tripods dedicated to Apollo were among the most prized victory-offerings a Greek city could make. The Serpent Column at Delphi -- looted from Delphi in the sixth century and now in Istanbul -- was the base of one such tripod, dedicated after the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo had one plant sacred to himself above all others. Before speaking her prophecies, the Pythia chewed its leaves; Apollo's prize-winners were crowned with a wreath of it; and the Vale of Tempe, where Apollo went to purify himself after killing the serpent, was where he broke off his first branches. What was the plant?
context: In myth the nymph Daphne, fleeing Apollo's pursuit, was turned by her father into the first laurel tree -- and Apollo, unable to marry her, wore her leaves in his hair ever after. Ivy is sacred to Dionysus; olive to Athena; myrtle to Aphrodite. Roman generals in triumph wore the laurel of Apollo.  (Legend.)

question: Above the entrance to the temple of Apollo at Delphi, two short Greek mottoes were carved for every pilgrim to read before going in to hear the god. One of the two was 'Know thyself' (gnothi seauton). What was the other?
context: Pausanias 10.24.1; Plato, Protagoras 343a-b. Ancient sources attributed these two maxims (and a third, 'Surety is ruin') to the legendary Seven Sages of Greece, dedicated at Delphi as the first-fruits of their wisdom. 'Know thyself' became the founding motto of Greek philosophy from Socrates onward.

question: Croesus, the enormously wealthy king of Lydia, sent envoys with gold to Delphi to ask the oracle what would happen if he attacked the growing Persian empire. The Pythia answered that if he crossed the river Halys, he would destroy a great empire. Croesus crossed the Halys -- and which empire was destroyed?
context: Herodotus 1.53 and 1.86-91. Cyrus of Persia defeated Croesus in battle, took Sardis, and burned Croesus on a pyre before pardoning him at the last moment. The story became the ancient world's founding lesson about the ambiguity of oracles: the god had not lied, but the questioner had not thought to ask WHOSE empire.

question: Killing the great serpent at Delphi had stained the sanctuary with blood, and Zeus commanded Apollo to atone. For a term of years the god had to serve as a plain mortal servant in the household of King Admetus of Pherae. What kind of work did the god do there?
answer: He herded the king's cattle in the pastures
choices: He herded the king's cattle in the pastures
He copied scrolls in the king's library
He guarded the palace gate as a spearman
He served wine at the king's table
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.10.4; Callimachus, Hymn to Apollo 47-49. During his service Apollo became so fond of Admetus that he later intervened with the Fates to spare Admetus's life on the day he was to die -- the seed of the Alcestis story dramatised by Euripides.  (Legend.)

question: Athena wove the first tapestry. In the centre she showed her own famous victory over another god for the naming of the city of Athens -- her olive tree beating what he had struck from the rock. Which god did Athena show herself defeating in that central scene?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.70-82. In the story Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident and made a salt-spring gush out; Athena struck the same rock and made an olive tree grow. The people of Athens chose the olive, and the city took her name. Around the borders Athena wove four cautionary scenes of mortals turned into mountains and birds for having challenged the gods.  (Legend.)

question: Then it was Arachne's turn at the loom. Instead of praising the gods, she wove twenty-one scenes of gods disguising themselves as animals or objects to trick and abduct mortal women. Which god appeared MOST OFTEN in her twenty-one scenes?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.103-128. Ovid lists nine of Arachne's twenty-one scenes as Zeus in one disguise or another -- swan, eagle, satyr, shower of gold, flame, shepherd, snake, and other shapes -- each targeting a different mortal woman. Poseidon has six, Apollo four, and Bacchus and Saturn one each.  (Legend.)

question: One of Arachne's twenty-one panels showed a particular scene: on the shore of Sidon a great white BULL walks up to a princess picking flowers, kneels for her to climb on his back, and then charges into the sea and swims her all the way to Crete. Who was the bull, and who was the princess?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833-875 (the fuller telling) and 6.103-104 (Arachne's panel). Europa was a Phoenician princess; the continent of Europe is named after her. Arachne wove other Zeus-disguise scenes into the same tapestry -- as a swan to Leda, as a golden shower to Danae -- but the bull-and-princess panel is the most famous of the twenty-one.  (Legend.)
