question: Arachne's weaving was so technically perfect that Athena, staring at the finished tapestry, could not find a single fault with the craftsmanship. What did the enraged goddess do to the tapestry itself?
answer: She ripped it to shreds with her own hands
choices: She ripped it to shreds with her own hands
She turned it into smoke with a wave
She buried it under the loom's stones
She threw it into the sea from a cliff
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.129-133. Ovid is explicit that the craftsmanship was flawless -- so flawless that the goddess of every craft could not fault the workmanship. That is what pushed her past control: not that Arachne had botched the work, but that she had matched a goddess AND used the skill to make Athena's family look like a family of predators.  (Legend.)

question: Having ripped up the tapestry, Athena took the small wooden tool Arachne had been weaving with and struck her three or four times on the forehead. Ovid names the tool and even the mountain the wood came from. What was the tool?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.132-133 -- boxwood shuttle from Mount Cytorus, a boxwood-famous mountain on the Black Sea coast. The shuttle is the small tool that carries the weft-thread back and forth through the warp. The spindle is for spinning raw wool into thread; the distaff holds the unspun wool; the reed-comb beats the weft down. Athena beat the mortal weaver with the weaver's own weft-tool.  (Legend.)

question: After Athena struck her three times on the forehead, Arachne could not bear the disgrace. Ovid says she took something from her own weaving and turned it against herself. What did she do?
answer: She hanged herself with a rope of her own thread
choices: She hanged herself with a rope of her own thread
She poisoned herself by chewing dyed wool
She wound the warp around her wrists and drowned
She burned the tapestry-scraps and breathed the smoke
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.134-135. It is one of the darker beats in the Metamorphoses -- the rope of her own weaving is the instrument of her death. Athena, seeing her hanging there, spoke aloud -- 'Live then, wicked girl -- and yet hang, and be forever anxious for the future, all your race' -- and only then reached out to touch her.  (Legend.)

question: As Arachne hung there, Athena sprinkled her with the juice of the witch-goddess Hecate's herb and said 'live, but hang forever.' The girl's hair fell out, her ears and nose vanished, her head shrank to a dot, and her fingers stuck to her sides as long thin legs. What tiny creature had she become?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.140-145. Ovid ends: 'even now, still she spins a thread; and, as a spider, weaves her ancient web.' The word 'arachne' is simply the Ancient Greek word for spider -- and the scientific class Arachnida (spiders, scorpions, mites) takes its name from this story.  (Legend.)

question: On Olympus one god was known for the fury of the killing-field itself -- not the strategy of it, but the joy of the slaughter -- while Athena kept the craft of war. Which Olympian is the god of that furious, blood-loving side of war?
context: Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, is the Olympian of war-fury and slaughter; Athena is his opposite, the goddess of war-craft. Apollo is archery, music, and prophecy. Hermes is the messenger. Hephaestus is the smith.  (Legend.)

question: Ares almost never rode into battle alone. Two of his own sons went with him -- one named 'Terror' and the other named 'Fear' -- and a goddess called the sacker-of-cities kept pace with them. What are the names of the two sons who went beside him?
context: Hesiod names Deimos ('Terror') and Phobos ('Fear') as Ares's sons by Aphrodite; Enyo the sacker-of-cities also rides with them. Castor and Pollux are the Dioscuri twins. Kratos and Bia (Strength and Force) attend Zeus. Hypnos and Thanatos are Sleep and Death.  (Legend.)

question: In the fifth book of the Iliad, a mortal Greek hero speared Ares in the belly with the goddess Athena guiding his arm. The god of war fled back to Olympus wounded and bleeding, whimpering to his father. Which mortal hero was it who put a spear through the god of war?
context: Iliad 5.855-863: Diomedes, with Athena driving his spear, wounds Ares in the belly. Achilles never fights a god face-to-face like this. Ajax and Odysseus never wound one either. Diomedes's rampage in Book 5 is called the first great aristeia of the poem.  (Legend.)

question: The hero Odysseus was gone from his island kingdom of Ithaca for twenty years -- ten fighting a famous war and ten struggling to sail home. Which war took the first ten years?
context: Odysseus spent ten years at Troy and another ten years wandering home across the sea. Book 17 of Homer's Odyssey shows him finally reaching Ithaca in disguise. Source: Wikipedia, Argos (dog).  (Legend.)

question: When Odysseus at last lands on Ithaca, the goddess Athena hides who he is by changing his appearance. She turns the king of Ithaca into someone no one at the palace will notice. Into what does she disguise him?
context: Athena disguises Odysseus as an aged beggar so he can enter his own palace unrecognized and take the measure of the suitors before revealing himself. Source: greekmyths-greekmythology.com, Odysseus's Return to Ithaca.  (Legend.)

question: The disguised Odysseus is led up from the harbor to his own palace by a loyal servant -- one who has kept his post on the far side of the island for twenty years, never joining the suitors. This servant does not recognize his beggar-master. Which servant is he?
context: Eumaeus the swineherd is one of the few Ithacans who stayed loyal to Odysseus's household. He leads the beggar-disguised Odysseus up to the palace without knowing who he is. Source: greekmyths-greekmythology.com, Odysseus's Return to Ithaca.  (Legend.)

question: At the outer gate of Odysseus's palace on Ithaca, an old creature named Argus has been left uncared-for in his last days. When the beggar-disguised Odysseus walks up, on what strange thing is Argus lying?
context: Homer places Argus on a pile of mule- and cattle-dung outside the palace door, piled up until servants can spread it on the fields (Odyssey 17.297-303, Lattimore). The image is Homer's whole point: the master's dog abandoned to the manure heap. Source: Wikipedia, Argos (dog).  (Legend.)

question: As the beggar-disguised Odysseus passes through his own gate, the swineherd Eumaeus beside him does not recognize him, Penelope in the palace does not know he is home, and his old nurse Eurycleia has not seen him yet. But the old hound Argus, lying on the dung heap, knows his master at once. He is too weak from age to stand. What small thing does Argus do?
context: Argus, too weak from age to stand, lifts his head, drops his ears, and wags his tail once. He is the first living thing on Ithaca to recognize the returned king. Source: Wikipedia, Argos (dog).  (Legend.)

question: The old hound Argus, lying on the dung heap outside the palace gate, has waited twenty years for this moment -- he lifts his head as the disguised Odysseus passes and becomes the first creature on Ithaca to know his master is home. Odyssey 17 tells what happens to Argus in the very same breath. What is it?
answer: he dies the moment Odysseus passes
choices: he dies the moment Odysseus passes
he crawls after his master to the door
he barks once and falls asleep
he rises to his feet for the first time in years
context: Odyssey 17.326-327 (Lattimore): 'The doom of dark death now closed down over the dog Argos, when after nineteen years had gone by, he had seen Odysseus.' The recognition is the last thing he does. Source: Wikipedia, Argos (dog).  (Legend.)

question: Apollo has a twin sister among the Olympians -- born the same day on the island of Delos. She is the virgin goddess of the hunt, the wild woodland, and the silver bow, and she runs the mountains with a band of nymphs and hunting dogs. Who is she?
context: Artemis is the daughter of Zeus and the Titaness Leto; her sacred animal is the deer; her Roman name is Diana. Athena is a virgin goddess but she is goddess of wisdom and war-craft, not of the wild hunt. Hera and Demeter are married mother-goddesses.  (Legend.)

question: A young Theban prince named Actaeon spent his days hunting on a great mountain of central Greece with a huge pack of hounds and a company of hunt-companions. On what mountain was Actaeon hunting the day he died?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.155-172; Euripides, Bacchae 1290-92. Cithaeron is the great mountain between Thebes and Athens and appears in many tragic stories -- it is also where the baby Oedipus was exposed and where Pentheus was torn apart by the Bacchae. Actaeon had been trained in hunting by the centaur Chiron.  (Legend.)

question: Actaeon the stag turned and ran through the woods of Cithaeron. Behind him he heard the noise of the hunt closing in. He tried to shout his own name but only a stag's bellow came out. In Ovid's telling, what actually killed Actaeon in the woods that day?
answer: His own hunting-hounds, who did not recognise him
choices: His own hunting-hounds, who did not recognise him
A wild lion that sprang from the thicket at the noise
A fall from the crag above the pool of Gargaphie
Artemis with a silver arrow through the throat
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.225-252. It is the specific horror of the story: not that Artemis killed him, but that his own pack, unable to recognise their master in stag form, ran him down and killed him without knowing what they were doing. Ovid drags out his death across dozens of lines as the dogs pull him apart while he tries to call their names.  (Legend.)

question: As Actaeon was being pulled down by his own hounds, his hunt-companions came running up through the woods behind them -- shouting a name into the trees, wanting the master of the hunt to hurry so he would not miss the kill. Whose name were they shouting?
choices: Chiron's, calling on his old teacher
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.242-248. It is Ovid's grimmest touch: the friends call Actaeon by name to come and see the stag his dogs have brought down, while the stag they are looking at IS Actaeon, unable to answer. Chiron the centaur had trained him, Cadmus was his grandfather, and Aristaeus (a rural god) was his father -- all real relations, none of them present in the woods that day.  (Legend.)

question: In Arcadia a king wanted a son so badly that when his queen bore a daughter, he had the newborn carried up to Mount Parthenion and left there to die. The infant was Atalanta, who would grow up the greatest huntress in Greece. What creature, sacred to Artemis, found the baby and nursed her?
context: The she-bear was sacred to Artemis; her own cubs had been killed by hunters, and she suckled the exposed infant at the same teats before hunters found the wild girl and raised her. The she-wolf is the Roman story of Romulus and Remus; the hind belongs to Artemis's chariot-team; the eagle to Zeus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Aelian, De Natura Animalium 13.1; Apollodorus 3.9.2.  (Legend.)

question: Atalanta grew up in the wild, dedicated to Artemis and sworn to virginity, and she never missed her mark. When two centaurs came at her in the forest and when the great boar of Calydon burst through the beaters, one weapon killed for her both times. What did she hunt with?
context: Atalanta shot the centaurs Rhoecus and Hylaeus with the bow when they attacked her, and drew first blood on the Calydonian Boar with an arrow. The spear belongs to Meleager; the net to fishermen; the sickle-knife is Perseus's Harpe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta.  (Legend.)

question: The kings of Greece gathered to hunt the monstrous boar Artemis had sent against Calydon -- Theseus of Athens, Peleus of Phthia, Jason of Iolcus, and many others. One woman was let in among them: Atalanta of Arcadia. What did she do that made Meleager award her the boar's hide?
answer: her arrow drew first blood on the boar
choices: her arrow drew first blood on the boar
she wrestled the boar to a standstill
she cornered it in a thicket with her hounds
she killed it with a single spear-cast
context: Atalanta's arrow struck the boar first; Meleager killed it with a spear and gave her the hide, which set off the fatal quarrel with his uncles over a trophy going to a woman. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.380-420.  (Legend.)

question: Her father recognized Atalanta as an adult and welcomed her back to his court, but he wanted her married. She agreed to one condition: any suitor must beat her in a footrace, and she was the fastest runner in Greece. What was the price of losing to her?
answer: the loser was put to death
choices: the loser was put to death
the loser was banished from Arcadia
the loser served her father seven years
the loser was branded on the cheek
context: Many young men tried the race and were executed as she overtook them; Atalanta expected the condition to keep her free. Banishment, servitude, and branding are other Greek shame-penalties (Cain-mark parallels), but the price at this race was the sword. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.560-600.  (Legend.)

question: A young man named Melanion watched the executions and knew he could not outrun Atalanta on his own legs. He went to a temple and prayed for help. Which goddess did he pray to?
context: Aphrodite, goddess of desire, answered Melanion's prayer with a very specific gift for the race. Athena helps Bellerophon and Perseus with cleverness; Hera protects marriage from outside; Demeter's gifts are the harvest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.640-660.  (Legend.)

question: The goddess who answered Melanion's prayer gave him three shining things and told him to carry them into the race. Each time Atalanta drew alongside him, he was to throw one off to the side of the track. What were the three things?
context: The three golden apples came from the garden of the Hesperides (or in some tellings from Aphrodite's own grove at Tamasus in Cyprus); Aphrodite made them so beautiful that Atalanta stopped to pick each one up, and by the third she was too far behind to catch him. The Hesperides' apples are the same tree Heracles fetched in his eleventh labor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.644-680.  (Legend.)

question: Melanion won the footrace by his trick, married Atalanta as the terms required, and then made a mistake that would ruin them both -- he forgot to thank the goddess who had given him the apples. In her anger she struck the couple with sudden desire inside a sacred precinct. What did she do to them for the sacrilege?
answer: turned them into a pair of lions
choices: turned them into a pair of lions
turned them into a pair of stags
turned them into a pair of stones
turned them into a pair of stars
context: Aphrodite made them lie together in a temple of Cybele (in Ovid), and for defiling the holy place the pair were transformed into lions and yoked to the chariot of Cybele, the Mother of the Gods, forever after. Stag-transformation is Actaeon's punishment from Artemis; stone is the fate of Niobe; stars belong to Callisto and Orion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atalanta; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.681-707.  (Legend.)

question: While Metis was pregnant, Gaia (earth) and Ouranos (sky) came to Zeus with a warning: after this child, Metis was fated to bear a SON who would grow up to overthrow his father -- just as Zeus had overthrown his own father Cronus. What did Zeus do about the warning?
answer: He swallowed Metis whole while she was still pregnant
choices: He swallowed Metis whole while she was still pregnant
He locked Metis in a bronze chamber under Olympus
He hurled Metis down into the pit of Tartarus
He turned Metis into a lark and set her free
context: Hesiod, Theogony 886-900. Zeus tricked Metis into shrinking small and gulped her down. It was a family trait: Zeus's own father Cronus had swallowed all his children whole, and Zeus escaped only because his mother Rhea substituted a stone. Zeus repeats the pattern here, one generation later, to break the prophecy.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus had swallowed the Titaness Metis while she was pregnant with his daughter. Some time later Zeus began to suffer a physical torment unlike anything the gods had known before. What ailed him?
choices: A burning fever in his chest
A ringing in his ears like bronze bells
context: In the Homeric tradition it is a headache of unnatural size -- the daughter growing inside him has reached full size and demands to come out, and the only way out is through his head. Zeus is otherwise unwoundable; the pain drives him to summon the blacksmith of the gods.  (Legend.)

question: Athena did not come out as a naked baby. She emerged fully GROWN and wearing a complete war-outfit -- helmet, breastplate, and one particular weapon that she would carry throughout Greek myth. Which weapon did she leap from Zeus's head shaking?
context: Homeric Hymn 28. The spear is Athena's mark; she carries it in almost every ancient statue, alongside her aegis-shield with the Gorgon's head. The silver bow is Artemis's; the sickle is Cronus's harvest-weapon; the thunderbolt is Zeus's own. Metis, still living inside Zeus, is said to have forged Athena's helm and spear from within.  (Legend.)

question: The Homeric Hymn 28 says Athena's arrival on Olympus was so violent that the whole cosmos reacted. All Olympus trembled at her war-cry, the sea heaved with dark waves -- and one specific god had to stop what he was doing in the sky and wait for her to take her war-gear off. Who was that god, and what did he stop?
answer: Helios stopped his sun-chariot in the sky
choices: Helios stopped his sun-chariot in the sky
Selene stopped her moon-chariot in the sky
Boreas stopped the north wind blowing
context: Homeric Hymn 28, lines 8-16. Helios pulls the sun across the sky every day in a fiery chariot; the Hymn says he halted the horses at the sight of Athena in her armour, and only when she disarmed did he take up the reins again. Selene is his sister the moon; Boreas is the north wind; Iris the rainbow-messenger. All four move across the sky, but Helios is the one the Hymn names.  (Legend.)

question: A young North African rhetorician was teaching in Milan in the mid-380s CE, listening to the sermons of the bishop Ambrose but unable to change how he lived. His mother had followed him from Africa and kept praying for him. What was the young rhetorician's name?
context: Aurelius Augustinus, born 354 CE in Thagaste (modern Souk Ahras in Algeria), was in his early thirties teaching rhetoric to the imperial court in Milan. His mother Monica had come north from Africa to be near him. Jerome, Anselm and Origen are also famous early or medieval Christian thinkers, but none is the man in the Milan garden. Source: Confessions, Books V-VIII.

question: The young rhetorician's mother, who had followed him all the way from North Africa to Italy and prayed for years that he would change his life, is remembered as one of the most famous mothers of Christian tradition. What is her name?
context: Monica of Hippo followed her son from Thagaste to Rome and then to Milan. Helena was the mother of the emperor Constantine; Perpetua and Felicity were the young North African women martyred at Carthage in 203. Monica appears throughout the Confessions and dies at Ostia later in 387 on the journey home.

question: In Book VIII of the Confessions the young Augustine looks back at a prayer he himself used to pray as a student, one he now finds embarrassingly honest. He asked for a virtue -- but with a delay clause tacked on the end. What did he ask for?
answer: 'Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.'
choices: 'Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.'
'Take from me this cup, but if it be your will.'
'Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth.'
context: Confessions VIII.7.17 -- 'da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo.' Augustine says he was afraid that God would hear him too soon. The other three are also real prayers from scripture (Christ in Gethsemane, Proverbs 30, Psalm 141) but none is the one that has become the byword for wanting to be good later.

question: On a late summer day in 386, in the middle of a bitter conversation with his friend Alypius, the young rhetorician tore himself away, walked to the far end of the garden of the house they were staying in at Milan, threw himself on the ground and wept -- 'How long, how long? Tomorrow and tomorrow? Why not now?' Under what kind of tree does he say in the Confessions he lay?
context: Confessions VIII.12.29: 'sub quadam ficu' -- 'under a certain fig-tree.' The fig-tree in the Milan garden became one of the icons of the whole conversion tradition and was painted in western art from the Middle Ages onward. Olive, cypress and laurel are all real trees of the Mediterranean garden but not the one in the text.

question: As Augustine lay weeping under the tree in the garden, from the house next door he heard the voice of a child -- boy or girl he could not tell -- chanting and repeating one short line, over and over, like a game. What were the Latin words the child was chanting?
context: Confessions VIII.12.29. Augustine writes that the chanting was so persistent he began to wonder whether it was a real children's game he had never heard or a divine command. The other three are all real Christian formulas -- the priest's greeting, the psalm of repentance, the Greek 'Kyrie' still sung in the liturgy -- but none is what the voice in the neighbouring house was singing.

question: After the chanting voice made him stop crying, Augustine wiped his tears, went back to the bench where his friend had been sitting, and picked up the book that lay there. Whose writings did he pick up and open?
answer: the letters of the apostle Paul
choices: the letters of the apostle Paul
context: Confessions VIII.12.29. It was a codex of the Pauline epistles that Alypius had left on the bench. Augustine treated it as sortes -- opening the book at random and taking the first verse he saw. Gospels, psalms and Isaiah were also common in ancient Christian libraries, but the specific book on the bench that afternoon was Paul.

question: Augustine opened the codex at random and his eye fell on a verse from Romans 13 -- a hard-edged sentence that begins by warning against rioting, drunkenness and wantonness, and then swings on the word 'but' to a command. What does the second half of the verse tell the reader to do?
answer: put on the Lord Jesus Christ
choices: put on the Lord Jesus Christ
walk honestly, as in the day
cast off the works of darkness
context: Confessions VIII.12.29 quotes Romans 13:13-14: 'Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying: but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.' 'Walk honestly, as in the day' is Romans 13:13a; 'cast off the works of darkness' and 'awake out of sleep' are both from Romans 13:11-12, the sentences immediately preceding. All four are real Pauline commands from the very same passage; only one is the pivot verse Augustine's eye landed on.

question: Augustine's friend who had been sitting with him in the garden asked to see the book after he had read the verse. This friend read the very next line -- 'Him that is weak in the faith, receive' -- applied it to himself, and joined Augustine in the decision. What was this friend's name?
context: Confessions VIII.12.30. Alypius, Augustine's oldest friend from Thagaste, had followed him through Manichaeism and to Milan; the verse in Romans 14:1 read against himself decided him too. Ambrose is the bishop who preached in Milan; Ponticianus is the courtier whose earlier visit that afternoon set the whole crisis in motion by telling them the story of Anthony of the Desert; Nebridius is another close friend of the circle. All four are real, but only one was on the bench.

question: On the Easter Vigil, the night between 24 and 25 April 387 CE, in the great cathedral at Milan, the bishop baptised the young rhetorician together with his son -- a boy whose name means 'gift-of-God' in Latin. What was the son's name?
context: Adeodatus, the son of Augustine's long-standing common-law partner, was baptised alongside his father and Alypius that night. He died as a teenager not long after the family's return to Africa. Deusdedit is a real Latin name of the same meaning (borne by later popes); Theodosius and Athanasius are also real fourth-century Christian names but do not belong to Augustine's son.

question: The bishop who did the baptising in the Milan cathedral that Easter night in 387 was already famous across the empire as a preacher and had for years drawn Augustine into the pews to listen. Who was he?
context: Ambrose of Milan (c. 339 - 397 CE) was one of the four great Latin doctors of the western church. Augustine had gone to hear him partly for his oratory and stayed for the argument. Athanasius (Alexandria), Basil (Caesarea) and Jerome (translator of the Vulgate) were his eastern and western contemporaries but not the bishop of Milan.

question: After his baptism Augustine sailed home to North Africa, was made bishop of the small port city of Hippo Regius, and went on to write the two most influential Christian books of the millennium after the Bible: the Confessions -- the first work in the western tradition to be called an autobiography -- and one other, a huge answer to those who blamed Christianity for the sack of Rome in 410. What is the second book?
context: De Civitate Dei, written between 413 and 426 CE, sets an 'earthly city' of self-love against a 'heavenly city' of love of God and reads the whole of history through the pair. The Imitation of Christ is a fifteenth-century book by Thomas a Kempis; the Consolation of Philosophy is by Boethius (c. 524); the Divine Comedy by Dante (c. 1320). All four are landmarks of western literature but only one is Augustine's.

question: The best-loved of all the Aesir gods is a young man so fair and gentle that light itself shines from him -- the son of Odin the All-Father and the goddess Frigg. What is his name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 22 and 49: Baldr is the shining son of Odin and Frigg, the fairest and most gentle of the gods. Bragi is the god of poetry; Vidar is the silent god of vengeance; Forseti is Baldr's own son, god of justice. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: Odin's shining son Baldr begins to have terrible dreams that keep waking him -- always the same subject. What do the dreams warn him about, in Snorri's Prose Edda?
choices: the loss of the sun and moon
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Baldr's dreams of his coming death alarm both him and the whole hall of the Aesir. The famine, the giant-war, and the swallowing of the sun and moon all belong to the wider Ragnarok prophecy, not to Baldr's private dreams. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: The goddess Frigg walks through all the nine worlds to save her son Baldr, taking an oath from every kind of thing that could ever hurt him. In Snorri's catalogue she binds fire, water, iron and every other metal, stones, earth, trees, beasts, birds, poisons and serpents -- and one more class of things that surprises modern readers. What ELSE does Frigg make swear?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Frigg's oath-list explicitly includes sicknesses alongside fire, water, metals, stones, trees, beasts, birds, poisons, and serpents -- so no illness could take Baldr either. The winds and clouds are not named in the list; the giants of Jotunheim were Frigg's enemies and not asked; the dead in Hel are outside her reach. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: Loki, the trickster of Asgard, decides to worm the one dangerous secret out of Frigg herself. He does not walk into her hall as Loki -- he changes his shape and comes to her fireside pretending to be a harmless visitor, and gets her chatting. WHAT shape does Loki take to fool Frigg?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Loki takes the form of an old woman and visits Frigg at Fensalir. He wonders aloud whether truly EVERYTHING has sworn -- and Frigg, unguarded, mentions the young mistletoe east of Valhalla. Loki goes straight there to cut it. Loki does take other shapes in other tales (a mare, a salmon, a fly) but never a skald, a serving-maid, or Odin's raven. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: After Baldr falls dead with Loki's dart in him, the gods must send a rider down through the black roads into Hel to beg the queen of the dead for Baldr's return. Who is the rider they send, and on whose horse?
choices: Bragi on foot with his harp
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Hermod (sometimes Hermod the Bold, a son of Odin) is chosen, and Odin lends him Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse. Thor's chariot is drawn by the goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr; Skidbladnir is Freyr's ship that folds up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: The one giantess who refuses to weep for Baldr, ensuring he stays in Hel, gives herself a bitterly ironic name -- an Old Norse word that literally means 'thanks'. What is her name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: the giantess names herself Thokk ('thanks'). Snorri adds that most people believe Thokk was Loki in disguise, doing his last damage. Skadi is Njord's wife; Gerd is Freyr's wife; Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover, mother of Fenrir and Hel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldr  (Legend.)

question: Baldr's funeral ship is the greatest ship ever built, and the gods themselves cannot budge it down the rollers into the sea. They have to send for a giantess to launch it -- and she arrives riding a wolf bridled with live vipers. What is the name of the SHIP she launches?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Baldr's ship is Hringhorni, the greatest of ships. The giantess Hyrrokkin comes riding her viper-bridled wolf and shoves the ship with such force that sparks fly and the earth shakes -- to Thor's fury. Skidbladnir is Freyr's folding ship; Naglfar is the nail-ship of the dead that sails at Ragnarok; Sessrumnir is Freyja's hall, not a ship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hringhorni  (Legend.)

question: After Ragnarok has burned down the old world and a new green earth has risen from the sea, Snorri says Baldr comes back up from Hel to rule the reborn world -- and he comes back with ONE companion, at peace with him at last. Who returns with Baldr from Hel?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 53: after Ragnarok, Baldr and Hodr come back from Hel together, sit down with the surviving Aesir on the new grass, and speak of old things -- one of the loveliest post-apocalypse promises in Norse myth. Odin has been swallowed by Fenrir; Loki has been killed by Heimdall; Nanna died of grief and was burned with Baldr but is not named among the returned. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodr  (Legend.)

question: In Irish myth the sea-monster people who lived in Ireland before the Tuatha De Danann arrived -- misshapen, often one-legged and one-eyed, and cruel -- were the enemies of every wave of settlers. Their king at the Second Battle of Moytura is the most terrible figure in the whole tradition. What are these sea-monster people called?
context: The Fomoire (Fomorians) precede the Tuatha De and are their great enemies. The Milesians (Gaels) come last and displace the Tuatha De; the Fir Bolg and the Nemedians are earlier settler-waves who lose to the Fomorians. Wikipedia: Fomorians.  (Legend.)

question: The king of the Fomorians has ONE eye, and it is so poisonous that whatever it looks upon dies. He is the most terrible figure in the whole tradition, the one the Tuatha De must face at the Second Battle of Moytura. What is his name?
context: Balor na Suile Nimhe -- 'Balor of the Evil Eye' -- is the Fomorian king. Bres is the half-Fomorian who briefly rules the Tuatha De; Elatha is Bres's father; Indech is another Fomorian chief. Wikipedia: Balor.  (Legend.)

question: Balor was not born with the poisoned eye. When he was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a magic potion in a great cauldron. Balor peered in over the rim. What went into the eye that gave it its killing power?
answer: the fumes rising off the druids' brew
choices: the fumes rising off the druids' brew
a splash of hot blood from the cauldron
a curse spoken by a rival druid
the light of a comet reflected in the pot
context: The Cath Maige Tuired traces the origin: the fumes of the brew infected the eye and left it venomous ever after. Wikipedia: Balor.  (Legend.)

question: Over the years Balor's eyelid grew so thick and heavy from the poison inside that Balor could no longer lift it alone. Whenever he needed the eye open on the battlefield, a team of warriors had to haul the lid up by a ring set into it, using hooks and ropes. How many warriors did it take?
context: The Cath Maige Tuired and Donegal folk-tradition agree: four warriors, hauling by a ring in the lid. Wikipedia: Balor; Cath Maige Tuired.  (Legend.)

question: Once the four warriors had hauled Balor's eyelid up and the gaze fell on the enemy line, the effect was not a wound or a spell but something total. What happened to soldiers the open eye looked at?
answer: whole armies fell dead where they stood
choices: whole armies fell dead where they stood
they were turned instantly to stone
they went blind on the spot but lived
they aged a hundred years in a heartbeat
context: The gaze does not wound, does not petrify, does not blind -- it kills outright, at rank-scale. Wikipedia: Balor.  (Legend.)

question: A druid brings Balor a prophecy he never forgets: he will be killed one day, not by an enemy king, not by another Fomorian, but by ONE particular family relation. Who does the prophecy say will kill him?
context: The grandson-prophecy is the whole engine of the story: Balor's attempt to prevent it sets everything else in motion. It is a direct parallel to the Greek myth of Acrisius, killed by his grandson Perseus. Wikipedia: Balor.  (Legend.)

question: To prevent the prophecy, Balor takes his only child -- his daughter Ethlinn -- and locks her away where no man can reach her. He puts her in a crystal tower on an island that ever after bears his name and the ruins of his stronghold. Which island?
context: Tory Island (Toraigh), off the coast of Donegal in northwestern Ireland, is Balor's stronghold in every version of the tale; the ruins on the island are still called Balor's Fort. Skellig Michael is off Kerry, Inishmore is one of the Aran Islands off Galway, Rathlin is off Antrim -- all real Irish islands, none Balor's. Wikipedia: Balor; Tory Island.  (Legend.)

question: A young warrior of the Tuatha De reaches Ethlinn in the tower anyway, with the help of a druidess named Birog who ferries him across on a magic cloak. He is the father of the prophesied grandson. Who is he?
context: Cian mac Cainte, son of Dian Cecht the healer, is the father of Lugh. Ogma, Goibniu, and Nuada are all major Tuatha De men and adjacent-real distractors. Wikipedia: Balor; Cian.  (Legend.)

question: Grandfather and grandson meet at last on the field of the Second Battle of Moytura. The four warriors bend to haul Balor's eyelid up, and the eye starts to open toward the Tuatha De line. Before the lid is fully raised, Lugh strikes. He is not close enough for spear-work. What weapon does he use?
context: Lugh casts a single sling-stone -- named in some medieval sources the Tathlum, a 'concrete-ball' made of enemy brains hardened with lime. The stone strikes the half-open eye before Balor can use it. Wikipedia: Balor; Cath Maige Tuired.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh's sling-stone hits Balor square in the opening eye and drives clean through the skull, bursting out the back of his head. The gaze fires one last time as Balor falls. WHO does it kill?
choices: the Tuatha De line in front of Balor
Balor's own daughter Ethlinn watching from the tower
no one -- the eye is destroyed by the stone
context: This is the strangest and most memorable image in the whole battle: the stone drove the eye backwards through Balor's skull, so the death-gaze fired the wrong way and killed the Fomorian ranks standing behind their own king. The prophecy is fulfilled and the Fomorians are broken forever. Wikipedia: Balor; Cath Maige Tuired.  (Legend.)

question: One of the Twelve apostles is always paired with Philip in the synoptic apostle-lists -- Matthew, Mark, and Luke all put the two names side by side. Which apostle is Philip's list-partner?
context: Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14. This pairing is why Christian tradition often identifies Bartholomew with the Nathanael of John's gospel -- John pairs Nathanael with Philip in the same way.

question: The name 'Bartholomew' is not really a first name at all. In Aramaic it means 'son of Tolmai' -- a patronymic. Which apostle in John's gospel do Christian scholars often say is the same man under his personal name?
context: John never lists a 'Bartholomew' and the synoptics never list a 'Nathanael'; the two names never appear in the same gospel. John also pairs Nathanael with Philip, matching the synoptic Bartholomew-Philip pairing.  (Legend.)

question: A stronger and later-dominant tradition sends Bartholomew not east to India but to the kingdom where he converts a king named Polymius at a city called Albanopolis. Which country does this tradition name as the site of his death?
context: This became the standard Christian story from the medieval Golden Legend onward. King Polymius is not attested in any Armenian royal list, so the tale is legendary, but Armenia is the traditional site.

question: It is not King Polymius himself who orders Bartholomew's death. Tradition names another figure who is furious about the king's conversion and takes matters into his own hands. Whom does the legend name?
context: The medieval Passio Bartholomaei and the Golden Legend name Astyages, the king's own brother, as the one who takes vengeance on the apostle. He orders Bartholomew arrested and killed to punish the conversion.

question: The Golden Legend, and Christian art ever since, tell one specific and horrifying way Bartholomew was killed. Kids will know it from the emblems he carries in painting. What does the dominant tradition say was done to him?
answer: He was flayed alive and then beheaded
choices: He was flayed alive and then beheaded
He was crucified upside down like Peter
He was thrown from a high tower
context: Other traditions have Bartholomew crucified head-down or simply beheaded, but the flaying is the version that entered Western imagination. Because of it he became patron of certain trades whose emblem is the knife and the hide.  (Legend.)

question: Because of the manner of his death, Bartholomew became the patron saint of a specific trio of trades. Which three trades claim him as their heavenly patron?
context: All three trades work with hide and skin -- animal hides for the tanner and leather-worker, meat and hide for the butcher. Bartholomew's flaying made him their heavenly patron.

question: In Michelangelo's great altar-wall fresco, Bartholomew holds up his own hanging skin -- and the face painted on the pelt is not Bartholomew's at all. Whose face did Michelangelo put onto that empty skin?
context: It is one of the most personal signatures in Western art: the artist as a hollow, empty skin held by a flayed saint on the wall behind the altar where popes celebrate Mass. Scholars read it as everything from a prayer for redemption to bitter protest at being made to paint the fresco at all.

question: Every apostle has a traditional feast day in the Christian calendar. In late summer, four famous saints share the season -- Mary at the Assumption on 15 August, Augustine on 28 August, John the Baptist's beheading on 29 August. Which August date does the Church keep as Bartholomew's?
context: 10 August is Lawrence, roasted on his gridiron; 6 August is the Transfiguration; 1 August is Lammas (loaf-mass). Bartholomew's 24 August is one of the oldest apostle-days in the calendar.

question: Around the year 731 Bede finished his greatest book in five volumes at Jarrow and dedicated it to the reigning Northumbrian king, who had received an earlier draft. Which king was this dedicatee?
context: The Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum ('Ecclesiastical History of the English People') is dedicated in its preface to Ceolwulf of Northumbria, who received a draft and returned comments. Oswald and Edwin were earlier Northumbrian kings featured inside the book; Aethelbald ruled Mercia at the time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede.

question: In Book IV of the Historia Ecclesiastica, Bede tells of an illiterate cowherd at Whitby Abbey under Abbess Hilda who used to leave the feast whenever the harp came around to him, because he had no gift for song. One night in the cattle-shed he dreamt of a stranger who told him to sing, and he woke able to compose religious verse in English. What was the cowherd's name?
context: Bede's account in HE IV.24 is the earliest witness to Caedmon and his nine-line hymn, the oldest recorded Old English poem. Cynewulf was a later Old English religious poet; Cuthbert was the bishop of Lindisfarne whose life Bede also wrote; Cedd was a 7th-century missionary bishop of the East Saxons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caedmon.  (Legend.)

question: In Book II of the Historia Ecclesiastica, Bede repeats a story about a pope who walked through the Roman slave market, saw fair-haired boys for sale from Britain, and made a pun on their tribe: 'Not Angles, but angels.' The pun is said to have inspired the mission that sent Augustine to Canterbury. Which pope does Bede name?
context: Bede records the story at HE II.1: Gregory saw the boys, asked their people, and said 'Non Angli, sed angeli' ('Not Angles, but angels'). He then sent the Roman mission under Augustine to Kent in 597. Leo the Great faced Attila at the walls of Rome; Nicholas the Great was a strong 9th-century pope; Sylvester the First baptized Constantine in later legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede.

question: Bede did not invent the practice of dating years from the birth of Jesus, but by using it throughout the Historia Ecclesiastica and his textbook on time-reckoning he made it the standard of Western Europe. Which earlier monk had first devised the method of counting years 'Anno Domini' about two centuries before?
context: Dionysius Exiguus ('Denis the Little'), a Scythian-born monk in Rome, worked out the AD count in 525 while calculating an Easter table. Bede adopted it in De Temporum Ratione (c. 725) and cemented it. Cassiodorus founded the Vivarium; Isidore of Seville wrote the Etymologiae; Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede.

question: A medieval Latin epitaph carved over Bede's stone tomb reads 'Hac sunt in fossa Bedae venerabilis ossa' ('Here in this grave are the bones of the venerable Bede'). The tomb stands today in the Galilee Chapel of a great English cathedral, to which Bede's relics were translated in the Middle Ages. In which cathedral does that tomb stand?
context: Bede's bones were moved to Durham in the 11th century and now rest in the Galilee Chapel at the west end of the nave, with the Latin epitaph carved on the tomb slab. Pope Leo XIII declared Bede a Doctor of the Church in 1899, the only native of Britain to hold that title. York Minster was Alcuin's cathedral; Canterbury was Augustine's see; Winchester held the West Saxon kings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede.

question: On the eve of Ascension Day 735 Bede lay dying in his cell at Jarrow and spent his last hours dictating a translation into English of a book of the New Testament. His disciple Cuthbert's letter records that this was the final book Bede was rendering into the tongue of his own people. Which book was Bede translating?
context: Cuthbert's Epistola de Obitu Bedae is the eyewitness source. Bede had reached the last chapters of John when the boy scribe Wilberht told him one sentence remained. The other three are all plausible New Testament books but the letter specifies John. Source: christianity.com Venerable Bede article.

question: According to Cuthbert's letter on the death of Bede, on the last evening the boy scribe Wilberht bent over the dictation and said, 'There is still one sentence, dear master, that we have not yet written down.' In two Latin words, what did the dying Bede answer him?
context: Cuthbert records the exchange in the Epistola de Obitu Bedae. When Wilberht answered 'It is finished,' Bede replied 'Thou hast well said, it is finished,' then sat on the floor of his cell singing the 'Gloria Patri' ('Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit') until he died. 'Ora et labora' is the Benedictine motto; 'Deo gratias' is a common liturgical response; 'In manus tuas' is the psalm-verse said by Jesus on the cross. Source: christianity.com Venerable Bede article.

question: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the last battle of Arthur's reign is fought against his own son Mordred, on a bare field where nearly every knight on both sides is killed. Arthur himself is mortally wounded there. What is the name of the battle where the fellowship of the Round Table falls?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.4. Camlann is the final battle where Arthur meets Mordred; the two kill each other. Roncesvalles is Roland's last stand in the Chanson de Roland. Badon is the earlier historical victory of the Britons over the Saxons. Bosworth is the real 1485 English battle where Richard III fell.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur, weakening fast, calls Sir Lucan to help him stand. Lucan is himself badly wounded from the battle. He bends down to lift the heavy king, and one specific thing happens to Lucan in that moment that leaves Bedivere the only man on his feet. What happens to Sir Lucan when he tries to lift the king?
answer: his own wounds burst and he dies
choices: his own wounds burst and he dies
he is struck by a stray arrow
he faints and cannot rise again
he is dragged off by Mordred's men
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5: 'the king swooped, and Sir Lucan fell in a swoon with the lift, that the part of his bowels fell out of his body, and therewith the noble knight's heart brast.' Lucan tears himself open on the strain and dies at the king's feet. Mordred is dead already. There is no stray arrow at this moment in the chapter.  (Legend.)

question: Bedivere walks down to the water carrying Excalibur, but when he looks at the pommel set with precious stones and the gold of the hilt, he thinks it a shame to lose so rich a thing. Instead of obeying the king, he hides the sword and goes back with a lie. Where does Bedivere hide Excalibur at the water's edge?
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5. Bedivere lays Excalibur under a tree at the water's edge and comes back empty-handed. The other hiding places are the kind of detail a listener might supply, but the exact word Malory gives is 'under a tree'.  (Legend.)

question: Bedivere comes back to the king and lies about what he saw at the water. Arthur, weakening but sharp, knows at once that no wonder happened -- because throwing Excalibur in should have produced a marvel -- and sends the knight back. What does Bedivere claim he saw on the first return?
choices: a black barge on the far shore
a red knight riding down the beach
three queens weeping on the water
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5: 'I saw nothing but waves and winds.' Because a proper obedience should have brought a wonder up from the water, Arthur knows it is a lie and sends Bedivere out again. The three queens in the black barge are the next scene of the chapter, not part of this first lie.  (Legend.)

question: Bedivere goes back to the water a second time, looks again at the jewelled hilt, hides Excalibur again, and returns with another lie. The line Malory gives him this time is one of the most quoted single sentences in the whole Morte d'Arthur -- a line quoted and translated for five centuries. What does Bedivere say he saw on the second return?
answer: the waters wap and the waves wan
choices: the waters wap and the waves wan
the moon lay white upon the lake
an island rose dark in the west
a bell tolled from beneath the water
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5 -- 'I saw nothing but the waters wap and the waves wan.' 'Wap' means lap; 'wan' means grow pale. The rhythmic Middle English line has been quoted and translated for five centuries. The other three lake-images sound the part but are not in the chapter.  (Legend.)

question: When Bedivere reports the pale waves the second time, Arthur turns on him in fury and gives one of the harshest speeches in the book. 'Ah traitor, untrue,' Arthur says, 'thou wouldest for my rich sword' do what?
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5: 'Ah traitor, untrue, who would have weened that thou that hast been to me so lief and dear... would betray me for the riches of the sword.' Arthur accuses Bedivere of choosing gold over loyalty, and threatens to kill him with his own hands if he lies a third time.  (Legend.)

question: Shamed by the king's rebuke, Bedivere goes down to the water a third time. This time he winds one specific thing about the hilt so that the sword will fly cleanly from his hand, whirls the blade around his head, and hurls it as far out over the water as his strength will send. What does Bedivere wind about the hilt before the third throw?
choices: a scrap torn from his cloak
a linen strip from his wound
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5 -- Bedivere 'bound the girdle about the hilts' before hurling Excalibur out over the water. The girdle is the sword-belt itself. It is a small practical detail easy to miss but it is Malory's own.  (Legend.)

question: The moment Excalibur clears Bedivere's hand and touches the water on the third throw, a wonder rises up to meet it. Bedivere stands staring, then runs back to the king and tells him what he saw at last. What did Bedivere see rise from the water?
answer: an arm clothed in white samite
choices: an arm clothed in white samite
a barge draped in black cloth
a knight in red on a pale horse
a swan with a chain of gold
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5: 'there came an arm and an hand above the water, and met it, and caught it, and so shook it thrice and brandished.' The arm is 'clothed in white samite' -- the same rich silk that clothed the arm which first GAVE Arthur the sword in Book I ch.25. The story closes its own circle. The black barge is the next scene of the chapter; the swan with the golden chain belongs to the Lohengrin story; the red-knight-on-a-pale-horse belongs to Perceval's road.  (Legend.)

question: The arm that rises from the water catches Excalibur, and before it sinks beneath the surface the hand does one exact ceremonial motion with the sword. Malory names it with a precise verb and a precise number of times. What does the arm do with the sword before it vanishes into the water?
answer: shakes it thrice and brandishes it
choices: shakes it thrice and brandishes it
raises it in salute to the king
breaks it once across its wrist
lays it flat upon the water
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5 -- the arm 'caught it, and so shook it thrice and brandished, and then vanished away the hand with the sword in the water.' The number three closes the whole scene: Bedivere's three trips to the water, and now the arm's three shakes of the returned sword before it sinks. The gesture is a farewell brandish -- neither a salute nor a break.  (Legend.)

question: Bellerophon is the young Greek prince who tamed a winged horse at a famous spring in his home city and rode him into battle against the Chimera. From which Greek city did Bellerophon come?
context: Bellerophon was the grandson of Sisyphus and (in one tradition) son of Poseidon; his home city of Corinth commanded the isthmus between the Aegean and Ionian seas, and the Spring of Pirene where the winged horse came to drink was one of Corinth's landmarks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellerophon; Homer, Iliad 6.152-155.  (Legend.)

question: Bellerophon killed a man by accident and had to flee for purification to King Proetus of Tiryns. Proetus's wife tried to seduce him, and when he refused her, she went to her husband with a false story. Proetus would not break the guest-friendship code by killing a suppliant himself. What did he do instead?
answer: sent Bellerophon on with a sealed letter of death
choices: sent Bellerophon on with a sealed letter of death
handed Bellerophon over to his brother-in-law's guards
poisoned Bellerophon's wine that same night
drove Bellerophon out into the sea in a chest
context: Proetus sent Bellerophon to his father-in-law Iobates of Lycia carrying a sealed letter that ordered the bearer's execution -- the only reference to writing in the whole Iliad, called there 'baneful signs, deadly to look on.' The chest-on-the-sea is Perseus and Danae; poisoning-the-guest belongs to other stories; the brother-in-law's guards would still make Proetus the killer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellerophon; Homer, Iliad 6.155-170.  (Legend.)

question: King Iobates of Lycia entertained Bellerophon for nine days as an honoured guest before he broke the seal and read what the letter demanded. Unwilling to kill a guest himself, he sent Bellerophon on an errand meant to be certain death -- against a monster that was ravaging his kingdom. What was the monster?
context: The Chimera burned crops and cattle across Lycia; no man on foot could approach a fire-breathing beast, so Iobates counted the errand as good as a death-warrant. The Hydra, Nemean Lion, and Erymanthian Boar are all real Greek monsters, all faced by Heracles in the labors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellerophon; Homer, Iliad 6.178-183.  (Legend.)

question: The monster of Lycia was a single beast pieced out of three animals. A lion's head roared at the front, a serpent's tail lashed at the rear, and from her back sprang the head of a third creature. What was the third?
context: Hesiod's Theogony gives the classic three-part Chimera: lion in front, goat-head sprouting from the back, serpent behind, and fire from all three mouths. The word chimera in modern English -- any fanciful hybrid -- comes from this beast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimera_(mythology); Hesiod, Theogony 319-325.  (Legend.)

question: The seer Polyidus told Bellerophon there was only one way to fight a fire-breathing beast: from above. On his advice Bellerophon slept the night in a temple, and in a dream the goddess of that temple laid a gift beside him. When he woke it was really there. Whose temple was it?
context: Athena, patron of clever heroes, gave Bellerophon a golden bridle in the dream; when he woke the bridle lay on the floor of her temple. Pindar sings this scene in the Thirteenth Olympian. Hera and Artemis play no part in this story; Aphrodite helps other heroes in other stories. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellerophon; Pindar, Olympian 13.63-92.  (Legend.)

question: Bellerophon took the golden bridle from Athena's temple down to the Spring of Pirene at Corinth, where every morning a winged horse came to drink. He slipped the bridle over the horse's head and tamed him for the flight against the Chimera. What was the winged horse's name?
context: Pegasus was the winged horse born from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her; he came to drink at Pirene, and Athena's bridle was the one thing that could tame him. Arion is Poseidon's black horse from the Adrastus stories; Xanthus and Balios are Achilles's mortal-born team from Iliad 19. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus; Pindar, Olympian 13.63-92.  (Legend.)

question: Bellerophon killed the Chimera, then the Solymi, then the Amazons -- every task Iobates set to finish him off. In his pride he tried one flight too many. He turned Pegasus's head straight up and drove toward the summit of Olympus, to sit among the gods. What did Zeus send to stop him?
answer: a gadfly to sting Pegasus in the flank
choices: a gadfly to sting Pegasus in the flank
an eagle to knock him from the horse's back
a thunderbolt straight across the horse's path
a north wind to freeze both wings at once
context: The gadfly's sting made Pegasus buck, and Bellerophon fell all the way back to earth. Homer says he lived on afterward 'hated by all the gods, wandering the Aleian Plain alone, eating out his heart.' The thunderbolt and eagle are Zeus's usual instruments; the humbling insect is the specific touch here -- the greatest hero brought down by a fly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellerophon; Pindar, Isthmian 7.44-47; Homer, Iliad 6.200-202.  (Legend.)

question: The winged horse went on without his rider. He flew up to Olympus alone, and Zeus kept him there, giving him a permanent job in the sky-god's own household. What task was Pegasus set to?
choices: to guard the gates of Olympus
to guide the souls of dead heroes
context: Hesiod says Pegasus took up his station in the halls of Zeus, bringing thunder and lightning to the god at his command; he was later placed as the constellation Pegasus in the northern sky. The sun-chariot is Helios's own (or the boy Phaethon's disaster); the gate-guarding is the role of the Hecatoncheires; the soul-guiding belongs to Hermes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus; Hesiod, Theogony 285.  (Legend.)

question: The Chimera was one of a whole brood of famous monsters born to the same monstrous parents. Her siblings were the Nemean Lion that Heracles strangled, the many-headed Hydra of Lerna, and the three-headed hound Cerberus. Who were the parents of this whole brood?
context: Typhon, the storm-giant Zeus buried under Mount Etna, and Echidna, the half-woman half-serpent, produced the Nemean Lion, the Chimera, Cerberus, Orthrus, and the Lernaean Hydra between them. Uranus and Gaia are Sky and Earth; Cronus and Rhea are the Olympians' own parents; Nereus and Doris are the sea-parents of the fifty Nereids. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimera_(mythology); Hesiod, Theogony 306-325.  (Legend.)

question: In one of the most famous scenes of the Book of Daniel, a Babylonian king throws a drunken banquet for a thousand of his lords -- and in the middle of it, a disembodied hand starts writing on the wall. Which king?
context: Daniel 5:1 KJV. Nebuchadnezzar is his named predecessor (the one who sacked Jerusalem and had the fiery-furnace scene). Cyrus is the Persian who later frees the Jews. Sennacherib is the Assyrian king from Isaiah / 2 Kings.

question: At the height of Belshazzar's drunken feast in Babylon, something appears in the air by the great lampstand and begins writing on the plaster wall of the king's palace. What is it?
answer: The fingers of a man's hand
choices: The fingers of a man's hand
context: Daniel 5:5 KJV: 'In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace.' A pillar of fire led Israel out of Egypt; ravens fed Elijah; the four-faced cherub is Ezekiel's vision.

question: Belshazzar's crime at the feast is very specific: as the wine goes round, he orders in a hoard of golden objects taken by his predecessor Nebuchadnezzar out of an enemy city, so his guests can drink from them. Where had that hoard come from?
choices: The palace of the pharaoh in Egypt
The treasury of the king of Tyre
The oracle at Delphi in Greece
context: Daniel 5:2-3 KJV: 'Belshazzar, whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem.' Nebuchadnezzar carried the Temple vessels off in the sack of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:14-15). The desecration of THESE cups is the reason the writing appears.

question: As Belshazzar's guests drink wine from the stolen Temple cups, the text says they praise a specific list of gods -- one of the sharpest verses in the story. What are the gods a list of?
answer: Gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone
choices: Gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone
The sun, the moon, and the seven planets
The eagle, the lion, the ox, and the serpent
context: Daniel 5:4 KJV: 'They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.' The point of the list is that these gods are all just idols made of ordinary stuff -- and the drinkers are toasting them with the vessels of the LIVING God's temple.

question: None of Belshazzar's astrologers can read the writing. The queen-mother remembers a Judean captive from Nebuchadnezzar's day and calls him in. What three things does Belshazzar publicly promise this captive if he can interpret the writing?
answer: A scarlet robe, a gold chain about his neck, and to be third ruler in the kingdom
choices: A scarlet robe, a gold chain about his neck, and to be third ruler in the kingdom
A tenth of the royal grain, a hundred cattle, and a house in the citadel
A daughter of the king to wife, and a province, and a bodyguard of a hundred spears
A crown of thorns, a purple cloak, and a scepter of reed
context: Daniel 5:16 KJV. 'Third ruler' -- likely because Belshazzar himself was second, ruling as co-regent under his father Nabonidus (a detail archaeology later confirmed). The crown of thorns and purple cloak is what the soldiers mock Jesus with (Mark 15:17). The other two options are invented parallels.

question: Daniel refuses the king's gifts and reads the words the disembodied hand has written on the plaster of the palace wall. Preserved in Aramaic in the original text, they are among the most famous foreign words in English literature. What did the hand write?
context: Daniel 5:25 KJV. 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' is Jesus's cry from the cross ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?', Mark 15:34). 'Talitha cumi' ('little girl, arise') and 'Ephphatha' ('be opened') are Jesus's Aramaic healing words. Maranatha ('the Lord comes'), Hosanna, and Abba are other preserved Aramaic phrases.

question: Reading Daniel's interpretation of the writing on the wall, one phrase in particular has passed straight into the English language for a moment of moral judgment -- said face to face to king Belshazzar about his own kingship. What does Daniel tell the king to his face?
answer: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting
choices: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting
Thou art the man whom the Lord hath chosen
Thou hast sold thyself to work evil in the sight of the Lord
Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee
context: Daniel 5:27 KJV, the meaning Daniel gives for the middle word on the wall. 'Thou art the man' is Nathan the prophet naming David's sin (2 Sam 12:7). 'Sold thyself to work evil' is Elijah to Ahab (1 Kings 21:20). 'This night thy soul shall be required' is Jesus's parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:20).

question: The end of Daniel chapter 5 is famously blunt: after Daniel finishes reading the writing, the very next verse tells us what happens to the king. What does the KJV say happened to Belshazzar?
answer: In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain
choices: In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain
He was driven from among men to eat grass as an ox seven years
He was carried off by the whirlwind up into heaven
He was struck dumb and lived out his days in silence
context: Daniel 5:30 KJV. The verse right after tells us Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old (5:31). Eating grass seven years is Nebuchadnezzar's madness (Daniel 4). Carried off in a whirlwind is Elijah (2 Kings 2). Struck dumb is Zacharias, John the Baptist's father (Luke 1).

question: This young Italian nobleman from Norcia in central Italy, later called the father of Western monasticism, was sent to Rome to study in the late fifth century CE. Disgusted by what he saw in the city, he walked out and took to the mountains east of Rome to live alone. What was his name?
context: Benedict of Nursia (traditional dates c. 480 - 547 CE). Anthony of the Desert was the earlier Egyptian hermit, Basil of Caesarea the great fourth-century eastern monastic legislator, and Columba the sixth-century Irish founder of Iona. All four are real monastic founders; only one is the Italian who walked out of Rome for the Simbruini mountains.

question: Word of Benedict's holiness spread and a nearby community of monks invited him to become their abbot. His discipline was too strict for them and at dinner one night they slipped poison into a cup in front of him. According to Gregory the Great's Dialogues, what happened to the cup when Benedict blessed it in the usual way?
context: Gregory, Dialogues II.3. Benedict is said to have simply made the sign of the cross over the cup as any Christian would before drinking, and the vessel broke apart on the table. He got up calmly, told the monks they had shown him what they thought of him, and went back to his cave.  (Legend.)

question: Around 529 CE, with a growing band of disciples, Benedict left the Subiaco valley and travelled south to a hilltop between Rome and Naples to found a new great mother-house. The site was already occupied by a pagan sanctuary, which he tore down before building. Which god's temple did he tear down on that hill?
context: The hilltop at Monte Cassino had held a temple of Apollo when Benedict arrived. He replaced it with oratories to John the Baptist and Martin of Tours. Mars, Mercury and Diana were all still worshipped in Italy in the fifth and sixth centuries, but the specific god of the shrine at Monte Cassino was Apollo.  (Legend.)

question: Before Benedict moved south to found his great hilltop mother-house, he had already organised his growing band of disciples in the Subiaco valley into a chain of small monasteries -- traditionally the same neat number of houses, each with the same number of monks in it. What number appears on both sides?
context: Twelve small monasteries of twelve monks each, matching the number of the apostles. When the settlement grew unmanageable Benedict left for the south and founded Monte Cassino around 529 CE. Seven, forty and seventy-two are all real symbolic numbers in the Bible (days of creation, days in the wilderness, disciples sent out in Luke), but the tradition attached to Subiaco is twelve.  (Legend.)

question: Benedict had a twin sister, herself the founder of a parallel community for women near Monte Cassino, and once a year the two of them met at a house halfway between the monasteries. What was her name?
context: Scholastica is buried in the same tomb as her brother at Monte Cassino. Her feast day is 10 February, Benedict's 11 July. Radegund, Hilda and Etheldreda are all real historical women who founded major sixth- and seventh-century monasteries (Poitiers, Whitby, Ely), but the twin sister on the hill was Scholastica.

question: Gregory the Great's Dialogues tell that at their very last meeting Scholastica begged her brother to stay talking through the evening, and when he refused because his own rule forbade it she prayed for a storm so violent he could not leave. Three days later she died -- and Benedict, in his cell at Monte Cassino, saw her soul leave the earth in the form of what animal?
context: Gregory, Dialogues II.33-34. The dove ascending from the sister's deathbed became a standard image in western monastic art. Eagle, swan and lark all appear as soul-birds in other medieval traditions -- the eagle in Roman imperial apotheosis, the swan in Celtic and Germanic story, the lark in later English hymnody -- but the bird in Gregory's Dialogues at Scholastica's death is the dove.  (Legend.)

question: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the young Geat hero has sailed to Denmark to help King Hrothgar defend his mead-hall Heorot from a monster that has been terrorising it every night for twelve years. What is the name of the monster Beowulf has come to fight?
context: Beowulf lines 86-193: the monster is Grendel, a descendant of Cain, who hates the sound of harp-song in Heorot and comes each night to devour Hrothgar's men. Fafnir is the Norse dragon on Gnitaheid. Humbaba is the forest-guardian killed by Gilgamesh. Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the Greek underworld. Grendel is the specific enemy of the poem's first half.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf and his fourteen Geat thanes settle down in Heorot for their first night. Before lying down among his men, Beowulf makes a striking choice about how he will meet Grendel when the monster comes -- a choice that shocks the Danes watching. HOW does Beowulf plan to meet Grendel?
answer: bare-handed, with no weapon at all
choices: bare-handed, with no weapon at all
with a sword blessed by Hrothgar
with a spear thrown from the doorway
with a torch to blind the monster
context: Beowulf 677-687: Beowulf gives his sword away, takes off his mail-shirt and helmet, and lies down bare-handed among his fourteen thanes to pretend to sleep. The Danes who watch him do this are astonished -- warriors of his day would never sleep unarmed under monster-threat. The poet tells the reader the reason at once: Grendel scorns weapons and Beowulf will not shame his opponent with an advantage the monster cannot use.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf has a very specific reason for setting his sword and mail aside before Grendel comes. What is his stated reason for going unarmed against the monster?
answer: Grendel uses no weapons himself, and Beowulf takes no advantage
choices: Grendel uses no weapons himself, and Beowulf takes no advantage
iron cannot cut Grendel's skin, so a sword is useless
his king has forbidden him to draw a blade in a foreign hall
his sword was lost overboard on the voyage to Denmark
context: Beowulf 677-687: Beowulf refuses the advantage because Grendel scorns weapons. Iron does turn out to fail against Grendel's hide -- the poet mentions this LATER, after the fight -- but Beowulf's stated reason for lying down unarmed is honour, not futility. The other reasons are not in the poem.  (Legend.)

question: At midnight Grendel came stalking to Heorot from the moors. When he reached the mead-hall the first thing he did was tear one specific thing off with a single blow of his hand -- the poem lingers on this moment as the first proof of the monster's strength inside the walls. What did Grendel rip off in his first act inside Heorot?
context: Beowulf 720-724: Grendel wrenches Heorot's iron-bound door off its hinges with one hand and strides in. The poet stresses the door's iron bands to make the ease of Grendel's entry more terrifying. The smoke-vent, king's seat, and harp are all real features of an Anglo-Saxon mead-hall but not what Grendel tears loose.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel came through the doorway and the first Geat he saw sleeping was closest to him. He did not fight the man; he ATE him on the spot before anyone else in the hall could rise. Later in the poem, when Beowulf retells the story to his own king Hygelac back in Geatland, the poet actually gives the eaten thane a name. What is the name of the Geat that Grendel ate first?
context: Beowulf 740-745 and 2076: the sleeping Geat Grendel devoured first is named Hondscioh, in the retelling to Hygelac. Wiglaf is the young thane who alone stays with Beowulf against the dragon fifty years later. Aeschere is Hrothgar's closest counsellor, killed by Grendel's mother the following night. Unferth is the Dane who taunts Beowulf at the feast.  (Legend.)

question: The two of them WRESTLED UPRIGHT in the pitch-dark hall, so fiercely that a specific thing broke apart all around them -- the poet uses the destruction to show how the fight is shaking Heorot itself. What broke apart around Beowulf and Grendel as they wrestled in the darkness?
answer: the mead-benches burst from their pegs
choices: the mead-benches burst from their pegs
the roof-beams sagged with the noise
the fire-pit collapsed in on itself
the wall-hangings caught fire from the torches
context: Beowulf 767-771: the great mead-benches sprang from their iron pegs as the two fighters slammed against them. Everything else in the hall stayed standing, and Heorot did not burn until decades later. The bursting benches are the poet's single sound-and-vision cue for the fight's violence.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel fled from Heorot with his life-blood spurting into the night. He ran back the way he had come, across the moors, headed for one specific place he had always considered safe. Where did the wounded Grendel flee to die?
choices: the deep forest north of Heorot
the sea-cliffs of the Geat coast
context: Beowulf 819-836: Grendel dies in the cave he shares with his mother beneath a haunted mere (lake). Beowulf will follow him there the day after next to face Grendel's mother in the very cave. The Geat coast is Beowulf's homeland, not Grendel's. The burial-barrow of the dragon is a different location fifty years later.  (Legend.)

question: When morning came the Danes and Geats crowded into Heorot to see the proof of Beowulf's victory. Beowulf had hung the trophy in one specific place in the hall so that everyone entering could see it at once, and so that all the tribes of Denmark would come to view it. Where did Beowulf hang Grendel's torn-off arm as the trophy of his fight?
choices: at the great door where Grendel had entered
outside the hall on a spear
context: Beowulf 833-836: 'under the vaulted roof' -- Beowulf hoisted Grendel's whole shoulder, arm, and clawed hand up into the rafters of Heorot to hang there as proof of the kill. The image is the most-remembered visual in all of Old English poetry: a monster's arm dangling from the mead-hall roof at dawn.  (Legend.)

question: The Beowulf poem, and the whole scene of Grendel's arm coming off in Heorot, has come down to us across a thousand years through a single object. In 1731 that object was nearly destroyed. What happened in 1731 that almost cost the world the Beowulf poem forever?
answer: a fire at Ashburnham House scorched the manuscript
choices: a fire at Ashburnham House scorched the manuscript
a Danish raid burned the monastery library
a monk erased the vellum to reuse the parchment
a shipwreck lost the copy sent to France
context: The Nowell Codex (Cotton Vitellius A.xv), containing the only copy of Beowulf, was in the Ashburnham House library when it caught fire on 23 October 1731. The manuscript survived but was scorched at the edges; every page has some fire-damage, and some words are lost to the burn. The Grendel-fight passage sits on folios 143r-146v of this single scorched book, now kept in the British Library.

question: Around 1113 a 22-year-old Burgundian noble talked about thirty of his own brothers, cousins, and friends into renouncing their careers with him and walking together into the struggling new reformed abbey of Citeaux, saving it from dying out. What was this young man's name?
context: Bernard of Clairvaux (c. 1090 to 1153) was born at Fontaine-les-Dijon and led his kinsmen into Citeaux in 1113; the mass entry rescued the Cistercian mother-house. Anselm was an 11th-century archbishop of Canterbury; Dominic founded the Dominicans a century later; Norbert founded the Premonstratensians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Clairvaux.

question: Three years after joining Citeaux, Bernard was sent by Abbot Stephen Harding into a wilderness on the river Aube in Burgundy to found a new daughter house. He led it as its only abbot for the next 38 years and became better known by its name than by his birthplace. What did he call the new abbey?
context: The name means 'bright valley' (clair val); Bernard's writings and reputation soon made the daughter-house better known than its mother-house. Cluny was the great older Benedictine abbey Bernard often clashed with; Fontenay was another Cistercian foundation; Melrose was the Cistercian house planted in Scotland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Clairvaux.

question: For eighteen years Bernard preached a running series of sermons at Clairvaux on a single book of the Bible, reaching 86 sermons before he died with the work still unfinished. Which book was he expounding?
context: The Sermones super Cantica Canticorum became foundational for medieval Christian mysticism. He was still working on them when he died in August 1153. The other three are all long books commonly preached through in the medieval schools. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Clairvaux.

question: On Christmas Eve of 1144 the atabeg Zengi captured the first of the crusader states in the East to fall to Muslim reconquest, a shock that prompted the Pope to summon a new crusade. Which crusader county did Zengi take?
context: Edessa was the northernmost and most exposed of the four Latin states founded after the First Crusade. Its fall in December 1144 was the trigger for Pope Eugenius III to commission Bernard to preach a new expedition. Antioch, Tripoli, and Jerusalem were the other three crusader states and all still stood at that date. Source: deremilitari.org/2014/03/the-origin-of-the-second-crusade/.

question: On Easter Sunday 1146 at Vezelay, Bernard preached the Second Crusade to a hillside crowd so large the basilica could not hold it. When the volunteers surged forward and the pre-cut cloth crosses ran out, Bernard tore up a piece of cloth on the spot to make more crosses for the vow-takers. What cloth did he tear up?
context: Odo of Deuil, King Louis VII's chaplain, is the eyewitness; his De profectione Ludovici VII in Orientem (c. 1148) records Bernard tearing his own white Cistercian robe into strips when the supply ran out. King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine were both present in the crowd. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_V%C3%A9zelay.

question: The Second Crusade that Bernard had preached ended in disaster; the joint French and German army made it to the East but its most famous set-piece attack collapsed after only four days. Which great city's siege was the debacle that ended the campaign in July 1148?
context: The four-day siege of Damascus by Louis VII and Conrad III fell apart amid quarrels and a poor water-supply choice; the crusade broke up soon after. Aleppo and Mosul were Zengid strongholds inland; Antioch was a friendly crusader capital. Bernard wrote in De Consideratione II.1 that God had not shown him the reason for the failure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Clairvaux.

question: Luke's Christmas story has Mary and Joseph on the road because the emperor has ordered a headcount of the whole empire. Everyone must travel to their family's home town to be counted. Which emperor's decree sends them walking from Nazareth to Bethlehem?
context: Luke 2:1 KJV: 'And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.' Julius Caesar had been assassinated decades earlier; Tiberius was emperor later, during Jesus's adult ministry; Nero came a full generation after.

question: Luke's most famous nativity line explains WHY Mary and Joseph do not get a proper room in Bethlehem for the birth. Luke states the reason bluntly at the end of the verse. What does Luke give as the reason?
answer: there was no room for them in the inn
choices: there was no room for them in the inn
the shepherds asked them to move on
a star had come to rest above the stable
an angel had told them where to go
