context: Luke 2:7 KJV: 'And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.' The star belongs to Matthew's magi story, not Luke's shepherd story; no angel gives Mary and Joseph specific instructions about the room.

question: Luke tells us exactly what Mary lays the newborn baby into for want of a proper bed. It is the object every Christmas carol names -- one plain word. What is the word Luke uses?
context: A manger is a feeding trough for animals -- kids eat, animals eat, and the same Latin root ('manducare', to eat) gives us the word. Luke's choice of that particular object is why the ox and the donkey later get pulled into the picture from Isaiah 1:3, though Luke himself never mentions them.

question: When the angel appears to the shepherds on the hillside, Luke says one thing shines around them -- a specific phrase that appears three separate times in the same chapter. What does Luke say shone round about them?
context: Luke 2:9 KJV: 'and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.' The pillar of fire belongs to Moses and the Exodus; the burning wheel to Ezekiel's vision; the star of the east to Matthew's account of the magi -- not this scene.

question: Once the sky is full of angels, Luke gives their song verbatim in two halves. The FIRST half is 'Glory to God in the highest'. What does the SECOND half say, according to Luke 2:14?
answer: and on earth peace, good will toward men
choices: and on earth peace, good will toward men
and blessed be the name of the Lord forever
and let all the earth keep silence before him
and holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts
context: Luke 2:14 KJV: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.' 'Blessed be the name of the Lord forever' is from the Psalms; 'let all the earth keep silence before him' is from Habakkuk 2; 'holy, holy, holy' is the seraphs' song in Isaiah 6.

question: After the shepherds have run to Bethlehem, seen the baby, and told everyone in the house what the angel said in the field, Luke pauses on Mary alone -- one gentle verse about her response. What does Luke 2:19 say Mary did?
answer: kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart
choices: kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart
knelt beside the manger and prayed silently until dawn
closed her eyes and said nothing for a long time
sang a psalm under her breath over the sleeping child
context: Luke 2:19 KJV: 'But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.' Mary's louder song, the Magnificat ('My soul doth magnify the Lord'), came earlier in Luke 1 at her cousin Elisabeth's house -- not here at the manger.

question: In 1223 an Italian friar staged the FIRST live nativity scene ever performed -- a real hay-filled manger in a hillside cave, a live ox and donkey, and torches and candles carried by villagers on Christmas Eve. In which Italian town did he set it up?
context: Francis of Assisi asked his friend Giovanni Velita, the Lord of Greccio (a hill town about 50 miles north of Rome), to prepare the cave and the animals two weeks before Christmas 1223. Mass was said over the crib with the ox and the donkey standing by -- and every live nativity performed since traces its lineage to that night.

question: The letter names among the arrested Christians a young girl whose Christian mistress was arrested with her and had feared she would be too weak to hold under torture. Instead the torturers, working on her in relays from morning to evening, finally admitted they were exhausted and did not know what more they could do to her. What is the girl's name?
context: Blandina was a slave of a Christian household of Lyon and, according to Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica V.1, held out longer than any of her fellow-martyrs. Perpetua was the young noblewoman of Carthage killed in 203, Agnes and Cecilia the famous Roman virgin-martyrs of a later century; all four are real, but the slave-girl in Gaul is Blandina.

question: Under torture, the girl kept answering with a single sentence, over and over, to every question the interrogators put. According to the letter quoted by Eusebius, what did she keep repeating?
answer: 'I am a Christian, and we do nothing to be ashamed of.'
choices: 'I am a Christian, and we do nothing to be ashamed of.'
'Into thy hands I commend my spirit.'
'Not my will, but thine, be done.'
'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.'
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.19. The Latin martyr formula is 'Christiana sum'. The other three are also famous sayings from the western tradition -- the last words of the psalm and of Jesus on the cross, the prayer in Gethsemane, and Tertullian's line from his Apology written a generation later. Only one belongs to the Lyon slave-girl.

question: That day the wild beasts that were sent into the arena would not touch her. The Roman officials had her taken back to prison and saved for the last day of the games, when she was brought out again -- this time paired with a fifteen-year-old boy. What was the boy's name?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.53. Sanctus, Attalus and Maturus were all also martyrs of the same Lyon pogrom named in the letter -- Sanctus the deacon of Vienne, Attalus the Roman citizen, Maturus a recent convert. But the fifteen-year-old boy at the climax, whom Blandina encouraged until he died, was Ponticus.

question: After the fifteen-year-old boy died at her side, the letter says, it was the slave girl's turn. The Romans had prepared several torments for her, one after the other, and the first of them was to fasten her to a piece of red-hot metal and burn her before the crowd. What piece of metal was it?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.56 says the iron chair was heated red-hot. The iron grid (gridiron) belongs to the third-century Roman deacon Lawrence; the copper altar to various Old Testament sacrifices; the bronze bull is the tyrant Phalaris's roasting-machine of Sicilian legend. All four are real instruments in the western imagination, but the one at Lyon in 177 was the iron chair.

question: The wild animal into whose horns the girl was thrown, after being wrapped in the net, tossed her again and again until an executioner finally finished her with a dagger. What animal was it?
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.56 -- a young bull, driven at her by the arena-keepers. A wild cow was the beast at Carthage that killed the noblewoman Perpetua in 203, a close and deliberate parallel arena-death for a Christian woman; boars and bears also appear in other martyr-accounts. But the animal at Lyon was the steer.

question: After the games the Romans burned the bodies of all the Lyon martyrs and threw the ashes into flowing water so the current would carry them away and no relics could ever be gathered. Into what river did they throw the ashes?
context: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.61-63, says the pagans deliberately scattered the ashes in the Rhone 'so that not a single relic of their bodies might be left on earth' -- which shows the pagan authorities already understood exactly what the young Christian custom of relic-veneration was going to become. The Saone joins the Rhone at Lyon; the Loire and the Garonne are the other great rivers of Gaul, running to the Atlantic. Only the Rhone carries the Lyon ashes in the letter.

question: The bishop of Lyon at the time of the pogrom was a very old man -- over ninety, the letter says -- dragged before the tribunal and asked point-blank 'Who is the god of the Christians?' What did he answer?
answer: 'If you are worthy, you will know.'
choices: 'If you are worthy, you will know.'
'A god who is greater than Caesar.'
context: Historia Ecclesiastica V.1.29-31. The old man's name was Pothinus; he was beaten so badly that day that he died in prison two days later. The other three are all real Christian answers of the martyr age (from Polycarp, Justin, and the Apostles' Creed) but only one is Pothinus's reply at Lyon in 177.

question: The River Boyne in County Meath runs past the great mound of Newgrange and out to the Irish Sea. In Irish myth the river is the body of a Tuatha De Danann goddess who drowned at its source and became the water. Which goddess?
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: Boann is the eponymous goddess of the River Boyne (Irish An Bhoinn). Brigid is the goddess of poetry, healing, and the smith-fire at Kildare; Danu is the mother-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann as a whole; Aine is a Munster sun-and-fertility goddess.  (Legend.)

question: At the mythic heart of Ireland stood a hidden well guarded by the Tuatha De god Nechtan and only three of his cup-bearers. It was the sacred source of wisdom and its waters were forbidden to all others. What was that well called?
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann and Nechtan (mythology): the Well of Segais (also called Connla's Well) was the mythic source of the Boyne. Only Nechtan and his three cup-bearers could approach it. The Well of Urd is the Norse well beneath Yggdrasil where the Norns sit; the Cauldron of Dagda is a different Tuatha De treasure; the Spring of Aengus is not a named source.  (Legend.)

question: Around the Well of Segais grew a ring of magical trees, and their nuts fell into the water and drifted downstream. These are the same trees whose nuts, dropping into a Munster pool, feed the Salmon of Knowledge in the Fionn mac Cumhaill story. What kind of trees are they?
context: The Well of Segais is ringed by hazel trees whose nuts carry wisdom -- they drop into the water, the salmon eat them, and any human who eats such a salmon gains the salmon's knowledge (Fionn burns his thumb on such a salmon and sucks it, gaining the gift). Oak, rowan, and yew are all sacred Irish trees but do not carry the wisdom-nut motif.  (Legend.)

question: Boann was forbidden to approach the Well of Segais at all. She went anyway. What did she do at the well as an act of open defiance?
answer: walked three times around it counter-sunwise
choices: walked three times around it counter-sunwise
spoke a curse into the water
cut down one of the hazel trees
washed her hair in the source
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: Boann walked three times around the Well of Segais tuathal -- against the sun, counter-clockwise, which in Irish tradition is the direction of ill omen and of ritual challenge. Sun-wise (deiseal) is the direction of blessing; counter-sunwise is the direction of defiance and destruction.  (Legend.)

question: The waters of Segais answered Boann's defiance immediately. They burst up out of the well and chased her down the plain of Meath, tearing her apart as they went. What THREE parts of her body did the flood strip away before drowning her?
answer: an arm, a leg, and an eye
choices: an arm, a leg, and an eye
her hair, her hands, and her tongue
her voice, her sight, and her memory
her cloak, her sword, and her name
context: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boann: the risen waters tore off Boann's arm, her leg, and her eye as they pursued her -- the classic Irish triple-blemish, the same body-perfection-broken that puts a king off the throne (Nuada's hand, Bres's boils). She drowned in the flood; the flood kept running and became the river.  (Legend.)

question: Boann's lover among the gods was the Dagda -- 'the good god,' chief of the Tuatha De -- and their child became one of the most beloved figures of Irish myth, later reckoned the god of love and youth, who owns Bru na Boinne. Who is that son?
context: Aengus (Aengus Og, 'Aengus the Young') is the son of the Dagda and Boann. The Dagda made the sun stand still for nine months so Boann's husband would not notice the pregnancy: Aengus is thus born in the space of a day. Lugh is a later Tuatha De hero (grandson of Balor); Ogma is the god of eloquence and inventor of ogham writing; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: The Boann story survives in a whole medieval Irish genre of place-name origin-tales -- one for every hill, lake, ford, and river of importance, gathering the story of how each landmark got its name. What is that genre called?
choices: the Annals of the Four Masters
context: The Dindshenchas ('lore of places') is the medieval Irish body of place-name origin-tales, preserved in prose and metrical (verse) forms in the Book of Leinster and other manuscripts. The Annals of the Four Masters is a much later (17th-century) chronicle of Irish history; the Fenian Cycle is the Fionn stories; the Cath Maige Tuired is one specific battle-tale, not a whole genre.  (Legend.)

question: In the early 8th century an English monk born Winfrid in Devon crossed the Rhine to preach to the pagan Franks and Hessians, sent with a commission from Pope Gregory II. The pope gave him a new Latin name, and by that name he became the great missionary bishop of the Germans and later archbishop of Mainz. What name did the pope give him?
context: Winfrid was renamed Boniface ('good deeds') by Gregory II in 719 and made a missionary bishop for Germania. Willibrord was his older colleague, the apostle of the Frisians; Columbanus was the Irish monk who evangelized Gaul and Italy a century earlier; Aidan founded Lindisfarne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Boniface.

question: In the year 723 in Hesse, Boniface walked up to a great sacred tree of the German pagans, took hold of an axe, and began to chop while a crowd of Hessians stood watching, expecting their thunder-god to strike him dead on the spot. What kind of tree was it?
context: The tree at Geismar near Fritzlar was an oak, the species most often held sacred in Germanic paganism (Roman writers had already identified Jupiter/Thor with the oak). The yew was sacred in Celtic tradition; the ash was Yggdrasil in Norse cosmology; the linden was the classic village gathering-tree of medieval Germany. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: According to Willibald's Vita Bonifatii, after Boniface had made only a few cuts a great blast of wind rose and the huge oak crashed to the ground, splitting cleanly into equal trunks. Into how many parts did the tree burst?
context: Willibald's account (chapter 6, c. 760) specifies four trunks of huge size and equal length lying on the ground. The crowd who had been cursing Boniface as an enemy of their gods now believed and blessed him when Donar sent no lightning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: From the wood of the fallen oak at Fritzlar, Boniface immediately built a small wooden chapel on the same spot, turning the old pagan cult-site into a Christian shrine. To which saint did he dedicate the new chapel?
context: Willibald says the oratory was dedicated to Saint Peter the apostle, tying the Hessian mission directly to Rome and to the pope who had sent Boniface. Michael and Martin were the two other patrons most common for German early-medieval churches; Paul was less commonly the sole dedicatee of missionary chapels. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donar%27s_Oak.  (Legend.)

question: On June 5 in the year 754, an elderly Boniface waited by the river Borne in Frisia for a group of new converts he was to confirm. An armed pagan band attacked him and about fifty companions instead. At what Frisian town was Boniface killed?
context: The martyrdom took place near Dokkum in what is now the northern Netherlands. Utrecht was the see of his colleague Willibrord; Nijmegen and Deventer were later Carolingian centers. The attackers, expecting treasure in the missionaries' chests, broke them open and found only manuscripts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Boniface.

question: Tradition says that when the pagan band struck at Dokkum, Boniface held a book up over his head to shield himself, and the killing sword-blow cut clean through it. A codex kept in the cathedral treasury at Fulda still bears the deep gashes and is venerated as that very book. What is this manuscript called?
context: The Ragyndrudis Codex is a late 7th or early 8th century collection of fourteen Latin exegetical and dogmatic texts (interestingly, not actually a gospel, though the 10th-century Utrecht vita of Boniface calls the shield-book 'a gospel'). Its original binding and pages bear cuts long identified with the martyrdom. The Codex Amiatinus was made at Bede's Wearmouth-Jarrow; the Book of Kells and Lindisfarne Gospels are Insular gospel books unrelated to Boniface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragyndrudis_Codex.  (Legend.)

question: In the Fenian tales of Ireland, Fionn mac Cumhaill leads the warrior-band called the Fianna and hunts across Ireland with a great pack of hounds. Two of his hounds are his favourites, named in every Fenian tale, and they can outrun any deer and understand what he says to them. What are the two hounds called?
context: Bran and Sceolang (Sceolan, Sgeolan) are Fionn's chief hunting hounds in the Fenian Cycle. Cerberus and Orthrus are the three-headed and two-headed guardian hounds of the Greek pillar (Hades and Geryon). Garmr is the hound at the gate of Hel and Fenrir the wolf who kills Odin in the Norse pillar. Argus is Odysseus's dog and Laelaps the Greek hound that always caught its prey.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn mac Cumhaill's two favourite hunting hounds, Bran and Sceolang, ride at his stirrup on every chase. In the Fenian tales the two hounds are not only clever animals; they are Fionn's own KIN, closer to him than any other pair of dogs on earth. What kinship do they bear to him?
context: Bran and Sceolang's mother, Uirne (also called Tuiren), was the sister of Fionn's own mother Muirne, which makes the hounds his first cousins. In a variant Uirne is Fionn's sister and the hounds are his nephew and niece, but the cousin-relation is the most common version. Fionn treats them accordingly.  (Legend.)

question: In the Irish tale The Birth of Bran, the mother of Fionn's two great hounds is a woman of Ireland who was carrying twins in her womb when she was struck with a druid's rod and TRANSFORMED into a hound. She gave birth to her pups in that changed shape. What was her name?
context: Uirne / Tuiren was married to Iollan of the Fianna. She was transformed while pregnant, hence her twin children were born as hounds. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of Longes mac nUislenn in the Ulster Cycle; Grainne elopes with Diarmuid from Fionn himself; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife, also in the Ulster Cycle.  (Legend.)

question: In The Birth of Bran, the woman who cursed Fionn's aunt with hound-shape while she was pregnant was not a witch or a warrior but a JEALOUS RIVAL: an earlier lover of the husband, come to punish the new wife who had replaced her. To what people did the jealous woman Uchtdealb belong?
context: Uchtdealb (also spelled Uct Dealv) was a woman of the Sidhe, the faery folk, and had been the lover of Iollan before he married Tuiren. The Sidhe in Irish tradition are what the Tuatha De Danann became after their defeat, retreating into the hollow hills. The Fomorians are the older sea-monsters defeated at Mag Tuired; the Milesians are the ancestors of the modern Irish; the Fir Bolg are one of the older invader-peoples.  (Legend.)

question: In The Birth of Bran, the jealous Uchtdealb of the Sidhe came to Fionn's aunt disguised as one of Fionn's own messengers. She lured her out of her husband's house alone into the woods, and struck her on the shoulder to change her shape. With what object did she strike the blow?
context: The hazel is the Irish tree of magic and wisdom (the hazels of Segais drop their nuts into the Salmon of Knowledge's pool); the druid's rod of transformation is characteristically hazel. A sword-stroke would have killed rather than transformed. The golden apple is a Greek pillar object (Atalanta, the Judgement of Paris). Yew is the tree of death in Irish tradition, not of shape-shifting.  (Legend.)

question: After the jealous Uchtdealb had struck Uirne with a hazel rod and turned her into a hound, Fionn eventually found out what had happened and forced the woman of the Sidhe to break the enchantment. The mother was made a woman again. But her two whelps, Bran and Sceolang, stayed hounds for the rest of their lives. Why could the spell on them not be undone?
answer: they had been conceived and born entirely under the enchantment
choices: they had been conceived and born entirely under the enchantment
they had drunk from a faery well after birth
they had been named by Fionn before their mother was freed
the Sidhe queen had bound them separately with a golden collar
context: Uirne was already pregnant when she was transformed; the whelps were shaped as hounds from their first breath, and the enchantment could not be lifted from a body that had never known any other. It is the rule of shape-magic in the Fenian tales. The other three are inventions of the choices.  (Legend.)

question: In one of the Fenian traditions, Sceolang met her death during a great hunt in the woods called the Chase of Thrush Glen. She and the pack were running down what strange quarry, half black and half white, when the chase ended in her death?
choices: a wild boar with iron bristles
a black horse with a red mane
context: The half-black, half-white deer of the Chase of Thrush Glen was an enchanted creature, and Sceolang died in the chase. Enchanted deer run through many Fenian tales, echoing the shape of Fionn's own wife Sadhbh. The boar of Ben Bulben kills Diarmuid, not the hounds; the black horse with red mane is a horse-of-the-Sidhe motif but not the quarry here; a giant hare belongs to Welsh Mabinogi tales, not to Bran and Sceolang.  (Legend.)

question: After the Tuatha De god Nuada lost his hand in battle and had to give up the throne (Irish law forbade a blemished king), the Tuatha De chose a new king known as the handsomest man of his generation. He was called 'the Beautiful.' What was his name?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 14-24: Bres (Bres mac Elathan) was elected king of the Tuatha De after Nuada stepped down, chosen partly for his looks and partly for his half-Fomorian blood, which was meant to make peace with the enemy. Ogma is the god of eloquence; Dian Cecht is the god of healing (who later replaces Nuada's hand with a silver one); Manannan is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: Bres was chosen partly for a political reason -- his blood was half Tuatha De and half something else, a peace-offering to Ireland's oldest enemies. His mother was the Tuatha De goddess Eriu; his father was a prince of which other people?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 14: Bres's father was Elatha, a Fomorian prince (the Fomorians were the sea-raiders and monstrous elder-race of Irish myth, ruled by Balor of the Evil Eye). The Milesians are the human ancestors of the modern Irish who arrive AFTER the Tuatha De; the Fir Bolg are an earlier people the Tuatha De defeated at the FIRST Battle of Moytura; 'the Danaans' is another name for the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: Under Bres's rule the Fomorians began to impose crushing tribute on the Tuatha De -- so heavy that the gods themselves had to work the fields like slaves. What menial job was the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De, forced to do?
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 25: under Bres's tyranny the Dagda ('the good god,' chief of the Tuatha De and owner of the club, the harp, and the cauldron of plenty) was forced to dig ditches and trenches around forts like a common labourer -- an especial humiliation for a god of abundance. Ogma was the one made to carry firewood; grinding grain and sweeping the hall are jobs from other tales.  (Legend.)

question: Old Irish kingship rested on one great obligation above all: a king must give food, drink, and gifts freely to any guest, and above all to poets. Bres broke this obligation. When a Tuatha De poet arrived at his hall for a night's stay, what was he served for dinner?
answer: three dry cakes and no meat or ale
choices: three dry cakes and no meat or ale
a single slice of raw pork
a bowl of watered barley porridge
nothing but a cup of cold water
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 39: Bres housed the poet in a small dark room and had him served three small dry cakes on a plate -- no meat, no butter, no ale. For an Irish king of the heroic age this was a shocking insult; hospitality (Irish oigidecht) was the king's first sacred duty.  (Legend.)

question: The insulted poet left Bres's hall the next morning, walked out onto the hillside, and did something with his voice that no bard in Ireland had ever done before. What did he compose?
answer: the first satire ever made in Ireland
choices: the first satire ever made in Ireland
the first battle-hymn ever sung in Ireland
the first curse ever cast in Ireland
the first lament ever wept in Ireland
context: Cath Maige Tuired sec 39 and the medieval Irish tradition on satire: Cairpre's poem against Bres is said to be the first satire (Irish aer) ever composed in Ireland. Satire in old Irish law was so feared that satirists had legal protection and named damages; the story of Bres is the mythic charter for that whole power.  (Legend.)

question: The instant the satire was spoken, something appeared on Bres's face that Irish law refused to accept in a king. It was the same category of unfitness that had put Nuada off the throne when he lost his hand. What broke out on Bres?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: at Cairpre's word red boils sprang up on Bres's face. Old Irish law required a king to be bodily perfect -- ainmech ('a blemish') of any kind was disqualifying, which is why Nuada had to step down for his lost hand. Bres was deposed on the spot: the first Irish king brought down by a poem.  (Legend.)

question: In the Irish legends, a young girl of the fifth century keeps giving her father's food and cloaks and cattle to the poor until he lets her take the veil; she grows up to found a great monastery and becomes one of the three patron saints of the whole island. What is her name?
context: Brigid (Old Irish Brigit), traditional dates c. 451 to 524/525 CE, daughter of the Leinster chieftain Dubthach and (in most Lives) a Christian slave-woman Broicsech baptized by Patrick. Hilda ruled the Northumbrian abbey of Whitby in the seventh century; Clare founded the Poor Clares at Assisi in the thirteenth; Genevieve is the patroness of Paris. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: The Irish word Cill Dara means 'church of the oak'; it is the town from which Saint Brigid takes her byname, and where she founded her great monastery around 480 CE. What is the modern English form of the town's name?
context: All four are real Irish towns whose names begin with Cill, meaning 'church'. Kildare (Cill Dara) is the church of the oak; Killarney (Cill Airne) the church of the sloes; Kilkenny (Cill Chainnigh) the church of Cainneach; Kilbeggan (Cill Bheagain) the church of Beagan. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Brigid takes her name from an older Irish figure of the same name, a pre-Christian goddess of poetry and healing and smithcraft and above all of fire; the goddess was said to be the daughter of a great chieftain-god of the Tuatha De Danann. Who was that father-god?
context: In Irish myth the goddess Brigit is a daughter of the Dagda ('the good god'), chief of the Tuatha De Danann. Lugh Lamhfhada is the spear-wielding sun-hero; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god; Nuada Silver-Arm is the earlier king of the Tuatha. The saint inherits her fire-associations, her name, and her feast-day from this goddess. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Brigid's feast is 1 February. On the older Gaelic calendar the same day was already a great festival, the traditional first day of spring and the day the lambing began. What was that older festival called?
context: The four great fire-festivals of the Gaelic year are Imbolc (1 February, ewes coming into milk), Beltane (1 May, cattle driven between fires), Lughnasadh (1 August, the first harvest), and Samhain (1 November, the year's end when the dead walk). Brigid's feast overlays Imbolc exactly. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: The famous kitchen miracle of the girl Brigid: her mother came home in a rage after Brigid had given the whole family food-crock away to a beggar that morning, but when the crock was opened it was found full again, fuller than before. What food had Brigid given away, in the version told across Ireland for centuries?
context: The specific food is butter, and the miracle makes Brigid the patron of dairy work, milkmaids, and the safe keeping of the family cow. All four are staples of an early-medieval Irish household kitchen. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.  (Legend.)

question: The cloak legend is set in the flat green plains of one of Ireland's five ancient provinces, the one whose king refused Brigid the ground for her convent until her miraculously stretching cloak covered acres of his land. In which of the ancient Irish provinces did the story take place, the province in which Kildare still stands today?
context: Kildare lies in Leinster, the province of the east, whose king in the legend grants Brigid the ground her stretched cloak covers. Munster is the south, Ulster the north, and Connacht the west; the fifth province Meath contained the High King's seat at Tara. Source: Brigidine Sisters, 'Legend of St Brigid's Cloak'; Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Gerald of Wales, visiting Ireland in the twelfth century, described a perpetual fire kept alight day and night at Kildare in Brigid's honour, with the nuns of the community taking turns to tend it, one each night in a fixed rota. How many nuns were in the rota?
context: Gerald of Wales wrote in Topographia Hibernica (c. 1188) that nineteen nuns took turns keeping the fire, one per night; on the twentieth night, the tradition ran, Brigid herself came and tended it, and the flame never went out. He said the fire had been burning since Brigid's own lifetime. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.  (Legend.)

question: Kildare was rare in all of Christendom: it was a double monastery with separate communities of nuns and monks under one head, Brigid herself, ruling alongside a hermit she had invited to be its first bishop. What was that first bishop's name?
context: Conleth (Conlaed) was a metal-worker and hermit whom Brigid invited to Kildare as its first bishop; the two are traditionally buried together in the old cathedral. Ciaran founded Clonmacnoise; Kevin founded Glendalough; Finnian founded Clonard. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: Brigid is counted one of the three patron saints of Ireland. Two other Irish saints of the fifth and sixth centuries share that honour with her. Which pair?
context: The three national patrons of Ireland are Patrick (fifth-century British-born missionary bishop who converted the island), Brigid (Kildare, fifth to sixth century), and Columba, also called Colum Cille (sixth-century abbot who left Derry and founded Iona in 563). Kevin (Glendalough), Ciaran (Clonmacnoise), and Malachy (twelfth-century reformer) are all major Irish saints but not among the three national patrons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brigid of Kildare'.

question: One of the greatest goddesses of the Tuatha De Danann is a daughter of the Dagda. She is the patron of THREE crafts at once -- poetry, healing, and the making of weapons at the forge -- so the Irish call her by three matching titles: 'of the Poets', 'of the Healers', 'of the Smiths'. What is her name?
context: Brigid is uniquely the goddess who owns all three crafts, and her name is thought to mean 'the Exalted One'. Danu is the mother-figure of the Tuatha De; Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne; the Morrigan is the war-and-crow goddess. Wikipedia: Brigid.  (Legend.)

question: Brigid's sacred site in Ireland is a place in Leinster whose old Irish name -- Cill Dara -- means 'church of the oak'. The town still bears that name today, in an anglicised form. What is the town called?
context: Cill Dara = Kildare, county town of County Kildare in Leinster. Killarney is in Kerry (a lake town); Kilkenny is a different Leinster town; Kilcullen is a village in Kildare county but not Brigid's shrine. Wikipedia: Kildare; Brigid of Kildare.

question: The 9th-century glossary Sanas Cormaic ('Cormac's Glossary') calls Brigid 'the goddess whom poets adored' -- and explains that she is really THREE sisters, all bearing the same name, one for each of her crafts. In Irish mythology this pattern of one-goddess-as-three appears again in which other figure?
context: The Morrigan is likewise a triple-goddess (Morrigan, Macha, and Badb, or in other lists Morrigan, Nemain, and Badb) -- a war-goddess made of three sisters. Danu, Boann, and Aine are single goddesses. Wikipedia: The Morrigan; Sanas Cormaic.  (Legend.)

question: Brigid's festival is the great Irish quarter-day at the beginning of spring, when the ewes first begin to give milk. It falls on the first of February. What is the festival called?
context: Imbolc (February 1) is the first of the four great Irish quarter-days. Samhain (November 1), Beltane (May 1), and Lughnasa (August 1) are the other three. Wikipedia: Imbolc.  (Legend.)

question: At Brigid's shrine in Cill Dara a fire was kept burning day and night -- a perpetual flame that never went out. It was tended in strict rotation by a fixed number of women, each keeping the flame for one night. How many women were on the rotation?
context: The nineteen priestesses (and later nuns) each guarded the flame for one night; on the twentieth night Brigid herself was said to tend it. Gerald of Wales records the practice in the late 12th century. Wikipedia: Brigid of Kildare.  (Legend.)

question: On the eve of Imbolc (February 1) Irish families still weave a small four-armed shape from fresh-cut rushes, with a woven square at the centre, and hang it above the front door of the house for protection through the coming year. What is this woven rush object called?
context: The Brigid's cross is one of the most recognisable Irish folk-objects: rushes cut fresh on February 1, woven in a few minutes, hung above the threshold. Wikipedia: Brigid's cross.  (Legend.)

question: The 9th-century Old Irish life of St. Brigid, Bethu Brigte, tells of a startling moment at her consecration. When Mel reads over her, he uses the wrong ordinal by accident and refuses to withdraw it, saying the honour has come from God. Into what office did the Bethu Brigte say he had ordained her -- an office no woman was supposed to hold?
choices: an abbot of a men's house
context: Bethu Brigte, ch. 19: Mel reads the ordinal for a bishop over Brigid and refuses to withdraw it, saying the honour has come from God. Many scholars read the episode as the priestess-authority of the goddess absorbed into the saint. Wikipedia: Bethu Brigte; Brigid of Kildare.  (Legend.)

question: The Lebor Gabala Erenn ('Book of Invasions') credits the goddess Brigid with a set of sacred animals -- specifically two named oxen, a 'king of boars' named Torc Triath, and a 'king of wethers' named Cirb. The story says all of these animals share ONE strange ability. What can they do?
answer: cry out whenever plundering happens in Ireland
choices: cry out whenever plundering happens in Ireland
speak human speech on Samhain night
context: The Lebor Gabala reports that Brigid's beasts raise a cry across Ireland the moment any theft or raid is done -- a guardianship shared across her whole animal household. Wikipedia: Brigid.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse Volsung cycle, the young hero Sigurd -- fresh from killing the dragon Fafnir and the smith Regin -- rides his horse Grani along a road the birds pointed him to, up a great mountain. From miles off he sees the mountain's crown ringed with a blaze so tall that no bird flies through it. What name does the Volsunga Saga give to this mountain?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 21 and the prose introduction to the Poetic Edda's Sigrdrifumal: the mountain is Hindarfjall, meaning 'Hind Mountain.' Gnitaheid is the heath where Sigurd killed Fafnir the dragon in the previous story. Bifrost is the rainbow-bridge between Midgard and Asgard. Yggdrasil is the world-tree. Hindarfjall is the specific peak of this wake-scene.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd rides straight at the wall of flame ringing the mountaintop. Only one horse in all the north will leap through fire without flinching -- the horse Odin himself chose for Sigurd out of a whole herd of mountain stallions. What is the name of Sigurd's horse, the only one that carries him through the fire?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 13-21: Grani is Sigurd's horse, chosen for him by Odin in disguise as an old man, and descended from Odin's own eight-legged steed Sleipnir. Sleipnir belongs to Odin, not Sigurd. Gullfaxi is the golden-maned horse of the giant Hrungnir, later given to Thor's son Magni. Hofvarpnir is the goddess Gna's horse. Grani leaps through Hindarfjall's fire because Sleipnir's blood is in him.  (Legend.)

question: Grani leaps through the flames of Hindarfjall and Sigurd comes down on the other side unharmed. Inside the ring of fire he finds a hall, and inside the hall lies a figure in full war-armour, helm on the head, sword at the side. Sigurd bends to unlace the helm expecting to see a slain warrior's face. What does Sigurd find under the helm?
choices: a stone carving with no face
a wolf curled in a heap
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21 and Sigrdrifumal prose 2-5: under the helm is a sleeping woman. The saga lingers on Sigurd's mistake -- he came expecting a dead warrior and found a living Valkyrie. There is no carving, no dwarf-corpse, and no wolf in the hall. The whole point of the scene is the shock of unlacing armour and finding a woman's face.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd finds the sleeping woman on Hindarfjall and cannot wake her by touch or by voice. Only when he takes his sword Gram and slits open the mail-coat 'as though cutting cloth,' the saga says, does she open her eyes. She sits up and speaks the first words: 'Who has broken the byrnie and waked me from long sleep?' What is her name?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21; Sigrdrifumal prose 5. She names herself Brynhild. Freyja is the Vanir goddess of love and battle who owns half of Valhalla's slain. Sigrun and Skuld are two other named Valkyries from the Norse corpus. Brynhild is the specific Valkyrie of this ladder.  (Legend.)

question: The Valkyrie Brynhild tells Sigurd how she came to be sleeping on Hindarfjall. Odin had already promised victory in her last battle to an older king named Hjalmgunnar. Brynhild disobeyed and awarded the day to a younger king instead. What is the name of the young king Brynhild wrongly gave victory to?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 21; Sigrdrifumal prose 4: the young king is Agnar. Hrothgar is the Danish king in Beowulf. Sigmund is Sigurd's own father, a previous Volsung. Helgi is Sigurd's half-brother, hero of the Helgi lays. Agnar is the specific name in the Brynhild-punishment story.  (Legend.)

question: The Hindarfjall wake-scene of Sigurd and Brynhild became the climax of one of the most famous operas of the 19th century, staged in 1876 as the third part of a four-opera cycle. In the opera the hero is renamed Siegfried and the Valkyrie is renamed Brunnhilde. Who composed the opera whose Act III is Sigurd's climb through the fire to Brynhild?
context: The opera is Siegfried (1876), the third of Wagner's four-opera Ring cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen. Verdi wrote Italian operas (Aida, La Traviata). Bizet wrote Carmen. Mussorgsky wrote Boris Godunov. Wagner's ring-cycle is the reason so many modern audiences meet Brynhild first as Brunnhilde on a stage-mountain with a stage-fire.

question: The old poem Sigrdrifumal, which tells the Hindarfjall wake-scene in the Poetic Edda, breaks off in mid-sentence in the Codex Regius manuscript. What has happened to the manuscript at this point, forcing scholars to fill in the rest of Sigurd's story from the prose Volsunga Saga?
answer: a whole gathering of pages is missing
choices: a whole gathering of pages is missing
a monk erased the vellum to reuse it
the ink faded in a house-fire
a page was cut out and sent abroad
context: The Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda has a physical gap at this point -- an entire gathering (a folded set of vellum sheets) is lost. Editors call it 'the great lacuna.' There was no erasure and no fire; the leaves simply went missing before the codex was rebound. Because of the lacuna, everything between Sigurd leaving Hindarfjall and arriving at the Gjukungs' court has to be reconstructed from the later prose Volsunga Saga.

question: In the Norse Volsung cycle Sigurd is married to Gudrun; her brother Gunnar is married to Brynhild, who still believes it was Gunnar who crossed the ring of fire to wake her. One morning the two queens go to a river to wash their hair, and there they quarrel. What do the queens quarrel about?
answer: whose husband is the greater warrior
choices: whose husband is the greater warrior
which brother should sit on the high seat
who owns the golden hoard of Fafnir
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 30: the argument at the river is a rivalry over the husbands' honour -- whose man is greater. The bathing-place quarrel is a folktale echo but not this scene's substance. The high-seat quarrel comes at Atli's court later. Fafnir's hoard is owned by Gjuki's sons jointly and is not what they dispute. It is the boast about husbands that starts the whole doom.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild boasts that her husband Gunnar is the greatest of men because he alone crossed the ring of fire around her mountain. Gudrun laughs and answers that Gunnar never crossed the fire -- Sigurd crossed it wearing Gunnar's face -- and to prove it she holds up a single object she says Sigurd took from Brynhild that first night on the mountain. What object does Gudrun hold up as proof?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 30: Gudrun holds up the ring Andvaranaut, which Sigurd had taken from Brynhild's finger during the shape-swap night and given to Gudrun. The lock of hair belongs to a different Norse story (Sif's hair, cut by Loki). A broken helm and a torn shift are not in this scene. The ring is the object that makes the quarrel deadly, because Brynhild recognises it at once.  (Legend.)

question: After Gudrun's revelation at the river, Brynhild goes home to her hall, lies down on her bed, and does one specific thing that shocks the whole household for three whole days. What does Brynhild do for three days after learning she was tricked by Sigurd?
choices: burns her wedding-gifts on the hearth
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 30-31: Brynhild lies down and will not speak or eat for three days. In the saga her silence is more terrifying than shouting -- everyone in the hall knows something dreadful is coming. She does not weep openly, does not sharpen a blade, and does not burn her goods. The muteness is the specific detail the saga returns to.  (Legend.)

question: When Gunnar finally comes to Brynhild's bedside and asks what is wrong, she tells him plainly what she demands. What does Brynhild demand of Gunnar for Sigurd's deception?
choices: that Sigurd be banished across the sea
that Sigurd swear a new oath in her presence
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 31: Brynhild tells Gunnar: 'Sigurd betrayed both of us. I want him dead, or I will die myself. Choose.' She does not ask for exile, for the gold, or for a fresh oath -- only for his death. The rest of the cycle turns on Gunnar's answer.  (Legend.)

question: Brynhild has demanded Sigurd's death, but Gunnar and his brother Hogni cannot lift a hand against him. Years earlier at Gjuki's hall the three men had sworn an oath that now binds Gunnar and Hogni from raising a weapon against Sigurd. What oath had Gunnar, Hogni, and Sigurd sworn to each other?
choices: a joint quest for Andvari's gold
loyalty to King Gjuki their father
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 26-32: Sigurd, Gunnar, and Hogni had mingled blood from their arms in the earth and sworn foster-brotherhood -- Old Norse fostbraedralag. The marriage to Gudrun was a separate transaction. The quest for Andvari's gold was over long before Sigurd came to Gjuki's court. Loyalty to King Gjuki did not bar personal murder. The oath specifically forbade one of them to raise a hand against another, and that is why Gunnar must find someone else.  (Legend.)

question: Guttorm is a boy, not a killer, and would not lift a sword against the greatest hero in the north on his own. To make him wild enough for the deed, his older brothers prepare a stew of two animals' flesh mixed with beer and feed it to him. What two kinds of flesh are cooked into the spell-stew fed to Guttorm?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 32: the stew is wolf-flesh mixed with serpent-flesh, boiled with beer. Raven and goat, hare and salmon, and bear and stag are all Norse animals but not this recipe. The saga calls the concoction geri-flesh -- one of the very few named magical foods in Norse myth, and the sole reason Guttorm is fierce enough that night to walk into the bedroom of Sigurd Fafnir-slayer with a drawn blade.  (Legend.)

question: That night Guttorm walks into Sigurd's bedroom. Gudrun is sleeping beside her husband. Guttorm drives a sword through Sigurd's chest in one blow. But Sigurd does not die at once -- he wakes to the death-blow, reaches beside the bed, seizes his own sword, and hurls it after the fleeing killer. What is the name of the sword Sigurd throws after Guttorm?
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 32: the sword is Gram, the blade Regin re-forged from Sigmund's shards and Sigurd used to kill Fafnir. Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Hervarar saga. Hrunting is the sword Unferth lends Beowulf. Naegling is the sword that breaks in Beowulf's dragon-fight. Gram is Sigurd's sword through the whole cycle -- and now his dying weapon.  (Legend.)

question: The thrown sword Gram catches the fleeing Guttorm from behind and cleaves him clean in two. The Volsunga Saga preserves the exact place on Guttorm's body where Gram struck him. Where did Gram strike Guttorm?
choices: at the base of the skull
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 32: Gram catches Guttorm between the shoulders and cuts him clean in two -- one half falling forward into the hall, one half falling backward into the bedroom where Sigurd lies dying. It is one of the most-remembered images in the whole saga.  (Legend.)

question: The evening Sigurd dies, Brynhild does not weep. She stands in the hall, laughs once aloud, dresses herself in her finest clothes, takes up a sword, and stabs herself through the chest. Before she dies she asks a very specific favour of her people -- what does Brynhild ask them to do with her body?
answer: to burn her on Sigurd's funeral pyre
choices: to burn her on Sigurd's funeral pyre
to bury her at the foot of Hindarfjall
to lay her in Freyja's temple at Uppsala
to place her body back inside the ring of fire
context: Volsunga Saga ch. 33 and Sigurdarkvida hin skamma stanzas 49-71: Brynhild asks to be burned on the same pyre with Sigurd, and asks that the sword Gram be laid unsheathed between their bodies -- as it had lain between them on the shape-swap night when Sigurd first slept beside her wearing Gunnar's face. She is not buried at Hindarfjall, not sent to Uppsala, and not returned to the ring of fire. The pyre-with-sword-between-them is the specific request the saga preserves.  (Legend.)

question: The death of Sigurd was retold across medieval Germanic literature and, in the 19th century, ended one of the most ambitious operas ever composed -- the fourth and final part of a four-opera cycle staged in 1876. What is the name of the opera in which Wagner tells this same murder-of-Siegfried scene?
context: Gotterdammerung ('Twilight of the Gods'), 1876, is the fourth opera in Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen. Siegfried is the third opera, which ends with the wake-scene on Hindarfjall. Die Walkure is the second, and Das Rheingold is the first. All four together make up the Ring cycle -- and the murder Guttorm strikes here is the climax of Gotterdammerung.

question: In the Arthurian stories King Arthur has a favourite city that serves as the seat of his court, the hall where his knights feast, and the place every completed quest is dedicated to. What is the name of Arthur's capital city?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, passim; Wikipedia: Camelot. Tintagel is where Arthur was conceived by Uther Pendragon. Avalon is the enchanted island where the wounded Arthur is carried at the end. Glastonbury is a real Somerset abbey where medieval monks later claimed to have found Arthur's tomb.  (Legend.)

question: The Norman poet Wace, writing his Roman de Brut around 1155, gives a very practical story-reason for the shape of Arthur's famous table: Uther Pendragon's court had suffered years of one specific ugly problem at every feast, and Arthur meant to end it. What problem did Wace say the Round Table was designed to prevent?
answer: barons quarrelling over who sat highest
choices: barons quarrelling over who sat highest
assassins hiding behind the hall pillars
spies overhearing counsel through open doors
poison being slipped along the high table
context: Wace, Roman de Brut (c.1155): 'Arthur created the Round Table to prevent quarrels among his barons, none of whom would accept a lower place than the others.' A round table has no head and no foot, so every seat is equal in dignity. Assassins, spies, and poisoners are all real medieval court-worries, but the Round Table specifically solves the seating-rank problem.  (Legend.)

question: Every year at Camelot Arthur holds a great feast on one particular high Christian holiday. At this feast the whole fellowship of the Round Table gathers, and Arthur famously refuses to sit down to eat until he has heard of some wonder or adventure. Which feast day is the great yearly gathering of the Round Table at Camelot?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur (throughout). Pentecost (Whitsunday, fifty days after Easter) is Arthur's great gathering day; it is at Pentecost that Galahad arrives and takes the Siege Perilous, and at Pentecost the Grail quest begins. Christmas is the feast of the Green Knight scene at Camelot in a different poem. Easter and All Saints' Day are important feasts but not Arthur's court-day.  (Legend.)

question: When Arthur marries Guinevere in Book III of Malory, her father sends the Round Table with her as her dowry -- it had been in his keeping since the days of Uther Pendragon. Which king gives the Round Table to Arthur as Guinevere's dowry?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1. Leodegrance is Guinevere's father and the king of Cameliard; he had the Table from Uther Pendragon. Pellinore is the king who broke Arthur's first sword. Uriens is Morgan le Fay's husband. Bagdemagus is the king of Gorre in Chretien's Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: Malory gives an exact seating capacity for the Round Table -- and says every seat around it has the name of the knight worthy to sit there written in gold letters. How many knights, in Malory's telling, does the Round Table seat?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1: Leodegrance sends the Table 'and a hundred knights' with it -- Arthur later fills the remaining seats. Twelve is the round number of Charlemagne's Twelve Peers of France, not Arthur's fellowship. Twenty-four fits the smaller Arthurian jousting-lists, not the Table itself. Three hundred is the count of Roman senators.  (Legend.)

question: One seat around the Round Table is always kept empty -- not out of respect for an absent knight, but because any knight who sits in it who is not perfectly worthy will die on the spot. Which seat at the Table carries this deadly reputation?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.4; Vulgate Cycle 'Queste del Saint Graal' (c.1220). 'Siege' comes from Old French 'sege' meaning seat or throne; 'perilous' is the modern English word. The Siege of Judas is the empty place at the Last Supper that the Vulgate Queste explicitly says the Siege Perilous mirrors. The Perilous Bed is Chretien's 'lit merveilleux' from Perceval, a magical bed that hurls spears at whoever lies on it. Uther Pendragon had his own high seat, but it is not the deadly one.  (Legend.)

question: In all the many years of the Round Table only ONE knight in the whole story is able to sit in the perilous seat and live. He arrives at Camelot on Pentecost, the letters of his own name appear on the empty seat, and he takes it. Who is the only knight to sit in the Siege Perilous?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.4. Galahad, the son of Lancelot, is the pure knight who alone can occupy the seat and later achieves the Grail. Percival is one of the three Grail companions but has his own seat. Lancelot -- Galahad's father -- is too flawed by his love for Guinevere to sit there. Gawain is the great courtier but not the pure knight.  (Legend.)

question: The name 'Camelot' does not appear in any of the earliest Arthurian material -- not in Geoffrey of Monmouth, not in Wace. It is coined by one specific twelfth-century French poet, in a poem about Lancelot rescuing Guinevere from the kingdom of Gorre. Who first named Camelot?
context: Wikipedia: Camelot; Wikipedia: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart. Chretien de Troyes coins 'Camelot' in his 1170s poem 'Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart'. Wace (Roman de Brut, c.1155) invented the Round Table motif but never used the name Camelot. Geoffrey of Monmouth (Historia Regum Britanniae, c.1136) placed Arthur's court at Caerleon, not Camelot. Wolfram von Eschenbach wrote Parzival (c.1210), long after Chretien.

question: The Great Hall of Winchester Castle in England has, hanging on its wall, a real physical Round Table of oak -- eighteen feet across, weighing over a ton. The table itself was built in the 1200s but was left bare wood for centuries. Later an English king ordered it painted with Arthur and his knights, reportedly to impress the visiting emperor Charles V. Which king ordered the paintwork now on the Winchester Round Table?
context: Wikipedia: Round Table. The oak table itself was built c.1250-1280 in the reign of Edward I but was left plain. It was Henry VIII who ordered the surviving paintwork -- Arthur enthroned above a Tudor-rose centre, the names of the knights around the rim -- to impress Charles V during his 1522 state visit. Richard the Lionheart lived a century before the table was built; Alfred the Great five centuries before.

question: In 1542 the antiquary John Leland rode through the west country and reported that the local people around one particular hill still called it the site of the real Camelot. Modern archaeologists dug there from 1966 to 1970 under Leslie Alcock and found a major refortification from Arthur's era, though no proof it was his. Which hill did Leland record as the local Camelot?
context: Wikipedia: Camelot. John Leland recorded the Cadbury tradition in 1542; Leslie Alcock's 1966-1970 excavations at the hillfort found evidence of major refortification 'by a Brittonic ruler and his war band from c. 470' -- exactly the era of the historical Arthur, if there was one. Cadbury Castle is in Somerset. Glastonbury Tor is a nearby Somerset religious hill. Maiden Castle is a huge Iron Age hillfort in Dorset. Silbury Hill is a neolithic mound in Wiltshire.

question: When the fellowship of the Round Table finally breaks apart in the last books of Malory, the whole Arthurian order goes with it. The specific quarrel that shatters the Table starts with an accusation against Lancelot -- that he has been sleeping with Arthur's queen -- and it splits the knights into two warring parties. Which knight leads the party demanding Lancelot be punished?
context: Malory, Books XX-XXI. Gawain leads the party demanding Lancelot's punishment after Lancelot kills Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris in the rescue of Guinevere from the stake. Sir Bors is Lancelot's own kinsman and stays loyal to him. Percival has gone on the Grail quest. Kay has faded by the end of the book. The Gawain-Lancelot feud is what ends the Round Table.  (Legend.)

question: In the Ulster Cycle the chief druid at the royal fort of Emain Macha runs a school for young pupils, teaching them to divine what will come to pass. He is King Conchobar mac Nessa's adviser and, in one strand of the tradition, Conchobar's own father by the warrior-woman Nessa. What is this chief druid's name?
context: Cathbad is the chief druid at Emain Macha and stands beside Conchobar throughout the Ulster tales. Amergin was the great druid of the Milesian invasion who chanted the land into their possession; Mug Ruith is the huge blind wheel-riding druid of Munster; Fintan mac Bochra is the salmon-shaped survivor of the Flood in Irish tradition. All are druids, but Cathbad is the Ulster chief.  (Legend.)

question: The chief druid at Emain Macha teaches his pupils outside the fort one morning, reading the fitness of the day. He tells them that if any warrior takes up arms for the very first time on this day, that warrior will win FAME everlasting through Ireland. But there is a price attached to the day of arms. What is the price?
answer: he will live only a short life
choices: he will live only a short life
he will lose the use of one eye in his first battle
he will father no son to carry his name
he will never sleep under a roof again
context: Cathbad's day-of-arms prophecy is the Irish equivalent of Achilles's choice: fame or long life, not both. Losing an eye is Odin's price for wisdom in the Norse pillar; the son-less price echoes Cuchulainn's later grief over Connla; sleeping under no roof is a geis (taboo) on other heroes, not the day-of-arms condition.  (Legend.)

question: When the chief druid Cathbad discovered that Conchobar had actually armed the boy Setanta that morning, he came before the king in anger and rebuked him for it. The boy answered his uncle's druid with a single line that sealed his character for the rest of the Tain. What did he say?
answer: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
choices: that a short life with lasting fame is better than a long life without it
that no druid's word could bind a warrior of Ulster
that his mother had already promised the fate to him
that only the sword would tell what the day would bring
context: The boy's answer is the Ulster Cycle's version of the Achilles-choice speech from the Iliad and it seals his character for the rest of the Tain. Denying druid-authority is Ferghus's later stance, not the boy's here. His mother Deichtine is not part of this scene. The 'sword will tell' line is not attested.  (Legend.)

question: The chief druid Cathbad appears at ANOTHER birth in the Ulster Cycle -- the newborn daughter of Feidlimid, who would grow into the fairest woman in Ireland. Cathbad's prophecy over the infant terrified the whole court of Ulster, who demanded she be killed at birth. Whose birth was this?
context: The tale is Longes mac nUislenn, 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu'. Cathbad prophesied that Deirdre would bring blood, ruin, and exile on the men of Ulster. Medb is the Connacht queen who raises the Tain against Ulster; Macha (of the twins) is the goddess-figure who curses the Ulstermen with their debility; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife, and no such prophecy is attached to her birth.  (Legend.)

question: Cathbad prophesied at Deirdre's birth that she would bring ruin on the men of Ulster. The warriors of Ulster demanded the infant be killed at once. King Conchobar refused. What did Conchobar do with the infant Deirdre instead?
answer: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
choices: had her raised in isolation so he himself could marry her when she was grown
gave her in fosterage to a smith of the border country
sent her to be reared by the druids of Emain Macha
cast her adrift in a leather bag on the western sea
context: Conchobar's plan was to keep Deirdre hidden away with tutors and never let her see any young man until she was of age for him. She saw Naoise anyway, one of the sons of Uisliu, and eloped with him -- which set off the tragedy Cathbad had foretold. The smith-fosterage recalls the Setanta / Culann story; druid-fosterage is Finn Emna's youth in a different tale; the leather bag on the sea is the birth-exposure of Taliesin in the Welsh tradition.  (Legend.)

question: The men of Ulster's greatest warrior went into exile at the court of Queen Medb of Connacht after Conchobar treacherously killed the sons of Uisliu -- the very ruin Cathbad had foretold over the newborn Deirdre. This is why he then leads the Connacht army against his own former Ulster people in the great cattle-raid of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Which warrior was he?
context: Fergus mac Roich had guaranteed safe conduct to the sons of Uisliu, and Conchobar's treachery in killing them dishonoured Fergus so utterly that he left Ulster forever. In the Tain he is the great Ulster exile in Medb's army. Conall Cernach and Loegaire Buadach stayed with Ulster and fought for Conchobar. Sualtam is Cu Chulainn's mortal father, not an exile.  (Legend.)

question: At the newborn Deirdre's cradle, Cathbad laid a prophecy over her -- three things she would bring on the men of Ulster because of her beauty. The warriors on hearing it drew their swords and demanded the child be killed at once. Which three things did Cathbad name?
context: The prophecy of Longes mac nUislenn -- 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu' -- is Cathbad's most famous cradle-word. Blood: the killing of the sons of Uisliu. Ruin: the burning of the royal hall at Emain Macha in the retaliations that followed. Exile: Fergus mac Roich and his followers going over to Connacht, which set up the whole Tain Bo Cuailnge. The other three options are invented distractors; blood, ruin, and exile are the three named in the tale.  (Legend.)

question: In 1347 in Siena, a wool-dyer named Jacopo Benincasa and his wife Lapa had a baby daughter, Caterina -- Catherine. Her twin sister died in infancy. Catherine and her twin were near the tail end of how many children born to the couple?
context: Catherine was the 24th of 25 children of the wool-dyer Jacopo Benincasa. Her twin sister died shortly after birth. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: At about six years old, walking home with her brother, Catherine of Siena looked up at the sky above her city's great Dominican basilica and froze in the street. Her brother had to shake her to make her move. According to her later account, what had she seen in the sky?
answer: Christ dressed as a pope, blessing her
choices: Christ dressed as a pope, blessing her
A giant silver key crossed with a sword
A ladder of angels reaching to the piazza
A ring of white fire around the bell tower
context: The child Catherine reported seeing Christ in papal vestments seated above the Basilica of San Domenico, blessing her. She ran home changed. Source: Dominican Sisters (dominicansisters.co.uk); Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Catherine had privately vowed her life to God as a small girl. When her family later tried to force her to marry the widower of her older sister, she went into her room and did something drastic to make the match impossible. What did the teenage Catherine do to refuse the marriage?
answer: She cut off her long hair
choices: She cut off her long hair
She burned her dowry chest on the hearth
She smashed her wedding cup at the door
She locked herself in the cellar for a week
context: Catherine cut off her hair to make herself an unfit bride. Her family finally relented and let her take a Dominican habit. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: In June 1376 Catherine of Siena undertook her boldest journey. She traveled to a walled city where seven popes in a row had lived for nearly seventy years under the shadow of the French crown, and she confronted Pope Gregory XI face to face, urging him to move his court back to Rome. In what city did she find him?
context: The Avignon Papacy (1309-1377) had kept seven popes on the Rhone. Catherine's June 1376 visit is credited with pushing Gregory XI to leave; he re-entered Rome on 17 January 1377. Source: Wikipedia, Catherine of Siena.

question: A young Roman noblewoman of the third century, born into an old plebeian house, is married against her wish to a pagan husband; she converts him on their wedding night and is later put to a slow martyrdom in her own home, which becomes one of the great house-churches of the city. Which martyr is she?
context: Cecilia takes her name from the plebeian Caecilii, one of the great Roman families; her feast is already in the Depositio Martyrum of 354 CE. Agnes was another young Roman martyr (feast 21 January); Lucy was martyred at Syracuse in Sicily; Perpetua was martyred at Carthage in 203 with her slave Felicity. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.

question: On the wedding night Cecilia tells her new pagan husband that an angel guards her virginity and that he too will see the angel if he is baptised. He agrees, is baptised by the pope on the Via Appia, sees the angel, and is martyred before her. What was the husband's name?
context: Valerian is baptised by Pope Urban at the third milestone on the Via Appia and, seeing the angel on his return, converts and is later martyred before Cecilia. Turcius Almachius is the prefect who later orders her death. Sebastian is another Roman soldier-martyr, shot with arrows a generation later. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: Cecilia's convert-husband brings home a brother, who is baptised at the same milestone on the Via Appia and martyred with him before Cecilia's own death. What was the brother's name?
context: Tiburtius is Valerian's brother; the two are venerated together as the martyred brothers of Cecilia's household. Cyprian was a third-century bishop of Carthage; Pancras a fourteen-year-old Roman martyr; Cornelius a mid-third-century pope. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: After the failed beheading Cecilia did not die at once; she lay teaching the Christians who gathered at her bedside and asked the pope to convert her house into a church, then died. How long is she said in the Passio to have lingered after the sword-strokes before she died?
context: Cecilia lives three days after the wounds, teaching from her bed, giving her property to the poor, and asking Pope Urban to make the house a church. The number three shapes the martyrdom: three strokes, three days. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Cecilia'.  (Legend.)

question: In Chaucer's late-fourteenth-century pilgrimage cycle, one of the pilgrims tells the story of Cecilia at length as her contribution to the tale-telling contest on the road to Canterbury. She is not named as a major character but is identified only by her office in the party. Which of the pilgrims tells Cecilia's story?
context: The Second Nun's Tale is Chaucer's Middle English hagiography of Cecilia, drawn largely from Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend; its prologue offers the fanciful etymology of the name Cecilia as caeli lilia, 'lily of heaven'. The Prioress tells the tale of the little clergeon; the Wife of Bath tells a knight-and-old-hag Arthurian story; the Parson closes the cycle with a long prose sermon. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Second Nun's Tale'.

question: In St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III came up behind the kneeling Frankish king during Mass, placed a crown on his head, and hailed him as Emperor of the Romans. Charlemagne (his biographer Einhard says) claimed he had not expected it and would not have entered the church that day if he had known. On what day of the year 800 did this happen?
context: Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor during Christmas Mass at St. Peter's on 25 December 800. Einhard reports Charlemagne's later claim of surprise. Source: Britannica; Wikipedia.

question: In 781 at Parma, in northern Italy, Charlemagne met an English deacon traveling home from Rome. The deacon was already famous across Europe as the finest scholar of the age, trained at his home city's great library. Charlemagne persuaded him to come south to run the palace school at Aachen. Which English center had trained this deacon?
context: Alcuin (c. 735-804) was schooled at York Minster's library, one of the finest in Latin Europe. Charlemagne met him at Parma in 781. Source: Britannica, Alcuin.

question: The stone chapel Charlemagne built at Aachen -- the oldest surviving stone church of its region north of the Alps -- was consciously modeled on an older basilica the emperor had admired on a visit to Italy. He even shipped columns and marble north from that Italian city for the new chapel. Which basilica did he take as his model?
choices: St. Paul's Outside the Walls at Rome
context: Ravenna's sixth-century octagonal Basilica of San Vitale, with its mosaics, provided the model. Charlemagne shipped marble columns north from Ravenna. Source: Wikipedia, Palatine Chapel, Aachen.

question: At Charlemagne's palace school the scholars gave each other classical or biblical nicknames. Alcuin was Albinus. Angilbert was Homer. Charlemagne himself took the name of a great biblical king. Which king?
context: Charlemagne = David in the court's poetry; Alcuin = Albinus / Flaccus; Angilbert = Homer. The comparison flattered Charlemagne as the ideal warrior-king united with his priest (Alcuin/Nathan). Source: Medievalists.net (Garrison, 'Nicknames at the Carolingian Court').

question: Einhard, who knew Charlemagne personally and wrote his life story, reports a strange domestic detail about the emperor: for all his conquests and his palace school full of scholars, Charlemagne never mastered one ordinary skill. At night he kept wax tablets and notebooks tucked in a particular place so he could practice whenever he woke -- but he never got good at it. What did Charlemagne keep the tablets and notebooks tucked under, and what was he trying to learn?
answer: Under his pillow, to practice forming letters
choices: Under his pillow, to practice forming letters
Under his saddle, to practice Latin verses
Under his throne, to practice Greek
Under his crown, to practice arithmetic
context: Einhard's Vita Karoli Magni reports that Charlemagne kept wax tablets and notebooks under his pillow to practice forming letters at night, but never learned to write well. He could read, and dictated fluently, but the hand of a scribe eluded him. Source: Wikipedia, Vita Karoli Magni.

question: Out of Alcuin's scriptoria came a clear rounded lowercase hand, with real spaces between the words, invented so scribes across the empire could copy the Bible accurately. It is called Carolingian minuscule. Six hundred years later, Renaissance humanists in fifteenth-century Italy dug it out of old manuscripts and enthusiastically copied it -- because they had made a mistake about what it was. What did those humanists think they were copying?
choices: The lost script of the druids
The private hand of the apostles
context: Fifteenth-century humanists took the Carolingian manuscripts in monastic libraries to be ancient Roman originals and copied the script as 'lettera antica'. From their humanist minuscule descends modern Roman printed type -- the lowercase letters you are reading right now. Source: Wikipedia, Humanist minuscule; Britannica, Carolingian minuscule.

question: Charlemagne died in 814 and was buried inside his Palatine Chapel at Aachen. In the chapel's upper gallery still stands the throne on which German kings were crowned for six centuries after him -- Otto I first sat on it in 936, and Ferdinand I last in 1531. The throne itself is older than any of them: it was built from re-used pieces of a much earlier civilization's stonework. What civilization's stone was recycled to make Charlemagne's throne?
context: The Aachen throne is four ancient marble slabs (some reworked from Roman spolia) clamped in bronze, reached by six marble steps. About thirty German kings were crowned on it between 936 and 1531. Source: Wikipedia, Palatine Chapel, Aachen; Throne of Charlemagne.

question: In the chanson de geste of the Frankish rearguard at Roncesvalles, Charlemagne rushes his army back over the pass and arrives too late -- Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, and the twelve peers lie dead on the mountainside beside their young captain. What was the young captain's name?
context: The Song of Roland (Oxford Digby 23, c. 1100) centres on Roland, Charlemagne's nephew and leader of the rearguard. Baligant is the pagan emir who arrives later; Marsile is the Saracen king of Zaragoza who plotted the ambush; Ganelon is the Frankish traitor who sold Roland out and is judged in this closing section of the poem.  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne pursued the Saracen force that had killed Roland deep into Spain. He caught them at a great Iberian river and drove them into the water; the pagans drowned in the current as the Franks pressed them from behind. Which river?
context: Song of Roland: the Saracens are driven into the Ebro, the largest river in northeast Spain, and drown. The Tagus runs through Toledo and Lisbon in the centre-west; the Duero cuts across Castile and northern Portugal; the Guadalquivir flows through Cordoba and Seville in the south -- all Iberian, but none the Ebro of the Roland pursuit.  (Legend.)

question: At the trial in Charlemagne's hall the traitor's guilt was not decided by testimony alone. Frankish law let it be decided by a JUDICIAL DUEL: one champion for the accuser fighting one champion for the accused, God granting victory to the just side. Who was the champion who fought FOR Charlemagne, on Roland's side?
context: Song of Roland laisses 273-291: Thierry, Roland's kinsman, argues that Ganelon's revenge is treason and offers his body against Ganelon's champion. Naimon is Charlemagne's wise old counsellor (already retired from the fighting); Ogier the Dane is another peer; Oliver is Roland's sworn brother, already dead at Roncesvalles.  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne's vengeance did not stop with Ganelon himself. Ganelon's whole extended kin-group had backed Pinabel and been implicated in the treason; on the same day, Charlemagne had a large number of them HANGED. How many of Ganelon's kinsmen were hanged?
context: Song of Roland: 'All those thirty kindred were swiftly hung.' The number is significant -- thirty pieces of silver in the Christian pillar, but also simply a large clan-remnant, marked as forfeit for their kinsman's treason. Twelve, three, and one hundred are wrong counts.  (Legend.)

question: At the very end of the poem, as the aged Charlemagne prepares to sleep, an angel appears to him in a dream commanding him to ride out YET AGAIN to another war -- to aid King Vivien besieged by pagans at Imphe. Which angel brought the summons?
context: Song of Roland (final laisses): Saint Gabriel appears to Charlemagne with the summons to Imphe. Gabriel is the messenger-angel of the Christian tradition, associated in this poem with prophetic word to the emperor. Michael is the warrior-angel who judges souls; Raphael is the healer of the Book of Tobit; Uriel appears in later apocryphal tradition.  (Legend.)

question: One of the most-quoted lines in the whole Old Testament ends: 'but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' It is spoken by an old warrior at the end of his life, gathering the tribes for a farewell speech. Which Israelite leader gives that speech?
context: Joshua 24:15 (KJV): 'And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye shall serve ... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' Samson pulled down the Philistine temple; Gideon fought Midian with 300 men and a trumpet-and-pitcher trick; Elijah confronted Ahab and Baal's prophets on Mount Carmel.

question: Joshua's farewell in Joshua 24 is not held just anywhere. He summons the elders, heads, judges, and officers of every tribe of Israel to one specific old covenant town in the hill country of Ephraim -- the same town where Abraham first pitched a tent and where Jacob later bought a parcel of ground for a hundred pieces of silver. Which town?
context: Joshua 24:1: Joshua 'gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem.' Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim is the town where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan (Genesis 12:6-7), and where Jacob bought the parcel of ground (Genesis 33:19). Bethel is where Jacob dreamed of the ladder; Hebron holds the tombs of the patriarchs; Beersheba is far to the south.

question: Long before the farewell at Shechem, Joshua had led the walk around Jericho. For the first six days the procession went around the city once a day, priests carrying rams' horn trumpets before the ark. On the last day the procession went around a certain number of times before the trumpets blew and the walls came down. How many times did they march around on that final day?
context: Joshua 6: seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns; the people march once a day for six days, and on the seventh day seven times around; then the priests blow a long blast, the people shout, and the wall falls down flat. Three days marks Jonah in the fish and the resurrection; twelve is the tribes and the apostles; forty is the wilderness years and Jesus's fast.

question: Joshua 24 closes with two burials -- one for the old warrior himself, one for a set of bones the Israelites had carried out of Egypt more than forty years earlier and had lugged all the way through the wilderness (Genesis 50:25). Whose bones were finally buried at Shechem, in the parcel Jacob had bought for a hundred pieces of silver?
context: Joshua 24:32: 'And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought ... for an hundred pieces of silver.' Aaron was buried on Mount Hor (Numbers 20); Moses on a mountain in Moab, in a grave no one knows (Deuteronomy 34); Jacob himself was carried back to the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (Genesis 50:13).

question: The name Christopher is a compound of two Greek words. What does the whole name mean, in a literal translation from the Greek?
context: Greek Christophoros = Christos (Christ) + phero (to bear or carry). The name is a story unto itself: the man who bore Christ across the river. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'.

question: Before his baptism and the river-crossing the giant of the Golden Legend went by a very different name, which the text uses until his encounter with the child on his shoulders. What was he called then?
context: Reprobus, from Latin reprobus ('rejected, reprobate'), is the name the giant carries in the Golden Legend until his baptism and the river-crossing. Ignatius, Marcellus, and Cassian are all real early Christian martyrs. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: In the Golden Legend Reprobus is measured in cubits, the old forearm-length unit, and the number is deliberately huge -- a size no ordinary man could reach. How many cubits does the Golden Legend say he stood?
context: Twelve cubits (a cubit being roughly a foot and a half) works out to about eighteen feet. Later medieval retellings sometimes push him higher, but the Golden Legend's figure is twelve. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.
