question: The giant sets out to serve the strongest master in the world. He first pledges himself to a great earthly king; then he sees the king flinch at a name and leaves in search of that master instead. Whom did the great earthly king fear, sending the giant off on the second leg of his search?
choices: the ghost of a dead prince
context: In the Golden Legend the earthly king fears the devil, so the giant leaves to serve that stronger master; the devil in turn flinches at another name, and the giant leaves again in search of the master the devil fears. It is a giant's plain step-by-step logic about what deserves service. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: On the far bank the giant, gasping, says he thought he had carried the whole world across the ford. The child answers with a specific line about what he has actually just done. What does the child tell him he has borne on his shoulders?
answer: him that made all the world
choices: him that made all the world
the last of the Hebrew prophets
context: The Golden Legend has the child answer: 'Thou hast not only borne all the world upon thee, but thou hast borne him that created and made all the world upon thy shoulders.' It is the moment that gives the giant his name Christophoros. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: On the far bank the child asks the giant to plant his walking-pole in the ground as a sign that the story is true. In the morning the dry wood has done something no dead wood does. What did the planted staff do overnight?
context: The Golden Legend has the staff put forth leaves, flowers, and dates by morning, echoing the Old Testament blossoming rod of Aaron. Source: CatholicSaints.info, 'Golden Legend: Life of Saint Christopher'.

question: Eastern Christian icons sometimes depict Christopher not as a bearded giant but as a man with a startling animal feature in place of his usual head, an image scholars trace to a scribal misreading of one Latin word about his origin. What animal's head do these Eastern icons give him?
context: The Latin word Cananeus, 'Canaanite', was garbled by a scribe into canineus, 'dog-like'; from there the story that Christopher came from a Canaanite tribe of dog-headed men grew, and Eastern icons still sometimes show him cynocephalos. Bulls, lions, and rams appear on the heads of other traditions' figures (the Egyptian Apis, the Assyrian lamassu, the Egyptian Khnum) but never on Christopher. Source: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'.  (Legend.)

question: On his long voyage home from Troy, Odysseus and his crew land on a wooded island called Aeaea and see smoke rising from a stone house in a forest clearing. Inside lives an enchantress who invites strangers in for a feast and then turns them into animals. What is her name?
context: She is a daughter of the sun god Helios. Calypso is the nymph who keeps Odysseus seven years on Ogygia later; Medea is Circe's niece and a sorceress in her own right; Nausicaa is the princess who finds him washed up on Scheria. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: The witch of the wooded island welcomes Odysseus's men in and gives them a warm feast of cheese, meal, honey, and wine. Then she touches each of them with her wand -- and they become animals, driven out to a pen. Into which animal are the men transformed?
context: Circe already has tame wolves and lions in her yard from earlier visitors; the crew is turned specifically into swine and fed acorns. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus sends only half his men to investigate Circe's house, led by an officer who suspects the invitation and hangs back at the door while the others go inside for the feast. When the men turn to pigs, this officer escapes and runs back to warn Odysseus. Who is he?
context: Elpenor is the crewman who later falls drunk off Circe's roof; Polites is another crewman; Antiphates was the Laestrygonian king who ate the earlier scouts. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: The pigs in Circe's sty are strange animals: they have pig bodies and pig snouts, but they weep. Why do they weep?
answer: They still have their human minds inside
choices: They still have their human minds inside
They are hungry for the acorns Circe throws down
Circe has laid a curse of sorrow on the pen
The moon has risen and the spell weighs on them
context: This is the horror of the punishment -- the men know they are men, and remember Odysseus, but can only grunt. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus sets out alone from the ship to rescue his men. On the forest path a god meets him and hands him a magical plant as an antidote to Circe's drugs -- Homer names it and describes it 'black at the root, white as milk at the flower.' Which god gives him the plant?
context: The messenger god, patron of travelers and tricksters -- the obvious ally against a sorceress. Source: Wikipedia, Moly (herb); Odyssey 10.302-306.  (Legend.)

question: The antidote plant Hermes hands to Odysseus has a black root and a milk-white flower. Homer says only the gods can safely pluck it from the soil. By what name does Homer call this plant?
context: Nepenthe is another Homeric drug, the sorrow-killer served at Helen's table in Odyssey 4; silphium is a real medicinal plant from Cyrene; asphodel is the flower of the meadow of the dead. Odyssey 10.302-306. Source: Wikipedia, Moly (herb).  (Legend.)

question: Hermes tells Odysseus exactly how to break Circe's magic: when she strikes with her wand and orders him to the sty, draw the sword -- she will drop the wand and offer to sleep with him. What must Odysseus force her to do before he agrees?
answer: Swear a great oath to do him and his men no more harm
choices: Swear a great oath to do him and his men no more harm
Cut a lock of her golden hair and burn it on the hearth
Give up her wand and throw it into the sea
Kneel before him and name him her master
context: Hermes coaches him line by line; the oath by the gods is what makes the alliance safe. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus does exactly what Hermes said. Circe strikes with the wand; the moly holds; he draws the sword and rushes her. She stares at him and drops the wand, and greets him by a phrase from a warning Hermes had given her long ago. Which phrase does she use?
context: The famous Homeric epithet 'polytropos' -- of many ways, many turns, many tricks. 'Breaker of horses' is Hector's epithet; 'son of Peleus' is Achilles. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: After the oath, Circe reverses the spell and the pigs are men again. Homer describes how they look after the change. How does he say they come back?
answer: Taller, younger, and handsomer than they had been before
choices: Taller, younger, and handsomer than they had been before
Shrunken and old, their beards suddenly white
The same as they had been the moment Circe struck
Silent, and unable to speak for three days
context: A rare gift on top of the mere reversal. Source: Cliffs Notes, Odyssey Book 10.  (Legend.)

question: The crew are men again and Circe is now their host. They stay in her feast-hall a very long time before they can even bear to think of Ithaca -- Homer says a specific length of time. How long do they stay on Aeaea?
context: It is Eurylochus and the crew who finally shake Odysseus and remind him of Ithaca. Seven years is what Calypso keeps him on Ogygia much later. Source: Wikipedia, Aeaea.  (Legend.)

question: When Odysseus at last asks Circe for the way home, she tells him he cannot sail straight to Ithaca -- he must first make a terrible detour and consult a specific blind seer, wherever he can be found. Which seer must Odysseus consult, and where?
context: The reason the next book of the Odyssey is the Nekyia -- the descent to Hades. Calchas was the seer of the Greek army at Troy; Melampus and Mopsus are other famous Greek seers. Source: Wikipedia, Circe.  (Legend.)

question: In the Umbrian hill-town of Assisi in the early 1200s, a girl named Chiara Offreduccio -- Clare -- listened from an upstairs window while a strange young preacher named Francis, roughly twelve years older than she was, gathered crowds in the piazza below. What sort of home had Clare grown up in?
answer: A noble palazzo near the cathedral
choices: A noble palazzo near the cathedral
A shepherd's cottage in the hills
A merchant's house on the market square
A stonemason's workshop by the church
context: Clare (b. 1194) was of the Offreduccio family, Assisi nobility. Her family lived in a palazzo near the cathedral of San Rufino. Source: Wikipedia, Clare of Assisi.

question: On the night of Palm Sunday, 18 March 1212, the eighteen-year-old Clare of Assisi -- refusing an arranged noble marriage -- slipped out of her family's palazzo after dark and ran down the hill through the fields, alone. At the bottom she found the chapel where Francis and his brothers were waiting for her by torchlight -- Francis's own mother-house. Which chapel was it?
context: The Portiuncula ('little portion') -- the tiny chapel of St. Mary of the Angels below Assisi -- was Francis's mother-house. Clare met him there on Palm Sunday night 1212. Source: Franciscan Media; Wikipedia.

question: Clare escaped her father's palazzo that night through a narrow side-door built into the wall of the house. In Assisi the palazzos actually had these small doors, and they had only one everyday purpose. What was that side-door used for?
answer: Carrying a corpse out of the house
choices: Carrying a corpse out of the house
Leading a bride out to her wedding
context: The porta dei morti -- 'door of the dead' -- was a small side-door reserved by tradition for taking a body out to burial. Clare using it to run to Francis is a beat kept by later biographers. Source: Christian History Institute.  (Legend.)

question: When Clare of Assisi reached the little chapel where Francis and his brothers waited for her by torchlight, she gave up her old life on the spot. Francis received her vows and clothed her in a rough tunic like his own. What did he do with her long hair?
answer: He cut it off with shears
choices: He cut it off with shears
He wound it around a cross
He burned it in the altar lamp
He buried it in the churchyard
context: Francis cut off Clare's long hair as the visible sign of her renunciation of the world -- the same gesture Catherine of Siena would later make on herself. Clare was 18. Source: Franciscan Media; Wikipedia.

question: Clare's family soon discovered where she had gone. Her uncle and armed relatives arrived at the convent where Francis had placed her for safety and tried to drag her home to be married. She ran to the altar, clung to the altar cloth, and did something that stopped them cold. What did she do at the altar?
answer: Threw back her veil to show her shorn head
choices: Threw back her veil to show her shorn head
Called down a curse on her uncle by name
Broke the wedding ring meant for her finger
Held up a burning coal from the altar lamp
context: Shorn hair marked a woman consecrated to God -- legally, her family could no longer marry her off. The gesture ended the argument. Her sister Agnes joined her days later. Source: Christian History Institute; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: In September 1240, mercenary Saracen troops in the pay of the Emperor Frederick II attacked Assisi and reached the walls of Clare's little house. Clare was too sick to stand. She had the sisters carry her out to the courtyard and lift into her hands a covered vessel from the chapel. When she raised it toward the soldiers, they turned back without attacking. What was she holding?
answer: The consecrated host from the altar
choices: The consecrated host from the altar
The sword Francis had once carried
A relic of the true cross
The rule of the order in a silver box
context: Clare had the pyx (or later monstrance -- the vessel is anachronistically depicted in art) containing the consecrated eucharistic bread brought out; the Saracens withdrew. Clare died three years later, on 11 August 1253. Source: Franciscan Foundation for the Holy Land.  (Legend.)

question: A high-born Irish monk of the O Neill royal line, born around 521 CE and trained as a scribe under Finnian at Movilla, would end up sailing off to Scotland to found the most famous island monastery in the Atlantic west. His Irish name was Colum Cille -- what did that name mean?
context: Colum Cille (later latinised as Columba) literally means 'dove of the church'. He was descended from Niall of the Nine Hostages through his father's line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: Around 560 CE the young monk Columba stayed up nights in secret at Movilla, transcribing a beautiful psalter that belonged to his old teacher Finnian. When Finnian found out he claimed the new manuscript as his own. The Irish High King Diarmait was asked to judge, and his ruling became a famous line of medieval law. What was the ruling?
answer: To every cow her calf, and to every book its copy
choices: To every cow her calf, and to every book its copy
A borrowed book is a borrowed sword
What the scribe writes, the abbey keeps
The pen has no owner but the psalm
context: In Irish: 'le gach boin a boinin, le gach leabhar a leabhran.' Later Irish tradition called this the first copyright judgment in Western history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cul_Dreimhne.  (Legend.)

question: In 561 CE the O Neill met High King Diarmait's forces near Drumcliff in County Sligo. About three thousand men lay dead by the end of the day. This clash, blamed by tradition on the scholar-monk who had transcribed his teacher's book, was later called the Battle of Cul Dreimhne. What did a synod of Irish abbots impose on Columba as his penance for it?
answer: An exile, to win as many souls to the faith as had died in the fighting
choices: An exile, to win as many souls to the faith as had died in the fighting
A year of silence and fasting on bread and water at Clonmacnoise
The building of a great high cross at every monastery he had known
A pilgrimage on foot to Rome and back, with only a psalter for a purse
context: The synod's judgment sent Columba across the sea; the exile is what made Iona possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.  (Legend.)

question: In 563 CE the exiled Columba pushed a wicker-and-hide boat off the Irish shore and sailed north-east to the western coast of Scotland, where his kinsman King Conall of Dal Riata granted him a small barren island for a monastery. How many companions sailed with him?
context: Twelve companions -- the same number as Christ's apostles -- crossed with Columba in a curragh. The island he was given, later mother-house of the northern British church, became Iona. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: In 565 CE at the River Ness in Pictish territory, Columba's companion Lugne was swimming across the water on the abbot's order when a great beast rose out of the current and lunged for him. Columba raised his hand, made the sign of the cross, and spoke a single sharp command at the creature -- Adomnan's Life records that the beast then fled as if pulled back by ropes. What did Columba say to it?
answer: Go no further, do not touch the man, go back at once
choices: Go no further, do not touch the man, go back at once
In the name of the Father, be still and drown no more
Return to the deep places, beast, and trouble none
Peace, creature, and leave this man his life
context: Adomnan places the encounter at the River Ness itself, not the loch of the same name -- so the very first 'Loch Ness monster' account is on the river, not the loch. The three other options are plausible saint-commands but not what the Vita Columbae records. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Ness_Monster.  (Legend.)

question: On the evening of Whitsun 597, the old abbot of Iona sat copying out Psalm 33 in his cell when he reached the verse 'they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing' and laid down his pen. He said 'here I must stop; let another write what follows', walked alone to the church, and died in front of the altar. Which of his brothers did he name to take up the pen?
context: Baithene, Columba's cousin, succeeded him as second abbot of Iona and finished the psalter. Aidan was the later missionary to Northumbria; Diarmait was Columba's personal attendant in some accounts; Oran was an earlier companion buried on the island. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.  (Legend.)

question: For roughly two centuries after Columba's death, the scriptorium at Iona was one of the great manuscript workshops of the Atlantic west, and around 800 CE its monks began an illuminated gospel book so richly painted that later ages called it the finest surviving manuscript of the early Middle Ages. Viking raids drove the monks and the book off the island. What is the book now called?
context: Kept today at Trinity College Dublin. The Book of Durrow is an earlier Iona-family manuscript, the Book of Armagh is a Patrick-tradition compendium, the Book of Deer is a small Aberdeenshire gospel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columba.

question: Mark's gospel names the desperate father who falls at Jesus's feet at the start of the raising scene: a local religious official whose only daughter is dying. What was this man's name?
context: Mark 5:22 KJV: 'And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name.' Zacchaeus is the tax-collector up the sycamore tree in Luke 19; Cornelius is the Roman centurion in Acts 10; Nicodemus is the Pharisee who comes to Jesus at night in John 3.

question: At Jairus's house Jesus tells the professional mourners the girl is only sleeping, not dead. Mark records their reaction to Jesus in one blunt phrase before Jesus puts them all out of the house. What did the mourners do?
context: Mark 5:40 KJV: 'And they laughed him to scorn.' The scene turns on Jesus then putting them all out of the house and taking only the parents and the inner three disciples in -- the laughing crowd sees nothing of what follows.

question: In the room Jesus takes the dead girl's hand and speaks in the ordinary language Galilean children spoke at home -- Aramaic. Mark preserves the actual words, then translates them for his Greek readers as 'Damsel, arise'. Which Aramaic words does Jesus speak?
context: Mark 5:41 KJV: 'And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.' Ephphatha is what Jesus says to a deaf man in Mark 7; Eli lama sabachthani is his cry from the cross in Mark 15; Maranatha is a very early Christian greeting preserved in Aramaic at the end of Paul's first letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22).

question: Right after the twelve-year-old gets up and walks, Mark records one final instruction from Jesus in the room -- a startlingly ordinary, physical, non-miraculous one, almost like a checklist item. What does Jesus tell the parents to do?
choices: keep her indoors for seven days
walk her three times around the house
context: Mark 5:43 KJV: '...and commanded that something should be given her to eat.' It is Mark's touch of realism -- a girl who has just crossed back has to eat like a girl. The other three instructions are invented.

question: The other great raising scene is in John's gospel. The dead man's two grieving sisters live with him in a village two miles from Jerusalem, and the sisters send urgent word to Jesus. Whom does John name as the sisters at Bethany?
context: John 11:1 KJV: 'Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha.' This Mary is Mary of Bethany -- not Mary Magdalene and not Mary the mother of Jesus. Rachel and Leah are Jacob's two wives; Naomi and Ruth are the mother-in-law and widow of the Book of Ruth; Priscilla and Lydia are early Christian women from Paul's letters and Acts.

question: John says the sisters send word that Lazarus is sick -- but Jesus deliberately does not set out at once. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has already been sealed in the tomb long enough for Martha to warn Jesus, at the stone, that the body 'stinketh'. HOW many days does John say Lazarus has been in the tomb?
context: John 11:17 KJV: 'Then when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.' Repeated in Martha's protest in verse 39. Forty is the wilderness number; twelve is Jairus's daughter's age; seven is the day-count for the Genesis creation week.

question: In the Ulster Cycle, the greatest Irish warrior sails away as a young man to train in arms with a fearsome war-woman named Scathach on an island called the Isle of Shadow. Who is this Ulster warrior?
context: Cu Chulainn ('the Hound of Culann') is the central hero of the Ulster Cycle. Conall Cernach is his foster-brother and Ulster's second-greatest warrior; Ferghus mac Roich is the exiled Ulster king; Conchobar mac Nessa is the reigning king of Ulster. All four are the great Ulstermen -- but the trip to the Isle of Shadow to learn from Scathach belongs to Cu Chulainn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: During his training on the Isle of Shadow, Cu Chulainn defeats in single combat a rival warrior-queen whose lands lie next to Scathach's. He spares her life, and she bears him a son. What is this warrior-queen's name?
context: Aife (also spelled Aoife) is the Scottish warrior-queen Cu Chulainn defeats and lies with for one night. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife back in Ulster; Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale; the Morrigan is the war-goddess who both loves and torments Cu Chulainn. All four are real Ulster-Cycle women, only one is the mother of his son. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: Before Cu Chulainn sailed home from the Isle of Shadow, he left the pregnant Aife a small token of gold and told her that when their son had grown enough to wear it, she should send the boy after him to Ireland. What was the token?
context: The thumb-ring is the recognition-token that drives the whole tragedy: its size doubles as the age-test (the boy is old enough only when he fits it), and it is the ONLY way father and son will know each other. A brooch, a torc, and an arm-band are all real early-Irish gold ornaments -- but a fitted ring is what the story chooses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aided_Oenfhir_Aife.  (Legend.)

question: Along with the ring, Cu Chulainn laid three commandments on the son he had never seen -- three unbreakable geasa meant to shape the boy into a great warrior. He must never turn back once he set out, and he must never refuse a challenge. What was the THIRD commandment?
answer: he must never give his name
choices: he must never give his name
he must never draw first blood
he must never sleep on the ground
he must never eat the flesh of a hound
context: The three geasa -- never turn back, never refuse, never name yourself -- are the whole engine of the disaster: they make it impossible for father and son to recognise each other in time. 'Never eat the flesh of a hound' is a REAL geis in Irish myth, but it is Cu Chulainn's OWN geis (his name means 'Hound'), not Connla's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: Word of the champion-slaying boy reaches Cu Chulainn at Dun Dealgan, and he sets out for the strand. His wife runs after him, catches him, and pleads with him NOT to go down -- she has heard the story and guessed who the child must be. What is her name?
context: Emer, daughter of Forgall Manach, is Cu Chulainn's wife -- famed as one of the six women of the perfect gifts. She reads the situation faster than he does, but he goes down anyway. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale (Longes mac nUislenn); Fedelm is a prophetess in the Tain; Nes is Conchobar's mother. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connla.  (Legend.)

question: The Irish tale of a father unknowingly killing his warrior son in single combat is not unique. Scholars point to two exact parallels from wholly separate traditions -- so exact that a common Indo-European origin has been proposed. One is the German Hildebrandslied (Hildebrand and Hadubrand). What is the other, from the Persian Shahnameh?
context: In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c.1010), the Persian champion Rustam meets his son Sohrab in single combat without knowing him, kills him, and recognises him only from the arm-clasp Rustam himself had left with the mother. The pattern -- token, unrecognised son, father's fatal blow, too-late recognition -- matches Aided Oenfhir Aife almost beat-for-beat. Kai Khosrow, Farud, Bahram, and Iskandar (Alexander) are all major Shahnameh figures but not the father-son duel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aided_Oenfhir_Aife.  (Legend.)

question: As a young shepherd on the hills of Northumbria in 651, a boy named Cuthbert saw a vision in the night sky of angels carrying a soul to heaven. In the morning he learned that an Irish missionary had died at the very same hour, and the boy decided to become a monk. Whose soul had Cuthbert seen carried up?
context: Aidan, an Irish monk from Iona, had founded Lindisfarne in 635 and was its first bishop. Cuthbert soon entered Melrose Abbey to begin his own monastic life. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert.  (Legend.)

question: Wanting greater solitude than even a tidal monastery could give him, Cuthbert withdrew in 676 to a tiny rocky outcrop in the North Sea, dug a well in the rock, grew barley to eat, and built his cell with walls high enough that he could see only the sky. Which island did he choose?
context: Inner Farne is the largest of the Farne Islands, a cluster of low rocky islands a few miles south of Lindisfarne. Coquet Island is another Northumberland island Cuthbert is recorded visiting. He built his cell so that nothing but the sky was visible from inside. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert.

question: Eleven years after Cuthbert was buried, in 698, the monks of Lindisfarne opened his coffin intending to lift his bones out into a reliquary. What they found instead became the most famous miracle told of him for the next thousand years. What did they find inside?
context: The body was reported whole and uncorrupted, the vestments still fresh. The coffin was opened again at Durham in 1104, and once more in 1827, when it was found in fragments but with recognizable relics. Source: sites.nd.edu/manuscript-studies/2023/03/23/by-the-bones-of-saint-cuthbert.  (Legend.)

question: When Viking raids began smashing Lindisfarne in 793, the monks lifted Cuthbert's coffin and carried it with them across the north of England for more than a century, looking for somewhere safe. In which English city did they at last set the coffin down, so that the cathedral was afterward built over his tomb?
context: The Community of Saint Cuthbert rested for over a century at Chester-le-Street before finally settling at Durham around 995. Durham Cathedral, begun in 1093, was built over the tomb, and Cuthbert lies there still. Source: durhamworldheritagesite.com/learn/history/st-cuthbert/body.

question: Two Greek brothers from a Byzantine port where the Slavic language was widely heard on the streets grew up to become the missionaries who first put Slavic into writing. The elder was named Methodius; the younger took the monastic name by which the whole family is now remembered. What was the younger brother's monastic name?
context: The younger brother was born Constantine and only took the name Cyril late in life in Rome. Athanasius was the 4th-c. Alexandrian bishop; Basil the great Cappadocian; Jerome the Latin translator of the Vulgate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_and_Methodius.

question: On the road north to Moravia, Cyril sat down and designed a brand new writing system to render the sounds of Slavic -- the first alphabet Slavonic manuscripts were ever written in. What do historians call his original design?
context: The name Glagolitic comes from the Slavic 'glagol', meaning 'word'. The alphabet later named Cyrillic was actually developed after Cyril's death by his students at the Preslav Literary School, based largely on Greek majuscule letters. Ogham was the early Irish script cut on stone edges; Uncial was a Latin manuscript hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_and_Methodius.

question: In 867 Cyril stopped in Venice and defended, against the local clergy, his right to celebrate the liturgy in Slavic. His opponents insisted that God could only be praised in the three languages Pilate had written above the cross. Which three languages did they name?
context: John 19:20 says the inscription above the cross was in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The Slavonic sources call the trilingualist position the 'Pilatian heresy' after this passage. Aramaic, Syriac, and Arabic are all real languages of the region, but not the three named at the cross. Source: scribd.com/Ss-Cyril-and-Methodius-and-a-Mythical-Western-Heresy-Trilingualism.

question: One of the most famous scenes in the Book of Daniel has the elderly prophet sealed overnight in a pit of hungry beasts as punishment for praying. What kind of beasts fill the pit?
context: Daniel 6:16 KJV: 'they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions.' Bears appear in the Elisha / mocking-boys story (2 Kings 2:24); serpents in the Moses / brazen serpent scene (Numbers 21); wolves are metaphorical only.

question: The moment Daniel learns the decree has been signed, he does not hide. He goes home and does exactly what he has always done. In what direction does the KJV say Daniel's windows are open when he kneels to pray?
context: Daniel 6:10 KJV: 'his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem.' Jews in exile prayed toward Jerusalem (the Temple) -- the tradition Daniel is honoring. The rising sun is a sun-worship posture the OT condemns (Ezek 8:16). Mount Sinai is where Moses received the law. 'Toward the four winds' is Ezekiel's phrase for scattering.

question: When Daniel was first brought to Babylon as a young captive of Nebuchadnezzar, he was given a new Babylonian court name (Daniel 1:7). What was the name they called him at court?
context: Daniel 1:7 KJV. Belteshazzar is Daniel's Babylonian name (do not confuse with king Belshazzar, a different figure). Abednego and Meshach are the Babylonian names of Daniel's three companions (Hananiah and Mishael); the fourth companion Azariah became Shadrach.

question: After Daniel is caught praying and cast into the pit, a great stone is rolled over the mouth of the den. To make sure no one in the night can dig Daniel out and cheat the decree, the stone is sealed. Whose seal is put on it?
answer: The king's own signet, and the signets of his lords
choices: The king's own signet, and the signets of his lords
The high priest's ephod, and the seals of the Levites
A tablet of clay bearing the name of Marduk
A cord of scarlet and blue, tied by the palace guard
context: Daniel 6:17 KJV: 'a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that the purpose might not be changed concerning Daniel.' The double sealing is why not even the king himself can rescue Daniel until dawn.

question: The king cries down into the pit fearing Daniel is torn to pieces. Daniel answers up out of the darkness with one of the most quoted verses of the story -- explaining WHY the lions have not eaten him. What does Daniel say his God has done?
answer: Sent his angel, and shut the lions' mouths
choices: Sent his angel, and shut the lions' mouths
Sent a whirlwind, and driven the beasts back
Laid his hand upon them, and made them tame as sheep
Blinded their eyes, that they should not see me
context: Daniel 6:22 KJV: 'My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me.' The other options are stylistic parallels drawn from other OT rescue-vocabulary but not from Daniel's answer.

question: Daniel is drawn up from the pit unhurt. Then king Darius turns on the men who plotted against him. Daniel 6:24 records the fate that falls on the accusers. What does the KJV say happens to them?
answer: Thrown into the pit with their wives and children, and torn by the lions
choices: Thrown into the pit with their wives and children, and torn by the lions
Stoned outside the city walls with their wives and children
Beheaded with their households, their heads set on the palace gate
Cast with their wives and children into a burning furnace
context: Daniel 6:24 KJV: '...the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den.' The famous 'furnace heated seven times' belongs to the Daniel 3 story of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego -- a different scene in the same book.

question: 2 Samuel 11 opens 'at the time when kings go forth to battle.' Israel's general Joab is off besieging Rabbah of the Ammonites, but King David is not with the army. Where is David?
answer: in Jerusalem, at his own palace
choices: in Jerusalem, at his own palace
hiding in the cave of Adullam
keeping his father's sheep at Bethlehem
context: 2 Samuel 11:1-2 KJV. Kings normally rode out with the army in spring; David has stayed behind. The next verse puts him walking on the palace roof at evening. The three wrong choices are all real David locations from earlier in his story -- Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), Gath under Achish (1 Samuel 27), the Bethlehem sheepfold (1 Samuel 16:11).

question: One evening David gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof in Jerusalem. Looking down from the roof he sees a beautiful woman doing something below, and sends to find out who she is. What is she doing?
context: 2 Samuel 11:2 KJV: 'from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.' The messenger returns and tells him her name and the name of her husband -- the next rung.

question: David asks his servants about the woman on the roof. They tell him her name is Bathsheba, and that she is the wife of a soldier the king knows well -- a foreigner serving in Israel's army, and one of the thirty listed later in the book as David's own mighty men. What is her husband's name and background?
context: 2 Samuel 11:3 KJV, with Uriah listed among David's thirty at 2 Samuel 23:39. The three wrong choices are also real foreign warriors around David: Ittai the Gittite followed David out of Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:19-21); Doeg the Edomite was Saul's chief herdsman (1 Samuel 21:7); Zelek the Ammonite is another of the thirty (2 Samuel 23:37).

question: After the killing, God sends the prophet Nathan to David. Nathan tells the king a story: a rich man with vast flocks and herds, and a poor man with only ONE small animal in his household. The poor man had raised it in his own house, fed it from his own plate, given it his own cup to drink, and let it lie in his bosom -- 'it was unto him as a daughter.' What one animal did the poor man have?
context: 2 Samuel 12:1-3 KJV. The rich man refuses to spend one of his own flock on a traveler and takes the poor man's lamb instead. The three wrong choices are all real OT sacrificial animals but none is in the parable.

question: David listens to Nathan's parable about the rich man who stole and killed the poor man's household lamb, and his anger flares up. He swears an oath that the rich man deserves to die. Nathan answers with one short sentence that turns the parable on David himself. What does Nathan say?
context: 2 Samuel 12:5-7 KJV. David has just sworn 'the man that hath done this thing shall surely die.' Nathan replies, 'Thou art the man,' and then names the ewe lamb as Bathsheba and the traveler as David's own lust. It is one of the sharpest lines in the Hebrew Bible.

question: Bathsheba's baby is struck sick. David fasts, lies on the ground, and refuses food for seven days. When his servants finally tell him the child has died, he rises, washes, changes his clothes, and asks for a meal -- terrifying them, because they expected him to break down. He explains himself in one line to his servants. What does David say?
answer: 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.'
choices: 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.'
'The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away.'
'Naked came I out of my mother's womb.'
'The days of my mourning shall be ended.'
context: 2 Samuel 12:20-23 KJV. David's answer is a working father's theology: he fasted while there was any hope, and stopped when there was none. The three wrong choices are all real famous OT grief lines -- Job 1:21 (twice, from the ash-heap) and Genesis 27:41 (the mourning of Esau) -- but none is the one David gives here.

question: The Philistines camp on one hill, Israel on another, with a valley between them. Every day the Philistines send out a champion to shout across at Israel and demand single combat. In which valley does 1 Samuel 17 set the standoff?
context: 1 Samuel 17:2-3 KJV. The three wrong choices are all real named valleys in the Hebrew Bible: Hinnom outside Jerusalem (the child-sacrifice site, later Gehenna), Jezreel where Ahab's dynasty falls, and Achor where Achan is stoned in Joshua 7.

question: Every morning and every evening the Philistine champion steps out into the valley and challenges any Israelite to fight him one-on-one. Not one Israelite comes down. For how long does 1 Samuel 17 say the stand-off drags on before David arrives?
context: 1 Samuel 17:16 KJV: 'And the Philistine drew near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days.' Forty is the Bible's long-wait number -- forty days of the Flood, forty years in the wilderness, forty days of Jesus fasting in the wilderness -- so the number is doing work.

question: David is not with the army. His father Jesse sends him from the sheepfold to the camp with food for his three oldest brothers and their captain. Jesse packs an ephah of parched corn, ten loaves of bread, and one very specific dairy item to be given to the captain of the thousand. What does Jesse send for the captain?
context: 1 Samuel 17:17-18 KJV. Ten cheeses for the officer is one of those specific homely details the storyteller preserves. The three wrong choices are all real OT foodstuffs in gift-lists elsewhere (Abigail's stores at 1 Samuel 25, Jonathan's honey in the wood at 1 Samuel 14).

question: Instead of Saul's kit, David goes down to the brook that runs through the valley and stoops to pick something up out of the water. He picks out several of them, chooses them for their smoothness, and puts them in the shepherd's bag he already carries. What does he pick up, and how many?
context: 1 Samuel 17:40 KJV: 'he chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip.' He will use only one -- the other four are the answer to why kids remember this story.

question: David answers the giant back. He names the giant's own weapons -- sword, spear, shield -- and says what he himself is coming in the name of. He finishes with why the fight is going to happen this way: 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.' What does David say he is coming in the name of?
answer: 'the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel'
choices: 'the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel'
'the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob'
'the LORD, the God who brought thee out of Egypt'
'the Rock of Israel, the shield of my salvation'
context: 1 Samuel 17:45-46 KJV: 'I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.' The wrong choices are all real OT divine-title formulas (Exodus 3:6, Exodus 20:2, 2 Samuel 22 in David's own song) -- but not the one he uses in the valley.

question: David runs at the giant, reaches into his bag for one stone, and slings it. The stone sinks into the giant. The giant falls face-first to the earth. Where in the giant's body does the stone strike?
context: 1 Samuel 17:49 KJV: 'the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.' A helmeted target with an exposed forehead is a real puzzle scholars raise -- most read Goliath's helmet as leaving the brow open, or read the giant as raising his visor to shout.

question: Years later David flees Saul unarmed and takes refuge with the priest Ahimelech, who feeds him and arms him. Saul soon orders Doeg the Edomite to butcher Ahimelech and eighty-five priests of his house. At which sanctuary town does the massacre happen?
context: 1 Samuel 21:1-9 (Ahimelech gives David the giant's sword and the showbread at Nob) and 1 Samuel 22:9-19 (Doeg the Edomite butchers the eighty-five priests on Saul's order). The wrong choices are all real OT sanctuary towns: Shiloh where the ark rested under Eli, Bethel of Jacob's ladder, Gilgal where Joshua's twelve stones stood.

question: There is a well-known textual puzzle deep in the David story. At 2 Samuel 21:19 a different Israelite is named as the killer of Goliath -- 'the Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.' What is the name of this other Bethlehemite the second book gives credit to?
context: 2 Samuel 21:19 KJV; the parallel at 1 Chronicles 20:5 smooths the puzzle by saying Elhanan killed 'Lahmi the brother of Goliath.' The wrong choices are all real named champions of David's thirty from 2 Samuel 23: Benaiah who killed a lion in a pit in the snow, Abishai who lifted his spear against three hundred, Eleazar who fought the Philistines until his hand cleaved to the sword.

question: That day the king's son seals the friendship with a gift. He strips off what he is wearing and hands it to David, giving him the outward marks of the throne he himself stands to inherit: his royal robe, his belt, his bow, and one more thing. What is the fourth item he gives?
context: 1 Samuel 18:4 KJV: 'And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.' The prince is handing his heir's kit to the man the LORD has chosen to replace him -- and doing it with his eyes open.

question: David becomes Saul's court musician, playing the harp to calm the king's dark moods. Twice the king reaches for a weapon and hurls it across the room at David's head while David is playing. What weapon does Saul throw at him?
context: 1 Samuel 18:10-11 and 19:9-10 KJV: 'Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it.' David slips out from under it both times. Saul carries the javelin as his royal token throughout the story -- it stands beside him when he sleeps in the camp at Hachilah.

question: David flees the palace and hides in a field. Jonathan works out a signal to tell him whether it is safe to come back. At the new-moon feast Jonathan will tell his father David is away visiting family; then Jonathan will come to the field pretending to practice, and shoot arrows past a boy servant. If Jonathan calls out that the arrows are on THIS side, it is safe; if he calls that they are BEYOND, David must flee. How many arrows does Jonathan shoot as the signal?
context: 1 Samuel 20:20-22, 36-37 KJV. Jonathan shoots three, cries to the boy 'Is not the arrow beyond thee?' and adds 'make speed, haste, stay not' -- the coded warning for David hiding in the rocks. The two friends then meet one last time in secret before David runs.

question: In the field after the arrows are shot, the two friends meet in secret. They fall on each other's necks and weep. Before they part, Jonathan makes David swear an oath. It uses one repeated phrase: 'The LORD be between me and thee, and between ______ and ______ for ever.' What two words fill the blanks?
context: 1 Samuel 20:42 KJV: 'The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever.' The oath about seed -- descendants -- is what saves Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth years later, when David is king and Saul's whole house should have been wiped out.

question: Years pass. The Philistines break the Israelite line on a mountain in the north; the king's sons are cut down around him and Saul himself is wounded by archers. Saul asks his armour-bearer to run him through so he will not be captured, and when the man refuses, the king does it himself. On what mountain do Saul and his sons -- including Jonathan -- die?
context: 1 Samuel 31:1-6 KJV. Saul falls upon his own sword after his armour-bearer refuses; the armour-bearer then does the same. The wrong choices are all real famous mountains of the OT -- Carmel of Elijah's contest, Tabor of Deborah and Barak, Hermon on Israel's north border.

question: The Philistines fasten Saul's body and his sons' bodies to the wall of Beth-shan. One town in Israel that had once been rescued by Saul from the Ammonites remembers the debt. Its valiant men march all night, take the bodies down from the wall, and burn them under a tamarisk tree back home, then fast seven days. What town's men come at night to recover Saul and Jonathan?
context: 1 Samuel 31:10-13 KJV. Saul had saved Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite at the start of his reign (1 Samuel 11); the town pays the debt at the end. The wrong choices are other real towns from the surrounding books, none of which does this deed.

question: Inside the same lament, David turns from Saul and the army to Jonathan alone. He addresses his dead friend as 'my brother' and gives one line about the quality of their friendship that has been quoted for three thousand years, comparing it to another kind of love and saying it surpassed it. How does David's line finish? 'Thy love to me was wonderful, passing ______.'
context: 2 Samuel 1:26 KJV: 'I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.' The line has been read as poetic hyperbole for sworn heroic brotherhood (the OT match to Achilles and Patroclus, Roland and Oliver, Fionn's Fianna) and, by other readers, as something closer -- the bank tells the story and lets the line speak.

question: In the hill country of Ephraim, between Ramah and Bethel, the prophetess who judged Israel held court and settled quarrels sitting beneath what?
context: Judges 4:5 KJV: 'And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment.' The oak and terebinth are real judgment-trees elsewhere in scripture (Abraham's oak at Mamre, Gideon's terebinth); the cedar of Lebanon is a real temple wood but no one sat under one for judgment.

question: The prophetess summoned Barak son of Abinoam and told him to gather ten thousand men against Sisera. Barak answered that he would go on only one condition. What did he demand?
answer: that the prophetess come with him
choices: that the prophetess come with him
that a lamb be offered first
that the king of Hazor be named
that the tribes of Judah lead
context: Judges 4:8 KJV: 'If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go.' Deborah agreed to go, but told him the glory of the day would not be his: the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:9).

question: Sisera, captain of Jabin king of Hazor, marched out against the Israelite muster at Mount Tabor with what fearsome force at his command?
context: Judges 4:3 KJV: 'he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel.' Iron chariots were the terror-weapon of the Canaanite lowlands; Israel's foot-levy had nothing that could stand against them on open ground.

question: Deborah drew Sisera's iron chariots down to one particular watercourse, where rain and mud swallowed his wheels and his host was routed. What was the trap?
context: Judges 4:7 KJV: 'I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his multitude.' The Song later says the Kishon swept them away. The Kidron runs by Jerusalem; the Arnon and Jabbok are east-Jordan rivers of other stories.

question: His chariots bogged and his army broken, Sisera ran on foot to a tent for shelter. Jael welcomed him in, and when he begged for water she opened a bottle and gave him what instead?
context: Judges 4:19; the Song of Deborah remembers it more richly: 'He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish' (Judges 5:25 KJV). The full stomach and the warmth of the mantle she then covered him with sent him straight to sleep.

question: Jael watched Sisera sink into sleep under the mantle. Deborah had promised the Lord would sell him into the hand of a woman. What did Jael use to kill him?
choices: a bronze dagger from his own belt
the leg-bone of a young ram
a rope drawn tight round his neck
context: Judges 4:21 KJV: 'Then Jael Heber's wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground.' Ehud killed King Eglon with a dagger and Samson killed a thousand with the jawbone of an ass; Jael's weapon was neither warrior's blade nor hero's improvisation but a peg and a mallet from her own tent.

question: Deborah's victory song does not credit Barak's spearmen or even Jael's hammer alone; it says something else fought against Sisera from the sky. What did the song claim came down against him?
context: Judges 5:20 KJV: 'They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.' Read with the next verse ('the river of Kishon swept them away'), the song turns the storm that flooded the Kishon into a cosmic army answering Deborah's call.

question: The Song of Deborah ends far from the battlefield, in a Canaanite palace, on a woman waiting at a lattice and crying 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?' Who is the song watching?
context: Judges 5:28 KJV: 'The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming?' Her wise ladies reassure her the men must be dividing the spoil ('to every man a damsel or two'); the reader knows the truth. Ending the war-hymn on a grieving enemy mother is one of the oldest and strangest moves in Hebrew poetry.

question: In the Greek myth of the seasons, Demeter is the older sister of Zeus and the mother of Persephone. Which Olympian domain is Demeter's?
context: Demeter is the Olympian goddess of grain, cereals, and the harvest. She and Zeus are siblings, children of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Source: Wikipedia (Demeter).

question: Demeter had only one child, a daughter she had by Zeus. What was this daughter's name -- the maiden whose story explains why the earth has winter?
context: Persephone (also called Kore, 'the Maiden') is the only child of Demeter and Zeus. Source: Wikipedia (Persephone).  (Legend.)

question: Persephone was gathering flowers in a meadow when she reached for one especially beautiful bloom that Earth had grown as a trap -- and the ground split open. Which flower was the lure?
context: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 8-14) describes a marvellous narcissus Earth made to grow at Zeus's will, with a hundred blooms from a single root, put there to lure the girl. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: As Persephone reached for the flower the earth split open beneath her, and out sprang a god in a golden chariot pulled by four immortal horses. He seized the girl and carried her below to be his queen. Which god took her?
context: Hades, lord of the dead and Zeus's brother, seizes Persephone in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 15-20) with Zeus's silent consent. Poseidon rules the sea, Apollo brings prophecy and the sun's light, and Hermes conducts souls to the underworld gates but does not rule there. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Demeter wandered the earth searching for her daughter for nine days and nine nights, tasting neither ambrosia nor nectar. What did she carry in her two hands as she searched?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 45-50: 'for nine days queenly Deo wandered over the earth with flaming torches in her hands.' Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Only two beings in the Homeric Hymn had heard Persephone cry out as she was seized. Demeter came first to Helios the sun-god, who had seen everything from above. Which goddess was the second witness?
context: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 24-27), only Helios the Sun and Hecate the goddess of the crossroads witnessed or heard Persephone's abduction. After the compromise, Hecate becomes Persephone's attendant in the underworld. Nyx is Night, Eos the Dawn, and Selene the Moon -- all night-sky goddesses who might plausibly have witnessed, but the Hymn names Hecate. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Disguised as an old woman, Demeter came to the town of Eleusis and was hired as nurse to the royal baby prince Demophoon. To make the child immortal she anointed him with ambrosia by day and hid him at night in the heart of one dangerous thing -- until the mother caught her. What was he hidden in?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 236-248: Demeter hid Demophoon 'like a brand in the heart of the fire.' Queen Metaneira spied by night, cried out, and stopped the rite. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Still furious over her lost daughter, Demeter blighted the whole earth. The oxen dragged the plows in vain and humans starved. But what finally forced Zeus himself to send Hermes down to fetch Persephone back?
answer: The gods received no sacrifices from the empty altars
choices: The gods received no sacrifices from the empty altars
The other Olympians rose up against Zeus
Hera demanded it as her price
context: Demeter's blight starved mortals, but the pressure that broke Zeus was divine: with no grain there were no offerings, and the Olympians received no sacrifices from the empty altars. Zeus then sent Hermes to Hades to negotiate Persephone's return. Source: Wikipedia (Demeter); Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus sent Hermes down to bring Persephone back to her mother. But Hades had slyly given the girl one thing to eat before she left -- and anyone who tastes food in the underworld cannot fully leave it. What did Hades give her?
context: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (line 371) Hades gives Persephone a single sweet pomegranate seed; Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 5) gives the number as seven, and later tradition settled on six seeds for six months. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.  (Legend.)

question: The compromise Zeus arranged: because Persephone had tasted food in the underworld, she must return there for part of every year as Hades's queen and the rest above with her mother. In the oldest version, the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, what share of each year does she spend below?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 395-400: Persephone spends 'a third part of the seasons every year' with Hades and two-thirds with Demeter. Later poets Ovid and Hyginus give half the year (six months, matching six seeds). Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: In gratitude to the royal family that had welcomed her as an old woman, Demeter revealed her secret rites to them, and taught the prince Triptolemus how to grow grain. Her rites were held for over a thousand years, and their central secret was famously never written down -- every initiate was sworn to silence. What is the name of these rites?
context: Homeric Hymn to Demeter lines 473-479: Demeter taught her rites to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, and Celeus at Eleusis. The Mysteries ran from the Mycenaean period to the 4th century AD; initiates were sworn to never reveal what they saw, and the secret was kept for the entire history of the cult. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Homeric Hymn 2.  (Legend.)

question: The Eleusinian prince who learned agriculture from Demeter did not keep the gift for Greece alone. She gave him a flying chariot to travel the world and teach farming, and it was pulled by two of the strangest animals in Greek myth. What drew Triptolemus's chariot across the sky?
context: In the fuller Eleusinian tradition, Triptolemus flew a winged serpent-drawn chariot given by Demeter and spread grain-farming across the world -- shown often in Attic vase-painting. Source: Wikipedia (Triptolemus).  (Legend.)

question: One mortal couple was warned in time to survive the great flood: a king of Phthia in Thessaly and his wife. The husband was named Deucalion. What was the name of his wife -- the woman who threw stones over her shoulder with him?
context: Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, was the wife of Deucalion and the only mortal woman to survive the flood. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly).  (Legend.)

question: Deucalion's father was a Titan who could foresee the future, and it was he who warned his son of the coming flood in time to build the chest. Which Titan was Deucalion's father?
context: Deucalion was the son of the Titan Prometheus, whose name means 'forethought' and who could foresee the future. Iapetus was Prometheus's own father; Menoetius and Atlas were his brothers. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion).  (Legend.)

question: Warned by his father Prometheus, Deucalion built a wooden chest and rode out the flood inside it with Pyrrha, drifting on the drowned world until the waters began to fall. For how many days and nights did Ovid say they floated?
context: In Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 1, Deucalion and Pyrrha float on the flood for nine days and nine nights before the waters begin to recede and the chest grounds. Forty days and nights is the length of the rain in the Noah story of Genesis. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.318-320.  (Legend.)

question: For nine days and nights Deucalion and Pyrrha floated on the drowning world until the chest at last grounded on the great mountain that towers above Delphi -- the same peak sacred to Apollo and the Muses. Which mountain did they land on in the canonical version?
context: In Ovid the chest grounds on Mount Parnassus, above Delphi in central Greece. Helicon is also sacred to the Muses; Cithaeron and Pelion are other famous mountains of Greek myth. Variant traditions of the landing name Etna, Athos, or Othrys, but Parnassus is the settled canonical landing. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.316-317.  (Legend.)

question: The oracle answered them in a chilling riddle: cover your heads, unloose your girdles, and throw behind you 'the bones of your great mother'. Deucalion thought a while and then told Pyrrha what the words really meant. What did he say the 'great mother' was?
context: Deucalion realised the great mother was the Earth (Gaia), and the bones of the Earth were stones scattered on the ground. Pyrrha at first believed the oracle was demanding she desecrate her own mother Pandora's grave. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.383-390.  (Legend.)

question: Once Deucalion had solved the oracle's riddle, the two did not simply pick up stones -- the oracle had ordered a particular ritual done to their bodies before they threw. What did they do to themselves before hurling the stones behind them?
answer: Veiled their heads and unloosed their girdles
choices: Veiled their heads and unloosed their girdles
Removed their sandals and cut their hair
Turned their faces east and knelt
context: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.381-383, the oracle commands them to cover their heads, unbind their girdles, and throw behind them the bones of their great mother. The stones Deucalion threw became men and those Pyrrha threw became women. Source: Wikipedia (Pyrrha of Thessaly); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.395-415.  (Legend.)

question: Deucalion and Pyrrha had a son whose own three sons -- Aeolus, Dorus, and Xuthus -- gave their names to the great tribes of Greece, and from him the whole Greek people took their name. What was the father's name?
context: Hellen is the eponymous ancestor of the Hellenes. His sons Aeolus, Dorus, and Xuthus (father of Achaeus and Ion) gave their names to the Aeolians, Dorians, Achaeans, and Ionians. Cadmus was the Phoenician founder of Thebes; Danaus was the ancestor of the Argives; Pelasgus was the mythic ancestor of the pre-Greek Pelasgians. Source: Wikipedia (Deucalion).  (Legend.)

question: In the Fenian Cycle, the aging warrior-leader Fionn mac Cumhaill -- now older than the High King himself -- is promised in marriage to the young and beautiful daughter of Cormac mac Airt, the High King at Tara. What is the young princess's name?
context: Grainne (pronounced GRAWN-ya) is the girl who will not have old Fionn. Sadhbh is Fionn's earlier wife, the mother of Oisin (she is a deer under enchantment); Etain is the heroine of Tochmarc Etaine in a different cycle; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife from the Ulster Cycle. All four are famous women from Irish mythology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: One of the finest young warriors in Fionn's own Fianna carries a magical beauty-mark placed on his brow by a faery woman -- the ball seirce, or 'love-spot' -- that makes any woman who catches a glimpse of it fall instantly in love with him. Who is he?
context: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne (Diarmuid of the love-spot) is one of the finest and most beloved young warriors of the Fianna. Oisin is Fionn's poet son; Caoilte mac Ronain is Fionn's runner-messenger; Goll mac Morna is Fionn's older rival within the Fianna. All four are Fenian heroes, only one carries the ball seirce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: At the betrothal feast at Tara, Grainne looks around the hall at old white-haired Fionn and refuses the match in her heart. She sees Diarmuid across the room -- his love-spot showing under a cap -- and takes decisive action. What does she do to the rest of the hall?
answer: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
choices: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
sings a lullaby that puts them to sleep
throws a druidic mist over them
sets a spell of silence on the tables
context: Grainne passes the drinking-cups herself, dosing every guest EXCEPT Diarmuid. The sleeping-cup at the feast is one of the most famous images in the tale. The other three -- lullaby-sleep, druidic mist, spell of silence -- are all real motifs elsewhere in Irish myth (druidic mist is very common), but the tool here is a straightforward drugged cup. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: With the hall asleep, Grainne goes to Diarmuid and speaks. He refuses her at first, out of loyalty to Fionn. So she binds him with an unbreakable magical vow to elope with her that same night, one he cannot refuse. What is the Irish name for this kind of unbreakable vow?
context: A geis (plural geasa) is an unbreakable magical prohibition or command in Irish myth -- to break it is to invite destruction. Grainne's geis leaves Diarmuid no choice. Fian is the warrior-band itself; rath is a ringfort; ban is a plain English word here (not the Irish word). All four sound Irish and start with the right shape -- only geis is the term for the vow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: Bound by the vow, Diarmuid takes Grainne and flees the hall at Tara. Fionn and the Fianna pursue them across Ireland for a very long time -- so long that Ireland's oral tradition remembers the exact count. About how many years does the pursuit last?
context: The pursuit is remembered as sixteen years -- long enough for Diarmuid and Grainne to have five children on the run. Seven is the standard folk-year (as in the seven years' service of Jacob); three years is the geasa-year; twenty-one is a marker in Fenian tales too. Only sixteen matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/pursuit-of-diarmuid-and-grainne.  (Legend.)

question: Diarmuid's foster-father is one of the Tuatha De Danann, master of the great passage-tomb Brugh na Boinne on the Boyne. Throughout the flight he shelters the lovers again and again with mist and trickery, and eventually mediates a peace with Fionn. Who is Diarmuid's foster-father?
context: Aengus Og (Aengus 'the Young') is the god of love, master of the great passage-tomb at Newgrange (Brugh na Boinne). Lugh Lamhfhada is the many-skilled hero; the Dagda is the 'good god' with the club and the cauldron; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god. All four are Tuatha De Danann -- only Aengus is Diarmuid's foster-father. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: Years after the peace, Fionn organises a great boar-hunt on a real Irish mountain in County Sligo -- a limestone table-mountain with a sudden northern cliff, still visible from Sligo town today. It is here that Diarmuid meets his death. Which mountain is it?
context: Ben Bulben (Beann Ghulbain, 'peak of Gulba') is a real 526-metre limestone mountain in County Sligo, its flat top and prow-like north face famous in Irish landscape (Yeats is buried in its shadow at Drumcliffe). Slieve Bloom is the mountain-range of central Ireland; Cnoc Aine is the fairy-hill of the goddess Aine in Limerick; Slieve Mish is a range in Kerry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.  (Legend.)

question: The boar on Ben Bulben is no ordinary beast. It was once a human boy, changed into an enchanted boar by a druid after being killed as a child, and set under a prophecy binding it to be the death of one Fenian warrior. In the boy's identity lies the whole tragedy. WHO was the boy?
answer: a half-brother of the doomed man
choices: a half-brother of the doomed man
a stable-boy of Cormac mac Airt
context: The half-brother -- Roc's son -- was killed as a child by Diarmuid's father Donn (crushed between his knees when Donn feared the boy was not his own); the boy's father, the druid Roc, then turned the body into a boar bound by prophecy to be Diarmuid's death. So Fionn's boar-hunt on Ben Bulben deliberately sends Diarmuid against a beast fated by druidic craft to kill him. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: The boar gores Diarmuid, but he mortally wounds it in return. Fionn arrives to find him dying. Long ago Fionn had gained a certain gift from the Salmon of Knowledge -- the ability to heal any wound with well-water, if only he carries it back to the wounded man in a very specific way. HOW must he carry it?
answer: cupped in his own two hands
choices: cupped in his own two hands
soaked into a folded oak leaf
wrung from a cloth on his sword
context: The healing-water in Fionn's cupped hands is the whole hinge of the death-scene: he CAN save Diarmuid, and the whole Fianna is watching. Fionn walks to the well three times -- and the first two times the water is gone before he reaches Diarmuid. Oak leaves, sword-cloths, and drinking-horns all appear as folk vessels elsewhere in Irish tradition, but the gift attached to Fionn is his own cupped hands. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn walks to the well twice. Both times he brings the healing water back close to Diarmuid, and both times it is gone before it can touch the wound. He goes back a third time and does deliver it -- but by then it is too late. HOW, exactly, does the water get away from Fionn on the first two trips?
answer: it slips through his cupped fingers
choices: it slips through his cupped fingers
it evaporates in the noon sun
his hound-pups drink it from the bowl
a raven of the Morrigan strikes it out of his hand
context: Fionn LETS the water fall through his cupped fingers twice on purpose -- remembering Grainne, remembering the sixteen years of pursuit, remembering the humiliation. On the third trip he brings the water, but Diarmuid has already died. It is one of the darkest moments in the Fenian Cycle: the leader murdering a friend by deliberate omission, in front of witnesses. Grainne curses Fionn when she hears, and the Fianna is never the same again. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.  (Legend.)

question: The shape of the tale -- an old king, a young queen, a young knight bound by involuntary love to elope with her, and a long pursuit -- is so close to a great Continental romance that scholars regard the Irish tale as its direct ancestor, and debate the direction of borrowing. Which later romance grew from this shape?
context: Tristan (nephew of old King Mark of Cornwall), the young Irish princess Iseult he escorts home to marry his uncle, the love-potion, the flight into the forest, the pursuit -- the beat-list matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne almost exactly. Most scholars now think the Irish material fed the Continental Tristan through Brittany. Lancelot and Guinevere is a different Arthurian love-triangle; Roland and Aude are the doomed betrothed of the Chanson de Roland; Aucassin and Nicolette is a 13th-c. French chantefable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek god Dionysus, later called Bacchus by the Romans, was the god of wild rites, madness, and one drink in particular. Which drink was Dionysus the god of?
context: Dionysus is the Greek god of wine, the grape harvest, ecstatic madness, and the theatre. His Roman name is Bacchus. Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: The jealous Hera came to Semele disguised as an old nurse and whispered that her lover might not really be a god. She told Semele to demand that Zeus prove himself by appearing to her in one particular way. What was Hera's fatal suggestion?
answer: Appear to her in his true form
choices: Appear to her in his true form
Give her a cup of ambrosia
Sacrifice a bull at her altar
Take her up to Mount Olympus
context: Hera, disguised as an old nurse (in some versions Semele's old nurse Beroe), persuades Semele to make the request that will kill her. Source: Wikipedia (Semele); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.259-315.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus had already sworn an unbreakable oath -- by the river Styx -- to grant Semele any request. He begged her not to ask this one, but he was bound. When he appeared to her in his true form, one thing about him killed her instantly. What killed Semele?
answer: The lightning of his divine glory
choices: The lightning of his divine glory
A single glance from his eyes
context: Zeus appeared to Semele with thunderbolts and lightning; the divine glory burned her to death on the spot. Source: Wikipedia (Semele); Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.308-309.  (Legend.)

question: Moving fast, Zeus snatched the unborn baby Dionysus out of Semele's burning body and carried the child to term hidden inside one part of his own body. Where did Zeus sew the baby to finish growing him?
context: Zeus sewed the unborn Dionysus into his own thigh and carried him there until he was ready to be born a second time. (Athena burst from Zeus's forehead -- a different birth story.) Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: Grown up, Dionysus travelled with a wild retinue of female followers dressed in fawnskins, carrying a fennel-stalk wand tipped with a pine cone and wound with ivy. What were these ecstatic followers called?
context: The maenads -- the name means 'raving women' -- are Dionysus's ecstatic female followers; the wand they carry is the thyrsus, a fennel stalk topped with a pine cone. Nereids are sea nymphs, oreads are mountain nymphs, and the graces are the three Charites. Source: Wikipedia (Dionysus).  (Legend.)

question: In Euripides's Bacchae, the young king of Thebes refused to accept Dionysus as a god and tried to stop his rites. Dionysus lured the king up an evergreen tree on Mount Cithaeron to spy on the maenads. What was this doomed king's name?
context: Pentheus, king of Thebes and Dionysus's own cousin, is the tragic figure of Euripides's Bacchae. Actaeon was another Theban torn apart on Cithaeron (by his own hounds after seeing Artemis bathing); Creon and Laius are other Theban kings. Source: Wikipedia (The Bacchae).  (Legend.)

question: When the maenads spotted the king spying on them from the tree, they pulled him down and tore him limb from limb in bacchic frenzy. His own mother led the killing and carried his head back to Thebes on her thyrsus, believing until the madness lifted that it was the head of one particular wild animal. What did she believe she was holding?
context: Agave, Pentheus's mother, led the maenads that tore him apart and returned to Thebes carrying his bloodied head, convinced it was a mountain lion until the divine frenzy faded. Source: Wikipedia (The Bacchae).  (Legend.)

question: Sailing across the sea one day disguised as a handsome young man, Dionysus was captured by Tyrrhenian pirates who planned to sell him as a slave. As the ship put out, vines grew up the mast, wine ran across the deck, the oars turned into serpents, and Dionysus himself took the form of a great beast on the deck. What beast did he become?
context: In Homeric Hymn 7 to Dionysus, the god takes the form of a lion (and, in some lines, creates a bear beside him) on the deck. Source: Mythopedia, Evelyn-White translation of Homeric Hymn 7.  (Legend.)

question: The terrified pirates leapt overboard to escape the god's transformations. They did not drown -- they were transformed mid-leap into another kind of sea creature entirely. What did the Tyrrhenian pirates become?
context: In Homeric Hymn 7 to Dionysus, the pirates leap overboard and are transformed into dolphins mid-leap -- said ever after to swim beside ships. Only the good helmsman, who had recognised the god and begged the crew to release him, was spared. Source: Mythopedia, Evelyn-White translation of Homeric Hymn 7.  (Legend.)

question: Dionysus later married a Cretan princess whom the hero Theseus had abandoned on the island of Naxos after she had helped him escape the Labyrinth with a ball of thread. Whom did Dionysus marry?
context: Dionysus wed Ariadne on Naxos and set her bridal crown among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis; he also brought his mother Semele up from the underworld to Olympus, where she was given the new name Thyone. Phaedra was Ariadne's sister, Europa her ancestress, Pasiphae her mother. Source: Wikipedia (Ariadne).  (Legend.)

question: In the Castilian village of Caleruega around 1170, a noblewoman named Jane of Aza was pregnant with a son. Tradition says she dreamed one night that an animal ran out of her womb carrying a burning torch in its mouth and set the world on fire. Which animal was in her dream?
context: The son grew up to be Dominic, and later a Latin pun read his order's name as Domini canes, 'the Lord's dogs'. Jane of Aza was herself later beatified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.  (Legend.)

question: As a young canon of the cathedral of Osma in Castile, Dominic traveled in 1203 with his bishop Diego through the south of France and saw a heretical movement flourishing there whose traveling preachers walked barefoot while the Catholic legates rode with baggage-trains. Which heretical movement did Dominic set himself against?
context: The Cathars, also called Albigensians after the town of Albi, were a dualist movement particularly strong in Languedoc. The Waldensians were a poverty movement of the same period; the Bogomils were the eastern dualist parent; the Iconoclasts were an earlier Byzantine controversy over images. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: Dominic gathered a small band of preachers at Toulouse, and in 1216 Pope Honorius III gave them papal approval as the Ordo Praedicatorum, the Order of Preachers. What did the Dominican habit look like?
context: The two colors gave the Dominicans their English nickname 'Blackfriars'; the white is said to stand for purity and the black for penance. The Carmelites wore brown-and-white; the Franciscans wore all-brown with a knotted cord; the Cistercians wore all-white. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: As soon as Dominic had his handful of brothers together, he scattered them across Europe to preach and to study, sending them at once to the two great universities of the age. Jordan of Saxony records the reason he gave for the risk: 'Hoarded seed does not bear fruit.' To which two university cities did Dominic send his first brothers?
context: Paris was the great northern university, Bologna the great southern one. Oxford and Cambridge were still young in 1217; Naples had no university until 1224; Salamanca and Coimbra rose later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic.

question: Nearly three centuries after Dominic was buried in Bologna, a young Florentine sculptor came into that city while fleeing the political upheaval at home and was given the commission to finish the small marble figures still missing from Dominic's tomb-arca in San Domenico. He carved a Saint Petronius, a Saint Proculus, and a candle-bearing angel there. Who was that young sculptor?
context: Michelangelo was nineteen when he fled Florence in 1494 after the expulsion of the Medici; the senator Aldrovandi sheltered him in Bologna and got him the arca commission. Nicola Pisano had begun the tomb-arca two centuries earlier; Donatello worked a generation before Michelangelo; Bernini was a 17th-century Roman. These three small figures are Michelangelo's earliest signed sculptures in Bologna. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arca_di_San_Domenico.

question: The magical gold arm-ring worn by the chief of the Norse gods earns its name from what it does over and over -- gold falls off it in fresh rings like drops of water off a wet blade. The Old Norse name simply means 'the dripper'. What is the ring called?
context: Old Norse Draupnir literally means 'the dripper'. Gungnir is Odin's spear; Andvaranaut is the cursed ring the dwarf Andvari gives up to Loki in the Volsung cycle; Gjallarhorn is Heimdall's warning-trumpet at the rainbow bridge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: The magic of Odin's ring Draupnir runs on a strict schedule -- new gold rings of equal weight fall from it at set intervals, forever. In Snorri's account, how often does the ring produce new rings, and how many at a time?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: 'every ninth night there fell from it eight gold rings of equal weight.' The number nine echoes through Norse myth -- the nine worlds of Yggdrasil, Odin's nine nights hung on the tree, Thor's nine paces after killing the World-Serpent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: During the great mourning after Baldr's death, Odin walks up to his dead son on the funeral ship Hringhorni and lays his own most precious object on the pyre with the body. WHICH of Odin's treasures does he put on Baldr's pyre?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: Odin lays Draupnir on Baldr's pyre as the last gift. Gungnir the spear he keeps for himself; Huginn is his living raven, not a burnable object; there is no wolf-pelt cloak in the myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)
