question: Loki lost the wager with Sindri and Brokkr and owed the dwarves his HEAD. He wriggled free on a technicality -- his neck, he pointed out, had not been part of the bet. Furious, the dwarf Brokkr instead did something else to Loki's face. What did Brokkr do?
answer: sewed Loki's lips shut with wire
choices: sewed Loki's lips shut with wire
cut off Loki's beard at the chin
branded Loki's cheek with the anvil
poured molten gold in Loki's ear
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr took an awl and thread and sewed Loki's lips shut with wire, silencing the trickster (at least until Loki ripped the thread out). No branding, beard-cutting, or gold-pouring appears in this scene. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: In the Poetic Edda's Skirnismal, Freyr the fertility god falls in love with a giantess from Jotunheim and sends his servant Skirnir to woo her. Skirnir arrives with a bag of bribes, including Odin's dripping ring itself. Which giantess is Skirnir sent to?
context: Skirnismal 21-22: Skirnir offers Gerd eleven golden apples and Draupnir the dripping ring; she refuses gold and only yields under threat of a magic curse. Skadi is Njord's giantess-wife; Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover, mother of Fenrir; Hyrrokkin is the giantess who launched Baldr's ship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupnir  (Legend.)

question: The Song of Roland is the great French epic of the paladin Roland, nephew of Charlemagne, who dies at the pass of Roncesvalles. Throughout the poem Roland carries a single named sword that he treasures more than his own life. What is the name of Roland's sword?
context: Roland's sword in the Chanson de Roland is Durandal, called the sharpest blade in Charlemagne's army. Joyeuse is Charlemagne's OWN sword (a separate weapon in the same poem). Tizona is one of the two swords of El Cid. Excalibur is King Arthur's sword. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'; Wikipedia, 'Song of Roland'.  (Legend.)

question: Roland's sword Durandal is named for a quality the poem prizes above sharpness or speed. The word 'Durandal' comes from the Latin root DURARE. What does that root mean -- what quality is Durandal named for?
answer: to endure -- Durandal is 'the enduring one'
choices: to endure -- Durandal is 'the enduring one'
to strike -- Durandal is 'the striking one'
to shine -- Durandal is 'the shining one'
to sing -- Durandal is 'the singing one'
context: Durandal comes from the French 'dur' (hard) and Latin 'durare' (to endure), yielding 'the enduring one' or 'the hard one'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'.  (Legend.)

question: Roland's sword Durandal is also a portable RELIQUARY. Its hilt is described in the Chanson de Roland as being hollow, and packed inside the pommel are holy fragments taken from famous saints -- a piece of the Virgin Mary's robe among them. Which apostle's TOOTH is also named in the poem as sealed inside the hilt?
context: Song of Roland, laisse 173: the hilt of Durandal holds a tooth of Saint PETER, the blood of Saint Basil, the hair of Saint Denis, and a scrap of the Virgin Mary's robe. Peter was the chief of the apostles for the medieval church, which is why his relic tops the collection. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'.  (Legend.)

question: Charlemagne, the emperor Roland serves, also carries a famous named sword in the Song of Roland -- a separate blade from his nephew's, said in the poem to shine like the sun and change colour thirty times a day. What is the name of Charlemagne's sword?
context: Joyeuse means 'the joyful one' -- it is Charlemagne's own sword in the chanson tradition, described as changing colour thirty times a day and shining like the sun. Curtana is the sword of mercy carried at English coronations. Notung and Balmung are two names for Sigurd's sword in the Volsung / Nibelung cycle. Source: Wikipedia, 'Joyeuse'.  (Legend.)

question: At the pass of Roncesvalles the rearguard of Charlemagne's army is broken. Roland lies dying, and he realises that his sword must not be captured by the enemy and turned against Christian knights. He rises up one last time to destroy Durandal himself. What does the dying Roland do to try to destroy the sword?
answer: smashes it against a great rock at his side
choices: smashes it against a great rock at his side
throws it into a deep gorge below the pass
buries it under a heap of the fallen
sets it in the flames of a burning cart
context: Song of Roland: with his last strength Roland brings Durandal down again and again on the rock beside him, meaning to shatter the blade so that no pagan hand can carry it home. Source: Medievalists.net, 'Roland's Sword Goes Missing'.  (Legend.)

question: As the dying Roland strikes Durandal against the great rock at his side, something astonishing happens under the blade. What does the ROCK itself do as Roland brings Durandal down on it?
choices: melts to slag around the point
swallows the blade to the hilt
rings out like a struck bell
context: The stone cracks and shatters under Durandal's edge, but the blade itself does not break -- that is the moment Durandal earns its name of 'the enduring one'. Roland cannot destroy the sword no matter how hard he tries. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'; Song of Roland.  (Legend.)

question: After Roland has failed to break Durandal on the rock, he lies at the point of death and turns his face in one deliberate direction, so that Charlemagne will find him fallen forward and still on the attack. In which direction does the dying Roland turn his face?
context: Song of Roland: unable to break the sword, Roland hides Durandal beneath his body and lies down with his face turned toward Spain -- toward the enemy -- so that Charlemagne, returning, will find him fallen forward, still on the attack rather than in retreat. Aachen was Charlemagne's northern capital, which would have signalled flight. Source: Wikipedia, 'Song of Roland'.  (Legend.)

question: Later medieval legend gave Durandal a much older lineage than the Chanson de Roland alone allowed -- it named a hero of the ancient world as the sword's ORIGINAL owner, long before it passed through many hands and came at last to Roland. Which hero of the ancient world was said in these later legends to have wielded Durandal first?
context: In later chivalric tradition Durandal is said to have belonged to Hector of Troy first, and to have passed through a chain of owners across centuries before reaching Roland. This is a typical medieval move -- tying the great weapons of French chivalric myth back to the Trojan founding-legends of European kingship. Achilles carried the shield made by Hephaestus and (later) armour taken from Patroclus's corpse. Aeneas carried a shield forged by Vulcan. Source: Wikipedia, 'Durendal'.

question: In the forests of Boeotia, a mountain nymph could no longer speak first. She could only wait for someone else to talk, then repeat their last words back. What was the name of the nymph cursed to only repeat what others said?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.359-401. Echo is an oread (mountain nymph). Daphne is the nymph turned into a laurel to escape Apollo; Calypso keeps Odysseus seven years on Ogygia; Arethusa is the nymph turned into a spring in Sicily to escape the river-god Alpheus. The English word 'echo' -- a repeating voice -- comes directly from her name.  (Legend.)

question: There was a beautiful young hunter in the same Boeotian forest, so cold to every girl and boy who loved him that they all went away in tears -- and one spurned lover finally prayed to Nemesis against him. What was the name of this beautiful, cruel young hunter?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-350, 3.404-406. His father was the river Cephissus, his mother the nymph Liriope. Adonis is the beautiful youth Aphrodite loved, killed by a boar; Hyacinthus is the youth Apollo killed by accident with a discus; Endymion is the shepherd the Moon loved in his sleep. The English word 'narcissism' -- love of self -- comes from Narcissus.  (Legend.)

question: When Narcissus was born, his mother Liriope carried him to the Theban seer who would one day speak to Odysseus in the underworld, and asked whether her child would live to old age. The seer gave a strange, riddling answer nobody understood at the time. Who was the seer she asked?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-348. Tiresias is the Theban seer of the Odyssey and of Sophocles. Calchas is the Greek seer at Troy; Melampus is an earlier seer of Argos; Amphiaraus is the seer of the Seven Against Thebes. Tiresias's answer -- that the boy would live long only if he never came to know himself -- would prove exact.  (Legend.)

question: Echo followed the beautiful hunter through the trees, longing to speak but unable to begin. He called out 'Is anyone here?' -- she called back 'Here!' -- 'Come!' 'Come!' -- 'Let us come together!' 'Let us come together!' She stepped out to embrace him -- and what did he say to her?
answer: 'I would rather die than have you touch me'
choices: 'I would rather die than have you touch me'
'Away, foul thing -- I have vowed to Artemis'
'Speak first, or leave me in peace'
'You are a shade -- return to the wood'
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.379-392. Narcissus shoves Echo away with the words 'I would rather die than have you touch me' -- and she can only cry back the last words, then flee and hide her face in the leaves. She wastes away until only her voice is left.  (Legend.)

question: One of the boys Narcissus had rejected lifted his hands to the sky and prayed a specific prayer against him -- 'May he love as I have loved, and never win the loved one'. Which goddess heard the prayer and answered it?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.404-406. Nemesis is the goddess of righteous retribution -- the punisher of pride. Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft and crossroads; Eris is strife (the golden apple at the wedding of Peleus); Ate is reckless folly. Nemesis's answer will fall on Narcissus at a clear pool in the woods.  (Legend.)

question: On a hot day, tired from the hunt, Narcissus knelt at a clear pool to drink. As he bent down he saw a beautiful face rising to meet him from the water -- and he did not realise one thing about that face. What did Narcissus fail to realise about the face in the pool?
choices: it was the ghost of a rejected lover
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.407-436. Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection without knowing what he is looking at -- and Nemesis's answer, and Tiresias's oracle, both come true in that instant.  (Legend.)

question: Narcissus leaned down again and again -- tried to kiss the face and to embrace it -- but every time he touched the water something happened that made him weep. What happened each time Narcissus reached for the face in the pool?
answer: the water rippled and the arms in it dissolved at his touch
choices: the water rippled and the arms in it dissolved at his touch
a cold hand from the pool pushed his own hand away
the face closed its eyes and turned aside from him
a black fish rose up between them and hid the face
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.427-436. Every reach broke the surface -- so the beautiful arms in the water reached back to him and dissolved the instant he touched them. Narcissus refused to leave the pool, unable to eat, unable to sleep, weeping for a body that vanished at his fingertips.  (Legend.)

question: Narcissus lay dying at the pool day and night, unable to eat or leave. Echo -- still nothing but a voice -- watched him from the trees. When he cried out his last words to himself, what could she do?
answer: repeat his 'Alas!' and 'Farewell!' back to him
choices: repeat his 'Alas!' and 'Farewell!' back to him
step out at last and lay her hands on his face
sing his mother Liriope to the pool
call up Nemesis to break the curse
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.494-501. Echo's curse still held -- she could not speak first, could not comfort him, could only give back the last words: 'Alas!' -- 'Alas!' -- 'Farewell!' -- 'Farewell!' Two doomed lovers, each stranded from the object of longing, one at the pool and one in the trees.  (Legend.)

question: The nymphs came for the boy's body to burn it on a pyre, but where he had lain by the water they found no body at all -- only a small flower with white petals and a golden centre, growing at the edge of the pool. What is that flower still called?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.509-510. The nymphs found only the flower we still call the narcissus. The hyacinth grew from the blood of Hyacinthus (Apollo's discus); the anemone from the blood of Adonis (the boar); the crocus from the youth Crocus who loved the nymph Smilax. Three flowers from three doomed loves; Narcissus's is the one that loved only itself.  (Legend.)

question: The great Castilian hero of the eleventh-century Reconquista was born RODRIGO DIAZ in the village of Vivar near Burgos. He became so famous as a warrior that both his Christian countrymen and his Muslim enemies gave him the same nickname -- the one by which the whole world remembers him today. What is the nickname by which Rodrigo Diaz is remembered?
context: Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar (c. 1043-1099) is called El Cid ('the lord' -- see the next rung for the language it comes from). El Conquistador ('the conqueror') is the standard title given to the New World Spanish invaders of centuries later. El Rey means 'the king'; El Caballero means 'the knight' -- both generic titles, not his nickname. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: The oldest surviving Castilian epic poem, the Cantar de Mio Cid (c. 1207), opens on Rodrigo Diaz weeping. He is weeping because his king has just unjustly ordered him into exile from all Castile on the whispers of enemies at court. Which king of Leon and Castile pronounces the exile that opens the poem?
context: Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile (r. 1065-1109) exiled the historical Rodrigo Diaz twice, in 1081 and 1089; the Cantar de Mio Cid conflates the two into one dramatic opening exile. Alfonso VII was Alfonso VI's grandson. Sancho II of Castile was Alfonso VI's brother, murdered before the story starts. Ferdinand I was Alfonso VI's father. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part I; Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: The exiled Rodrigo Diaz did not sulk in the wilderness. He had to feed the small band of men who followed him into exile, so he raised his sword for pay wherever it was wanted. The historical Cid was for a time in the pay of the Muslim EMIRS of which Iberian city, fighting for them against both Christians and other Muslims?
context: For years in his historical exile the Cid served the Muslim Banu Hud emirs of ZARAGOZA in the Ebro valley, campaigning for them against neighbouring Christian and Muslim powers alike. The Cantar tidies this into a purely Christian arc; the history is messier. Cordoba was by then a fading caliphate remnant, Granada and Seville were rival Taifa emirates the Cid did NOT serve. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: In the Cantar de Mio Cid, Rodrigo carries TWO named swords, and both are given the honour of a proper name of their own. One is called COLADA, won in battle from the Count of Barcelona. What is the name of the OTHER of the Cid's two swords, the one he won from the Moroccan king Bucar?
context: The Cid's two named swords in the Cantar are COLADA (from the Count of Barcelona) and TIZONA (from king Bucar of Morocco). Durandal is Roland's sword; Joyeuse is Charlemagne's; Curtana is the English coronation sword of mercy -- all real named blades from other traditions. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tizona'.  (Legend.)

question: The great victory the historical Cid is remembered for is his siege and capture in 1094 of one of the richest cities of Muslim al-Andalus -- he then ruled it as his own princedom until his death there in 1099. Which city did Rodrigo Diaz take in 1094?
context: The Cid took Valencia in 1094 after a long siege and ruled it as his own princedom until his death there in 1099. Toledo had already been taken by Alfonso VI in 1085. Cordoba fell to Ferdinand III much later, in 1236. Malaga was taken by the Catholic Monarchs at the very end of the Reconquista, in 1487. Source: Britannica, 'El Cid'.

question: The third and last cantar of the Poem of My Cid centres not on more battles but on a wrong done to Rodrigo's two DAUGHTERS by their new husbands, the Infantes de Carrion. What did the Infantes do to the daughters that turns the whole final third of the poem?
answer: stripped, beat, and abandoned them in a forest
choices: stripped, beat, and abandoned them in a forest
poisoned them at a banquet in Carrion
sold them into slavery in Africa
shut them up in a convent at Leon
context: Cantar III: the Infantes de Carrion take Elvira and Sol into the oak-wood of Corpes, strip them, beat them mercilessly with their belts and spurs, and leave them for dead. It is a shocking scene by any age's standards. The daughters are rescued by their cousin Felez Munoz and the Cid demands justice from King Alfonso. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part VI.  (Legend.)

question: At the close of the Poem of My Cid, once the Infantes de Carrion are shamed and defeated, Alfonso VI arranges MUCH better second marriages for Rodrigo's two daughters. The poem says with pride that from these second marriages descend all the Christian kings of Spain thereafter. To the princes of which two Iberian kingdoms are Elvira and Sol re-married at the end of the poem?
context: Cantar III's closing lines re-marry Elvira and Sol to the princes of Navarre and Aragon; the poem claims this is why 'today the kings of Spain descend from Mio Cid'. The other pairs are real Iberian kingdoms of the age but not the ones the poem names. Source: Poetry in Translation, El Cantar de mio Cid Part VI.  (Legend.)

question: The Museum of Burgos displays an eleventh-century sword long identified as one of Rodrigo Diaz's own two named blades. In 2007 the regional government of Castile and Leon paid 1.6 million euros to keep the blade in Spain and put it on public display, though academic historians still argue over whether it really was the Cid's. Which of the Cid's two swords is the Burgos blade venerated as?
answer: Tizona -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
choices: Tizona -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
Colada -- the one from the Count of Barcelona
Tizona -- the one from the Count of Barcelona
Colada -- the one from king Bucar of Morocco
context: The Burgos sword is TIZONA -- the sword won from king Bucar of Morocco. It is an eleventh-century blade the regional government bought in 2007 for 1.6 million euros. Its bill of ownership traces back through Spanish noble families but the identification with the Cid's actual sword is disputed by historians. Colada, the other of the Cid's two swords, was the one taken from the Count of Barcelona -- no surviving blade is claimed as Colada. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tizona'.

question: The prophet Elijah the Tishbite stands before King Ahab of Israel and swears there will be no dew and no rain in the land except by his word. God then tells him to slip away and hide by a brook east of the Jordan, where he can drink from the water. What creatures does God send to feed him bread and flesh there, morning and evening?
context: 1 Kings 17:6 KJV: 'And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook.' The brook is called Cherith. Ravens are ritually unclean birds in the law -- part of the story's shock is that unclean birds keep God's own prophet alive.

question: Elijah has sworn before King Ahab of Israel that no rain will fall except by his word. From that moment God keeps the prophet fed and hidden -- by a brook east of the Jordan, with wild birds bringing him meals at sunrise and sunset. Ahab's foreign-born queen is the one driving the hunt for Elijah's life, and she is killing the prophets of the LORD across Israel. Who is she?
context: 1 Kings 16:31; 18:4, 13. Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and she was cutting down the prophets of the LORD while Elijah was in hiding. Athaliah is her daughter, later queen of Judah; Bathsheba is Solomon's mother; Delilah belongs to the Samson story.

question: God tells the fugitive prophet Elijah to leave Israel and stay with a widow in a town of Sidon -- inside the homeland of the very queen who is killing the prophets of Israel. What is the widow's town called?
context: 1 Kings 17:9. Zarephath sits between Tyre and Sidon. Tyre is the other great Phoenician city; Tishbe is Elijah's own hometown ('the Tishbite'); Shunem will appear later in Elisha's stories.

question: Elijah arrives at the gate of the foreign town and calls to a widow gathering firewood; he asks her for water and a bite of bread. She swears she has nothing baked, only a scrap of flour and a little oil left in the house. She has come out for the last time, she says, to gather enough wood to bake one final little cake for herself and her son before they starve. How many sticks does the widow say she is gathering?
choices: As many as her arms could hold
context: 1 Kings 17:12 KJV: 'behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.' The number matters -- two sticks is barely a fire, and it makes the widow's poverty concrete.

question: At the widow's house Elijah promises that if she bakes him a little cake first, God has said her stores will not run out until the day rain returns. In the KJV, what two everyday household containers become the sign of the miracle?
answer: A barrel of meal and a cruse of oil
choices: A barrel of meal and a cruse of oil
A jar of meal and a flask of oil
A sack of meal and a jug of oil
A pot of meal and a horn of oil
context: 1 Kings 17:14 KJV: 'The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.' The 'cruse' is a small clay flask; the 'barrel' is a large storage jar. Modern translations often say 'jar of flour and jug of oil' -- the barrel/cruse pairing is the KJV's signature phrasing.

question: Time passes; the flour and oil have not run out. Then the widow's son falls sick and stops breathing. Elijah carries the boy up to the loft where he is staying, lays him on his own bed, and stretches himself out on the child, crying to God. How many times does the story say he stretches himself upon the boy?
context: 1 Kings 17:21 KJV: 'And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the LORD.' Seven and forty are recurring biblical numbers in other stories -- seven for Naaman's dips, forty for the wilderness -- so all three feel plausible until you know the verse.

question: The widow's boy is dead in the upper room. Elijah has stretched himself on the child three times and cried to God. The child's breath returns; the prophet carries him back down the stairs and hands him to his mother. In the KJV, what does Elijah say to her as he gives back the boy?
context: 1 Kings 17:23 KJV. This is the first raising-of-the-dead scene in the Hebrew Bible; Elisha will do the same thing later for the Shunammite woman's boy. 'Rise up and walk' and 'Thy faith hath saved him' come from the New Testament (the paralytic and the woman with the issue of blood).

question: While Elijah is in hiding and Jezebel is killing prophets across the land, King Ahab's own steward -- a man named Obadiah, who secretly fears God -- gathers a hundred prophets and hides them in caves, feeding them bread and water. In the story, how does he split them between hiding places?
context: 1 Kings 18:4 KJV: 'Obadiah took an hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.' Two caves, fifty each. Obadiah is Ahab's governor of the household -- the parallel to Elijah is deliberate: God is feeding his prophet with ravens, and this quiet insider is feeding a hundred more with bread and water.

question: The New Testament twice looks back at Elijah's drought and gives a specific length: once in Luke, when Jesus reminds the crowd at Nazareth of the widows in Israel in those days, and once in the letter of James, when he cites Elijah as a model of prayer. In both verses, how long is the drought said to have lasted?
context: Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 KJV both give 'three years and six months.' 1 Kings itself only says 'in the third year' the word came to Elijah to return (1 Kings 18:1) -- the exact 3.5-year figure is the New Testament's gloss, which is why later Christian tradition speaks of a three-and-a-half-year drought.

question: The young shepherd David is summoned to King Saul's court because the king is being tormented by a spirit that makes him rage. David plays for him, and the king is 'refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.' What is the instrument David is playing in the story?
context: 1 Samuel 16:23 KJV. The Hebrew word is kinnor -- technically a small lyre rather than a modern concert harp, but the KJV chose 'harp,' and that is the word the story is remembered by (David the harpist, the Psalms as harp-songs).

question: The prophet Elijah has been told his time is nearly up. He finds his chosen successor, Elisha son of Shaphat, plowing in a field with twelve yoke of oxen -- that is, twenty-four beasts. Elijah passes by and, without a word, casts the sign of his prophet's office over the young man's shoulders. What is that object called in the story?
context: 1 Kings 19:19 KJV: 'Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.' Elijah's own look is described later: 'an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins' (2 Kings 1:8) -- but the specific object that names the prophet's office, and that Elisha will later inherit at the Jordan, is the mantle.

question: Elijah's own everyday look is described in only one verse -- a passerby recognizes him from it. The king asks 'what manner of man was he?' and the servants answer that he was a hairy man wearing a specific belt (KJV: 'girdle') about his loins. Centuries later, when John the Baptist appears out of the wilderness, he wears the same signature belt with a garment of camel's hair. What is the girdle made of?
context: 2 Kings 1:8 KJV: 'He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins.' Matthew 3:4 says John the Baptist wore 'a leathern girdle about his loins,' the same phrase word-for-word. When the crowds thought John was Elijah come back, this outfit was the reason.

question: King Solomon builds the temple in Jerusalem and sets up two enormous bronze columns in front of the porch of the sanctuary. Each is given its own proper name. The right-hand pillar is called 'he shall establish' and the left-hand one is called 'in him is strength.' Under what two names does the story remember them?
context: 1 Kings 7:21 KJV. Jachin (right) means 'he shall establish'; Boaz (left) means 'in him is strength.' Urim and Thummim were the two lots on the high priest's breastplate; Alpha and Omega belongs to the Book of Revelation; Cherubim and Seraphim are ranks of angels.

question: The strangeness of the biblical named objects is that some of them are just alive. In one story, a wooden rod for each tribe of Israel is placed overnight before the ark to settle a dispute among the tribes. In the morning one rod has grown -- it has budded, blossomed, and even yielded ripe almonds. Whose rod is it?
choices: the rod of the tribe of Judah
context: Numbers 17:8 KJV: 'the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds.' Moses's rod is famous for turning into a serpent and for striking the rock; 'the rod of Jesse' is a phrase from Isaiah 11 about David's line; the tribe of Judah had a rod placed alongside the others -- but only Aaron's, for the house of Levi, budded and bore almonds, marking Levi as the priestly tribe.

question: The old prophet Elijah walks up to a young farmer named Elisha son of Shaphat, who is working in his father's field behind a huge team of animals drawing the plow. Without a word Elijah throws his hairy prophet's garment across the young man's shoulders. What is this garment called, the object that becomes the sign that Elisha will take Elijah's place?
context: 1 Kings 19:19 KJV: 'Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.' Elisha then slaughters his oxen, boils the flesh over the burning plow-wood, feeds the people, and follows Elijah as his servant. The mantle is the physical sign of the succession -- and the same cloak will later part the Jordan for Elisha.

question: The young farmer Elisha has just been called by Elijah. To show he is not going back, he slaughters his own oxen and gives a farewell feast to his village. What does the KJV say he uses as firewood to boil the meat -- a no-turning-back gesture aimed at his old life?
context: 1 Kings 19:21 KJV: 'and took a yoke of oxen, and slew them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen.' The 'instruments' are the plow-gear -- the wooden yokes and plow-frame. Elisha is deliberately burning the tools of his old life so he cannot return to it.

question: Elijah and Elisha have crossed the Jordan on dry ground; the older prophet asks his successor what final gift he would want before he is taken away. Elisha does not ask for silver, or for long life, or for a kingdom -- he asks for a particular measure of Elijah's own prophetic power. In the King James Bible, what is the exact phrase Elisha uses for what he wants?
answer: A double portion of thy spirit
choices: A double portion of thy spirit
A share of thy prophetic gift
All the strength thou canst spare me
The full weight of thy anointing
context: 2 Kings 2:9 KJV: 'let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.' The 'double portion' echoes an Israelite inheritance law -- the firstborn son received a double share of the father's estate. Elisha is asking to be treated as the firstborn heir of Elijah.

question: The prophet Elisha climbs the road up to the town of Bethel. A gang of small children pours out of the town and mocks him with a jeering taunt they shout at him, twice. The King James Version records the exact words. What did they shout at him?
choices: 'Where is the word of the LORD?'
context: 2 Kings 2:23 KJV. They shout it twice: 'Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.' The 'go up' is likely a jeer about Elijah having been taken up in the whirlwind -- as if to say, 'why don't you go up too and leave us alone?' Compare the taunt Amaziah's priest throws at Amos: 'Get thee hence, thou seer' (Amos 7:12).

question: The children at Bethel have jeered at the prophet Elisha for his bald head. Elisha turns, looks at them, and curses them in the name of the LORD. Out of the woods come two she-bears and tear a specific number of the children. The number is one of the hardest and most quoted specifics in the whole story. How many children do the bears maul?
context: 2 Kings 2:24 KJV: 'and tare forty and two children of them.' The bears are SHE-bears, and there are two of them, and the count is forty-two. The story is deliberately disturbing -- the bank tells it as it is, without softening.

question: A young prophet is chopping wood by the Jordan when his borrowed axe head slips off the handle, splashes into the river, and sinks. He cries out to Elisha in a panic -- he borrowed the tool and cannot afford to replace it. Elisha cuts a stick, throws it into the water at the spot, and something impossible happens. What?
answer: The iron head floats up to the surface
choices: The iron head floats up to the surface
A great fish carries the head to shore in its mouth
The river dries in a circle around the sinking spot
An angel appears standing on the water holding the head
context: 2 Kings 6:6 KJV: 'And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim.' 'The iron did swim' is one of the strangest four-word phrases in the Old Testament -- the whole miracle is that iron floated, which iron does not do.

question: The Syrian general Naaman has been told by Elisha's messenger to go dip in the Jordan seven times to cure his leprosy. Naaman rages -- the muddy Jordan is nothing next to the great rivers back home in Damascus. In the King James Bible, what are the two Damascus rivers he names, insisting they are better than 'all the waters of Israel'?
context: 2 Kings 5:12 KJV: 'Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?' Naaman's servants talk him down, he wades in and dips seven times, and 'his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child.'

question: A wealthy woman of Shunem keeps feeding Elisha whenever he passes through her town. She tells her husband the prophet is a holy man, and together they build him a private guest-room up on the wall of their house. In the King James Bible, four pieces of furniture are named specifically as what they put in the little chamber for him. Which set does the story list?
answer: A bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
choices: A bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
A pallet, a jug, a bench, and a hanging lamp
A cot, a chest, a footstool, and an oil-lamp
A couch, a bowl, a chair, and a brazier
context: 2 Kings 4:10 KJV: 'Let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick.' The specific four-item list is why the story is remembered -- 'the Shunammite's little chamber' becomes a proverb for hospitality to holy men.

question: Elisha's servant Gehazi is a real problem. When his master refuses payment from the great Syrian general for the leprosy cure, Gehazi secretly runs after the general and lies -- says his master needs silver and clothes for two visiting young prophets. He pockets the silver. When he returns, Elisha already knows and pronounces a terrible curse. What does the KJV say happens to Gehazi?
answer: Naaman's leprosy cleaves unto him and unto his seed for ever
choices: Naaman's leprosy cleaves unto him and unto his seed for ever
His hands turn as leprous as Miriam's when she mocked Moses
A leprosy breaks out in his brow like Uzziah's at the altar
The plague that killed the firstborn of Egypt falls upon his house
context: 2 Kings 5:27 KJV: 'The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever. And he went out from his presence a leper as white as snow.' The moral is on the surface: the disease is transferable but so is the greed that draws it.

question: The rich Shunammite woman's promised son grows up and one day, out in the harvest field, cries to his father that his head hurts. He is carried home to his mother's lap and dies at noon. She rides out to fetch Elisha; the prophet comes, sends everyone out, and lies down upon the dead child. The child comes back to life -- and in the King James Bible he does one particular thing a specific number of times before he opens his eyes. What is it?
context: 2 Kings 4:35 KJV: 'and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.' The sneezing detail is one of the most oddly specific miracle-endings in the Bible -- kids remember it because sneezes are the last thing you expect from a resurrection story.

question: Even after Elisha's death the story is not done with him. Years later, during a burial in Israel, a Moabite raiding party is spotted rushing down on the funeral. The mourners panic and shove the corpse into the nearest tomb -- which turns out to be Elisha's own. What happens the moment the dead man touches the prophet's bones?
answer: The dead man revives and stands up on his feet
choices: The dead man revives and stands up on his feet
The bones flare with fire and consume the whole corpse
The tomb seals shut and the raiders retreat in terror
The corpse turns to salt and the stone tomb splits open
context: 2 Kings 13:21 KJV: 'when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.' Elisha's miracles keep going after his death -- the closing beat of his whole cycle, and the reason his bones were later treated as holy relics in Christian tradition.

question: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, one of the great foretales of the Tain is a courtship-story rather than a battle-tale: Cu Chulainn's own wooing of the young woman he chose above every daughter of Ireland. What is the tale called in Old Irish?
context: Tochmarc Emire means 'The Wooing of Emer' -- one of the great foretales of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Longes mac nUislenn is 'The Exile of the Sons of Uisliu' (Deirdre's tale); Serglige Con Culainn is 'The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn' (the Fand tale); Aided Con Culainn is 'The Death of Cu Chulainn'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: Emer's father hated the match and did not want any Ulster warrior for a son-in-law. Rather than refuse Cu Chulainn to his face he DISGUISED HIMSELF, travelled to King Conchobar's court, and told the young hero that no warrior of his promise was complete without training abroad -- with the warrior-woman Scathach on the Isle of Shadow. What was the father's real hope in sending him?
answer: that Cu Chulainn would die on the perilous journey
choices: that Cu Chulainn would die on the perilous journey
that Scathach would refuse him and shame him home
that a rival hero would seize Emer while he was away
that the sea-voyage would humble his pride
context: The father-in-disguise trick is the whole engine of Tochmarc Emire and the reason Cu Chulainn ends up trained by Scathach. The father assumed he would never return; he did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: The father who set the Isle of Shadow trap for Cu Chulainn had a fort at Lusk in what is now north County Dublin. When the young warrior returned alive from a year's training with Scathach, he came straight back for the daughter. What was the name of the father who had tried to kill him?
context: Forgall Manach ('Forgall the Wily') was chief of Lusk. Ailill mac Mata is King Medb's husband at Cruachan; Daire mac Fiachna is the Ulster owner of the Brown Bull of Cooley; Sualtam mac Roich is Cu Chulainn's own mortal father. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emer  (Legend.)

question: When Cu Chulainn returned from Scathach he stormed the Wily One's fort at Lusk. Twenty-four of the fort's warriors fell in the fight; the girl was carried off and the treasure with her. But the master of the fort himself died in a way that had nothing to do with Cu Chulainn's sword. How did Forgall Manach die?
answer: he fell from the ramparts of his own fort trying to escape
choices: he fell from the ramparts of his own fort trying to escape
he choked on the poisoned cup he had prepared for the raider
he drowned in the fort's own well hiding from the sack
he was crushed by his own gate as he swung it shut
context: The trap-setter died by his own walls -- narrative justice the Irish sagas are fond of. The three wrong choices are invented parallels. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: Long after the wooing, in the tale Serglige Con Culainn ('The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn'), Cu Chulainn fell into love with a woman of the sea-people -- the wife of Manannan mac Lir himself. Emer came to the meeting with a troop of women armed with knives, meaning to kill her rival. What did Emer do when she saw the strength of the fairy woman's love for Cu Chulainn?
answer: she decided to give her husband up to her
choices: she decided to give her husband up to her
she stabbed the fairy woman where she stood
she cursed her husband and left the country
she asked the druids to divide his years between them
context: Emer's magnanimity is the turn of the tale. Moved in return by Emer's magnanimity, the fairy woman decides not to take Cu Chulainn and returns to her own husband. The other three are invented parallels of the same shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: The name of Cu Chulainn's fairy-lover in Serglige Con Culainn -- the woman Emer confronted with a troop of knife-armed noblewomen and then, seeing the strength of her love, decided to give her husband up to -- is one of the most famous names in the Ulster Cycle. What was the fairy woman called?
context: Fand is the sea-fairy of Serglige Con Culainn, wife of Manannan mac Lir. Aife is the warrior-queen who bore Cu Chulainn's son Connla; Uathach is Scathach's daughter; Sadhbh is Fionn's wife in the later Fenian Cycle (mother of Oisin). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: At the end of Serglige Con Culainn, once the sea-fairy has gone home, one god of the Tuatha De comes forward and does one specific act between Cu Chulainn and the woman he has just given up, so that the two will never see each other again in this world. Which god acts, and what does he do?
answer: Manannan mac Lir shakes his cloak between them
choices: Manannan mac Lir shakes his cloak between them
Lugh Lamhfhada casts his spear between them
the Dagda plays his harp until she forgets
Aengus Og calls his four swans to carry her away
context: Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god and the fairy woman's own husband; his shaken cloak (an-fharraige) is the sea itself set forever between Cu Chulainn and Fand. Cu Chulainn and Emer then drink a druid's potion of forgetting. Lugh's spear, the Dagda's harp, and Aengus's swans are all real Tuatha powers but do the wrong work. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serglige_Con_Culainn  (Legend.)

question: A stranger falls in beside the two travellers on the Emmaus road and asks what they are talking about. He walks and talks with them for nearly the whole seven miles -- and they never realise who he is. Luke gives one specific short reason. What does Luke say?
answer: their eyes were holden that they should not know him
choices: their eyes were holden that they should not know him
the noonday sun stood full in front of their faces
he had wrapped a traveller's cloak over his head
a great dust rose up around him on the road
context: Luke 24:16 KJV: 'But their eyes were holden that they should not know him.' Luke names the reason directly -- not weather, not disguise. 'Holden' is an old English past-participle of 'hold', meaning 'kept'.

question: The two disciples reach the village at evening and invite the stranger to stay for the meal. He sits down at the table, takes bread, blesses it, and breaks it -- and IN THAT MOMENT Luke says something specific happens to the two disciples. What?
answer: their eyes were opened, and they knew him
choices: their eyes were opened, and they knew him
the room shook, and a voice spoke
the bread turned into flame in his hands
a white dove flew down through the doorway
context: Luke 24:31 KJV: 'And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight.' The recognition happens over broken bread, and Jesus disappears the same instant -- one full beat. The other three details are invented.

question: After the stranger has vanished out of their sight, the two Emmaus travellers look at each other and say one memorable line about what they had FELT during the long conversation on the road. What did they say to each other?
answer: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way
choices: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way
Surely the Lord was in this place, and we knew it not
Blessed be his name from generation to generation
How is it that we have not perceived until this hour
context: Luke 24:32 KJV: 'And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' The 'surely the Lord was in this place' line is Jacob at Bethel in Genesis 28; the other two are invented.

question: That same Sunday evening the frightened disciples are gathered together behind LOCKED DOORS 'for fear of the Jews'. Jesus suddenly stands among them, doors still shut, and speaks first. What is his opening word to the terrified room, according to John 20:19?
context: John 20:19 KJV: 'came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.' 'Weep not for me' is on the way to the crucifixion in Luke 23; 'Follow me' is the calling of the fishermen; 'Behold, it is I' is close to but not the wording of the walking-on-water scene.

question: The apostle called 'Doubting Thomas' in English tradition is called something else in John's Greek: a nickname that means 'twin'. What Greek nickname does John 20:24 give him?
context: John 20:24 KJV: 'But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.' Didymus is Greek for 'twin' (no one knows who Thomas's twin was). Boanerges ('sons of thunder') is what Jesus nicknamed James and John in Mark 3; Iscariot is Judas's second name; Barabbas is the prisoner released instead of Jesus.

question: Thomas is not in the room the first evening. When the other disciples tell him they have seen Jesus alive, he refuses to believe on hearsay. He names two specific things he must SEE AND TOUCH -- and the second is not the hands. What does Thomas say he must thrust his hand into?
context: John 20:25 KJV: 'Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.' The side-wound is from the Roman soldier's spear thrust in John 19:34. Feet were also nailed at crucifixion, but that is not the wound Thomas names.

question: Eight days later Jesus appears in the same locked room, doors still shut, and turns straight to Thomas. He shows Thomas his hands and offers his side. Thomas answers with FIVE quiet words that John records. What does Thomas say?
context: John 20:28 KJV: 'And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.' The scene turns on it being a startled man's line to someone he thought was dead. The other three options are invented paraphrases in the same five-word shape.

question: John's final chapter has the disciples back on the Sea of Galilee. Peter and six others have fished ALL NIGHT and caught nothing. A figure on the shore at dawn tells them to cast the net on the RIGHT side of the boat -- and the net fills. Peter drags it to land and John records the EXACT count. HOW many fish?
context: John 21:11 KJV: 'and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.' 144 (thousand) is the sealed of the tribes in Revelation 7; 5,000 is the crowd fed with five loaves and two fish; 490 is seventy times seven, Jesus's forgiveness count in Matthew 18.

question: As the boat draws near the shore in the dawn light on the Sea of Galilee, one disciple in the boat recognises the figure standing on the beach before any of the others do. He is called 'the beloved disciple' in this scene, and he says one blunt short line to Peter. What does he say?
context: John 21:7 KJV: 'Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved saith unto Peter, It is the Lord. Now when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girt his fisher's coat unto him, (for he was naked,) and did cast himself into the sea.' Peter cannot wait for the boat -- he jumps and swims for the shore. Traditionally the beloved disciple in the fourth gospel is identified with the apostle John.

question: After the disciples eat the breakfast Jesus has cooked for them on the shore, Jesus turns to Peter and asks him ONE question -- and then asks it again, and then asks it a THIRD time. Peter is grieved by the third asking. What is the question Jesus asks Peter three times?
answer: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?
choices: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?
Simon, son of Jonas, wilt thou follow me?
Simon, son of Jonas, whom sayest thou that I am?
Simon, son of Jonas, canst thou drink of my cup?
context: John 21:15-17 KJV records the question three times. The threefold asking mirrors Peter's three denials on the night of the arrest -- and the shore fire in John 21:9 uses the same rare Greek word for 'charcoal fire' (anthrakia) that appears back at Peter's denial fire in John 18:18. That word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The other three questions are famous exchanges Jesus has with Peter elsewhere.

question: After each of Peter's three answers on the beach, Jesus gives Peter the same short commission back -- almost the same three-word instruction each time, with only one word varying between the rounds. What is the commission Jesus gives Peter?
context: John 21:15-17 KJV. The exact three variations across the three rounds are 'Feed my lambs' (v.15), 'Feed my sheep' (v.16), and 'Feed my sheep' (v.17) -- Peter, who denied Jesus at a fire in a courtyard, is restored at a fire on a beach and told to look after the flock. 'Take my yoke upon you' is Matthew 11; 'wash one another's feet' is the Maundy Thursday scene in John 13; 'let him deny himself' is Mark 8.

question: Erasmus writes his most famous satire in about a week, as the guest of a good friend at that friend's London house. The Latin title 'Encomium Moriae' has a second sense in Latin -- it also reads as a joke on the host's own Latinised surname. Whose name is being punned on?
context: More's surname was Latinised as Morus, and Moriae ('of Folly') doubles as 'of More'. Erasmus wrote the book in about a week at More's house in London in 1509. Colet, Warham and Fisher were all English scholarly friends of Erasmus in this period, but the pun is on More. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Praise_of_Folly.

question: In 1516, printed at Basel by Johann Froben, Erasmus publishes the Novum Instrumentum. It is a book that had never been printed before in the history of Europe: the New Testament in its original language, with a fresh Latin translation of his own set alongside it. In which original language did Erasmus print it?
context: The New Testament was written in Koine Greek in the first century; Erasmus's 1516 edition was the first ever put in print in the original. Hebrew is the language of most of the Old Testament; Aramaic was the everyday language of first-century Palestine but not of the New Testament writings; Coptic is a much later Egyptian translation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.

question: In 1524 Erasmus finally broke with Luther in print. Luther fired back in 1525 with De Servo Arbitrio -- On the Bondage of the Will. What Latin title did Erasmus use for the book Luther was answering?
context: Erasmus's 'De Libero Arbitrio' (On Free Will, 1524) drew Luther's crushing 'De Servo Arbitrio' (On the Bondage of the Will, 1525) in reply; the exchange marked the final break between humanist reform-from-within and Protestant break-from-without. De Copia and De Ratione Studii are earlier Erasmus works on Latin style and education; De Contemptu Mundi is an early monastic-life treatise of his -- all real Erasmus titles, none the anti-Luther book. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.

question: Erasmus, a Latinist all his working life whose Latin correspondence fills volumes, dies at Basel on 12 July 1536. His friend Beatus Rhenanus records that in his last words he slipped out of Latin altogether and cried out in his childhood tongue instead -- 'Dear God'. In which language did he say it?
context: Beatus Rhenanus reports Erasmus's dying words as 'Lieve God' -- 'Dear God' in Dutch, the language he had grown up with in Rotterdam and largely abandoned in adult life for Latin. German was the language of his printer's city Basel; French of the great university at Paris; English of his English friends. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus.  (Legend.)

question: When Queen Vashti refuses to be paraded before the drunken Persian lords, King Ahasuerus deposes her and orders a beauty search across the empire. A young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, raised by her cousin, is brought to the palace at Shushan and crowned queen. By what royal name is she known?
context: Esther 2. Hadassah (myrtle) is her Hebrew name; Esther is her Persian throne name. The other three are all real named Jewish women -- Deborah the judge, Judith of the Assyrian general, Miriam sister of Moses.

question: The Jewish orphan crowned queen of Persia was raised by an older kinsman who sat daily at the king's gate. He warned her not to reveal she was a Jew, and the story of Purim is built around him and her. Who was he?
context: Esther 2:5-7, 2:20. Mordecai is Esther's older cousin who raised her after her parents died. The others are all real Jewish figures from adjacent books -- Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, Ezra the scribe led a return from exile, Boaz married Ruth.

question: At the opening of the story King Ahasuerus throws a colossal feast at Shushan the palace for the princes and servants of Persia and Media, showing off the riches of his kingdom. How long does the feast last?
context: Esther 1:3-4. The 180-day feast is followed by a further seven-day feast for the people of Shushan; it is at the close of that shorter feast that Vashti refuses to appear.

question: A courtier furious that Mordecai the Jew would not bow to him at the palace gate cast a LOT (pur) to pick the day for a massacre, and offered ten thousand talents of silver to buy an edict destroying every Jew in the empire. Who was he?
context: Esther 3:1-13. Haman is called 'the Agagite'. The others are all real named officers of Ahasuerus's court from the same book -- Hegai kept the women, Harbonah was a chamberlain who later pointed out Haman's gallows, Shaashgaz kept the concubines.

question: Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, then sent word begging Esther to go in to the king. She sent back word to fast three days and nights on her behalf, saying she would then go in unbidden even though it was against the law and could cost her life. What were her last words in that message?
choices: into thy hand I commit my spirit
context: Esther 4:16 KJV. The three-day fast is why Purim is preceded by the Fast of Esther. The other three lines are all real biblical quotations -- Psalm 23, Isaiah 6, Psalm 31.

question: Mordecai's message to Esther in Esther 4:14 has become one of the most quoted lines in the whole Bible: 'who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom' for what?
answer: for such a time as this
choices: for such a time as this
to break the yoke of thine enemies
context: Esther 4:14 KJV. The line is Mordecai's warning that if Esther keeps silent, deliverance will come from another quarter but her house will perish -- and God may have raised her up precisely for this crisis. The others are biblical-sounding but not the verse.

question: In the Persian court, anyone who entered the king's inner court without being called was put to death -- unless the king held out a specific object to spare them. Esther risked this on the third day of her fast. What did Ahasuerus hold out to her?
context: Esther 5:1-2. The sceptre is the physical sign of the king's favor; Esther touches its tip. The signet ring is a real palace object -- it seals the edicts -- but is not what he holds out.

question: The night before he planned to ask permission to hang Mordecai, Haman built an execution frame in his own courtyard at his wife Zeresh's suggestion. How tall was it?
context: Esther 5:14 KJV. A cubit is roughly 18 inches, so about seventy-five feet -- absurdly, deliberately huge, meant as public humiliation. The others are real biblical measurements (Solomon's porch, Noah's ark, the walls of Jericho).

question: The night between Esther's two banquets, the king could not sleep and had the chronicles of his reign read aloud to him. He learned there that Mordecai had once uncovered an assassination plot by two of his own doorkeepers and had never been rewarded. What were the plotters' names?
context: Esther 2:21-23, 6:1-3. Bigthan and Teresh are two eunuchs who guarded the door and conspired against Ahasuerus; Mordecai overheard them and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name. The others are all real named officers of the same Persian court -- Hegai and Shaashgaz kept the women, Hatach carried messages to Esther and Harbonah later pointed out the gallows, Carshena and Memucan were princes of Persia and Media in Esther 1.

question: When Haman arrived at dawn to request Mordecai's death, the king asked him first what should be done for a man he wanted publicly honoured. Haman -- thinking of himself -- named royal robes, the king's own horse, and a herald crying a specific line. The king then made Haman himself do all of it, for Mordecai. What was the line the herald was to cry?
answer: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour
choices: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour
Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the king
Bow the knee, ye people of Shushan
Long live the king of Persia and Media
context: Esther 6:7-11 KJV. Haman himself must lead Mordecai on horseback through the city street crying the words he had designed for his own honour. He goes home mourning with his head covered.

question: At the second banquet Esther named Haman as the enemy. The king stormed into the palace garden in fury; Haman fell across Esther's couch pleading for his life; the returning king took it for assault. A chamberlain named Harbonah pointed to Haman's own courtyard. What did the king say?
choices: Let him be cast into the pit
context: Esther 7:9-10 KJV. Harbonah's aside about the fifty-cubit gallows Haman had raised for Mordecai is the pivot; the king answers in three curt words and Haman dies on the frame he built. 'The wrath of the king was pacified.'

question: The book that closes with the founding of Purim is famous for one specific absence in its text that has puzzled readers for two thousand years. What is it?
answer: God is never named in it
choices: God is never named in it
no miracle is ever performed in it
no law of Moses is ever cited in it
no prophet is ever consulted in it
context: Esther. God is never named -- not YHWH, not Elohim, not Adonai. Traditional Judaism reads this as the point: providence works through what looks like coincidence (a sleepless night, a chronicle read aloud). The Song of Songs also omits the divine name in some counts, so this is the classic case rather than the strictly unique one.

question: Early in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (Book I ch.24), the young Arthur rides out with Merlin and meets a very tall, very proud king on the road who challenges him to single combat. The two fight until Arthur's first sword -- the one he drew from the stone -- shatters in his hand. Which king breaks Arthur's first sword?
context: Malory, Book I ch.24. Pellinore is the questing knight who nearly kills the young Arthur in this duel until Merlin intervenes. Pellinore later becomes an ally and a companion of the Round Table. Uriens is Morgan le Fay's husband; Lot is Gawain's father; Rience is the giant northern king who demands the beards of eleven kings for his cloak.  (Legend.)

question: After the sword breaks, Merlin leads Arthur to a wide, still lake. Merlin points to something at the very center of the water where an enchantress makes her home. What does Merlin show Arthur in the middle of the lake?
answer: a low rock rising above the water
choices: a low rock rising above the water
a floating chapel of white marble
a bridge of glass to the far shore
a whirlpool that swallows passing ships
context: Malory, Book I ch.25: Merlin explains 'there is within that lake a rock, and thereon is as fair a place as any on earth, and richly beseen; and this damosel will come to you anon, and then speak ye fair to her that she will give you that sword.' The floating chapel belongs to certain later Grail tales; the glass bridge to Chretien's Lancelot; the whirlpool to the Greek Odyssey (Charybdis).  (Legend.)

question: Once Arthur takes the sword from the arm in white samite, Merlin tells him it has a famous name. The Vulgate Merlin (and Malory following it) glosses 'Excalibur' with an Old French phrase. In this medieval gloss, what does the name Excalibur mean?
context: Wikipedia: Excalibur. The Vulgate Merlin says the name means 'cuts iron, steel, and wood' in French. Earlier the sword is called 'Caledfwlch' in Welsh ('hard-cleaver') and 'Caliburnus' in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin. The other three glosses sound heroic but are inventions.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur rows out in a barge and takes both the sword and its scabbard from the arm in the water. Riding home, Merlin turns to the young king and asks him which of the two he likes better. Arthur says the sword. Merlin sharply corrects him -- and the reason is a specific magical property of the second object. What does Merlin say the scabbard does?
answer: stops all bleeding from any wound
choices: stops all bleeding from any wound
makes its bearer invisible in shadow
lets its bearer ride without tiring
context: Malory, Book I ch.25 verbatim: 'the scabbard is worth ten of the swords, for whiles ye have the scabbard upon you, ye shall never lose no blood, be ye never so sore wounded.' The magic is bleed-prevention, not invisibility, blow-turning, or endurance. Merlin's blunt lesson is that gear you can't see is often worth more than gear you can.  (Legend.)

question: In that same speech Merlin uses a specific rule of thumb to tell Arthur just how much more valuable the scabbard is than the sword. The line is one of the most quoted single sentences in Malory's whole Excalibur scene. In Merlin's phrase, the scabbard is worth what?
context: Malory, Book I ch.25: 'the scabbard is worth ten of the swords.' A hundred horses and a king's ransom are the ordinary medieval measures of great value, but Merlin's exact rule of thumb is ten of the swords -- and that ratio is what makes losing the scabbard a catastrophe later.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin's warning proves right. Later in Malory (Book IV ch.14), someone close to Arthur steals the scabbard away from him while he sleeps and throws it into a deep lake, where no one can ever find it. Who steals and disposes of Excalibur's scabbard?
context: Malory, Book IV ch.14. Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister and one of the great villains of the middle books; she steals the scabbard during her intrigue against him. The Lady of the Lake GAVE the scabbard in the first place. Nimue (also Viviane) is Merlin's sorceress-apprentice who traps him in a cave later. Guinevere is Arthur's queen, not his enemy.  (Legend.)

question: Without the scabbard, Arthur can bleed again -- and at the final battle of Camlann he takes the mortal wound that ends his reign. He then orders the sword itself thrown back into a lake. His last surviving knight has to try three times before the arm in white samite rises to catch it and take Excalibur down beneath the water. Which knight throws Excalibur back on the third try?
context: Malory, Book XXI ch.5. Bedivere is the old one-handed veteran who is the last knight standing at Camlann; the arm in white samite catches the sword on his third throw. Lancelot has been in exile after his affair with Guinevere shattered the Round Table. Gawain has died of head wounds before Camlann. Kay -- Arthur's foster-brother -- is long dead by then.  (Legend.)

question: Malory says that when the giver of Excalibur first offered the sword to Arthur, she made him promise her a gift in return, to be named later. In Book II ch.3 she comes to Arthur's court to collect. Before Arthur can rule on her demand, a knight steps forward in the hall -- his mother has been wronged by her family -- draws his sword, and cuts her head off on the spot. Which knight beheads the Lady of the Lake in Arthur's hall?
context: Malory, Book II ch.3. Balin le Savage -- fresh out of Arthur's prison -- recognizes the Lady of the Lake as the woman who destroyed his mother and beheads her before Arthur can stop him. It is a shocking scene: Arthur exiles Balin for the killing, and Balin's own doom follows soon after (the Dolorous Stroke that wounds the Fisher King and lays waste to the land). The other three are real Round Table knights but play no part in this hall.  (Legend.)

question: The oldest name for Arthur's sword is not Excalibur at all but an older name meaning 'hard-cleaver', appearing in one of the earliest surviving Arthurian tales -- a story where the hero must complete forty impossible tasks to marry Olwen. What is the sword's oldest known name?
context: The Welsh tale 'Culhwch and Olwen' (c. late 11th-12th century) is the earliest surviving Arthurian story; Arthur's sword there is Caledfwlch (from 'caled' hard + 'bwlch' breach/cleft). Caliburnus is Geoffrey of Monmouth's later Latin form; Escalibor is the Old French of the twelfth century, from which English 'Excalibur' comes. Durendal belongs to a different hero -- Roland of the Chanson de Roland.  (Legend.)

question: In Geoffrey of Monmouth's 'Historia Regum Britanniae' (about 1136) -- the book that put Arthur into European literature -- the sword is already famous and Geoffrey names the place it was made. In Geoffrey's Latin history, where was Caliburnus, the sword that would become Excalibur, forged?
choices: on the anvil of the Dagda
context: Wikipedia: Excalibur, from Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book IX. Geoffrey says the sword 'was forged in Avalon.' Annwn is the Welsh otherworld from Culhwch and Olwen. The Dagda is the Irish father-god with his own great club. Weyland the Smith is the Anglo-Saxon smith-hero -- a real English legend, but not the maker of Excalibur.

question: By the river Chebar in Babylon, a young exile priest sees the heavens open in his thirtieth year -- a cloud from the north with fire enfolding itself and a brightness around it -- and becomes the strangest visionary in the Hebrew Bible. Who is he?
context: Ezekiel 1:1-4. Ezekiel is a priest deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles under Jehoiachin (597 BC). The other three are all real major prophets -- Jeremiah stays behind in Jerusalem, Isaiah lived a century earlier, Daniel is a court official in the same exile.

question: Out of the fiery cloud in Ezekiel's opening vision come four living creatures. Each has four wings, feet like a calf, and burnished-brass gleam -- and each has four different faces on one head. Which set of four faces does the text name?
answer: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle
choices: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle
a bull, a serpent, a hawk, and a jackal
a ram, a goat, a lion, and a leopard
a lamb, a dove, a lion, and a child
context: Ezekiel 1:5-10 KJV. These four faces are later picked up by Revelation 4 and become the traditional symbols of the four Gospel-writers -- Matthew (man), Mark (lion), Luke (ox), John (eagle). The other sets are drawn from other real ancient iconography (Egyptian, Persian).

question: Ezekiel 1:18 says the rims of the wheels beside the four creatures were 'so high that they were dreadful'. What did those rims have all the way around them?
context: Ezekiel 1:18 KJV: 'their rings were full of eyes round about them four'. It is the eyes, not the height, that make the wheels most memorable -- the whole apparatus is a chariot-throne that sees in every direction.

question: Above the wheels and the four creatures Ezekiel sees a firmament like crystal, and above the firmament a throne of one specific gemstone -- with 'the appearance of a man' upon it surrounded by a rainbow. What stone was the throne?
context: Ezekiel 1:26 KJV: 'the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone'. Compare Moses in Exodus 24:10 who sees under God's feet 'a paved work of a sapphire stone'.

question: In his commissioning vision, Ezekiel is handed a scroll covered in 'lamentations, and mourning, and woe' and told to eat it. He puts it in his mouth and it tastes surprisingly like one specific sweet thing. What does the text say the scroll tasted like?
context: Ezekiel 3:1-3 KJV: 'it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness'. The prophet has to swallow the message before he can speak it. John in Revelation 10 eats a similar scroll -- sweet in the mouth, bitter in the belly.

question: As a sign against Jerusalem, God tells Ezekiel to lie on his LEFT side to bear the iniquity of the house of Israel for three hundred and ninety days, then to flip and lie on his RIGHT side for the house of Judah. For how many days does he lie on his right side?
context: Ezekiel 4:4-6 KJV. Each day counts for a year -- 390 years for Israel, 40 for Judah. It is one of the most physically demanding sign-acts in the Old Testament: over a year on one side of his body, then more than a month on the other.

question: Ezekiel prophesies over the valley and hears a noise and a shaking begin. The KJV catches the first stage of what happens next in a four-word phrase that has been quoted ever since. What is the phrase?
context: Ezekiel 37:7 KJV: 'the bones came together, bone to his bone'. Then sinews and flesh and skin come up, and when the wind comes in verse 10 they stand upon their feet 'an exceeding great army'. The other three are real biblical phrases from Genesis 3, Genesis 2, and Genesis 1.

question: In the middle of his ministry Ezekiel is told, calmly and in advance, that his wife -- 'the desire of thine eyes' -- will die suddenly at evening, and that he is to give the mourners no sign at all: no weeping, no bare feet, no torn clothes. The point is a sign to the exiles about what?
answer: the coming fall of the Temple
choices: the coming fall of the Temple
the birth of a great king
context: Ezekiel 24:15-24. His wife dies at evening; the next morning he does as commanded. When the exiles ask why, he tells them that they too will lose 'the desire of your eyes' -- the Temple -- and will not be able to mourn it publicly.

question: The Tain Bo Cuailnge tells of a young Ulster champion who holds off Queen Medb's whole invading army by killing her champions one after another at river fords. What is his name?
context: Cu Chulainn is the great hero of the Ulster Cycle and the sole defender of Ulster in the Tain, killing champion after champion at the fords to slow Medb's army. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: When Queen Medb of Connacht runs out of champions willing to face the young Ulster defender at the fords, she sends for one man from her own army who once trained beside him under the same warrior-woman on the Isle of Shadow. What is that champion's name?
context: Ferdiad, son of Daman, of the Fir Domnann, is the only warrior in Medb's whole host who trained under Scathach beside Cu Chulainn and so knows every one of his feats. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: In the Tain, Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad had been foster-brothers in arms, having eaten from the same dish and slept under the same shield while training together as boys. Who was the warrior-woman on the Isle of Shadow who taught them both?
context: Scathach ran a warrior-school on the Isle of Shadow (Dun Scaith) where the young men of Ulster were sent to learn feats of arms. Ferdiad and Cu Chulainn learned side by side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad refuses to face his foster-brother at the ford. Queen Medb calls in a class of person from her court whose public verse could physically shame a warrior into fighting or dying. Whom does she call in?
context: In early Irish culture the satire of the filid was a genuine weapon: their public verse could raise three blisters on the target's face, named Blame, Blemish and Disgrace, and to be so shamed was social death. Ferdiad said he deemed it better to fall by the shafts of valour than by the shafts of satire. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/20-the-combat-of-ferdiad-and-cuchulain/  (Legend.)

question: The two foster-brothers meet at the ford. On the first morning of their combat, from dawn until noon, they hurl one class of weapon at each other again and again and neither can draw blood. With what do they fight on that first day?
context: The Tain lays out the four days as an escalating scale. Day one is small darts and light casting-spears from morning's early twilight till noon; each day the weapon grows heavier. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/20-the-combat-of-ferdiad-and-cuchulain/  (Legend.)

question: On the fourth day at the ford, Ferdiad has been raising his high shield against Cu Chulainn's throws all morning. Cu Chulainn shouts down to his charioteer Loeg to bring the one feat-weapon Scathach reserved for him alone and never taught to any other pupil. Which does he call for?
context: All four are feats or weapons from Scathach's warrior-school on the Isle of Shadow, so a player must actually know which one Scathach withheld from every other pupil. The Gae Bolg, the 'belly-spear', was that feat. Ferdiad had no defence against it because he had never learned it, and Loeg readied it in the river-stream for the throw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: The Gae Bolg comes at Ferdiad from a place he cannot guard against with his high shield. In the Tain, Cu Chulainn does not throw it from his hand at all. From where does he launch it?
answer: From between the toes of his foot, in the water
choices: From between the toes of his foot, in the water
From the back of his chariot
context: The Tain is exact: 'with the stream it was made ready, and from between the fork of the foot it was cast.' Cu Chulainn stood in the river and kicked the barbed spear up at Ferdiad from underneath the shield-rim. It made the wound of a single spear on entry but opened into thirty barbs inside the body. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/20-the-combat-of-ferdiad-and-cuchulain/  (Legend.)

question: The four-day combat between Cu Chulainn and his foster-brother is the emotional heart of the Tain Bo Cuailnge, and the river ford where they fought is still named for the man who died there. What is the modern Irish town on that ford?
context: The ford was called Ath Fir Diad, 'the Ford of Ferdiad', and the town that grew there kept the name: Ardee (Baile Atha Fhirdhia) in County Louth. Every other choice is a real Irish site of the Ulster Cycle era: Armagh the church seat, Navan the modern town near the royal fort of Emain Macha, and Tara the seat of the High King. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdiad  (Legend.)

question: In Norse mythology, the world does not end quietly. Almost every named Aesir god dies in one great final battle, the sky splits, and the sea rises to swallow the earth. What is the Norse name for this doom of the gods?
context: Ragnarok is prophesied in the Voluspa (the opening poem of the Poetic Edda) and retold by Snorri Sturluson in Gylfaginning chapters 51-52. Yggdrasil is the world-tree at the centre of the nine worlds. Valhalla is Odin's warrior-hall in Asgard. Midgard is the middle earth where humans live. Ragnarok is the specific name for the ending.  (Legend.)

question: The great ending of Norse myth does not come out of nothing. Snorri Sturluson says in Gylfaginning 51 that a monstrous winter comes first, sent as a warning-sign to the whole world -- snow blowing in from every direction, the sun giving no warmth, and no growing season to break it. What is the name of the winter that comes before Ragnarok?
context: Snorri Gylfaginning 51: the winter is Fimbulvetr, the 'Great Winter' (Old Norse fimbul- 'mighty' + vetr 'winter'). Skidbladnir is the folding-ship of the god Freyr. Nastrond is the shore of corpses in Hel. Muspelheim is the fire-realm of Surt in the south. Fimbulvetr is the specific name of the winter, and Snorri names it plainly.  (Legend.)

question: The Great Winter that precedes Ragnarok is not just cold. Snorri says the snow blows in from every direction, the sun gives no warmth, and one very specific thing does not happen between the winters. How many winters does Fimbulvetr last, one after another with no summer between them?
context: Snorri Gylfaginning 51 and Vafthrudnismal stanzas 44-45: three winters in a row with no summer between. The number nine is Norse for cosmology (nine worlds of Yggdrasil), forty is the Biblical wilderness number, seven has no place here. Three is the specific count in the Prose Edda, and it is what makes the winter unlivable -- no growing season means no food.  (Legend.)

question: During Fimbulvetr the food runs out and the sky stays grey. The Voluspa poem sums up what human society becomes in a famous chain of names for the era -- 'an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cloven, a wind-age, a ___-age, before the world plunges.' Which age fills the blank in that stanza?
context: Voluspa stanza 45 (Bellows translation): 'an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cloven, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world plunges.' The same stanza says brothers will murder brothers and sisters' sons will violate the kinship-bond. Fire belongs to Surt at the end; frost belongs to the giants at the beginning of the world; iron-age is a Greco-Roman scheme, not Norse. The Voluspa's specific word here is wolf-age -- the wolves Skoll and Hati are about to catch the sun and moon.  (Legend.)

question: In the sky above the frozen earth, one very old chase finally ends. Since the beginning of the world, according to Snorri Gylfaginning 12, a wolf has run behind the sun's chariot trying to catch it. During Ragnarok the wolf finally succeeds. What does the sky-wolf do to the sun?
context: Gylfaginning 12 and 51: the wolf catches the sun-chariot at last and swallows the sun whole. He does not shatter, burn, or drown it. Norse eschatology is precise on this -- the sun goes DOWN a wolf's throat, and the stars go out. The image is meant to be simple and terrifying to a child listening at a hearth.  (Legend.)

question: The wolf that swallows the sun has a name in the Prose Edda: it means 'treachery' in Old Norse. What is this sky-wolf called?
context: Gylfaginning 12: the wolf is named Skoll, meaning 'treachery.' Fenrir is a different much larger wolf -- the one who bites off Tyr's hand and eventually kills Odin himself. Garmr is the hound at the gate of Hel. Managarmr ('Moon-hound') is a variant name given by some sources. Skoll is the specific name Snorri gives the sun-chaser.  (Legend.)

question: Only after the Great Winter, the kin-slaughter, and the swallowing of the sun and moon do the roosters crow and one of the gods lift a great horn to summon the Aesir to their final battle. Which god blows the horn that starts Ragnarok proper?
context: Voluspa stanzas 42-43 and Gylfaginning 51: Heimdallr, the watchman of the rainbow-bridge Bifrost, lifts the Gjallarhorn and blows it. Thor rides out to fight the Midgard-serpent when he hears it. Bragi is the god of poetry. Forseti is the god of justice. The horn is specifically Heimdallr's, and its blast is the summons.  (Legend.)

question: In the poem Vafthrudnismal Odin visits a giant and asks who, if anyone, will survive the Great Winter that ends the world. The giant Vafthrudnir answers that two people -- a man and a woman -- will live through it by hiding in a forest called Hoddmimir's holt, and will come out afterwards to repopulate the earth. What are the names of the two survivors of Fimbulvetr?
context: Vafthrudnismal stanzas 44-45: the survivors are Lif ('Life') and Lifthrasir ('Life-yearner'), who shelter in the wood called Hoddmimir's holt through the winter and step out into the new world. Ask and Embla are the first humans, made by Odin and his brothers at the beginning of the world -- a different pair. Njord and Skadi are a Vanir god and a giantess couple.
