Sigyn is Loki's faithful wife and Vali her son. Lif and Lifthrasir are the specific after-winter pair.  (Legend.)

question: Just before Heimdallr lifts the Gjallarhorn to summon the gods, the Voluspa says three roosters crow at the same moment across three worlds -- one in Asgard on the world-tree, one among the giants, and one down in the halls of the dead. Which rooster crows in Odin's Valhalla to rouse the einherjar?
context: Voluspa stanzas 42-43: Gullinkambi ('Golden-comb') wakes the warriors in Odin's Valhalla. Fjalar is the red rooster who wakes the giants in Jotunheim. A third un-named rooster (called only 'Hel's rooster') crows in the halls of the dead. Vidofnir is a different mythical bird sitting in the branches of Mimameid. Chanticleer is the rooster of Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale, not a Norse creature. Gullinkambi is the specific Asgard rooster.  (Legend.)

question: The Fenian Cycle of Irish myth tells of a great hero who becomes chief of the Fianna, the roving warrior-band that guards the High King. What is his name?
context: Fionn mac Cumhaill, anglicised 'Finn MacCool', is the central hero of the Fenian Cycle and captain of the Fianna. Cu Chulainn belongs to the older Ulster Cycle; Conaire Mor is a High King in the Cycles of the Kings; Oisin is Fionn's son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: In the Boyhood Deeds of Fionn, the boy who will grow up to captain the Fianna is hidden away in the forest of Sliabh Bladhma because a rival killed his father Cumhall at the Battle of Cnucha before he was born. Who is the rival who killed Cumhall and took command of the Fianna?
context: Goll mac Morna led the rival clan Morna against Cumhall's clan Baiscne at Cnucha. He took the captaincy of the Fianna and would have killed the infant heir if he could find him. Later Goll and the grown Fionn reconcile and Goll serves under him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: To hide the infant heir of Cumhall from the men of clan Morna, his mother gave him to two women who raised him in secret in the forest for years. One was a druidess, the other a warrior-woman. What was the boy's given name in those forest years, before he ever ate the salmon?
context: The boy's birth-name was Deimne, meaning 'sureness' or 'certainty', a word that also names a young male deer. The druidess Bodhmall and the warrior-woman Liath Luachra raised him in Sliabh Bladhma. Setanta is Cu Chulainn's boyhood name from a different cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: When the boy Deimne was old enough to leave the forest, he was sent to a hut on the banks of the River Boyne to study with an old poet who had been fishing the same pool for years. What was that poet's name?
context: Finnegas (Finn Eces, 'Finn the seer') lived by the Boyne teaching poetry and waiting for one particular fish. Amergin is the poet who chanted the Milesians ashore; Cathbad is the Ulster druid who prophesied over Cu Chulainn's cradle; Mog Ruith is a Munster wizard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: Finnegas had spent years by the Boyne trying to catch one particular fish, an unremarkable-looking salmon that would grant all the world's knowledge to whoever ate it. How had that ordinary salmon come by all the world's knowledge?
answer: By eating nine hazelnuts that fell from the trees of wisdom into the Well of Segais
choices: By eating nine hazelnuts that fell from the trees of wisdom into the Well of Segais
By swallowing a ring cast into the pool by the Dagda
By drinking from the Cauldron of Rebirth at Bran's court
By living a hundred years under the standing stone at Tara
context: In Irish tradition the hazel is the tree of knowledge just as the apple is the tree of knowledge in Genesis. Nine sacred hazels stood over the Well of Segais at the source of the Boyne; their nuts fell into the water and the salmon that ate them gained the wisdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: In the Boyhood Deeds of Fionn, Finnegas had waited by the river Boyne for one particular fish for a very long stretch of his life before he finally caught it. How many years had the old poet been fishing?
context: The tale specifies seven years: Finnegas had been fishing that one pool for seven full years for the Salmon of Wisdom before finally hooking it. That is why his rage at being cheated of the wisdom in the end is so bitter and his grace in giving it up so remarkable. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: The day Finnegas finally lands the great salmon, he hands the fish to Deimne and gives him one strict order before going away to fetch something. What was Finnegas's order?
answer: Cook it but do not taste even a bite of the flesh
choices: Cook it but do not taste even a bite of the flesh
Bury it under the hazel tree till nightfall
Cast the hazelnuts back into the well first
Bring it whole and uncooked to the elder-druid
context: The prophecy said the wisdom would go to whoever FIRST tasted the salmon, not to whoever caught it. Finnegas trusted the boy to turn the fish over a fire without stealing so much as a crumb. Source: https://www.askaboutireland.ie/reading-room/life-society/irish-language-legends/the-salmon-of-knowledge/

question: As the boy turned the great salmon on a rowan spit over the fire, a blister rose on the fish's skin. He pressed the blister down with his thumb to smooth the flesh, and a drop of hot juice burst onto him. What did the boy do next that, in that instant, transferred all the salmon's wisdom into him?
answer: He put the burnt thumb into his mouth
choices: He put the burnt thumb into his mouth
He shook the burnt hand in the river to cool it
He wiped the burnt thumb on the rowan spit
He wrapped the burnt thumb in a strip of his tunic
context: The tale turns on an instinct: burnt fingers go into a child's mouth. All the salmon's wisdom had gathered into that one drop of hot fat, and in the instant the boy sucked his thumb the wisdom passed into him rather than to the poet who had waited seven years for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: Finnegas returned to the fire, saw the changed look on the boy's face, and asked whether he had tasted the salmon. When the boy told him about the burnt thumb, Finnegas did something remarkable rather than raging over the seven wasted years. What did the old poet do?
answer: Gave the whole fish to the boy and gave him a new name, Fionn
choices: Gave the whole fish to the boy and gave him a new name, Fionn
Cast the boy out and forbade him ever to return to the Boyne
Demanded the boy split all future wisdom equally with him
Kept silent and never told the boy what he had eaten
context: Finnegas said the salmon had chosen its own eater and the prophecy was for a boy named Fionn, not for himself. He gave the fish over and gave the boy the name he would carry for the rest of the tales: Fionn, 'the fair one'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The pattern of Fionn's story, a hero who gains second sight by accident from a burnt taste while cooking a magical creature for someone else, appears also in Norse myth. Which Norse hero tastes a drop of dragon-blood off his finger and suddenly understands the language of the birds?
answer: Sigurd, roasting Fafnir's heart for Regin
choices: Sigurd, roasting Fafnir's heart for Regin
Beowulf, cutting off Grendel's arm at Heorot
Odin, hanging nine nights on Yggdrasil
Thor, wrestling Elli in Utgard-Loki's hall
context: In the Volsunga Saga, Sigurd kills the dragon Fafnir and roasts the heart for the smith Regin. He burns his finger on the roasting heart, sucks it, and immediately hears the birds warning him that Regin means to murder him for the treasure. The 'accidental eater who gains second sight from a burnt taste' pattern is a shared Indo-European motif of Irish and Norse tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_of_Knowledge  (Legend.)

question: In one popular Irish folk-tradition, a great Irish warrior-chief does not have a death-tale at all. He is said to be lying inside a cave beneath an Irish hill, surrounded by all his sleeping warriors in full armour, waiting for the day Ireland needs him most. Which Irish warrior is this sleeping figure?
context: Fionn mac Cumhaill leads the Fianna in the later Fenian Cycle and the folk-tradition retires him into a sleeping cave rather than a death-tale. Cu Chulainn is the Ulster Cycle hero who has a very famous death-tale (tied upright to a standing stone). Conall Cernach is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and avenger. Lugh Lamhfhada is a Tuatha De Danann warrior of an older cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: In the folk-tale of the sleeping warriors of the Fianna, they lie in a great circle inside the cave, weapons at their sides, sleeping in full armour. In the middle of the circle one thing hangs -- the object that will wake them when the day comes. What hangs in the middle of the sleeping circle?
context: The hunting horn of the Fianna hangs in the middle of the ring of sleepers. A silver harp belongs to the Dagda; a druid's rod is Cathbad's or Uchtdealb's; a crowned helmet belongs to no Fenian scene. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The hunting horn hanging in the middle of the sleeping Fianna in the cave has a name of its own, spoken in every retelling of the wake-and-return legend. What is the horn called?
context: Dord Fiann means 'the horn (or humming-chant) of the Fianna' in Old Irish. The Olifant is Roland's ivory war-horn at Roncesvalles in the Western-medieval pillar. Gjallarhorn is Heimdall's horn on Bifrost in the Norse pillar. The Horn of Bran is a Welsh instrument. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The Dord Fiann hanging over the sleeping Fianna must be sounded a specific number of times before the warriors will fully wake, rise, and ride out to defend Ireland. How many times must the horn be sounded?
context: Three blasts of the Dord Fiann fully wake Fionn and the Fianna. The tale that turns on the exact number is coming up in the ladder. The other three counts belong to unrelated Irish and Norse rites (nine is the Norse ritual number). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: In the folk-tale of the cave, a lone shepherd who had wandered inside by accident lifted down the Dord Fiann and blew it. He blew it ONCE. The Fianna in the circle stirred, half-rose on their elbows, opened their eyes. The shepherd panicked. What did the shepherd then do?
answer: dropped the horn and ran out of the cave
choices: dropped the horn and ran out of the cave
blew the second blast at once and fled
prayed aloud and asked their forgiveness
cut a chip from Fionn's shield as a token
context: The horn falls, the shepherd bolts, the Fianna are left only half-awake and sink back into sleep -- and they cry out that he has left them worse than he found them. It is the shape the whole tradition preserves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: As the Fianna, half-woken by the single blast on the Dord Fiann, sank back into their sleep, they cried out to the fleeing shepherd one bitter sentence -- the sentence the tale hangs on and by which folklorists know the story. What did the sinking warriors cry after him?
answer: you have left us worse than you found us
choices: you have left us worse than you found us
the age of heroes has ended in shame
the horn has broken faith with us
we sleep now for a thousand years
context: In Irish the sentence is 'Is measa a dfhag na mar a fuair' -- 'worse have you left us than as you found us'. It is the folk-formula that fixes the tale in memory. The other three are invented parallels of the same shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fionn_mac_Cumhaill  (Legend.)

question: The Fenian sleeping-hero pattern is one of the widest folk-patterns in Europe. In another kingdom of legend, a great king is said to lie in a similar sleep on a mist-hidden island of apples, waiting to return -- and the Latin epitaph on his supposed tomb calls him rex quondam rexque futurus, 'the once and future king'. Who is this parallel sleeping-king?
context: Arthur at Avalon is the parallel Malory refuses to resolve: 'yet some men say... that King Arthur is not dead, but... he shall come again' (Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI). Barbarossa is the Holy Roman Emperor asleep under the Kyffhauser mountain with his red beard growing through the stone table -- another once-and-future-king, but not the one on the apple-island. Olger Danske sleeps in the vaults of Kronborg in Denmark. Charlemagne was buried at Aachen with elaborate ceremony and does not carry the sleeping-return legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_in_the_mountain

question: In the 1760s a Scottish editor published what he claimed were 3rd-century Scots-Gaelic poems by 'Ossian son of Fingal' -- Fingal being the Scots-Gaelic form of Fionn. The publication swept Europe: Napoleon carried a copy on campaign, Goethe cited it in Werther. Later scholarship judged the work largely a forgery drawing freely on real oral Fenian tradition. Who was the editor?
context: James Macpherson (1736-1796) issued Fragments of Ancient Poetry in 1760 and Fingal in 1761-2. Hugh Blair was the Edinburgh professor who championed and defended Macpherson's Ossian in print. John Home was the Scottish playwright who first put Macpherson onto the Highland poetry trail. Allan Ramsay was an earlier Scots-vernacular editor. Only Macpherson issued the Ossian publications themselves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossian

question: The Scots-Gaelic form of Fionn -- FINGAL -- gave its name to a real sea-cave on the uninhabited isle of Staffa off Scotland's west coast. In 1829 a German composer visited the cave, heard the ocean-swells roll into its hexagonal basalt chamber, and wrote an overture built around the sound he heard there. Which composer wrote it?
context: Felix Mendelssohn visited Fingal's Cave on Staffa in August 1829 and completed The Hebrides Overture (Op. 26, sometimes called 'Fingal's Cave Overture') in 1830. Wagner wrote sea-legend music (The Flying Dutchman) but not this piece; Sibelius's Swan of Tuonela is Finnish; Berlioz's Corsair is a Byron piece. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hebrides_(overture)

question: Late one afternoon a huge crowd has followed Jesus into a lonely, grassy place beside the Sea of Galilee. The disciples want to send them home to buy supper. Jesus tells the disciples to feed the crowd themselves -- but he starts with what one boy has brought for his own lunch. How many loaves does the boy have?
context: John 6:9 (KJV): 'There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?' All four gospels agree on five loaves (Matthew 14:17, Mark 6:38, Luke 9:13, John 6:9).

question: In a lonely place beside the Sea of Galilee, evening is coming on and a crowd of thousands has followed Jesus out from the towns. The disciples ask him to send everyone away to buy food. Jesus refuses, and gives them a short instruction instead. What does he say?
choices: Let the children come to me
Sit and rest, they will not stay
context: Matthew 14:16 (KJV): 'They need not depart; give ye them to eat.' Also in Mark 6:37 and Luke 9:13. The instruction is directed at the disciples -- the miracle begins as a task laid on them.

question: In a lonely place beside the Sea of Galilee, evening is coming on and a huge crowd has followed Jesus out from the towns. Matthew counts the men who are fed that day 'beside women and children'. About how many men does he count?
context: Matthew 14:21 (KJV): 'And they that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children.' The true total, women and children included, is likely much higher -- perhaps twice that.

question: In John's version of the feeding by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus first turns to one disciple and asks where they can buy bread for such a crowd -- testing him, John says, for Jesus already knows what he will do. That disciple protests that even two hundred days' wages worth of bread would not be enough for each person to have a little. Which disciple?
context: John 6:5-7 (KJV): Jesus asks Philip, and Philip answers, 'Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.' A 'pennyworth' here is a Roman denarius, roughly a day's wage for a laborer.

question: John alone tells us where the loaves and fishes actually came from. As the disciples cast about for food, one of them brings forward a small boy from the crowd who has offered up his own lunch. Which disciple brings the boy forward?
context: John 6:8-9 (KJV): 'One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, saith unto him, There is a lad here...' Andrew is Peter's brother; the boy and his picnic are unique to John's account.

question: In Mark's telling, Jesus does not just feed the crowd on the Sea of Galilee shore in a chaotic press -- he first has the disciples organize them. They sit down 'upon the green grass' in an unusual, orderly arrangement. What arrangement does Mark describe?
answer: In ranks, by hundreds and by fifties
choices: In ranks, by hundreds and by fifties
In two rings of five hundred each
In twelve companies of four hundred
In rows of ten, four hundred rows deep
context: Mark 6:39-40 (KJV): 'And he commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass. And they sat down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties.' The image is almost military -- easy for the disciples to count as they distribute the bread.

question: In John's account, the loaves the boy hands over are made of the humblest grain, the bread of the poor. What grain are the loaves made of?
context: John 6:9 (KJV): 'five barley loaves'. Barley was cheaper than wheat and associated with poorer diets -- the detail marks the boy's lunch as ordinary and small, which sharpens the point.

question: After the crowd has eaten and is full, Jesus tells the disciples to gather up what is left over so that nothing is lost. When they finish walking the grass, all four gospels record the same striking count of baskets filled with fragments. How many?
context: Mark 6:43 (KJV): 'And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments'. Matthew 14:20, Luke 9:17, John 6:13 all agree on twelve -- one per disciple. There was more food AFTER the miracle than the boy had brought BEFORE it.

question: Later in Mark, Jesus catches the disciples worrying that they have forgotten to bring bread on a boat trip -- and quizzes them on the two feeding miracles to shame them. About the smaller of the two feedings, he asks how many baskets of fragments they took up. What answer do the disciples give?
context: Mark 8:19-20 (KJV): 'When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve. And when the seven among four thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? And they said, Seven.' The number of baskets mirrors the starting loaves.

question: Right after his baptism, Jesus goes out alone into the wilderness. He eats nothing, and stays there a specific stretch of time that Matthew and Luke both give the same figure for. How long?
context: Matthew 4:2 (KJV): 'And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.' The number echoes Moses's forty days on Sinai (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah's forty days walking to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8).

question: At the end of Jesus's forty-day fast in the desert, when he is starving, a visitor comes to him and tests him three times, each time trying to get him to prove himself or bow down. Who comes?
context: Matthew 4:3 (KJV) calls him simply 'the tempter'; Matthew 4:10 has Jesus name him: 'Get thee hence, Satan'. Luke 4:2 uses 'the devil' throughout. The scene is a plain, three-round contest between two figures alone.

question: At the very end of the wilderness testing, when Jesus has refused every temptation and the devil has departed, Matthew describes the arrival of one final group who tend to him. Who arrives?
choices: The twelve disciples, come to find him
Shepherds from the nearby hills, drawn by the story
His mother and brothers, worried for him
context: Matthew 4:11 (KJV): 'Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.' The disciples have not yet been called at this point in the story; the family and shepherds appear in other Gospel scenes but not this one.

question: The Christian season of Lent -- six weeks of penitence before Easter, not counting Sundays -- is timed to and named after one specific scene from the life of Jesus. Which scene?
answer: His time alone in the wilderness before his ministry
choices: His time alone in the wilderness before his ministry
The time between his resurrection and his ascension
The time he spent teaching in the Temple as a boy
The time he spent hidden in Egypt as a child
context: Lent runs the six weeks minus Sundays before Easter -- forty days -- and its liturgical readings recall the wilderness testing. Ash Wednesday opens the season; Palm Sunday closes it.

question: In the first temptation, the devil finds Jesus starving after forty days without food. He points at the ground and dares Jesus to prove he is the Son of God by turning the objects in front of them into bread. What objects?
context: Matthew 4:3 (KJV): 'If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.' The Judaean wilderness floor is littered with pale limestone rocks roughly the size and shape of small loaves.

question: In the second temptation the devil takes Jesus to Jerusalem and sets him on the highest point of one building, then dares him to jump -- quoting a psalm about angels catching him. Which building's pinnacle?
context: Matthew 4:5-6 (KJV): 'Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, And saith unto him... he shall give his angels charge concerning thee.' The psalm the devil quotes is Psalm 91:11-12.

question: In the third and last temptation the devil takes Jesus up 'into an exceeding high mountain' and shows him something all at once, then offers to give the whole of it to Jesus if he will fall down and worship him. What does the devil show?
answer: All the kingdoms of the world
choices: All the kingdoms of the world
The twelve tribes gathered in one place
context: Matthew 4:8-9 (KJV): 'sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.'

question: Offered every kingdom in the world in exchange for one bow of worship, Jesus dismisses the devil with a short, sharp command in the King James wording. What does he say?
context: Matthew 4:10 (KJV): 'Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.' Jesus then closes with a third Deuteronomy quotation (6:13). The devil leaves; the angels arrive.

question: Francis of Assisi's father Pietro Bernardone made the family fortune not in banking or in war but in a single trade -- one that took him regularly across the Alps to France for merchandise. What did Pietro Bernardone sell?
context: Pietro dealt chiefly in fine French cloth and silks, so much so that he nicknamed his son Francesco -- 'the little Frenchman'. Francis worked in the family shop as a boy and later gave the merchandise away. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Long before founding any order, the young Francis of Assisi was riding on the road below his town when he met a figure his old life had taught him to dread. Francis dismounted, embraced the man, and pressed money into his hand; in his own Testament he later named this meeting as the turning point of his life. Whom did Francis embrace on that road?
context: Francis dictated the Testament in the last year of his life (1226) and opens it with this scene: 'What had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body.' Lepers lived apart in colonies below the towns; a rider would normally throw coins from horseback and hurry past. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Around 1202 the young Francis rode out with the Assisi cavalry against a neighbouring city and was taken prisoner at the battle of Collestrada. He spent a full year in an enemy dungeon and came home broken by illness. Which nearby Umbrian city held him prisoner?
context: Perugia sat just across the Tiber from Assisi and was the region's traditional rival. Francis's captivity and subsequent illness are marked by his biographers as the first opening of his old life. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: Praying in an old chapel below Assisi, the young Francis reported that a painted crucifix on the wall spoke to him three times. According to the Legend of the Three Companions, what did the icon tell him to do?
answer: Repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.
choices: Repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin.
Sell all you have and give it to the poor.
Feed my sheep and my lambs.
Leave your family and follow me into the desert.
context: The chapel was San Damiano, just outside the walls of Assisi. Francis first took the command literally and rebuilt the stones; only later did he understand it as a call to renew the whole Church. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.  (Legend.)

question: Standing in the piazza before the bishop, the crowd, and his furious father, Francis of Assisi did not argue. He simply peeled off every stitch of his clothing -- shirt, cloak, and even his undergarments -- laid the whole heap at his father's feet along with a purse of the coins he had taken, and stood there naked in the square. What did the astonished bishop do next?
answer: Wrapped his own cloak around Francis
choices: Wrapped his own cloak around Francis
Ordered the crowd to be silent
Called for a scribe to record the renunciation
Blessed the coins and returned them to Pietro
context: Giotto's fresco cycle in the Upper Basilica of San Francesco at Assisi, painted around 1297-1299, shows the moment: Francis naked on one side of the piazza, Bishop Guido leaning across to cover him. Sources: cac.org/daily-meditations/naked-before-god-2019-10-04/.

question: Over the next four years Francis attracted followers -- Bernard of Quintavalle sold everything to join him, then Peter Catani and Giles. In 1210, when the little band numbered twelve, Francis walked to Rome and won provisional approval from Pope Innocent III for a new order. What did he call his brothers?
context: Ordo Fratrum Minorum in the Latin -- the 'lesser brothers'. Dominic's Order of Preachers came a few years later; the White Monks are the Cistercians; the Hermits of Saint Augustine were formed decades on. Innocent III gave verbal approval in 1210; Honorius III confirmed the Rule in writing in 1223. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi.

question: On Christmas night 1223, in a hilltop village of the Rieti valley in central Italy, Francis of Assisi staged the first live nativity scene -- a real ox, a real ass, and a manger of straw, so the local peasants could picture the poverty of Bethlehem. Every crib and presepio since descends from that night, and the village gave its name to the whole custom. What is the name of the village?
context: Greccio sits about fifty miles north of Rome on a rocky hillside above the Rieti valley. Assisi was Francis's hometown; Rieti is the valley's main town; Gubbio was where the legend of Francis taming the wolf is set. The sanctuary at Greccio still preserves the small chapel where the tableau was staged. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_scene, wantedinrome.com/news/greccio-home-of-the-worlds-first-nativity-scene.html.

question: For the first nativity scene, staged at Christmas 1223, Francis of Assisi refused statues and refused a play. He wanted the villagers to smell and hear the stable of Bethlehem. So beside the manger of straw he tethered two live animals -- the same pair that stand in every crib today. Which two animals?
context: The pairing comes from a line in the prophet Isaiah about the ox knowing its owner and the ass its master's crib -- read from early times as a foreshadowing of Bethlehem. Thomas of Celano wrote up the Greccio scene in his Vita Prima about three years later. Sources: franciscanmedia.org/st-anthony-messenger/greccio-and-the-first-live-nativity-800-years-of-tradition/.

question: A count of Tuscany, whose name was Orlando of Chiusi, was so moved after hearing Francis of Assisi preach that in May 1213 he gave the friars an entire mountain in the central Apennines -- a savage, wooded peak fit for prayer and penance. What is the name of that mountain, where Francis kept returning for solitude?
context: La Verna (also spelled Alverna) rises on Monte Penna in the Tuscan Apennines. Monte Cassino was Benedict's monastery, Subiaco his earlier cave; both are real distractors from Benedictine history. The sanctuary Francis built on La Verna still stands. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Verna.

question: In early August 1224, Francis of Assisi climbed La Verna with only a few companions to keep a forty-day fast in preparation for Michaelmas. He took with him the brother he trusted most as scribe and confessor -- the friar whom Francis called 'God's little sheep' and to whom he later dictated the Canticle of the Sun. Who was that closest companion?
context: Leo (Frate Leone) was Francis's secretary in the last years and one of the very few witnesses left alive to describe the La Verna events. Elias later became Minister General; Giles was one of the first three companions; Masseo was famed for his simplicity. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Verna.

question: Praying at dawn on a cliff of La Verna on or about September 14, 1224 -- the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross -- Francis of Assisi saw a burning Seraph descending from the sky, with the form of the crucified Christ fixed within its wings. Isaiah 6 gives the Seraphim a very particular wing-count, and Celano's Vita Prima keeps that count exact. How many wings did the Seraph carry?
context: In Isaiah 6 each Seraph has six wings -- two covering the face, two covering the feet, two for flight. Bonaventure took the six-winged vision as the pattern for his Journey of the Mind to God, mapping the wings onto six stages of contemplation. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stigmata.  (Legend.)

question: In the Umbrian hill town of Gubbio, people were so afraid of a beast killing sheep AND people outside the walls that they would only leave in armed bands. Francis walked out alone to meet it. What kind of animal was it?
context: The story is told in chapter 21 of the Fioretti (Little Flowers of Saint Francis), a Tuscan vernacular retelling of the earlier Latin Actus beati Francisci et sociorum eius. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_of_Gubbio  (Legend.)

question: As the beast of Gubbio charged him with open jaws, Francis made the sign of the cross and called out to it as kin — a greeting that stopped it in its tracks and made it lie at his feet. What did he call it?
context: In the Fioretti Francis addresses the animal 'Frate Lupo' — Brother Wolf — the same fraternal address he uses for Brother Sun and Sister Moon in the Canticle. Source: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/ugolino/flowers.iii.xxi.html  (Legend.)

question: Francis brokered a pact between the wolf and the townspeople of Gubbio: the town would feed the wolf every day for the rest of its life, and the wolf would stop killing. How did the wolf SEAL the pact in front of Francis?
answer: It placed its right paw in his hand
choices: It placed its right paw in his hand
It licked his open palm three times
It bowed its head to the ground
It rolled onto its back at his feet
context: In chapter 21 of the Fioretti Francis asks the wolf to shake on the promise a second time before the whole town, 'and the wolf raising his right paw, placed it in the hand of Saint Francis.' Source: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/ugolino/flowers.iii.xxi.html  (Legend.)

question: Walking with his companions through the plain near Bevagna in Umbria, Francis saw a huge flock of many kinds of birds — doves, crows, jackdaws — sitting in a field. He left the road, walked in among them, and preached. How did he address them?
context: The sermon to the birds is Fioretti chapter 16. Francis tells them they are much beholden to God their creator for giving them 'liberty to fly everywhere' and 'clothing double and triple.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sermon_of_St._Francis  (Legend.)

question: Near the end of his life in 1224, weak and nearly blind and sheltered at San Damiano, Francis composed a long poem of praise — the first known poem written in the Italian vernacular by a named author. What is it called?
context: Also called the Canticle of the Creatures (Cantico di frate Sole). It is the earliest surviving vernacular Italian poem with a known author, in the Umbrian dialect. The 'Peace Prayer of Saint Francis' is a much later French composition from around 1912, often misattributed to him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canticle_of_the_Sun

question: Francis's Canticle praises God through a whole household of siblings: 'Brother Sun,' 'Sister Moon,' Brother Wind, Sister Water, Brother Fire. What phrase opens each verse?
context: 'Praise be to you, my Lord.' Pope Francis (elected 2013) took his name from Francis of Assisi and titled his 2015 encyclical Laudato Si' after this opening line. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laudato_si%27_(disambiguation)

question: Francis Xavier, later the great Jesuit missionary to Asia, was born in 1506 in the castle of Xavier, into a noble family of one of Europe's oldest peoples -- neighbours of both France and Spain in the Pyrenees. What people were his family?
context: Xavier's mother Maria de Azpilcueta was heiress to Xavier castle in the Kingdom of Navarre. His older brothers fought against the Spanish crown in the conquest of Navarre in 1512. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: At the College Sainte-Barbe in Paris in the late 1520s, a young Francis Xavier dreamed of a chivalric career restoring his ruined family fortunes. His limping roommate -- a much older student and former soldier -- wore him down over six years by repeating a single line from the Gospel of Mark. Which line did that older roommate keep asking him?
answer: What shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?
choices: What shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?
Who among you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?
How can a camel pass through the eye of a needle?
Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye and not the log in your own?
context: The roommate was Ignatius of Loyola, wounded at the siege of Pamplona and turned pilgrim. Mark 8:36. Xavier finally joined the little band of companions around 1533. Sources: jesuits.org/stories/the-feast-of-st-francis-xavier-sj/.

question: On August 15, 1534, Ignatius of Loyola and six companions -- Francis Xavier among them -- climbed a hill outside Paris and, in a crypt beneath a chapel there, took private vows of poverty and chastity that became the seed of the Society of Jesus. On which Parisian hill did the seven meet that day?
context: The vows were taken in a crypt under the chapel of the martyr Denis on Montmartre ('mount of the martyr'). The formal Society of Jesus was approved by Pope Paul III in 1540. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: In 1540, when King John III of Portugal asked Rome for missionaries for his new Asian empire, Nicolas Bobadilla fell ill and Ignatius called Xavier at short notice. Xavier packed in two hours, sailed from Lisbon in April 1541, and after a thirteen-month voyage stepped ashore in May 1542 at the capital of Portuguese India. What port was that?
context: Goa on the Konkan coast was the seat of the Portuguese viceroy of India from 1510. Xavier used it as his base for the next decade, ranging as far as the Moluccas and Japan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: In Malacca in the 1540s Xavier met a fugitive Japanese samurai named Anjiro, who had fled his homeland after killing a man. Anjiro learned Portuguese, was baptized at Goa as Paulo de Santa Fe, and guided Xavier back to his home island. On August 15, 1549 the two landed at a port on Kyushu, and Xavier became the first Christian missionary to Japan. At which Kyushu port did he step ashore?
context: Anjiro was from Satsuma in southern Kyushu, and Kagoshima was his own home city. Nagasaki grew into the great Christian port only decades later. The Japanese converts came to be called kirishitan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anjir%C5%8D; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: Convinced that if China were converted the rest of Asia would follow, Xavier sailed from Goa in 1552 for the Chinese coast. Chinese law forbade any foreigner to enter, so he waited on a small offshore island near Canton, trying to bribe a merchant to smuggle him ashore. He caught a fever in a straw hut on the beach and died there on December 3, 1552, aged 46, within sight of the coast he never reached. What was the name of that offshore island?
context: Shangchuan (Sancian in Portuguese sources) lies off the coast of Guangdong. Macau was not yet a Portuguese enclave; that came a few years later. A stone chapel now marks the spot on Shangchuan where Xavier is said to have died. Sources: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Francis-Xavier.

question: Xavier's body, reported incorrupt after burial and exhumation, was carried from the China coast to Malacca and finally to Goa in 1554, where it lies today in the Basilica of Bom Jesus. In 1614, at Vatican request, a piece of the body was cut off and taken to Rome, where it is still displayed in a silver reliquary in the Jesuit mother church, the Gesu. Which body part was sent to Rome?
context: The forearm -- the arm that had baptized, by tradition, some thirty thousand converts -- is displayed in a raised silver reliquary at the Chiesa del Gesu in Rome. The rest of the body remains in Goa and is exposed for public veneration once a decade. Xavier was canonized in 1622 alongside Ignatius, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri, and Isidore. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Xavier.

question: In Norse myth, the goddess Freyja rides across the sky in a chariot -- but her chariot is not pulled by horses or by goats. What pulls Freyja's chariot?
context: Snorri Sturluson gives the two cats plainly as her team in Gylfaginning 24 of the Prose Edda. Thor's chariot IS pulled by goats, and Freyr owns the golden boar Gullinbursti -- both are used here as honest wrong choices, not joke options. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, the goddess Freyja's hall in the afterworld -- where warriors slain in battle come to her -- has a name that means 'People-Field'. What is the name of her hall?
context: Folkvangr is her whole realm; Sessrumnir is the great HALL inside that realm. All four distractors are real named halls of the Norse gods used honestly -- Bilskirnir is Thor's hall, and Vingolf is another goddess-hall. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, Freyja's most famous single possession is a necklace -- the most brilliant piece of jewellery in all Nine Worlds. What is the name of that necklace?
context: Brisingamen means roughly 'the necklace of the Brisings'. All four distractors are real named Norse treasures used honestly -- Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night, Andvaranaut is the cursed ring of the Volsung cycle, Sviagris is a legendary Swedish king's ring. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'.

question: In Norse myth, the goddess Freyja's necklace Brisingamen was forged deep in the earth by a company of four dwarves whose names the Sorla thattr preserves for us. What are the four dwarves' names?
context: The Sorla thattr (a story preserved in the 14th-century Flateyjarbok manuscript) names the four smiths as Alfrigg, Dvalin, Berling, and Grerr. All four distractor quartets are real named Norse dwarves used honestly -- Sindri and Brokkr forged Mjolnir; Fjalar and Galar brewed the Mead of Poetry; Nordri, Sudri, Austri, and Vestri are the four dwarves who hold up the four corners of the sky. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, Freyja owns a magical cloak of feathers -- the valshamr -- and its wearer can fly. Loki borrows it more than once, including to rescue Idunn from a giant. What kind of bird's feathers is Freyja's cloak made from?
context: Valshamr means literally 'falcon-skin'. Loki borrows it to fetch Idunn back from the giant Thjazi (Skaldskaparmal 3) and again to spy out where the giant Thrym has hidden Mjolnir (Thrymskvida 3-5). Freyja lends it grudgingly the second time. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, Freyja's husband is named Odr -- and he has wandered away from her, and she cannot find him. What does Freyja weep for her missing husband, so much that the poets made a kenning out of it?
context: Snorri says in Gylfaginning 35 that Freyja's tears turn to red gold as they fall. In Norse skaldic poetry, 'Freyja's tears' became a standing kenning (poetic phrase) for gold itself (Skaldskaparmal 37). She searches for Odr under many names -- Mardoll, Horn, Gefn, Syr. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, Loki once stole the Brisingamen right out of Freyja's bedchamber by turning into a fly to slip past her locked door. Which of the Aesir tracked him down and won the necklace back from him?
answer: Heimdall, the watchman of the gods
choices: Heimdall, the watchman of the gods
Tyr, the one-handed god of oaths
Vidar, the silent son of Odin
context: Heimdall found Loki with the necklace; both took the shape of seals and fought over it at a rock called Singasteinn out at sea. Heimdall won and gave the Brisingamen back to Freyja. All four distractors are real named Aesir used honestly. Source: Wikipedia, 'Brisingamen'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, the Aesir and Vanir were once at war. When the war ended, the two groups of gods exchanged hostages, and the Vanir sent three: Freyja, her brother Freyr, and a third -- Freyja and Freyr's father. What was his name?
context: Njord is the Vanir god of the sea, of shores, and of wealth from the sea-trade. His two children Freyr and Freyja came with him to Asgard. All four distractors are real named Norse gods or primordial beings used honestly -- Aegir is a sea-giant, Ymir is the first frost-giant, Mimir is the wise head at the well. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth, the two daughters that Freyja bore to her wandering husband Odr both have names meaning 'treasure' or 'precious jewel', as though even her children were more gold. What are the two daughters' names?
context: Both names in Old Norse literally mean 'treasure' -- Hnoss is a word for a precious jewel or a treasure, and Gersemi is a word for something exquisite and prized. All four distractor pairs are real Norse duos: Sol and Mani are sun and moon, Nott and Dag are night and day, Skuld and Verdandi are two of the three Norns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Freyja'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the god of sunshine, good weather, harvest and peace is not one of the Aesir by birth. He belongs to the older tribe of gods who were traded to the Aesir as hostages after their war. Which tribe is he from?
context: Freyr, his father Njord, and his sister Freyja are the three Vanir hostages who came to live in Asgard after the Aesir-Vanir war. The Jotnar are the giants (their enemies); the Alfar are the elves; the Aesir are the tribe he was given to, not the one he came from. Snorri, Gylfaginning 23-24.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr's home in the nine worlds is a bright realm the gods gave him as a baby present when he cut his first tooth. What is the name of Freyr's realm?
context: Grimnismal 5 in the Poetic Edda: 'Alfheim the gods to Frey gave in days of yore for a tooth-gift.' The name literally means 'Elf-Home'. Asgard is the whole home of the Aesir; Svartalfheim is the home of the dark elves / dwarves; Midgard is the human world.  (Legend.)

question: One afternoon Freyr sneaks onto a special high seat in Asgard that only two gods are supposed to use. From it a god can see into every world at once. Whose high seat has he climbed?
context: Only Odin and his wife Frigg are allowed to sit on Hlidskjalf. Freyr's trespass is what sets the whole Skirnismal story in motion. Skinfaxi is a horse, not a seat; Himinbjorg is Heimdall's hall, not a watching-seat; Fensalir is Frigg's hall.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr comes home from the forbidden high seat unable to eat, unable to sleep, unable to speak. The gods finally send his own servant to find out what has happened to him. What is the servant's name?
context: Skirnir means 'the Shining One' and he is Freyr's messenger throughout Skirnismal. Skidbladnir is Freyr's magical ship (not a person); Skadi is Njord's giantess wife; Skoll is one of the wolves that chases the sun.  (Legend.)

question: Off in Jotunheim, far to the north, a giant-girl steps out of her father's hall and reaches her arm up to open a door. The plain skin of that one arm shines so brightly that the sea and the sky light up all the way to Asgard. Freyr sees it from the high seat and falls silent. What is her name?
context: Gerdr is the daughter of the giant Gymir. Skirnismal stanzas 4-7 describe the bare-arm-shining moment; it is one of the most sudden coup-de-foudre scenes in Norse verse. Gunnr is a valkyrie; Gefjun is an Aesir goddess; Grid is another giantess but the mother of Vidar.  (Legend.)

question: When Skirnir reaches Gerdr's hall, he first tries to buy her hand with treasure. He offers her a set of golden apples and then a very famous named dwarf-made object. Which of these dwarf-made treasures does Skirnir offer Gerdr?
context: Draupnir is Odin's ring, dwarf-made, which drips eight matching golden rings every ninth night. Skirnir offers eleven apples and then Draupnir itself -- Gerdr refuses both, saying the Vanir have gold enough (Skirnismal 19-22). Andvaranaut is the cursed dragon-treasure ring from the Sigurd cycle; Sviagris is a Swedish royal ring (Hrolf Kraki's saga); Brisingamen is Freyja's necklace -- all real dwarf-made Norse treasures, but only Draupnir is the one Skirnir offers.  (Legend.)

question: When gifts and drawn steel both fail to move Gerdr, Skirnir stops asking and starts cursing. He tells her exactly the kind of husband she will get instead if she keeps refusing -- a monstrous mate she cannot escape. What kind of husband does Skirnir promise her?
context: Skirnir's curse in Skirnismal 27-36 is one of the darkest passages in Norse poetry: Gerdr will pine forever, be mocked by gods and men, sit weeping under the giants' gate, and be married to a three-headed frost-giant she loathes. The threat, not the treasure, is what finally breaks her.  (Legend.)

question: The curse works. Terrified, Gerdr names a time and place where she will meet Freyr in nine nights and become his bride. She picks a small, quiet wood far from the giants' halls. What is the name of the grove where Gerdr promises to meet Freyr?
context: Skirnismal 39: Gerdr sets the meeting in the grove Barri after nine nights (nine is the sacred Norse number -- nine worlds, Odin's nine nights on the tree, Heimdall's nine mothers). Glasir is the golden-leaved tree beside Valhalla; Jarnvid ('Iron-Wood') is where the giantess-mother of wolves dwells; Myrkvid ('Mirk-Wood') is the dark border-forest between worlds.  (Legend.)

question: At the end of the world, out of Muspelheim in the south, a fire-giant comes riding to burn the nine worlds. He carries a sword that shines brighter than the sun. Freyr rides out to meet him. What is the fire-giant's name?
context: Surt (Surtr, 'the Swart One') leads the fire-giants of Muspelheim at Ragnarok. Fenrir is the wolf that swallows Odin; Jormungandr is the world-serpent that fights Thor; Hrym is the giant who steers the ship Naglfar. Voluspa 52-53; Gylfaginning 51.  (Legend.)

question: The Merry Men in Sherwood Forest include a stout, jolly churchman in a friar's robe with a rope belt around his middle. When Robin Hood first stumbles across him at a riverside, the friar does not run and does not preach -- he draws a weapon and squares up to fight. What weapon did Friar Tuck swing at Robin Hood the first time they met?
context: Friar Tuck carries a sword throughout the ballad Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child Ballad 123). Church law of the day officially forbade a friar from shedding blood -- clerics were supposed to fight only with bludgeoning weapons like clubs or maces -- and the joke of Tuck is that he cheerfully ignores this and fights like any yeoman with a blade. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: In the ballad Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar (Child Ballad 123), Will Scadlock tells Robin that a stout friar has beaten every man that came against him, and Robin sets out to find him. The friar lives at a real Yorkshire monastery, still standing today as a ruin. Which abbey does the ballad name?
context: The ballad places the friar at Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire -- a Cistercian house founded in 1132, dissolved by Henry VIII, and now a UNESCO ruin. All four choices are real Yorkshire abbeys of the same era. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: When Robin Hood first meets the fighting friar at a riverside, he draws his sword and forces the friar to carry him across the water on his back. The friar carries him in silence -- but halfway across, he gets his revenge. What does the friar do to Robin midstream?
context: In Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar, the friar dumps Robin into the river halfway across in payment for being made to carry him. Both men then draw swords in the shallows and fight until they are exhausted. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.  (Legend.)

question: After Robin Hood and the fighting friar have fought with swords in the river until both are exhausted, Robin blows his horn to summon the Merry Men. The friar answers by whistling up a pack of his own beasts that had helped him guard his abbey. What kind of dogs come running out of the woods?
context: The friar whistles up his pack of mastiffs -- massive English guard-dogs bred for war and estate defence. Robin's men come with bows; the friar's mastiffs come with teeth; neither side can beat the other. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar; boldoutlaw.com, Friar Tuck.  (Legend.)

question: The full title of Child Ballad 123 is Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar. A curtal friar was known at a glance by one feature that told a medieval villager he was a mendicant on the road, not a cloistered monk. What was it?
context: A curtal friar wore a short robe -- 'curtal' is from Old French 'curt', meaning short. The short robe was the mark of a mendicant on the move, walking preaching roads instead of staying cloistered like a black-robed Benedictine monk. All four choices were real marks of medieval clergy, but only the short robe gave the 'curtal' name. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar.

question: Friar Tuck is not one of the original Merry Men. He is missing entirely from the earliest Robin Hood ballads. He joins the tradition only around 1475, first appearing as a character in what kind of medieval source?
context: Friar Tuck first appears in a fragmentary text of a May Day play, Robin Hood and the Friar, dated around 1475. The Curtal Friar ballad (Child 123) was written down later. Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son are in the earliest ballads; Tuck is a later arrival. Source: robinhoodlegend.com, Plays and the May Festivities.

question: Twice in 1417, royal writs from King Henry V demanded the arrest of an outlaw who called himself 'Frere Tuk' and led a band that murdered, robbed, and burned forest wardens' lodges across Surrey and Sussex. A 1429 letter later gave his real identity. In real life he was actually what?
answer: a chaplain of Lindfield in Sussex
choices: a chaplain of Lindfield in Sussex
a friar of Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire
a hermit of the Weald of Sussex
a monk of Battle Abbey in Sussex
context: The 1429 letter identifies the outlaw 'Frere Tuk' as Robert Stafford, chaplain of the village of Lindfield in Sussex. He was a real churchman who took up outlawry and borrowed a colourful nickname; the ballad-Tuck grew up on top of his memory. Source: boldoutlaw.com, The Search for a Real Robin Hood; Lindfield Life history articles.

question: In a house in Nazareth, in Galilee, an angel appears to a young woman named Mary and greets her -- 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' -- and tells her she will bear a son called Jesus. Which angel?
context: Luke 1:26-28 (KJV): 'the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth... And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.' All four choices are named angels in Jewish and Christian tradition.

question: The angel tells Mary she will conceive a son. Mary's astonished reply is a short, honest question, quoted in Luke in the King James wording. What does she ask?
answer: How shall this be, seeing I know not a man
choices: How shall this be, seeing I know not a man
Why hast thou chosen me above all women
What sign wilt thou give me for a token
Where shall this thing come to pass
context: Luke 1:34 (KJV): 'Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?' 'Know' in this construction is the biblical euphemism for marital relations.

question: As a sign to Mary that nothing is impossible, the angel tells her that one of her older female relatives -- long thought unable to bear a child -- is already six months into a pregnancy of her own. Which relative?
context: Luke 1:36 (KJV): 'And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren.' Elizabeth's child is the future John the Baptist.

question: Mary hurries into the hill country of Judea to visit her older cousin. The moment Mary calls out her greeting at the door, one specific thing happens that Luke uses to open the whole scene. What?
answer: The baby in her womb leaps
choices: The baby in her womb leaps
A dove lands on the roof
The oil in her lamp catches fire
context: Luke 1:41 (KJV): 'And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost.' Elizabeth explains at verse 44: the child 'leaped in my womb for joy'.

question: In answer to Elizabeth's blessing, Mary bursts into a long poem of praise that Catholic, Lutheran and Anglican monasteries have sung every evening at Vespers for more than a thousand years. What is its traditional Latin name?
context: Luke 1:46-47 (KJV): 'And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.' All four choices are famous canticles named for their opening Latin word; three come from Luke's first two chapters alone (Benedictus = Zacharias's song, Nunc Dimittis = Simeon's song).

question: The Magnificat is famous for one line in particular -- the line that Christian reformers, radicals and poets have quoted for centuries as the song's political sting. In the King James wording, which line comes from Mary's song and not from somewhere else in scripture?
answer: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree
choices: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth
The kingdom of this world is become the kingdom of our Lord
context: Luke 1:52 (KJV). This reversal image echoes the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2 ('the bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength'). It is why the Magnificat has always been sung at evening prayer, night after night, in monasteries.

question: The same angel who later visits Mary had already appeared, months before, to Elizabeth's husband -- the priest Zacharias -- while he was carrying out his priestly duty inside the Temple in Jerusalem. Where in the Temple was he standing when Gabriel spoke to him?
context: Luke 1:9-11 (KJV): 'his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord... And there appeared unto him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense.' The incense altar stood in the Holy Place, the inner room. The angel appears on the right side of it.

question: When the priest Zacharias doubts Gabriel's promise that his old wife will bear a son, the angel strikes him with a specific disability that lasts until the child is born. Which one?
context: Luke 1:20 (KJV): 'And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words.' 'Dumb' in the King James English means unable to speak.

question: In the last books of Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, one young knight rides into Camelot on the feast of Pentecost in red armour, led by an old hermit, and takes an empty seat at the Round Table that had killed every other man who ever sat in it. In the story he is the pure knight who alone achieves the Holy Grail. What is his name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.4. Galahad is the pure Grail-knight of the Vulgate Queste and Malory. Percival and Bors are his two Grail companions but only Galahad may sit in the Siege Perilous. Lancelot, his father, is the greatest fighter in the world but is barred from the Grail by his love for Guinevere.  (Legend.)

question: Galahad's mother is a young noblewoman who tricks Sir Lancelot into her bed by enchantment -- the sorceress Dame Brusen gives her a magic ring that makes her appear as Queen Guinevere for one night, and Galahad is conceived. Who is Galahad's mother?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XI. Elaine of Corbenic is the daughter of King Pelles the Fisher King; Dame Brusen brought Lancelot the magic ring that made Elaine appear as Guinevere for the night. Elaine of Astolat is a DIFFERENT Elaine -- the tragic lily-maid who dies of love for Lancelot in a boat drifting down to Camelot. Nimue is Merlin's sorceress-apprentice; Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister and a great villain.  (Legend.)

question: On the same Pentecost, a strange thing comes drifting up the river to Camelot. A great STONE floats on the water, with a bright sword driven through it; letters on the stone say only the best knight in the world shall draw it. Sir Lancelot tries first and fails; Sir Gawain tries and fails. Which knight then puts his hand to the sword and draws it easily?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XIII ch.2. This floating stone with a sword is the SECOND sword-in-a-stone of the whole cycle -- Arthur drew the first as a boy to be crowned king of Britain; Galahad draws this one to be crowned king of holiness. Percival and Bors are the two knights who will go with him on the Grail quest, but the floating sword is Galahad's alone.  (Legend.)

question: When the Grail quest ends, only THREE knights of the whole fellowship of the Round Table actually achieve the Grail -- Galahad the pure, plus two others. Which two knights complete the Grail quest with Galahad?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII. Percival and Bors are the two companions who ride the whole quest with Galahad and see the Grail at Corbenic. Gawain and Lancelot both attempt the quest and both fail. Kay and Bedivere are old household knights of Arthur. Tristan and Palamedes belong to a different romance-cycle -- the Tristan story of Cornwall.  (Legend.)

question: The three Grail-knights ride at last to a castle where the wounded Fisher King rules -- the same castle where Galahad had been conceived. In its chapel they see the Grail uncovered before them. What is the name of the Fisher King's castle?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII; Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal. Corbenic is King Pelles's castle -- the same castle where Elaine tricked Lancelot and conceived Galahad. Camelot is Arthur's own city. Joyous Gard is Lancelot's personal castle. Tintagel is where Uther Pendragon fathered Arthur.  (Legend.)

question: In the Vulgate Queste's telling of what happens in the chapel at Corbenic, the Grail is uncovered and the three knights receive communion -- but it is not a priest who serves them. Someone else steps out of the Grail vessel and hands them the bread. Who serves the three knights communion from the Grail?
context: Vulgate Queste del Saint Graal c.1220. The scene is the mystical centre of the whole cycle -- Christ steps from the vessel and communicates the three knights with his own hand. Joseph of Arimathea is the figure who FIRST brought the Grail to Britain in the older backstory. The Fisher King is Corbenic's wounded lord. Michael is the warrior archangel of the Book of Revelation.  (Legend.)

question: After the wonder at Corbenic, Galahad and his companions carry the Grail overseas to a mystical city said to lie somewhere in the East. There Galahad is crowned king and rules for one year before his death. What is the name of that city?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.20-22. Sarras is a mystic city of the Grail cycle -- sometimes said to be in the Holy Land, sometimes further east, never really pinned down on any real map. Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Constantinople are the great real Christian cities of the eastern Mediterranean and would each have been an obvious choice -- the poet's use of a made-up name Sarras is deliberate.  (Legend.)

question: During Mass in Sarras, Galahad kneels before the Grail and beholds it uncovered. Malory says the wonder of that sight is so great that a particular thing happens to him at that very instant. What happens to Galahad when he beholds the Grail directly?
answer: he dies of joy on the spot
choices: he dies of joy on the spot
he goes blind for the rest of his life
he is turned to stone in the chapel
he is carried off in his sleep
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.22. Galahad had asked earlier that he might die at the moment of his greatest joy -- and here the wish is granted. The wonder of the uncovered Grail simply kills him; his soul is carried up by angels. Being blinded belongs to Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus; petrification belongs to Perseus's Medusa (Greek pillar); a sleeping abduction belongs to fairy-story.  (Legend.)

question: At the instant Galahad dies in the Mass at Sarras, and his soul goes up, something comes DOWN from above the altar and takes the Grail out of the world for good. Malory says no one ever sees it again. What comes down from heaven and takes the Grail?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.22. A single HAND reaches down from above the altar, takes the Grail and the holy spear with it, and is gone. This is the very end of the Grail on earth. The white dove belongs to the Grail's arrival scenes (and to the baptism of Jesus in the gospels); Jacob's ladder belongs to Genesis; the pillar of fire is Israel's guide out of Egypt in Exodus.  (Legend.)

question: When the Grail quest is finished, one knight rides back alone to Arthur's court and tells the whole tale of Corbenic and Sarras -- he is the only Grail-witness left in the world, and years later he will stand with Lancelot in the war that ends the Round Table. Which knight is this?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII ch.23. Bors alone returns to Camelot and tells the whole tale -- Galahad died at the Mass in Sarras and Percival took vows and died a hermit not long after. Later Bors stands with Lancelot in the war that ends the Round Table. Gawain, Kay, and Lancelot all attempted the quest and all failed to reach Corbenic.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, a tall handsome young man arrives at Camelot at Pentecost and refuses to give his name. Sir Kay the seneschal, scorning him, gives him a mocking French nickname meaning 'Fair-Hands' and puts him to work scrubbing pots. What was the nickname?
context: Beaumains is Old French for 'fair hands' (beau + mains). Malory Book VII opens with the scene. Le Bel Inconnu ('the Fair Unknown') is a parallel French romance by Renaut de Beaujeu, not a name in Malory; La Cote Male Taile ('the badly cut coat') is another Round Table nickname, given by Kay to Sir Breunor; Perceval le Gallois ('Perceval the Welshman') is the Grail knight of Chretien de Troyes.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's Tale of Sir Gareth, the young man who took the kitchen nickname Beaumains asked King Arthur for three gifts on arrival. Which was his very first gift?
answer: food and shelter for a year
choices: food and shelter for a year
a place at the Round Table
the hand of a lady of the court
context: Malory Book VII. The other two gifts would be named a year later. His plan was to earn his knighthood without the advantage of anyone knowing his name. A sword and horse would have marked him as noble; a Round Table seat was not something asked as a gift; marriage came only at the tale's end, to Dame Lyonesse.  (Legend.)

question: After a year in the kitchens, Beaumains asked his second gift: the quest of a damsel who had arrived seeking a knight to rescue her besieged sister. What was the damsel's name?
context: Lynette (sometimes Lyonet) rode beside Beaumains all the way to the castle, mocking him from behind as a kitchen-boy who smelled of grease, until his deeds converted her mockery to admiration. Elaine of Astolat dies of unrequited love for Lancelot; Nimue is the Lady of the Lake figure who imprisons Merlin; Enid is the wife of Geraint in the parallel Welsh and French tales.  (Legend.)

question: The damsel Lynette had come to Camelot seeking rescue for her sister, who was besieged in her own castle by a great enemy. What was the besieged sister's name?
context: Dame Lyonesse held Castle Perilous against the Red Knight of the Red Launds. Beaumains married her at the tale's end. Guinevere is Arthur's queen; Igraine is Arthur's mother; Morgause is Gareth's own mother (which he does not yet know he is proving himself to marry into).  (Legend.)

question: On the road to Castle Perilous, Beaumains fought and defeated in turn four knights known by the colours of their arms: the Black Knight Sir Percard, a Green Knight, a Red Knight, and one more, sending each defeated foe back to Arthur as prisoner. What colour was the fourth?
answer: the Blue Knight Sir Persaunt of Inde
choices: the Blue Knight Sir Persaunt of Inde
the White Knight Sir Balin the Savage
the Golden Knight Sir Ector de Maris
context: Malory Book VII. Persaunt's territory is called 'Inde', hence the deep blue of his arms. Sir Balin the Savage is a wholly different tragic knight (the Dolorous Stroke); Sir Ector de Maris is Lancelot's brother; Sir Palamedes is the Saracen knight of the Tristan cycle.  (Legend.)

question: At Castle Perilous the besieger who had held Dame Lyonesse locked in her tower was a giant knight in red arms. The knight in red had done a shameful thing around his own pavilion, meant to intimidate any challenger who rode up: what?
answer: hanged nearly forty defeated knights by their necks from trees
choices: hanged nearly forty defeated knights by their necks from trees
chained a lion at each of the four corners
planted the ground with sharpened stakes and burning oil
set his slain foes' heads on pikes along the palisade
context: Malory Book VII. To be hanged by the neck was the most shameful death a knight could suffer, reserved for common criminals; the Red Knight had done it to nearly forty defeated foes as a warning and a boast. Beaumains cut the corpses down for honourable burial after the fight.  (Legend.)

question: Beaumains fought the giant Red Knight of the Red Launds all day at Castle Perilous, spared his life on condition he yield at Camelot, and cut the hanged knights down for burial. What was the Red Knight's true name, later revealed?
context: Malory Book VII. Ironside explained he had sworn to a former love, whose brother had been killed by Lancelot or Gawain, that he would kill any of Arthur's knights he could reach. Sir Turquine is a different giant who imprisoned dozens of Arthur's knights and was slain by Lancelot; Sir Breunis Sans Pite ('without pity') is another wandering villain; Sir Marhaus is the Irish champion killed by Tristan.  (Legend.)

question: When Beaumains finally revealed his true identity, he was named as the youngest son of a king; his father was the king whose sons Gawain, Agravain, Gaheris, and Mordred were also known at Arthur's court. What was his father's name and kingdom?
context: Malory Book VII closes with the revelation. Lot's queen was Morgause, half-sister to Arthur; this makes all four brothers Arthur's nephews. King Ban is Lancelot's father; King Pellinore is father of Perceval and Lamorak; King Uriens of Gore is husband of Morgan le Fay and father of Yvain.  (Legend.)

question: Gareth's story ends happily with his marriage to Dame Lyonesse, but the later Round Table cycle turns the beloved young knight into the trigger of the fellowship's collapse. During whose rescue is Gareth accidentally killed by Sir Lancelot, turning his brother Gawain into Lancelot's mortal enemy?
choices: King Arthur from the siege of Joyous Gard
Sir Bors from the dungeon of Sir Meliagrance
context: Malory Book XX. Arthur had condemned Guinevere to the pyre for adultery with Lancelot; Lancelot's rescue party cut a bloody path through the guards, unknowingly killing the unarmed Gareth (who was there only out of loyalty). Gawain, who had loved Gareth most of all his brothers, refused ever to make peace with Lancelot; his rage kept the two great captains fighting while Mordred took the throne.  (Legend.)

question: On New Year's Day at Camelot, King Arthur's court is at feast in the great hall when a huge stranger rides in on horseback. Everything about the man and the horse is one single startling colour -- his skin, his beard, his armour, and the horse under him are all the same shade. What colour is the strange rider who bursts into Arthur's court?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 150-220. The Green Knight -- skin, beard, armour, and horse all green -- is one of the most striking single images in medieval literature. Red is the colour of a different Arthurian arrival (Galahad in his red armour at Pentecost); the Black Knight is a common romance figure; a silver rider is not a fixed medieval type.  (Legend.)

question: The green stranger who rides into Camelot on New Year's Day is armed for the exchange he has come to propose. He holds two things at once as he stops before Arthur's high table -- a heavy weapon in one hand and a branch of an evergreen plant in the other, offered as a sign that he comes in peace. What weapon does the Green Knight carry?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 206-209. The Green Knight carries a huge axe in one hand and a bough of holly in the other -- the holly is the peace-sign, the axe is the game-piece. The whole story turns on which knight will use the axe on his neck. The spear, broadsword, and mace are the other standard knightly weapons of the poem's period but are not the tools of this particular game.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight proposes what he calls a Christmas game to Arthur's court. The rule is simple and terrible: any knight who takes up the axe may strike him one blow with it right now -- BUT that knight must swear on his honour to receive one return blow, at the Green Knight's hand, at a set time later. When must the return blow be given?
answer: a year and a day later
choices: a year and a day later
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. 'A year and a day' is the medieval formula for a full year's completion of an oath or a legal claim (used in English law of ownership, in fairy-tale, and here in the beheading game). The other three periods sound the part but do not match this poem.  (Legend.)

question: The whole court is silent at the Green Knight's proposal. King Arthur himself starts to rise to take up the axe -- but a young knight of the Round Table steps forward and asks Arthur's leave to take the game in the king's place. Which knight of the Round Table volunteers to strike the Green Knight?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. Gawain -- son of King Lot of Orkney and Arthur's sister Morgause, and youngest of Arthur's chief knights -- takes the game to spare his uncle. Lancelot, Percival, and Kay are all present at the court in the wider Arthurian tradition but this poem makes Gawain its hero.  (Legend.)

question: Gawain takes the axe and strikes off the Green Knight's head with a single stroke -- and something very strange then happens. The headless body does not fall. Instead it does one very deliberate thing before mounting its horse. What does the headless Green Knight do next?
answer: picks up its own severed head
choices: picks up its own severed head
kneels and prays before the high altar
sheds its green armour on the floor
cuts off its own left hand at the wrist
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I lines 435-459. The headless body walks calmly across the hall, lifts its own severed head from the flagstones by the hair, and mounts its horse. The head then OPENS ITS EYES and speaks aloud to Gawain from the Green Knight's own hand -- telling him to meet him a year hence.  (Legend.)

question: The Green Knight's severed head, held up in his own hand from horseback, opens its eyes and speaks to Gawain -- naming the place where Gawain must come, one year from that New Year's Day, to receive the return blow. What is the name of the meeting-place the Green Knight names?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt I. The Green Chapel turns out to be no chapel at all but a low hollow mound with an opening in it in the northern wilderness -- an old barrow. The other three names sound the medieval-romance part (the Perilous Ford is a testing-place in Chretien, the Waste Land is the Grail-realm, Castle Adventurous is a Malory name) but the Green Knight names none of them.  (Legend.)

question: A year later Gawain rides north through the winter to keep his oath. On Christmas Eve he finds shelter in a fine castle in the wilds and is welcomed by its lord, a big red-faced hunter. The lord proposes a second game to fill the days until New Year's: while he goes out hunting each day, Gawain will rest at the castle, and each night the two men will exchange whatever each has won that day. What is the name of this lord?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt II-III. Sir Bertilak de Hautdesert is the lord of the castle. Balin is the tragic knight of the Dolorous Stroke in Malory. Bedivere is Arthur's last steward. Sir Baudwin of Britain is one of Arthur's Table but not this lord. The exchange-of-winnings game is Bertilak's own contribution.  (Legend.)

question: While Bertilak is out hunting each day, his own lady comes to Gawain's chamber and tries to seduce him. Gawain, courteous but resolved, refuses her bed but each night gives Bertilak the KISSES she pressed on him during the day. On the third day the lady also gives Gawain one particular gift -- and Gawain, terrified of the axe waiting for him tomorrow, keeps this gift secret and does NOT give it to Bertilak. What is the gift Gawain hides?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt III. The lady swears the green silk girdle (a woven belt) will keep its wearer from being killed. Gawain, believing he will die at the axe tomorrow, wraps it around his waist under his armour and does NOT hand it to Bertilak that night. Rings and phials and locks of hair are the ordinary courtly-love gifts but the girdle is the one the poem uses.  (Legend.)

question: On New Year's Day Gawain rides to the Green Chapel and finds the Green Knight sharpening the axe by a stream. Gawain bares his neck and kneels. The Green Knight swings the axe THREE times in all. The first swing he pulls up because Gawain flinched; the second he pulls up because Gawain kept still; only the third comes down. What does the third swing do to Gawain?
answer: nicks his neck and draws blood
choices: nicks his neck and draws blood
cuts off his ear on the left side
breaks his collarbone but not the skin
misses him entirely and on purpose
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV lines 2260-2330. The third swing shaves the skin of Gawain's neck and just breaks it -- one small cut, one drop of blood. That single nick is the punishment for the one day Gawain hid the girdle from Bertilak. Had he kept the exchange bargain faithfully, the axe would have missed him entirely.  (Legend.)

question: After the three swings the Green Knight reveals who he really is. The huge green stranger and Gawain's cheerful host of the last three days turn out to be the SAME man, transformed. He then names the enchantress who put him in green skin and sent him to Arthur's court in the first place, to test the honour of the whole Round Table. Who sent the Green Knight to Camelot?
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV. Morgan le Fay -- Arthur's half-sister and a great mistress of enchantments -- shaped the whole scheme; Bertilak is her servant. The old woman Gawain saw beside the lady at the castle turns out to have been Morgan herself, watching in disguise. Nimue is Merlin's apprentice. Guinevere is Arthur's queen. The Lady of the Lake gave Excalibur.  (Legend.)

question: Genevieve is born around the year 420 in a village a few miles west of the Roman town of Lutetia, which is the old Latin name for what will become one of the great capitals of Europe. In the story she will spend her life protecting that city and become its patron saint. Which city is it?
context: Lutetia (Lutetia Parisiorum) was the Roman name for the town on the Ile de la Cite; it became Paris in the late Empire. Genevieve was born in the outlying village of Nanterre around 419-422. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.

question: When Genevieve is about seven years old a travelling bishop of Auxerre stops in her village on his way to Britain (he is going to argue against the Pelagian heresy there). He notices the child, recognises her seriousness, and consecrates her to God on the spot. What is the bishop's name?
context: Germanus of Auxerre was a well-attested Gallo-Roman bishop who did travel to Britain to argue against the Pelagian heresy; his consecration of the child Genevieve at Nanterre is one of the earliest scenes in her Vita. Athanasius was in Alexandria a century earlier; Ambrose was bishop of Milan; Boniface was an eighth-century missionary. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.
