question: In the summer of 451 a huge army has crossed the Rhine, is burning cities across Gaul, and word has just reached Paris that its line of march will bring it straight through the city. The Parisians are packing their households onto carts to flee south. Which warlord is leading the army?
context: Attila the Hun's western invasion of 451 is one of the best-attested events of late Roman history. Alaric was the Gothic king who sacked Rome in 410; Genseric was the Vandal king who sacked Rome in 455; Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor in 476. Source: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Genevieve.

question: As the Parisians pack to flee, Genevieve -- then a consecrated woman in her early thirties -- steps into the panic and stops it. She gathers a very particular group of the city's people into the churches for many days of fasts, prayers and vigils, and tells them the city will be spared if they hold. Whom does she gather into the churches?
choices: the Roman soldiers of the garrison
context: The Vita Genovefae is explicit that Genevieve organised the women of Paris into what modern historians call a 'prayer marathon'; her own explanation was that she was following the biblical models of Esther fasting in Persia and Judith praying before facing Holofernes. Source: britannica.com/biography/Saint-Genevieve.  (Legend.)

question: Some of the men of Paris are furious at Genevieve for stopping the flight, and the Vita Genovefae says a group of them plotted to seize her and put her to death. A messenger from the absent bishop arrived just in time to save her. What method did they mean to use?
choices: stone her outside the city gate
starve her in a locked church
context: The Vita Genovefae records the drowning plot; it was broken up when the archdeacon of Auxerre arrived from her old protector Germanus's see with a letter defending her. The Seine is the river that Paris straddles and is central to Genevieve's story throughout. Source: newadvent.org/cathen/06413f.htm.  (Legend.)

question: The Huns do turn aside from Paris. Attila's army wheels south, is intercepted, and is bloodily defeated at a great battle in the Champagne region of Gaul in 451. The Roman general Aetius fought alongside a barbarian king who was killed on the field that day. Which king?
context: The battle is known as the Catalaunian Plains (or Chalons); Theodoric I of the Visigoths was killed leading his men in the Roman-Visigothic line. Clovis was king of the Franks born decades later; Alaric was the earlier Gothic king who sacked Rome in 410; Gaiseric was the Vandal king. Parisians credited the deliverance to Genevieve's prayer marathon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.

question: Genevieve dies aged over 80 and is buried on the hill above the Left Bank of Paris that still bears her name. Fourteen centuries later King Louis XV builds a great domed church to her there. In 1791 the Revolution rededicates the building. What is it called today?
context: The domed church of Sainte-Genevieve, designed by Jacques-Germain Soufflot 1758-1790, was rededicated by the Revolution in 1791 as the Pantheon to house the tombs of Mirabeau, Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo and others. It still stands on the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve above the Sorbonne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_of_Saint_Genevieve.

question: The Parisian custom of carrying Genevieve's relics in procession to protect the city outlasts the fifth century by a long way. In 885, when raiders lay siege to Paris and the city seems about to fall, the same relics are carried along the walls and the besiegers finally withdraw. Which raiders were besieging Paris in 885?
context: The 885-886 Viking siege of Paris was led by the Norse jarl Sigfred with hundreds of longships; the defence by Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin, with Genevieve's relics carried on the walls, became one of the founding stories of the Capetian monarchy. Magyars raided further east; the Moors were in Spain; the Mongols came four centuries later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve.  (Legend.)

question: The historical George whom the medieval world made into its most famous dragon-slaying knight was in real life a Christian soldier of the Roman army, executed on 23 April 303 CE at Lydda in Palestine. Which Roman emperor was the one who ordered the persecution that killed him?
context: Diocletian's persecution (303-311) is called the Great Persecution -- the last and worst systematic Roman effort to stamp out the church. Nero killed Peter and Paul two centuries earlier; Marcus Aurelius killed the martyrs of Lyon; Julian (the Apostate) ruled long after the persecutions had ended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: The famous story of a knight riding by a lake, spearing a dragon, and leashing it with a princess's belt was NOT originally a story about George at all. It first appeared in the 9th and 10th centuries in Cappadocian frescoes about a different Christian warrior-saint, and only transferred to George in an 11th-century Georgian text. To which earlier warrior-saint did the dragon story originally belong?
context: Theodore Tiro ('Theodore the Recruit') is another martyred Roman soldier. Michael slays a dragon in the Book of Revelation but is an archangel, not a saint; Demetrios of Thessalonica is a lance-bearing warrior-saint but not the dragon's original owner; Mercurius is a mounted warrior-saint but again not the dragon's owner. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.  (Legend.)

question: The version of the George story that fixed itself in Western memory -- dragon in a lake, princess by the water, knight with a lance, town baptised on the spot -- comes from a great 13th-century collection of saints' lives compiled by Jacobus de Voragine. What is this famous book called?
context: 'Legenda Aurea', compiled around 1260 by Jacobus de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa. The Little Flowers is a much later Franciscan collection of Francis stories; the Roman Martyrology is a Church calendar of saints' feast-days; 'Book of the Saints' is not a specific canonical title. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: In the Golden Legend, when the lot at last falls on the king's own daughter, the townspeople dress her for the sacrifice and lead her out to the water's edge. In what clothing is the princess led out to the dragon?
context: The bride-of-the-dragon image is the same one the Greeks gave Andromeda chained to the rock as an offering to the sea-monster -- the pre-Christian ancestor of this scene. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.  (Legend.)

question: George rides by the lake, sees the weeping princess, hears her story, and charges the beast; he wounds it with his lance but does not kill it. He then tells the princess to fasten one thing on the wounded dragon so that she can lead it, tame, back into the city. What does he tell her to fasten on it?
answer: Her girdle around its neck as a leash
choices: Her girdle around its neck as a leash
A strand of her hair looped round its horn
A ribbon from her sleeve tied to its foreleg
Her nurse's rosary hung at its throat
context: Girdle = the belt or sash of her dress. In the Golden Legend the leashed dragon follows her meekly through the city gates so that the townspeople can see the miracle for themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: George told the terrified people of the city he would publicly kill the dragon in the town square if, and only if, they all agreed to be baptised. They agreed, and the beast was beheaded with a single sword-stroke in front of everyone. According to the Golden Legend, how many men were baptised in the square that day, not counting the women and the children?
context: 'Fifteen thousand men, without counting women and children' is the Golden Legend's own number. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: The Golden Legend leaves the princess unnamed. Later English tellings, from the sixteenth century onward, gave her a name that stuck in the popular version -- especially in Richard Johnson's 'Seven Champions of Christendom'. What was the princess's late-medieval name?
context: Sabra is late medieval / early modern -- not in the Golden Legend itself. Cleodolinda and Aia appear in some regional variants; Margaret of Antioch is a different saint entirely, whose own legend also involves a dragon (she is swallowed and bursts out unharmed). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George_and_the_Dragon.

question: George was a Cappadocian saint of the Eastern church for a thousand years before the English kings made him their own. He became patron of England in the fourteenth century when a warrior-king placed his new order of chivalry -- the Order of the Garter -- under George's banner, and turned George's red cross on white into England's flag. Which English king made George patron of England?
context: Edward III founded the Order of the Garter around 1348 under George's patronage. Henry V famously invoked 'God for Harry, England, and Saint George' at Agincourt, but the patronage had already been fixed a lifetime earlier. Richard I (the Lionheart) had used the red cross on crusade but had not made George patron; Alfred is centuries too early. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: The later Passios of George, written down long after his death, pile up an outrageous list of tortures -- among them broken on a wheel and boiled in molten lead -- but say that none of them killed him. Only one final punishment finally did. How, in the later Passios, did the historical George at last die?
choices: Buried alive in a lime pit
context: Beheading was the standard Roman military-privileged execution for a citizen soldier. Crucifixion upside down is the Peter tradition; wild horses is the death of Hippolytus of Rome in another legend; buried alive is a Vestal-Virgin punishment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_George.

question: The Midianites' camel raids had driven Israel into caves. An angel found Gideon at Ophrah trying to hide his harvest from the raiders in the strangest place. Where was he beating out his wheat?
context: Judges 6:11 KJV: 'Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.' A winepress is a sunken pit for stamping grapes; threshing normally needs an open, breezy floor to winnow chaff. Gideon was doing the job in the wrong place because doing it in the right place would get him raided.

question: The angel who found Gideon crouched in the winepress opened with a greeting that has become one of the most quoted lines in the book of Judges. What did he call the frightened man?
choices: thou faithful servant of the vine
thou watchman of the high hills
context: Judges 6:12 KJV: 'The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.' The joke is on Gideon: he is HIDING in a winepress from camel raiders. The line is spoken as a promise, not a description, and the rest of the story is Gideon growing into it.

question: Wanting proof he had heard right, Gideon spread a piece of wool on the threshingfloor overnight and asked for a sign involving the morning dew. What did he ask should happen?
answer: the wool wet with dew and the ground dry around it
choices: the wool wet with dew and the ground dry around it
dew on the fleece and on the ground alike
the fleece frozen stiff and no dew anywhere else
dew on the wool the first night and none the second
context: Judges 6:36-38: he laid a fleece of wool on the threshingfloor and asked that dew be on the fleece only, dry on all the earth around. In the morning he pressed the fleece and wrung out a bowlful of water. The word 'fleece' comes to English from this scene by way of the KJV.

question: One night's sign was not enough for Gideon. The next night he asked God for a second dew-sign on the same fleece on the same threshingfloor. What did the second morning show?
answer: the wool dry and the ground wet with dew
choices: the wool dry and the ground wet with dew
the wool wet again and the ground wet as well
the wool doubled in weight with dew
the wool white with frost and the ground bare
context: Judges 6:39-40 KJV: 'let it now be dry only upon the fleece, and upon all the ground let there be dew.' God obliged him a second night. The double sign became the pattern behind the English phrase 'putting out a fleece' for asking a doubt-quieting proof.

question: Gideon mustered thirty-two thousand men against the Midianite camp. God told him the army was too many, so any man who was fearful and afraid was sent home. About how many left?
context: Judges 7:3 KJV: 'there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand.' God's reason: if Israel won with a huge army it would 'vaunt itself against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me' (Judges 7:2). Ten thousand was still too many; the second cut was coming at the water.

question: God told Gideon to bring the ten thousand down to the water for one more cut. Only three hundred were kept, chosen by the way they drank. What did the three hundred do?
answer: they lapped with their tongues like dogs
choices: they lapped with their tongues like dogs
they knelt and drank slowly from cupped hands
they drank standing with the pool up to the knee
they took only a mouthful and spat it back out
context: Judges 7:5-6 KJV: 'Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself; likewise every one that boweth down upon his knees to drink.' Three hundred lapped, putting hand to mouth; the rest knelt. The kneelers were sent home.

question: At the signal three hundred men blew trumpets and smashed their pitchers all at once around the Midianite camp. Then they raised a shout naming a weapon. What did they cry?
answer: The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon
choices: The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon
The bow of the Lord, and of Gideon
The shield of the Lord, and of Gideon
The fire of the Lord, and of Gideon
context: Judges 7:20 KJV. The Midianites in the sudden torchlight, hearing the shout from every side at once, panicked; 'the Lord set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host' (Judges 7:22 KJV). The three hundred did not have to fight the battle; they only had to make the noise.

question: In the Norse stories, Loki has three monstrous children by the giantess Angrboda: the death-goddess Hel, a great serpent that will grow long enough to circle the whole world, and a third child that terrifies the Aesir most of all -- called Fenrir. What kind of creature is Fenrir?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Fenrir (Old Norse Fenrisulfr, 'the Fenris-wolf') is the wolf-child of Loki and Angrboda. His siblings are Jormungand the world-serpent and Hel the death-goddess. Baldr's father Odin himself will fall to this wolf at Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: While Fenrir the wolf is still growing up in Asgard, every one of the Aesir is afraid to go near his cage -- except a single god who alone will bring the wolf his meat. Which god was brave enough to feed Fenrir?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: 'Tyr had the courage to go to him and give him food.' Tyr is the Norse war-god; Thor kills giants with Mjolnir but does not tend the wolf; Baldr is the shining son later killed by mistletoe; Heimdallr stands watch at Bifrost. Tyr's name gives us the English weekday Tuesday, 'Tyr's day'.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir see Fenrir growing bigger every day and hold a council: they must bind him before he becomes too strong. They forge a first heavy fetter and put it on him as a game -- but Fenrir breaks free at his very first kick. What was the name of that first failed fetter?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: 'Leyding he loosened at the first kick.' Dromi is the second, stronger fetter that Fenrir also shatters. Gleipnir is the silken third fetter forged by the dwarves that finally holds him. Gelgja is the cord threaded through the stone Gjoll that anchors Gleipnir. Leyding is often anglicised as Loeding.  (Legend.)

question: After the first fetter snaps, the smiths of the Aesir forge a second one twice as strong and clap it on Fenrir. He strains once and shatters this one so hard its pieces fly far away across the plain. What was the second fetter called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: 'Dromi was made half again as strong, and it broke apart so that the pieces flew far into the distance.' Gleipnir is the silken third fetter that actually holds. Gungnir is Odin's spear. Gelgja is the cord that later ties Gleipnir to a rock.  (Legend.)

question: With both iron fetters in pieces, Odin sends a messenger down into the dark below the earth, to the world of the dwarves, and orders them to make a fetter no wolf can break. In which of the nine worlds do those dark smiths live?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the messenger Skirnir goes down to Svartalfheim, the world of the 'dark elves' or dwarves, and commissions the fetter. Muspelheim is the fire-world of Surt; Alfheim is the shining home of the light-elves; Jotunheim is the giants' country.  (Legend.)

question: The dwarves hand up a fetter that looks nothing like a chain -- it is smooth and soft as a silk ribbon, thin enough to wrap round a finger, and yet the strongest thing ever made. What is the name of this fetter the dwarves forged for Fenrir?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Gleipnir means 'the ensnarer' or 'open one', and was 'smooth and soft as a silken ribbon, yet strong and firm.' Gelgja is the cord threaded through the stone Gjoll to anchor Gleipnir once Fenrir is bound. Dromi and Leyding are the two iron fetters Fenrir has already snapped.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri lists the six impossible ingredients the dwarves used up making that ribbon. One is taken from a cat. What ingredient of the ribbon does Snorri say the dwarves took from a cat?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: 'It was made of six things -- the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird.' Snorri uses the list as an etiology: cats now make no sound on their paws because the dwarves used the sound up in Gleipnir; likewise women have no beards and mountains no visible roots.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir row Fenrir out to a lonely island in the middle of a black lake to test this thin silk ribbon on him. Snorri gives the island a name -- the last place Fenrir will stand free. What is that island called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the gods take Fenrir 'to a certain island called Lyngvi, in a lake called Amsvartnir.' Hlesey is a real Danish island associated with the sea-giant Aegir in the sagas; Sokkvabekk is the hall of the goddess Saga; Idavoll is the plain where the Aesir gather in Asgard.  (Legend.)

question: The gods do not stop with the ribbon. They drive a huge stone slab called Gjoll deep into the earth and pass Gleipnir through it, then anchor it with an even greater rock. They also wedge Fenrir's jaws open with something driven point-up so he cannot bite them shut again. What did the Aesir set upright in the wolf's mouth?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: 'Then they took a sword and thrust it into his mouth so that the hilt stood on the lower jaw and the point in the palate; that was his gag.' Fenrir's slaver, running over the blade, forms the river Van that flows from his mouth until Ragnarok breaks him free to swallow Odin.  (Legend.)

question: In the middle of King Volsung's great hall stands a living oak the family call Barnstokk -- 'child-trunk' -- with its branches spreading up through the roof-beams. On the night of Signy's wedding-feast a one-eyed stranger walks in and does one shocking thing to Barnstokk before he leaves. What does the stranger do to the tree?
answer: drives a sword into the trunk up to the hilt
choices: drives a sword into the trunk up to the hilt
hangs a golden ring from the highest branch
carves a runic curse into the bark
sets a torch to the roots
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 3 (Morris translation); Barnstokkr (Wikipedia). The stranger -- Odin in his wanderer-disguise -- walks straight to Barnstokk and drives a sword into the living wood up to the hilt, then leaves without a word. He does not hang a ring, carve runes, or burn the tree. The buried sword is what the whole saga hangs on: only the man who can pull it free will own it.  (Legend.)

question: After driving the sword into the tree the stranger turns to the hall and speaks his one condition, then walks out and is never seen leaving. What does he say the sword will be worth to the person who can pull it free?
answer: he shall never bear a better sword
choices: he shall never bear a better sword
he shall be king of the North
he shall never die of iron
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 3: the stranger says whoever pulls the sword shall have it as a gift and 'shall never bear in hand a better sword.' The offer is not a crown, not immortality, not a bride -- it is that specific weapon. Kingship of the North is nowhere promised. 'Never die of iron' is Balder's mother's charm, not this scene. Marriage to Signy is already being celebrated at this very feast.  (Legend.)

question: The bride whose wedding is being celebrated in the great hall the night the sword appears in the tree is not the daughter of a foreign king but Volsung's own daughter, Sigmund's sister. She will become one of the darkest figures in the saga. What is her name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 2-8. Signy is Sigmund's sister, married against her will to Siggeir at this feast; after Siggeir massacres the Volsungs she will engineer his own death and Sigmund's revenge. Sigrid is a name from other sagas. Gudrun is the woman Sigmund's son Sigurd will marry generations later. Brynhild is the valkyrie Sigurd wakes on Hindarfjall.  (Legend.)

question: The name of the great tree in Volsung's hall is not a random word. Old Norse Barnstokk breaks into two parts: barn (a common Norse word) plus stokk ('trunk' or 'stock'). What does the first half of the word barn mean in Old Norse?
context: Barnstokkr (Wikipedia); Old Norse dictionaries (Cleasby-Vigfusson). Old Norse barn means 'child' (the same word survives in modern Scandinavian languages -- barn is still 'child' in Swedish, Norwegian, and Danish today). So Barnstokk means 'child-trunk' or 'family-trunk' -- the tree stands in the hall as the visible symbol of the Volsung line. Iron in Old Norse is jarn; raven is hrafn; north is nordr. Barn is the specific meaning here.

question: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has torn off the arm of a monster named Grendel and hung it in the rafters of the mead-hall Heorot as a trophy. That same night a second monster comes to Heorot for revenge. What relation is the second monster to Grendel?
context: Beowulf lines 1251-1309 (Klaeber edition). The second attacker is Grendel's mother; the poem never names her, describing her only as 'the mother of that terror' and 'the mere-woman.' Grendel has no father in the poem, no brother, no cousin -- only his mother, herself descended from Cain according to the poem's genealogy. She is the specific attacker on the second night.  (Legend.)

question: The night she attacks Heorot the mother of Grendel takes two things away with her. She snatches Hrothgar's dearest counsellor, an old warrior named Aeschere -- and she also takes back a trophy the Danes had hung in the rafters. What does she take down from the rafters of Heorot?
context: Beowulf lines 1294-1309. She takes back the arm Beowulf had torn from her son the night before, and she takes Aeschere as a hostage. Grendel's skull is not the trophy in the hall (Beowulf will bring it back himself in the next scene). Beowulf's helmet and Hrothgar's cloak do not appear in this raid. The arm is the specific trophy.  (Legend.)

question: Hrothgar warns Beowulf about the dark tarn in the moors where the monsters live. To make plain how cursed the water is, he tells Beowulf about a hart -- a large stag -- that a pack of hounds chases to the very bank of the mere. What does the hart do at the water's edge rather than jump in?
answer: it turns back and lets the hounds take it
choices: it turns back and lets the hounds take it
it drinks and dies at once
it hides in the frost-bitten trees
context: Beowulf lines 1368-1372 (Heaney translation): 'Though the heather-stepper harried by the hounds takes refuge in the wood, he will lose his life on the bank sooner than plunge in.' The stag would rather die of the hunt than touch the water. Drinking and dying, swimming across, or hiding in the trees are not the story -- the stag REFUSES the water. It is one of Old English poetry's most quoted horror-images.  (Legend.)

question: Before Beowulf dives into the mere he is loaned a sword by one of Hrothgar's own men -- the same warrior who had earlier tried to shame Beowulf at the mead-bench with a story about a swimming-contest against a friend named Breca. Who lends Beowulf his sword?
context: Beowulf lines 1455-1472 (Klaeber). Unferth, whose earlier taunt Beowulf had answered in full, now hands Beowulf his own sword as a peace-offering. Aeschere is Hrothgar's counsellor -- already dead in this scene, killed the previous night. Wiglaf is the young kinsman who will help Beowulf in the DRAGON fight fifty years later. Wealhtheow is Hrothgar's queen. Unferth is the sword-giver here.  (Legend.)

question: The sword that Unferth lends Beowulf is a famous named blade. The poem says it had never failed the hand of any warrior who had carried it before. What is this sword called?
context: Beowulf lines 1455-1472; Hrunting (Wikipedia). The sword is Hrunting, an heirloom of Unferth's family. Naegling is Beowulf's OWN sword, from the dragon-fight fifty years later at the end of the poem -- a common test pitfall. Durendal is Roland's sword in the Chanson de Roland, a completely different tradition. Tyrfing is Hervor's cursed family sword in Hervarar Saga. Hrunting is the specific loaner here.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf arms himself in mail and helmet and jumps into the black water of the mere. The poem is deliberately clear about how long it takes him just to REACH the bottom, and it is longer than any real dive by a man in armour could possibly last. How long does the poem say Beowulf spends swimming down through the water?
answer: the better part of a day
choices: the better part of a day
the length of a slow hour
context: Beowulf lines 1490-1512; CliffsNotes and LitCharts summaries. The poem gives 'the space of a day' or 'nearly a day' -- physically impossible, which is the poem's point: the mere is a supernatural descent, not an ordinary lake. A slow hour is too short for the poem's cosmic scale. Three heartbeats belongs to boasting fighter-scenes elsewhere. Seven days is Noah-scale Biblical language. Nearly a day is the specific figure.  (Legend.)

question: When Beowulf finally reaches the bottom of the mere, Grendel's mother seizes him and drags him into her own hall -- a dry, roofed chamber lit by an unearthly light, at the bottom of the water. There he lifts the sword Unferth loaned him and swings it at her head. What happens to Hrunting when its edge strikes her neck?
choices: it sticks fast in the bone
context: Beowulf lines 1518-1528 (Heaney translation). Hrunting, which had never failed any warrior before, bounces off her neck 'and could not bite' -- Beowulf casts it aside. Snapping in half is Roland's Durendal on the rocks (a different story). Sticking in bone is the trope of a lesser sword. Burning his hand is nowhere in Beowulf. The bounce is the specific detail, and its whole point is that ordinary named weapons cannot harm this creature.  (Legend.)

question: With Hrunting cast aside and the monster-woman grappling him, Beowulf's eye falls on the wall of the underwater hall. Hanging there is a huge weapon the poem describes as 'the work of giants, from the days before the flood, that no ordinary warrior could carry.' What does Beowulf do with the giant-forged sword?
answer: strikes off her head with one blow
choices: strikes off her head with one blow
burns her body with it as a torch
throws it up through the water to Hrothgar
wedges it against the door to trap her
context: Beowulf lines 1557-1569 (Klaeber and Heaney): Beowulf seizes the giant sword two-handed and takes her head off with a single stroke. He does not use it as a torch, does not throw it away, and does not use it as a barricade. Decapitation is the specific act and matches the arm-tearing of the first fight (a Grendel-kin dies by having a body-part removed).  (Legend.)

question: The moment after Grendel's mother falls dead, Beowulf sees something else in the underwater hall: the body of Grendel himself, dead from the arm-wound Beowulf gave him the night before. Beowulf goes over and does one more thing to Grendel's corpse before he leaves. What does he do?
answer: strikes off the head as a trophy
choices: strikes off the head as a trophy
burns the body on the hall's floor
buries it under the giant sword's blade
cuts open the chest and takes the heart
context: Beowulf lines 1584-1590. Beowulf beheads Grendel's corpse as a trophy for Hrothgar; the head will need four men to carry back to Heorot on a spear-shaft. He does not burn, bury, or open the body. The double beheading (mother alive, son dead) is the specific pattern -- Grendel-kin are ended by losing heads and arms.  (Legend.)

question: As Beowulf stands over the two corpses, he notices something strange happening to the giant-forged sword in his hand: its blade begins to shrink, 'like an icicle when the Father lets go of the frost-fetters,' dissolving in the hot blood of the monsters. By the time he swims back to daylight, only ONE part of the weapon is left in his hand. Which part remains?
context: Beowulf lines 1605-1617 (Heaney translation); Hrunting (Wikipedia). The blade melts away in the monster-blood and only the hilt is left. The pommel is only the ornamented cap on top of the hilt; the scabbard is empty by the time Beowulf dives; the point melts first, not last. The hilt is what Beowulf carries back to Hrothgar and hands to him -- and it is one of Old English literature's most-quoted supernatural details.  (Legend.)

question: When Beowulf swims back up out of the mere he brings with him the melted sword's hilt and one huge trophy from the fight below. Back at Heorot, no single warrior can lift the trophy. How many of Beowulf's men are needed to carry it back to Heorot on a spear-shaft?
context: Beowulf lines 1633-1639. Four of Beowulf's men are needed to carry Grendel's severed head back to Heorot, lashed to a spear-shaft between them. The number is precise and deliberate: it is the poet's way of driving home how monstrous the skull is. Two, seven, and twelve are common poetic numbers elsewhere but the poem is specific: four men, one head.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf is not a Dane. He has crossed the sea to Hrothgar's kingdom to fight the monster of the mere because Hrothgar had once done a favour for Beowulf's father. What people does Beowulf lead -- the tribe he sails home to when the whole adventure is over?
context: Beowulf lines 194-200, 1830-1839. Beowulf is a Geat, from the south of what is now Sweden; his uncle Hygelac is king of the Geats. The Frisians are a coastal North Sea people Beowulf raids much later. The Saxons are a different Germanic group (some settled England). The Suebi are a Central European tribe from Roman-era sources. The Geats are Beowulf's specific people.  (Legend.)

question: The old king Gjuki of the Rhine has a queen who is far more dangerous than he is: a powerful sorceress who knows how to brew charmed drinks and speaks spells over them. She will engineer every disaster in the second half of the Volsunga Saga. What is this queen's name?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 25-30; Grimhild (Wikipedia). Grimhild is the queen and the schemer. Gudrun is her DAUGHTER, the woman she wants Sigurd to marry. Brynhild is the flame-ringed warrior-woman Sigurd has already sworn to. Signy is Sigmund's sister from the earlier generation. Grimhild is the specific mother-in-law here.  (Legend.)

question: The queen of the Rhine sees at once that Sigurd is the greatest hero of the age, and she wants to bind him to her family through her only daughter. Her plan has one problem: Sigurd is already sworn to another woman, a valkyrie on a burning mountain. What is the name of Grimhild's daughter, the woman she wants Sigurd to marry instead?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 26. Gudrun is Grimhild's only daughter; the marriage-plot is her plot. Freyja is a Vanir goddess, not a Rhine princess. Sigrid is a name from later Norse historical sagas. Signy belongs to the earlier Volsung generation -- Sigmund's sister. Gudrun is the specific bride Grimhild picks.  (Legend.)

question: Grimhild brews something at the hearth-fire and hands it to Sigurd in a cup at the welcome-feast; he drinks it in one swallow and something specific inside him changes. What does the cup contain?
choices: a healing draught for his wounds
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 26 (Morris translation): 'she gave to Sigurd a cup of mead wherein was a drug, that he should forget utterly Brynhild.' The potion does not poison him, does not weaken him, and does not heal him -- it erases one specific memory. This is the fork-point where everything begins to go wrong.  (Legend.)

question: The drug Grimhild slips into Sigurd's cup is precisely targeted -- it erases one person entirely from his memory. Who?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 26 (Morris translation): the drink wipes only Brynhild from his memory -- the ring of fire, the runes she taught him, the oath he swore, the ring on her finger, everything about her. Hjordis is Sigurd's own mother from the earlier Volsung chapters; Signy is Sigmund's sister from two generations back; Gudrun is the Gjukung daughter Grimhild is about to make him marry. The specificity is the horror of the drug: it erases exactly one person -- the one woman he had sworn to.  (Legend.)

question: Once Sigurd has drunk the memory-drug he goes through with the marriage Grimhild has arranged and takes a second oath at the same feast, with two of Gjuki's sons. What oath does Sigurd swear with Gjuki's sons Gunnar and Hogni after the wedding?
choices: the oath of a Christian knight
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 27. Sigurd, Gunnar, and Hogni mix their blood and swear to be brothers -- the strongest Norse bond outside kinship, and the same bond whose betrayal will get Sigurd murdered in his sleep by the third brother, Guttorm. Vassalage, Christian knighthood, and midsummer-truces belong to other medieval-romance traditions. Blood-brotherhood is the specific Norse oath.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd and Gunnar ride together to Hindarfjall so Gunnar can cross the fire and claim the valkyrie as his bride. Gunnar first tries his own horse; it refuses the flames. He climbs onto Grani, Sigurd's horse -- a horse sired from Odin's own stock -- and tries again. What does Grani do?
answer: stands still and will not move
choices: stands still and will not move
rears once and plants his hooves
turns his head aside and will not face the fire
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 29. Grani, of Sleipnir's line, senses the rider is not Sigurd and simply refuses to take a single step. The other quiet refusals in the choices are the shape of Norse animal-lore but not what Grani does in this scene. It is the horse's refusal -- an animal knowing the truth the woman on the mountain cannot see -- that forces Grimhild's next spell into action.  (Legend.)

question: Grimhild has taught Sigurd and Gunnar a spell for exactly this moment. Sigurd sits on Grani a second time -- but not as himself. What has Grimhild's spell done to the two men?
answer: Sigurd and Gunnar have swapped faces
choices: Sigurd and Gunnar have swapped faces
Sigurd has been made invisible under a cloak of shadow
Sigurd has been shape-shifted into a wolf
Sigurd has been wrapped in a mist that hides his features
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 29; Grimhild (Wikipedia). Grimhild's shape-swap spell exchanges the men's faces (and voices): Sigurd wears Gunnar's outward form, Gunnar wears Sigurd's. Invisibility cloaks, wolf-shifting (as in Sigmund and Sinfjotli's earlier chapters), and mist-veiling are all real Norse magical shapes -- but the Volsunga Saga is specific about this scene: it is a face-swap. Wagner in Gotterdammerung Act I keeps the swap almost intact but uses the Tarnhelm (magic helmet) instead of Grimhild's spell.  (Legend.)

question: On the third morning, before he rides back through the fire and swaps faces with Gunnar again, Sigurd takes one small object off the valkyrie's hand and puts a different ring in its place. The ring he takes is the cursed gold circle he won from Fafnir's hoard and gave to her the first time they met on Hindarfjall. What is this ring called?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 14, 21, 29; Andvaranaut (Wikipedia). Andvaranaut ('Andvari's Gift') is the cursed dwarf-ring -- originally lost by Andvari the dwarf, then wrested from Fafnir's hoard by Sigurd. Sigurd's theft of it back from Brynhild's hand is the moment that will make her, on discovery, want him dead. Draupnir is Odin's arm-ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night -- a different Norse ring. Sviagris is a Swedish royal ring. The Sampo is a Finnish artifact, not a ring. Andvaranaut is the specific one.  (Legend.)

question: When the shape-swap ends and everyone is married to someone, the deception sits in the hall like a time-bomb. Later, when the valkyrie learns the truth, she demands Sigurd's death. Grimhild feeds one of her sons a stew of wolf-flesh and serpent-flesh to work him into a killing rage, and it is he who murders Sigurd in his own bed. Which of Grimhild's sons is the killer?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 32. Guttorm, the youngest Gjukung brother, is fed wolf-flesh and serpent-flesh by Grimhild until he is savage enough to stab his sworn brother-in-law in his sleep. Gunnar and Hogni are the two elder Gjukung brothers -- Sigurd's sworn blood-brothers, and so bound by oath they cannot strike him themselves; that is why Grimhild uses Guttorm, who never swore. Hjalli is a thrall from the same saga's later Atli chapters. Guttorm is the specific assassin.  (Legend.)

question: The queen of Arthur's Camelot, whose long secret love-affair with Sir Lancelot of the Lake finally shatters the Round Table, has a name that has passed into English from a Welsh original meaning roughly 'white phantom'. What is the name of Arthur's queen?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books III-XXI; Wikipedia: Guinevere. The Welsh original is Gwenhwyfar -- 'gwen' (white) + 'hwyfar' (phantom, spirit). Isolde is the tragic queen of the parallel Tristan story in Cornwall. Morgause is Arthur's sister, mother of Gawain and Mordred. Nimue is the sorceress-apprentice of Merlin.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur's queen is not the daughter of a nobody. Her father is the ruling king of the neighbouring realm of Cameliard, an ally of Arthur, and when she marries Arthur she brings with her one great gift that will become the centerpiece of his court. What does Arthur receive as Guinevere's dowry?
choices: the horn of Bran the Blessed
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book III ch.1. Guinevere's father King Leodegrance of Cameliard sends the Round Table to Arthur along with a hundred knights to sit at it. Excalibur was given to Arthur separately by the Lady of the Lake. Uther Pendragon's crown Arthur already held. The horn of Bran the Blessed is a treasure of Welsh myth (in Culhwch and Olwen) outside the Arthurian marriage story.  (Legend.)

question: The twelfth-century French poet Chretien de Troyes wrote a romance in which Guinevere's lover rides in a cart of shame to reach her, sacrificing his knightly honour to prove his devotion. Who is Guinevere's lover through nearly the whole Arthurian cycle?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot ou le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177); Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books XVIII-XX. The romance is titled Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette ('Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart') -- the cart of shame Lancelot rides in to reach the queen when she is kidnapped costs him his knightly honour but proves his devotion. Sir Tristan is Isolde's lover in the parallel Cornish story; Gawain and Percival have no such affair.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Agravaine and one other knight lie in wait with twelve armed men outside Guinevere's chamber to catch Sir Lancelot in the act. Which knight joins Agravaine in setting the trap that exposes Lancelot and the queen?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.2-4. Mordred is Arthur's illegitimate son by Arthur's own half-sister Morgause -- the future usurper of Camelot. Gaheris and Gareth are two more of Gawain's brothers (Agravaine, Gaheris, Gareth, and Gawain are the four sons of King Lot and Morgause). Sir Bors is Lancelot's kinsman and stays LOYAL to him.  (Legend.)

question: Trapped inside the queen's own chamber and given no chance to explain, Sir Lancelot arms himself, throws open the door, and fights his way out through the ambush waiting in the corridor. When the fight is over one of the ambushers -- Sir Agravaine himself -- lies dead among the rest. How many knights in all does Lancelot kill on the way out of the queen's chamber?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.4. Malory gives the exact tally: Lancelot kills thirteen knights (including Agravaine himself) fighting his way out. Three would be the fair-fight number; twenty-four is a Round-Table capacity; a hundred is the number of Round-Table seats in Malory Book III ch.1 -- all wrong for this scene.  (Legend.)

question: With Lancelot escaped and the queen arrested for treason, Arthur is caught: by the law of his own kingdom he must pass sentence on his own wife, and he does so with grief. What sentence does Arthur pass on Guinevere?
answer: to be burned at the stake
choices: to be burned at the stake
to be beheaded on Tower Hill
to be walled up in a nunnery
to be drowned in a sack in the river
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.7. Burning at the stake is the specific medieval punishment for a queen's adultery -- a form of high treason against the king. Beheading on Tower Hill is the Tudor-era punishment (Anne Boleyn, Catherine Howard). Being walled up alive is a late-legend punishment. The sack-and-drowning is the ancient Roman poena cullei for parricides.

question: At the pyre in the courtyard at Carlisle, the guard leads Guinevere out to the fire in what Malory names exactly. What is Guinevere wearing at the stake?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.8. The 'smock' is a plain linen undergarment (later called a shift or chemise) -- the medieval condemned wore a smock alone as a mark of stripped honour. Wedding gown, crown, and mourning-robes would each have signalled a different scene entirely; the smock is Malory's exact word.  (Legend.)

question: As the fire is being kindled at Carlisle, hoofbeats sound in the yard. Sir Lancelot and his kinsmen ride in at full charge, cut through the guard around the pyre, sweep the queen up onto Lancelot's horse, and ride out again. But in the melee Lancelot's own sword kills two of Arthur's household knights -- both unarmed, both there because they had refused to bear arms against him. The killing turns their eldest brother, who had loved Lancelot best of all the Round Table, into his mortal enemy. Which two knights does Lancelot kill by mistake at the pyre?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XX ch.8. Gareth (nicknamed Beaumains, 'fair hands') and Gaheris are two of Sir Gawain's four brothers; they had been on guard at the pyre unarmed because they honoured Lancelot too much to want to fight him. Kay and Bedivere are Arthur's oldest household. Percival and Bors are Grail-knights. Ector is Lancelot's brother; Balin is a tragic loner from earlier in the book.  (Legend.)

question: When it is all over -- Arthur dead of the wound at Camlann, Mordred killed by his own father, and Lancelot in exile -- Guinevere does not stay at court. She takes vows and enters a nunnery to live out her days in penance, and dies there as its abbess. Which abbey does Guinevere retire to at the end of the story?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.7. Amesbury Abbey in Wiltshire is a real Anglo-Saxon foundation (later a Benedictine nunnery); Malory places Guinevere there. Glastonbury is where Arthur's tomb was later claimed to be found. Iona is Columba's Scottish island monastery. Whitby is the great Northumbrian house of Hilda's synod.  (Legend.)

question: In the very last chapter of Malory, Sir Lancelot, hearing that Guinevere has become a nun, rides once more to her abbey -- hoping to take her out of it and away with him at last. The queen comes to hear he is at the gate. What does Guinevere do when Lancelot arrives at Amesbury for her?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.9-10. Guinevere sends word from the cloister that she will not see Lancelot again in this life; she asks only that he pray for her soul. Lancelot rides away, takes his own vows at Glastonbury, and dies a hermit soon after -- the last scene of the book. The other three answers are all endings the poet might have chosen and did not.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the harvest-and-sunshine god of the Vanir owns a chariot pulled by a shining beast forged of solid gold. That god is Freyr, twin brother of Freyja. What animal draws Freyr's chariot?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43 and Gylfaginning 49: Freyr's mount is a golden boar. Boars were sacred to Freyr in the Viking age -- warriors wore boar-crested helmets called hildisvin, and roast boar was offered at midwinter feasts in his honour. Freyja rides a chariot pulled by cats, and also has her own separate boar Hildisvini.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr the god of harvest and sunshine belongs to a family of gods separate from Odin's family of the Aesir -- his people arrived in Asgard as hostages after the first war of the gods. Which family of gods does Freyr come from?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 24: Freyr, his sister Freyja, and their father Njord are the three Vanir gods who came to live in Asgard after the Aesir-Vanir war. The Aesir are Odin's family. The Jotnar are the giants. The Alfar are the light-elves of Alfheim, which Freyr was given as a tooth-gift when he cut his first tooth.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr's shining boar was forged in a wager between Loki and two dwarf brothers. One brother worked the anvil, the other pumped the bellows. Loki turned himself into a biting fly and stung the bellows-brother's hand, but the dwarf kept pumping. Which pair of dwarves made the golden boar?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) at the anvil, Brokkr at the bellows. The Sons of Ivaldi were a rival dwarf-team who made Odin's spear and Sif's golden hair. Fjalar and Galar are the two dwarves who murdered Kvasir to brew the Mead of Poetry. Nordri and Sudri are the two dwarves holding up the sky.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr's golden boar has a second name besides the one meaning 'gold-bristled'. Snorri also calls it by a name that boasts about its dangerous tusks -- 'cutting-tusk' or 'fearsome tooth'. What is the second name of Freyr's boar?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the boar is called both Gullinbursti ('gold-bristled') and Slidrugtanni ('cutting-tusk'). Hildisvini ('battle-swine') is Freyja's separate boar. Saehrimnir is the boar cooked and eaten every night in Valhalla and reborn every morning. Freki is one of Odin's two wolves.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri says the golden boar can carry Freyr not only over the land but through two other elements just as fast as any horse -- faster, in fact, than any horse alive. Over which pair of elements can the boar run at full speed?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Freyr's boar 'runs through the air and over the sea better than any horse.' The boar is one of the Norse cosmos's few land-sea-sky mounts, alongside Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir and Freyr's own folding ship Skidbladnir.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the All-Father Odin, chief of the Aesir and lord of the slain in Valhalla, carries a signature weapon into every battle -- the same weapon he takes with him on his last ride out at Ragnarok. What kind of weapon does Odin carry?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43 and Gylfaginning 51: Odin's weapon is a spear (Gungnir). The hammer Mjolnir belongs to Thor; axes belong to warriors like the berserkers but not to a named god; the bow is Ullr's weapon. Every Odin-carving from the Viking age shows him with a spear.  (Legend.)

question: The Norse gods are split into two families that fought a war before the age of mortals: Odin's family that includes Thor and Baldr, and a second family of harvest and sea gods that includes Freyr and Freyja. Which family does Odin belong to?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 20: Odin, Thor, Baldr, Tyr, and Frigg belong to the Aesir. The Vanir include Freyr, Freyja, and Njord. The Jotnar are the giants of Jotunheim. The einherjar are not a family at all but the chosen dead warriors who feast in Valhalla.  (Legend.)

question: Odin's spear has its own name in Snorri, and every treasure of the Aesir carries its own name the way a king's sword did. What is the name of Odin's spear?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: 'Odin has the spear called Gungnir.' The name is thought to mean 'the swaying one' or 'the trembler'. Mjolnir is Thor's returning hammer. Draupnir is Odin's dripping gold arm-ring. Skidbladnir is Freyr's folding ship that can hold every Aesir and still fit in a pocket.  (Legend.)

question: Odin's spear was forged in a dwarf-workshop in Svartalfheim by a team of three brothers -- the same dwarf brothers who made a wig of spun gold for Sif after Loki had shaved her bald in the night. Which dwarf-team forged Odin's spear?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki takes his commission to the Sons of Ivaldi, who forge Sif's replacement golden hair, Freyr's ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear. Sindri and Brokkr are the rival dwarf-team who then forge the ring Draupnir, the boar Gullinbursti, and the hammer Mjolnir. Fjalar and Galar are the killers of Kvasir.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri writes one line about Odin's spear that is quoted more than any other: he says the weapon does one specific thing that no other spear in Norse myth can do. In Snorri's line, what does the spear do once it has been thrown?
answer: it never stops in its thrust
choices: it never stops in its thrust
it returns to Odin's hand each time
it splits into three points in flight
it drinks the blood of the slain
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Odin's spear 'never stopped in its thrust' -- once thrown, no shield or wall stops it. The returning weapon is Thor's hammer Mjolnir. Three-pointed spears and blood-drinking weapons appear elsewhere in world myth but not with Odin's.  (Legend.)

question: The Voluspa, the seeress-poem of the Elder Edda, opens the very first war ever fought between the two families of gods. Odin begins it with one act aimed at the whole Vanir army as a formal challenge, dedicating them all to him. What did Odin do to open the war?
answer: hurled his spear across the enemy host
choices: hurled his spear across the enemy host
sent his ravens Huginn and Muninn to circle above them
context: Voluspa 24: 'Odin cast his spear, hurled it into the host' -- the opening act of the Aesir-Vanir war. In Norse tradition the flying spear across the heads of an army was a legal dedication of every man on the other side to Odin. Gjallarhorn is what Heimdallr will blow at the start of Ragnarok, not Odin's gesture. Huginn and Muninn are Odin's scout-ravens, not battle-openers.  (Legend.)

question: The mythic spear-cast from the Voluspa was not just an Elder-Edda story -- Viking-age captains imitated it before real land battles. According to the sagas, what was every man on the far side of the flying spear then reckoned to be?
choices: a war-band already claimed by the valkyries
a host consecrated to Freyr for the harvest
context: Eyrbyggja saga and Styrbjarnar thattr both record the pre-battle spear-cast as a legal dedication of the enemy to Odin, imitating Voluspa 24. The men on the far side of the flying spear were then reckoned already-dead, already-owed. Old Norse law even had a term for this: they were 'given to Odin' before a blow had fallen. The valkyries choose after the fight, not before; Freyr is a peace-and-harvest god, not a war-claimant; and no saga records a Loki-dedication.  (Legend.)

question: In the Sigrdrifumal, the valkyrie Sigrdrifa wakes on her mountain and teaches the young hero Sigurd a whole lesson in runes -- where power-runes are carved in the Norse world. She names one place on Odin's own gear where runes are carved. Where does Sigrdrifa say the runes are carved on Odin's spear?
context: Sigrdrifumal 17 (Poetic Edda): the valkyrie lists rune-places -- Odin's horse Sleipnir's teeth, the Norn Urd's tongue, the paws of a bear, Bragi's tongue, and 'on the point of Gungnir'. The runes on the point are what make the spear never miss.  (Legend.)

question: Norse tradition held one bond was heavier than any other: break it and doom would follow you, and even the Aesir used it to seal their own most sacred promises. What was the highest oath-object in the Norse world?
choices: the ring of the Thingvellir temple altar
the blood of a black horse spilled on the hof floor
the roots of Yggdrasil at Urd's well
context: Norse oath-tradition holds that the spear-point of Gungnir was the highest bond. The temple oath-ring (used at Iceland's Thingvellir) and blood-of-a-horse sacrifices existed alongside, but only the spear-point carried the doom of Odin himself. Breaking such an oath meant giving yourself over as one of Odin's own. The Norns sit at Urd's well but no oath was sworn on Yggdrasil's roots.  (Legend.)

question: At the end of the world Odin himself rides at the head of the einherjar out of Valhalla, spear in hand, to face his oldest enemy. For all the never-missing power of the spear, Odin does not survive the fight. Which creature swallows Odin whole at Ragnarok?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 51: 'Fenrir will swallow Odin, and that will be his death.' Jormungand is killed by Thor, who then dies of the serpent's venom nine paces away. Surt burns the whole world and kills Freyr. Garm and Tyr kill each other at the gates of Hel. Odin's son Vidar avenges his father by tearing Fenrir's jaws apart.  (Legend.)

question: In the darkest ballad of the Robin Hood cycle, a fearsome bounty hunter comes stalking through Sherwood to kill Robin for the price on his head. He wears a whole animal's hide as a cloak -- head and tail still attached -- to make himself terrifying. From which ANIMAL is his hide-cloak made?
context: Stanza 7 of Child Ballad 118 'Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne': 'A sword and a dagger he wore by his side / Had beene many a mans bane / And he was cladd in his capull-hyde / Topp, and tayle, and mayne.' 'Capull-hyde' is Middle English for horse-hide. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: The horse-hide-clad bounty hunter of Child Ballad 118 has not come to Sherwood for adventure -- he has been HIRED by a powerful enemy of Robin's to collect the bounty on the outlaw's head. Who has hired the hunter?
context: In the ballad the Sheriff of Nottingham is at once hunting Robin's men in the forest and has commissioned Guy to hunt Robin himself; the Sheriff and Guy meet in the wood while Guy is on his errand. The Bishop of Hereford, the Abbot of St Mary's, and the Prioress of Kirklees are all real enemies of Robin from other ballads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Guy_of_Gisborne.  (Legend.)

question: Robin and Little John have QUARRELLED and gone their separate ways in the wood. Robin, alone, meets the hunter in the horse-hide cloak, not knowing who he is. The two men fight -- for two hours of a summer's day, the ballad says. With what WEAPONS do they fight?
context: Stanzas 33-38 of the ballad: 'To see how together these yeomen went / With blades both browne and bright / To see how they hewed on eche other / It was a wonderous fight.' The fight is with 'blades' -- swords. The bow-shot in this ballad is only an earlier target-shooting contest, not the killing fight. Source: traditionalmusic.co.uk/child-ballads/ch118.htm.  (Legend.)

question: Recovering from his stumble, Robin kills the hunter with 'an awkwarde stroke' and then does something shocking with the corpse. Stanza 41: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his...' -- on WHAT does Robin fix the severed head?
context: 'He tooke Sir Guys head by the hayre / And sticked itt on his bowes end.' Robin walks with the head raised on his own longbow like a standard. It is one of the grimmest single images in any Robin Hood ballad. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Not content with the beheading, Robin then draws a KNIFE and slashes at the dead hunter's face until 'hee was neuer on a woman borne / Cold tell who Sir Guy was' -- ruined past recognition. What KIND of knife does the ballad say Robin draws?
context: Stanza 42: 'Robin pulled forth an Irish kniffe / And nicked Sir Guy in the face.' Irish knives -- long, single-edged blades of Gaelic manufacture -- circulated in the English borderlands and had a reputation for cruel work; the ballad specifies the kind. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Robin then strips the horse-hide from the dead hunter and pulls it on over his own body. What does he do with his OWN Lincoln-green gown after taking it off?
answer: throws it over the hunter's corpse
choices: throws it over the hunter's corpse
hangs it on the branch of an oak
buries it under a heap of leaves
carries it rolled up under his arm
context: Stanza 44: 'Robin did off his gowne of greene / Sir Guye hee did it throwe / And hee put on that capull-hyde / That cladd him topp to toe.' The disguise-swap is total: Robin becomes the horse-hide hunter and the hunter is dressed as Robin. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Wearing the horse-hide, Robin walks out of the trees toward the Sheriff of Nottingham -- who thinks the hunter he hired is coming to report the kill. Robin fools him with a signal the Sheriff has been waiting for. What SIGNAL does the disguised Robin give?
answer: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
choices: he blows the hunter's hunting horn
he waves the hunter's Lincoln bow
he holds up a green rag on a stick
context: Stanza 46: 'Robin sett Guyes horne to his mouth / A lowd blast in it he did blow.' The Sheriff hears Guy's own horn and rides toward it thinking Guy has won -- and Robin is waiting. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Meanwhile the Sheriff has captured LITTLE JOHN in the woods, away from Robin. In the ballad the Sheriff's men do a very specific thing to Little John while they wait for the hunter's kill -- stanza 19 says 'they haue tane Litle Iohn / And bound him fast to a...'. Bound him fast to a WHAT?
context: Stanza 19 of Child 118: 'And they haue tane Litle Iohn / And bound him fast to a tree.' The point is grim symmetry -- the Sheriff wants to hang Little John from that tree once Robin is confirmed dead. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: Robin cuts Little John's ropes with the Irish knife, and Little John looses one arrow at the fleeing Sheriff -- who dies with a broad arrow that 'did cleaue his heart in twinn.' In the ballad's poetic justice, WHOSE bow launches that killing arrow?
choices: a bow snatched from a Sheriff's man
context: The point of the ballad's poetic justice: the hunter's own bow finishes the hunter's employer. Robin hands Little John Guy's bow, and stanza 58 reads: 'But Litle Iohn, with an arrow broade / Did cleaue his heart in twinn.' The Sheriff dies with Sir Guy's arrow in him. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal118-gisborne.html.  (Legend.)

question: A grim old boatman waits on the far shore of a black river in the land of the dead. The newly-dead who reach him must pay one small bronze coin -- placed under their tongue at burial -- before he will pole them across. What is his name?
context: The coin is called an 'obol', and archaeologists have found real bronze coins in the mouths of Greek burials. Those who could not pay had to wander the near shore for a hundred years. Source: Wikipedia, 'Charon'.  (Legend.)

question: A monstrous dog crouches at the gate of the underworld. He fawns on any soul coming IN, and rages at any soul trying to LEAVE. In the standard picture-books and vase-paintings, how many heads does he have?
context: In Hesiod's Theogony (line 311) the dog actually has FIFTY heads, and Pindar gives him a hundred, but later art and story almost universally settle on three. His name is Cerberus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cerberus'.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus borrowed a piece of magical headgear from Hades to approach the sleeping Medusa unseen -- the same cap Athena wears in Iliad Book 5 to slip past the war-god Ares. Which craftsmen forged this cap for Hades in the beginning?
context: The Greek name of the cap is 'kynee' -- literally 'dog-skin cap', because the earliest such caps were made from dog-hide. The one-eyed Cyclopes also forged Zeus's thunderbolt and Poseidon's trident. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cap of invisibility'.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek land of the dead is threaded by a fixed set of dark named rivers, each one carrying a different meaning. How many rivers does the classical count give?
context: Styx (hatred / oath), Acheron (woe), Cocytus (wailing), Phlegethon (fire), and Lethe (forgetfulness). Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: One river in the underworld is so sacred that even the gods swear their most unbreakable oaths on its black waters -- a god who breaks such an oath is struck mute for a year and cut off from Olympus for nine. It rings the underworld nine times. Which river is this?
context: The Styx's name means 'hatred'. The Acheron is the river of woe (the one Charon actually ferries across in most Greek sources), the Cocytus of wailing, the Phlegethon of fire. Source: Wikipedia, 'Styx'.  (Legend.)

question: Three JUDGES sit at a crossroads in the land of the dead and route each newly-arrived soul to its final home. Two are brothers -- Minos, the former king of Crete, and Rhadamanthys. Who is the third judge, the grandfather of the hero Achilles?
context: Aeacus was king of Aegina and Achilles's grandfather on his father Peleus's side. Tantalus and Sisyphus are among the punished IN the underworld, not judges. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: In Tartarus, the deepest pit of the underworld far below the ordinary land of the dead, one condemned man is doomed forever to push a huge boulder up a hill -- only to watch it roll back down every time he nears the top. What is his name?
context: Tantalus stands in Tartarus under fruit he can never reach; Ixion is bound to a spinning wheel; Prometheus was chained to a mountain in the Caucasus (outside Tartarus proper) where an eagle ate his liver each day. Source: Wikipedia, 'Greek underworld'.  (Legend.)

question: The Greeks were so afraid to say Hades's real name aloud that they gave him a EUPHEMISM meaning 'the Rich One' -- because all the gold and gems come from beneath the earth. The Romans kept the meaning and made it his Roman name. What was this euphemism?
context: 'Plouton' becomes the Roman 'Pluto' -- same word, same wealth-meaning. 'Chthonios' just means 'of the earth' and is an epithet of many underworld gods. 'Aidoneus' is another byname of Hades. Nyx is the primordial goddess Night, not an underworld euphemism. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hades'.  (Legend.)

question: In Genesis, Sarah has waited years for a child of her own and cannot bear one. She hands her Egyptian handmaid Hagar to Abraham as a second wife so that he may have a son. Hagar bears the boy, and Abraham names him. What is the name of that first son?
context: Genesis 16:15 KJV: 'And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael.' Isaac is the LATER son Sarah herself bears; Esau and Jacob are the grandsons of Isaac, two generations later.

question: Years after Ishmael's birth, Sarah bears her own son Isaac and demands the handmaid and her boy be cast out. Early in the morning Abraham puts two things on Hagar's shoulder and sends her into the wilderness. What two things does he give her?
answer: bread and a bottle of water
choices: bread and a bottle of water
a sack of grain and a lamb
a mantle and a walking staff
context: Genesis 21:14 KJV: 'And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away.' The narrator is deliberately spare: nothing else -- no gold, no beast to carry them, no escort.

question: After Abraham sends her away, Hagar wanders lost with her boy in one particular wilderness of the Negev, where the water runs out. Genesis 21:14 names the region. Which wilderness is it?
context: Genesis 21:14 KJV: 'she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.' Paran comes LATER in the story, after Ishmael grows up and settles there as an archer (Genesis 21:21). Sinai is where Moses receives the tablets, a generation later. Moab lies east of the Jordan, out of the picture.

question: The water is spent and Hagar cannot bear to watch the boy die of thirst. She lays him under a shrub and walks a specific distance away before she sits down to weep. Genesis 21:16 measures the distance in an ordinary unit of the ancient world. How far off does she sit?
context: Genesis 21:16 KJV: 'she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child.' A bowshot -- roughly two hundred yards -- is far enough that she cannot hear him, close enough that she is still with him. The stone's-throw measure belongs to Luke's Gethsemane scene; a day's journey belongs to Elijah under the juniper tree.

question: Hagar weeps, saying 'Let me not see the death of the child'. Then Genesis 21:19 says God opens her eyes and shows her something she had not seen before -- one specific object that saves the boy's life. What does she suddenly see?
choices: a stream running from a rock
a stag standing in the thicket
context: Genesis 21:19 KJV: 'And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.' The raven bringing bread belongs to Elijah at the brook Cherith; the stream from the rock belongs to Moses at Horeb -- both real other wilderness-miracles, both wrong for this scene.

question: Long before this second flight, Hagar had run from Sarai's harshness once already, met an angel by a spring on the way to Shur, and done something no other human being in the whole book of Genesis does. What did Hagar do at that first spring that is unique in Genesis?
context: Genesis 16:13 KJV: 'And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me.' In Hebrew: El-Roi -- 'God who sees me'. The well itself became known as Beer-lahai-roi, 'the well of the Living One who sees me'. Wrestling God for a blessing is Jacob at Peniel, a later Genesis story (Genesis 32). No one in Genesis writes God a letter, and refusing God a sacrifice does not fit the scene.

question: In the Norse myths a shining god stands on the arch of the rainbow that joins the world of humans to the world of the gods. His whole duty is to watch: no giant may cross without his seeing it first. Which Aesir god is this rainbow-bridge watchman?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 27. Heimdallr is the watchman posted at the top of Bifrost. Bragi is the god of poetry who greets warriors in Valhalla. Forseti is the god of justice who holds court in Glitnir. Vidar is the silent son of Odin who avenges his father at Ragnarok. Heimdallr is the specific bridge-watcher.  (Legend.)

question: The shining span that Heimdallr guards is no ordinary rainbow: it is a burning three-coloured arch reaching from Midgard up to the wall of Asgard, and only the gods and Heimdallr may safely cross it. What did the Aesir call this three-coloured span?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 13 and 27. Bifrost is the burning rainbow span to Asgard. Gjallarbru is the gold-roofed bridge over the river Gjoll on the road to Hel. Naglfar is the corpse-nail ship that sails at Ragnarok. Gleipnir is the silky-thin ribbon that binds Fenrir. Bifrost is the specific rainbow.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri makes Heimdallr the sharpest-sensed being in the nine worlds: he needs less sleep than a bird, he can see for a hundred leagues by day or night, and Snorri pairs his hearing of the wool on the sheep's back with one other silent thing on the earth. What is that other silent thing Heimdallr can hear?
choices: the sap in the ash tree
the tread of a cat's paw
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 27. The paired image is 'he can hear the grass grow on the earth and the wool grow on the sheep's back' -- one from the soil, one from the animal, both silent to any other ear. The distractors are real Norse-flavoured images (Yggdrasil's sap, Mimir's well, the padding of a cat) but not from Snorri's grass-and-wool line.  (Legend.)

question: The instant Heimdallr's horn-blast fades from the nine worlds, the Aesir gather at once on the plain of Idavoll to hold their last council. Odin himself does not stay with them: he rides off alone one more time to a certain well beneath a root of Yggdrasil, to ask counsel of a severed head. Whose head does Odin ride to consult one last time?
context: Voluspa stanza 46; Snorri, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Mimir's severed head, preserved by Odin with herbs and spells, sits beside the well of wisdom under Yggdrasil's root and speaks counsel to Odin. Kvasir is the wise man from whose blood the Mead of Poetry was brewed. Ymir is the primordial giant from whose body the world was made. Vafthrudnir is a giant Odin once out-riddled. Mimir is the specific counsellor.  (Legend.)

question: One Poetic Edda poem tells of Heimdallr walking Midgard among humans under a different name. Sleeping three nights each in three different farmhouses, he fathers the ancestors of the three classes of Norse society: thrall, farmer, and jarl. Under what alias does Heimdallr wander Midgard in this poem?
context: Rigsthula (Poetic Edda), whose title literally means 'the lay of Rig.' Heimdallr calls himself Rig ('king') as he walks among humans. Grim is one of Odin's many wandering names (from Grimnismal, 'the masked one'). Bolverk ('evil-worker') is another Odin alias, from the theft of the Mead of Poetry. Ganglati is a servant in the hall of Hel, not a wandering god. Rig is the specific alias Heimdallr uses.  (Legend.)

question: The last thing the rainbow-bridge Bifrost will ever hear is Heimdallr's own horn-blast. The moment the muster begins, a great fire-giant rides up from Muspelheim with a flaming sword; he is the first to try Bifrost, and the bridge cannot bear him. Who is this fire-giant, whose crossing shatters the rainbow?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Surtr the fire-giant leads the host of Muspelheim, and Bifrost breaks beneath him into pieces as he crosses. Hrym captains the ship Naglfar in the flood; he does not ride the bridge. Thrym is the giant who stole Mjolnir long before Ragnarok. Fenrir is the great wolf who breaks his chain and swallows Odin -- but he comes at the muster on the plain, not by the bridge. Surtr is the specific bridge-breaker.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories, a rainbow bridge stretches from the world of humans up to the home of the gods. One god stands guard at its far end and lets no giant across. What is the name of the rainbow bridge?
context: Bifrost ('shimmering way' or 'trembling road') is the rainbow bridge in Snorri's Gylfaginning 13-15. Gjallarbru is the bridge over the river Gjoll on the road to Hel; Yggdrasil is the world-tree; Naglfar is the ship built from dead men's fingernails that carries the giants to Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: The watchman who guards the far end of that rainbow bridge is one of the sons of Odin. He is called the 'white god' and is famous for his sharp senses. What is the watchman's name?
context: Heimdallr (also spelled Heimdall) is described in Gylfaginning 27 as 'the whitest of the gods'; his gold teeth give him the alternate name Gullintanni ('gold-tooth'). Bragi is the god of poetry; Tyr is the one-handed war god; Forseti is a god of justice -- none of them stand watch.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri says the watchman-god was born in a very strange way. Where every other god has one mother, this god had a whole set of them who bore him together on the edge of the world. How many mothers did Heimdallr have?
context: Gylfaginning 27 quotes the lost poem Heimdalargaldr: Heimdallr was born of nine sisters. Nine is the sacred Norse number and it appears again in Heimdallr's own story -- Odin's throne can see everything but Heimdallr's ears can catch things the throne cannot, and the number nine belongs to him personally.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri lists two impossible growth-sounds Heimdallr can hear together in one line of Gylfaginning 27. Which pair does he name?
answer: grass on the earth and wool on sheep
choices: grass on the earth and wool on sheep
grain in the ear and hair on horses
roots in the soil and hair on goats
moss on stones and hooves on cattle
context: Gylfaginning 27, word-for-word: 'he hears grass as it grows on the earth, wool as it grows on sheep, and all things that make more noise.' This is the detail every Norse kid remembers about Heimdallr -- his ears are that fine.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri adds a second superpower after listing Heimdallr's hearing. What is the second thing Snorri says about him?
answer: he sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day
choices: he sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day
he needs no sleep at all, ever
he can taste poison in any drink
he can smell a giant a league off
context: Gylfaginning 27: Heimdallr 'sees a hundred leagues off just as clearly by night as by day.' Snorri also says he needs less sleep than a bird -- less sleep, not none -- and Snorri never gives him poison-tasting or giant-scenting powers.  (Legend.)

question: The watchman-god carries an instrument that will be sounded only once. It is kept hidden under one of the roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil, beside Mimir's well of wisdom. What is the instrument called?
context: Gjallarhorn means 'Yelling Horn' or 'Hollering Horn'. Voluspa 27 and Gylfaginning 15 place it beside Mimir's well under Yggdrasil. Odhroerir is one of the vessels of the Mead of Poetry; the horn of Bragi is a drinking-horn of the god of poetry; Mimir's head is also kept by the well but it is a severed head, not a horn.  (Legend.)

question: When the watchman finally lifts that horn to his lips and blows it, the sound will travel further than any horn in Norse story. Snorri says how far: it reaches through every last one of a specific number of worlds. Across how many worlds is Gjallarhorn's blast heard?
context: The Norse cosmos has nine worlds (Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim, Vanaheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Helheim). Voluspa 46 says the horn's blast fills them all. Nine again -- the number that keeps returning around Heimdallr.  (Legend.)

question: Heimdallr blows Gjallarhorn only once in the whole story of the world. Snorri says that when they hear that blast, the warriors of Valhalla and every Aesir do one specific thing together. What do they do?
answer: take up their weapons and go out to fight
choices: take up their weapons and go out to fight
kneel and swear a new oath to Odin
run to bar the gates of Asgard shut
sail out from Asgard on Skidbladnir
context: Voluspa 46 and Gylfaginning 51: at the first sight of the giants coming for Asgard, Heimdallr raises Gjallarhorn and blows. Every Aesir hears it, every warrior in Valhalla hears it, and they arm themselves and march out onto the field. There is no oath-scene and no shutting of Asgard's gates -- the point is to go out and meet the end.  (Legend.)

question: At Ragnarok itself Heimdallr does not fight a giant or a wolf. He goes out to meet an old personal enemy of his -- the one god who has been his opposite from the beginning, and the two of them kill each other on the field. Which god does Heimdallr die killing?
context: Gylfaginning 51: 'Heimdallr and Loki shall meet and each shall slay the other.' The two have been enemies for ages -- in one older tale (Snorri's Skaldskaparmal) they fought in seal-form over Freyja's necklace Brisingamen. Freyr dies fighting Surt at Ragnarok; Hodr is already dead by then; Bragi has no death-scene.  (Legend.)

question: Heimdallr's own hall stands right at the top of the rainbow bridge, where the road from earth arrives at Asgard. Its name means 'Sky-Cliff'. What is the name of Heimdallr's hall?
context: Himinbjorg is listed in Grimnismal 13 and Gylfaginning 27. Valhalla is Odin's hall of slain warriors; Bilskirnir is Thor's; Sessrumnir is Freyja's. His horse there is called Gulltoppr ('Golden-Top').  (Legend.)

question: In the poem Rigsthula the watchman-god goes walking on earth in disguise, under a different name. He visits three couples in three houses on three nights, and out of those visits three different social groups of humans are born. Under what name does Heimdallr do this?
context: Rigsthula ('the List of Rig') tells the story: the three couples produce the ancestors of the thralls, the karls (farmers), and the jarls (nobles). Grimnir, Vegtamr, and Bolverkr are all disguise-names Odin uses in other stories -- Heimdallr's own disguise-name is Rigr.  (Legend.)

question: Long before the last battle, an older story has Heimdallr and Loki wrestling in the shape of seals on a rock in the ocean, fighting over a stolen treasure of Freyja's. Which treasure of Freyja's are they fighting over?
context: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal (and a lost skaldic poem, the Husdrapa) tells that Loki stole Brisingamen from Freyja; Heimdallr fought him in seal-form off Vagasker to get it back. Brisingamen is Freyja's most famous necklace; the falcon-cloak is a shape-shifting cloak she lends to other gods; the chariot drawn by cats is her ride; Hildisvini ('battle-swine') is her golden boar. All four are real Freyja possessions -- only Brisingamen is the one Loki stole.  (Legend.)

question: Menelaus, king of Sparta, comes home from a trip to Crete to find his wife gone and much of his palace treasure gone with her. She has sailed east across the Aegean with a prince from Troy. What was the name of Menelaus's wife?
context: Andromache is the wife of the Trojan Hector; Hecuba is queen of Troy; Iphigenia is Agamemnon's daughter. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: The prince of Troy who takes Helen east across the Aegean is a son of King Priam. He is the same young prince who, as a shepherd boy on Mount Ida, was made to judge a beauty contest between three goddesses. Who is he?
