context: He chose Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful woman in the world -- Helen. Hector is Paris's older brother, Troy's greatest warrior; Aeneas is a cousin of the Trojan royal house; Deiphobus is another brother, who will marry Helen after Paris is killed. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: Years before Helen ever married Menelaus, so many Greek kings and princes came to court her that her stepfather feared the losers would go to war over the loss. A young Odysseus proposed a clever solution: every suitor should swear an oath binding them to defend the winner. Who was the stepfather?
context: Tyndareus was king of Sparta; Icarius was his brother and Penelope's father; Peleus is the father of Achilles; Priam is king of Troy. Source: mythologystories.net, The Oath of Tyndareus.  (Legend.)

question: In return for the advice about the suitors' oath, the young Odysseus asked the king of Sparta to help him win the hand of another woman -- a girl he had come to Sparta hoping to court in the first place. Whom did Odysseus want as his own wife?
context: Penelope was the daughter of Icarius, Tyndareus's brother, so Tyndareus had the family standing to arrange the match. Clytemnestra is Helen's sister and Agamemnon's wife; Cassandra is Priam's prophetic daughter; Briseis is Achilles's captive. Source: mythologystories.net, The Oath of Tyndareus.  (Legend.)

question: When Paris carries Helen off to Troy, Menelaus calls in the old suitors' oath and every former suitor is legally sworn to sail east and get her back. Menelaus goes first to his own older brother, the overlord of the Achaeans, to lead the whole expedition. Who is Menelaus's brother?
context: Agamemnon becomes commander of the entire Greek force. Nestor, Diomedes, and Idomeneus are real Achaean chieftains, all wrong for 'Menelaus's brother.' Source: Wikipedia, Catalogue of Ships.  (Legend.)

question: One of the sworn suitors tries hardest to dodge the summons. An oracle has warned him he will be gone for many years if he sails to Troy. When the envoys arrive he pretends to be mad, ploughing his own field with an ox and a donkey yoked together and sowing the furrows with salt. Which Greek king does this?
context: It is the same young Odysseus who first invented the oath years before. Source: Wikipedia, Palamedes (mythology).  (Legend.)

question: The king who yoked an ox and a donkey to his plough almost gets away with the madness ruse. Another Greek exposes him: he takes the king's baby son and lays the child down in the path of the plough. The father swerves to save the baby, and is drafted. What is the baby's name?
context: The exposer is Palamedes; the father's grudge against him lasts the whole war. Neoptolemus is Achilles's son; Astyanax is Hector's baby; Eurysaces is Ajax's son. Source: Wikipedia, Palamedes (mythology).  (Legend.)

question: The whole Greek fleet finally gathers at one port to sail east across the Aegean together. It is where the ships collect, and where -- becalmed by the anger of a goddess -- the expedition will pay a terrible price before it ever leaves Greece. Which port is this?
context: Aulis is in Boeotia, on the strait between mainland Greece and Euboea; the setup for the sacrifice of Iphigenia. Piraeus is the port of Athens; Nauplia is the port of Argos; Pylos is Nestor's port on the west coast. Source: Wikipedia, Catalogue of Ships.  (Legend.)

question: The most famous English line about Helen is Christopher Marlowe's -- 'the face that launched a thousand ships.' The number a thousand is a poet's round figure, not Homer's. In the Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad Book 2, Homer gives a much larger total. About how many Greek ships does Homer name?
context: Twenty-nine contingents under 46 captains. Agamemnon brings the largest single contingent, 100 ships. Marlowe wrote his line in Doctor Faustus (1604), roughly 2,300 years after Homer. Source: Wikipedia, Catalogue of Ships.  (Legend.)

question: Not every Greek storyteller believed Helen ever reached Troy. A rival tradition -- told by the poet Stesichorus and dramatised by Euripides, and reported by the historian Herodotus in Book 2 -- said the real Helen never went there at all, and only a phantom in her shape fought the ten-year war. Where did that tradition say the real Helen actually spent the war?
context: Herodotus (2.113-115) says Paris's ship was blown to Egypt, King Proteus took Helen for safekeeping, and Menelaus recovered her there after Troy fell. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: In Iliad Book 3, in a scene the Greeks called the 'Teichoscopia' -- the view from the walls -- Helen stands beside old King Priam on the walls of Troy and does something specific for him as the Greek army moves on the plain below. What does she do?
answer: Names each Achaean chieftain for him one by one
choices: Names each Achaean chieftain for him one by one
Weaves the great tapestry Priam later burns
Sings a lament in Trojan for the coming siege
Draws a map of the Greek camp in the dust
context: One of the great catalogue scenes of Greek literature; Homer's way of introducing the Greek commanders through Helen's eyes. Source: Wikipedia, Helen of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: The greatest surviving poem in the Old English language tells of a young warrior who sails across the sea to kill a hall-monster and, decades later, dies fighting a dragon. What is the name of this poem?
context: Klaeber's Beowulf, 4th edition (University of Toronto Press). Beowulf is 3,182 alliterative lines long and is named for its hero. The Wanderer and The Seafarer are shorter Old English elegies about exile at sea. The Dream of the Rood is an Old English dream-vision in which the cross of the crucifixion speaks. All four are real Anglo-Saxon poems; Beowulf is the one with the hall-monster and the dragon.

question: The poem Beowulf opens in Denmark, at the court of an old king of a people called the Scyldings. He has built the greatest mead-hall in the north and gives out rings to his warriors after every feast. What is this Danish king's name?
context: Beowulf lines 78-83; Klaeber's Beowulf. Hrothgar is the king of the Danes at the story's start. Hygelac is Beowulf's own king back in Geatland. Scyld Scefing is the legendary founder of Hrothgar's dynasty, whose ship-burial opens the poem. Wiglaf is the young Geatish warrior who stands with Beowulf against the dragon at the end. Hrothgar is the specific host of the great hall.

question: King Hrothgar builds the greatest mead-hall in the north and gives it a name that means 'the hart,' from the great pair of antlers mounted on its gables. What is the name of Hrothgar's hall?
context: Beowulf lines 78-83; Klaeber's Beowulf. Heorot ('the hart') is Hrothgar's antler-gabled hall. Valhalla is Odin's hall of slain warriors in Norse myth. Camelot is King Arthur's court in the Arthurian legends. Barnstokk is the tree that stands in the middle of King Volsung's hall in the Volsunga Saga. All four are famous halls, but only Heorot is Hrothgar's.

question: For a long time Heorot is a hall of feasting and song, but soon it becomes a place of grief: a monster comes out of the marshes at night to break in and eat Hrothgar's sleeping warriors. What is the name of this monster?
context: Beowulf lines 86-193; Klaeber's Beowulf. Grendel is the fen-monster who raids Heorot. Fafnir is the dragon Sigurd kills in the Volsunga Saga -- a different Germanic monster. The Nemean Lion is Hercules's first labour, from Greek myth. The Balrog is Tolkien's invention in The Lord of the Rings, drawn on Norse hints but not itself old. Grendel is the specific Heorot-raider.  (Legend.)

question: The whole poem of Beowulf survives in ONE medieval manuscript, which was very nearly lost in a fire at Ashburnham House in London in 1731 -- the flames scorched its edges but the pages held. Under what shelfmark is this manuscript catalogued today?
context: British Library manuscript description; Kiernan, Beowulf and the Beowulf Manuscript. Cotton Vitellius A.xv (also called the Nowell Codex) is the sole Beowulf manuscript. Codex Sinaiticus is a 4th-century Greek Bible in Saint Catherine's Monastery. The Book of Kells is an illuminated Latin gospel-book in Trinity College Dublin. The Exeter Book is another Old English poetry manuscript in Exeter Cathedral (it holds The Wanderer and The Seafarer, but NOT Beowulf). Cotton Vitellius A.xv is the specific Beowulf codex.

question: The Beowulf poet, writing in a Christianised Anglo-Saxon world, roots his fen-monster's ancestry in the book of Genesis rather than in the Norse giant-genealogies. From which biblical ancestor is Grendel said to descend, in one of the poem's few explicit Christian framings?
context: Beowulf lines 102-114; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poet traces Grendel to Cain, the first murderer -- the killing of Abel put a curse on Cain's line, and the poet imagines Grendel as a distant, monstrous descendant of that curse. Nimrod is the mighty hunter and would-be builder of Babel. Esau is Jacob's cheated elder brother. Ham is Noah's son whose descendants were cursed for the tent-vision. All four are real Genesis figures around whom cursed lineages were built in medieval commentary; Cain is the specific one the Beowulf poet chose.  (Legend.)

question: The Beowulf poet stresses that Hrothgar's own warriors are helpless against Grendel not because they lack courage but for a specific reason -- something about the monster that the poet returns to more than once. What does the poem say happens when Hrothgar's warriors try to strike Grendel with an ordinary blade?
answer: no sword can wound him at all
choices: no sword can wound him at all
his skin turns to iron in the fight
he vanishes in mist before the blow
he catches every blade in his teeth
context: Beowulf lines 801-805; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poet writes that Grendel had laid a charm on the edges of all weapons -- 'no sword could bite the sinner' in translation. He does not turn to iron, does not vanish, does not disarm his attackers by mouth. The point is that ordinary weapon-craft, however brave, is useless against this enemy; only bare-handed strength will do.  (Legend.)

question: News of Hrothgar's twelve years of grief reaches a young warrior across the sea at the court of King Hygelac. To which people does the young Beowulf belong?
context: Beowulf lines 194-228; Klaeber's Beowulf. The Geats were a people of what is now southern Sweden. The Danes are Hrothgar's people, the ones being saved. The Franks are the Germanic people of continental Europe from whom France takes its name. The Angles are one of the two peoples (with the Saxons) who gave England its name and its language. The Geats are the specific nation of Beowulf and his fourteen thanes.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf chooses the best fighters he can find, boards a ship, and sails from Geatland to Denmark to help Hrothgar. The poet gives an exact count of the war-band that lands at Hrothgar's door. How many thanes does Beowulf bring with him besides himself?
context: Beowulf lines 194-228; Klaeber's Beowulf. The poem names 'the sturdiest thane he could find' and gives a total of fifteen sea-crafty warriors -- Beowulf plus fourteen others. Seven, twelve, and thirty are round Germanic and biblical numbers (the seven sleepers, the twelve apostles, the thirty pieces of silver) but not the number Beowulf brings to Denmark. Fourteen is the specific count.  (Legend.)

question: On his first night in Heorot, Beowulf makes a boast before Hrothgar's court about how he will meet Grendel. What does Beowulf declare he will fight Grendel with?
choices: only a spear and a shield
a magic blade of the giants
context: Beowulf lines 675-687; Klaeber's Beowulf. Beowulf's boast is that Grendel wields no sword, so he will match him hand to hand. He does not use a spear, does not carry a torch, and the giants' blade appears only LATER in the poem, in a different fight -- against Grendel's mother, under the water. Bare-handed is the specific vow of the first night in Heorot.  (Legend.)

question: Grendel comes at dark, tears open the door of Heorot, and eats one of Beowulf's sleeping men. Then he reaches for Beowulf -- who is only pretending to sleep -- and finds a grip stronger than any he has ever felt. What does Beowulf do to Grendel in the fight that leaves the monster mortally wounded?
answer: tears his arm from its socket
choices: tears his arm from its socket
breaks his neck against a pillar
chokes him with a chain from the wall
context: Beowulf lines 710-836; Klaeber's Beowulf. In the wrestling in the dark, Beowulf holds Grendel's arm so hard that when the monster tries to pull free the arm rips from the shoulder; Grendel flees back to the fen to die. He is not broken against a pillar, not thrown into fire, not chained. The severed arm is hung as a trophy above Heorot's door the next morning.  (Legend.)

question: The Beowulf poem places Heorot at a specific location in Denmark that Danish tradition remembers as a real village on the island of Zealand. Archaeologists digging at that village in the 20th and 21st centuries uncovered the foundations of a huge Viking-age long-hall exactly where the poem places the king's seat. At what village in Zealand did they find these hall-foundations?
context: Tom Christensen, Lejre beyond the Legend (Roskilde Museum, 2015). At Lejre on Zealand, Danish archaeologists have excavated a series of massive 6th-11th century long-hall foundations that Danish tradition (from the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus onward) identifies with the seat of the Scyldings. Uppsala is the ancient royal-cult centre of Sweden. Jelling is the site of Harald Bluetooth's rune-stones in Jutland. Ribe is Denmark's oldest surviving trading town. Lejre is the specific place where the hall-foundations were found.

question: Every Olympian god has a specialty -- Zeus rules, Poseidon storms, Apollo shoots the bow. One god runs the FORGE: he hammers out the thunderbolts of Zeus, the armour of heroes, and every impossible metal thing the other gods need. Which god is he?
context: In Hesiod's Theogony Hera bore him alone, in jealous revenge after Zeus produced Athena from his own head without a mother. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Of all the twelve Olympian gods, one is famously and permanently different in body from the others -- he limps, because he fell from the sky when he was young. Which god walks with the limp?
context: He walks with special support-braces of his own devising. The other gods on Olympus are all portrayed as flawlessly formed; only the smith is not. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Book 1 of the Iliad, the smith-god himself explains why he limps: long ago, while defending his mother in a quarrel, he made his father Zeus so angry that Zeus GRABBED HIM BY THE FOOT and flung him off Olympus. He fell for an entire day. On what island did he finally land?
context: Iliad 1.590-594. The people of Lemnos were the first to find him and worshipped him ever after. Delos is Apollo's birth island, Crete is Zeus's own, Ithaca is Odysseus's home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Homer's Iliad actually tells TWO different stories of the smith-god's fall from Olympus -- in one, his father Zeus throws him; in the OTHER (Book 18), his own MOTHER hurls him out at birth for being ugly, and he falls into the sea. Which two sea-goddesses catch him and raise him for nine years in a cave under the waves?
context: Iliad 18.394-405. Thetis is later the mother of Achilles -- which is why she can walk into Hephaestus's forge and ask him to make her son a shield. That's the debt he owes her. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: Cast out of Olympus for being ugly, the smith-god plots quiet revenge. He forges a beautiful GOLDEN THRONE and sends it up to his mother as a peace-gift. She sits down proudly -- and cannot get up. What springs from the throne to hold her?
context: No other god can undo them; only their maker can. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus' and 'Return of Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: The smith-god has been married off, as compensation, to a goddess who has taken the war-god Ares as her lover -- and one day he catches the two of them in his own bed. He forges a fine metal snare, invisibly thin, and drops it over them where they sleep. Which goddess has he trapped in the net with Ares?
context: Odyssey 8.266-366 -- the blind bard Demodocus sings this story at the court of the Phaeacians. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: The smith calls all the male Olympians into the bedroom to look at Aphrodite and Ares tangled in his invisible net; the gods burst into laughter. Poseidon awkwardly negotiates the couple's release. Ares slinks off to Thrace. Where does the shamed Aphrodite flee?
context: Odyssey 8.362-363: 'And laughter-loving Aphrodite went to Cyprus, to Paphos'. Cyprus and Paphos are her sacred island and city -- she was born from the sea-foam off Cyprus. Cythera is also a birth-story island for her but the Odyssey text names Cyprus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: When the smith-god works in his forge he does not work alone -- a crew of monstrous ancient giants swings the hammers beside him, the same beings who hammered out Zeus's thunderbolts and Poseidon's trident. What race of giants are these forge-assistants?
context: Not the same as Polyphemus the Odyssey cyclops (a wild son of Poseidon) -- these are the elder, craftsman Cyclopes. The Hecatoncheires had a hundred hands, the Gigantes were snake-legged rebels, the Titans were the older generation of gods. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cyclopes'.  (Legend.)

question: Even the smith's helpers inside the forge itself are his own work. Homer describes bronze handmaidens who wait on him -- and these bronze women are astonishing because, unlike normal statues, they can actually do something specific that no other statue could do (Iliad 18.417-421). What can these bronze women do?
context: Iliad 18.417-421 -- Homer's own words: 'in whom is understanding in their hearts, and in whom is speech and strength'. The oldest robot story in Western literature. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hephaestus'.  (Legend.)

question: The smith-god is famous even in Rome, where he is called by a different name; and in Roman legend his forge lies not on Lemnos but deep beneath a still-active volcano -- Vulcan's fire is what makes the mountain smoke. Under which mountain does the Roman forge lie?
context: Etna sits in Sicily; Vesuvius is the volcano that buried Pompeii; Stromboli is a smaller volcanic island north of Sicily; Santorini (ancient Thera) is the Greek volcano whose Bronze Age eruption may have inspired the Atlantis legend. Source: Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (mythology)'.

question: Zeus is the king of the Olympian gods. His sister -- and also his WIFE -- is queen beside him, the divine patron of marriage and the mother of Ares. Which goddess is this?
context: Hera is one of the six children of Cronus and Rhea; her brothers include Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades, and her sisters include Demeter and Hestia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hera'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera's greatest temple in the Greek world stands in the Peloponnese, in a city so devoted to her that the whole nearby region is her sacred country. In which Greek city does the queen of the gods have her most famous temple, the Heraion?
context: The Argive Heraion is one of the oldest large stone temples in the Greek world. It is why Homer calls Hera 'Argive Hera' throughout the Iliad. Source: Wikipedia, 'Heraion of Argos'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus, always unfaithful, falls for a young mortal priestess -- who serves in Hera's own temple, of all places. Desperate to hide her from his wife's eyes, he turns the girl into an animal. What kind of animal does Zeus turn Io into?
context: The transformation does not fool Hera at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Io (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: To make sure Zeus can never rescue Io, Hera assigns the cow a special watchman -- a monstrous giant whose entire body is covered in eyes, so that some can always stay open while others rest. What is this hundred-eyed giant's name?
context: 'Panoptes' means 'all-seeing' -- the same root as the modern word 'panopticon'. Talos was the bronze guardian of Crete; Antaeus was a giant who drew strength from the earth; Tityos was chained in the underworld and had his liver eaten. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argus Panoptes'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus needs Argus killed so he can free Io. He sends one god down disguised as a shepherd, who plays a lulling tune on a shepherd's pipes and tells the giant the long, sleepy story of how those pipes were invented, until the watchman finally sleeps -- and then strikes off Argus's head. Which god does the deed?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.668-721. Apollo is the greater musician but Hermes is the trickster and messenger who slips between worlds; Ares is the crude war-god, no place for pipes and stories; Dionysus's tools are the vine and the frenzy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argus Panoptes'.  (Legend.)

question: Argus is dead, Io is freed, and Hera grieves her loyal watchman. She takes his hundred eyes from the corpse and sets them, one by one, into the tail-feathers of her own sacred bird -- and every bird of that kind carries them still. Which bird did she choose?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.722-723: 'excipit hos, volucrisque suae Saturnia pennis / conlocat' -- Saturn's daughter caught the eyes and set them in the feathers of her bird. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argus Panoptes'.  (Legend.)

question: Hera hates the baby Heracles from birth -- he is her husband's son by yet another mortal woman. While he is still in his cradle she sends two deadly serpents to kill him in his sleep. What does the infant Heracles do to them?
choices: Frightens them off with a shout
Sets them on fire with a coal
context: The scene is painted on Greek vases and Roman coins. His own name -- Heracles -- literally means 'Glory of Hera', because it is Hera's persecution across his whole life that drives him to the twelve labours that make him famous. Source: Wikipedia, 'Heracles'.  (Legend.)

question: In Thebes lived a mortal princess named Alcmene, married to the general Amphitryon. While Amphitryon was away at war, a god disguised himself as her husband and came to her bed. Which god?
context: Zeus took Amphitryon's shape (Apollodorus 2.4.8). Ares (war), Apollo (prophecy), and Hermes (messenger) are real Olympians who did many wonders, but the shape-shifting seduction of Alcmene is a signature Zeus trick, like the swan with Leda or the shower of gold with Danae.  (Legend.)

question: Amphitryon returned from his war that same long night and also lay with his wife Alcmene. So Alcmene gave birth to two boys at once, one from each father. What was Zeus's son called?
context: Alcmene bore twins: Heracles (Zeus's son) and Iphicles (Amphitryon's son) - a rare condition called heteropaternal superfecundation. Perseus, Theseus, and Bellerophon are famous Greek heroes but sons of other parents (Perseus from Danae, Theseus from Aethra, Bellerophon from Glaucus).  (Legend.)

question: Alcmene had been in labor for days with Eileithyia's spell holding her closed. Her clever servant Galanthis finally broke the spell by running out of the house and doing what?
answer: Shouting that the baby had already been born
choices: Shouting that the baby had already been born
Setting the door of the birthing-room on fire
Untying every knot she could find in the palace
Sacrificing a black goat at the front gate
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.281-323: Galanthis lied out into the courtyard that the baby was already delivered. Eileithyia jumped up in shock, breaking her cross-legged posture and her knots, and Heracles was born. A furious Eileithyia later turned Galanthis into a weasel.  (Legend.)

question: Still angry after Heracles was safely born, Hera sent two giant creatures into the nursery to kill him in his cradle. He was eight months old, and his mortal twin Iphicles was in the cradle beside him. What did Hera send?
context: Pindar (Nemean 1.35-50) and Apollodorus (2.4.8) both describe the two snakes gliding across the nursery floor. Lions, eagles, and wolves are all real threats in Greek myth (the Nemean Lion, Prometheus's eagle) but Hera's cradle-attack is specifically two serpents.  (Legend.)

question: Iphicles screamed and tried to crawl away, but the eight-month-old Heracles did something no baby should be able to do. When his nurse rushed in what did she find him doing in the cradle?
answer: Playing with two dead serpents, one in each hand
choices: Playing with two dead serpents, one in each hand
Standing on his feet with a torch already lit
Holding a bright bronze sword he could not lift the day before
Laughing while a great white bird flew above him
context: Pindar's Nemean 1: the eight-month-old Heracles grabbed one snake in each fist and strangled them both, then lay in his cradle playing with the corpses. This is the first proof that he is Zeus's son and not Amphitryon's - and it foreshadows every labor to come.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles's Theban music tutor tried to correct him too harshly during a lesson. The boy Heracles hit him over the head with his own instrument and killed him. What was the tutor's name?
context: Linus, brother of Orpheus, was Heracles's music tutor; Heracles struck him dead with the lyre. Chiron (the centaur) tutored Achilles and Jason, not Heracles. Phineus was a blind seer from the Argonauts' story. Nestor was the old king of Pylos in the Iliad.  (Legend.)

question: In the Homeric Hymn that opens with a nymph bearing Zeus a son in a cave on Mount Cyllene, the newborn will grow up to be the messenger of the Olympian gods and the guide of souls to the underworld. Who is his mother?
context: Maia was a Pleiad, one of the seven daughters of Atlas, and she bore Hermes to Zeus in secret in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia. Calypso kept Odysseus on Ogygia; Callisto was turned into a bear by Hera; Echo faded away pining for Narcissus. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 1-9; Wikipedia, 'Hermes'.  (Legend.)

question: On the very morning Hermes is born he climbs out of his cradle, walks to the mouth of his mother's cave, and finds a small creature passing along the ground. He kills it, cleans it out, and by that afternoon has invented the first lyre from its body. What creature did the newborn Hermes turn into the first lyre?
context: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes lines 24-61 describe the newborn god finding a tortoise crawling past the cave, praising its shell as a fine covering for a musician, and stretching seven cow-gut strings across the hollowed shell to invent the lyre. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 24-61.  (Legend.)

question: Still on the same first day of his life, the newborn Hermes slips out of the cave again, crosses the mountains into Pieria, and steals fifty sacred cattle grazing in the meadows. The herd belonged to Hermes's own elder brother, an Olympian. Which brother did the baby rob?
context: Apollo pastured the sacred cattle of the gods in Pieria; the newborn Hermes drove fifty of them off, kicking off a quarrel that ended in the trade of the lyre. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 72-75; Wikipedia, 'Hermes'.  (Legend.)

question: The baby thief knows a tracker will follow the hoof-prints of the stolen herd straight back to his cave. To make the trail read the wrong way, he does something to the cattle themselves before he drives them home. What did the newborn Hermes do to the cattle?
choices: he tied brushwood to their tails
he split the herd in three
he crossed them through a river
context: In Homeric Hymn 4 lines 75-78, Hermes drives the cattle backwards along the road, so the hoof-prints point away from his cave rather than toward it. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 75-78.  (Legend.)

question: The tracks the cattle leave behind may point the wrong way, but a baby's tiny footprints beside them would give the thief away at once. So Hermes weaves an oversized pair of sandals for his own feet from whatever grew close by the road. What did he weave the disguising sandals from?
context: Homeric Hymn 4 lines 79-86 describe Hermes weaving huge sandals of tamarisk and myrtle branches so that no one seeing the prints would guess an infant made them. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 79-86.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo finally tracks the impossible backwards trail all the way back to a cave in the mountains and finds a tiny baby swaddled in his cradle, insisting innocently he is far too small to have stolen cattle. Apollo drags the newborn up to Olympus and demands justice from Zeus. What is Zeus's response to the scene?
answer: he laughs at his infant son's cheek
choices: he laughs at his infant son's cheek
he strikes Hermes with a thunderbolt
he orders the cattle chained to Hades
he refuses to speak until Hera decides
context: In the Hymn's Olympus scene, Zeus bursts out laughing at the sight of the baby denying everything, and orders the two brothers to work it out between themselves. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 388-396; Wikipedia, 'Hermes'.  (Legend.)

question: Told by Zeus to settle the quarrel with his elder brother, Hermes pulls out the new instrument he invented that morning and begins to play. Apollo, the god of music himself, is so charmed by the sound that on the spot he trades away one of his greatest possessions to keep the instrument. What does Apollo hand over to Hermes in the trade?
context: Apollo accepts the lyre and gives up all claim on the fifty cattle; from then on the lyre is Apollo's instrument, and Hermes takes the herd. Homeric Hymn 4 lines 418-502. Source: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes 418-502.  (Legend.)

question: Hildegard later dictated to her secretary Volmar that she had been seeing visions of a brilliant light — 'a light so great my soul quaked' — since a specific age of her own childhood. What age did she name?
context: The claim appears in her Vita Sanctae Hildegardis. She called the visions 'umbra viventis lucis' — the reflection of the Living Light. Source: https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2022/09/17/hildegard-of-bingen-voice-of-the-living-light/

question: In 1141, aged 43, Hildegard heard a command she called the Living Light: 'Write what you see and hear.' She resisted, fell ill, and only recovered when she obeyed. It took her ten years to complete the resulting book of twenty-six visions. What is it called?
context: The title is short for 'Scito vias Domini' — Know the Ways of the Lord. Her friend Volmar served as her scribe. Confessions is Augustine (c. 400); The Cloud of Unknowing is a 14th-c. English mystical work; The City of God is Augustine's late apology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hildegard_of_Bingen

question: At the Synod of Trier in 1147-48, extracts of Hildegard's book of visions were read aloud — and the pope himself gave formal approval for her to keep writing and preaching, an almost unheard-of authorization for a medieval woman. Which pope?
context: Eugenius III (r. 1145-1153) was a Cistercian and a former pupil of Bernard of Clairvaux, who had personally endorsed Hildegard's writings. Innocent III came later (1198-1216); Gregory VII was the reformer of the 1070s; Urban II called the First Crusade in 1095. Source: https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2022/09/17/hildegard-of-bingen-voice-of-the-living-light/

question: Alongside her theology and about 77 pieces of liturgical music, Hildegard wrote two long reference works still studied today — Physica and Causae et Curae. What subject did those two books cover?
context: Physica is a catalogue of the healing properties of plants, animals, stones, and elements; Causae et Curae covers the human body and diseases. Both draw on herbal and monastic-infirmary tradition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hildegard_of_Bingen

question: Hours after fire fell from heaven on his sacrifice at Carmel, the greatest of the prophets learned that Queen Jezebel had sworn by her gods to have him killed by the next day. He ran for his life -- a day's journey into the wilderness -- and sat down under a lonely tree to die. Who was this prophet?
context: 1 Kings 19:1-4. The Carmel contest (1 Kings 18) is the high moment of Elijah's ministry; the wilderness collapse right after it is the low. Elisha is Elijah's successor -- easy to confuse.

question: The tree Elijah sits under in the wilderness, right after Jezebel's threat, is named specifically in the text. He asks under it to die. Which tree is it?
context: 1 Kings 19:4 KJV. It is a solitary desert bush (Hebrew rotem, a broom-plant). Under it he prays 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.' The others are all real biblical trees.

question: Elijah is asleep under the juniper when an angel touches him and points to food already prepared beside his head. He eats, drinks, sleeps, and is woken a second time to eat again. What food is set beside him?
answer: a cake baken on the coals and a cruse of water
choices: a cake baken on the coals and a cruse of water
a bowl of red pottage and a jug of goat's milk
quails from the sky and manna on the ground
unleavened bread and a cup of blessing wine
context: 1 Kings 19:5-6 KJV. On the strength of that food he walks forty days and forty nights. The others are real biblical meals -- Jacob's pottage, Israel's wilderness rations, Passover.

question: Fed twice by the angel, Elijah walks forty days and forty nights across the wilderness and lodges in a cave on the mountain of God -- the same peak where he will hear the still small voice. What mountain is his destination?
context: 1 Kings 19:8-9. Horeb is another name for Sinai. He lodges in a cave there -- traditionally identified with the cleft in the rock where Moses had been hidden centuries earlier.

question: Told to stand on the mountain, Elijah watches three tremendous things pass by in turn. First a great wind rends the mountains and breaks the rocks -- but the LORD is not in the wind. Then an earthquake -- but the LORD is not in the earthquake. Then what?
context: 1 Kings 19:11-12 KJV. And after the fire, of course, comes the still small voice. The other three are all real biblical theophanies -- Noah's flood, the seventh plague on Egypt, the ninth plague on Egypt.

question: After three tremendous natural forces have passed by the cave at Horeb -- and the LORD has not been in any of them -- Elijah hears one more thing, described in a KJV phrase now proverbial in English. What is that phrase?
context: 1 Kings 19:12 KJV. At the sound of it Elijah wraps his face in his mantle and steps to the mouth of the cave. The other three are real biblical divine sounds -- Pentecost, Sinai, Revelation.

question: At the cave's mouth the still small voice gives Elijah three orders -- three people to anoint. Two are new kings (Hazael over Syria and Jehu over Israel). Who is the third?
answer: Elisha as prophet in his place
choices: Elisha as prophet in his place
Nathan as prophet to the king
Aaron as priest over the tribes
context: 1 Kings 19:15-16. The KJV wording is 'prophet in thy room' -- 'room' here is archaic for 'place/stead'. God adds that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed the knee to Baal. The other three are real biblical figures from other reigns.

question: At the end of his ministry Elijah crosses the Jordan on foot with Elisha beside him. He takes one thing off his own body, wraps it together, strikes the water with it, and the river parts so both prophets cross dry-shod. Which item does he use?
context: 2 Kings 2:8 KJV: 'Elijah took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and smote the waters.' The mantle becomes the physical sign of prophetic succession -- Elisha will pick it up minutes later and part the river back the other way with it.

question: As Elijah and Elisha still walked and talked on the far side of the Jordan, two fiery things suddenly parted them -- 'a chariot of fire, and horses of fire' -- and Elijah was taken up into heaven. By what mode of ascent, according to the KJV text?
context: 2 Kings 2:11 KJV: 'Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.' The chariot and horses of fire appear -- but the wording says the whirlwind carries him, not the chariot. It is one of only two people in the Hebrew Bible who never die (Enoch is the other).

question: In Snorri Sturluson's Skaldskaparmal, the strongest of all the giants has a stone heart, a stone head, a stone shield -- his whole body is made of rock. What is the name of this stone-giant who takes on Thor?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Hrungnir is the stone-giant Thor duels. Thrym is the giant who stole Mjolnir and demanded Freyja as a wife (Thor recovered it in a bridal veil). Geirrod is the giant Thor visits with only Grid's iron gloves. Utgardaloki is the illusionist-giant of the giant-city.  (Legend.)

question: The stone-giant Hrungnir was proud above all of his horse -- so proud that he raced it against Odin's own eight-legged horse Sleipnir, with each rider wagering his own head on the outcome. What is the name of Hrungnir's horse?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Gullfaxi means 'Golden-Mane' (Old Norse gull = gold, faxi = mane). Blodughofi is Freyr's horse; Skinfaxi ('Shining-Mane') pulls the day; Hrimfaxi ('Frost-Mane') pulls the night. Odin let Hrungnir into Asgard because of the race -- and Hrungnir got drunk and started boasting.  (Legend.)

question: Drunk on Odin's mead in Asgard, Hrungnir began to boast very badly: he would kill all the gods, carry Valhalla back to Jotunheim, and take home two goddesses as trophies. Which two goddesses did Hrungnir say he would drown in his own drinking?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Freyja is the great goddess of love and gold; Sif is Thor's golden-haired wife. Frigg is Odin's wife; Idunn keeps the apples of youth; Skadi is a ski-goddess; Nanna is Baldr's wife; Hel rules the dead; Gerd is Freyr's wife. Threatening Sif specifically was threatening Thor -- Thor got called home from the east to fight.  (Legend.)

question: Because Hrungnir had been under Odin's hospitality, Thor could not just kill him -- Thor had to challenge him to a formal duel on giant-ground. The giants, terrified of losing their strongest, decided to build Hrungnir a bodyguard. What was Hrungnir's bodyguard made of?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. The giants raised a huge man-shape out of clay -- nine leagues tall and three leagues wide -- called Mokkurkalfi ('Mist-Calf'). They needed a heart big enough to fit inside him, but the only heart they could get was a mare's heart, and it was too timid.  (Legend.)

question: The giants stuffed the huge clay bodyguard Mokkurkalfi with a heart -- but they could only find a mare's heart, and it was the wrong size and the wrong nerve. What did the mare's heart cause the clay bodyguard to do when Thor came into view?
answer: tremble helplessly and wet the ground beneath him
choices: tremble helplessly and wet the ground beneath him
sing a mourning song for the mare
turn and run east into the mountains
call out to Odin for mercy
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. The mare's heart made Mokkurkalfi shake with terror at the sight of Thor -- Snorri says he wet the ground where he stood. Thor's servant Thialfi ran him through easily, and the clay-giant fell 'with little glory'. The real duel was Thor against Hrungnir alone.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's swift servant Thialfi ran ahead of the thunder-god to the duelling ground and shouted a lie across at Hrungnir about which direction Thor was coming from. What did Thialfi tell Hrungnir?
answer: that Thor was coming up from under the ground
choices: that Thor was coming up from under the ground
that Thor was coming down out of the clouds
that Thor was coming from behind the mountain
that Thor was coming across the sea from the east
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Thialfi lied so that Hrungnir, panicked and thinking Thor would strike upward at his legs, made a fatal choice about his shield. Hrungnir laid his stone shield flat on the ground and stood on top of it -- leaving his body wide open when Thor actually came over the horizon overhead.  (Legend.)

question: Thor went home from the duel with the whetstone-shard still stuck in his forehead. A wise-woman was called in to sing charms over the wound so the shard would loosen and slip out. What was the name of the wise-woman who came to sing the charm?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Groa (Old Norse for 'to grow / to heal') was a volva -- a Norse seeress. Angrboda is Loki's giantess wife and mother of Fenrir, Jormungand, and Hel; Sigyn is Loki's other wife who holds the bowl over him under the serpent; Hyndla is the seeress of the Hyndluljod. When Groa began to chant, Thor felt the shard move.  (Legend.)

question: As Groa chanted, Thor -- meaning to reward her with joyous news -- began telling her that he had lately met her long-lost husband Aurvandil and carried him home in a basket across the icy river Elivagar. One of Aurvandil's toes had stuck out of the basket and frozen off. What did Thor say he did with the frozen toe?
answer: threw it up into the sky as a star
choices: threw it up into the sky as a star
gave it to the ravens to eat
set it on Aurvandil's mantel for luck
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 17. Thor threw the frozen toe up into the sky, where Snorri says it still shines as the star called Aurvandil's Toe (Aurvandilsta). Later commentators have guessed the star was Rigel in Orion, or the Morning Star, or Alcor -- Snorri does not fix it. But the news of her husband's rescue overcame Groa: she forgot the words of the charm, and the shard stayed in Thor's forehead forever after.  (Legend.)

question: Odin sits on his high seat in Asgard, but he cannot be in every corner of the world at once. To keep watch on all of Midgard he sends out two of the same kind of bird every dawn to fly the whole earth and come back at breakfast. What kind of bird does Odin send out?
context: Snorri's Gylfaginning 38 describes the two ravens flying from Odin's shoulders each dawn, ranging over the whole earth, and returning at the morning meal. Eagles belong to Thjazi and to the tree of Yggdrasil; owls do not carry this errand; sparrows are not Norse omen-birds.  (Legend.)

question: Inside Valhalla Odin keeps two wolves at his feet, and Grimnismal 19 says the wolves devour everything set on his table -- every scrap of meat the war-father is served. Odin himself, the poem says, never touches the food at all. What does Odin himself live on?
context: Grimnismal 19: 'Geri and Freki the war-glorious sates, the battle-hardened Father of Hosts; but on wine alone weapon-magnificent Odin ever lives.' The two wolves are the mirror-pair to the two ravens -- birds for what he knows, wolves for what he feeds. Mead belongs to the poetry-story (Odin steals the Mead of Poetry from Suttungr); blood-drinking is not Odin's marker.  (Legend.)

question: The two wolves at Odin's feet in Valhalla have names in Grimnismal 19, and like the ravens' names they are plain descriptive Old Norse words. One means 'Greedy' and the other means 'Ravenous'. What are the wolves called?
context: Geri = 'Greedy', Freki = 'Ravenous'. Skoll and Hati are the wolves that chase the sun and moon across the sky. Fenrir is the wolf who swallows Odin at Ragnarok; Garm is the hound at the gates of Hel. Sleipnir and Gulltoppr are horses -- Odin's and Heimdallr's.  (Legend.)

question: Long before the Viking sagas were written down, Norse and Germanic warriors were already carving Odin with the two ravens. On 6th to 8th century helmet plates dug up in Sweden a helmeted figure appears with a spear -- and one bird flanking him on either side. At which two Swedish sites do those helmet plates come from?
context: The Vendel and Torslunda helmet plates (Sweden, ca. 550-800 AD) are among the oldest surviving pictures of the raven-flanked warrior; they show the two ravens beside Odin centuries before Snorri wrote the myths down. Uppsala was Odin's great temple site; the others are famous Viking trading and burial places, but not the plate sites.

question: In the Norse stories the Aesir stay young because one goddess of Asgard keeps a wooden box of golden fruit and hands them around at every feast. The gods eat from her box; without it they would age like any mortal. What kind of fruit does this goddess keep in her box?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1 and Gylfaginning 26: Idunn keeps a wooden box of golden apples that the Aesir eat to stay young. The pomegranate is Persephone's fruit in Greek myth; figs and pears belong to other traditions. Apples of immortality are one of only a handful of Norse-specific food-of-life motifs.  (Legend.)

question: Odin, Loki, and Hoenir are wandering the wilds. They kill an ox for supper and lay it in the coals, but the meat will not cook no matter how long the fire burns. A great eagle in a nearby oak calls down that the fire will only take the meat if the bird gets his share first. What does Loki do to the eagle in a rage?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: Loki swings a pole at the bird -- the pole sticks fast to the eagle and Loki's hands stick fast to the pole, and the eagle takes off dragging Loki through rocks and brambles until he begs for mercy. This is how the trap on Idunn begins.  (Legend.)

question: The eagle in the oak is not really a bird at all -- he is a giant in feathered disguise, and once Loki is stuck to the pole and begging in the air, the giant names his price. What does the eagle demand in exchange for setting Loki down?
answer: Idunn and her box of fruit
choices: Idunn and her box of fruit
Frigg and her ring of keys
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: the eagle is the giant Thjazi, and his price is Idunn together with her apples -- if the Aesir lose her, they lose their immortality. Freyja's necklace is Brisingamen (a different story); Sif's hair is what Loki himself shaved off in another episode; Frigg keeps the household keys of Asgard but is not ransomed here.  (Legend.)

question: In the Prose Edda the giant who steals the box of youth-fruit from Asgard has a name and a mountain hall. He carries the goddess in his talons all the way home, and the Aesir will not know where to find her until Loki confesses. What is the name of this giant?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: Thjazi (or Thiazi) carries Idunn to his hall Thrymheim in Jotunheim. Suttung is the giant who hoards the Mead of Poetry. Thrym is the giant who steals Mjolnir and demands Freyja as bride. Hymir is the giant whose cauldron the gods borrow for Aegir's ale-brewing.  (Legend.)

question: Weeks pass and the box does not come back to Asgard. In Snorri's Prose Edda the effect is written straight into the bodies of the gods -- Bragi grows a grey beard, the goddesses wrinkle, Odin's shoulders begin to bend. The Aesir gather in council and quickly work out one thing about the day Idunn disappeared. What?
answer: Loki was the last one seen with her
choices: Loki was the last one seen with her
an eagle had circled Asgard for a week
the box had been left standing empty
she had spoken of going out alone
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: the gods meet, ask each other what was last known of Idunn, and the last thing anyone saw was that she had gone out through the gate with Loki. They seize Loki and threaten him with death or torture until he agrees to bring her back.  (Legend.)

question: To fly north into Jotunheim after Idunn, Loki cannot go on his own feet -- he needs the shape of a bird. He borrows a set of feathered gear from another Aesir goddess. Which goddess owns the flying-plumage that Loki borrows?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: Loki borrows Freyja's falcon (or hawk) plumage and flies as a falcon into Jotunheim. Freyja is the Vanir goddess who owns the necklace Brisingamen and this plumage. Frigg keeps the household of Asgard; Nanna is the wife of Baldr; Skadi (Thjazi's daughter) will not enter the story until after her father is dead.  (Legend.)

question: Loki reaches Thrymheim while the giant is out fishing on the sea, and finds Idunn alone in the hall. To carry a full-grown goddess back to Asgard in a bird's claws he does not just grab her -- he changes her shape so she is small enough to fly with. What shape does Loki turn Idunn into for the journey home?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: 'Loki turned her into the shape of a nut and grasped her in his claws and flew his utmost.' The nut-shape in the talons is one of the neatest small-and-hidden rescue-transformations in Norse myth, parallel to Zeus hiding Metis or Vishnu hiding worlds in a leaf.  (Legend.)

question: The pursuing giant comes home, sees Idunn gone, takes eagle-shape and chases Loki across the sky. The Aesir on the walls of Asgard have prepared a trap for the moment the falcon crosses the wall ahead of the eagle. What have the gods heaped on top of the wall to spring on Thjazi?
answer: a pile of wood-shavings ready to light
choices: a pile of wood-shavings ready to light
a net of chains ready to drop
a rank of archers ready to loose
a wall of shields ready to raise
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 1: the Aesir pile wood-shavings on the wall; the instant Loki-as-falcon crosses inside with Idunn in his claws, they light the pile, and Thjazi's eagle-feathers catch fire so he falls inside the walls of Asgard, where the gods kill him. His daughter Skadi comes armed for blood-price and is granted a husband chosen by his feet -- she picks the fairest pair thinking they are Baldr's, but they belong to Njord.  (Legend.)

question: Inigo Lopez de Loyola — later Ignatius — was born in 1491 at his family's castle in the mountainous northern region of Spain where he grew up a court page and then a soldier fond of chivalric romances. Which people was he from?
context: The castle of Loyola sits in the Basque province of Gipuzkoa. Ignatius was the youngest of thirteen children. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/St-Ignatius-of-Loyola

question: On May 20, 1521, Ignatius was defending a fortress in northern Spain against a French army during a Habsburg-Valois war. He refused to surrender, and a single French projectile shattered his right leg. What kind was it?
context: The fortress was Pamplona in Navarre. The cannonball passed between his legs; the French, respecting his courage, treated him gently and had him carried home to Loyola. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Pampeluna

question: Recovering from his leg wound at Loyola, Ignatius insisted his surgeons rebreak and reset the bone TWICE — without anesthetic, nearly killing him. What was his reason?
answer: The stump would show through his tight courtier's hose
choices: The stump would show through his tight courtier's hose
The pain would prove his worthiness as a knight
A vow to Saint Sebastian required a threefold ordeal
His confessor had ordered a penance for battlefield pride
context: Ignatius, still vain of his courtier looks, could not bear the thought of the deformity showing through his leg-hugging stockings. He limped the rest of his life. He tells the story in the third-person Autobiography he dictated near the end of his life. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ignatius_of_Loyola/

question: Bedridden and bored, Ignatius asked his family for the chivalric romances he loved — knights, damsels, adventures. But the only books in the castle were two very different ones his sister-in-law brought instead. What were they?
answer: A life of Christ and a book of saints' lives
choices: A life of Christ and a book of saints' lives
A Roman history and a book of court manners
A pilgrim's guide and a bestiary
A book of hours and a farmer's almanac
context: The books were Ludolph of Saxony's Vita Christi and the Flos Sanctorum ('Flowers of the Saints'). Reading them, Ignatius noticed that fantasies of chivalric love left him restless while dreams of imitating the saints left him at peace — his first discovery, which he called discernment of spirits. Source: https://www.jesuits.org/about-us/ignatius-of-loyola/

question: In March 1522, converted and traveling to Jerusalem, Ignatius climbed to the Benedictine mountain shrine of Montserrat in Catalonia. He kept an all-night vigil there and marked the moment with a single unmistakable gesture. What was it?
answer: He hung his sword and dagger at the altar
choices: He hung his sword and dagger at the altar
He knelt on a bed of raw barley grains
He recited every Psalm of David from memory
He kept watch beside a single burning taper
context: He also exchanged his fine clothes with a beggar for sackcloth. This vigil of arms deliberately imitated the ritual of a knight before being girded — but in reverse, as Ignatius was laying his soldier's life DOWN. The sword is still shown at Montserrat by tradition. Source: https://www.foreverbarcelona.com/st-ignatius-in-barcelona-montserrat-and-the-manresa-cave/

question: On August 15, 1534, Ignatius and six companions from the University of Paris — Francis Xavier, Peter Faber, Diego Lainez and three others — knelt in a small chapel and swore vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience to the pope. Where in Paris did they gather?
context: This is the moment traditionally taken as the founding of the Society of Jesus — the Jesuits — though the order was formally approved by Pope Paul III only in 1540, in the bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae. Ignatius was elected first Superior General; the Society's motto Ad Maiorem Dei Gloriam (AMDG) — 'to the greater glory of God' — is associated with him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits

question: Around 108 CE a Christian bishop was arrested in the Syrian capital under the emperor Trajan and sentenced to be sent to the arena. He would spend the last months of his life walking under guard all the way to Rome to die there. Of which great Syrian city was Ignatius the bishop?
context: Antioch on the Orontes, in Syria -- founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals, in Roman times the third-largest city of the empire after Rome and Alexandria, and the place where Christ's followers were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch.

question: Ignatius was marched overland from Syria under the guard of a squad of ten Roman soldiers. In his Letter to the Romans he gave those soldiers a memorable nickname. What did Ignatius call his ten military escorts?
context: Letter to the Romans, chapter 5: 'From Syria even to Rome I fight with wild beasts, by land and sea, by night and by day, being bound to ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers, who, even when treated well, only become worse.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch.

question: Along the road, Christian communities in the towns they passed came out to meet the condemned bishop, and Ignatius wrote each of them a letter -- letters that have survived as one of the earliest and most vivid glimpses of the very early church. How many authentic letters did Ignatius write on that final journey?
context: The seven letters are addressed to the churches at Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Philadelphia, Smyrna, Rome, and personally to Polycarp the young bishop of Smyrna. Scholars call this the 'middle recension'; a longer 4th-century version with spurious extras is not accepted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch.

question: The single most famous line Ignatius ever wrote comes from that same Letter to the Romans, chapter 4. Explaining why he wanted the beasts to have their way with him, he chose one homely image from ordinary Roman life and cast himself as it. In Ignatius's own words, what did he call himself?
context: Letter to the Romans 4: 'I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch.

question: Ancient tradition puts Ignatius's death in the arena at Rome, torn apart by wild beasts as he had asked. Later Church Fathers filled in details: Jerome was the first writer to specifically name the animal, and John Chrysostom the first to name the great amphitheatre. What animal did Jerome name as the one that killed Ignatius?
context: Chrysostom's amphitheatre is the Flavian Amphitheatre -- the Colosseum. Leopards are memorable in the story only as Ignatius's nickname for his GUARDS, not the beasts of the arena; bears and wild boars did appear in Roman venationes but not in the Ignatius tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch.  (Legend.)

question: A thousand Greek ships bound for Troy sit becalmed in the harbor, sails limp, day after day; the men grow restless waiting for a wind that never comes. In which port do the ships lie waiting?
context: The mustering-place of the Greek fleet in the Trojan War tradition is Aulis, a small harbor on the Euripus strait in Boeotia, across from Euboea. Euripides opens Iphigenia at Aulis with the fleet stalled there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_in_Aulis.  (Legend.)

question: At Aulis Agamemnon calls in the army's reader of omens -- Homer says he had no rival in the Greek camp for reading birds and entrails -- to explain why the wind will not come. Which seer stands before him?
context: Calchas son of Thestor is the seer who marches with the Greek army through the whole Trojan War tradition; Homer (Iliad 1.69-72) calls him the best of bird-readers, who knew what is and what will be and what was before. Tiresias is the blind Theban seer of Oedipus's story; Melampus is the older seer who understood the speech of animals; Amphiaraus is the seer of the Seven Against Thebes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calchas.  (Legend.)

question: The seer Calchas gives his answer to the whole army: the calm at Aulis is a punishment. The commander Agamemnon has offended one of the Olympians, and she alone is holding back the wind. Which goddess?
context: In one strand of the story Agamemnon killed a stag in her grove and boasted he was a better hunter than she; in another it is an older family curse. Either way, the huntress is the one holding back the wind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calchas.  (Legend.)

question: Agamemnon cannot simply order his daughter dragged to camp; she is far away with her mother Clytemnestra. So he writes home a letter with a lie: come at once to Aulis, because a marriage has been arranged for the girl. Which Greek hero does the letter falsely name as the bridegroom?
context: The false-wedding letter names Achilles as the bridegroom precisely because he is the most glorious young warrior in camp; no mother would refuse the match. Mother and daughter set out for Aulis joyfully. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_in_Aulis.  (Legend.)

question: When the young warrior whose name Agamemnon borrowed for the false wedding-letter learns that his own name was used as bait to bring a girl to a killing, he does something the whole army does not expect. What does he do?
answer: swears to defend the girl with his own sword
choices: swears to defend the girl with his own sword
sails home for Phthia in disgust
demands his share of the sacrifice
refuses to sail for Troy at all
context: In Euripides's play Achilles is furious that his name was borrowed for a killing; he offers to stand with drawn arms against the whole Greek host on the girl's behalf. It is one of the few moments Achilles's honor is used to protect rather than to demand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_in_Aulis.  (Legend.)

question: In the older, harder tradition of Aeschylus's Agamemnon, the sacrifice at Aulis goes through: the girl is gagged so her curses cannot spoil the omen, the knife falls, and the chorus later says her prayers and her cries of 'Father' the war-lords heeded not. Years later, on the day Agamemnon comes home from Troy, someone kills him in his bath for that killing. Who?
context: In Aeschylus's Agamemnon the chorus recalls the sacrifice at Aulis in unforgettable detail (parodos, lines 228-247). When Agamemnon returns from Troy his wife Clytemnestra murders him in his bath; her stated reason is the killing of their daughter. Her lover Aegisthus helps, but the axe is hers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon_(play).  (Legend.)

question: In the softer, later tradition of Euripides's Iphigenia at Aulis, the goddess who demanded the girl's life takes pity at the last moment. As the knife falls she snatches the girl away and leaves a different living creature bleeding on the altar in her place. What animal appears there?
context: The substitution echoes Artemis's own emblem: she is goddess of the hunt, and the beast that appears under the knife is a hind of the forest. Compare the ram substituted for Isaac in Genesis 22 (a different tradition's version of the same terrible moment). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_in_Aulis.  (Legend.)

question: In Euripides's Iphigenia at Aulis the girl has one of the most famous change-of-heart speeches in Greek tragedy. Where she began pleading for her life, she now walks calmly to the altar veiled like a bride, and tells her father what her death will earn. What does she say she gives?
answer: her body to Greece, that the fleet may sail
choices: her body to Greece, that the fleet may sail
her name to Artemis, that the goddess be honored
her marriage to Achilles, that he fight the harder
her tears to her mother, that Clytemnestra be spared
context: Iphigenia at Aulis 1375-1401: 'I give my body to Greece. Sacrifice it, and sack Troy. This shall be my monument for ages: this is my marriage, my children, my glory.' The speech is what turns her from a victim into a heroine in the Euripidean version. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iphigenia_in_Aulis.  (Legend.)

question: A young Jerusalem prophet, standing in the Temple, saw the Lord sitting upon a throne 'high and lifted up' -- and the hem of the robe alone filled the whole Temple. Above the throne blazed six-winged burning ones crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' Who was that prophet?
context: Isaiah 6:1-3 KJV: 'In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.' The three distractors are all 8th-century BC prophets working in the same era as Isaiah -- Micah in Judah, Amos and Hosea in the northern kingdom of Israel -- but the throne-vision with the seraphim belongs to Isaiah alone.

question: In Isaiah's Temple vision the seraphim above the throne each had six wings arranged in three pairs -- and two of those pairs were not for flying at all. Two wings covered what two parts of the seraph's own body?
context: Isaiah 6:2 KJV: 'with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly.' The name seraphim is from Hebrew saraph, 'burning one' -- they appear only in this chapter of the Hebrew Bible, distinct from the cherubim who guard the Ark and Ezekiel's four-winged living creatures.

question: One of the seraphim flew to the trembling Isaiah with a burning coal in its hand -- a coal it had just picked up from the altar. What did the seraph carry the coal with?
context: Isaiah 6:6 KJV: 'having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar.' The distractors are all real Temple implements -- golden censers for incense (Numbers 16), fire-shovels of gold (Exodus 27:3), and the priestly hem used for handling holy things.

question: After the seraph laid the live coal upon Isaiah's mouth and his sin was purged, the prophet heard the voice of the Lord ask: 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Isaiah answered in a single short line that has become the classic prophet's reply. What did he say?
choices: Behold the handmaid of the LORD
context: Isaiah 6:8 KJV. The three distractors are the boy Samuel at the LORD's midnight call (1 Samuel 3:9), Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42), and Mary at the Annunciation (Luke 1:38) -- other famous scriptural yes-answers.

question: Isaiah promised King Hezekiah, sick unto death, that the LORD would give him fifteen more years -- and gave him a sign on the sundial of Ahaz. What did the shadow on the sundial do?
answer: went backward ten degrees on the dial
choices: went backward ten degrees on the dial
leapt forward ten degrees on the dial
stood still for a full hour at noon
doubled in length across the dial
context: 2 Kings 20:9-11 KJV. Isaiah offered Hezekiah forward ten degrees or backward ten; Hezekiah said forward was 'a light thing' and asked for backward. Isaiah cried unto the LORD and it did. One of the most striking miracle-signs in the Hebrew Bible -- the sun itself running backward on the sundial of Ahaz.

question: Esau came in from the fields half-starving and begged his brother for a bowl of something cooking on the fire. In exchange for that one meal Esau gave away what?
choices: a full year of his labour
context: Genesis 25:29-34. The pot on the fire was a stew of red lentils; because of its red colour Esau got the nickname Edom, meaning 'Red'. The birthright of the elder brother was a double share of the inheritance and the headship of the family, and Jacob traded a bowl of soup for it.

question: Jacob's mother Rebekah wrapped his arms and neck in what to help him fool his blind father Isaac, who wanted to feel Esau's rough skin before giving the blessing?
context: Genesis 27:16 KJV: 'And she put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck.' Isaac, blind and suspicious, still says 'The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau' (27:22), yet blesses him. When Esau comes in later with the real venison, the blessing is already spent.

question: Fleeing Esau's fury alone at nightfall, Jacob stopped at a certain place and lay down to sleep in the open. What did he use as a pillow?
context: Genesis 28:11 KJV: 'he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep.' The unlikely pillow becomes the point: what he lays his head on becomes the marker of holy ground in the next verses.

question: As Jacob slept on the stone, he dreamed of a ladder set on the earth whose top reached to heaven. What did he see moving on the ladder?
choices: the four beasts of the throne
context: Genesis 28:12 KJV: 'and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.' The other visions are real from other Bible scenes (Zechariah's seven lamps, Ezekiel's four living creatures, the cherubim east of Eden with the flaming sword). Only Jacob's ladder shows angels going both ways at once.

question: Jacob woke shaken from the ladder-dream and said, 'Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.' He set up the pillow-stone as a pillar and poured oil on the top of it. What new name did he give the place?
context: Genesis 28:19 KJV: 'And he called the name of that place Bethel: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.' Beth-el in Hebrew means 'house of God'. Mizpah, Peniel, and Gilgal are all real named stones and shrines from later scenes; Bethel is the ladder's stone.

question: Twenty years later Jacob was coming home to face Esau. On the last night he sent his wives, his handmaids, and his eleven sons ahead across a certain ford and was left alone on the far bank. What brook did they cross?
context: Genesis 32:22 KJV: 'he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok.' The Jabbok is an east-Jordan tributary; its name puns on the Hebrew for 'wrestle' (avaq), setting up what happens next.

question: Alone on the bank of the Jabbok in the dark, Jacob was attacked. A stranger wrestled him until the sky began to lighten. When he could not throw Jacob, what did the stranger do to end the match?
answer: touched Jacob's hip and put it out of joint
choices: touched Jacob's hip and put it out of joint
breathed on Jacob's eyes and darkened them
seized Jacob's tongue so he could not cry
cut a lock of Jacob's hair with a fingernail
context: Genesis 32:25 KJV: 'when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.' Jacob walked with a limp the rest of his life; to this day, the text says, the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh (Genesis 32:32).

question: As dawn broke Jacob still had hold of the stranger and would not let him go without a blessing. The stranger blessed him by taking his name away and giving him a new one, saying he had prevailed with God and with men. What was the new name?
context: Genesis 32:28 KJV: 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.' Jacob then named the place Peniel, 'for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved' (32:30). Ishmael is Abraham's other son; Immanuel is 'God with us' from Isaiah; Isaac is Jacob's father.

question: The apostle James, son of Zebedee, worked with his father and his brother John in a fishing boat before Jesus called them. On what body of water did the two brothers cast their nets?
context: James and John were sons of Zebedee, a Galilean fisherman; Jesus called them from their boat as they mended nets (Mark 1:19-20). Source: Mark 1:19-20; Wikipedia: James, son of Zebedee.

question: Jesus gave James and his brother John a matching Aramaic nickname -- 'Boanerges' -- for their fiery tempers. What did the nickname mean in plain speech?
context: 'And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder' (Mark 3:17 KJV).

question: Jesus took only Peter, James, and John up a high mountain apart; there his face and clothes changed, and two long-dead figures from the Hebrew scriptures appeared beside him. Which two men stood there with him?
context: Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8, Luke 9:28-36. The scene is called the Transfiguration; the same inner three -- Peter, James, John -- also alone accompanied Jesus into the inner garden at Gethsemane.

question: James and his brother John came to Jesus asking to sit at his right hand and his left hand in his kingdom. Jesus answered them with a question. What did he ask?
answer: 'Can ye drink of the cup that I shall drink of?'
choices: 'Can ye drink of the cup that I shall drink of?'
'Have ye left all to follow me?'
'Will ye watch with me one hour?'
context: Matthew 20:20-23 KJV: 'Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of...? They say unto him, We are able.' The 'cup' is the cup of suffering -- and James would be first to drink it.

question: About the year 44, when a king began to persecute the Jerusalem church, James son of Zebedee became the first of the Twelve to be put to death. What did the king have him killed with?
context: 'Now about that time Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword' (Acts 12:1-2 KJV). This one line is the only martyrdom of the Twelve actually narrated inside the New Testament.

question: After King Herod Agrippa had James killed with the sword, he saw the crowd approved -- and reached for another apostle next. Whom did he arrest, setting up the famous Acts 12 jailbreak by an angel?
context: 'And because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also' (Acts 12:3 KJV). That night an angel struck Peter's chains off and led him out of the prison past the sentries (Acts 12:6-11).

question: One line in the New Testament says Herod 'killed James the brother of John with the sword' -- and out of that one line grew one of the three great pilgrimage roads of medieval Europe, alongside Rome and Jerusalem. Where does that road end?
context: Medieval Spanish tradition holds that James's body was brought by boat to Galicia. 'Santiago' is a contraction of 'Sant Iago' -- Saint James in Spanish. Pilgrims on the Camino carry a scallop shell, his emblem, home from Galicia as proof of the walk. The relic-transfer story is legendary; the pilgrimage road is entirely real.

question: A man named James, called 'the Just' or 'the Righteous', is identified in Mark 6:3 as a brother of which figure in the Gospels?
context: 'Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon?' (Mark 6:3 KJV). Paul also identifies him in Galatians 1:19 as 'James the Lord's brother'. This James is distinct from the two apostles named James (son of Zebedee and son of Alphaeus).

question: After the Resurrection, James the Just stayed in one city and became the head of its church, later presiding over a decisive council on Gentile converts. What city?
context: James delivered the decisive ruling recorded in Acts 15 that Gentile converts need not be circumcised. Peter, Paul, and Barnabas all deferred to his judgment in that room.

question: The second-century historian Hegesippus wrote that James the Just was so often on his knees in the Temple praying for the people that the skin of his knees grew hard and callused. To what animal's knees did Hegesippus compare them?
context: 'The skin of his knees became horny like that of a camel's, by reason of his constantly bending the knee in adoration to God' (Hegesippus, quoted in Eusebius, Church History 2.23).  (Legend.)

question: According to Hegesippus, James the Just kept a strict lifelong discipline about what he would put into his body. Which two ordinary things did he refuse for life?
context: 'He drank no wine or other intoxicating liquor, nor did he eat flesh' (Hegesippus in Eusebius, Church History 2.23). Ascetic disciplines like these were common among Jewish holy men of his generation.  (Legend.)

question: About the year 62, during Passover in Jerusalem, scribes and Pharisees stood James the Just up on a high place and demanded he denounce Jesus to the crowd below. Where exactly did they stand him?
answer: On the pinnacle of the Temple
choices: On the pinnacle of the Temple
On the wall of the Antonia fortress
On the stairs of Pilate's palace
On the roof of the Sanhedrin
context: Hegesippus in Eusebius, Church History 2.23. The same 'pinnacle of the Temple' is the setting of Jesus's second temptation in Matthew 4:5.  (Legend.)

question: The crowd threw James from the pinnacle of the Temple, but the fall did not kill him. Broken on the ground below, he did one thing that turned the crowd from throwers into stoners. What did he do on the ground?
answer: He knelt and prayed for them
choices: He knelt and prayed for them
He cursed his attackers by name
He tore the veil of the Temple
He called down fire from heaven
context: Hegesippus (in Eusebius 2.23) says James rose to his knees and prayed for the crowd -- and the crowd began to stone him for it.  (Legend.)

question: As the crowd stoned James the Just on the ground below the Temple pinnacle, one man ran in with the tool of his own daily working trade and struck James on the head, killing him. What was that man's trade?
context: 'One of them, who was a fuller, took the club with which he beat out clothes and struck the just man on the head' (Hegesippus in Eusebius, Church History 2.23). A fuller was a laundry-worker; his club was the wooden mallet used to beat dirt and oil out of wet cloth.  (Legend.)

question: King Pelias of Iolcus had received a chilling oracle: he was to beware a certain kind of stranger who would one day arrive at his court. What was the warning sign the oracle told him to watch for?
answer: A man wearing only one sandal
choices: A man wearing only one sandal
A boy carrying a golden bough
A rider on a white bull
context: The one-sandal oracle is Pelias's undoing -- it turns him into a man who cannot sit at his own table without watching feet. (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.9.16.)  (Legend.)

question: On his way home to claim his throne, Jason met an old woman at a swollen river and carried her across on his back. She was not old at all -- she was a goddess in disguise, one who nursed a private grudge against King Pelias, and she remembered Jason's kindness for the rest of his life. Which goddess had he carried across the river?
context: Hera hated Pelias for slighting her rites, and the river-crossing bought Jason her lifelong help. In the current Jason lost one of his sandals, which fulfilled the oracle Pelias had been warned about. Athena will help build the Argo, but the river-crossing kindness is Hera's. (Apollodorus 1.9.16.)  (Legend.)

question: Jason returned as a grown man to his uncle Pelias's court to claim the throne. Pelias did not dare kill his nephew openly, so instead he set him what was meant to be an impossible errand at the far eastern end of the Black Sea -- a treasure guarded by a sleepless dragon in the grove of Ares. What did Pelias order Jason to fetch?
choices: The girdle of Hippolyta the Amazon
The head of the Gorgon Medusa
context: The Golden Fleece hung in a grove of Ares in Colchis, guarded by a sleepless dragon and King Aeetes -- an errand Pelias fully expected Jason to die on. (Apollodorus 1.9.16.)  (Legend.)

question: For his voyage Jason needed a ship greater than any yet built. On the beach at Pagasae in Thessaly, Athena herself stood over a master shipwright, guiding his hands as he laid the planks and fitted the timbers for the vessel that would carry the heroes to Colchis. Who was the shipwright who built her?
context: Argus son of Arestor is the builder; the ship was named the Argo after him, and her crew were called the Argonauts. Tiphys was the Argo's helmsman, not her carpenter, and Daedalus is Cretan (the Labyrinth, the wings), not Argonaut. (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1; Apollodorus 1.9.16.)  (Legend.)

question: Athena fitted the Argo with something no other ship ever carried: a piece of a certain sacred tree, set into the prow. Because of that timber the ship herself could speak aloud and warn her crew of what was coming. From what oracle-grove did Athena take the wood?
answer: The oak of Zeus at Dodona
choices: The oak of Zeus at Dodona
The laurel of Apollo at Delphi
The olive of Athena on the Acropolis
The cypress of Hades at Cumae
context: Dodona was the oldest Greek oracle -- Zeus spoke through the rustling of the sacred oak-leaves. A plank of that tree in the prow gave the Argo her voice. (Apollodorus 1.9.16.)  (Legend.)

question: The crew Jason gathered was the greatest muster of heroes ever seen in one place before the Trojan War, and every one had his specialty. One rowed on the benches with a lyre across his knees; when the Sirens later tried to sing the ship onto the rocks, he outsang them and saved the Argo. Which Argonaut was this musician?
context: Orpheus of Thrace, whose music moved trees and stones. Amphion built the walls of Thebes with music, but he was never an Argonaut. (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.23-34; 4.891-919.)  (Legend.)

question: On the coast of Thrace the Argonauts came upon a blind old prophet who was starving because every time he sat down to eat, filthy winged monsters swooped in and snatched or fouled his food. The Argonauts drove the monsters off, and the grateful seer told them how to survive what lay ahead. What was the name of this blind prophet?
context: Phineus of Thrace was tormented by the Harpies until two of the Argonauts drove them off, and in gratitude Phineus told the crew the trick for the Clashing Rocks. (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.178-499.)  (Legend.)
