question: At the mouth of the Black Sea stood two mountainous cliffs called the Symplegades that would slam together every few seconds and crush any ship between them, then reopen. Following the blind seer's advice, the Argonauts sent a small living thing through first as a test; the rocks crashed on it, missed all but its tail, and in the moment the cliffs sprang open again the crew rowed for their lives. What did they send through ahead of the Argo?
context: The dove lost only her tail-feathers; the Argo lost only the tip of her stern-post. And after that day the Clashing Rocks were fixed in place forever, never to move again. (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.549-609.)  (Legend.)

question: In Colchis King Aeetes agreed to give up the Golden Fleece only if Jason first performed a task designed to kill him: yoke two bronze-hoofed, fire-breathing bulls forged by Hephaestus to a plow, drive them across a wide field, and then sow the fresh-turned furrows with a handful of strange seed the king would put into his hand. What did Aeetes make Jason sow into the plowed field?
context: Each tooth sprang up as a full-grown armed warrior -- the Spartoi, 'sown men.' The teeth were left over from the dragon Cadmus killed at Thebes, given to Aeetes by Athena. Jason survived only because Medea's potion made him proof against fire and steel. (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 3; Apollodorus 1.9.23.)  (Legend.)

question: In the days of King Josiah of Judah, the LORD's word came to a young Jerusalem priest's son, who objected: 'Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.' The LORD reached out, touched his mouth, and told him he would carry His words to the nations. Who was this young prophet?
context: Jeremiah 1:6-9 KJV. Jeremiah is called the 'weeping prophet' because he lived to see Jerusalem burn in 586 BC. Isaiah was called a century earlier; Ezekiel and Daniel prophesied after Jerusalem fell, in Babylonia.

question: To teach Jeremiah a lesson about the LORD and Israel, God told him to go DOWN to one specific working craftsman's house and watch him at his craft. To whose house did God send him?
context: Jeremiah 18:1-2 KJV: 'Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words.' All four craftsmen appear in the Old Testament -- Isaiah 7 has the fuller's field, Nahum 3 the smiths, Isaiah 38 the weaver -- but only the potter carried this lesson.

question: Watching the potter at his craft, Jeremiah saw the vessel of clay come out marred in the man's hand. The potter did one specific thing that became the LORD's whole lesson to the house of Israel. What did the potter do with the marred vessel?
answer: he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to him
choices: he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to him
he burnt it in the furnace as a warning to his apprentices
he set it high on the shelf as an example of failed work
he cast it into the street to be trodden of the men of Judah
context: Jeremiah 18:4 KJV: 'the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.' The point of the sign is REMAKING, not discarding -- the LORD can reshape a marred people. Verse 6: 'as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.'

question: Jeremiah gave Judah a bitter proverb about people so used to evil that they can no more choose to do good than an Ethiopian can change his skin. Which beast did Jeremiah pair with the Ethiopian in the same KJV verse?
context: Jeremiah 13:23 KJV: 'Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.' Wolves, serpents, and lions are all real biblical predators; only the leopard has the spots that carry the proverb.

question: The LORD told Jeremiah to buy a certain garment, put it on without ever washing it, then carry it far east to the great river Euphrates and hide it in the cleft of a rock. When he dug it up many days later it was marred, good for nothing -- a sign against the pride of Judah. Which garment was it?
context: Jeremiah 13:1-11 KJV. The 'linen girdle' is a loincloth worn next to the skin, meant to cleave closely to a man -- that is the whole point of the sign, cleaving. He hides it in a hole in a rock by the Euphrates. The distractors are all real biblical garments -- Jesus's robe, Elijah's mantle, the priestly ephod.

question: As the Babylonians closed in on Jerusalem, Jeremiah's enemies threw him into the empty cistern of Malchiah -- no water, only deep mire; he sank in it up to his armpits and was left there to die. One court official went to the king, got permission, and pulled him out. What was the rescuer's name?
context: Jeremiah 38:6-13 KJV. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian eunuch of the king's house, is one of the small heroes of the book; his name means 'servant of the king.' Baruch is Jeremiah's own scribe; Nebuzaradan is the Babylonian captain who burns the Temple; Gedaliah is the governor Nebuchadnezzar appoints after the fall.

question: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian took thirty men, went to Jeremiah in the miry pit, and lowered a very odd assortment of things by cords into the pit -- then called down and told Jeremiah exactly what to do with them. What did he lower down?
answer: old cast clouts and rotten rags
choices: old cast clouts and rotten rags
a wooden ladder tied together with strips of goat's hide
a hollow reed lowered for the prophet to breathe through
a broad leather bucket to lift him bodily out of the mire
context: Jeremiah 38:11-13 KJV: 'Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords.' 'Armhole' is KJV for armpit -- the padding kept the ropes from cutting Jeremiah as they hauled him up. The other three are plausible rescue tools but not the biblical ones.

question: Even with Babylonian siegeworks around Jerusalem, Jeremiah bought a family field at Anathoth from his cousin Hanameel as a public sign that houses and fields would one day be bought here again. Witnesses signed, the deed was sealed, and Baruch stored it away for the future. What price did Jeremiah weigh out for the field?
context: Jeremiah 32:6-15 KJV. Seventeen is an oddly specific number -- exactly the point, the transaction is a legal deed with a receipt. The distractors are all real biblical prices -- Judas at Matthew 26:15, Abraham's cave at Genesis 23:16, David's threshingfloor at 1 Chronicles 21:25.

question: Jeremiah's scroll of judgments was read aloud in the winter house of King Jehoiakim, who sat before a hearth fire in the ninth month. As Jehudi the reader finished three or four leaves at a time, the king took a small blade, cut those leaves off, and dropped them in the fire, until the whole scroll was consumed. What blade did the king use?
context: Jeremiah 36:23 KJV: 'when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the PENKNIFE, and cast it into the fire.' The penknife was a scribe's small tool for trimming reed pens -- the king used a scribe's own instrument to destroy the scribe's work. Jeremiah then dictated the scroll again, with more added.

question: When Jeremiah sealed the deed to Hanameel's field at Anathoth, he told his scribe Baruch to preserve both the sealed copy and the open copy for a long time -- because someday houses and fields would be bought and sold in Judah again. In what kind of container did Baruch store the deeds?
context: Jeremiah 32:14 KJV: 'put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.' A baked clay jar was cheap, common, and outlasted armies -- the Dead Sea Scrolls survived two thousand years by the same trick. The distractors are all real biblical containers for treasures or letters.

question: In a cave-cell in Bethlehem, an old scholar named Jerome bent over his lamp-lit desk for the last thirty-four years of his life, working on ONE enormous project. What was he making?
answer: A single Latin Bible for all of Western Europe
choices: A single Latin Bible for all of Western Europe
A commentary on the sayings of the Egyptian desert monks
A history of the persecutions under the Roman emperors
A rule of life for hermits in the eastern deserts
context: Pope Damasus in Rome had commissioned Jerome to fix the mess of divergent Latin Bibles then in circulation. Jerome went to Bethlehem in 386 and worked on the project until his death on 30 September 420. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate.

question: One evening in Jerome's Bethlehem monastery, while the monks were reading with him, a great animal limped in from the dusk with a bleeding paw. The monks fled; Jerome quietly took the paw in his hands and pulled out a thorn. According to the legend told in the Golden Legend, what kind of animal was it?
context: The story is told in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend (compiled c. 1259-1266). It is why Renaissance painters (Antonello da Messina, Ghirlandaio, Durer) show Jerome as an old scholar with the beast curled at his feet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Legend; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome.

question: Before Bethlehem, Jerome spent about three years (c. 382-385) in Rome as personal secretary to a specific pope, until scandal over his close friendships with wealthy Roman women drove him out of the city. Which pope was his patron?
context: It was Damasus who first put the idea of a single reliable Latin Bible into Jerome's head and formally commissioned the work. Siricius was his successor, Liberius his predecessor, Innocent I later served in the early 400s. When Damasus died in 384, Jerome lost his protector and soon left Rome for good. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome.

question: Jerome made a choice for his Old Testament that shocked many other Christians of his day. Instead of translating from a Greek version that most churches had used for three hundred years, he insisted on going back to the older Hebrew text -- what he called Hebraica veritas, 'the Hebrew truth.' Which Greek Old Testament was he refusing to rely on?
context: The Septuagint was the standard Greek Old Testament used by most Christian communities for three centuries. Origen's Hexapla arranged six versions in parallel columns; Aquila and Symmachus produced later Jewish Greek revisions. Jerome believed the Hebrew was closer to the source; his opponents feared it broke unity with the eastern churches. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate.

question: In the medieval version of the lion story, Jerome's grateful lion did not just curl at his feet -- he was given a JOB in the monastery. He had to walk beside a specific working animal to guard it on its trips for firewood. When some passing merchants stole that animal, the disgraced lion had to do its work himself, hauling loads on his own back, until the thieves were caught. What working animal was the lion supposed to be guarding?
context: The story is a favorite of Renaissance painters. It comes from Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, chapter 146 (compiled c. 1259-1266). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Legend.

question: At about thirteen, a farmer's daughter in the village of Domremy began hearing voices in her father's garden. One voice named itself the Archangel Michael. The other two said they were early-church women martyrs. Which two saints did the voices claim to be?
answer: Catherine of Alexandria and Margaret of Antioch
choices: Catherine of Alexandria and Margaret of Antioch
Ursula of Cologne and Barbara of Nicomedia
context: The girl was Jeanne d'Arc. Over four years the voices grew insistent that she must go to the Dauphin Charles, drive the English out of France, and see him crowned at Reims. All four choices name real early-church women martyrs whose cults were strong in medieval France. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.  (Legend.)

question: At sixteen, Joan of Arc rode to the nearest French garrison at the town of Vaucouleurs to ask for an escort to the Dauphin's court. The commander there twice refused her before finally agreeing. Who was the commander of the garrison at Vaucouleurs who eventually gave her the escort?
context: Robert de Baudricourt was the French captain who commanded Vaucouleurs on the eastern frontier. Jean de Metz was one of the men-at-arms who did escort her; La Hire was a famous French captain who fought beside her later at Orleans; Jean d'Aulon became her squire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.

question: Joan's escort to the Dauphin was an eleven-day cross-country ride from Vaucouleurs to Chinon, straight through country held by English and Burgundian troops. Before setting out, she made two changes to her appearance meant to help her survive the ride. What did she do to her hair and her clothing?
answer: Cut her hair short and dressed in men's clothing
choices: Cut her hair short and dressed in men's clothing
Braided her hair with iron beads and dressed in a nun's habit
Covered her head with a widow's veil and wore black mourning
Bound her hair in a snood and put on a farmer's smock
context: The short hair and man's dress were practical for a long armed ride, but at her trial fifteen years later the men's clothing became one of the central charges against her. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.

question: In late February 1429, Joan arrived at the Dauphin's court at Chinon castle after an eleven-day ride through enemy country. Charles decided to test her: he dressed as an ordinary courtier and had another man dress in royal robes on the throne. According to the traditional account of the meeting, what did Joan do when she entered the great hall?
answer: Walked straight past the impostor and knelt to the true Dauphin
choices: Walked straight past the impostor and knelt to the true Dauphin
Refused to speak until every man present removed his hat
Asked for a mirror and named the true Dauphin from his reflection
Called out the Dauphin's baptismal name from the doorway
context: The story is preserved in early accounts of the Chinon meeting on 25 February 1429; she then told Charles she wanted to make war against the English to open his way to Reims for coronation. Source: www.tourainevaldeloire.com/en/discover/the-loire-valley-chateaux/historical-figures-of-touraine/joan-of-arc/.  (Legend.)

question: For her ride to besieged Orleans in April 1429, Joan was given white armor and carried a large white banner made of boccassin cloth. The field was sprinkled with lilies; two angels flanked a painted world in the center; and above them she had two names stitched in bold letters. Which pair of names did Joan have stitched at the top of the banner?
context: Joan later told her judges she loved this banner forty times more than her sword. She carried it into every assault, even when wounded. Alpha and Omega is a Greek Christian symbol; Louis and Denis are the two patron saints of the French crown. Source: thehistorianshut.com/2021/02/04/joan-of-arcs-holy-banner/.

question: The English fort called Les Tourelles guarded the southern end of the great bridge across the Loire at Orleans; while it held, the city was cut off. On 7 May 1429 Joan led the French assault on Les Tourelles in person. During the attack she was struck and driven back, then returned to the fight by evening and the fort fell. Where on her body did the crossbow bolt strike her?
answer: Between the neck and the shoulder, above her breastplate
choices: Between the neck and the shoulder, above her breastplate
Through the thigh, below the tasset plates
Through the left palm as she gripped her banner
Across the eye through her raised visor
context: Joan reportedly pulled the bolt from the wound herself, wept briefly, then returned to the attack. The English abandoned Les Tourelles and the whole siege the next day - the first major French victory of the war in living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.

question: Twenty-five years after Joan's death, a new tribunal took testimony from surviving villagers of Domremy about her childhood. Several of them - and the trial prosecutors before them - kept coming back to one detail: a huge old beech at the edge of the village where the village children, Joan among them, would dance and hang garlands on feast days. What did the villagers call that tree?
choices: L'Arbre du Pendu (the Hanged Man's Tree)
L'Arbre de la Vierge (the Virgin's Tree)
context: At the 1431 trial the prosecution tried to use the tree to suggest Joan had dabbled in pagan or fairy customs; she said she had only danced there as a child with the others. The nullification witnesses from Domremy confirmed the tree and the dances as harmless village custom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.  (Legend.)

question: In May 1430, Joan of Arc rode out of the besieged town of Compiegne to attack an enemy camp. As her rearguard covered the retreat, the town's captains closed the drawbridge behind her too early, and she was pulled from her horse into enemy hands. Which force captured her at Compiegne?
choices: French royal troops sent to relieve the town
context: The Burgundians were French but allied with the English through most of the Hundred Years' War. They sold Joan to the English six months later for 10,000 livres tournois. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.

question: For months after her capture Joan was moved between castles. At one of them, Beaurevoir, held by a Burgundian noble, she made a desperate escape attempt: from the top of a tower she leaped from a high window, hoping either to break out or to warn Compiegne, which was still besieged. Roughly how high was the tower window she jumped from?
choices: About one hundred and twenty feet
context: Joan survived the fall without permanent injury. She later told her judges her voices had scolded her for the jump; she said she had asked forgiveness for it and been granted it. Sixty feet is roughly a six-story fall - astonishing to survive, but recorded by multiple witnesses at the nullification. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc.

question: In November 1430 the Burgundians sold Joan to their English allies for 10,000 livres tournois. The English handed her over to a French bishop for trial - a man loyal to the English regency and openly hoping to be promoted to the archbishopric of Rouen in return for his work on the case. Which bishop presided over Joan's trial?
context: Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, would spend the rest of his life defending the trial he had run; the nullification of 1456 tore his verdict apart. Jean Gerson was chancellor of the University of Paris and had actually written cautiously in Joan's favor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: The court tried to catch Joan on the question of whether she knew that she was in a state of grace - either 'yes' would be prideful heresy, and 'no' would be a confession of sin invalidating her voices. Joan, unlettered and nineteen, gave an answer the theologians in the room recognized at once as clever enough to walk between the two traps. What did she reply?
answer: If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God so keep me
choices: If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God so keep me
Only my confessor may know that, not the court
The voices tell me nothing on that point, so I will not say
Grace is a gift; a gift cannot be measured, only received
context: The exchange is preserved in the trial minutes; several assessors reportedly went quiet after her reply. It was cited at the nullification as evidence of her sincerity and native theological instinct. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: On 24 May 1431, taken to the cemetery of Saint-Ouen and shown the stake built for her, Joan collapsed and signed a document giving up men's clothing and submitting to the church, in exchange for her life. What did she use in place of a signature on the abjuration?
choices: Her banner's motto, drawn by another and touched by her thumb
A drop of her own blood
A ring pressed into hot wax
context: Joan was unlettered and could not write her name; contemporary accounts differ on whether the mark was a cross or a circle. Within a few days she was back in men's clothes in her cell, and Pierre Cauchon declared her a relapsed heretic on 28 May 1431. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: On Wednesday morning, 30 May 1431, Joan was taken in a cart to a public square in Rouen, where a tall plaster stake had been built high enough that the crowd could watch her burn. Above the stake a wooden placard listed the four crimes for which she was being executed. Which four words were written on the placard?
context: The placard's four charges were formal church-court categories; 'relapsed' meant she had returned to a condemned position after abjuring it - the trigger for the death sentence. The square was the Place du Vieux-Marche, the Old Market. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: Tied to the stake and weeping, Joan asked for a cross to hold as the fire was lit. An English soldier in the crowd tied two small sticks together and passed her the improvised cross; then a Dominican friar ran to the nearby church of Saint-Sauveur and brought back the great processional crucifix, holding it up close enough for her to see through the flames. Which Dominican friar was the one who brought the church crucifix and held it up?
context: Isambard de la Pierre and Martin Ladvenu were both Dominicans with Joan at the end - Isambard is the one the 1456 witnesses named as running for the church cross. Jean Massieu was the trial usher; Jean Beaupere was one of the interrogators. Source: maidofheaven.com/joanofarc_nullification_rouen_testimony2.asp.

question: After the flames died, Joan's executioner - a man named Geoffroy Therage - was ordered to gather what was left of her body and get rid of it. Where did he put her ashes?
choices: Into a common lime-pit outside the walls
Into an unmarked grave at the cathedral
Into an iron chest stored at the Tower of London
context: The point of scattering the ashes in the river was to prevent a cult of relics; Therage is later reported to have said he feared he was damned for burning a saint. Twenty-five years later Charles VII ordered a retrial - the Nullification of 1455-1456 - and 115 witnesses testified; the 1431 sentence was overturned. Joan was canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joan_of_Arc.

question: Around 1400 a priest in Prague filled a chapel of about 3,000 townspeople week after week by preaching in the everyday speech of the streets, when almost every other pulpit in Europe used one fixed church language for sermons. Which language did almost every other pulpit in Europe use for its sermons at that time?
context: The priest was Jan Hus, and the chapel was the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, founded in 1391 with the explicit rule that all preaching there be done in Czech. Latin was the ordinary church language of the medieval West; German was a spoken vernacular but not the pulpit standard; Church Slavonic was the liturgical language of Orthodox Slavs, not the Bohemian Latin-rite; Greek belonged to the Eastern church. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Chapel, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hus.

question: At his degradation from the priesthood in July 1415 the churchmen cut Hus's tonsure with scissors, stripped him of his liturgical robes, and set on his head a tall paper cap painted with three demons - the sign of a condemned heretic. Looking at it, Hus made a comparison. Whose crown did he say had been much heavier and more painful than his?
context: His full recorded words: 'My Lord Jesus Christ for my sake wore a much heavier and more painful crown of thorns.' The three other choices are all real famous crowns in Christian tradition, so the parallel is genuine, but only the crown of thorns is the one Hus named. Source: christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/hus-reformation-connection.

question: In the Castilian town of Medina del Campo a small brilliant friar, barely five feet tall, is preparing in 1567 to leave the Carmelites for the stricter Carthusians when a determined fifty-two-year-old nun buttonholes him and talks him into launching her reform among the men instead. Which nun changed his mind?
context: Teresa had begun her Carmelite reform among women and wanted parallel houses for the friars. Ana de San Bartolome was Teresa's own nurse and secretary; Maria de San Jose Salazar was a leading discalced prioress at Seville; Anne of Jesus led the reform into France -- all sixteenth-century Discalced Carmelite nuns, but Teresa was the founder who recruited John at Medina del Campo.

question: The little friar the nun recruited took a new name -- John of the Cross -- and on November 28, 1568, opened the first reformed men's Carmelite house in a broken-down farmhouse. In what Castilian village did he set it up?
context: The Duruelo foundation, with Antonio de Jesus de Heredia, launched the male Discalced Carmelites. Mancera and Pastrana were later small Discalced houses of that first generation; Fontiveros was John's own birthplace in Old Castile, not a foundation site.

question: Bitter fighting between reformed and unreformed Carmelite friars came to a head on the night of December 2-3, 1577. Unreformed friars raided the house of John of the Cross in Avila, seized him, and took him under guard to their monastery -- where they locked him in a windowless disused room barely six feet wide and ten feet long. In which Castilian city did they imprison him?
context: The Toledo Carmelite monastery held him from December 1577 to August 1578 in a room described as a converted latrine off a friar's cell. Salamanca, Segovia, and Granada were all real Discalced houses John later worked in, but the imprisonment was Toledo.

question: In the Toledo cell John was fed only bread, water, and scraps of salt fish on the floor, and three times a week was brought to the friars' refectory and publicly whipped across the shoulders before the community -- leaving scars visible until his death. For how many months did the unreformed friars keep him there?
context: From December 3, 1577, to the night of his escape in August 1578 -- nine months of the tiny cell, the vermin in his clothing, the summer bake and winter cold of Toledo, and the beatings.

question: On a night in August 1578 John broke out of the Toledo cell. He had spent weeks loosening the door hinges; when he was ready he lowered himself from a high window on a rope made by tearing up and knotting together strips of an ordinary object in the cell. What did he tear up to make the rope?
context: Testimony from the jailer Fray Juan de Santa Maria describes John tying blanket strips together and fastening an old tunic at the bottom; even so the rope ran short and he had to drop the last ten feet or so onto a wall.

question: The rocky island where John was exiled and where he wrote down his visions is named in the opening of the last book of the Bible. What is the island called?
context: 'I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation... was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:9 KJV). Patmos is a small volcanic island in the Dodecanese, off the coast of Asia Minor.

question: On Patmos, John hears a voice like a trumpet behind him and is told to write letters to churches in the province of Asia. How many churches receive letters?
context: The seven are Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea (Revelation 1:11). Smyrna's letter is where 'be thou faithful unto death' is spoken; Laodicea's is the 'neither cold nor hot' rebuke.

question: When John turned to see who was speaking to him on Patmos, he saw a figure whose eyes were like a flame of fire -- and out of whose mouth came a strange weapon. What came from the mouth?
context: 'And out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength' (Revelation 1:16 KJV).

question: In heaven John sees a great scroll sealed shut, and as each seal breaks a rider comes out. As the first seal breaks, a rider comes out on a WHITE horse. What weapon does the rider on the white horse carry?
context: 'And I saw, and behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer' (Revelation 6:2 KJV).

question: The rider of the pale horse is the only one of the four horsemen given his own name in the text of Revelation -- a single terrible word. What is his name?
context: 'His name that sat on him was Death' (Revelation 6:8 KJV). The names War, Famine, and Plague are popular labels invented later for the first three riders; the text names only the fourth.

question: In chapter 12 John sees a woman appear in heaven, clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, pregnant and crying out in labor. Around her head is a crown -- of how many stars?
context: 'And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars' (Revelation 12:1 KJV).

question: As the woman clothed with the sun cries out in labor, a great dragon appears in the sky, seven-headed and ten-horned, waiting to devour her child the moment it is born. What COLOR is the dragon?
context: 'And there appeared another wonder in heaven; and behold a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and seven crowns upon his heads' (Revelation 12:3 KJV). The child is caught up to God, and the woman flees into the wilderness.

question: In Revelation 12, war breaks out in heaven when a single named archangel and his angels fight the seven-headed dragon and cast him down to the earth. Name the archangel.
context: 'And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels' (Revelation 12:7 KJV). Michael is the warrior-archangel; Gabriel is the announcer; Raphael and Uriel appear in earlier Jewish tradition and in the deuterocanonical books.

question: At the end of John's vision a New Jerusalem comes down from heaven, dressed like a bride. The city has twelve gates -- and each single gate is made out of one enormous piece of one precious thing. What is each gate made of?
context: 'And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass' (Revelation 21:21 KJV). The wall itself is jasper, and 'there shall be no night there' (Revelation 22:5).

question: Out in the desert country east of Jerusalem, a wild preacher stood by the river and called the crowds to turn their lives around. He dressed like the old prophets -- a rough coat woven from the hair of one particular animal, cinched with a leather belt. What animal's hair was his coat made of?
context: Matthew 3:4 KJV: 'And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins.' The outfit was a deliberate echo of the prophet Elijah, who wore 'a garment of hair' and a leather girdle (2 Kings 1:8). Camel-hair cloth was coarse and cheap -- the opposite of the fine wool a rich man would wear.

question: The wild preacher John lived off whatever the wilderness gave him. The gospel names two foods -- wild honey scraped from rocks, and one other, listed in Matthew 3:4. What did he eat with the honey?
context: Matthew 3:4 KJV: 'his meat was locusts and wild honey.' The Greek word akrides means the insect, not carob pods -- a later medieval reading tried to soften it. Leviticus 11:22 lists locusts as clean food. Locusts are still eaten today across the Arabian peninsula. So: real insects, roasted or dried, chased by honey scraped out of rocks. That was dinner.

question: John did his preaching in the wilderness, but people walked out from Jerusalem to hear him. When they wanted to show they were washing away their old lives, John dunked them in a particular river -- the river that gave him the title 'the Baptist' (Greek for 'the dipper'). Which river?
context: Matthew 3:5-6 KJV: 'Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, And were baptized of him in Jordan.' The Greek word baptizein means to dip or immerse -- so 'the Baptist' is literally 'the Dipper.' The Jordan is the river Joshua crossed to enter the promised land, so John dunking penitents in it carried a strong echo of a fresh start.

question: Luke opens his gospel with the parents of John. His father was a priest named Zacharias, on duty in the temple when an angel told him his elderly wife would bear a son. His mother was a kinswoman of Mary, and it is her house Mary visits during the Visitation. What was the mother's name?
context: Luke 1:5, 1:36, 1:39-45 KJV. Zacharias served in the priestly course of Abijah. Elizabeth was 'of the daughters of Aaron' and, Luke says, a cousin of Mary; she felt her own child leap in her womb when Mary walked in the door -- the Visitation scene. Both parents were said to be old and long past hope of a child.

question: When a delegation of Pharisees and Sadducees walked down to the river to be baptized, John greeted them with a stinging insult that Jesus himself would later reuse on the same crowd (Matthew 23:33). Matthew 3:7: 'O ______, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?' Fill in the blank.
context: Matthew 3:7 KJV. 'Generation of vipers' -- a brood of snakes. Jesus would later use the same insult on the same crowd (Matthew 23:33). 'Whitewashed tombs' and 'blind guides' are also real -- but both are Jesus's lines from Matthew 23, not John's. 'Sons of Belial' is Old Testament language for lawless men.

question: John kept telling the crowds that someone far greater was coming after him -- someone whose humblest servant John was not fit to be. Mark 1:7: 'I am not worthy to stoop down and ___ his sandals.' Fill in the blank.
context: Mark 1:7 KJV: 'the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.' The 'latchet' is the leather thong that tied the sandal on -- untying it was the household slave's job. Washing feet (John 13) comes later, when Jesus does it for his disciples -- a different scene entirely.

question: Jesus walked down from Galilee to the river and stepped into the water in front of John. John was appalled and tried to stop him -- Matthew 3:14 gives his exact protest. What does he say?
answer: I have need to be baptized of thee
choices: I have need to be baptized of thee
Depart from me, for I am a sinful man
Who am I, that I should come?
Let this cup pass from me
context: Matthew 3:14 KJV in full: 'I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?' Jesus insists -- 'Suffer it to be so now' -- and John gives in. The other lines are also real but come from very different scenes: 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man' is Peter after the great catch of fish (Luke 5:8); 'Who am I, that I should come?' is David (2 Samuel 7:18); 'Let this cup pass' is Jesus in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39).

question: The moment Jesus came up out of the water at his baptism, Matthew says the sky opened and something living came down and settled on him. All four gospels agree on the exact bird. Matthew 3:16: he saw the Spirit of God descending like WHAT, and lighting upon him?
context: Matthew 3:16 KJV: 'the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him.' All four gospels use the dove image -- one of the very few details all four agree on word-for-word. Ravens carry a very different mythology (Elijah in 1 Kings 17, Noah's raven in Genesis 8, Odin's Huginn and Muninn); eagles belong to Roman legionary standards, not this scene.

question: The dove settled on Jesus, and then a voice came out of the open heavens. It was short -- one sentence -- and it named who Jesus was and how the speaker felt about him. Matthew 3:17 gives the exact words. What did the voice say?
answer: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased
choices: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased
Behold my servant, whom I uphold, mine elect in whom my soul delighteth
I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee
context: Matthew 3:17 KJV. The voice returns nearly word for word at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), where it adds 'hear ye him.' The distractors are real prophetic 'voice from God' lines from elsewhere in scripture: Isaiah 42:1 (a servant song sometimes read as messianic), Isaiah 43:1 (to Israel), and Jeremiah 1:5 (to the young prophet Jeremiah).

question: John was later thrown in prison for calling out Herod Antipas over his marriage to his brother's wife Herodias. At Herod's birthday feast Herodias's daughter danced, and Herod swore to give her anything. Prompted by her mother she asked for John's head -- carried in on one specific item, named in Mark 6:25. What was it?
context: Mark 6:25 KJV: 'I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist.' A 'charger' is a large flat serving platter -- the King James word for a big dish. Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2) locates the imprisonment and execution at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Notice the gospels never actually name the dancing daughter -- the name 'Salome' comes only from Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.4).

question: When John's own disciples came to him worried because Jesus was now drawing bigger crowds, John cut them off with one line about his own role. John 3:30 KJV -- the closing line of his last recorded speech in the fourth gospel. What does he say?
answer: He must increase, but I must decrease
choices: He must increase, but I must decrease
The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away
I am not worthy to be called an apostle
Not I, but Christ liveth in me
context: John 3:30 KJV -- the closing line of John's last recorded speech in the fourth gospel. The distractors are Job (Job 1:21), Paul on his unworthiness (1 Corinthians 15:9), and Paul again on the changed self (Galatians 2:20) -- all real, none John's.

question: The LORD told a Hebrew prophet -- son of Amittai -- to go east and cry against the wickedness of a certain great enemy city. Instead he went down to the port of Joppa, paid his fare, and boarded a ship sailing the opposite way, toward far Tarshish. Who was this runaway prophet?
context: Jonah 1:1-3 KJV. Jonah son of Amittai is a real prophet mentioned at 2 Kings 14:25. The other three are also 8th-century northern-kingdom prophets whose books stand next to Jonah in the Bible -- easy to confuse.

question: The LORD sent a mighty tempest after Jonah's ship out of Joppa; the sailors threw the cargo overboard and cried each man to his own god. Meanwhile Jonah himself, the one whose flight had caused it all, was doing what -- and where on the ship?
answer: fast asleep down in the sides of the ship
choices: fast asleep down in the sides of the ship
up on the mast pleading with the LORD to spare the crew
at the helm shouting orders at the terrified sailors
kneeling in the prow tearing his robes in repentance
context: Jonah 1:5 KJV: 'Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.' The KJV 'sides of the ship' means the inner hold. The captain has to wake him and ask him to pray.

question: The terrified sailors on Jonah's storm-tossed ship did one specific thing to find out for whose sake this disaster was hunting them. When the answer pointed at the sleeping stranger down in the hold, they still tried to row to shore before they finally threw him overboard. What did they do to name the guilty man?
choices: they questioned each man under oath
context: Jonah 1:7 KJV: 'Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.' Casting lots was the standard biblical way of asking heaven a yes/no question -- the priests used them, the apostles used them to replace Judas.

question: Once the sailors flung Jonah overboard the sea was calm at once, and the LORD prepared one huge creature to swallow him up alive. He stayed inside it for a very specific stretch of time before it spat him out on dry land. How long was Jonah inside?
choices: one full day from dawn to dawn
context: Jonah 1:17 KJV: 'the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.' Note the KJV says GREAT FISH, not whale -- the whale image is later tradition. The distractors are all real biblical durations -- Noah's rain, Job's mourning silence, a fast.

question: From inside the belly of the great fish Jonah prayed a psalm to the LORD, and at the end of it the LORD spake to the fish and gave it a single order. The fish obeyed. In what unglamorous way, according to Jonah 2:10, did the prophet finally get free?
answer: it vomited him out upon the land
choices: it vomited him out upon the land
it swam onto a beach and died open-mouthed
it split down its own belly to release him
it carried him three days more toward the east
context: Jonah 2:10 KJV: 'And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.' The unglamorous ending is the point -- the prophet is spat out where he should have started. Only after this does he finally go to Nineveh.

question: Jonah finally reached the enormous Assyrian capital -- so vast the text calls it a three-days' journey across -- and walked in one day's journey preaching a single blunt line. That line named an exact number of days until Nineveh's destruction. What was the number?
context: Jonah 3:4 KJV: 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.' Forty is a recurring biblical span -- Noah's rain, Moses on Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Elijah walking to Horeb, Jesus fasting in the wilderness. The distractors are also all real biblical countdowns.

question: One morning after the shade plant God had made grow over Jonah's booth had sprung up, the LORD prepared one small living thing at dawn that killed the whole plant -- and the sun and a hot east wind then beat Jonah's bare head until he fainted and asked to die. God's whole final lesson turns on this tiny creature. What was it?
context: Jonah 4:7 KJV: 'But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered.' The book ends with God's rebuke: Jonah pitied the plant he did not labour for -- should God not pity Nineveh, wherein are 'more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much cattle?'

question: Pharaoh dreams that seven fat, sleek beasts come up out of the river Nile and feed in the meadow. Then seven lean and ill-favoured beasts of the same kind climb out after them and eat the fat ones up, and Pharaoh wakes shaking. What animal is it?
context: Seven fatfleshed kine and seven leanfleshed kine, Genesis 41:1-4 KJV. The Nile setting is exact; cattle grazing in the river-meadows would have been the everyday sight along its banks in Egypt.

question: Pharaoh falls back asleep and dreams a second time. He sees seven ears of grain, full and good, growing on a single stalk. Then seven thin ears sprout after them, blasted with the east wind, and the thin ears swallow the seven full ones. When morning comes, whom does he first send for to read the dreams?
answer: The magicians and wise men of Egypt
choices: The magicians and wise men of Egypt
The high priest at the temple of Ra
The desert oracle at the oasis of Siwa
His own mother the queen dowager
context: Genesis 41:5-8 KJV. Pharaoh calls for all the magicians of Egypt and all the wise men, and none of them can interpret the two dreams. Only then does the chief butler remember the young Hebrew in the prison.

question: The chief butler, still cupbearer to Pharaoh, suddenly remembers a young Hebrew he met in prison who read his own dream true. Pharaoh sends for the man at once, and he is brought hastily out of the dungeon. Before he can stand in front of Pharaoh, what two things does he do first?
answer: He shaves himself and changes his raiment
choices: He shaves himself and changes his raiment
He fasts three days and drinks only water
He bows to the four corners and casts lots
He binds his forehead and washes his feet
context: Genesis 41:14 KJV: 'Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.' Clean-shaven faces were Egyptian court style; a bearded Hebrew prisoner had to be made presentable.

question: Joseph listens to both dreams and tells Pharaoh they are one and the same warning. Seven years of great plenty are coming across all Egypt, he says, and after them seven years of famine so terrible the plenty will be forgotten in the land. What does he advise Pharaoh to do during the plenty?
answer: Appoint a wise man to store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities
choices: Appoint a wise man to store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities
Send the army east to conquer the granaries of Canaan
Build a great temple to the sun to turn the famine aside
Ration the people at once so they learn to live on little
context: Genesis 41:33-36 KJV. Joseph advises setting officers over the land and taking up the fifth part of the harvest during the seven plentiful years to lay up food against the seven years of famine.

question: To finish making Joseph an Egyptian, Pharaoh gives him a new Egyptian name and marries him to Asenath, the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of the sun-city of On. Joseph is thirty years old the day he stands before Pharaoh. What is the Egyptian name Pharaoh gives him?
context: Genesis 41:45-46 KJV. Jewish interpreters (Targum Onkelos, Rashi) read the name as 'revealer of hidden things', fitting the dream-reader. He was thirty when he went out from before Pharaoh and went throughout all the land of Egypt.

question: The afternoon of the crucifixion, a wealthy man walked in to see the Roman governor Pilate and boldly asked for the body of Jesus. Mark 15:43 introduces him as 'an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God' -- a member of the Jewish ruling council. What was his name?
context: Mark 15:43 KJV. The 'counsellor' in Mark's phrasing means a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish supreme court. Luke 23:51 KJV specifies that Joseph 'had not consented to the counsel and deed of them' -- he had voted against condemning Jesus. Not the same as Joseph the father of Jesus. Simon of Cyrene carried the cross (Mark 15:21); Lazarus was the man Jesus raised in Bethany (John 11); Cleopas walks the road to Emmaus (Luke 24).

question: After Joseph took the body down from the cross, he had to wrap it before burial. Mark 15:46 says he went and bought fine cloth to wrap the body in. What kind of cloth did he buy?
context: Mark 15:46 KJV: 'And he bought fine linen, and took him down, and wrapped him in the linen.' Linen was the traditional Jewish burial cloth -- plain, white, and undyed; the Shroud of Turin, whether it belongs to this scene or not, is a linen cloth. Sackcloth is the coarse mourning material worn BY the grieving, not wrapped around the dead.

question: When Joseph asked for the body, Pilate reacted with surprise -- Mark 15:44 says he 'marvelled' at one specific thing about Jesus's condition. Roman crucifixion was designed to take days; something was unexpected here. Pilate even sent for the centurion to check. What surprised him?
choices: That Joseph was on the council
That the sky had gone dark
context: Mark 15:44 KJV: 'Pilate marvelled if he were already dead: and calling unto him the centurion, he asked him whether he had been any while dead.' Crucifixion typically killed slowly over days by exhaustion and asphyxiation; Jesus was on the cross roughly six hours. Pilate only released the body once the centurion confirmed the death. The darkness (Matthew 27:45) and Joseph's Sanhedrin membership were real but not the marvel Mark records here.

question: Joseph did not carry the body to a common grave. Matthew 27:60 says he laid it in a NEW tomb of his own, one he had just had cut for himself out of solid rock, and then rolled something heavy across the entrance to seal it. What did he roll to the door?
context: Matthew 27:60 KJV: 'And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.' Rock-cut tombs sealed by a disc-shaped rolling stone are archaeologically documented in first-century Judea -- the stone sat in a channel and had to be pushed. The Sunday-morning women worry aloud on the way there about who can roll it back for them (Mark 16:3).

question: Before dawn on Sunday, women set out for the tomb carrying spices to finish anointing the body properly -- the Friday burial had been rushed before the sabbath. Mark 16:1 names three of them. Which group is it?
answer: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome
choices: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome
Mary the mother of Jesus, Martha, and Joanna
Mary of Bethany, Susanna, and Elizabeth
Mary the wife of Cleopas, Anna, and Rhoda
context: Mark 16:1 KJV. The four gospels give slightly different lists: Matthew has Mary Magdalene and 'the other Mary'; Luke adds Joanna; John names only Mary Magdalene. Mark's Salome here is a different woman from Herodias's daughter -- 'Salome' was a common name. Mary of Bethany (Martha and Lazarus's sister) is a different Mary; the 'daughters of Jerusalem' are the women Jesus addressed on the way to the cross (Luke 23:28).

question: As the women walked toward the tomb in the half-dark, they kept discussing one practical worry aloud among themselves -- Mark 16:3 records the exact question. What did they keep asking each other?
answer: Who shall roll us away the stone
choices: Who shall roll us away the stone
Who will lend us fresh oil
Who will open the outer gate
Who will speak for us to the guards
context: Mark 16:3 KJV: 'And they said among themselves, Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?' The three women were carrying spices alone, with no man to help them, and the great stone Joseph had rolled across the door was far too heavy for them to shift. The next verse resolves it in the driest way possible -- 'And when they looked, they saw that the stone was rolled away: for it was very great.' It is one of the small human touches Mark is famous for.

question: Matthew 28 alone gives the scene of the stone being moved. An angel of the Lord comes down, rolls the stone back, and sits on top of it as if to make a point. Matthew describes his appearance in two vivid images. His face was like WHAT, and his raiment white as snow?
context: Matthew 28:2-3 KJV: 'the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it. His countenance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow.' Note the almost cheeky detail -- he SITS on the very stone that had sealed the tomb. The other images are real biblical descriptions of divine or angelic beings elsewhere: 'his feet like unto fine brass' (Revelation 1:15), 'the morning star' (Revelation 22:16), the sun-face of the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2).

question: In John 20 the other women leave, but Mary Magdalene stays behind at the tomb weeping. She turns around and sees a man she takes for the gardener; she asks where the body has been carried. He answers with a single word -- her own name -- and she suddenly knows him. She cries out one Aramaic word back. John 20:16 preserves it untranslated. What word does she say?
context: John 20:16 KJV: 'Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.' Rabboni is a heightened form of 'rabbi' -- 'my teacher.' The distractors are all real Aramaic words the New Testament preserves untranslated: Maranatha ('Our Lord, come,' 1 Corinthians 16:22), Hosanna ('save us,' from Palm Sunday), and Abba ('Father,' Mark 14:36). Jesus then tells her not to hold on to him but to go tell the others.

question: Famine has reached Canaan. Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain, and they come before the vizier and bow with their faces to the earth. The vizier knows them at once, but they have not seen his face for more than twenty years and do not know him. Who is the vizier?
context: Genesis 42:6-8 KJV. Joseph was seventeen when the brothers sold him to the Ishmeelites; he is now about thirty-seven, second only to Pharaoh in Egypt. He recognises them; they do not recognise him.

question: The governor makes himself a stranger to the ten brothers and speaks roughly to them through an interpreter. He accuses them of a crime that would carry a death sentence in Pharaoh's court and demand a search of their story from top to bottom. What does he accuse them of being?
context: Genesis 42:9 KJV: 'Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.' Border-crossing foreigners in a time of famine were the classic suspects; the charge lets Joseph hold them without seeming cruel.

question: Joseph tells the brothers he will hold one of them in prison in Egypt while the others fetch their youngest brother Benjamin down from Canaan. He binds one man before their eyes and keeps him behind. Which brother does he choose to hold as the hostage?
context: Genesis 42:24 KJV. Simeon is the second son of Leah. Some Jewish commentators (Rashi) note Reuben tried to save Joseph at the pit, so Joseph passed over him and chose the next brother in line.

question: The brothers murmur to each other in Hebrew, not knowing Joseph has understood every word because he spoke with them through an interpreter. What are they confessing to one another as they stand in front of him?
answer: That God has finally punished them for selling their brother into slavery
choices: That God has finally punished them for selling their brother into slavery
That the governor's harshness is a sign Simeon will die in prison
That Reuben was right to warn them not to harm the boy at the pit
That their father Jacob's grief has followed them all the way to Egypt
context: Genesis 42:21-23 KJV: 'We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear.' Joseph turns aside and weeps when he hears it.

question: The brothers come back with Benjamin, and Joseph invites all eleven of them to a feast at his own house. As they sit down, they look at one another and marvel: without a word spoken to any Egyptian, the seating has been arranged in a way that no Egyptian steward could have guessed. What order are they seated in?
answer: The exact order of their birth, from oldest to youngest
choices: The exact order of their birth, from oldest to youngest
The order of their mothers, Leah's sons first
By height, tallest at the head of the table
Alphabetical by name in the Egyptian tongue
context: Genesis 43:33 KJV: 'And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth: and the men marvelled one at another.' The seating is a private signal: only a brother could know it.

question: The feast is served, and Joseph sends portions from his own table to each of the brothers. To one of them he sends a portion far larger than the others, so large that no one at the table can miss the favour. Which brother, and how much more?
context: Genesis 43:34 KJV. Benjamin is Joseph's only full brother, Rachel's other son. Joseph is watching the ten half-brothers to see if the old jealousy over a father's favourite will flare up again.

question: Judah has stepped forward and begged to be made a slave in Benjamin's place, telling the vizier of an old father whose life is bound up in the lad's life. The vizier can hold in no longer. He orders every Egyptian sent out of the room, weeps aloud so the whole house hears him, and speaks. What are the first words he says to his brothers?
answer: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?
choices: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?
Come near to me, I pray you.
God did send me before you to preserve life.
Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
context: Genesis 45:1-3 KJV. His brothers cannot answer him, for they were troubled at his presence. The other three choices are real lines Joseph speaks moments later (Gen 45:4, 45:5) or after Jacob's death (Gen 50:19), but this is the first sentence out of his mouth. Later he tells them, 'Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good' (Genesis 50:20).

question: Jacob loves Joseph more than any of his other sons because Joseph is the son of his old age, born to Rachel. To mark him as the favoured son, Jacob gives him a gift so striking that his ten older brothers see it and cannot speak peaceably to him. What does Jacob give Joseph?
context: Genesis 37:3-4 KJV. The Hebrew is disputed (some read 'a long coat with sleeves'), but the KJV 'coat of many colours' is the phrase that stuck in Western imagination. It is the visible token of the favoured son.

question: Joseph tells his brothers a dream. They are all binding sheaves of grain in the field when suddenly his sheaf stands upright, and their sheaves gather round about it and bow down to it. He tells them a second dream in which the sun and moon and eleven stars also bow to him. When they see him coming, what do the brothers mutter to one another?
choices: Behold, the boy of the fine coat
context: Genesis 37:19 KJV. Immediately after they say it, they plan to kill him and cast him into a pit and say some evil beast has devoured him, and then, they say, 'we shall see what will become of his dreams.'

question: The brothers reach Dothan, strip Joseph of his coat, and throw him into a pit with no water in it. As they sit down to eat bread, a caravan comes along the road below, its camels loaded with spicery, balm, and myrrh going down into Egypt. To whom does the caravan belong?
context: Genesis 37:25 KJV. The Ishmeelites are descended from Ishmael, Abraham's other son; their spice-trade route runs from Gilead down through Canaan into Egypt. The detail is almost cinematic: the smell of balm and myrrh drifting past a pit.

question: As the spice-caravan passes by on the road down to Egypt, Judah speaks up. Killing their brother, he says, will not profit them; concealing his blood will only weigh on them. He proposes selling Joseph to the traders instead. For how many pieces of silver do they sell him?
context: Genesis 37:28 KJV. The distractor 'thirty' is the Judas price for Jesus in Matthew 26:15; different sale, different number. Twenty shekels was roughly the going market price for a young male slave in that era, according to Levitical valuation tables.

question: With Joseph on his way to Egypt, the brothers must explain the missing boy to their father. They kill a kid of the goats and dip the coat in its blood. They send the bloodied coat to Jacob with a short, cold message that will not even name Joseph. What do they tell him?
answer: Know now whether it be thy son's coat or no
choices: Know now whether it be thy son's coat or no
See now if this be the coat of the son thou lovedst
Come and see the beast that hath devoured thy son
Take up thy staff and search the hills for his body
context: Genesis 37:32 KJV. It is a cold sentence: they will not even name Joseph. Jacob knows the coat at once, rends his clothes, puts sackcloth on his loins, and mourns for his son many days. It is the first false evidence in the Hebrew Bible.

question: In Egypt Joseph is bought by Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard. He rises to run the whole household until Potiphar's wife tries to seize him, he flees, and she keeps a piece of him as false evidence against him. What does she keep in her hand?
context: Genesis 39:11-18 KJV. Once again a garment of Joseph's is used as false proof against him: the coat to his father, now the garment to Potiphar. He is thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners are bound, and there Pharaoh's officers will one day be sent.

question: In the prison Joseph interprets the dreams of two of Pharaoh's officers who have offended their king. To one he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up thy head and restore thee to thy office. To the other he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up thy head and hang thee on a tree. Which two officers are they?
answer: The chief butler and the chief baker
choices: The chief butler and the chief baker
The chief steward and the chief herald
The chief scribe and the chief physician
The chief cupbearer and the chief taster
context: Genesis 40:9-22 KJV. The butler is restored on Pharaoh's birthday and forgets Joseph for two full years, until Pharaoh dreams of the cows and the corn and needs a dream-reader. The baker's hanging is the tell that Joseph reads dreams true.

question: After Moses died on Mount Nebo looking into the promised land, one man took his place and led Israel across the Jordan to the walled city they would attack first. Who led them?
context: Joshua son of Nun succeeded Moses and led the crossing at the Jordan and the siege of Jericho (Joshua 1-6, KJV).

question: Rahab hid Joshua's two spies on the flat roof of her house, laying them under a crop she had spread there in orderly rows to dry. What crop covered them?
context: Joshua 2:6 (KJV): 'she had brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof.'

question: Rahab lowered the spies down from her window, and they told her to tie a single mark in that same window so her house would be spared when the city fell. What was the mark?
context: Joshua 2:18 (KJV): 'thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by.' Blue, purple, and scarlet are all real Tabernacle colors -- only scarlet is the sparing-mark.

question: Near Jericho, Joshua looked up and saw a man standing before him with a drawn sword, and Joshua asked, 'Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?' The stranger refused both sides. Who did he say he was?
answer: captain of the host of the Lord
choices: captain of the host of the Lord
prince of the tribe of Judah
watchman of the walls of Jericho
elder of the men of Gibeon
context: Joshua 5:14 (KJV): 'Nay; but as captain of the host of the Lord am I now come.' Joshua fell on his face; the captain told him to loose his shoe from off his foot.

question: For the march around Jericho, God told Joshua that seven priests would go before the ark, each one blowing a trumpet. What were the trumpets made of?
context: Joshua 6:4 (KJV): 'seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams' horns.' Numbers 10:2 describes a different pair of trumpets, of solid silver, for calling the assembly -- not these.

question: For six days Israel marched once around Jericho in silence. On the last day they rose early and circled the city more than once before Joshua gave the shout. How many times around on that final day?
context: Joshua 6:15-16 (KJV): 'on the seventh day... they compassed the city after the same manner seven times.' Then the priests blew, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat (6:20).

question: After Jericho fell, Israel was routed at little Ai and about thirty-six men were killed. Achan confessed he had coveted and buried in his tent a wedge of gold, two hundred shekels of silver, and one stolen luxury cloak. Where was the cloak from?
context: Joshua 7:21 (KJV): 'I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment... I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent.' Israel's early defeat at Ai was blamed on Achan's hidden loot.

question: Judas Iscariot was one of the Twelve disciples, but he had a particular job among them the gospels remember him for. What did Judas carry for the disciple band?
context: John 12:6 and 13:29 say Judas 'had the bag' -- he kept the disciples' shared purse. John's gospel then adds a sharp aside: 'this he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag'.

question: At a dinner in Bethany a woman named Mary poured an expensive perfumed ointment over Jesus's feet. One of the disciples spoke up loudly, complaining that the ointment should have been sold and the money given to the poor. Which disciple objected?
context: John 12:3-6. John's narrator adds that Judas said this 'not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag'.

question: After the anointing at Bethany, Judas Iscariot went in secret to the chief priests and offered to hand Jesus over to them. Matthew's gospel names the exact price they weighed out to him. How much silver did they agree on?
context: Matthew 26:14-15. Thirty pieces of silver was also the compensation set in Exodus 21:32 for a slave killed by an ox -- a bitterly pointed sum.

question: Late at night in the garden of Gethsemane, Judas came with a mob carrying torches and swords, and gave them a pre-arranged signal so they would know which man to seize in the dark. What sign did Judas use to point Jesus out?
context: Matthew 26:48-49: 'Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast. And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.' Jesus answered, 'Friend, wherefore art thou come?'

question: Later Jewish law recorded in Exodus 21:32 set thirty pieces of silver as the compensation for a very particular kind of loss. Matthew keys the price of the betrayal to that same sum. What did Exodus 21:32 value at thirty pieces of silver?
answer: A slave killed by an ox
choices: A slave killed by an ox
A field of barley in harvest
context: Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels of silver as the payment an ox's owner must give if the ox gores a slave to death. Matthew echoes the price to underline what Jesus was being sold for.

question: In Matthew's gospel, once Judas Iscariot saw that Jesus had been condemned to die, he was seized with remorse. He rushed back into the Temple, flung the thirty pieces of silver down on the floor, went out, and killed himself. How did Judas take his own life in Matthew's account?
choices: He fell on his own sword
He threw himself from the Temple wall
He drank poison in the courtyard
context: Matthew 27:3-5: 'and cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.' Matthew's ending is one of two very different accounts of the death of Judas in the New Testament.

question: The book of Acts tells the end of Judas Iscariot in a very different way from Matthew. Acts 1:18 says Judas bought a field with the reward of his treachery, and there something gruesome happened to his body. According to Acts, what happened to Judas in that field?
answer: He fell headlong and his body burst open
choices: He fell headlong and his body burst open
He was struck dead by lightning at the gate
He was stoned by a crowd of pilgrims
He wandered into the desert and starved
context: Acts 1:18 (KJV): 'and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.' Both accounts sit in the New Testament side by side -- Matthew has the hanging in the Temple, Acts has the falling in the field; the church has never smoothed them into a single story without inventing extra detail.

question: In Matthew's account, when Judas hurled the silver back at the priests and ran out, the chief priests picked the coins up but faced a problem: their own Temple law said it was blood-money and could not go back into the treasury chests. What did the priests decide to do with the silver instead?
answer: They bought a potter's field as a graveyard for foreigners
choices: They bought a potter's field as a graveyard for foreigners
They sent it as tribute to the Roman governor
They gave it to the widows of the city
They melted it into a lampstand for the sanctuary
context: Matthew 27:6-8: 'It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in.'

question: The graveyard the priests bought with Judas's returned silver picked up a grim Aramaic nickname among the people of Jerusalem, and both Matthew 27 and Acts 1 record it. By what name did that field become known?
context: Acts 1:19: 'insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.' Golgotha was the place of Jesus's execution; Gehenna was the burning refuse valley south of the city; Bethesda was the pool of the healing at the sheep gate.

question: In Acts chapter 1, before Pentecost, the remaining eleven apostles wanted to fill Judas's empty seat and bring their number back to twelve. Two men were put forward as candidates and the lot fell on one of them. Who was chosen to replace Judas Iscariot?
context: Acts 1:23-26. The two candidates were 'Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias'; they prayed, cast lots, and 'the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.'

question: In Matthew 27:9-10 the writer stops the narrative to say the potter's-field purchase fulfilled words of a prophet, quoting a passage about thirty pieces of silver being 'cast to the potter in the house of the LORD'. Which Old Testament prophet's book actually contains that line about the thirty pieces and the potter?
context: The line is Zechariah 11:12-13 -- 'And they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter... and I cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD.' Matthew's gospel names Jeremiah at the head of the quotation, a wording puzzle scholars still argue about.

question: In May 1373, in an English city on the eastern coast, a woman about thirty and a half years old lay dying of a mysterious illness. A priest at her bedside held up a wooden cross so her fading eyes could rest on it -- and instead of dying she began to see visions that made her one of the great mystical writers of Europe. In which English city was she?
context: Norwich was then a plague-stricken port on the eastern coast, one of the largest towns in England. Canterbury, York, and Ely are all real English cathedral cities, but the visionary of May 1373 was in Norwich -- and she takes her name from a church there.

question: The Norwich visionary's birth name has been lost -- her mother, her father, the neighbours who knew her as a child, all gone from the record. We call her by another name, taken from an unusual source. Where does the name we use for her come from?
answer: the parish church her later cell was built against
choices: the parish church her later cell was built against
the ship her father sailed on out of Norwich harbour
the older nun who taught her at a Norwich priory
the pen name she signed at the end of her book
context: The parish church of St Julian, Conisford, in Norwich gave her the name Julian; her birth name is genuinely lost. She never gave herself a pen name; no father-and-ship story is recorded; no priory teacher is named in her Long Text.

question: Julian says that in one of her visions she looked at the palm of her hand and saw a small round thing lying there -- so small she marvelled it did not fall to nothing for littleness -- and she understood it was 'all that is made'. What did she say the little round thing was the size of?
context: 'A little thing, the quantity of an hazelnut, lying in the palm of my hand, as it seemed, and it was as round as any ball' (Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 5). The mustard seed and the pearl of great price come from Jesus's parables in the Gospels; the poppy pod is not a scripture image.

question: Over the five hours between four and nine one morning in May 1373, Julian says she was shown a whole sequence of visions -- Christ's Passion in vivid physical detail, the mother of Jesus, the hazelnut in her palm. She calls each one a 'shewing'. Exactly how many shewings does the Long Text say she received that morning?
context: Sixteen shewings between roughly four and nine in the morning, according to the opening of Julian's Long Text; she spent the next twenty years working out what she thought they meant. The other numbers are famous elsewhere (seven sacraments, twelve apostles, forty days in the wilderness).

question: Twenty years after her visions Julian finished a book working out what she had seen -- known as the Long Text, or Revelations of Divine Love. What distinction does that book hold in the history of English writing?
answer: the earliest surviving book in English by a woman
choices: the earliest surviving book in English by a woman
the earliest English translation of the Bible
the earliest printed book in England
the earliest hymnal used in an English cathedral
context: Julian's Long Text (c. 1393) is the earliest book in the English language whose named woman author is known. The first printed book in England was William Caxton's, more than eighty years later; the earliest full English Bible translation was Wycliffe's, at about the same time as Julian; hymnal history goes back centuries earlier.

question: In chapter 27 of the Long Text Julian gives the line that would become perhaps the most quoted in all English mysticism -- Christ's reply to her about sin and suffering. What kids often miss when they quote it is that the promise is stated THREE TIMES in a single breath, not once. Which of these is the exact threefold form Julian records?
answer: All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well
choices: All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well
Blessed be the name, and blessed be the name, and blessed be his holy name
Peace, peace be with you, peace be with you always, peace be with you now
Fear not, and fear not still, and fear no more the doom that comes
context: The threefold repetition is the whole point -- kids often shorten it to one 'all shall be well' and miss the drumbeat. The other threefold forms are pastiche; Julian's line comes from Revelations of Divine Love ch. 27, given as Christ's answer about sin.

question: Around 1413 a much louder, tearful, wandering visionary made a special trip to Norwich to sit at Julian's window and ask her whether her own noisy sobbing fits were really from God -- Julian told her they were. The visitor went home and wrote the days at the window into what is now considered the first autobiography of its kind. Who was the visitor at Julian's window?
context: The Book of Margery Kempe records the days Margery of Bishop's Lynn sat with Julian at the anchorage window in Norwich; it is the first surviving autobiography in English. Bridget of Sweden died in 1373, the year of Julian's visions; Catherine of Siena died in 1380; Hildegard of Bingen died in 1179 -- all real medieval visionaries but far too early for a 1413 visit.

question: In 1942, as the Blitz was falling on England, T. S. Eliot closed the fourth of his Four Quartets by quoting Julian's threefold promise word for word -- ending with a rose and a flame folded together. Which of the Four Quartets is that poem?
context: 'And all shall be well and / All manner of thing shall be well / When the tongues of flame are in-folded / Into the crowned knot of fire / And the fire and the rose are one.' Little Gidding, published September 1942, closes the sequence; the other three Quartets are titled after other English and American places Eliot cared about.

question: In the Arthurian legends, one knight is Arthur's foster-brother: they grew up together in the same household believing they were natural brothers, before the sword-in-the-stone revealed Arthur's true parentage. What is the foster-brother's name?
context: Sir Kay (Welsh Cei, French Ke) is the son of Sir Ector, in whose house Merlin had hidden the infant Arthur. Lancelot is fostered by the Lady of the Lake, not Arthur; Gawain is Arthur's blood nephew, not foster-brother; Bedivere is another Round Table knight but not the foster-brother.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory Book I, on the day the sword-in-the-stone was pulled, Sir Kay and young Arthur rode to a New Year's tournament in London with Kay's father. What was the father's name, the knight in whose house Arthur had been secretly fostered from infancy?
context: Merlin gave the infant Arthur to Sir Ector to raise, so no one would know he was Uther's son. Sir Bors is one of the Grail knights; Sir Uwain is Morgan le Fay's son; Sir Kynon is a companion of Owain in the Welsh tradition.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory Book I, on the morning of the New Year's tournament outside London, Kay realised on the road that he had left a crucial piece of gear back at the inn and sent Arthur to fetch it. What had Kay left behind?
context: Arthur rode back, found the inn locked, saw a blade standing in the stone in a nearby churchyard, and pulled it out to bring to Kay. A knight might arrive at a tournament without a spare shield or helm and borrow; a blade was harder to borrow at short notice.  (Legend.)

question: When Arthur returned from the locked lodging carrying the sword he had pulled from the stone, Kay recognised it and briefly tried to claim credit for the deed himself. Who forced Kay to admit the truth about who had actually drawn the sword?
context: Malory Book I. Ector had Kay lay hand on holy relics and swear how he had come by the sword; Kay confessed, and Ector then had Arthur put the sword back in the stone and pull it out again in front of him. Merlin arranged the sword-test but was not present at this exact moment; the Archbishop presided at the churchyard trials that followed; the Lady of the Lake gives Excalibur later, a different sword.  (Legend.)

question: Kay's defining trait in Malory's Round Table stories is his sharp tongue. Which of the following knights did Kay famously mock and put in the kitchen for a whole year under a scornful nickname, before that knight rode out and proved himself?
context: Malory Book VII. Kay named the disguised Gareth 'Beaumains' ('Fair-Hands') and set him scrubbing pots for a year. In Chretien de Troyes Kay also mocks the young Perceval when he first arrives at court, but Percival is not the knight Kay puts in the kitchen for a year in Malory; Bors and Tristan arrive at court fully known as noble.  (Legend.)

question: In the old Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen (about 1100), Kay is called Cei and is a magical warrior, not just a sharp-tongued seneschal. Cei can hold his breath underwater for a striking stretch of time. How long?
context: Culhwch and Olwen names several magical powers Cei has: nine days without breath, nine days without sleep, and the ability to grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. Nine is a number of mythic completion in the Welsh tradition (as in the Nine Witches of Gloucester).  (Legend.)

question: In the Welsh Arthurian tradition, two warriors are Arthur's chief companions long before Lancelot arrives in the later French romances. Kay (Cei) is one of the two. Who is the other?
context: Bedwyr (later Bedivere in French and English) is Kay's constant companion in Culhwch and Olwen and other early Welsh tales; the pair are Arthur's inner circle. Owain (later Yvain), Peredur (later Perceval), and Geraint all belong to the Welsh corpus of Arthurian heroes but are protagonists of their own separate tales, not Arthur's paired inner companions.  (Legend.)
