question: In the Norse origin of poetry itself, the two families of gods -- the Aesir and the Vanir -- ended their long war by sealing peace in one shared act at a great vat. What did every god on both sides do into that vat to seal the truce?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the Aesir and Vanir sealed their peace by all spitting together into a vat. From that spittle grew the wise-man Kvasir. The oath-ring belongs to Icelandic Thing-law, not to this scene; blood-oaths and wine belong to other traditions.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse peace-story of the Aesir-Vanir war, the spittle of every god in a shared vat took on a life of its own and grew into a full-grown man. He was said to be the wisest being that had ever lived -- no question could be put to him that he could not answer. What is his name?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: from the peace-vat spittle grew Kvasir, wisest of all beings. Mimir is the guardian of the well of wisdom whose severed head Odin keeps to counsel him. Bragi is the god of poetry. Heimdall is the watchman of Bifrost.  (Legend.)

question: The wise-man Kvasir walked the worlds answering every question that was put to him, until he came at last to the hall of two dwarves who invited him inside as a guest. There they killed him. What are the names of the two dwarves who murdered Kvasir?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: Fjalar and Galar invited Kvasir to their hall and killed him. Sindri and Brokkr are the dwarf-brothers who forged Mjolnir. Nordri and Sudri (with Austri and Vestri) hold up the four corners of the sky. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf trapped by Thor at daybreak; Andvari owns the cursed ring of the Volsung cycle.  (Legend.)

question: In the Prose Edda the two dwarves drain Kvasir's blood into two vats and a kettle and mix it with one common hall-ingredient, then brew it into a drink so powerful that whoever tastes it becomes a poet and a wise-man on the spot. What did the dwarves mix Kvasir's blood with to make the Mead of Poetry?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the dwarves drained the blood into two vats (Son and Bodn) and a kettle (Odrerir), mixed it with honey, and brewed a mead. Mead is the honey-fermented drink of the Norse hall; ale was made from grain. The dwarves later told the Aesir that Kvasir had 'choked on his own wisdom' because no one was clever enough to ask him a question.  (Legend.)

question: Gilling's son avenged his parents by seizing the two murdering dwarves and stranding them on a rock in the tide, where the water would rise and drown them. The dwarves bought their lives by handing him one thing. What did they give him in ransom for their lives?
answer: the Mead brewed from Kvasir's blood
choices: the Mead brewed from Kvasir's blood
the millstone they had killed his mother with
a chest of gold rings from the workshop
the drill they used to bore into stone
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 5: the giant Suttung stranded Fjalar and Galar on a tidal skerry, and they bought back their lives with the Mead. He took it home to his mountain and set his own daughter to guard it -- and that is how the drink passed from dwarves into the hands of the giants.  (Legend.)

question: The giant who ransomed the Mead from the dwarves hid it deep inside a mountain of his own and set one guardian to watch it in an inner chamber. Who did the giant Suttung set to guard the Mead inside the mountain Hnitbjorg?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Suttung hid the Mead in the mountain Hnitbjorg and set his daughter Gunnlod to guard it. Baugi is Suttung's brother, whom Odin will use as his way in. Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover (mother of Fenrir, Jormungand, and Hel) -- not Suttung's wife. Gilling is Suttung's own already-dead father.  (Legend.)

question: Odin set out to steal the Mead disguised as a farm-labourer. He came to the fields of Suttung's brother and made himself so useful that nine slaves working there died in a quarrel over a single sharp thing he had brought with him. What did Odin bring that made the nine slaves kill each other in a scramble for it?
choices: a silver ring he had promised
a helmet he had worn in war
a spear he had brought from Asgard
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Odin, calling himself Bolverk, arrived at Baugi's farm and outworked nine slaves, then offered to sharpen their scythes with a whetstone. When they saw how well it worked they all lunged for the stone at once; Odin threw it in the air and the nine cut each other's throats. This is how he manoeuvred Baugi into needing him.  (Legend.)

question: The mountain that held the Mead had no door in it. To get Odin inside, Baugi bored a hole through the rock with a drill called Rati. Odin then had to slip through the drilled hole himself. What shape did Odin take to pass through the drill-hole into Suttung's mountain?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Odin turned himself into a snake and slithered through the hole Baugi had bored with the drill Rati. Baugi stabbed after him with the drill but missed. Inside the mountain Odin found Gunnlod alone.  (Legend.)

question: Inside the mountain Odin spent three nights with the giant's daughter, and each night she granted him one sip from the vessels of Mead she was guarding. Odin took three sips in three nights. In three sips what exactly did he drink?
answer: all three vessels dry to the bottom
choices: all three vessels dry to the bottom
one third of the smallest kettle
the surface layer of each vessel
half of the largest vat only
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: Gunnlod gave Odin one sip each of the three nights; in three sips he drained all three vessels (Son, Bodn, and Odrerir) to the last drop. Havamal 104-110 tells the same theft from Odin's own voice, and calls the sips the greatest bargain a woman ever gave.  (Legend.)

question: With every drop of the Mead swallowed and held inside him, Odin fled the mountain and raced for Asgard. Suttung woke, saw him going, and pursued in the same shape Odin himself had taken for the escape. What shape did both Odin and Suttung take for the chase across the sky?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: both took eagle-shape for the pursuit. The Aesir on the walls saw Odin coming and put out great vats; he spat the Mead into them as he crossed. Suttung the eagle arrived just after, and the Aesir lit a fire on the wall that burned him to death. The story is carved on the Stora Hammars III picture-stone on Gotland from around 700 CE.  (Legend.)

question: In his hurry to reach the vats with Suttung right behind him, Odin lost a portion of the Mead out the OTHER end of his body -- not into the vats. The Norse have a name for that spilled portion, and they say it explains something about the world of verse. What is the spilled Mead said to be?
answer: the share of the bad poets
choices: the share of the bad poets
the drink of the fallen valkyries
the tears of the giant's daughter
the wine of the buried kings
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 6: what Odin lost out his rear end is called 'the share of the bad poets' and belongs to any hack-versifier who can pick it up. The good stuff Odin spat into the vats belongs to Asgard and to the true skalds. That is why 'Kvasir's blood' remains the standard kenning for poetry itself.  (Legend.)

question: A monstrous beast was ravaging the town of Nemea in the northern Peloponnese, eating farmers and their flocks. King Eurystheus of Mycenae sent Heracles to kill it as the very first of his twelve labors. What kind of animal was it?
context: The Nemean Lion was the first of the twelve labors (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.1). The Erymanthian Boar, the Ceryneian Hind (golden-horned stag), and the Lernaean Hydra are later labors, all real Heracles monsters.  (Legend.)

question: The Nemean beast was no ordinary animal. Its coat, said to gleam like polished metal in the sun, was famous through Greece for a single terrifying property that made every hunter before Heracles give up. What was it?
answer: No mortal weapon could pierce it
choices: No mortal weapon could pierce it
It shed its skin like a snake each dawn
It caught fire when touched by iron
context: The lion's golden pelt turned aside bronze, iron and stone; even arrows glanced off. Its own claws were sharper than any mortal sword. This is what made the labor an execution, not a hunt.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles tracked the great beast to its den in the rocks at Nemea. Before he went in after it, he did one thing to make sure it could not slip past him. What?
answer: He blocked up one of the den's mouths with heavy boulders
choices: He blocked up one of the den's mouths with heavy boulders
He wedged burning brands in a ring around the mouth
He drove a javelin up under its foreleg
He waited three days for the beast to starve out
context: The den had two openings; with one sealed, the lion could not slip out the back while Heracles came in the front. He then went in unarmed to face it up close.  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the two-mouthed cave at Nemea, the golden-coated beast turned to fight. Heracles's arrows bounced, his sword-edge slid across the hide as if off polished stone. So he dropped every weapon he carried and killed it a very different way. How?
answer: He wrestled it and choked it to death with his bare arms
choices: He wrestled it and choked it to death with his bare arms
He rolled a heavy boulder down onto its skull
He drove a javelin up under its foreleg
He blinded it with a torch and let it starve
context: Heracles wrestled the lion in the dark of its own den and strangled it to death by main strength (Apollodorus 2.5.1). This is why his cult image shows him always with a lion-skin and empty hands.  (Legend.)

question: The lion was dead, but Heracles now had a fresh problem: he needed the hide to carry back to Eurystheus, and no blade of his would cut it. His patron goddess Athena watched him struggle and gave him one piece of advice that solved it. What did she tell him to use?
answer: One of the lion's own claws
choices: One of the lion's own claws
A shard of stone from the cave wall
A tooth from the lion's jaw
A shaft of sunlight through the cave mouth
context: The claws were the only things sharp enough to slice the invulnerable pelt. Athena is Heracles's constant patron; she appears again in the twelfth labor guiding him into Hades.  (Legend.)

question: After skinning the lion with its own claw, Heracles put the pelt on. From that day forward, in every vase-painting and statue for the rest of the twelve labors, he is shown wearing it in one particular way. How?
answer: As a cloak, with the head pulled up over his own as a hood
choices: As a cloak, with the head pulled up over his own as a hood
As a shield strapped across his left arm at the elbow
As a banner tied to the shaft of his olive-wood club
As a wide belt bound around his waist with a knot
context: The lion-head hood is Heracles's signature; combined with his olive-wood club, it is how the ancient world recognized him in art. The pelt was arrow-proof and sword-proof and served as his armor through every later labor.  (Legend.)

question: When Heracles finally hauled the huge corpse of the Nemean beast back to Mycenae, King Eurystheus was so terrified he had a permanent hiding-place set into the palace grounds. What was it?
answer: A large bronze jar sunk into the earth
choices: A large bronze jar sunk into the earth
A hidden chamber lined with sheets of lead
A stone cellar sealed with a bronze door
A tall tower with a single iron gate
context: From then on Eurystheus refused to meet Heracles face-to-face; new labors were passed to him through a herald named Copreus. The jar reappears at the twelfth labor when Heracles brings home Cerberus.  (Legend.)

question: Long before the labors began, Heracles had done something so terrible in a fit of divine madness that Eurystheus's whole punishment cycle was penance for it. Hera had driven him mad, and in that madness he killed the members of his own household. Whom did he kill?
answer: His wife Megara and their children
choices: His wife Megara and their children
His teacher Linus and his father Amphitryon
context: After the killing, Heracles went to the Pythia at Delphi for cleansing. The oracle told him to serve Eurystheus of Mycenae for ten years and perform whatever labors the king set. Linus (his music tutor) he had killed years earlier in a separate incident, not in the madness.  (Legend.)

question: Ancient poets disagreed about where the great beast at Nemea had actually come from. One strange tradition, preserved in scattered fragments, says Hera arranged for a certain goddess to hurl the lion down out of her own realm onto Greek soil for Heracles to hunt. Which goddess?
context: In this variant, Selene the moon-goddess threw the lion from the moon at Hera's request. Other traditions (Hesiod) make the lion a child of the two-headed hound Orthrus; Apollodorus makes it a child of Typhon. Iris is Hera's rainbow messenger; Hebe is her cupbearer; Nyx is Night herself.  (Legend.)

question: Because Eurystheus was now too afraid to face Heracles in person after the lion-carcass was laid before the palace, he set up a go-between to shout each new labor at Heracles from the walls. Sources name this herald. Who was he?
context: Copreus, a son of Pelops in exile at Eurystheus's court, delivered the labors from labor two onward. Iolaus is Heracles's nephew and chariot-driver; Hylas is his young companion on the Argo; Telamon is his comrade at Troy's first sack. All three fight alongside him, but the shouted-messages herald is Copreus.  (Legend.)

question: For his tenth labor Heracles was sent to the far western edge of the world, to an island called Erytheia, to drive home a herd of famous red-coated cattle. Who owned the herd?
context: Geryon, king of the red island of Erytheia -- a giant with three bodies joined at the waist, three shields, and three spears. Antaeus is the giant Heracles wrestles in Libya on a later trip; Cacus is the Italian cattle-thief we meet at the end of this same labor. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Geryon's cattle were not ordinary cattle. Herds all over Greece were dun or brown, but every ox in this herd was of one striking color that gave their island home the name Erytheia, 'the ___ land.' What color were the cattle of Geryon?
context: The setting sun over the western ocean, the storytellers said, dyed the cattle's coats red -- and the island's name Erytheia comes from the same root as the Greek word for red. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Hesiod, Theogony 287-294.)  (Legend.)

question: The hero's journey to the western edge of the world took him all the way across North Africa and Europe. At the narrow strait between Africa and Spain, one peak in Morocco and one in Spain still bear a matching name from Greek myth. What are those two matching peaks called?
context: The northern pillar is the Rock of Gibraltar; the southern is Jebel Musa in Morocco. In some versions the hero split a single mountain in two to open the strait, letting the Atlantic into the Mediterranean. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Britannica, 'Pillars of Heracles'.)  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the North African desert on his way west, the sun beat down so cruelly on Heracles that he could not walk another step. So he did something no hero had ever tried: he drew his bow and pointed the arrow straight at the sun-god himself. The sun-god, more amused than angry at this insolence, made him a loan. What did the sun-god lend Heracles for the last leg of the trip?
answer: A golden cup to sail in
choices: A golden cup to sail in
A chariot pulled by winged horses
A cloak that turned aside heat
A crown that lit its own path
context: The golden cup of Helios is the vessel the sun himself sails from west to east every night while he sleeps. Heracles sailed it out to Erytheia, then loaded the cattle into it and sailed home. (Athenaeus 11.469; Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Geryon's cattle were kept in shape by a herdsman -- himself a giant, and the son of the war-god Ares. Heracles killed him on Erytheia with the same olive-wood club he had used to drop the two-headed dog. What was the herdsman's name?
context: Eurytion the herdsman, son of Ares. (There is a separate Eurytion who is a centaur in a different story -- Greek myth is not shy about reusing names.) The olive-wood club is Heracles's signature weapon. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles landed on Erytheia and dropped Geryon's two-headed dog with a single blow of his club, then dropped the herdsman the same way. For the giant himself he saved a single arrow -- one so deadly no monster could survive its bite. What had Heracles dipped that arrow in to make it that deadly?
answer: The venomous blood of the Lernaean Hydra
choices: The venomous blood of the Lernaean Hydra
The waters of the river Styx
The blood of the centaur Nessus
context: Back in the second labor Heracles had killed the Hydra and dipped his arrows in her poisonous blood -- and those arrows kept killing for the rest of his life. Stesichorus's lost poem Geryoneis told how one such arrow pierced all three of Geryon's bodies at once. (Stesichorus fr.; Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: Long before Rome was built, on Heracles's cattle-drive back through Italy, a fire-breathing giant living in a cave on one of the seven hills that would one day belong to Rome came out and stole some of Geryon's red cattle. Heracles hunted the thief down and killed him in his own cave. What was this cattle-thief's name?
context: Cacus lived in a cave on what would become the Aventine Hill. Virgil's Aeneid Book 8 has old Evander tell the whole story to Aeneas at that very spot. (Virgil, Aeneid 8.185-275; Livy 1.7.)  (Legend.)

question: The killing of the fire-breathing giant on the Aventine, Livy wrote, is why Rome's oldest and most sacred altar -- in the cattle-market of the Forum Boarium -- was said to be dedicated to Heracles from Rome's very founding. What is the name of that ancient altar in the Forum Boarium?
context: The Ara Maxima ('greatest altar') stood in the Forum Boarium and was in continuous use for centuries. Livy 1.7 traces its founding straight back to Heracles thanking the site of his fight with Cacus. (Livy 1.7; Virgil, Aeneid 8.)  (Legend.)

question: Even at the last stage of the labor, on the drive back to Mycenae, Hera was not finished with Heracles. She sent a creature that panicked the herd and scattered the red cattle across the length of Thrace -- the same creature she had once used to torment the wandering princess Io. What did Hera send after Heracles's herd?
context: The gadfly is a small biting fly whose sting sends cattle mad -- exactly the insect Hera used to torment Io as a wandering cow. A Hera-signature weapon. (Apollodorus 2.5.10; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 566ff.)  (Legend.)

question: In Virgil's version of the Cacus story, the giant thief tried to hide the stolen cattle in his cave by driving them in backwards, so that the tracks led away from his lair, not toward it. So how did Heracles find the cave anyway?
answer: A stolen cow inside the cave lowed and gave the hiding place away
choices: A stolen cow inside the cave lowed and gave the hiding place away
A river running through the cave carried out a scrap of hide
Cacus's own footprint faced the wrong way in the mud
A raven flew straight to the cave's mouth
context: The lowing cow is the whole point of Virgil's telling in Aeneid 8: even the cleverest theft cannot silence a living animal. The rest of the herd, walking past outside, called back and forth with the ones inside. (Virgil, Aeneid 8.212-218.)  (Legend.)

question: When Heracles finally reached Mycenae with the red herd from the far west, King Eurystheus who had set the labor did not keep the cattle for himself or for the city. What did Eurystheus do with the cattle of Geryon at the end of the tenth labor?
choices: He set them free on the plain
He gave them to Heracles as reward
He drove them into the sea
context: Eurystheus was Hera's client-king throughout the whole labor cycle -- Hera made the labors happen through him. Sacrificing Geryon's cattle to Hera closes the loop: her enemy Heracles has done all the work, and her altar gets the prize. (Apollodorus 2.5.10.)  (Legend.)

question: For his eleventh labor Heracles was sent to steal a fruit no mortal was supposed to touch -- a fruit that grew at the western edge of the world in the garden of the Hesperides, whose name means 'daughters of Evening.' What kind of fruit was it?
context: The golden apples of the Hesperides -- a wedding gift from Gaia (the earth) to Hera when Hera married Zeus. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 215-216.)  (Legend.)

question: The tree of golden apples had not always grown at the western edge of the world -- it was a wedding present, given long before by the earth-goddess Gaia to a certain bride on the day of her wedding on Olympus. Who was this bride, the goddess to whom the golden-apple tree belonged?
context: Gaia gave the tree to Hera when Hera married Zeus. That is why the fruit can never be kept by a mortal thief -- it is Hera's, and Athena eventually returns it to the garden. (Apollodorus 2.5.11.)  (Legend.)

question: The tree of golden apples was guarded by a truly terrible serpent -- a dragon that never slept and that had, in Hesiod's telling, one hundred heads. What was the name of this dragon at the world's edge?
context: Ladon coiled around the tree and never let his eyes shut. Python was Apollo's dragon at Delphi; the Hydra was Heracles's second labor; Typhon was the world-monster Zeus fought in a much older war. (Hesiod, Theogony 333-336.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles did not know how to reach the garden. On the way west he caught an old sea-god who knew every path in the world, and refused to let go of him no matter how the old god struggled. The old god turned into water, then fire, then a serpent, then all manner of shapes trying to slip free -- but Heracles held on until he answered. Who was this shape-shifting old man of the sea?
context: Nereus, the 'old man of the sea' and father of the sea-nymph Nereids, has the gift of prophecy and the gift of shape-changing. Proteus is a similar shape-shifter but belongs to Menelaus's story in the Odyssey, not to Heracles. (Apollodorus 2.5.11.)  (Legend.)

question: On the same journey, high in the mountains of the Caucasus, Heracles passed a Titan chained to a crag with a great eagle tearing his liver out day after day. Heracles took up his bow, shot the eagle out of the sky, and broke the chains. Which Titan did Heracles free from that punishment?
context: Prometheus, chained by Zeus for giving fire to humanity. His liver grew back every night so the eagle could eat it fresh every morning -- until Heracles's arrow. Prometheus in gratitude tells Heracles the secret of the apples. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound.)  (Legend.)

question: Reaching the western edge of the world, Heracles came upon a lone Titan who had been bent under a punishment-burden since the Titanomachy, thousands of years before. This Titan was the only one nearby who could pick the apples from the garden, and Heracles came to bargain with him. Which Titan was this?
context: Atlas, condemned since the Titanomachy to stand at the world's edge with the sky on his shoulders. He would prove eager to set the burden down, even briefly -- which is exactly what Heracles was counting on. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 517-520.)  (Legend.)

question: Heracles's whole plan for reaching the golden apples came down to a single strange offer he made to the Titan at the world's edge -- he would do the Titan's punishment-work for him if the Titan would fetch three apples from the garden. What was the punishment-work Heracles offered to take on?
choices: Rolling a boulder up a hill
context: Atlas jumped at the chance to be free of the sky for even a little while, gave the burden to Heracles, and walked off to the garden. That opened the trap the whole labor turns on. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Hesiod, Theogony 517-520.)  (Legend.)

question: The constellation Draco winds around the north celestial pole -- a long, coiled shape of stars that never sets. Hyginus in his Astronomica says that this coil of stars is a memorial placed in the sky by Hera for the slain guardian of her golden-apple tree. Which guardian does Hyginus say Draco commemorates?
context: Hyginus, Astronomica 2.3, identifies Draco at the pole as Ladon, put up by Hera in memory of her lost hundred-headed guardian. Python was Apollo's dragon at Delphi; Typhon was the world-monster Zeus fought; Cetus is the sea-beast Perseus killed. (Hyginus, Astronomica 2.3.)  (Legend.)

question: The Titan came back from the garden with three golden apples in his hand -- and then had an idea of his own. He would carry the apples to Mycenae himself; Heracles could just keep the punishment-burden forever. Rather than argue, Heracles agreed cheerfully -- but asked one small favor first. What was the favor?
answer: Take the sky back while he padded his shoulders with his lion-skin
choices: Take the sky back while he padded his shoulders with his lion-skin
Take the sky back while he stretched his cramped arms a moment
Take the sky back while he shifted his footing on the stones
Take the sky back while he tied a knot in the burden's edge
context: The moment Atlas took the sky back to let Heracles adjust his lion-skin as a shoulder-pad, Heracles snatched up the apples and walked away. The whole trick works because Atlas asked for it. This is the single cleverest moment in the twelve labors. (Apollodorus 2.5.11; https://www.greekmyths-greekmythology.com/apples-of-hesperides/)  (Legend.)

question: The cowardly king Eurystheus, who had set Heracles a series of impossible labors, saved the very worst for last: descend into the land of the dead and bring back the great hound that guards its gates so no soul can leave and none escape. What is the name of that hound?
context: The twelfth and final labor set by Eurystheus (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.12). Orthrus is Geryon's two-headed dog (also a Heracles labor); Argus is the hundred-eyed watchman of Hera; Laelaps is the hound that always caught its prey.  (Legend.)

question: When Heracles walked into the throne-room of the underworld and asked leave to take away the great three-headed hound at the gates, Hades answered with a single condition. What did he demand?
answer: That Heracles subdue the dog using no weapons
choices: That Heracles subdue the dog using no weapons
That Heracles give up his lion-skin cloak
That Heracles first free a mortal from a chair
That Heracles swear never to return
context: Hades granted the request on the sole condition that Heracles overpower the beast with brute strength alone (Apollodorus 2.5.12). Heracles wrapped himself in his invulnerable Nemean-lion cloak for armor but kept his hands empty.  (Legend.)

question: Before descending, Heracles first traveled to the priest Eumolpus to be initiated into a famous secret cult whose rites promised the initiated safe passage through the underworld. Which cult was it?
context: Heracles went to Eumolpus at Eleusis to be initiated before descending. The Orphic mysteries are a separate secret cult; Dodona and Delphi are oracle sites, not initiation cults for the underworld.  (Legend.)

question: Which of the pair stuck to the chair in Hades did Heracles wrench loose by main force, leaving chunks of the man's thighs fixed to the stone?
choices: Both -- Heracles took them out together
context: Pirithous was the main offender (he had wanted to abduct Persephone as his bride) and could not be moved; he stayed in Hades forever. Heracles tore Theseus free but had to leave pieces of his thighs stuck to the chair.  (Legend.)

question: The magical seat in Hades that fused itself to Theseus and Pirithous was named for one of the five rivers of the underworld. Which river gave the seat its name?
context: The Chair of Lethe, also called the Chair of Forgetfulness after Lethe the underworld river of forgetting. Hades sat the pair down at a feast and coils of serpents wound them fast to the stone. Styx, Acheron, and Cocytus are the other named rivers of the classical underworld.  (Legend.)

question: Vase-paintings of Heracles's descent to fetch Cerberus almost always show him flanked by the same two divine guides through the dark of Hades. Which pair?
context: Hermes Psychopompos escorts souls; Athena is Heracles's lifelong patron and had already advised him at the very first labor. The other pairs are real god-pairs but not tied to Heracles's descent.  (Legend.)

question: Barred from using his club, his bow, or his sword, Heracles walked up to Cerberus at the gates of Hades wearing only the pelt of his very first labor for armor. How did he take the three-headed dog?
answer: He wrapped his arms around the necks and squeezed until the beast went limp
choices: He wrapped his arms around the necks and squeezed until the beast went limp
He fed it a drugged honey-cake and put it to sleep at the third head
He blinded all three heads with the light of a burning torch
He tied all three heads together with a strong braided rope
context: Apollodorus 2.5.12: Heracles used the Nemean lion-skin as armor against Cerberus's bite and choked the dog. The drugged honey-cake belongs to the Sibyl in Virgil's Aeneid VI, a different underworld story.  (Legend.)

question: Ovid tells that as Heracles dragged Cerberus up into the daylight the dog was blinded by the sun, twisted against the grip, and slavered white foam onto the Greek soil. Wherever a fleck of the drool fell, a poisonous plant is said to have sprung up. Which plant?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.408-419. Aconite (wolfsbane) is a real and deadly Greek mountain plant that Ovid traces to Cerberus's foam. Hemlock was famously used to execute Socrates; mandrake and nightshade have their own separate poison traditions.  (Legend.)

question: Down in Hades every shade fled from Heracles except one heavily armed ghost who was not afraid of him. When Heracles recognized his old comrade, the shade wept and asked him to marry his unwed sister Deianira on his return to the living. Who was the ghost?
context: The scene is preserved in Bacchylides, Ode 5. Meleager's request bound Heracles to marry Deianira, whose jealousy years later sent him the shirt of Nessus, poisoned with Hydra-blood, that finally killed him. Achilles and Patroclus die at Troy long after; Ajax kills himself at Troy.  (Legend.)

question: For his second labor, Eurystheus sent Heracles into a poisonous swamp in the Argolid to kill a monster that had been burning crops and eating the local cattle. What kind of creature was it?
choices: A giant boar with iron tusks
context: The Lernaean Hydra, born of Typhon and Echidna, lived in the marsh at Lerna (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.2). The other choices are all real Heracles-cycle monsters (the Erymanthian Boar, Cerberus, the Stymphalian Birds), from different labors.  (Legend.)

question: In the swamp at Lerna, Heracles landed the first solid blow with his sword. But what happened next made him realize the fight could not be won this way at all. What did the wound do?
answer: Two new heads grew back from the stump
choices: Two new heads grew back from the stump
The severed head kept biting on its own
The stump spat venom that blinded him
The body split into two full serpents
context: This regeneration is the wonder of the story: cutting a head off doubled the problem. It is why Heracles needed a second-order idea and a helper to win.  (Legend.)

question: Watching his uncle drowning in new heads, a young hero-in-training who had ridden into the swamp as his charioteer figured out the trick that broke the deadlock. Who was Heracles's helper?
context: Iolaus, son of Heracles's twin Iphicles, is Heracles's regular chariot-driver and nephew. Telamon and Hylas fight with him elsewhere; Philoctetes is the friend who lights his funeral pyre years later, taking his bow as thanks.  (Legend.)

question: The nephew's answer was to stop the stumps from healing. He ran up beside Heracles as each new head fell to the sword and pressed something against the raw wound so no fresh heads could sprout. What did he press against the stumps?
answer: A burning firebrand from a torched grove
choices: A burning firebrand from a torched grove
A cold blade pulled from a bucket of well-water
A handful of clay from the swamp-bank
A bronze cup filled with wine from the road
context: In some versions Iolaus set fire to a nearby grove to keep a supply of burning branches. Cauterizing the wound with the flame is what finally cleared head after head. Cold, clay, and wine are all plausible-sounding but only heat sealed the stumps.  (Legend.)

question: One of the serpent's many heads had a special property that no fire could touch: it could never truly die. When Heracles reached that final head, he cut it off but could not destroy it. What did he do with it?
answer: He buried it under a huge rock beside the road
choices: He buried it under a huge rock beside the road
He hurled it into the sea from the cliffs at Malea
He gave it to Iolaus to guard for life
He fed it to Cerberus at the gates of Hades
context: The immortal head was pinned under a boulder on the road from Lerna to Elaeus. It could not be killed, only trapped. Ancient travellers pointed out the very rock.  (Legend.)

question: When the swamp battle was finally over, Heracles did something with the serpent's body that made him more dangerous for the rest of his career: he took a permanent weapon-upgrade from the corpse. What did he do?
answer: He dipped his arrows in the blood
choices: He dipped his arrows in the blood
He cut a bowstring from the sinew
He forged a helmet from the scales
He wove a cloak from the shed skin
context: The serpent's blood was so venomous that from then on every one of Heracles's arrows carried an incurable poison. This one act sets up several of the later stories, including the death of the centaur Nessus and, in the end, Heracles's own death.  (Legend.)

question: Years after Lerna, a stray arrow from Heracles's poisoned bow grazed one of his own oldest teachers, an immortal being who had trained Jason, Asclepius, and Achilles up on Mount Pelion. The wound was incurable, and the teacher traded his immortality to Prometheus just to be released into death. Which of Heracles's teachers did he kill by mistake?
context: Chiron the immortal centaur, tutor of heroes on Mount Pelion, was grazed by a stray Hydra-poisoned arrow during a brawl among centaurs and gave up his immortality to end the pain. Nessus is the ferryman-centaur killed by Heracles at the river Evenus; Pholus is another centaur friend who died examining one of the same arrows; Silenus is the drunken old satyr-tutor of Dionysus.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles brought the corpse home to Mycenae and expected the labor to be checked off. But Eurystheus refused to count this one, and added an extra task later to bring the total up to twelve. Why did he refuse?
answer: A nephew had helped, so it was not a solo victory
choices: A nephew had helped, so it was not a solo victory
Heracles had used a weapon Hades had forbidden
Heracles had brought back only pieces, not the whole body
A nephew had killed the immortal head, not Heracles himself
context: The rule was ten labors done alone; because Iolaus had cauterized the stumps, Eurystheus struck this one off, and later did the same for the cleansing of the Augean stables, adding two more labors to make twelve.  (Legend.)

question: The serpent Heracles killed in the swamp had famous siblings, all born of the same monstrous parents. When Heracles later strangled the Nemean Lion and dragged Cerberus up from Hades, he was killing or capturing his enemy's own brothers. Who were the parents of all these monsters?
context: Typhon (the storm-giant Zeus buried under Etna) and Echidna (half-woman, half-serpent) produced the Nemean Lion, the Chimera, Cerberus, Orthrus, and the Lernaean serpent. Uranus and Gaia are Sky and Earth; Cronus and Rhea are the Olympians' parents; Nereus and Doris are sea-parents to the fifty Nereids.  (Legend.)

question: Years after Lerna, the same swamp-poison finally killed Heracles himself. His second wife Deianira, tricked by a dying enemy who told her his blood would keep her husband faithful, soaked a tunic in that blood and sent it to Heracles as a love-gift; when he put it on, the Hydra-venom burned into his flesh and could not be pulled off. Under what name is that famous garment remembered?
context: The dying enemy was the centaur Nessus, killed by one of the Hydra-poisoned arrows after trying to carry Deianira across the river Evenus. Heracles climbed Mount Oeta, built his own pyre, and asked Philoctetes to light it. The robe of Medea is the poisoned wedding-gift she sent Jason's new bride; the gown of Glauce is that same bride's burning dress; 'the cloak of Iason' is a distractor tied to Jason's name.  (Legend.)

question: For his third labor, King Eurystheus sent Heracles after a deer that lived on Mount Ceryneia. Two things about this deer set it apart from any ordinary hind. Its horns were gold. And its hooves were made of what?
context: Gold horns and bronze hooves are the standard details for the Ceryneian Hind in Apollodorus and Callimachus; the striking metal-pairing is what marks her as a sacred beast. Iron is too late a metal for Bronze-Age myth; silver is Artemis's bow-metal; flint belongs to arrow-heads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3.  (Legend.)

question: The gold-horned, bronze-hoofed deer of Mount Ceryneia was no ordinary animal. She had escaped long ago from the chariot-team of an Olympian goddess -- one of a set of magical sisters the goddess had yoked, and the only one to slip her harness. Which goddess did the hind belong to?
context: Callimachus's Hymn to Artemis names her as the owner of the golden-horned chariot-hinds; the escaped fifth became the labor of Heracles. Aphrodite's chariot is drawn by doves or sparrows; Athena's beast is the owl; Demeter's is the harvest-serpent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 100-112.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles could not use his club or his poisoned arrows on the hind, and she could outrun even an arrow. So the chase went on, and on -- across Greece, north through Thrace, into the far north and back. How long did the pursuit last in Apollodorus's telling?
context: Apollodorus says the pursuit lasted a full year, ending at the river Ladon in Arcadia (or on Mount Artemisius, or as far as the Hyperboreans in the far north, depending on the source). Three years is Odysseus's stretch with Circe; seven is the epic long-service span; nine days is how long Hephaestus fell from Olympus when Zeus hurled him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3; Pindar, Olympian 3.  (Legend.)

question: On the trail of the hind Heracles ran clear off the edge of the Greek map, into the land where Apollo goes each winter and the sun never quite sets. What did the Greeks call the blessed people who lived there?
context: Hyperborea meant 'the land beyond Boreas', the north wind; Apollo wintered there each year, and Heracles is said to have chased the hind to their edge. The Scythians and Thracians were real northern peoples the Greeks traded and fought with; the Cimmerians lived in perpetual fog and gloom in Odyssey 11. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperborea.  (Legend.)

question: On the way back through Arcadia with the hind in his arms, Heracles was intercepted by two angry Olympians who demanded to know why he was carrying off a creature sacred to their family. One was Artemis herself. Who was with her?
context: Artemis and her twin brother Apollo confronted Heracles on the road; he explained that Eurystheus had set the labor and promised to return the hind alive, and the twins let him pass. Leto is their mother but does not travel with her adult children in the stories; Zeus is above such quarrels; Hera loathed Heracles and would not have helped Artemis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Apollodorus 2.5.3.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles carried the hind alive into the courtyard at Mycenae and set her before Eurystheus. The king demanded she be kept in the royal menagerie for his amusement. Heracles had promised Artemis to return the beast, so he pulled a trick to keep both promises at once. What did he do?
answer: let her bolt free the instant Eurystheus had seen her
choices: let her bolt free the instant Eurystheus had seen her
handed her to a huntsman who let her escape overnight
asked Eurystheus to fetch her himself and dropped the rope
carried her back to Ceryneia during the king's afternoon meal
context: Heracles kept the letter of both promises: Eurystheus had 'received' the deer with his own eyes, and Artemis had her beast back alive and free. The other options are all thin variants of the same trick -- the classic version is the sudden release the moment the king's eyes were on her. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind.  (Legend.)

question: Callimachus's Hymn to Artemis explains where the golden-horned hind came from in the first place. The goddess had once caught a whole set of these magical deer as a girl -- yoking most of them to her chariot-team, all but one, who escaped to Mount Ceryneia and became the future labor. How many did she catch in that hunt?
context: Callimachus says Artemis caught five golden-horned hinds as a girl, yoked four to her chariot, and the fifth got away to Mount Ceryneia in the northern Peloponnese -- setting up Heracles's labor generations later. Three, seven, and twelve are the standard mythic small-numbers (three Graces, seven Pleiades, twelve Olympians), but the hinds are five. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceryneian_hind; Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 100-112.  (Legend.)

question: On the road to the boar, Heracles broke his journey at the cave of a wise centaur who set roasted meat before him but hesitated to open a jar of wine, saying it belonged to all the centaurs in common. What was the name of the friendly centaur who hosted him?
context: Pholus, the son of Silenus in Apollodorus, was one of the two civilised centaurs of Greek myth (Chiron the other). Nessus is the centaur Heracles kills later at the river-crossing with Deianira, whose poisoned shirt kills Heracles himself. Eurytion and Rhoecus are lesser centaurs of the wilder sort. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles opened the shared wine-jar in Pholus's cave anyway. The fragrant smell drifted out and drew the other centaurs down the mountain armed with rocks and pine-trunks. What weapon did Heracles use to drive the enraged centaurs back?
answer: arrows dipped in the blood of the Hydra
choices: arrows dipped in the blood of the Hydra
the jawbone of the Nemean Lion
a torch snatched from Pholus's fire
the club of olive-wood he cut on Helicon
context: The venom Heracles had drawn from the Hydra in his second labor becomes the poison on every arrow he shoots for the rest of his life -- and eventually the poison Nessus's shirt uses to kill him. The club, the lion-hide and the torch are all real Heracles gear but the centaur-rout is arrow-work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: One of the fleeing centaurs took refuge at the cave of the wise elder Chiron, tutor of Achilles and Jason. In the confusion Heracles fired one shot too many and the poisoned arrow struck Chiron himself. Chiron was immortal -- but the Hydra-poison meant he could not heal, only suffer. How did the story end his agony?
answer: Prometheus traded his own immortality with Chiron so Chiron could die
choices: Prometheus traded his own immortality with Chiron so Chiron could die
Zeus struck Chiron with a thunderbolt as a mercy
Apollo drew the poison out with a hymn of healing
Chiron leapt from the cliffs of Pelion into the sea
context: In one of the great cross-linked twists of Greek myth, Chiron's agony from the accidental arrow-wound is what frees Prometheus from the eagle -- Prometheus inherits Chiron's immortality and Chiron is allowed at last to die. Zeus later sets Chiron among the stars as the constellation Centaurus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiron.  (Legend.)

question: The wine-jar fight had a second casualty besides Chiron. Pholus, the very host whose cave the brawl began in, was picking through the aftermath -- some say he was marvelling at the arrows, some that he was helping bury the dead. How did Pholus die?
answer: he dropped one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot
choices: he dropped one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot
the last centaur to flee turned and speared him
he choked on the wine he had been forbidden to serve
Heracles killed him by mistake in the twilight
context: In Apollodorus, Pholus draws an arrow from a dead centaur to examine it, wondering how so small a thing could kill so large a creature; it slips, falls point-first on his foot, and the Hydra-poison kills him almost at once. Heracles buries him where he lies. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pholus_(mythology); Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles went on alone to hunt the boar. The trick of the labor was that the animal was too huge to bring in alive by ordinary fighting -- one swing of the club and he would have a dead beast, not a live one. Heracles chased the boar with shouts up the mountain until it was exhausted. What terrain finished the capture for him?
choices: a pit trap the shepherds had dug
context: Apollodorus has the boar driven uphill into deep snow, where it sinks belly-deep and can no longer move; Heracles then binds it in chains. The bog, the gorge and the pit trap are the shapes of other capture-stories in Greek myth (Bellerophon's traps, the Calydonian Boar hunt), not this one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erymanthian_Boar; Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles hoisted the bound boar onto his shoulders and carried it into the courtyard at Mycenae. When Eurystheus looked out and saw his cousin coming with a live, chained monster over his head, the king lost his nerve completely. Where did Eurystheus hide?
answer: inside a great bronze jar sunk in the ground
choices: inside a great bronze jar sunk in the ground
under his own throne with a cloak drawn over him
in the treasury vault behind the double doors
up in the watchtower with the archers
context: The bronze pithos sunk into the palace floor became the king's favourite refuge whenever Heracles turned up with a live monster; he had first used it after the Nemean Lion. Eurystheus gave the rest of his orders through a herald called down through the jar's mouth. The scene is one of the most-painted Heracles moments on Greek vases. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erymanthian_Boar; Apollodorus 2.5.4.  (Legend.)

question: For his fifth labor, Eurystheus sent Heracles into the land of Elis to serve one of the great cattle-kings of Greece. Which king held the largest herds in the country?
context: Augeas ruled Elis in the western Peloponnese and was famous for the size of his herds. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: Eurystheus meant the fifth labor as a humiliation as much as a physical impossibility. What single-day chore was Heracles told to finish at the palace of Augeas?
answer: Muck out thirty years of dung from his cattle-yards
choices: Muck out thirty years of dung from his cattle-yards
Wrestle every one of his bulls to the ground
Count every animal in his herds
context: The stables had not been cleaned in three decades, and the surrounding fields had gone uncultivable. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: Augeas kept the largest herd in Greece, said to be a gift from his divine father. Which god fathered him?
context: Theocritus's Idyll 25 says the enormous herd was given by the Sun to his son. Augeas was one of several 'children of Helios' in Greek myth.  (Legend.)

question: Before starting the fifth labor, Heracles went to Augeas and offered to clean the stables in a single day if the king would give him a share of the herd. What share did he ask for?
context: Augeas laughed and agreed, thinking the job impossible. Heracles brought a member of the king's own household in as witness to the deal.  (Legend.)

question: Faced with thirty years of dung and a single day to shift it, Heracles did not lift a shovel. What did he do to the cattle-yard instead?
answer: Broke open the walls and ran two rivers through it
choices: Broke open the walls and ran two rivers through it
Burned the whole yard down with a torch
Called down a thunderstorm from Zeus
Set his bull-team to trample the yard flat
context: He knocked a gap in the upstream wall and another downstream, ran the water through, then closed the gaps so the rivers returned to their beds. Apollodorus 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: To flush the stables of Augeas, Heracles rerouted a pair of nearby rivers straight through the cattle-yard. Which pair did he use?
context: Both are real rivers of the western Peloponnese and still flow today. The Eurotas runs by Sparta, the Achelous through Aetolia; the Scamander and Simois are the rivers of Troy.  (Legend.)

question: The rivers came, the dung went, and Heracles walked back to the palace to collect his tenth of the cattle. How did Augeas answer him at the gate?
answer: Refused to hand over anything he had promised
choices: Refused to hand over anything he had promised
Ordered his household to sing Heracles's praises
Handed over twice the agreed share
Named Heracles his heir on the spot
context: Augeas even denied ever making the deal, once he learned the labor had been imposed on Heracles by Eurystheus.  (Legend.)

question: At the hearing over the unpaid cattle, someone from inside Augeas's own household stood up and testified that the king had indeed struck the bargain. Who spoke against him?
context: Phyleus was banished from Elis for testifying against his father, and settled on the island of Dulichium. Apollodorus 2.5.5.  (Legend.)

question: Years after the broken bargain, Heracles came back to Elis to deal with Augeas himself. How did that reckoning end?
answer: Heracles killed Augeas and set the banished son on the throne
choices: Heracles killed Augeas and set the banished son on the throne
Heracles spared Augeas and took the promised cattle at last
Heracles was defeated and driven back to Tiryns
Heracles married Augeas's daughter and inherited Elis
context: Phyleus, who had testified against his father and been exiled for it, came back as the rightful king of Elis after Augeas fell.  (Legend.)

question: Eurystheus refused to count the fifth labor toward the total of twelve, ruling that Heracles had broken a condition of the labors. What was the objection?
answer: Contracted to be paid for the job
choices: Contracted to be paid for the job
Killed one of the sacred bulls
Left the job unfinished by nightfall
Called on Iolaus for help again
context: The bargain with Augeas disqualified the labor. Combined with the Hydra (where Iolaus's help was ruled out), Heracles now owed two extra labors to reach twelve.  (Legend.)

question: Later tradition said that after his victory over Augeas, Heracles founded a great festival of games at a sanctuary on the banks of one of the rivers that had washed the stables clean. Which festival did he found?
context: The sanctuary at Olympia sat on the banks of the Alpheus, one of the very rivers that had washed the stables clean. The Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean Games are the other three Panhellenic festivals, each with its own founding story.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles is set twelve labors by King Eurystheus, and most involve grappling with one huge beast. But the SIXTH labor is different: he is sent to clear out a whole FLOCK that has terrorised a Greek countryside. What kind of animal is this flock made of?
context: The sixth labor targets the Stymphalian birds -- a whole flock of man-eating birds nesting in the marshes of Lake Stymphalia in Arcadia. Wild pigs recall the Erymanthian boar (a single beast, labor 4); wolves belong to no labor; goats to the Ceryneian hind's forest (a single deer, labor 3, not a flock).  (Legend.)

question: Which Greek hero, working through the famous set of twelve labors set by King Eurystheus, is sent to clear out the man-eating birds of Lake Stymphalia?
context: The Twelve Labors are Heracles's, imposed by King Eurystheus at Delphi's instruction. Perseus killed Medusa and rescued Andromeda; Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Cretan labyrinth; Jason led the Argonauts after the Golden Fleece -- and, later, was attacked by the SAME Stymphalian birds after they fled Heracles.  (Legend.)

question: The Stymphalian birds are not ordinary birds. Their beaks and feathers are made of one specific metal -- so hard the birds can shoot the feathers out like arrows -- and their droppings are poison. What metal are their beaks and feathers?
context: Pausanias 8.22 and later mythographers describe the Stymphalian birds' beaks and feathers as bronze; the birds can loose the feathers like arrows, and their droppings poison crops. Iron is later than the mythic Bronze-Age setting; silver and obsidian belong to other traditions (obsidian is Aztec/Meso-American, out of lane).  (Legend.)

question: Heracles arrives at the lake with his bow but cannot reach the flock: the birds refuse to fly, the reeds hide them, and the boggy ground will not carry his weight. He needs a way to make the whole flock take to the air at once. Which Olympian goddess appears to help him solve the problem?
context: Athena, the patron of most Greek heroes (Perseus, Odysseus, Bellerophon, Heracles himself), appears in the Stymphalian labor. Hera is Heracles's lifelong enemy who set the labors in motion by driving him mad; Aphrodite is the goddess of love (her interventions are Trojan-War romances); Demeter is grain and the seasons.  (Legend.)

question: Once the rattle drives the whole flock into the air, Heracles picks the birds off with his bow. His arrows are not ordinary -- they have been dipped in the venom of a monster he killed in an earlier labor, and a single scratch kills. Whose blood or venom coats those arrows?
context: In Labor 2, Heracles killed the many-headed Hydra of Lerna and dipped his arrows in its poisonous blood; those Hydra-tipped arrows recur across later labors -- Stymphalian birds, Geryon, the centaur Nessus, and finally Heracles's own death when Nessus's blood turns them against him. The Nemean Lion (labor 1) yielded a hide impervious to weapons, not venom; the Cretan Bull and the Erymanthian Boar were captured alive.  (Legend.)

question: The birds Heracles does not kill scatter far, and generations later Jason's Argonauts run into them on a lonely island in the Black Sea. The Argonauts, warned by the seer Phineus, drive the birds off by copying Heracles's noise-trick -- but with the equipment they already have, clashing spears against shields. To which Olympian's island had the surviving flock fled (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2)?
context: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.1030-1089: the surviving Stymphalian birds settle on the island of Ares (Aretias) in the Black Sea, where the birds are already sacred to the war-god; the Argonauts clash spears against shields to raise a wall of noise -- exactly Heracles's krotala trick reapplied. Hades has an underworld realm, no island; Dionysus's islands are Naxos and Chios (wine, not war); Hermes has no cult island of this kind.  (Legend.)

question: For his seventh labor, King Eurystheus sent Heracles across the sea to bring back alive a magnificent white bull that was running wild through the fields and orchards. On which island was the bull loose?
context: Apollodorus places the seventh labor on Crete, where the bull was uprooting crops and knocking down orchard walls. Rhodes is Helios's island; Naxos is where Theseus abandons Ariadne after Crete; Cyprus is Aphrodite's home. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 2.5.7.  (Legend.)

question: The white bull of Crete had not always been wild. Long before Heracles was sent for it, the beast had come out of the sea, as a sign from a god to King Minos that his rule of Crete was rightful. Which god sent the bull?
context: Poseidon, god of the sea and of bulls and horses, sent the bull walking out of the surf as the sign that Minos held Crete by divine right. In return Minos had sworn to sacrifice the bull straight back to Poseidon. Zeus's own bull-form is the one that carried off Europa; Apollo's animals are the swan and the deer; Hephaestus is the smith of the gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.3.  (Legend.)

question: The trouble with the bull began before Heracles was born. Minos had sworn to sacrifice the sea-bull straight back to Poseidon in thanks for the sign. When the animal walked out of the surf, though, Minos saw how magnificent it was and could not bring himself to burn it. What did Minos do instead?
answer: substituted an ordinary bull from his own herd for the sacrifice
choices: substituted an ordinary bull from his own herd for the sacrifice
sacrificed a hundred lesser bulls together in its place
sent it in secret to be hidden in the mountain caves
carved a wooden image of the bull and burned that
context: Minos kept the sea-bull for himself and sent up a common bull from his own herd to the altar. Everything that follows -- Pasiphae's curse, the Minotaur, Heracles's labor, the Marathonian Bull, Theseus's early fame -- runs out of that one broken promise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.3-4.  (Legend.)

question: Poseidon's anger at Minos's broken promise did not fall on the king. It fell instead on his wife, whom Aphrodite was told to curse. Who was the queen of Crete, cursed to fall in love with the white bull?
context: Pasiphae was daughter of the sun-god Helios and wife of Minos; Aphrodite laid the curse. Europa is the earlier bull-carried queen -- Zeus took her to Crete as a bull and she became Minos's mother. Ariadne and Phaedra are Pasiphae's own daughters, both later tied to Theseus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 3.1.4.  (Legend.)

question: When Heracles asked Minos for help capturing the bull, Minos gave him a single condition before the hunt. What did Minos require?
answer: Heracles could take the bull if he could capture it alone
choices: Heracles could take the bull if he could capture it alone
Heracles must return the bull unharmed to Crete after the labor
Heracles must first swear an oath at the palace altar
Heracles must pay a tribute of a hundred cattle for the beast
context: Minos gave permission and no help. Heracles did the capture single-handed, wrestling the bull to the ground bare-handed -- exactly the pose on the black-figure vases, arm hooked over the horn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull; Apollodorus 2.5.7.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles carried the captured bull back across the sea and dumped it in front of Eurystheus at Mycenae. Eurystheus tried to dedicate it, as he had tried before with Heracles's other live catches. To which goddess did he try to dedicate the bull, only to have her refuse the gift?
context: Hera hated Heracles from the day he was born -- he was Zeus's son by another woman, and his very name means 'glory of Hera' as a taunt at her. She refused every gift that came from him, and this bull was no exception; it was set loose. Athena is Heracles's usual patron among the gods; Artemis owns the Ceryneian Hind; Demeter has no quarrel with him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_Bull.  (Legend.)

question: For his eighth labor, King Eurystheus sent Heracles to Thrace to bring back the four wild mares of King Diomedes, chained in bronze because no rope would hold them. What made these mares so feared across Greece?
answer: they had been fed on human flesh
choices: they had been fed on human flesh
they breathed fire like the bulls of Colchis
no bit or bridle could touch them
context: Diomedes had trained them on the flesh of travellers and shipwrecked strangers, an outrage against every rule of Greek hospitality; that outrage is what makes the labor a punishment as well as a task. Fire-breathing belongs to Aeetes's bulls in Colchis; winged horses to Pegasus and to the horses of the Sun; the bit-and-bridle line is a distractor -- the mares WERE controllable, they just had to be tamed the hard way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: The eighth labor took Heracles to the kingdom of Diomedes in the far north, up on a coast famous for its wild horses and its warlike tribes. In which country did King Diomedes rule?
context: Diomedes was king of the Bistonian people on the Thracian coast. This is NOT the Diomedes who fights at Troy in the Iliad -- that Diomedes is a Greek prince from Argos, on the other side of the Aegean. Colchis is where the Golden Fleece hangs; Thessaly is Achilles's country; Lydia is where Heracles later serves Queen Omphale. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Hyginus preserves the names of Diomedes's four mares. Three of them were Podargos, Lampon, and Xanthos. What was the fourth?
context: The four names in Hyginus's Fabulae are Podargos ('swift-foot'), Lampon ('shining'), Xanthos ('yellow'), and Deinos ('terrible'). Aithon ('blazing') is one of the sun-horses; Balios is one of Achilles's own horses at Troy (his brother is a different Xanthos); Phlegon is another sun-horse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Hyginus, Fabulae 30.  (Legend.)

question: The horses of Diomedes were kept in a stable no rope would hold. What material were the chains and mangers made of, in the traditional telling?
context: Bronze chains to bronze mangers -- the hero-age metal, the same material as Talos and as Eurystheus's own hiding-jar. Iron is a later metal that mostly stays out of Bronze-Age myth. Silver has no strength in it. Doubled hemp is the shape of a distractor -- the whole point of the mares is that NO rope held them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles did not sail alone to Thrace for the mares. He brought a small band of companions, and one of them was a young friend of his (some sources say his lover) whom he trusted enough to leave in charge of the captured horses while he went back to fight the king. What was the young man's name?
context: Abderus is the friend Heracles brings on this labor. Hylas was the boy who drowned when Heracles took him on the Argo (the nymphs pulled him into a spring). Iolaus is the nephew who helped with the Hydra and stays with Heracles for most of the labors -- so he is often confused with Abderus, but he SURVIVES this one. Philoctetes is much later, the boy who lights Heracles's funeral pyre. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles surprised the mares in the stable, broke the bronze chains, and drove them down to the shore. The king's own people, his tribe, came after him in force to take the horses back. What was the tribe called?
context: The Bistones were Diomedes's Thracian people. The Myrmidons are Achilles's men from Phthia. The Amazons will be Heracles's ninth labor, for Hippolyta's belt. The Lapiths fought their own famous battle -- with the centaurs, at Pirithous's wedding. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Apollodorus 2.5.8.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles ran back to the shore to fight the Bistones and killed King Diomedes in the battle. When he came back to the horses, though, the news was awful: his young friend was dead, torn apart and eaten by the very mares he had been guarding. In grief, Heracles founded a city on that coast in the friend's name. What city rose there?
context: The real Greek colony of Abdera on the Thracian coast traced its founding-legend to this labor and to Heracles's grief for his friend. Abdera was later famous as the birthplace of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras. Byzantium is the Bosphorus city (later Constantinople); Miletus and Ephesus are Ionian cities in Asia Minor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdera,_Thrace.

question: After Heracles killed King Diomedes in the fight with the Bistones, he had to deal with the mares themselves -- they were still wild with the taste of human flesh. What did Heracles do that finally calmed them?
answer: fed the king's body to them
choices: fed the king's body to them
made them drink from the river Nestos
yoked them to a plow for a full day
sang to them with Orpheus's lyre
context: In Diodorus and Apollodorus, Heracles throws Diomedes's body to the horses. Once they had tasted their own master, the beasts became calm and controllable -- the horror ended the horror. It is the same shape as Perillos the bronze-smith roasted in his own hollow bull, or Haman hung on his own gallows in the Book of Esther: the tyrant destroyed by his own instrument. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mares_of_Diomedes; Diodorus Siculus 4.15.  (Legend.)

question: The ninth of Heracles's twelve labors sent him far from Greece to the land of a tribe of warrior women beyond the Black Sea. What did King Eurystheus order him to bring back from their queen?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Eurystheus set Heracles to fetch the girdle -- Greek 'zoster', a warrior's war-belt -- of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. Older English translations call it a 'girdle', which is why the labor keeps that name.  (Legend.)

question: In the ninth labor Heracles was sent to bring back the war-belt of the queen of the Amazons, a tribe of warrior women whose city stood on a river on the south coast of the Black Sea. What was the name of the Amazon queen who owned the war-belt?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: the queen was Hippolyta. Andromache is the Trojan wife of Hector; Cassandra the Trojan seer-daughter of Priam; Iphigenia the daughter of Agamemnon sacrificed at Aulis -- all real names from adjacent Greek stories.  (Legend.)

question: Hippolyta's belt was not just a piece of armor -- it had been given to her by her own father, a great god of Olympus, as the token that she ruled the Amazons. Which Olympian was Hippolyta's father?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Ares, god of war, fathered Hippolyta and gave her the belt in token of her supremacy over the Amazons. In myth the whole Amazon tribe descend from Ares.  (Legend.)

question: Eurystheus, the king who set the labors, did not want Hippolyta's war-belt for himself. He wanted it as a present for a specific woman in his own household -- a priestess of Hera. Who did Eurystheus intend the belt for?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: the labor was set at the request of Admete, Eurystheus's daughter and a priestess of Hera. She wanted the Amazon queen's war-belt as a temple treasure.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles sailed with a small band of companions to the Amazon city of Themiscyra, expecting a fight. The queen came out to meet him at the shore. What did Hippolyta do?
answer: agreed to give him the war-belt willingly
choices: agreed to give him the war-belt willingly
sent him to consult the Amazon oracle
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hippolyta was impressed by Heracles and agreed to hand the belt over peacefully. For one moment the ninth labor was a friendly diplomatic errand -- which is what makes what happens next so bitter.  (Legend.)

question: Just as Hippolyta was about to hand over the war-belt in peace, a figure ran through the Amazon ranks in disguise, crying that Heracles was carrying the queen off by force. In the panic the Amazons armed and rushed the Greek ships. Who was the disguised troublemaker who started the battle?
answer: Hera in the shape of an Amazon
choices: Hera in the shape of an Amazon
Athena in the shape of an old woman
Aphrodite in the shape of a priestess
Artemis in the shape of a huntress
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hera hated Heracles as the son of Zeus by a mortal, and she went down to the Amazons herself in Amazon-shape to spread the rumor that turned the peace into a slaughter. The scene is a mirror of Loki in disguise or the Morrigan in disguise -- a goddess as a story-mover.  (Legend.)

question: The city of the Amazons, where Hippolyta welcomed Heracles and where Hera in disguise turned the peace into a battle, stood at the mouth of a river on the south coast of the Black Sea. What was the name of the river the Amazon capital stood on?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9; Herodotus 4.110: the Amazon capital Themiscyra stood on the Thermodon on the south coast of the Black Sea. The Styx is an underworld river; the Scamander runs at Troy; the Eurotas runs at Sparta.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles saw the Amazon warriors charging the shore in arms and believed Hippolyta had betrayed him -- that the offer of the belt had been a trap. What did Heracles do to the queen who had welcomed him?
answer: killed her and took the belt from her body
choices: killed her and took the belt from her body
took her prisoner and dragged her aboard
wounded her and left her on the shore
spared her and fled without the belt
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: believing Hippolyta had betrayed him, Heracles killed her, stripped the belt from her body, and fought his way back to the ships. Hera's disguise-and-rumor trick had turned a peaceful labor into the death of a queen who had done him no harm.  (Legend.)

question: Sailing home from the Amazons with Hippolyta's war-belt aboard, Heracles put in at Troy -- and found the king's daughter chained naked to a rock at the water's edge as a sacrifice to a sea-monster sent by Poseidon. Who was the Trojan princess Heracles found chained to the rock?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9: Hesione was the daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. Andromeda is the Ethiopian princess Perseus rescued (a very similar scene, different heroine). Iphigenia was sacrificed by her father Agamemnon at Aulis. Chryseis was Agamemnon's captive in the Iliad.  (Legend.)

question: King Laomedon of Troy had a habit of cheating his rescuers. He had cheated Poseidon over the building of the walls of Troy -- and when Heracles killed the sea-monster and freed Hesione, Laomedon cheated Heracles too by refusing the promised divine horses. Heracles came back later with an army and did what to Troy?
answer: sacked the city and killed Laomedon
choices: sacked the city and killed Laomedon
besieged the city and made a treaty
burned the walls but spared the king
carried off the temple treasures only
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.6.4: Heracles returned with an army, breached the walls, killed Laomedon and all his sons except young Podarces (who was ransomed and renamed Priam -- the same Priam who would rule Troy in Homer's war). This is the FIRST sack of Troy, a generation before Achilles.  (Legend.)

question: After sacking Troy the first time and killing King Laomedon, Heracles gave the rescued princess Hesione as a bride to the Greek friend who had been first over the walls in the fight. To which of his companions did Heracles give Hesione as bride?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.6.4 and 3.12.7: Telamon of Salamis was first over the wall in the sack and received Hesione as his war-bride. Their son was Teucer the great archer of the Trojan War; Telamon's other son Ajax the Great was born to his wife Periboea. Peleus of Phthia (father of Achilles) was on the same expedition. Nestor and Iolaus are other companions of Heracles from the wider cycle.  (Legend.)

question: After his father King Ban of Benwick dies of his wounds fleeing a burning castle, an infant is stolen from his mother's arms by a fairy who carries him down into her enchanted underwater realm and raises him there. He will grow up to be Arthur's greatest knight. Who is this fostered boy?
context: Vulgate Cycle, Lancelot en prose (c.1215-30); Wikipedia: Lancelot. Ban of Benwick's castle Trebes falls to King Claudas of Gaul; Ban dies fleeing, and the Lady of the Lake abducts the infant. Gawain is King Lot's eldest son. Tristan is the tragic hero of the parallel Cornish story. Percival is the innocent Grail-knight of the forest.  (Legend.)

question: The enchantress who fostered the boy taught him arms and letters and at last sent him out, still not knowing his own true name, to serve Arthur. He rode into Camelot with no device on his shield, no colour but plain white, and was announced only as the White Knight. By what title is his fairy foster-mother known?
context: Vulgate Cycle; Wikipedia: Lady of the Lake. The Lady (called Viviane in French tradition, Nimue in Malory) raises him in her otherworld realm and sends him out as a nameless White Knight. Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister and often his enemy. Igraine is Arthur's mother, not a foster. Ragnell is the loathly lady of Gawain's marriage tale.  (Legend.)

question: The first surviving romance to make Lancelot the queen's lover was written by the French poet Chretien de Troyes between 1177 and 1181 at the request of Countess Marie of Champagne. Its title names Lancelot the Knight of one particular object -- the object he climbs into to follow Guinevere after Meleagant carries her off. What is Lancelot called the Knight of in Chretien's title?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot ou le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177-1181); Wikipedia: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart. The cart is a criminal's tumbrel -- a shame-cart used to haul the condemned to the gallows; riding in it is a knight's disgrace, and Lancelot does it because it is the only way to follow the trail of the kidnapped queen. 'Knight of the Green Chapel' is Gawain's poem; 'Knight of the Two Swords' is Balin's tale in Malory; 'Knight of the Fountain' is Yvain's -- three real Arthurian titles.  (Legend.)

question: In Chretien's romance the queen is carried off to the otherworldly realm of Gorre by Meleagant, son of King Bagdemagus, and Lancelot chases him. To cross the river at Gorre's border Lancelot must pull off his gauntlets, grip a razor-edged span with his bare hands, and crawl across bloodied to the elbows. What weapon is that crossing shaped from?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Lancelot le Chevalier de la Charrette (c.1177-1181); Wikipedia: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart. The 'Pont de l'Espee' is a single giant sword laid edge-up as a bridge, one of the two entrances into Gorre. A spear-bridge, axe-bridge, or arrow-bridge would each be a plausible medieval-romance ordeal but is not the one Chretien invents.  (Legend.)

question: A daughter of King Pelles wants a child by Lancelot and enlists the sorceress Dame Brisen, who gives him drugged wine and gives the lady a ring of Guinevere's to fool him in the dark. He wakes in the morning next to the wrong woman -- but the night has already given him a son. What is the name of the child conceived at Corbenic that night?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XI; Wikipedia: Galahad, Elaine of Corbenic. Elaine of Corbenic is the mother; Galahad grows up to be the one pure knight who alone sees the Grail uncovered -- the purity Lancelot himself could not attain. Bors is Lancelot's cousin, also a Grail knight. Perceval finds the Grail castle first but does not achieve it. Mordred is Arthur's incest-son and the future usurper of Camelot.  (Legend.)

question: The lady who deceived Lancelot at Corbenic follows him to Camelot months later and tricks him a second time; this time Guinevere finds them together, and the queen in a rage drives Lancelot from court with words he cannot bear. He runs from the palace, throws himself from a window, and disappears into the forest, forgotten. For how long does Lancelot wander mad in the wilderness before he is found again?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books XI-XII; Wikipedia: Lancelot. Malory gives the interval as two years (some earlier French versions say five); Lancelot is fed by hermits and shepherds and does not know his own name. Forty days is the biblical wilderness. Seven weeks and twelve summers are period-plausible distractors that Malory does not use.  (Legend.)

question: The tie between Lancelot and the lady who conceived Galahad is not the sort a knight breaks lightly. Long after the Grail quest, when Malory looks back on the girl who tricked Lancelot into her bed with Brisen's wine and the borrowed ring, and afterward brought the mad Lancelot to the Grail to be healed, he still names her by the castle her father ruled. What is the full name Malory gives Galahad's mother?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books XI-XII; Wikipedia: Elaine of Corbenic. Malory has several Elaines and this one is the daughter of King Pelles at the Grail castle Corbenic. Elaine of Astolat is the Fair Maid who dies of unrequited love for Lancelot in a barge floated to Camelot. Elaine of Garlot is Arthur's half-sister, wife of King Nentres. Elaine of Benwick is Lancelot's own mother, wife of King Ban.  (Legend.)

question: In the last chapter of Malory (Book XXI ch.13), Lancelot dies as a hermit at Glastonbury after Guinevere is gone. His companions find him in the morning laid out with a smile on his face. And one of the hermits with him, a former bishop of Canterbury, wakes laughing -- he has dreamed something he tells them at once. What does the bishop dream at Lancelot's death?
choices: the Grail carried up the aisle
the Lady of the Lake returning Excalibur
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.13; Wikisource. The bishop tells them: 'here was Sir Launcelot with me with more angels than ever I saw men in one day, and I saw the angels heave up Sir Launcelot unto heaven, and the gates of heaven opened against him.' The other three answers are all Arthurian endings this scene is NOT -- the Grail is Galahad's ending; the Round Table breaks and is not remade; Bedivere returns Excalibur at Arthur's death, not Lancelot's.  (Legend.)

question: At Corbenic the covered Grail passes over sleeping Lancelot in the night and heals his madness, but for all his greatness he never sees it uncovered. Malory carries the vision on to the far city of Sarras, where one knight alone of all Arthur's court kneels before the Grail unveiled and dies in that same hour, taken up. Who is the one knight who sees the Grail unveiled at Sarras?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XVII; Wikipedia: Galahad, Sarras. Galahad -- Lancelot's own son by Elaine of Corbenic -- is the virgin knight who alone achieves the uncovered vision at Sarras and dies at that moment. Bors is the third companion who survives and returns to Camelot to tell the tale. Perceval reaches Sarras with Galahad and dies soon after as a hermit. Lancelot is shut out by the adultery with Guinevere -- the one flaw the Grail tests -- and his son achieves what he could not.  (Legend.)

question: Lawrence was in charge of the Roman church's silver plate, its help to the widows and the poor, and its ledger of every gift the church held -- the office ranked just below the bishop himself. What was Lawrence's title in the church of Rome?
context: The archdeacon was the chief of all the deacons of a city church, in charge of its property and its charity. Deacon, subdeacon, and acolyte are the ranks beneath him. Above the archdeacon stood only the bishop. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.
