question: The Roman prefect who arrested Lawrence had heard rumours that the Roman church was very rich, and demanded that Lawrence hand over its TREASURES. Lawrence's famous answer was to gesture at a line of people he had brought with him and to say, 'THESE are the treasures of the Church.' Who were the people standing behind him?
answer: The poor and crippled of Rome
choices: The poor and crippled of Rome
The bishops of Italy in exile
The other deacons of the city
The virgins who served the altar
context: Ambrose of Milan reports this scene about a century after the event. Lawrence had spent his three days' grace selling every gold vessel the church owned and distributing the money to the widows, sick, and poor of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: The emperor whose sharp 258 edict against the Christian clergy of the whole empire fell on Lawrence, on Pope Sixtus II in Rome, and on Bishop Cyprian in Carthage all in the space of a few weeks was a soldier-emperor sixty years old who would himself, two years later, be captured alive by the Persian king Shapur I -- one of only two Roman emperors ever taken alive by an enemy. Which emperor?
context: Valerian's edict of 258 fell heaviest on the church's leadership: Pope Sixtus II was beheaded on 6 August, Lawrence roasted on 10 August, Cyprian of Carthage beheaded on 14 September of the same year. Valerian himself was captured by Shapur I two years later in 260 and died in Persian hands. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: Lawrence's boss, the bishop of Rome, was arrested first and taken away to be beheaded. As they led him past Lawrence in the street the old bishop turned back to the weeping young deacon and told him he would follow within THREE DAYS. Who was the bishop of Rome executed just before Lawrence?
context: Sixtus II was beheaded on 6 August 258; Lawrence followed on 10 August, four days later. The scene of Sixtus's farewell on the road to execution is one of the earliest reported details of the story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: When the Roman prefect demanded Lawrence hand over the church's silver and gold, Lawrence did not refuse outright. He asked for a short window to gather it all -- just enough time to secretly sell every vessel and hand the money to the widows and crippled of Rome before he came back with his parade of the poor. How many days' grace did Lawrence ask the prefect for?
context: The three-day grace period is the hinge of the story: it is exactly enough time for Lawrence to convert every gold vessel in the Roman church into food, coin, and medicine for the poor, so that when the prefect arrived to collect gold he was shown a crowd of beggars instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman prefect, humiliated by Lawrence's answer about the 'treasures of the Church,' refused to grant him the simple beheading Pope Sixtus II had already received. He ordered something slow and theatrical enough to break the young deacon's nerve on the Esquiline Hill in view of the city. What did the prefect have Lawrence killed on?
context: The site of the martyrdom on the Esquiline Hill is now occupied by the church of San Lorenzo in Panisperna. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.  (Legend.)

question: Lawrence's death date is one of the sharpest dates in the Roman calendar. Italian folklore later tied it to a natural event in the summer night sky that happens every year within a day or two of it, and to the harvest of certain golden pears named after him. On what date did Lawrence die?
context: The Perseid meteor shower peaks on 12-13 August, right after Lawrence's 10 August feast. Sixtus II fell on 6 Aug; Cyprian of Carthage was beheaded on 14 September of the same year; 29 June is Peter and Paul. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: The Italian folk-name for the Perseid meteor shower, which peaks in the sky every August around the anniversary of Lawrence's death, is a poetic reference to the fire that killed him. What are the streaks of light called in that folk-name?
context: In Italian: 'le lacrime di San Lorenzo.' The peak of the Perseids falls on 12-13 August, right after his 10 August feast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: King Philip II of Spain built one of the largest Renaissance buildings in the world -- a colossal grey monastery-palace-tomb north of Madrid whose whole rectangular floor plan is deliberately shaped like a Roman cooking grill in Lawrence's memory. What is the palace called?
context: Full name San Lorenzo de El Escorial. Philip started it in 1563 in thanks for his victory at St Quentin on 10 August 1557 -- Lawrence's feast day. Construction ran 1563-1584 under Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Escorial.

question: One historian in the last century, Patrick J. Healy, has argued that the gridiron may not have been the real instrument at all. He suggests the tradition may rest on a single copying mistake in Latin: an earlier text saying 'passus est' (he suffered) misread by a scribe as one letter different -- 'assus est' (he was roasted) -- and then dramatised outward from there. If Healy is right, how would Lawrence actually have been killed?
answer: Beheaded, like Pope Sixtus II days before
choices: Beheaded, like Pope Sixtus II days before
Thrown to lions in the Colosseum
context: Healy's minority argument is that the standard Roman execution of a clergyman in 258 was the sword, and that the whole cooking-grill drama grew from that one-letter scribal slip. The gridiron is nonetheless what Ambrose and Prudentius already report within a century, so the tradition is deeply rooted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_of_Rome.

question: Jesus tells a parable in Luke 16 about two men who die on the same day. One is a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen who feasts every day at his own table; the other is a poor beggar covered in sores who lies outside the rich man's gate hoping for the scraps that fall. What is the poor beggar's name?
context: Luke 16:20 (KJV): 'a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores.' This is the parable-Lazarus -- NOT the historical Lazarus of Bethany whom Jesus raises from the tomb in John 11. Bartimaeus was the blind beggar of Jericho; Nicodemus came to Jesus by night; Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore tree. Source: Luke 16:19-21 (KJV).

question: In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the poor beggar is not alone at the rich man's gate: an unclean animal from the street keeps him company, coming to lick his sores as he lies there. What animals does Luke's gospel say came?
context: Luke 16:21 (KJV): 'moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.' The image doubles the horror of the rich man's neglect -- even street dogs pay Lazarus more mind than the master of the house. Source: Luke 16:19-21 (KJV).

question: In torment across the great gulf, the rich man cries out to Abraham with one small, desperate request. He does not ask to be freed, or brought over. He only asks that the beggar Lazarus be sent to him to do one specific thing to give him a moment's ease. In Luke 16, what does the rich man ask Lazarus to do?
answer: Dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue
choices: Dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue
Say a single prayer to Abraham on his behalf
Fetch a length of cloth to cover his burning eyes
Lead him quietly across the gulf to the other side
context: Luke 16:24 (KJV): 'send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.' The horror of the image is the smallness of the request against the size of the refusal. Source: Luke 16:19-31 (KJV).

question: Abraham refuses to send Lazarus with the drop of water, because -- he tells the rich man -- something has been set in place between the two sides of the dead that cannot be crossed by anyone from either direction. What image does Abraham use in Luke's gospel for this barrier?
context: Luke 16:26 (KJV): 'between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.' Source: Luke 16:19-31 (KJV).

question: In Matthew 25 the king welcomes the sheep on his right with a great blessing, because -- he tells them -- when he was hungry they fed him, when he was thirsty they gave him drink, when he was naked they clothed him, when he was sick they visited him. The sheep are baffled and protest that they never saw the king in any such state. The king answers with the line the whole parable turns on: 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of ______ of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' Fill in the missing word.
context: Matthew 25:40 (KJV): 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' From this scene the medieval church drew the Seven Corporal Works of Mercy -- feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the stranger, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, and (added later from the Book of Tobit) bury the dead -- which shaped hospitals, hospices, and prison-visiting orders across centuries. Source: Matthew 25:31-46 (KJV); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_works_of_mercy.

question: Robin Hood's second-in-command in the Merry Men is a giant of a man -- the ballads say he stands seven feet tall and is the biggest fighter in the band. Everyone calls him 'Little John' as a joke. What is his ACTUAL birth-name, the one the joke inverts?
context: His true name in the seventeenth-century broadside 'Robin Hood and Little John' (Child 125) is JOHN LITTLE; the outlaws swap his first name and surname to make 'Little John' as an ironic nickname. 'Nailer' or 'Naylor' is given as his surname in some late versions -- adjacent but not the joke-inversion form. Miller and Scarlet belong to other Merry Men (Much the Miller's Son and Will Scarlet). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: The joke behind the nickname 'Little John' is that the man is anything but little -- the ballads make a point of his enormous size. How TALL do the ballads say John Little stands?
context: The seventeenth-century broadside describes him as 'seven feet high, large-limbed, and fearsome to behold'; medieval Englishmen averaged about five foot seven, so a seven-foot man was a walking marvel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: The origin-story of how Little John joined the band is told in a seventeenth-century broadside ballad. Robin, walking alone through the forest, comes to a long narrow crossing over a stream and meets a stranger coming the other way -- neither will step aside. What kind of CROSSING are they standing on?
context: Child Ballad 125 'Robin Hood and Little John': 'They happened to meet on a long narrow bridge / And neither of them would give way.' The bridge duel becomes iconic -- every later film and pantomime uses it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: The stranger on the bridge is armed with the poor man's fighting-weapon of the English commons -- cheap, two-handed, needing no gentry training and no royal license. Robin, who is carrying only his longbow, lays it down and goes into a thicket to cut a matching one of his own from a young oak, so that the fight will be fair. Which COMMONER'S WEAPON is the duel fought with?
context: The quarterstaff was the standard peasant and yeoman weapon of medieval and early-modern England -- a two-handed wooden stave about six to nine feet long. Robin's own bow is put aside so the stranger is not disadvantaged. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: The two men trade blows 'thick and fast' on the narrow bridge. In the end, one of them lands a great stroke that sends the other tumbling off the bridge and into the water below. WHICH man wins the duel?
answer: the stranger knocks Robin into the brook
choices: the stranger knocks Robin into the brook
Robin knocks the stranger into the brook
the two men yield at the same moment
the stranger yields and swims away
context: Child 125: 'The blow it so bent his bones, / That he tumbled him into the brook.' The whole point of the story is that Robin -- the greatest outlaw in England -- is dunked in a stream by a total newcomer; that is why the man earns a place in the band. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal125.html.  (Legend.)

question: Dripping and laughing, Robin wades out of the brook and summons his men to meet the stranger who has just bested him. What INSTRUMENT does he sound?
context: The ballad: 'He blowd a loud blast on his fine bugle-horn.' The bugle-horn -- a curved cattle-horn with a mouthpiece -- is the standard summoning-signal of the Sherwood band. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood_and_Little_John.  (Legend.)

question: When the Merry Men arrive, one of them serves as 'godfather' in a mock baptism to give the stranger a new name in the band. He pours brook-water over the giant's head and announces the new name -- by INVERTING the man's first and last names. WHICH Merry Man performs the christening?
context: Child 125: 'William Stutely then said, this jocular blade / Shall be Godfather to him.' Stutely (also spelled Stukely or Stutley) is a Merry Man from several ballads. Much the Miller's Son, Will Scarlet, and Alan-a-Dale are all real named companions -- but the christening job in this ballad is Stutely's alone. Source: boldoutlaw.com/rhbal/bal125.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the great fifteenth-century poem 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (Child 117), Little John pulls off a piece of espionage against the Sheriff of Nottingham -- he goes into service inside the Sheriff's own household as a disguised servant. What FALSE NAME does he give the Sheriff at the hiring?
context: A Gest of Robyn Hode, Fytte 3: 'Reynolde Grenelefe' is Little John's alias in the Sheriff's kitchens -- an in-joke, since 'green leaf' hints at the greenwood he has come from. Holderness is a real district of the East Riding of Yorkshire. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.  (Legend.)

question: In A Gest of Robyn Hode, Little John carries Robin's message to an impoverished knight who has fallen into debt to the greedy Abbot of St Mary's Abbey. Robin lends the knight 400 pounds to redeem his lands. What is the KNIGHT'S name?
context: Fyttes 1-4 of the Gest turn on Robin's rescue of the poor knight Sir Richard at the Lee, who repays every penny with interest a year later. Sir Guy of Warwick is the hero of a different English romance; Sir Kay is Arthur's foster-brother; Aymer de Valence was a real Earl of Pembroke, unconnected. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.  (Legend.)

question: In the ballad of Robin's death at Kirklees Priory (Child 120), the prioress bleeds Robin to death by treachery. Little John smashes the priory doors to reach his old chief but is too late. From a window Robin looses his last arrow into the woods and gives Little John one final order about that arrow. What does he ask?
answer: bury me where the arrow falls
choices: bury me where the arrow falls
burn this priory to the ground
hang me from the greenwood oak
context: In the B-text of Child 120 'Robin Hood's Death', the dying Robin shoots one last shaft from the window and asks Little John to bury him on the spot where it lands. Robin explicitly REFUSES the burning of the priory -- 'I never hurt woman in all my life / Nor man in a woman's company.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: For centuries a Derbyshire churchyard has kept an unusually long grave-mound that local tradition points out as Little John's own burial place -- a modern tombstone still marks it. In WHICH English village is the traditional grave shown?
context: St Michael's churchyard in the village of HATHERSAGE, Derbyshire, has for centuries been shown to visitors as Little John's grave -- an over-long mound with a modern tombstone. There is no historical proof, but the tradition is old. Barnsdale is Robin's Yorkshire haunt; Loxley is the village some legends give as Robin's birthplace; Kirklees is where Robin died. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_John.

question: On the morning of the fatal battle in the Aided Con Culainn, the charioteer Loeg went out as usual to yoke the chariot. But the Grey of Macha would not let him. The horse turned his left side three times against Loeg; only when Cu Chulainn himself came out did the horse consent to the harness. As the harness was being set, one further omen came from the horse himself. What did the Grey do as the harness went on?
answer: he wept tears of blood onto Cu Chulainn's feet
choices: he wept tears of blood onto Cu Chulainn's feet
he tore his own bridle-rein in his teeth
he cast his own shoe into the fire
he stamped a print into the flagstones
context: The tears-of-blood omen is one of the darkest images in the whole cycle; the Grey knows what the day will bring. Loeg had never been refused before that morning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: The killings at the fatal battle came in a very deliberate order. Lugaid mac Con Roi held three magical spears and each was prophesied to kill a king. His FIRST spear did not take Cu Chulainn. Whom did the first of the three prophesied spears take instead?
answer: Loeg the charioteer -- 'the king of chariot-drivers'
choices: Loeg the charioteer -- 'the king of chariot-drivers'
the Grey of Macha -- 'the king of horses'
the Black of Saingliu -- 'the king of dark runners'
context: The three-spear order in the Aided Con Culainn: first spear takes Loeg (king of charioteers); second spear takes the Grey of Macha (king of horses); third spear takes Cu Chulainn himself. The prophecy attached to each spear is that it will fell a king, and each does. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1eg  (Legend.)

question: Loeg the charioteer was more than a driver: he carried out Otherworld errands for Cu Chulainn as well. In the tale Serglige Con Culainn ('The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn'), Loeg is sent alone into the fairy country with a strange guide to bring back a report on the woman his lord has fallen for. Who guides Loeg into the Otherworld to scout for his master?
answer: Li Ban, sister of the fairy Fand
choices: Li Ban, sister of the fairy Fand
Manannan mac Lir, sea-god of the wave
Cathbad the druid of Emain Macha
context: Li Ban is Fand's sister; she comes as messenger and takes Loeg into the Otherworld so he can describe Fand's country back to the bedridden Cu Chulainn. Manannan is Fand's own husband and closes the tale. The Morrigan and Cathbad are figures of a different cycle-strand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1eg  (Legend.)

question: After Cu Chulainn was dead upon the standing stone at the ford, and Medb's warriors held off at a distance, the wounded Grey of Macha turned back from the water and charged into the mass of the enemy to defend his master's body from being looted. The tradition counts the kill in specific numbers. What tally did the horse take with teeth and hooves alone?
answer: fifty men with his teeth and thirty with each hoof
choices: fifty men with his teeth and thirty with each hoof
twelve men with his teeth and twelve with each hoof
ninety men in total, evenly split among his four feet
a hundred and one -- one for each of the Fianna
context: The horse-tally is one of the most cited numbers in all of Irish heroic corpus: fifty by tooth, thirty by each of four hooves. It is the horse, not any man, that defends the corpse. The other three counts belong to no source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: When the wounded Grey of Macha had finished defending the corpse, he did not just run off to die. He crossed the country to Cu Chulainn's foster-brother -- Ulster's second-greatest warrior, the one bound to take the vengeance -- and led him back to the standing stone where the body lay. Which foster-brother did the Grey lead to Cu Chulainn's body?
context: Conall Cernach is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and the vengeance-taker of the Ulster Cycle; the Grey's guiding him to the body is what sets Conall on Lugaid mac Con Roi. Ferdiad was killed by Cu Chulainn himself at the Ford; Fergus was in Connacht exile; Loegaire had fled the beheading-bargain long before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liath_Macha_and_Dub_Sainglend  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories, one of the great banquet-hosts of the Aesir and Vanir is a sea-figure who brews ale in an enormous cauldron under the waves and invites the gods down to drink. Which Norse figure is this undersea host?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction (and Hymiskvida): Aegir (also called Hler or Gymir) is the sea-giant who hosts the gods in his undersea hall. Njord is the Vanir god of the coast (father of Freyr and Freyja). Jormungand is the Midgard serpent Thor will fight at Ragnarok. Utgarda-Loki is the giant-king who tricks Thor in the eastern lands.  (Legend.)

question: The sea-host has two named serving-men working the hall that night. The gods praise the first for his skill with cup and platter, and jealousy rises in one uninvited guest. What is the name of the servant whose praise sets off the trouble?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction: Aegir's two serving-men are Fimafeng and Eldir. The gods praise Fimafeng, and Loki kills him on the spot. Eldir is the second servant, who later meets Loki at the door when he tries to come back in. Skirnir is Freyr's messenger. Byggvir is Freyr's own servant, present at the feast and mocked by Loki later.  (Legend.)

question: When the gods heap praise on Aegir's serving-man Fimafeng, one guest at the table cannot bear it and does something that gets him driven out of the hall at once. What does Loki do to Fimafeng in his fit of jealousy?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna prose introduction: Loki, in jealousy at the praise the servant gets, kills Fimafeng on the spot. The gods shake their shields, howl at him, and drive him out into the forest before returning to their drinking. Loki will not stay outside for long.  (Legend.)

question: Loki, back in his seat at Aegir's hall, works his way down the benches -- one god at a time, one shame at a time, in matched verse. This old Germanic verse-form appears again in Beowulf when Unferth trades barbs with the hero at Heorot. What is the name of the form Loki is using here?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna: the poem is the great mythic exemplar of a flyting -- a formal verse-duel of insults. The same form appears in Beowulf when Unferth trades barbs with Beowulf at Heorot (lines 499-606), and later in Scots poetry. A saga is a prose narrative; a rune-cast is a divination; a nithing-pole is a real cursing-post erected against an enemy.  (Legend.)

question: Once Loki is seated again at Aegir's hall, he turns on Odin and throws in his face an accusation about magic Odin practised on the island of Samsey. What is the shameful thing Loki says Odin did on Samsey?
answer: dressed as a woman to work seidr magic
choices: dressed as a woman to work seidr magic
raised nine dead men to fight for him
sold his other eye for a second sip
murdered a sleeping king in his bed
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 24: Loki throws in Odin's face that on Samsey he beat a drum like a seeress and dressed as a woman to work seidr, a magic considered unmanly for a warrior. Odin does not really deny it -- he answers with an accusation about Loki's own strange forms (Loki once became a mare and bore Odin's own horse Sleipnir).  (Legend.)

question: Loki does not spare Odin's wife either. He accuses Frigg to her face of having gone to bed with two of Odin's own kin while Odin was long away from Asgard. Which two brothers of Odin does Loki accuse Frigg of sleeping with?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 26: Loki accuses Frigg of having slept with Vili and Ve, Odin's brothers, while Odin was away. Snorri's Ynglinga saga 3 echoes the same charge. Hoenir and Lodur are Odin's companions in creation-stories; Baldr and Hodr are Frigg's own sons; Bragi and Njord are guests at the same feast, insulted separately.  (Legend.)

question: Loki works his way down the benches of Aegir's hall. He does not spare Freyja either. He accuses her of the widest sexual shame he can invent -- but the sharpest point of his accusation is that among all her lovers she has also taken one specific member of her own family. Whom does Loki accuse Freyja of having slept with in her own family?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 30, 32: Loki accuses Freyja of having slept with every one of the Aesir and specifically with her own brother Freyr. Sibling-marriage was normal among the Vanir before their peace with the Aesir (Njord had married his own sister in Vanaheim, per Ynglinga saga 4). Njord is her father; Hnoss is her daughter by Od, her own missing husband.  (Legend.)

question: As Loki finally leaves the hall he throws one parting curse at his host -- a curse that promises the sea-hall itself will not survive the age of the gods. What does Loki curse Aegir's hall with, on his way out?
context: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna 65: Loki curses Aegir's hall that fire shall take it -- a curse fulfilled at Ragnarok when Surt's flames burn the nine worlds. The prose ending of the poem then names Loki's own coming doom: he will be bound with his own son's guts under a serpent whose venom drips on his face until the world ends.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the trickster Loki lives among the Aesir gods in Asgard, but Snorri opens Loki's genealogy by pointing out that Loki is not one of the Aesir by blood at all. What race are Loki's mother and father, according to Snorri's Prose Edda?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 33: Loki's father is the giant Farbauti ('cruel-striker', a poetic name for lightning) and his mother is the giantess Laufey (also called Nal, 'needle'). This giant-blood plus Asgard-oath split is why the gods keep having to punish and forgive him rather than execute him outright. The Vanir are the other tribe of gods (Njord, Freyr, Freyja); the elves and dwarves are separate races again.  (Legend.)

question: In the Poetic Edda poem Lokasenna, Loki walks uninvited into the sea-god Aegir's feast. Odin at once tells the other gods to bring a cup for Loki as well, and reminds them why he cannot be turned away. What bond does Odin invoke to make Loki welcome at the table?
answer: Odin and Loki are sworn brothers
choices: Odin and Loki are sworn brothers
Loki once saved Odin's life at sea
Loki is married to Odin's daughter
context: Lokasenna 9: Odin says he will not drink at the feast unless a cup is brought for Loki as well, because he and Loki once mingled their blood as sworn brothers. This oath -- an Aesir king and a giant-born trickster bound as brothers -- is the crack in Asgard through which everything Loki does gets in.  (Legend.)

question: Loki keeps a household in Asgard with a wife who bears him two sons named Narfi (or Nari) and Vali. Snorri names her only a few times, but her one great scene -- standing bowl-in-hand above her bound husband -- makes her one of the tenderest figures in Norse myth. What is the name of Loki's Asgard wife?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 33 (household), Gylfaginning 50 (the bowl-scene): Sigyn is Loki's Asgard wife and mother of Narfi and Vali. Angrboda is Loki's giantess-lover in Jotunheim, mother of Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel. Skadi is the giantess-goddess who fastens the snake over Loki's face. Idunn is the keeper of the golden apples.  (Legend.)

question: In Jotunheim Loki has a second household, with a giantess who bears him three children -- children so dangerous that Odin himself will one day throw them out of Asgard when they are still young. Who is the giantess who bears Loki's three monstrous children?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: Angrboda ('the boder of sorrows') bears Loki's three monster-children in Jotunheim. Gunnlod is the giant's daughter who guards the Mead of Poetry. Gerd is the giantess Freyr courts. Skadi is the huntress-giantess who becomes a goddess by marriage.  (Legend.)

question: Loki and the giantess Angrboda produce three children between them -- Snorri says the three are so dreadful that Odin has each one dealt with separately. Who are the three children Loki fathers on Angrboda?
answer: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the serpent, and Hel
choices: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the serpent, and Hel
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 34: the three are Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the Midgard-serpent, and Hel the queen of the dead. Sigurd, Fafnir, and Regin are the three central figures of the Volsung dragon-slaying cycle. Nidhogg is the serpent gnawing Yggdrasil's root, Garm is the hound at Hel-gate, and Managarm ('moon-hound') is one of the wolves that chase the moon. Skoll and Hati are the sun-and-moon chasers; Surt is the fire-giant of Muspelheim.  (Legend.)

question: At Ragnarok two of the great Aesir kings die at the jaws and fangs of two of Loki's own children -- one father-line producing the deaths of both. Odin is swallowed by Fenrir the wolf; Thor kills the second monster with his hammer Mjolnir but staggers only a few steps before dropping dead of its venom. How many steps does Thor take after killing Jormungandr before he falls?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 51; Voluspa 56: Thor kills the world-serpent Jormungandr with Mjolnir and staggers nine steps before dropping dead of its venom. Nine is a repeatedly sacred number in Norse cosmology (nine worlds of Yggdrasil, Odin's nine nights hanging on the tree). Odin, meanwhile, is swallowed whole by Fenrir; his son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart.  (Legend.)

question: The giant-mason who built the wall of Asgard on a wager was about to win the sun and the moon and the goddess Freyja for his fee. The gods forced Loki to sabotage the deal, and Loki lured away the mason's great stallion Svadilfari by turning himself into a mare. What was born of that horse-shape union with Svadilfari?
choices: the horse Gulltopp ridden by Heimdall
the horse Hrimfaxi that draws Night's chariot
the horse Blodughofi ridden by Freyr
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 42: Loki as a mare lured Svadilfari away for a night; some months later he returned to Asgard leading an eight-legged grey colt, Sleipnir, which he presented as a gift to Odin. Gulltopp ('gold-top') is Heimdall's horse. Hrimfaxi ('rime-mane') is the horse of Night whose bit-foam falls as dew on the earth. Blodughofi ('bloody-hoof') is one of Freyr's horses.  (Legend.)

question: In Snorri's smithing-contest of the six treasures, two dwarf-brothers named Brokkr and Sindri compete against the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi. When the gods judge which of the six is finest, the winning object goes to the god who will carry it into every battle for the rest of Norse story. Which of the six do the gods judge the greatest?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the gods judge Mjolnir the greatest of the six treasures because it will defend Asgard from the giants. Gungnir (Odin's spear, never misses) and Skidbladnir (Freyr's ship, folds into a pocket) were the Sons of Ivaldi's treasures. Draupnir (Odin's gold ring that drips eight copies of itself every ninth night) was Sindri and Brokkr's, alongside Mjolnir and the golden boar Gullinbursti.  (Legend.)

question: Loki had wagered on the outcome of the smithing-contest between the two dwarf teams -- and he had put up a very specific stake of his own body if he lost. When Brokkr wins the contest for the hammer, he comes forward to claim exactly what Loki had put up. What had Loki wagered against the dwarves' work?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki had wagered his head. Odin gave one eye for a drink from Mimir's well, and Tyr gave his hand to the wolf Fenrir. The tongue-cutting will come, in a way, later in the same scene -- but that is not what Loki wagered.  (Legend.)

question: Loki, cornered by Brokkr and about to lose his life, first tries to talk his way out. He offers Brokkr a rich alternative in place of the forfeit, and when the dwarf refuses, Loki bolts. Only one god is fast enough to run him down and drag him back for the dwarf. Which god catches Loki and hands him back to Brokkr?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor catches Loki and drags him back for the dwarf. Heimdall is the watchman at Bifrost. Tyr is the one-handed god of oaths. Vidar is Odin's silent avenger-son who will one day rip Fenrir's jaws apart. Note how ready Thor is to see Loki punished; he owes Brokkr a debt because the very reason Mjolnir's haft is too short is that Loki (as a fly) bit Brokkr during the forging.  (Legend.)

question: In the last moment before the dwarf's knife falls, Loki springs a lawyerly escape-clause on Brokkr -- pointing at the exact wording of the bet -- and the dwarf finds he cannot honour it. Which escape-clause does Loki suddenly name?
answer: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck
choices: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck
Brokkr must take the head without spilling a drop of blood
Brokkr must first speak Loki's true name backwards
Brokkr must take the head with his bare hand and no tool
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki tells Brokkr he may have the head but may not touch the neck -- because the wager named the head only. Brokkr cannot cut off a head without cutting a neck, and the exact wording of the bet gives Loki the wriggle. The move is one of the earliest surviving Indo-European trickster escape-clauses; it echoes into medieval legal riddles (compare Shylock's pound of flesh but no blood in Merchant of Venice).  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr's first attempt with his own awl fails -- the tool will not go through Loki's skin, however hard he presses. Snorri says Brokkr then wishes aloud for a very specific replacement, and the wish is granted at once. What does Brokkr wish for that finally punches through Loki's lip?
choices: a spark from the forge of Muspelheim
the point of a giant's tooth
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr wishes for his brother Sindri's awl, which is sharper, and it appears at once and punches straight through. Sindri is the master-smith of the two brothers; Brokkr is his bellows-worker and hands. Even in this dark comic scene the older-brother-and-younger-brother rhythm of the dwarf pair is preserved.  (Legend.)

question: With the sharper awl at last punching holes through the trickster's flesh, Brokkr sews Loki's lips shut with a length of leather thong. The thong itself has a name in Snorri -- the only named awl-and-thong in Norse literature. What is the name Snorri gives the leather thong Brokkr uses to stitch Loki's mouth?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the thong is called Vartari. Gleipnir is the ribbon-thin fetter that binds Fenrir the wolf (made from six impossible things -- a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, and so on). Vidofnir is the rooster on Yggdrasil's crown. Sviagris is the gold ring of the Yngling king Adils.  (Legend.)

question: The scene closes with the trickster stitched up and delivered back to Asgard. Snorri does not leave Loki that way forever -- he adds one grim note about what Loki's face carries from that day on. What does Snorri say remains?
answer: the scars where he tore the thong out of his own lips
choices: the scars where he tore the thong out of his own lips
a thin silver line where each stitch had been
a thong knotted at each corner of his mouth
a set of iron pins where the thong had been
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki rips the leather thong Vartari out of his own lips and the scars remain. The image of a trickster whose face carries the record of every lie he has been silenced for is one of the sharpest character-details in Snorri -- one of the very few places the Prose Edda lingers on a physical mark left by punishment.  (Legend.)

question: Before the wager even reached the head-forfeit, Loki had already tried to sabotage the forging itself. While Brokkr was working the bellows on the great hammer, Loki turned himself into a fly and bit him in one place hard enough to draw blood -- Brokkr took one hand off the bellows to wipe it, and that lost pressure is why Mjolnir's haft came out too short. Where did Loki-as-fly bite Brokkr during the third forging?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki as a fly bit Brokkr's eyelid during the third forging, and Brokkr took one hand off the bellows to wipe the blood away. That single moment of lost pressure is the reason (Snorri says) that Mjolnir's haft came out too short -- meaning even the flaw of the greatest hammer in the nine worlds is Loki's fault. Which makes Brokkr's later fury at the head-loophole richer still.  (Legend.)

question: The whole smithing-contest that ended with Loki's stitched mouth had begun because Loki had cut off a goddess's beautiful long hair while she slept, and had been forced to find the dwarves who could replace it or die. Whose hair had Loki cut off in her sleep to trigger the whole affair?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki cut off Sif's golden hair as a prank; Thor (Sif's husband) threatened to break every bone in Loki's body unless he brought her back real hair. Loki went to the Sons of Ivaldi, who spun the new hair from gold, and also produced Gungnir and Skidbladnir on the same visit. That is why Loki then goaded Brokkr and Sindri into a rival contest -- and how the whole six-treasures wager (and Loki's own head) came to be at stake.  (Legend.)

question: Loki flees the wrath of the gods and hides in the mountains. He builds himself a house of a strange shape on top of a mountain -- a paranoid architecture that turns the trickster's mind into a building. What is unusual about the house Loki builds himself on the mountain?
answer: it has one door on each of its four sides
choices: it has one door on each of its four sides
it is a tower with a single narrow door he can defend
it stands on high stilts with a ladder he can pull up
it is dug entirely into the earth with no windows
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki's house has four doors, one on each of the four sides, so he can watch the approach from every direction at once. The other three are inventions -- plausible watchtower shapes, but Snorri names only the four-door design.  (Legend.)

question: During the day Loki takes the shape of a fish and hides in a waterfall, catching food and watching for pursuers. Snorri names both the animal Loki becomes and the waterfall he swims in. What shape does Loki take by day, and in what waterfall does he hide?
answer: a salmon in the waterfall of Franang
choices: a salmon in the waterfall of Franang
a pike in the waterfall of Andlang
an eel in the waterfall of Elivagar
a trout in the waterfall of Vimur
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki becomes a salmon and hides in the waterfall of Franang ('the glistening'). The other three pair real Norse cosmological rivers/streams (Elivagar the primordial ice-rivers of Ginnungagap; Vimur the river Thor wades) with wrong fish -- the point is that only the salmon is named in the source, and salmon are the traditional wise-fish of Northern myth (compare Fionn's Salmon of Knowledge in Irish story).  (Legend.)

question: Sitting by the fire in his four-door house one evening, Loki idly weaves something out of linen thread that no one in the nine worlds has ever seen or made before. What does Loki accidentally invent while sitting by his own fire?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Loki weaves the world's first fishing-net from linen thread. When he sees the gods coming he throws the half-made net into the fire -- but the ashes preserve the pattern, and the gods copy it and use that first net to catch him at his own waterfall. It is a classic 'trickster caught by his own new tool' motif. The other three are real Northern catching-devices, but Snorri names only the net.  (Legend.)

question: Loki and his Asgard wife Sigyn had two sons named Narfi (or Nari) and Vali. When the gods drag Loki into a cave to punish him, they do not kill the sons themselves -- they turn one brother into an animal, and force him to kill the other. What do the gods turn the surviving brother into to make him kill his own brother?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: the gods turn Vali into a wolf, and he tears his brother Narfi (Nari) to pieces. The Loki-son called Vali here must not be confused with Odin's avenger-son Vali, who kills the blind god Hodr to avenge Baldr -- two different figures with the same name in Norse myth. The wolf is Norse myth's own recurring image of a family-killer (Fenrir will kill Odin at Ragnarok).  (Legend.)

question: With one son turned wolf and the other torn apart, the gods drag Loki himself into the cave to bind him. Snorri says they lash him to three flat stones -- one under his shoulders, one under his loins, one under his knees -- with a cord that then hardens into iron. What cord do the gods use to bind Loki to the three stones?
choices: a rope braided from his son Narfi's bones
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: the gods use Narfi's entrails, which then harden into iron -- an unusually cruel detail even by Norse standards, and one Snorri does not soften. The other three are body-derived bonds Snorri does NOT name; the horror in the source is specifically the entrails, laid on the father by his own son.  (Legend.)

question: Once Loki is bound to the three stones with the iron-hardened entrails, one goddess in particular steps forward to add her own cruelty to the punishment. She fastens a snake above his face so its venom will drip on him day after day. Who fastens the snake above Loki's face?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50: Skadi ('shadow') fastens a serpent above Loki's face so its venom will drip on him. Her father was the giant Thjazi, whom the gods had killed after Loki lured him into their fire-trap; Skadi had marched armed on Asgard for weregild and been made a goddess by marriage instead. The snake above Loki is her private revenge, at last, on the man behind her father's death. Frigg is Odin's wife; Freyja is the leader of the Vanir goddesses; Idunn keeps the golden apples.  (Legend.)

question: Loki's wife Sigyn, faithful even to a bound and shameful husband, does not abandon him in the cave. She takes her place beside him and holds one small thing above his face day and night. What does Sigyn hold above the bound Loki's face to protect him?
answer: a wooden bowl to catch the venom
choices: a wooden bowl to catch the venom
a mirror to reflect the venom back
a shroud to smother the snake
her own cupped hands to gather the venom
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 50 and the prose epilogue to Lokasenna: Sigyn holds a wooden bowl above her husband's face and catches the venom as it drips. The image of a wife standing over her criminal husband's centuries of torment is one of the tenderest in Norse myth -- and one of the earliest depictions of it survives in stone on the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria from around 900 CE, carved by a Christian mason who put it beside a Crucifixion scene.  (Legend.)

question: In Irish myth, a young warrior in a gold king's diadem came to the gates of Tara during King Nuada's feast, leading a company of warriors and asking to be let in. Who was this young stranger at the gate?
context: Lugh Lamhfhada, grandson of the Fomorian tyrant Balor through his mother Ethniu, arrived at Tara during King Nuada's feast wearing a diadem and leading a company of warriors. Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), CELT edition, sec. 53-55.  (Legend.)

question: At the gates of Tara the doorkeeper challenged the young Lugh with a single question, one every craftsman entering the royal hall had to answer. What was that question?
choices: How many battles have you won?
context: 'What art do you practice? For no one without an art enters Tara.' The rule turned the doorkeeper's post into a filter: Tara admitted skill, not birth. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 53.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh's epithet SAMILDANACH, given to him after the doorkeeper scene at Tara, is one of the most famous titles in Irish myth. What does Samildanach mean?
answer: Equally skilled in all the arts
choices: Equally skilled in all the arts
context: Samildanach is the honor Lugh earned at the gate by claiming every craft at once. His other epithet, Lamhfhada ('Long-Arm'), belongs to his skill with the spear. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55; Wikipedia, Lugh.  (Legend.)

question: At the gate of Tara, Lugh said 'I am a WRIGHT' (a builder). The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a wright and named him. Which of the Tuatha De was Tara's wright?
context: Luchta was the wright (carpenter) of the Tuatha De who made the shafts for their spears. Goibniu was the smith, Credne the brazier, Dian Cecht the physician. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: At the gate of Tara, Lugh said 'I am a SMITH'. The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a smith by that trade, forger of the weapons that would arm the Tuatha De at Moytura. Which of the Tuatha De was Tara's smith?
context: Goibniu forged the spearheads and blades of the Tuatha De and lent his name to the eternal Feast of Goibniu whose ale kept the gods young. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: At the gate of Tara, Lugh said 'I am a PHYSICIAN'. The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a physician by that trade, the healer who would restore the fallen at the Second Battle of Moytura. Which of the Tuatha De was Tara's physician?
context: Dian Cecht was the healer-god of the Tuatha De and would tend the Well of Slaine to revive the wounded at Moytura. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: In the doorkeeper scene at Tara, Lugh named craft after craft, and each time was told that Tara already had someone for that work. What was the one killing question he finally put to the doorkeeper that opened the gate?
answer: 'But have you one man who is ALL of these at once?'
choices: 'But have you one man who is ALL of these at once?'
'But which of your craftsmen can also swing a sword in the shield-wall?'
'But which of your smiths is also a poet of the court?'
'But which of your masters can beat the king at fidchell?'
context: 'Ask the king whether he has one man who possesses all these arts.' No craftsman inside could claim every trade Lugh had claimed; the doorkeeper ran to Nuada, who ordered the gate opened. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: In the doorkeeper scene, Lugh finally claimed to be a BRAZIER, a worker in brass. The doorkeeper answered that Tara already had a brazier, and named the smith-craftsman of the Tuatha De who worked in that softer metal. What was his name?
context: Credne Cerd was the brass-worker (cerd) of the Tuatha De, distinct from Goibniu the iron-smith. He would later forge the silver hand for Nuada. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 55.  (Legend.)

question: Once Lugh was inside Tara's hall, King Nuada decided the young man's arrival was so important that he made a sacrifice no king had made before. What did Nuada do?
answer: He gave up his own throne to Lugh for thirteen days
choices: He gave up his own throne to Lugh for thirteen days
He handed Lugh the sword he had carried at Moytura
He killed his own champion Ogma in single combat
He burned the royal hall to purify it before battle
context: Nuada rose from his seat so Lugh could sit in it for thirteen days to plan the coming battle with the Fomorians. Cath Maige Tuired sec. 74: 'it was easier that a king should stand for a champion than that a champion stand for a king.'  (Legend.)

question: One of the four great festivals of the medieval Irish year falls on the first of August and honors the foster-mother Tailtiu, who according to legend died clearing Ireland's plains for planting. What is this harvest festival called?
context: Lughnasadh ('Lugh's assembly') is the harvest festival Lugh founded in honor of his foster-mother Tailtiu. It survives as the August bank-holiday Lughnasa. Wikipedia, Lugh.  (Legend.)

question: Here is the surprise the modern films leave out. If you go back to the oldest Robin Hood ballads -- A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin Hood and the Monk, Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne -- and look for Maid Marian by name, how often does she appear in those three earliest ballads?
context: Maid Marian is never mentioned in any of the earliest extant Robin Hood ballads. The only woman in the Gest is the villainous Prioress of Kirklees, who eventually causes Robin's death. Marian is a much later addition to the legend.

question: In A Gest of Robyn Hode -- the great early ballad, and the oldest long Robin Hood text -- exactly one woman appears with a role in the story, and she is not a beloved: she is the villainess who eventually causes Robin's death. Who is the only named woman in the Gest?
context: In the Gest, the Prioress of Kirklees is the one woman with a role: she bleeds Robin to death under the pretence of a medicinal blood-letting. Marian does not appear at all in the Gest. The May-Queen belongs to the folk games. The Sheriff has no named wife in the ballads.  (Legend.)

question: Marian did not begin in the Robin Hood ballads at all. She began in the French pastourelle -- songs about a knight meeting a shepherdess -- and around 1283 a poet in Arras dramatized one such song as a musical play. In that play a knight rides up to the shepherdess Marion and tries to carry her off. Whom does Marion choose over the knight?
choices: no one -- she runs into the woods alone
context: In Adam de la Halle's Le Jeu de Robin et Marion (c. 1283), the shepherdess Marion resists the knight and stays with her shepherd-lover Robin. The play is considered the first musical drama on a non-religious subject written in French; it is the seed from which the English May-games pair of Robin and Marian later grew.

question: The French pastoral of the shepherdess Marion and her lover Robin crossed the Channel and took root in one particular English folk festival, where a village crowned its own Marian and paired her with a Robin. Which yearly English festival adopted them as its King and Queen?
context: In the English May-Day games a village girl was crowned May Queen and called Marian, paired with a village boy playing Robin. Twelfth Night and Plough Monday had their own customs (the Lord of Misrule; the plough-blessing). Michaelmas was a rent day, not a Marian festival.

question: For a long time the May-games Marian and the outlaw Robin Hood remained separate figures. In 1598 the English playwright Anthony Munday finally married them off in The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon, but with a twist: his Marian is really a noblewoman under a different name, and she only takes the name Marian when she flees to join Robin in the greenwood. What is her true name in Munday's version?
context: In Anthony Munday's plays The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1598) and The Death of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1601), the noblewoman Matilda takes the name Marian on joining Robin in the greenwood. Munday's two plays fixed Marian as Robin's wife and a full member of the outlaw band, the shape we know today.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir's third great treasure was a blade that no armor could turn aside, and whose point had a second, stranger power: when Manannan set the blade at a man's chest, that man could not tell a single lie. What is the sword called?
choices: Excalibur, the sword of the stone
context: Fragarach ('the Answerer') sliced through any armor and compelled its target to answer any question truthfully. Manannan later gave it to Lugh, and it walked through the whole later mythology. Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir did not keep his three great treasures for himself forever. He gave the Wave-Sweeper, Enbarr the horse, and the sword Fragarach as a gift to a young hero he had fostered. Who was the foster-son?
context: Manannan fostered Lugh in the otherworldly islands and armed him for the coming war with the Fomorians. Wikipedia, Enbarr; Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir rules a chain of paradise islands far out in the western sea, where dead heroes go and where nobody grows old. The first and most famous of these islands is called Emain Ablach. What does its name mean?
context: Emain Ablach ('Emhain of the Apples') is the paradise island of Manannan, filled with swans and yews and apple trees always in fruit. Wikipedia, Emain Ablach.  (Legend.)

question: Manannan mac Lir's Emain Ablach means 'Isle of Apples' in Old Irish. Centuries later, a paradise island appears in the Arthurian romances that also means 'Isle of Apples' and that scholars trace directly back to Manannan's realm. What is the Arthurian island called?
context: Avalon (Insula Avallonis in Geoffrey of Monmouth) shares its name and its whole picture with Emain Ablach: apple-orchard paradise where the wounded king is taken to be healed. Wikipedia, Emain Ablach.  (Legend.)

question: After the Milesians defeated the Tuatha De Danann and drove them underground, Manannan mac Lir took charge of what remained. He allotted each surviving god a sidhe mound of their own and fed them all at an eternal banquet whose ale kept them young forever. What was that feast called?
context: The Feast of Goibniu (Fled Goibnenn) was the eternal banquet whose ale conferred everlasting youth on the Tuatha De after their retreat into the sidhe mounds. Wikipedia, Manannan mac Lir.  (Legend.)

question: A goddess of Olympus invented a new instrument, the double-piped flute called the aulos. But when she sat beside a still pool to play it, she saw her own cheeks puffing out grotesquely in the reflection -- and she flung the flute away in disgust, cursing whoever should pick it up. Which goddess invented and then threw away the aulos?
context: Athena, patron of arts and crafts, invented the double-flute but cast it away when she saw how it disfigured her face; her curse falls on the satyr Marsyas, who picks it up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Fasti 6.697-710.  (Legend.)

question: When the Phrygian satyr Marsyas challenged Apollo to a music contest, the two brought their signature instruments. Marsyas brought his aulos, the double flute of loud reed-music. Which instrument did Apollo bring?
context: The contest is famously flute-against-lyre: Marsyas's wild reed-piping against Apollo's ordered stringed music. The syrinx (pan-pipes) belongs to Pan; the sistrum is an Egyptian temple rattle; the tambourine is the frame-drum of the ecstatic cults. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400.  (Legend.)

question: Before a note was played, the two musicians agreed on the terms of the contest -- and Marsyas, sure of his skill, agreed to a bargain no mortal should ever make with a god. What did the loser have to submit to?
answer: whatever the winner wished to do to him
choices: whatever the winner wished to do to him
a year of silent exile from Phrygia
context: The terms were open: the winner could inflict any penalty at all on the loser. It is a bargain made by trickster-figures and by fools; Marsyas is here the fool. Source: Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400.  (Legend.)

question: The first round of the contest ended in a tie: both musicians played beautifully. To break the tie, Apollo produced a new challenge -- one he could do with his lyre but Marsyas could never match. What was Apollo's trick?
answer: he played his instrument upside-down and dared Marsyas to do the same
choices: he played his instrument upside-down and dared Marsyas to do the same
he sang along with his instrument in the god's own voice
he played with his eyes shut behind a thick cloth
he handed his instrument to a Muse to play in his stead
context: Apollo inverted his lyre and played it just as sweetly upside-down, then challenged Marsyas to do the same with the aulos -- a physical impossibility for a flute-player whose breath drives the reeds. The Muses ruled for Apollo. Source: Theoi Project, 'Marsyas'; Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo carried out the punishment not on Olympus but in the Phrygian countryside, choosing a specific tree from which to hang the losing satyr upside-down. From what kind of tree was Marsyas hung?
context: Ancient tradition (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.391-393) places the flaying on a pine near Celaenae in Phrygia; the pine was already sacred to Pan and the satyrs. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.391-393; Wikipedia, 'Marsyas'.  (Legend.)

question: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, as the god's punishment begins, Marsyas cries out to Apollo in a single line that has become one of the most quoted in Latin poetry. What does Marsyas cry?
answer: Why do you tear me from myself?
choices: Why do you tear me from myself?
Give me back my breath, Apollo!
context: The Latin is 'quid me mihi detrahis?' -- Metamorphoses 6.385. The line has been read for two millennia as the cry of every artist stripped of his art. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.385.  (Legend.)

question: Long after the death of Marsyas, Apollo faced a second contest with a second flute-player: the goat-god Pan. This time only ONE mortal sat as judge, a king who happened to be listening in the hills. He alone judged the contest FOR Pan and against Apollo. Who was the mortal judge?
context: Midas of Phrygia -- the same king with the golden touch -- happened by while Pan and Apollo played, and alone judged for Pan. Priam ruled Troy; Croesus ruled Lydia; Tantalus is famous for his crime and eternal thirst. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.146-179; Wikipedia, 'Midas'.  (Legend.)

question: Apollo was so insulted by the mortal judge's verdict that he declared his ears must be as dull as an animal's, and reshaped them on the spot. Midas hid the shameful new ears under a tall Phrygian cap; only one servant, his barber, ever saw them. Unable to hold the secret in, the barber dug a hole in the ground, whispered the truth into it, and covered it over. What later grew from the covered hole and betrayed the secret to the wind?
context: Reeds grew from the covered hole, and every time the wind blew through them they whispered aloud 'King Midas has ass's ears'. The story is Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.180-193. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.180-193; Wikipedia, 'Midas'.  (Legend.)

question: One bitter winter night on the road into a city in northern Gaul, a young Roman cavalry officer named Martin came upon a beggar shivering nearly naked in the freezing wind. Martin had no money and nothing to give -- so he drew his sword, cut his only piece of gear in half, and handed one piece to the beggar. What did he cut in half?
context: The scene comes from Sulpicius Severus's Life of Saint Martin, chapter 3, written from Sulpicius's own conversations with Martin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: Martin was serving in a Roman cavalry unit at the gate of a specific city in northern Gaul when he met the beggar and gave away half his cloak. That city, still famous today for its great Gothic cathedral, is where the whole story happens. What city is it?
context: Roman-era Amiens was called Samarobriva. Martin was posted there with the Gallic cavalry around age 18. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: Martin was not born in Gaul but far to the east, in a Roman province of the middle Danube where his father served as a Roman military tribune. It is one of the four provinces the empire cut out of that stretch of frontier -- and the one Martin's birthplace of Savaria sat in. Which Danube province?
context: Martin was born around 316 in Savaria (modern Szombathely in western Hungary), inside the Roman province of Pannonia. Roman law required soldiers' sons to enter the army; Martin was pressed into cavalry service in his mid-teens. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: The night after he cut the cloak in half, Martin -- who was not yet baptised, just a catechumen learning about Christianity -- had a DREAM. In the dream he saw the beggar again, standing this time in the middle of a crowd of angels, still wrapped in Martin's half-cloak, and speaking Martin's name. Who did Martin recognise the beggar as?
context: Sulpicius Severus reports the words of the dream in Vita Martini 3: 'Martin, still only a catechumen, has clothed me with this cloak.' Martin was baptised at the following Easter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: Martin eventually got out of the Roman army when his unit was about to fight the Alemanni at Worms and he told his commander he could no longer serve as a soldier. Accused of cowardice, Martin made a startling offer to prove he was not afraid of the enemy. What did he offer to do?
answer: Stand unarmed in the front line of the army
choices: Stand unarmed in the front line of the army
Fight three of the enemy champions at once
Ride alone into the enemy camp with a message
Take his commander's place at the very front rank
context: Martin declared 'I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight,' and volunteered to stand at the front of the army without weapon or shield. The battle never happened -- the enemy sued for peace, and Martin was released. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: After his years as a hermit, Martin was chosen bishop of a city on the Loire in 371 -- against his own strong protest. The townspeople had to get him into the city by TRICKERY, because he would never have come willingly. How did they get him through the gates?
answer: They said a sick woman needed him to bless her
choices: They said a sick woman needed him to bless her
They said the city was under attack and needed prayers
They said his mother had arrived and was asking for him
They said a hunting bear was loose in the marketplace
context: Once Martin was inside the walls the townspeople of Tours acclaimed him bishop on the spot, and the neighbouring bishops confirmed the acclamation despite his protests. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.  (Legend.)

question: As bishop of Tours, Martin refused to live inside the city or in a bishop's palace. Instead he founded a monastery just outside the city on the bank of the Loire, and his own personal cell was dug into a soft rock cliff by the river. What was the name of that monastery, still remembered today?
context: The cliff-cells are still visible in the tufa above the Loire. Cluny, Fontevraud, and Fecamp are all famous French monasteries -- but they are all founded many centuries after Martin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: After Martin's death, the piece of the famous cloak he had NOT given to the beggar -- the half he kept for himself -- was preserved as a holy relic in the treasury of the Frankish kings. In Latin, that half-cloak has a specific name that became one of the most productive words in the whole of medieval Europe. What is the Latin word for Martin's half-cloak?
context: The other three -- toga, sagum, palla -- are all real Roman garments, but the Frankish relic of Martin's half-cloak is specifically called the cappa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours.

question: One of Jesus's twelve disciples had a job before he was called that made his neighbours despise him: he sat at a customs booth on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee, collecting money for Rome. Which of the Twelve came from that hated profession?
context: Matthew 9:9. In first-century Judea, publicans -- men who bought the right to collect Roman customs and taxes and skimmed a living off the top -- were treated as collaborators with the occupying power. Matthew's fellow Jews grouped them in a single scornful phrase with sinners.

question: Walking along the shore near Capernaum, Jesus stopped in front of Matthew's customs booth and spoke only two words to the man sitting there. What two words did Jesus say?
context: Matthew 9:9: 'and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.' Mark and Luke tell the same scene, using Matthew's other name -- Levi.

question: In Mark's gospel and Luke's gospel, the man sitting at the tax booth outside Capernaum is not called Matthew at all -- both books give him a different personal name for the calling scene. What other name do Mark and Luke use for him?
context: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 name him Levi (Mark adds that he was 'the son of Alphaeus'). Christian tradition identifies Levi and Matthew as the same man -- he seems to have gone by both.

question: Right after he was called, Matthew threw open his own house and put on a great banquet for Jesus. The Pharisees, watching from outside, were scandalised by the guest list -- Luke and Matthew's gospels sum up the crowd at the tables in one blunt phrase. What phrase names that dinner crowd?
context: Luke 5:29 says Levi 'made him a great feast in his own house', and Matthew 9:10 notes the guests were 'many publicans and sinners' -- fellow tax collectors and the outcasts who kept them company.

question: Around the year 130, a bishop named Papias of Hierapolis wrote a line about Matthew that the church historian Eusebius later preserved in his Church History (book 3, chapter 39). Papias claimed Matthew first put down Jesus's sayings in one particular language before they reached the wider Greek-speaking world. Which language did Papias say Matthew originally used?
context: Papias, quoted in Eusebius Church History 3.39: 'Matthew collected the oracles [logia] in the Hebrew language, and each one interpreted them as best he could.' The gospel we now read is in Greek; what Papias meant by the Hebrew original is one of the oldest puzzles in New Testament study.

question: Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew hangs in a specific Rome church, in the Contarelli Chapel, alongside two other Caravaggio paintings of the same apostle. All three canvases have been on those chapel walls since around 1600. In which Rome church is that chapel?
context: The Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi holds all three Caravaggio Matthew paintings: The Calling on the left wall, The Martyrdom on the right, and The Inspiration over the altar between them.

question: The Calling of Saint Matthew was not painted alone. Caravaggio delivered the Contarelli Chapel as a trio of scenes from the apostle's life, hanging together in the same small room: the Calling on one wall, the Martyrdom facing it, and a third canvas placed above the altar between them. What does the third painting show?
answer: Matthew being dictated to by an angel
choices: Matthew being dictated to by an angel
Matthew washing the feet of a beggar
Matthew preaching to a crowd in Ethiopia
Matthew asleep during a storm at sea
context: The altarpiece is Caravaggio's The Inspiration of Saint Matthew (1602). Matthew sits at a writing desk while an angel leans in from above, counting off points on its fingers -- the moment of the gospel's composition.

question: When Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, a young priestess-sorceress fell hopelessly in love with him and helped him at every turn. What was her name?
context: Medea, priestess of the witch-goddess Hecate, was a princess of Colchis. Hera and Athena arranged the love through Aphrodite. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.  (Legend.)

question: Medea was a princess of Colchis, daughter of the king who kept the Golden Fleece. Which king was her father?
context: Aeetes ruled Colchis at the far end of the Black Sea and was Medea's father. Pelias sent Jason for the Fleece; Creon ruled Corinth; Polydectes is from the Perseus story.  (Legend.)

question: Before Jason went out to face King Aeetes's first challenge, Medea slipped him a magic ointment to smear on his skin and weapons. What did the ointment protect him from for a single day?
context: The ointment guarded him against the bulls' fire and any weapon's blade for one day. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.828-878.  (Legend.)

question: The first task Aeetes set Jason was to yoke a monstrous pair of bulls and plough a field with them. These were the Khalkotauroi, made by Hephaestus himself. What were their hooves made of?
context: The Khalkotauroi had bronze hooves and breathed fire from their nostrils. Medea's ointment guarded Jason as he wrestled each bull down to the yoke.  (Legend.)

question: The second task was to sow the ploughed field with a serpent's teeth. What sprang up out of the furrows as Jason worked?
context: They were called the Spartoi, 'sown men' -- the same seed-crop Cadmus once sowed at Thebes.  (Legend.)

question: As the sown warriors stood up out of the furrows with drawn spears, Jason followed a trick Medea had taught him. What did he do?
answer: Threw a rock into their middle so they killed each other
choices: Threw a rock into their middle so they killed each other
Blew a horn that sent them back into the earth
Sang a lullaby that put them to sleep
Held up a bronze mirror so they turned to stone
context: Not knowing who had thrown it, the sown men turned on one another and cut each other down until none was left. Apollonius, Argonautica 3.1354-1407.  (Legend.)

question: The Golden Fleece hung on a tree in the sacred grove of Ares, guarded by an enormous serpent. What was uncanny about this particular serpent?
choices: It could not be wounded by iron
context: Ladon at the Hesperides had a hundred heads; Argus Panoptes had a hundred eyes; the Colchian serpent's uncanny mark was sleeplessness.  (Legend.)

question: Medea led Jason at night to the guardian serpent in Ares's sacred grove, coiled around the tree that held the Fleece. What did she do to the beast so Jason could climb up and take the Fleece?
answer: Sang a charm and sprinkled its eyes with the juice of magic herbs
choices: Sang a charm and sprinkled its eyes with the juice of magic herbs
Cut off all its heads with the harpe sword
Traded her own life to it for the Fleece
context: For the first time in its life the serpent slept. The harpe belongs to the Perseus story; there was no lamb offering here.  (Legend.)

question: Convinced by Medea's cauldron-demonstration, most of Pelias's daughters chopped up their father and put the pieces into her cauldron. What went wrong for Pelias?
answer: Medea did not add the herbs, and Pelias stayed dead
choices: Medea did not add the herbs, and Pelias stayed dead
The cauldron cracked from the heat, and Pelias was scalded
The ghost of Jason's father struck Medea down mid-spell
Pelias came out young but blind for the rest of his days
context: Alcestis alone of the daughters refused to lay a hand on her father. The trick was Medea's revenge for Pelias's usurpation of Iolcus.  (Legend.)

question: Years later at Corinth, Jason abandoned Medea to marry Glauce, the daughter of King Creon. What did Medea send Glauce as a wedding gift?
answer: A poisoned wedding dress that burned her alive
choices: A poisoned wedding dress that burned her alive
A cup of wine that turned her hair white
A gold ring that struck her mute
A basket of serpents in flowers
context: Euripides put the whole Corinth story on the stage in his Medea, first performed at Athens in 431 BCE. Medea also killed her own children by Jason before fleeing.  (Legend.)

question: The three Fates stood at the newborn Meleager's hearth and prophesied that his life was tied to a single ordinary thing already in the room -- burning right there in front of them. What did the Fates tie the baby's life to?
answer: a burning log on the hearth
choices: a burning log on the hearth
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.451-458; Apollodorus 1.8.2: the Fates declared that Meleager would live only as long as a particular firebrand -- a log then burning in the hearth -- was unburnt. A common Greek word for the log-brand is 'dalos'.  (Legend.)

question: The moment the Fates finished speaking, Meleager's mother Althaea sprang up from her seat, ran to the hearth, and did one urgent thing to save her baby's life. What did Althaea do the instant the Fates were finished?
answer: snatched the log from the fire and hid it in a chest
choices: snatched the log from the fire and hid it in a chest
carried the baby out of the room and up the mountain
sent a servant to the oracle at Delphi for counsel
sacrificed a black lamb on the household altar
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.457-461; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Althaea seized the burning log, doused the flames, and locked it away in a chest, where it stayed safe for years while Meleager grew into a man.  (Legend.)

question: Years later Meleager's father, King Oeneus of Calydon, offered first-fruits sacrifices to all the gods after the harvest -- but he forgot one goddess. She sent a monstrous boar to ravage Calydon's orchards and kill its farmers. Which goddess did Oeneus fail to honor?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.270-283; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Artemis, huntress and mistress of wild beasts, was passed over in the harvest sacrifice and in fury sent the giant boar. Athena is the war-goddess of Athens; Hera the queen of Olympus; Demeter the grain-mother -- none matches the Calydon story.  (Legend.)

question: To hunt the Calydonian Boar Meleager summoned the greatest heroes of Greece to Calydon -- Theseus, Jason, Castor and Pollux, Peleus, Telamon, his own uncles Toxeus and Plexippus. He also invited one hunter whose presence enraged the other men because she was a woman. Who was the woman Meleager invited to the hunt?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.317-328; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Atalanta, the huntress raised by a she-bear and trained as an archer, was the only woman on the hunt. Meleager was in love with her. Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus; Andromache the wife of Hector; Iphigenia the daughter of Agamemnon.  (Legend.)

question: The great hunt begins in a Calydonian thicket. Several hunters are gored or killed. Then one of the hunters strikes the boar behind the ear with an arrow and draws first blood. Whose arrow struck the Calydonian Boar first?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.380-383; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Atalanta's arrow struck the boar behind the ear -- first blood in the greatest hunt of the age. Jason, Theseus, and Castor were all on the hunt and all failed to land the first strike.  (Legend.)

question: As leader of the hunt Meleager had the right to award the boar's hide and tusks as trophy. He gave them not to himself and not to his uncles but to Atalanta, saying she had drawn first blood and had earned the prize. What did Meleager's uncles Toxeus and Plexippus do when they saw the trophy handed to a woman?
answer: tried to take the hide from Atalanta by force
choices: tried to take the hide from Atalanta by force
demanded a share of the tusks for themselves
walked out of the hunt-feast in silence
called on Artemis to judge between them
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.435-444; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Toxeus and Plexippus, enraged at seeing the greatest hunt-prize in Greek memory given to a woman, tried to snatch the hide from Atalanta by force. What happened next set the tragedy in motion.  (Legend.)

question: When his uncles Toxeus and Plexippus laid violent hands on Atalanta to take back the boar's hide, Meleager stepped in to defend her. What did Meleager do to his mother's two brothers in that moment?
answer: killed both of them on the spot
choices: killed both of them on the spot
wounded them and drove them out of the hall
cursed them and left the feast
swore an oath never to speak to them again
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.435-444; Apollodorus 1.8.2: Meleager killed Toxeus and Plexippus defending Atalanta. His mother Althaea now had to choose between vengeance for her brothers and love for her son -- the choice that ends the story.  (Legend.)

question: When Althaea learned that her son Meleager had killed her two brothers over Atalanta's prize, she went to the chest she had guarded for years, took out the log the Fates had spoken of at his cradle, and made her choice. What did Althaea do with the firebrand?
answer: threw it back onto the fire
choices: threw it back onto the fire
carried it to a temple altar
broke it in half over her knee
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.460-525; Apollodorus 1.8.3: Althaea, torn between mother-love and blood-vengeance for her brothers, threw the firebrand back into the hearth. Ovid gives her a long anguished speech before she casts the log in.  (Legend.)

question: Far away from his mother's hearth, Meleager was in perfect health when he suddenly felt his body catching alight from the inside as the firebrand crumbled to ash in the flames. His grieving sisters wept so long over him that they were turned into birds -- birds whose scientific genus is still named for Meleager today. What kind of birds did his sisters become?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.533-546: Meleager's weeping sisters were turned into guineafowl, called meleagrides in Greek. The bird's Latin scientific genus is still Meleagris today (which is also the genus of the wild turkey, named by Linnaeus by confusion with the true meleagris). Swans belong to Cygnus; nightingales to the Philomela story; ravens to Apollo.  (Legend.)

question: At the young Arthur's court an old white-bearded man in a long robe advises the king on every disaster before it comes, arranges Arthur's own conception and secret upbringing, and sets up the sword-in-the-stone test that would prove him rightful king. What is the wizard's name?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136); Malory Books I-IV. The Latin name Merlinus comes from the Welsh Myrddin. Blaise is Merlin's own confessor and chronicler. Bedivere is Arthur's steward-knight who returns Excalibur. Bagdemagus is the king of Gorre in Chretien's Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: When old King Uther Pendragon dies with no acknowledged heir and the barons of Britain gather to fight over the throne, the wizard sets a test in a churchyard: whichever man can draw a certain fixed weapon free from where it is set in an iron anvil will be the rightwise-born king of all England. The boy who draws it is Arthur. By what name is that test known?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.5-6. Arthur draws the blade as squire to his foster-brother Kay at a tournament. The horn on the hearth is a chastity-test in Arthurian romance. The bridge of glass is a distractor. The burning bush is Moses at Sinai (Christian pillar).  (Legend.)

question: In Robert de Boron's poem Merlin (c.1195-1210), a council of demons plot to sire their own antichrist on a sleeping virtuous woman. The plot fails at the very moment of the baby's birth, before he can be raised to their purpose: a single act performed on the newborn strips the devils' claim on his soul, though he keeps their gift of perfect memory of all things past and present. What act saves the newborn Merlin?
context: Robert de Boron, Merlin (c.1195-1210); Wikipedia: Merlin (Robert de Boron poem). The mother tells her confessor of the demonic pregnancy, and the child is baptised at birth, freeing him from the devil's power. Exorcism is the ritual expulsion of a demon already in possession. Circumcision is the Jewish covenant rite of the eighth day. Anointing with oil is a separate sacrament used at confirmation and last rites.  (Legend.)
