question: Uther Pendragon has fallen in love with Igraine, wife of the Duke of Cornwall, and cannot come to her while her husband lives. The wizard offers a way. He gives Uther the outward SHAPE of Duke Gorlois; and that same night, while the real Gorlois is being killed in battle, Uther comes to Igraine as her husband. The child conceived that night is Arthur. Where does the wizard arrange the deception?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book VIII; Malory Book I ch.1-2. Tintagel is Duke Gorlois's clifftop castle in Cornwall (still visitable today) where Igraine is guarded. Camelot is Arthur's own future capital. Carlisle is Arthur's northern seat in some romances. Winchester was later claimed as the site of the Round Table.  (Legend.)

question: The wizard takes the newborn Arthur from Uther and Igraine and hides him: he carries the baby out of the palace and gives him to a good country knight to raise as his own, with the knight's own son as the boy's foster-brother. The boy will grow up thinking he is the knight's second child, never told he is king. What is the name of Arthur's foster-father?
context: Malory Book I ch.3; Wikipedia: Sir Ector. Ector is the country knight; his son Kay grows up as Arthur's foster-brother and becomes Arthur's seneschal. Bors is Lancelot's cousin, not Arthur's foster-father. Balin is a tragic loner from Malory Book II.  (Legend.)

question: In Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (Book VIII), the king of the Britons wants a great memorial raised for the hundreds of British nobles the Saxon Hengist massacred at Amesbury; the wizard tells him he must send men across the sea to fetch a certain ring of ancient stones, and the wizard's magic will do the lifting. Which king does the wizard build the memorial for?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book VIII (c.1136); Wikipedia: Giant's Dance. Aurelius Ambrosius is Uther's older brother and king before him; the monument becomes Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain. Uther Pendragon leads the men who ship the stones but is not yet king. Vortigern is the earlier king who let the Saxons into Britain in the first place. Cadwallader is the last British king in Geoffrey's chronicle, centuries later.  (Legend.)

question: Geoffrey names the country the stone ring is dragged across the sea from, and gives it a specific mountain -- Mount Killaraus -- where the giants once set the ring down before Merlin comes for it. It is the same country the giants themselves are said to have carried the stones to long before, from Africa. Which country does Merlin bring Stonehenge from?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Book VIII; Wikipedia: Giant's Dance. Geoffrey names Mount Killaraus in Ireland; Waun Mawn in Pembrokeshire (Wales) is one modern candidate for a real dismantled circle behind the legend. Iceland has no Arthurian role. Norway is Beowulf's neighbour. Brittany is where Lancelot's father Ban is from.

question: In Malory Book III, the young Arthur has just broken his first sword in single combat and stands weaponless. The wizard leads him to a lake in the wilderness; a woman's arm clothed in white samite rises from the water holding a great blade above the surface, and Merlin tells Arthur to row out in a small barge and take it. What is the name of the second sword the wizard leads Arthur to?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.25 (the second sword; the first was the sword-in-the-stone). The arm in white samite is the Lady of the Lake's. Durendal is Roland's sword (Chanson de Roland). Tizona is El Cid's sword. Gungnir is Odin's spear (Norse pillar).  (Legend.)

question: In his old age the great wizard of Arthur's court falls in love with a beautiful young damsel of the Lady of the Lake's kin. He follows her wherever she goes like a lovesick fool, and cannot leave her side. He is Merlin. What is the young woman's name in Malory (Book IV chapter 1)?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1 (Caxton 1485). Malory's spelling is Nimue (with variants Nenive, Niviene); the French Vulgate calls her Viviane. Igraine is Arthur's mother. Enide is the heroine of Chretien's Erec et Enide. Iseult is the queen of the parallel Tristan story.  (Legend.)

question: The damsel does not love Merlin back. Malory says plainly that she is AFRAID of him because of what he was rumoured to be from birth -- a rumour rooted in the older origin story Robert de Boron had put in writing a century before Malory. According to Malory, what did the damsel think Merlin was?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1; Robert de Boron, Merlin (c.1200). Nimue's fear is rooted in de Boron's antichrist-plot origin story for Merlin. Fairy child, Saxon spy, and Roman priest are the sort of thing a distrusted stranger might be called in Arthur's Britain but not what Malory writes.  (Legend.)

question: The damsel is afraid, but she is also clever. She uses Merlin's infatuation against him. Whenever she wants him gone from her, she promises she will love him better if he teaches her only ONE MORE secret, and Merlin -- wanting the promise -- hands one over, and then another, and then another. What did Nimue coax out of Merlin secret by secret in Malory?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.1. Merlin hands over his spells one by one, and Nimue collects the whole arsenal -- which she will shortly use against him. The language of birds is Solomon's; naming saints is a monk's work; teaching Britain's geography is the sort of thing Merlin ALREADY tells Arthur (from prophecy). Only the magic is the fatal gift.  (Legend.)

question: The medieval traditions disagree on WHERE the trap happens. The French Vulgate Cycle moves it out of Cornwall and into a real forest in Brittany, still visited today for its Arthurian associations -- the Forest of Paimpont, on the road out of Rennes. What is the legendary name of that Breton forest?
context: French Vulgate Cycle; Wikipedia: Broceliande; the Forest of Paimpont in Brittany is the real forest identified with Broceliande. Argonne is a French forest famous from WWI. Sherwood is Robin Hood's forest in Nottinghamshire. Ardennes is the Belgian-French forest of Chretien's Cliges and later of many wars.  (Legend.)

question: The Victorian poet Alfred Tennyson retold the story of Merlin's trap in a poem published in 1859 as part of his long Arthurian cycle Idylls of the King. Tennyson changes the trap again: no stone, no tower of air, no hawthorn. Instead his Vivien waves her arms over the sleeping wizard and weaves her spell so that the hollow trunk of one great tree closes over him. Under what tree does Tennyson's Vivien trap Merlin?
context: Alfred Tennyson, Idylls of the King, 'Merlin and Vivien' (1859). Tennyson's Vivien puts the sleeping Merlin inside a hollow oak; Tennyson favours the oak because it is the great sacred tree of British antiquity, the tree of the druids. Apple, rowan, and walnut are other significant British trees but not this poem's.

question: In one of the most intricate stories in all Irish myth, a Tuatha De god of the sidhe mound of Bri Leith fell in love with the most beautiful woman ever born in Ireland and married her. Who was this god?
context: Midir, son of the Dagda, lived in the sidhe mound of Bri Leith (Ardagh Hill in modern County Longford). Tochmarc Etaine ('The Wooing of Etain'), Yellow Book of Lecan; Wikipedia, Midir.  (Legend.)

question: The beautiful woman that the Tuatha De god Midir brought home to his sidhe mound at Bri Leith had a name that Irish schoolchildren still learn. What was her name?
context: Etain was said to be the most beautiful woman ever born in Ireland. Tochmarc Etaine ('The Wooing of Etain') part I; Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: When Midir brought his new bride Etain home to Bri Leith, he already had a first wife: a powerful druidess of the Tuatha De who was consumed with jealousy the moment she saw the newcomer. Who was the first wife?
context: Fuamnach had been trained by the druid Bresal Etarlam and is described in the tale as 'intelligent, cunning, and versed in the knowledge and power of the Tuatha De Danann'. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: When Midir brought his new bride Etain home, his first wife Fuamnach struck her with a wand and worked a chain of transformations: first a pool of water, then a worm, and finally a creature Etain would live as for centuries. What did Fuamnach turn Etain into last?
context: The Old Irish text calls her cuil corcrai, a scarlet or purple fly. Even as a fly Etain was so beautiful that her wing-buzz was sweet music and her scent healed the sick. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: After turning Etain into a purple fly, Fuamnach was not finished. She raised a great wind that carried the fly through the sky over Ireland, never letting her land. How long did the wind blow Etain around?
context: Fuamnach's storm blew Etain the fly for seven years without rest. In one version Etain then reached Aengus's protective bower before a second storm drove her onward. Wikipedia, Fuamnach.  (Legend.)

question: The wind that Fuamnach raised finally carried the purple fly to a mortal hall, where Etain dropped into a golden cup on a woman's table. What happened next?
answer: The woman drank her down and later gave birth to Etain reborn
choices: The woman drank her down and later gave birth to Etain reborn
A hound leapt to the table and swallowed her whole
A druid caught her in a jar of honey
A crow snatched her out and dropped her at Bri Leith
context: The fly fell into the cup of the wife of a warrior named Etar; the woman drank without noticing, and nine months later gave birth to a girl who was Etain reborn, with no memory of her earlier life. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: By the time Etain was reborn as the daughter of Etar's wife and grew up, an enormous stretch of years had passed since her first birth. How long, according to Tochmarc Etaine?
context: Tochmarc Etaine sets the reborn Etain 1,012 years after her original marriage to Midir. This makes her one of the earliest recorded reincarnation stories in Western literature. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: In the second half of Tochmarc Etaine, the reborn Etain grows up in mortal Ireland and marries the High King at Tara. Which High King took her to wife?
context: Eochaid Airem sat at Tara when the reborn Etain grew up and did not know that his queen had once been the wife of a Tuatha De god. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: To win Etain back from the High King Eochaid Airem, Midir came in disguise to Tara and challenged the king to a series of games at an Irish board game of thought and strategy. What was the board game called?
context: Fidchell (Old Irish for 'wood-sense') was the great Irish chess-like game of kings. Midir's board was silver, its playing pieces gold, its corners jeweled. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: Midir let Eochaid win the early games of fidchell and paid every prize the king demanded, mounds of horses and treasure. Then he asked for a single last game, this time HIS choice of prize, and this game he won. What was the prize Midir asked for?
answer: An embrace and a kiss from Etain
choices: An embrace and a kiss from Etain
The sword of the high king
context: Midir named a modest-sounding prize: one embrace, one kiss. Eochaid agreed, thinking to guard against it, and set the day a month later. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: On the day set for Midir's kiss, Eochaid Airem barred every door of Tara's hall with armed men. Midir simply appeared inside the hall, took Etain in his arms, and the pair vanished out of Tara. How did they leave?
answer: Flying up through the skylight as two swans
choices: Flying up through the skylight as two swans
Melting into the flames of the great hearth
Riding out on Enbarr the sea-horse
Sinking through the floor into the sidhe below
context: 'The pair fly away through the skylight, turning into swans as they do so.' Eochaid dug up every sidhe mound in Ireland after them and never found her again. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: The two swans that flew up through the skylight of Tara carrying Midir and Etain away were bound together in a single striking detail from the story. What linked the two swans?
context: A chain of gold linked the two swans as they flew, a scene the Middle English romance Sir Orfeo (c. 1330) would later borrow and transfer to a British setting. Wikipedia, Tochmarc Etaine.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth the red-bearded god of thunder rides across the sky in a chariot pulled by two goats, and the flash of his weapon is what people down in Midgard see as lightning. What is that thunder-god's name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 21: Thor is the son of Odin and Jord (Earth), god of thunder, defender of Asgard and Midgard against the giants. Freyr is the harvest and fertility god; Tyr is the god of law and single combat (the one who lost a hand to Fenrir); Baldr is the shining god slain by mistletoe.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's weapon is short-handled and heavy, and no matter how far he throws it, it always flies back to his hand. What is this weapon called?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 21 and Skaldskaparmal 43: Mjolnir ('crusher') is the returning hammer of Thor. Gungnir is Odin's spear; Gram is the sword Sigurd uses to kill the dragon Fafnir; Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Volsung cycle.  (Legend.)

question: The gods needed the hammer made, so the smith-work was given to two dwarf brothers. The elder put a pig-skin in the forge and told the younger to keep pumping the bellows and never stop, no matter what happened. What are the names of the two dwarf brothers who forged Mjolnir?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (sometimes called Eitri) is the elder, Brokkr the younger who works the bellows. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder Kvasir to make the Mead of Poetry; Nordri and Sudri are two of the four dwarves holding up the sky; Alviss and Andvari are unrelated dwarves from other tales.  (Legend.)

question: The whole forging was really a bet. One of the Aesir had wagered his own head that a rival team of dwarves (the sons of Ivaldi) could out-craft Sindri and Brokkr, so he had good reason to want the pig-skin forging to fail. Which Aesir had bet his head against the two brothers?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki set up the whole contest by boasting that the sons of Ivaldi were the finest smiths in the nine worlds, then wagered his own head that Sindri and Brokkr could not beat them. Thor is the customer for the hammer, not the gambler; Odin and Heimdallr are not in the wager.  (Legend.)

question: Even with the short grip, the gods judged Mjolnir the finest of the six treasures made that day, so Loki had lost his wager and owed his head. He wriggled out with a lawyer's trick: the dwarves could have his head, but they could not touch one particular part of him, which had not been part of the bet. Which part of Loki was outside the bet?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki argued that he had wagered his head, not his neck, and cutting off the head would necessarily damage the neck -- which was not on offer. The dwarves conceded the argument.  (Legend.)

question: Cheated of Loki's head, Brokkr took an awl and a leather thong and stitched a different part of Loki shut in payment -- so Loki could not go on making mischief with words for a while. That thong has a name in the Prose Edda. What is the thong called?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43 names the thong Vartari. Brokkr sewed Loki's lips shut with it. Gleipnir is the ribbon-thin chain that binds Fenrir; Draupnir is Odin's dripping ring (made in the same forging session as Mjolnir); Gjallarhorn is the horn Heimdallr will blow at Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: The same pig-skin fire produced two other named treasures besides Mjolnir. Together with Mjolnir they were judged the three finest gifts at the wager. What are those two other treasures Sindri and Brokkr made in that session?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri and Brokkr produce Draupnir (Odin's gold ring that drips eight matching rings every ninth night) and Gullinbursti (Freyr's golden boar whose bristles light the dark and who outruns any horse) in the same session as Mjolnir -- three of the six treasures at the wager. Gungnir (Odin's spear) and Skidbladnir (Freyr's folding ship) are the OTHER three treasures, made by the rival dwarf-team, the sons of Ivaldi; Andvaranaut is Andvari's cursed ring from the Volsung cycle and Gram the sword Sigurd swings there; Sif's hair (also from the sons of Ivaldi) and Brisingamen (Freyja's necklace, made by four different dwarves) are unrelated forgings.  (Legend.)

question: Baldr's body has been laid on his burning ship Hringhorni. Before the pyre is lit, Thor steps up to the ship's side and does one thing with Mjolnir. What does Thor do with the hammer at Baldr's funeral?
answer: raises it to consecrate the pyre
choices: raises it to consecrate the pyre
throws it at a passing giant
smashes the mast of the ship
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 49: at Baldr's funeral aboard the ship Hringhorni, Thor stands and raises Mjolnir to hallow the pyre. The scene shows Mjolnir as a sacred object -- it is used the same way over births, marriages, and funerals in the sagas, not just in battle. The giant Litr is kicked into the flames at the same funeral, but by Thor's foot, not the hammer.  (Legend.)

question: Because Mjolnir hallows, Viking-age Scandinavians did not only tell stories about it -- they wore small silver copies of Thor's hammer on cords around their necks. Among the many kinds of Viking-age pendant known from graves and hoards, where do the surviving silver Mjolnir-pendants rank in the archaeological record?
answer: the most-collected single pendant type from the Viking age
choices: the most-collected single pendant type from the Viking age
about as common as silver cross-pendants of the same era
the second-most-collected pendant type after cross-pendants
context: British Museum and Nationalmuseet Copenhagen catalogues: silver Mjolnir-pendants are the most abundant single amulet type recovered from Viking-age burials and hoards (roughly 9th-11th centuries), found from Iceland to the Danelaw to Kievan Rus. Many were worn alongside crosses in the transition to Christianity -- direct evidence of the hallowing role Snorri describes.

question: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god carries a single signature weapon that the Aesir gods count on above every other blade in Asgard when the giants of Jotunheim come down from the mountains. What is the weapon Thor carries?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 21 and Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor's weapon is Mjolnir, a war-hammer. Odin's weapon is the spear Gungnir; the god Ullr is the bowman of Asgard; Tyr carries a sword. The hammer is unique to Thor and is the single most famous weapon in Norse myth.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's war-hammer has a proper name in the Norse stories -- the same name that turns up centuries later carved on Viking-age amulets worn around the neck. What is the name of Thor's hammer?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the hammer is called Mjolnir. Gungnir is Odin's spear; Draupnir is Odin's self-multiplying gold arm-ring; Gram is the sword Sigurd uses to kill the dragon Fafnir. Around a thousand hammer-shaped amulets have been dug up across Viking-age Scandinavia.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the two dwarf brothers who forge Mjolnir do the work as a wager against Loki. Snorri names one at the anvil and the other at the bellows. What are the names of the two smith-brothers who make Thor's hammer?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) stands at the anvil and his brother Brokkr works the bellows. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder the wise Kvasir. Baugi and Suttung are the giant brothers in the Mead of Poetry story. Nordri and Sudri are two of the four dwarves who hold up the sky. It is a common wrong answer to say the Sons of Ivaldi made Mjolnir -- the Sons of Ivaldi make Gungnir and Skidbladnir in the SAME wager, but not the hammer.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri lists three marvellous properties Mjolnir has when Thor uses it. Two of them are that it will never miss its mark when thrown, and that it can be shrunk down small enough to hide inside Thor's shirt. What is the third property Snorri names?
answer: it always returns to Thor's hand
choices: it always returns to Thor's hand
it grows red-hot when giants are near
it splits the earth wherever it lands
it can be lifted by no one but Thor
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor's hammer will never miss the mark, will always fly back to his hand, and can be shrunk small enough to hide inside his shirt. The distractor 'can be lifted by no one but Thor' is a modern comic-book addition, not from Snorri; the belt Megingjord is what lets Thor lift it at full strength.  (Legend.)

question: One evening the giant Thrym steals Mjolnir out of Asgard and hides it eight leagues underground. He sends word to the Aesir that he will give the hammer back only on one condition -- one of their goddesses must be brought to his hall to marry him. Which goddess does Thrym demand as the price of Mjolnir's return?
context: Poetic Edda, Thrymskvida: Thrym names Freyja specifically, and the gods must plan a trick because Freyja refuses to be handed over -- her rage shakes Asgard, and Brisingamen bursts from her neck. Heimdall then proposes that Thor go to Thrym's hall himself dressed in Freyja's bridal veil, with Loki as bridesmaid; when the hammer is finally laid in the 'bride's' lap Thor throws off the veil and kills Thrym and every giant present.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse religion of the Viking age, Mjolnir was not only a weapon in the stories but a symbol used in real ritual -- a small hammer-shape, or the sign of one, was raised over the participants and words were spoken over them to sanctify the moment. At what ceremony was the hammer-sign used in this way?
choices: a naming of a newborn child
context: Poetic Edda, Thrymskvida stanza 30 and Snorri after it: the hammer is brought forth and laid in the woman's lap to sanctify the union -- the story-detail preserves the real Viking-age custom. Naming ceremonies for newborns used water-sprinkling (ausa vatni) rather than the hammer; ship-launchings used sacrifice; there was no single Norse coronation-rite. The hammer-role at weddings is also why so many small Mjolnir-pendants have been dug up in Viking graves across Scandinavia -- around a thousand of them.  (Legend.)

question: After Thor kills the world-serpent at Ragnarok, he does not walk away from the fight. The serpent's venom is in his lungs, and the Voluspa gives the exact count of paces he manages to take from the corpse before he falls dead. How many steps does Thor walk before he dies?
context: Poetic Edda, Voluspa 56 and Snorri, Gylfaginning 51: 'Nine paces fares the son of Fjorgyn, and, slain by the serpent, fearless he sinks.' Nine is a sacred number all through Norse myth -- Odin hangs nine nights on Yggdrasil, the world-tree has nine worlds, Heimdall has nine mothers. Three, seven and twelve are more commonly Christian and Greek sacred numbers.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the young King Arthur one night sleeps with a queen who is a guest at his court, not knowing that she is his own half-sister. She conceives a son by him that night. In Malory, who is the queen whose son by Arthur will one day bring the kingdom down?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.19-20 (Caxton 1485). Morgause is Igraine's daughter by her first husband Gorlois of Cornwall and thus Arthur's half-sister; she is married to King Lot of Orkney. In the older French Vulgate tradition the mother of Mordred is Morgan le Fay -- also Arthur's half-sister -- and Malory's switch to Morgause is idiosyncratic. Guinevere is Arthur's queen, not his sister. Elaine of Astolat dies of unrequited love for Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: The child born of Arthur's night with Morgause is a boy. He is raised in secret, comes to Arthur's court years later as a young knight, half-brother to Gawain, and is eventually seated with the fellowship of the Round Table. In Malory, what is the name of Arthur's son by Morgause?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.27 and passim. Galahad is Lancelot's pure son by Elaine of Corbenic, the Grail-achiever. Bors is Lancelot's cousin, a Grail knight. Kay is Arthur's foster-brother and seneschal. Mordred is Arthur's own son by incest and the ruin of his reign.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin tells Arthur that the child born of his night with Morgause will one day destroy his kingdom -- and adds that the child was born on May Day. Arthur, terrified, orders that ALL noble children born on May Day be gathered up. He puts them into a single ship and sends them out to sea to drown, hoping the prophesied child will die among them. In Malory (Book I ch.27), what happens to the infant Mordred aboard that ship?
answer: he is cast up alive on shore
choices: he is cast up alive on shore
he is nursed to safety by a passing dolphin
Merlin himself lifts him from the wreck
Morgause hides him ashore before the ship sails
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.27. The ship wrecks and every other child drowns; the infant Mordred is thrown up alive on shore, is found by a good man, and is raised until age fourteen before being brought to court. Malory adapts the episode from the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin. Many of Arthur's lords are furious over the drowned children -- some blame Arthur, some blame Merlin.  (Legend.)

question: Years later Guinevere's love for Lancelot is exposed at court and Lancelot flees across the Channel. Arthur pursues him with an army and lays siege to Lancelot's castle at Benwick in France. Arthur cannot leave Britain kingless while he is away, so he must appoint someone to hold the kingdom in his absence. In Malory Book XXI, whom does Arthur leave as regent of Britain when he crosses the Channel to besiege Lancelot?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.1. Arthur trusts the regency to his own acknowledged son. Gawain is with Arthur on the campaign, driving him to press Lancelot for having killed Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris. Kay and Bedivere are Arthur's oldest household knights but neither is the regent. Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136) is the first to make Mordred the treacherous regent -- an invention that becomes central to the whole later legend.

question: With Arthur across the Channel, Mordred forges letters saying Arthur has been killed at Benwick, has himself crowned king in his father's place, and moves to take Guinevere -- Arthur's queen -- as his own wife by force. Guinevere refuses. In Malory Book XXI ch.1, where does Guinevere shut herself up to escape Mordred?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.1. Guinevere pretends to consent, asks Mordred's leave to go to London for her wedding-clothes, and instead shuts herself up in the Tower of London stocked with provisions and men-at-arms. Amesbury is the nunnery she retires to at the very end of the story after Arthur's death. Avalon is where Arthur is carried on the barge. Camelot is Arthur's own court and would be Mordred's stronghold, not her refuge.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur breaks off the siege of Lancelot at Benwick and races back across the Channel with his army to face his usurping son. The two armies meet on a plain in the west of Britain, placed in Cornwall in most later traditions and given as the year 537 by the earliest Welsh source. What is the name of the plain where Arthur and Mordred bring their armies to battle?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.3-4. Camlann is the name in Malory and in the earlier Welsh Annals under 537. Badon (Mons Badonicus) is Arthur's earlier victory in the Historia Brittonum, not his last battle. Roncesvalles is the pass where Roland's rearguard is destroyed in the Song of Roland (Western-medieval pillar) -- a parallel of a great order's last stand, but a different story. Bosworth is 1485, Richard III's death, real history not legend.

question: On the morning of the battle at Camlann, both sides agree a truce. The two armies are drawn up facing each other in the heather while Arthur and Mordred meet in a tent to sign the treaty; each side is instructed that if a single sword is seen drawn, they are to charge. Then a knight in the ranks is stung on the foot by something in the heather and instinctively draws his sword to kill it. What stings the knight in Malory's account of that morning?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.4. The adder in the heather is Malory's own vivid detail. Both armies see the drawn blade, take it for the signal of treachery, and charge. In one instant a truce is broken by a snake and the whole day is set on fire. Hornets and scorpions belong to warmer traditions; the marsh viper is a real snake but not what Malory names.  (Legend.)

question: The battle at Camlann lasts all day. By evening every knight of the Round Table on both sides is dead, and Arthur can see only two men standing beside him on the whole field -- his knights Sir Bedivere and Sir Lucan. Then across the field Arthur sees Mordred, alone, leaning on his sword among heaps of the dead. Arthur takes his spear and runs at him. What does Mordred do as Arthur drives the spear clean through his body?
answer: pulls himself up the spear shaft
choices: pulls himself up the spear shaft
hurls his sword to break Arthur's helm
kneels and calls for Morgause his mother
context: Malory Book XXI ch.4. Arthur's spear goes clean through Mordred's body, but the dying Mordred grips the shaft with both hands and drags himself up it until he can reach his father, then strikes Arthur through the helm and the skull with his sword. Both men fall together. Malory gives this act the whole weight of the ending: the son will not let the father live, even at the cost of his own last moment.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory, once Mordred has dragged himself up the spear and struck Arthur through the helm, both father and son fall on the field of Camlann. Mordred is dead where he lies, but Arthur is not yet dead -- he is carried from the field by Sir Bedivere, mortally wounded, and taken to be laid on a barge. In Malory Book XXI, where is the barge said to be taking the dying Arthur?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.5. The three queens on the black barge tell Bedivere they are taking Arthur to the vale of Avalon to heal him of his grievous wound. Glastonbury is the site LATER identified with Avalon by the monks of Glastonbury Abbey (who claimed in 1191 to have found Arthur's tomb), but Malory's own text names Avalon. Camelot is Arthur's court, empty now. Cornwall is where Camlann is placed.  (Legend.)

question: The oldest surviving reference to the battle where Arthur and Mordred fell is not Malory or Geoffrey of Monmouth -- it is a single bare line in a Latin chronicle compiled at St David's in Wales in the mid-10th century, listed under the year 537. That one line records only the strife of Camlann in which Arthur and Medraut fell. What is the name of that Latin chronicle?
context: Annales Cambriae (Welsh Annals), entry for the year 537: 'Gueith Camlann in qua Arthur et Medraut corruerunt' -- the strife of Camlann in which Arthur and Medraut fell. Medraut is the Welsh name for Mordred. The Historia Brittonum (c.828, attributed to Nennius) gives Arthur's twelve battles but not Camlann. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is the English royal chronicle and does not mention Arthur. Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica (731) mentions Badon but not Camlann.

question: The Welsh Annals under 537 record only the bare fact that Arthur and Medraut both fell at Camlann. The chronicle does NOT say that Medraut was Arthur's treacherous nephew or son, does NOT say they fought on opposite sides, does NOT say why they were there. Every detail of the treacherous-regent story -- Mordred forging the letter, seizing the crown, taking Guinevere -- is a later invention. Which writer is the first to turn Mordred into Arthur's treacherous regent?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136). Geoffrey invents the treacherous-regent story a full six centuries after the annals' bare line; every later Arthurian writer builds on his invention. Chretien de Troyes (c.1170-90) writes the great courtly Arthurian romances but not the Camlann story. Wolfram von Eschenbach (c.1210) writes Parzival, the German Grail poem. Malory (Caxton 1485) is 350 years after Geoffrey and gathers the whole tradition into English prose.

question: The Camlann shape -- a great order's last stand in which friend and foe kill each other to the last man on a single day -- is not unique to Arthur. The Norse tradition has its own version: Odin is swallowed by the wolf Fenrir, Thor and Jormungand the world-serpent kill each other, and Surt sets the world on fire. What name do the Norse give to that last day of the gods?
context: Ragnarok is the Norse doom of the gods, told in the Voluspa and in Snorri's Prose Edda: Odin falls to Fenrir, Thor and Jormungand kill each other, Surt burns the world. The binding of Fenrir is an earlier episode in which the gods trick the wolf into the fetter Gleipnir -- but Fenrir breaks free at Ragnarok. The death of Baldr, killed by mistletoe through Loki's trick, is the omen that Ragnarok is coming. The theft of Idunn's apples is another Loki episode entirely. The Song of Roland's rearguard destroyed at Roncesvalles (778) is the Western-medieval pillar's version of the same last-battle shape.  (Legend.)

question: Arthur has three older half-sisters, all daughters of his mother Igraine by her first husband Duke Gorlois of Cornwall, born before Igraine ever married Uther Pendragon. The most dangerous of the three is a sorceress who steals Excalibur's scabbard, sends a burning cloak to Camelot, and becomes Arthur's lifelong enemy at court. What is her name?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay. Her name in Old French is Morgain la Fee -- 'Morgan the Fairy'. Her sisters are Morgause (mother of Gawain and, in Malory, of Mordred) and Elaine of Garlot -- a DIFFERENT Elaine from Elaine of Astolat, who dies of love for Lancelot. Nimue is the chief Lady of the Lake, Morgan's opposite -- she saves Arthur repeatedly from Morgan's plots. Iseult belongs to the parallel Tristan cycle.  (Legend.)

question: When Morgan le Fay is grown, Arthur gives her in marriage against her will to a northern king who is later the father of Sir Ywain of the Round Table. Morgan hates the marriage, takes lovers at court, and eventually plots her husband's death as well as Arthur's. In Malory, who is the husband Arthur forces on Morgan?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV. Uriens of Gore is the father of Sir Ywain (Yvain), one of Arthur's Round Table knights. King Lot of Orkney is Morgan's SISTER Morgause's husband and the father of Gawain -- easily confused with Uriens because both are northern kings married to Igraine's daughters. Pellinore is the hunter of the Questing Beast. Bagdemagus is another northern king and Morgan does keep him at her court, but he is not her husband.  (Legend.)

question: When the Lady of the Lake first gives Excalibur to Arthur she gives him TWO gifts, not one -- the sword itself, and the sword's SCABBARD. Merlin later tells Arthur that of the two the scabbard is the greater gift, worth ten of the sword. What does the scabbard do for whoever wears it, in Malory Book IV?
choices: makes its wearer invisible in battle
turns aside every arrow in flight
gives its wearer courage in fear
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur. Merlin says the wearer of the scabbard, however sore he is wounded, shall never bleed to death. The other three are the sort of magical property a legendary sheath COULD carry (Perseus's cap of invisibility, the arrow-turning shields of Homer, courage-gifts to cowards) but Malory keeps the gift specific to blood.

question: Morgan le Fay does the worst thing in Malory that can be done to Arthur short of killing him. She goes secretly to the strong-room where Excalibur is kept and takes the scabbard -- the one gift that keeps Arthur alive in battle. Arthur pursues her hard across the country. When Morgan sees she cannot outrun him, she rides to the edge of a lake and, before she can be taken, hurls the scabbard far out into the deep water where it sinks forever. What does Malory say Morgan CRIES OUT as she throws it?
answer: whatever happens, her brother shall not have it
choices: whatever happens, her brother shall not have it
let the lake keep what the king has lost
so passes the pride of Camelot
may Merlin himself never find it
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV; https://sacred-texts.com/neu/trt/trt09.htm. Morgan rides to the edge of a lake on the plain at the forest's edge and, crying out that whatever happens her brother shall not have the scabbard again, throws it far into the deep water where it sinks -- gone forever. From that day forward Arthur can bleed and die, and eventually will.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan later sends Arthur what looks like a peace-offering to make amends -- a magnificent mantle covered in jewels, sent to Camelot by one of her damsels. Arthur is about to put it on when Nimue the Lady of the Lake steps forward and whispers to him to make the messenger try it on FIRST. The damsel is forced to put on the cloak. In Malory Book IV ch.16, what happens to the messenger the moment the cloak touches her?
choices: she falls into a bewitched sleep
she turns to stone standing there
her tongue is struck dumb forever
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book IV ch.16. The cloak has been enchanted to consume its wearer in fire; Nimue, who watches over Arthur, saves him at the last instant. The messenger burns to a cinder in front of the whole court. Sleep-curses, stone-curses, and dumbing-curses are the classic witch-gifts of a fairy-tale but not Morgan's here.  (Legend.)

question: The great alliterative poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Cotton Nero A.x, c.1400) tells how a huge green stranger rides into Camelot at the New Year's feast holding an axe, dares any knight to strike off his head if he may return the blow a year later, and leaves Gawain to keep the appointment. In the poem's final section (Fitt IV) the Green Knight -- revealed as Sir Bertilak of Hautdesert -- says the whole beheading-game was engineered by Morgan le Fay. What did Morgan send the Green Knight to Camelot to DO?
choices: shame Gawain out of the Round Table
test whether Arthur himself would take the blow
steal back the scabbard from Camelot
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Fitt IV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gawain_and_the_Green_Knight. Bertilak reveals that the old woman Gawain has ignored at his host's castle is Morgan le Fay in disguise, and that she sent the Green Knight to Camelot in the hope that the sight of a man picking up his own head would frighten Guinevere to death. Gawain survives the return-blow with only a nick on the neck.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay and her lover Sir Accolon plot together to kill Arthur. Morgan uses her magic to switch Excalibur and its scabbard for cheap copies at court and slips the real sword to Accolon; Accolon then challenges Arthur to a duel expecting to face him weapon against weapon while Arthur wields the fake. In Malory Book IV, who intervenes at the last moment to knock the real Excalibur out of Accolon's hand and put it back into Arthur's?
context: Malory Book IV; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accolon. Nimue the Lady of the Lake attends the duel invisibly and, at the moment Accolon's blade is about to fall, uses her magic to jolt Excalibur out of his hand -- Arthur grabs it and wins. Bedivere and Gawain are Arthur's household knights, present at court but not sorcerers. Merlin is by this point already sealed under the stone by Nimue herself (Malory Book IV ch.1) and cannot help.  (Legend.)

question: At the very end of Malory (Book XXI ch.5), after Arthur is mortally wounded at Camlann, Sir Bedivere carries him down to the edge of a lake at nightfall. A dark barge appears on the water, poled by three queens all veiled in black hoods, and they receive the dying king aboard with great weeping. Morgan le Fay is the queen at the head of the barge, and she takes Arthur's head into her lap. What does Malory say Morgan says to him as she cradles his head?
answer: Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?
choices: Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?
Sleep now, king, the wound is healed already.
The scabbard is returned, and the debt is paid.
Avalon has waited long for its rightful lord.
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book XXI ch.5; https://kingarthur.fandom.com/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay. Morgan is the queen at the head of the barge; she takes his head in her lap and says only 'Ah, dear brother, why have ye tarried so long from me?' Guinevere is at the same moment shutting herself into the nunnery at Amesbury -- she and Arthur do not meet again in this life. The barge carries Arthur to Avalon.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay is not always the villain. In the very earliest surviving text about her -- Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin poem Vita Merlini (c.1150) -- she is a benign healer-queen who rules the enchanted Isle of Avalon, described as the most beautiful and wisest of a company of magical sisters, able to heal any wound. How many magical sisters does Geoffrey say rule Avalon under Morgan?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c.1150). The Vita Merlini gives the benign healer-Morgan at the head of nine magical sisters on the Isle of Avalon; the malevolent Morgan is the invention of the later French Vulgate Cycle and of Malory, which blends both -- hostile in life, restorative at death. Three, seven, and twelve are the other classic magical numbers in medieval story (the three Fates, the seven sages, the twelve peers) but Geoffrey's Avalon-sisters are nine.  (Legend.)

question: Morgan le Fay and her sister Morgause are DIFFERENT women in Malory though many later retellings blur them into one. Both are Igraine's daughters by Gorlois; both are Arthur's half-sisters; both practise witchcraft; both have sons who trouble Arthur's court. In Malory, which of these characters does Malory make MORGAUSE's son (and NOT Morgan's)?
context: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book I ch.19-20. Malory's Mordred is Morgause's son by Arthur (born of Arthur's night with her in Book I). In the older French Vulgate tradition Mordred is Morgan's son by Arthur and Malory's switch is idiosyncratic -- the confusion between the two sisters starts in the medieval tradition itself. Accolon is Morgan's lover, not her son. Bertilak is Morgan's knightly tool in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, not her son. Ywain is Morgan's son by her husband Uriens of Gore -- a real son of Morgan's, but a loyal knight of the Round Table.  (Legend.)

question: A new Pharaoh who did not know Joseph enslaved the Hebrews and ordered a horror against every newborn Hebrew boy. What did he order done to them?
choices: shut in the temple of Ra
context: Exodus 1:22 (KJV): 'Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive.' The river is the Nile.

question: A Levite woman bore a son and saw he was a goodly child. Before she was forced to give him up, she managed to hide him quietly in her house for a time. How long?
context: Exodus 2:2 (KJV): 'when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.' Later tradition names her Jochebed.

question: The Levite mother wove a small ark to float her son on the Nile, and coated it inside and out to keep the water from soaking through. What was she said to daub it with?
context: Exodus 2:3 (KJV): 'she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein.'

question: While the ark floated among the flags at the river's brink, one member of the baby's family kept watch from a distance to see what would happen to him. Who?
context: Exodus 2:4 (KJV): 'And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him.' Miriam is named at Exodus 15:20. Aaron, Amram, and Korah are all real Levite men from Moses's family.

question: One woman came down to bathe at the river, spotted the ark among the flags, and sent her maid to fetch it. Who found the baby?
context: Exodus 2:5 (KJV): 'the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river... and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.'

question: When Pharaoh's daughter opened the little ark, one small thing the baby did moved her to compassion and made her decide to keep him. What did the babe do?
context: Exodus 2:6 (KJV): 'when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him.'

question: When the child was weaned and brought to the palace, Pharaoh's daughter gave him the name Moses. What did she say the name meant?
answer: because I drew him out of the water
choices: because I drew him out of the water
because he shall lead a people
because his cry moved my heart
because he was hidden three months
context: Exodus 2:10 (KJV): 'she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.' Hebrew mashah = to draw out.

question: Israel is suffering through a three-year drought, and King Ahab blames one man: the fierce prophet who had declared before the whole court that the sky would give no rain until he said so. What is that prophet's name?
context: 1 Kings 17:1 KJV -- Elijah the Tishbite tells Ahab there shall not be dew nor rain 'but according to my word.' The drought sets up the Mount Carmel duel in 1 Kings 18. Elisha is his student and successor; Isaiah and Jeremiah are prophets of later centuries.

question: The 850 prophets Elijah faces at the great fire-contest all eat at the table of King Ahab's wife -- the Sidonian queen who has hunted the LORD's prophets into hiding. What is her name?
context: 1 Kings 18:19 KJV -- 'the prophets of the groves four hundred, which eat at Jezebel's table.' Jezebel is daughter of the Sidonian king Ethbaal and Ahab's queen. Bathsheba is David's wife; Delilah is Samson's betrayer; Athaliah is Jezebel's daughter who later seizes Judah's throne.

question: On the mountaintop above the sea, Elijah faces the massed prophets of two gods sponsored by Queen Jezebel: the prophets of Asherah of the grove, and the prophets of the storm-god Baal. How many prophets of Baal stand against him alone?
context: 1 Kings 18:19 KJV -- 'the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of the groves four hundred.' The Asherah prophets are 400; the Baal prophets are 450. Total 850 against Elijah alone.

question: Two altars are built on Mount Carmel, one for Baal and one for the LORD; the wood is laid, the bullocks placed, but no human hand may touch it further. The rule Elijah lays down for the contest is: whoever answers by ____ , let him be God. What element decides it?
context: 1 Kings 18:24 KJV -- 'call ye on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the LORD: and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God.' The drought made rain the obvious sign -- but Elijah names fire, and gets rain as the aftershock.

question: From morning to noon the prophets of Baal cry aloud, cut themselves with knives, and no fire falls. Elijah steps forward mocking their silent god: 'Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or ______.' How does Elijah finish the taunt?
context: 1 Kings 18:27 KJV verbatim. 'Peradventure' is old English for 'perhaps.' The mockery is savage -- Elijah is saying maybe your storm-god is off in a bathroom, on a trip, or napping. The prophets of Baal then cut themselves with lancets 'till the blood gushed out upon them' (v.28) and still nothing.

question: Before the sacrifice, Elijah rebuilds the LORD's ruined altar on Mount Carmel, laying TWELVE STONES side by side -- but why twelve? What does each stone stand for?
context: 1 Kings 18:31 KJV -- 'Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob.' Every altar-stone rebuilds the covenant with the whole nation. Apostles-of-Jesus is a New Testament twelve; months and prophets are honest twelve-of-something distractors.

question: To prove no hidden spark could light the wood, Elijah orders barrels of water dumped over the sacrifice and the altar until the water fills a trench dug around the whole pile. How many separate rounds of water-pouring does he order before he prays?
context: 1 Kings 18:34 KJV -- four barrels each round, 'do it the second time... do it the third time.' Four barrels times three rounds equals twelve barrels of water soaking the wood before Elijah's short prayer in v.36.

question: Elijah's short prayer ends, and the fire falls from heaven. It burns the bullock and the wood -- and then it keeps eating things wood-fire cannot normally touch. Which THREE things does the KJV say the fire also consumes?
answer: the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench
choices: the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench
the ropes, the bones, and the oil of the sacrifice
the priests, the altar cloth, and the seven jars
the bulls of Baal, the wooden idols, and the grove
context: 1 Kings 18:38 KJV -- 'the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.' Twelve barrels of water and the fire still ate it.

question: Once the crowd falls on their faces crying 'The LORD, he is the God', Elijah takes the 450 defeated prophets of Baal down from the mountain and slays them beside a single small watercourse below Carmel. What is the name of that brook?
context: 1 Kings 18:40 KJV -- 'Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there.' Kidron runs by Jerusalem; Cherith is where ravens fed Elijah earlier (1 Kings 17); Jabbok is where Jacob wrestled the angel. All four are real Old Testament brooks.

question: After the killing at the brook, Elijah climbs back up Carmel, casts himself down with his face between his knees, and sends his servant to look toward the sea for a sign the drought will break. How many times does he send the servant to look before the sign comes?
context: 1 Kings 18:43 KJV -- 'Go again seven times.' The first six times the servant reports nothing; the seventh brings the cloud from the sea.

question: The rain finally breaks in a deluge. Elijah girds up his loins and runs on foot before King Ahab's chariot all the way to the entrance of a royal city where Ahab keeps his palace. To which city does Elijah run ahead of the chariot?
context: 1 Kings 18:46 KJV -- 'he girded up his loins, and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.' Jezreel was Ahab and Jezebel's royal residence in the valley below Carmel. Samaria was Ahab's other capital; Jericho and Bethel are other real Old Testament cities of the northern kingdom.

question: In the Norse story of Ragnarok, the sea rises up over Midgard, the wolf Fenrir breaks loose, and a great ship sails out of the east across the flooded world, carrying an army of giants and monsters to the last battle. What is the name of this ship?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapters 43 and 51; Voluspa stanza 50. Naglfar is the ship of the dead. Skidbladnir is Freyr's magical folding ship that always has a fair wind and can be folded into a pocket. Ringhorn is Balder's funeral-ship, which the giantess Hyrrokkin launches into the sea with a single push. Mannigfual is a giant ghost-ship of German North Sea sailor-legend, not Norse myth. Naglfar is the specific Ragnarok-ship.

question: Snorri Sturluson tells us that the Ragnarok-ship Naglfar is not built of oak or pine or any tree at all. Its planks are cut from a material harvested off the world's dead, one small piece at a time, for every generation since the beginning. What material is Naglfar built of?
answer: the fingernails and toenails of the dead
choices: the fingernails and toenails of the dead
the swords of every fallen warrior
the golden coins of every buried king
the black stones of the underworld
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Every corpse in the nine worlds contributes its clippings; the ship has been slowly assembling itself out of the leavings of the world's funerals for as long as there have been funerals. Norse myth is full of dark images -- this is arguably the darkest.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri turns from the myth to speak straight to his medieval Norse readers, giving them one plain funerary instruction to slow Naglfar's building. What does he tell them to do?
answer: clip the nails of every corpse before burial
choices: clip the nails of every corpse before burial
cover every corpse's mouth with a coin
burn every corpse instead of burying it
lay every corpse with its head toward the east
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51 (Brodeur translation): 'And there is this also to say concerning it, that any man who dies with untrimmed nails contributes materially to this ship's building -- both gods and men would fain the ship's completion be far off.' The other choices are real funerary practices from various cultures (Charon's obol, cremation, cardinal-direction burials), but none is Snorri's instruction. Cutting the dead's nails is the specific Norse practice.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri says that when Ragnarok comes, Naglfar breaks loose from its moorings on the flood, and a captain steps to the helm to steer it against the gods. In Snorri's version of the story, this captain is a frost-giant with a specific name. Who steers Naglfar in Snorri's account?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Voluspa stanza 50 ('Hrym steers from the east, the serpent writhes'). Hrym is the frost-giant helmsman. Thrym is the giant who once stole Mjolnir. Skrymir is the giant who tricked Thor with the illusion-glove in Utgard. Suttung is the giant who kept the Mead of Poetry in the mountain until Odin stole it. All four are real Norse giants -- Hrym is the specific captain of Naglfar.  (Legend.)

question: The Voluspa specifies not just how Naglfar comes but from what direction it sails. Snorri quotes the same line: 'Hrym steers from the ___, the serpent writhes.' Fill in the direction Naglfar sails from at Ragnarok.
context: Voluspa stanzas 50-51; Snorri, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Naglfar sails from the east; the fire-giants under Surtr come from the south (from Muspelheim). North and west are not directions given for either muster. The east-origin is the specific Voluspa detail.  (Legend.)

question: Naglfar comes to shore at the plain where every doomed pairing in the Norse myths -- Odin against Fenrir, Thor against Jormungandr, Heimdall against Loki, Freyr against Surtr -- will meet. Snorri says this plain stretches a hundred leagues on every side. What is the name of the plain of the last battle?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Vafthrudnismal stanza 18 ('a hundred leagues on every side'). Vigrid is the battlefield of Ragnarok. Idavoll is the meadow where the gods held council and where the survivors will re-gather AFTER the battle. Folkvang is Freyja's meadow where she takes half of the slain. Ginnungagap is the primordial abyss between fire and ice from before creation. Vigrid is the specific final-battle plain.  (Legend.)

question: Naglfar is not the only named ship in Norse myth. The god Freyr owns one made for him by the dwarf-smiths, the sons of Ivaldi -- it always has a fair wind at its back, and when he does not need it he folds it small enough to put in a pocket. What is the name of Freyr's folding ship?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 43; Grimnismal stanza 43. Skidbladnir is Freyr's magic folding ship, made for him by the sons of Ivaldi. Naglfar is the Ragnarok ship of the dead. Ringhorn is Balder's funeral-ship, launched by the giantess Hyrrokkin with a single push. Mannigfual is a giant ghost-ship of German North Sea sailor-legend. All four are named ships in Norse or adjacent lore -- Skidbladnir is Freyr's specific folding ship.

question: Long before Odysseus washes up on the beach where the princess Nausicaa will find him, he has been stuck for seven years on a far island with a woman who wants him to stay and be her husband. She even offers him immortality if he will forget his home. What is her name?
context: Calypso keeps Odysseus on the island of Ogygia; every morning he sits on the shore weeping for Ithaca. Circe is the earlier witch who turned his men to pigs; Athena is his patron goddess; Penelope is the wife he is trying to get home to. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calypso.  (Legend.)

question: The nymph finally lets Odysseus go on a raft, but the god who has hated him ever since he blinded the Cyclops smashes the raft in a storm. Odysseus swims two days and nights and crawls onto a strange beach. Which god broke his raft?
context: Poseidon is the father of the blinded Cyclops Polyphemus and has hunted Odysseus across the sea for the injury. Zeus rules Olympus but does not smash the raft; Hades rules the underworld; Hermes is the messenger who ordered Calypso to let him go in the first place. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Half-drowned and salt-caked and naked, Odysseus drags himself up above the beach into a thicket of scrub. To survive the cold night on the ground he scrapes something up around himself and falls asleep. What does he cover himself with?
context: The detail is Homeric and homely: no cloak, no hero-blanket, just leaves scraped up under an olive scrub. It matters because when he wakes up moments later he is still naked and covered in salt, and a princess is about to meet him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: That same morning, on the same island, a young princess is visited in her sleep by a goddess who has taken the shape of one of her girl friends. The dream-visitor tells her it is time she took the family's fine clothes down to the river-mouth to wash them for her wedding-day. Which goddess sends the dream?
context: Athena has been steering Odysseus's rescue at every step, and she chooses the princess Nausicaa's dream as her tool: a friendly-friend visit, a marriageable-girl errand, a wash-day that puts a wagon and a party of young women on the exact beach where Odysseus is sleeping. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus stops at a distance rather than clutch her knees as a suppliant would (touching a young woman would give offence). Instead he delivers a speech from where he stands, comparing her to a young tree he once saw shooting up beside Apollo's altar at Delos. What kind of tree does he compare her to (Odyssey 6.149-185)?
context: The palm at Apollo's altar on Delos was a real cult-object in Odysseus's world, and the compliment lands: a tall, slender, sacred, well-nurtured shoot beside a god's altar. Cypress and laurel are also Apollonian trees, but the shoot Odysseus actually names is the Delian palm. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: After Nausicaa gives Odysseus clothes and oil and lets him bathe, she thinks like the royal she is. If a princess is seen walking a strange man into the city, the whole town will gossip that she has picked him for a husband. So she gives Odysseus a very practical order about how he is to travel. What does she tell him to do?
answer: walk behind her chariot into the city
choices: walk behind her chariot into the city
wait outside the city walls until dark
come dressed as one of her handmaids
swear an oath he is not seeking her hand
context: The line is one of the shrewdest things any young character says in Homer: a princess who has just met a hero already knows the difference between a rescue and a scandal. She goes ahead in the chariot; he follows on foot at a distance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausicaa.  (Legend.)

question: Nausicaa also gives Odysseus a piece of court advice: when he reaches her father's great hall, do not stop at the throne of King Alcinous. Go past the king and clasp the knees of someone else in the room as your suppliant. Whose knees does she tell him to clasp?
choices: the old bard beside the fire
context: Nausicaa tells the stranger plainly: in Phaeacia any stranger my mother accepts is safe, because it is she who really rules. Odysseus does exactly that; the queen accepts him; the whole rescue turns on it. Homer is quietly saying who runs the palace. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaeacians.  (Legend.)

question: That night in the great hall the court bard Demodocus takes up his lyre and sings songs of Troy. The stranger sitting at Alcinous's table hears them, hides his face in his cloak, and weeps into it. The king, watching this, then gently asks him one thing that will unlock the whole poem. What does the king ask him?
choices: whether he was at the sack
context: Alcinous's simple question is the hinge of the whole Odyssey: it is what unlocks Odysseus's own after-dinner storytelling, and the entire flashback of books 9 through 12 (Cyclops, Lotus-eaters, Circe, Sirens, the underworld, Scylla and Charybdis) is his answer, told at Alcinous's table. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: King Nebuchadnezzar, the mightiest ruler of the ancient world, has torn Daniel and his three friends out of Judah and marched them east into captivity in his own great capital city. What is Nebuchadnezzar's empire?
context: Daniel 1:1-6 KJV. Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BC) sacks Jerusalem and carries the temple treasures and the royal youth home to Babylon. Assyria had already fallen; Persia will rise later and end the exile under Cyrus.

question: When Nebuchadnezzar demands his wise men not only INTERPRET a dream but tell him what the dream WAS, only one young Judean captive prays through the night and comes back with both. Which Judean interpreter is it?
context: Daniel 2:14-19 KJV -- 'Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision.' Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dream in Egypt; Ezekiel is a prophet of the exile; Ezra returns generations later to rebuild Jerusalem. All are honest OT dream-or-exile figures.

question: The dream Daniel describes for Nebuchadnezzar is a great image made of five materials, one for each part of the body. Starting at the top, what metal is the statue's HEAD?
context: Daniel 2:32-33 KJV -- 'This image's head was of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his thighs of brass, his legs of iron.' All three distractors ARE in the statue -- just lower down.

question: In the dream, as the great statue stands complete, one thing strikes it at the feet and breaks the whole colossus to pieces -- and it is not a hammer or a sword or a battering-ram. What smashes the statue?
answer: a stone cut out without hands
choices: a stone cut out without hands
context: Daniel 2:34 KJV -- 'a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet.' 'Without hands' means no human made it. The stone then becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth (v.35).

question: Later in the story, Nebuchadnezzar sets up a new golden image on a wide flat plain in the province of Babylon and orders everyone to bow before it when the music sounds. On what plain is the image raised?
context: Daniel 3:1 KJV -- 'he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.' Shinar is where Babel was built; Jezreel is Ahab's Israelite plain; Moab lies east of the Jordan. All real OT plains.

question: A herald cries that when the music sounds, every people and language must fall down and worship the golden image. The list of instruments is famous: cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery -- and one more with a name that feels wrong for a Babylonian court. What is the last instrument the herald names?
context: Daniel 3:5 KJV -- 'the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick.' The KJV translators chose 'dulcimer' for a stringed instrument that in Aramaic reads 'symphonia' -- probably a kind of bagpipe or drum, but the KJV word 'dulcimer' is the one every English reader remembers.

question: Three young Judean captives -- Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah -- have been given new names in Nebuchadnezzar's court, and it is those new names history remembers when the three refuse to bow. What are the three court names?
context: Daniel 1:6-7 KJV -- the chief of the eunuchs renames Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The distractors are all real Babylonian / Neo-Assyrian court names and titles that appear in the OT: Nebuzaradan is Nebuchadnezzar's captain of the guard, Ashpenaz is his master of eunuchs, Arioch is his captain who fetches Daniel; Rabsaris / Rabmag / Rabshakeh are court titles used as names in 2 Kings and Jeremiah; Belteshazzar is Daniel's own Babylonian name, Nergal and Sin are Babylonian gods appearing in courtier-names like Nergal-sharezer.

question: In his fury Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace stoked hotter than it has ever been. He does not say twice or thrice -- he names a specific multiple so extreme it will kill the strong men who carry the three young men up to it. How much hotter than usual does he order it heated?
context: Daniel 3:19 KJV -- 'he commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated.' Verse 22: 'the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.'

question: Standing before Nebuchadnezzar with the fiery furnace roaring behind them, the three Judeans first say their God is able to deliver them from the flames. But then they add three short words that make the refusal unbreakable -- even if no rescue ever comes, they still will not bow. What three words do they add?
context: Daniel 3:17-18 KJV -- 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.' Three of the boldest words in the Bible.

question: Peering into the seven-times-hot furnace, Nebuchadnezzar counts four figures walking in the flames when he threw only three men in. About the fourth walker he says: 'the form of the fourth is like _____.' What does the king say the fourth figure looks like?
context: Daniel 3:25 KJV verbatim -- Nebuchadnezzar's own words. The bank reports what the king says; Christian tradition later reads this fourth figure as a pre-incarnation appearance of Christ, Jewish tradition as a delivering angel. The line is the king's, not the bank's.

question: On a bend of a river in County Meath, Irish farmers five thousand years ago raised a great round mound of white quartz and dark stone, with a passage running deep inside it. In Irish myth this mound was the palace of the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann. What is the modern name of this ancient mound, older than the pyramids of Egypt?
context: Bru na Boinne (the palace of the Boyne) is the ancient Irish name for the mound known today as Newgrange, in the bend of the River Boyne in County Meath. Knowth and Dowth are its two great sister passage-tombs on the same bend of the Boyne. Loughcrew is another Irish megalithic complex, further west in Meath.

question: The great passage-tomb on the Boyne is famous partly for its age. Stone Age farmers built it before the first stone was set at Stonehenge and before the first block was cut for the Great Pyramid of Giza. Roughly how many years ago did Neolithic Ireland raise Newgrange?
context: Newgrange was constructed around 3200 BC, roughly 5,200 years ago -- older than the Great Pyramids of Giza by about six centuries and older than Stonehenge by more than a thousand years. Stone Age farmers, not Celts or Vikings, raised the mound; the Tuatha De story was attached to the site much later.

question: In Irish myth the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann, fell in love with a woman named Boann -- but she was already married to another god of the Tuatha De, Elcmar. To hide the affair the Dagda sent Elcmar off on an errand and cast a spell on the daylight. What did the Dagda's spell do to time while Elcmar was away?
answer: made a single day last nine months
choices: made a single day last nine months
reversed the sun's course across the sky
froze the moon at its full for a year
sank the sun beneath the sea for a winter
context: In the Old Irish tale Tochmarc Etaine and the fragment De Gabail in tSida, the Dagda enchanted the sun to stand still so that Elcmar would not notice time passing, and a single day lasted nine months. In that endless day Boann conceived their son Aengus and gave birth before Elcmar returned. Reversing the sun and freezing the moon are common in Greek myth (Atreus, Zeus with Alcmene) but are not the shape of this story.  (Legend.)

question: During that endless day the Dagda and Boann conceived a son, who was hidden away in fosterage before Elcmar returned. This boy grew up not knowing his father, and would one day trick the Dagda out of Newgrange itself. What is the name of the son of the Dagda and Boann?
context: Aengus (also spelled Oengus, or Aengus Og, 'the young Aengus') is the child of the Dagda and Boann. He is the god of love and youth in Irish myth, best known for the swan-maiden Caer, the dream-quest of Aisling Oenguso, and the Newgrange trick. Bres is the tyrant king of the Bres ladder; Ogma is the champion who invented the ogham alphabet; Nuada is the silver-handed first king.  (Legend.)

question: When Aengus grew up and learned who his father was, he came to the Dagda and asked for a portion of the earth like every other Tuatha De god. The Dagda gave him an answer that would set up the whole trick to come. What did the Dagda tell his son about the land of Ireland?
answer: all of it had already been divided; nothing was left
choices: all of it had already been divided; nothing was left
he would inherit only after the Dagda's death
he must fight another god to win his share
context: In De Gabail in tSida ('The Taking of the Fairy Mound'), the Dagda tells Aengus that all the sidhe mounds and lands of Ireland have already been distributed among the Tuatha De. There is no share left for the latecomer. That answer is what forces Aengus into wordplay to get any place of his own -- and the place he chooses is his father's own palace on the Boyne.  (Legend.)

question: Advised in some tellings by Manannan mac Lir and in others by his foster-father Midir, Aengus went back to the Dagda with a very small-sounding request. He asked to stay in Bru na Boinne for one specific length of time, and the Dagda agreed to it as a small favour. What length of time did Aengus ask to borrow the palace for?
answer: for a day and a night
choices: for a day and a night
for the length of a single feast
from one harvest to the next
context: In the Old Irish text, Aengus asks for the Bru 'la ocus aidche' -- literally 'a day and a night'. The Dagda, thinking his son wants only a brief visit, agrees. The whole trick will turn on the fact that this exact Old Irish phrase can be read two different ways.  (Legend.)

question: When the day and night were up and the Dagda came to take Newgrange back, Aengus refused to leave. He pointed out that the phrase he had used, 'la ocus aidche', could also be read another way in Old Irish -- and once the Dagda had granted the request in those exact words, that second reading stood. Which second meaning of the phrase did Aengus claim?
answer: 'day and night' -- meaning all days and all nights, always
choices: 'day and night' -- meaning all days and all nights, always
'a day into a night' -- meaning until the next dusk
'the day and its night' -- meaning until the following dawn
'day and night together' -- meaning a single full cycle of the sun
context: Old Irish 'la ocus aidche' with the definite article dropped can mean either 'a day and a night' (one span) or 'day and night' (all of them, always). Under early Irish law of the spoken word, once the Dagda had granted the request in those exact terms, the wider reading stood. The Dagda was tricked out of his own palace by his son's grammar. This is one of the earliest Irish stories of the clever-son-outwitting-the-old-father motif.  (Legend.)

question: Bru na Boinne is not the only great passage-tomb on that bend of the River Boyne. Two other giant Neolithic mounds of similar age stand within a few hundred metres of Newgrange and were built by the same Stone Age culture. What are the names of the two sister passage-tombs that make up the Bru na Boinne complex with Newgrange?
context: Knowth (the largest by area, ringed with more carved stones than any monument in Western Europe) and Dowth (whose passages face the winter solstice sunset, not sunrise) are the two sister mounds of Newgrange on the Boyne bend. Tara and Uisneach are inland royal seats. Emain Macha and Cruachan are the royal centres of Ulster and Connacht. Loughcrew and Carrowmore are other Irish megalithic complexes elsewhere in the country.

question: In the Netherlands, on the night before Nicholas's December feast, children still leave one particular household object out overnight, and in the morning it is full of treats and small gifts. What do Dutch children leave out for Nicholas to fill?
context: Dutch children leave a shoe by the fireplace on the eve of 6 December. The tradition crossed the Atlantic to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (later New York) and mixed with English Father Christmas customs to produce the modern Christmas stocking -- the shoe is the direct ancestor of the stocking. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: The most famous story about Bishop Nicholas begins with a poor merchant of Myra whose business had collapsed and who could no longer feed his family of three daughters. Under the custom of the fourth-century eastern Mediterranean, a father in that condition had one desperate option that the poorest really did resort to -- an option Nicholas heard about and moved to prevent. What was the merchant on the point of doing with his daughters to survive?
context: In the Roman world a girl without a dowry could not marry and, in a truly destitute family, was often sold into brothels. The threat to the three daughters is what triggers the Nicholas gift story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: Night after night Bishop Nicholas came to the poor merchant's house after dark carrying a heavy purse of gold coins -- one purse for each of the three daughters, so that each could have a dowry and be married. Nicholas did not knock and did not want the father to know it was him; instead he delivered each purse in one specific way, and that way has fixed the whole scene in Christian art ever since. How did he get the purses to the family?
context: The window version is the earliest and most widespread; in some later medieval retellings the purse is dropped down the chimney instead, which is why Santa Claus still comes down chimneys. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: For centuries after Nicholas, painters showed him at his feet or in his hand with the three purses of gold he tossed for the merchant's daughters -- simplified in the paintings into three GOLDEN BALLS. In medieval Europe one specific trade adopted those three balls as its shop sign and took Nicholas as its patron saint. The sign of three balls still hangs today over the doors of the old shops in that trade. Which trade?
context: Nicholas is the patron saint of pawnbrokers because the three purses of gold in the dowry story became the three golden balls of the pawnshop sign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: Nicholas is said to have taken ship on pilgrimage to the Holy Land; on the way a great storm caught the vessel and the crew were giving themselves up for lost. Nicholas stood, rebuked the wind and the waves as though they were disobedient servants, and the storm died away. Every Greek harbour to this day has a chapel of Ayios Nikolaos above the water. Because of that one scene, medieval Europe made Nicholas the patron of one working group. Which group?
context: Nicholas's image was carried on Mediterranean vessels for over a thousand years. Fishermen usually take Peter as patron (a fisher of Galilee); shipwrights take Joseph the carpenter; divers have no ancient patron. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.  (Legend.)

question: In a grisly medieval legend three young travellers stopped one night at a wayside inn and were never seen again. Bishop Nicholas, passing by, went straight to the innkeeper's back room, revealed the bodies and named exactly what the wicked innkeeper had done with them to hide the murders. What had the innkeeper done with the bodies?
answer: Salted them into brine to sell as ham
choices: Salted them into brine to sell as ham
Buried them under the cellar floor
Fed them to the pigs in the sty
Baked them into loaves in the oven
context: This 13th-century legend, told in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, has Nicholas find the three boys pickled in a barrel in the innkeeper's back room -- and raise them back to life out of it. It is why Nicholas is also patron saint of children. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: One very popular medieval legend, first written down about a thousand years after Nicholas's death, sends him to the Council of Nicaea in 325 as one of the 318 bishops there. The story says that during the debate Nicholas got so angry with the priest Arius, who was arguing that Jesus was not fully divine, that Nicholas physically attacked Arius in front of the whole council. What does the story say Nicholas did to Arius?
choices: Threw a cup of wine at him
Kicked him out of his chair
context: The slap is a late (14th-century) tradition with no historical support -- there is no evidence Nicholas was even at Nicaea. It has become one of the most beloved Nicholas legends anyway. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: The modern English name SANTA CLAUS is not from Latin or English at all; it is a slightly worn-down version of the name shouted every year on the night of 5 December by Dutch children waiting at their fireplaces for gifts. That Dutch name came across the Atlantic with the settlers of New Amsterdam (later New York) and became the American Santa Claus we know. Which Dutch name is Santa Claus a corruption of?
context: Sinterklaas is the Dutch contraction of 'Sint Nikolaas' (Saint Nicholas). Sint-Maarten is Martin of Tours (11 November); Kerstman is modern Dutch for 'Christmas Man'; Zwarte Piet is Sinterklaas's controversial helper. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Nicholas.

question: In the great flood, water came down from the sky for a set span of days and nights that Genesis names exactly. How long did the rain fall?
context: Genesis 7:12 (KJV): 'And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.'

question: Noah did not build the ark alone -- three grown sons helped him build it and rode it out with their wives. What were their names?
