context: Genesis 7:13 (KJV): 'In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah's three wives with them.' The other trios are real Genesis families -- not Noah's sons.

question: Genesis says water did not only pour DOWN from the sky in the flood; it also came UP from below on the same day. What burst open from beneath?
answer: the fountains of the great deep
choices: the fountains of the great deep
context: Genesis 7:11 (KJV): 'the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.'

question: On the SECOND flight the dove returned at evening with a freshly plucked leaf in her beak -- the sign to Noah that living plants were above water again. What kind of leaf?
context: Genesis 8:11 (KJV): 'the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated.' The olive branch as a peace-sign traces from here.

question: In Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland from four northern cities, and the first king to lead them onto the island carried a burning blade called the Sword of Light -- once drawn from its sheath, no enemy could escape it. What is the name of that first king of the Tuatha De Danann?
context: Nuada was the first king of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland. He carried Claiomh Solais, the Sword of Light, one of the Four Treasures brought from the city of Findias. Lugh and Bres come later in the story (Lugh becomes king after Nuada dies; Bres is the tyrant who rules while Nuada heals). Ogma is the great champion of the Tuatha De who invented the ogham alphabet, but he was never king.  (Legend.)

question: Nuada's blade was one of the Four Treasures the Tuatha De brought from the northern city of Findias, and once drawn from its sheath no enemy could escape it. Which name is given to Nuada's blade?
context: The Claiomh Solais, or Sword of Light, is Nuada's weapon from the city of Findias. It is one of the Four Treasures alongside the Dagda's Cauldron, the Spear of Lugh, and the Lia Fail (the Stone of Destiny). Gae Bolg is Cuchulainn's belly-spear from a later Ulster-cycle story. The Spear of Lugh is a different Treasure. Excalibur is Arthurian, not Irish.  (Legend.)

question: At the First Battle of Moytura the Tuatha De met the Fir Bolg, who then held Ireland. The Fir Bolg champion Sreng stepped out and, with a single stroke of his sword, shore clean through Nuada's guard. Which limb did Sreng take from Nuada with that stroke?
answer: Nuada's right arm at the shoulder
choices: Nuada's right arm at the shoulder
Nuada's sword hand at the wrist
context: In Cath Maige Tuired Cunga (the First Battle of Moytura) Sreng, the Fir Bolg champion, cut off Nuada's right arm at the shoulder with one blow. Nuada survived, but the wound would cost him his throne. Sreng was later offered Connacht as the Fir Bolg's share of Ireland after peace was made.  (Legend.)

question: While Nuada healed, two craftsmen of the Tuatha De worked together to fashion him a new arm of silver, jointed so cleverly that every finger moved as freely as a hand of flesh. Which pair of Tuatha De craftsmen made Nuada's silver arm?
answer: Dian Cecht the healer and Creidhne the wright
choices: Dian Cecht the healer and Creidhne the wright
Goibniu the smith and Luchta the carpenter
Ogma the champion and Bres the Beautiful
Manannan mac Lir and Aengus Og
context: Dian Cecht the physician-god crafted the arm itself, and Creidhne the wright helped with the jointing so that every finger moved as freely as flesh. From that day Nuada is called Nuada Airgetlam, Nuada of the Silver Hand. Goibniu and Luchta are the smith and carpenter of the Tuatha De -- makers of weapons, not this arm. Ogma and Bres are champion and king. Manannan and Aengus are sea-god and love-god, not craftsmen.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann were said to have come to Ireland from four northern cities, each sending one of the Four Treasures along with them. From which of those four cities was Nuada's Sword of Light brought?
context: The Four Cities and their Treasures: Findias gave the Sword of Light (Nuada's blade); Falias gave the Lia Fail, the Stone of Destiny that cried out under a rightful king at Tara; Gorias gave the Spear of Lugh; Murias gave the Dagda's Cauldron of plenty. All four are named in the Lebor Gabala Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: Dian Cecht was proud of the silver arm, but his son -- himself a greater physician -- would not leave things there. Working nine days and chanting 'joint against joint of it, sinew against sinew', the son took the silver arm off Nuada and grew back a living arm of flesh in its place. What is the name of Dian Cecht's son who healed Nuada with living flesh?
context: Cath Maige Tuired section 33 records the healing: Miach son of Dian Cecht set the arm to Nuada's shoulder and, over nine days of chant ('bone to bone, sinew to sinew'), grew back living flesh. Ogma is the champion who invented the ogham alphabet. Goibniu is the smith of the Tuatha De. Aengus is the young god of Newgrange -- a different son of a different father (the Dagda).  (Legend.)

question: When the healer-god Dian Cecht saw that his son Miach had done better healing on Nuada's arm than he himself was capable of, jealousy flared and he turned on the young physician. What did Dian Cecht do to his own son next?
answer: struck him dead with four sword-blows to the head
choices: struck him dead with four sword-blows to the head
banished him beyond the western sea forever
cursed him into the shape of a running wolf
shut him alive in a hollow standing stone
context: Cath Maige Tuired records the killing in awful detail: the first stroke cut only skin, the second reached bone, the third pierced the brain-membrane, and the fourth killed Miach outright. It is one of the darker set-pieces in early Irish myth. The lupine curse is a Norse or Anglo-Saxon shape; hollow-stone imprisonment belongs to the Bres and Aoife stories.  (Legend.)

question: Miach was buried, and from his grave grew a great many herbs -- one for every joint and sinew in the human body. His sister Airmed carefully laid them out in order on her cloak so that no healer would ever be without the knowledge of them. What exact number of herbs, in the Cath Maige Tuired reckoning, grew from Miach's grave?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 365 herbs grew from Miach's grave, 'as many as his joints and fibres'. Airmed the sister spread her cloak on the ground and laid each herb in its right place so that later healers could know which one cured which joint. The number matches the days of the year and is one of the oldest 'herbal correspondence' images in Western myth.  (Legend.)

question: Dian Cecht came upon his daughter Airmed's cloak of 365 ordered herbs at Miach's graveside, and jealousy took him a third time. What did Dian Cecht do to the cloak?
answer: overturned it so the herbs mixed beyond sorting
choices: overturned it so the herbs mixed beyond sorting
burned it and scattered the ashes to the sea
sold it to the Fomorians for a boat
buried it in the same grave as Miach
context: Dian Cecht, still enraged that his son Miach and his daughter Airmed had surpassed him, overturned the cloak and mixed the 365 herbs past any hope of sorting. Cath Maige Tuired ends the episode with the line that no human physician after that knew the powers of every herb -- 'only Airmed remembers'. The mixing-of-the-herbs is Irish myth's folk-etiology for the limits of the healing craft.  (Legend.)

question: As the Tuatha De Danann prepared for their great war against the Fomorians, the true king Nuada Silverhand did an unusual thing: he stepped off his own throne and put a younger champion in his place for the run-up to the battle. Who took Nuada's seat as war-leader?
context: Cath Maige Tuired (Elizabeth Gray trans.): Nuada rose up before Lugh Samildanach ('many-skilled') at the king's seat because a champion was needed to lead the preparations. Ogma is the god of eloquence; the Dagda is the club-and-cauldron chief; Manannan is the sea-god.  (Legend.)

question: Nuada did not give up the throne to Lugh for good -- only for a fixed run of days before the battle, on the reasoning that 'it was easier that a king stand in for a champion than that a champion stand in for a king.' How many days did Nuada yield the throne?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 'the king rose up before him till thirteen days had ended.' Seven, forty, and one hundred are all sacred numbers in other traditions (seven in Hebrew scripture, forty in the wilderness, one hundred in the Odyssey's suitors) but the Irish figure here is thirteen.  (Legend.)

question: On the eve of the great battle, the Dagda -- 'the good god' of the Tuatha De -- kept a tryst at the ford of the Unius with a Tuatha De goddess who promised him she would go herself against the Fomorian king Indech and 'take from him the blood of his heart and the kidneys of his valour.' Which goddess?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: the Morrigan ('the great queen') met the Dagda at the ford of the Unius in Corann and pledged Indech's heart-blood. Brigid is the poetry-and-flame goddess of Kildare; Danu is the mother-goddess the Tuatha De are named for; Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne.  (Legend.)

question: The war between the Tuatha De and the Fomorians was fought on a plain in County Sligo whose name means 'the plain of pillars' -- and this was the SECOND time a great battle had been fought there (the first was against the Fir Bolg). What is the plain called?
context: Cath Maige Tuired ('the battle of Moytura'): Mag Tuired in County Sligo. Tara is the seat of the High King in Meath; Tailtiu is where the Tuatha De later lose to the Milesians and where the Lughnasadh games are held; Emain Macha is the Ulster capital of Conchobar mac Nessa.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh's own people had judged him too valuable to lose in the fighting. Behind the ranks a set number of warriors had been posted to KEEP HIM AWAY from the front line -- but Lugh slipped his guard and ran to the battle anyway. How many warriors had been set over him?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 'his nine comrades keeping Lugh... then when the battle follows, Lugh escaped from the keeping in which he was.' Nine is a repeating Irish sacred number (the Nine Hazels of Segais, the nine worlds of Yggdrasil in Norse). Three, twelve, and twenty-one are the wrong counts.  (Legend.)

question: When Lugh reached the front he confronted his own grandfather Balor as Balor's poison eyelid was being lifted. Lugh loosed a single missile that drove the eye clean out the back of Balor's head and turned the deadly gaze back on the Fomorian ranks behind him. What weapon did Lugh use?
context: Cath Maige Tuired: 'Then Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye through his head.' Some later retellings substitute the Spear of Assal, one of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha De, but the primary text is explicit: a sling-stone. The turned gaze then destroyed the Fomorian rear ranks.  (Legend.)

question: After the victory the Tuatha De found Bres (the deposed half-Fomorian former king) alive and captive. Instead of killing him they SPARED him -- but only on condition that he teach them a set of skills the Fomorians had guarded from them until then. What did Bres have to teach them?
answer: how to plough, sow, and reap
choices: how to plough, sow, and reap
how to smelt iron and forge weapons
how to read the stars for war-omens
how to sail the western ocean
context: Cath Maige Tuired: Bres bought his life by teaching the Tuatha De the agricultural cycle -- ploughing, sowing, and reaping. The tale is a mythic charter for the Tuatha De's transition from a warrior-god people to farmers. Iron-smelting, star-reading, and ocean-sailing are staples of other myth-cycles.  (Legend.)

question: With Nuada dead and the Fomorians broken, Lugh was made KING of the Tuatha De Danann in Nuada's place -- and his reign became the golden age of the Tuatha De in Ireland. How long did Lugh rule as king?
context: Irish tradition (Lebor Gabala Erenn and later synchronisms): Lugh reigned forty years over the Tuatha De after Moytura. Forty is the number of the wilderness in the Christian pillar (Moses, Elijah, Jesus) -- an interesting cross-pillar echo. Seven, one hundred, and three hundred are other sacred spans.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse story of the last battle, a monstrous wolf breaks loose after ages of being bound, and races across the world to devour the All-Father Odin himself. What is the name of this wolf?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Voluspa stanza 53. Fenrir is the great wolf who kills Odin at Ragnarok. Garm is a different Ragnarok-hound who guards the gate of Hel and kills Tyr. Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's OWN sons -- the two wolves who chase the sun and the moon across the sky and swallow them at Ragnarok. Fenrir is the specific killer of Odin.  (Legend.)

question: Fenrir the great wolf was born to the trickster-god Loki and a giantess in Jotunheim. He has two full siblings equally famous in the Norse myths -- the great serpent that circles the world, and the queen who rules the dead. Who is the mother of Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 34. Angrboda ('grief-bringer') is the giantess who bore Loki's three monstrous children -- Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the world-serpent, and Hel the death-queen. Sigyn is Loki's actual wife, who holds the bowl above his face as he lies bound under a snake dripping venom. Skadi is the giantess wife of Njord. Gerd is the giantess wife of Freyr. Angrboda is the specific mother of the three monsters.  (Legend.)

question: When Fenrir was still a young wolf living in Asgard he was growing so fast that the gods were afraid to approach him. Only one god was brave enough to walk up to Fenrir every day and hand-feed him. Who was Fenrir's one keeper in Asgard?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 34. Tyr alone had the courage to feed the growing wolf. Bragi is the god of poetry, Vidarr is the silent god who will one day avenge Odin, Heimdall is the watchman of Bifrost. Tyr is the specific keeper -- which is why, when the gods later tricked Fenrir into being bound, it was Tyr's hand the wolf bit off at the wrist.  (Legend.)

question: The gods knew ordinary iron could not hold Fenrir, so they commissioned the dwarves of Svartalfheim to spin a silken ribbon out of six things that do not exist. It was called Gleipnir, and it is the ribbon that binds Fenrir to this day. Which of these was one of the six materials in Gleipnir?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 34. The six materials of Gleipnir are the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. That is why (Snorri jokes) you no longer see any of those things in the world -- the dwarves used them all up. The other three choices are plausible-sounding but not on the list.  (Legend.)

question: Odin's son who will one day step forward to avenge his father is one of the strangest of the Aesir: he almost never speaks a word, and Snorri names him the second-strongest of all the gods, after only Thor. What is the name of this silent son of Odin?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapters 29 and 51. Vidarr is the silent god, second-strongest of the Aesir after Thor. Vali is a different son of Odin -- born and grown in one day for the sole purpose of avenging Baldr, not Odin. Bragi is the god of poetry and eloquence (the opposite of silent). Forseti is the just-judging son of Baldr. Vidarr is the specific avenger of Odin.  (Legend.)

question: At the coming of Ragnarok the bindings of Gleipnir at last give way and Fenrir bursts loose. Snorri describes his jaws opening so far that one jaw touches heaven and the other drags on the ground, and something bursts from his eyes and nostrils as he runs. What comes from Fenrir's eyes and nose as he charges out onto the plain?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51: 'flames burst from his eyes and nostrils' as Fenrir runs. Poison is what the Midgard-serpent Jormungandr breathes over Thor a few lines later in the same passage, and what kills Thor nine steps after the serpent dies. Smoke and ice belong to other Ragnarok forces (Surtr's fire-smoke; the fimbulwinter). Fire is the specific detail Snorri gives Fenrir at the last battle.  (Legend.)

question: At the very end of the world Odin rides out to face the loose wolf in a golden helmet and mail-coat, carrying the weapon he has always borne into every battle. What is the name of the weapon Odin carries to his last fight with Fenrir?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51; Skaldskaparmal 35. Gungnir is Odin's spear, forged by the sons of Ivaldi -- it never misses its mark. Gae Bolg is the belly-spear of the Irish hero Cuchulainn, given him by the warrior-woman Scathach. Areadbhair is the spear of Lugh Lamhfhada of the Tuatha De Danann, one of the four treasures. The Lance of Longinus is the Roman soldier's spear from the Passion story. Gungnir is the specific spear Odin carries to his death.  (Legend.)

question: In the greatest single loss of the Norse pantheon, Fenrir does not merely bite or gore the All-Father. What does the wolf do to Odin at the last battle, as Voluspa and Snorri agree in the same words?
context: Voluspa stanza 53; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Fenrir swallows Odin whole -- the All-Father, wisdom-god of a hundred and seventy names, the hanged god of the runes, goes down the wolf's throat. Odin's missing eye was long ago pledged to Mimir's well for wisdom. Sleipnir the eight-legged horse carries him to and from the battle. The wolf's specific killing of Odin is the swallowing.  (Legend.)

question: The silent son who steps forward to avenge his father wears one very special piece of armour on one foot -- the thick-soled shoe Vidarr will need when he steps inside a wolf's mouth. What is Vidarr's shoe made of?
answer: leather scraps trimmed from every boot
choices: leather scraps trimmed from every boot
iron bands worked by the sons of Ivaldi
the scales of a fallen dragon
the tanned hide of Fenrir's father
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. The shoe is made of the strips of leather trimmed from the toes and heels of every boot ever made in the human world. It has been growing since the beginning of time and it must be thick enough to protect the foot that will one day step inside a wolf's mouth.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri does not merely describe Vidarr's shoe in Gylfaginning -- he stops the narrative and gives his medieval Norse readers a plain instruction about what THEY must do at home, at their own workbenches, if they wish to help the Aesir at Ragnarok. What does Snorri tell every cobbler to do?
answer: throw away the trimmings from his own workbench
choices: throw away the trimmings from his own workbench
keep the trimmings and place them in his grave
burn the trimmings on a bonfire at midwinter
hand the trimmings to his lord as tribute
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51: 'That shoe has been being made since the beginning of time. Any man who wishes to help the Aesir must throw away the strips of leather he cuts off the ends of his own boot when making it.' Discarded scraps drift somehow to Vidarr's foot -- the myth turns every cobbler in the medieval North into a small contributor to the vengeance of a god. The other three choices are plausible medieval practices, but only discarding the scraps is what Snorri asks.  (Legend.)

question: Wearing that thick-soled shoe, Vidarr meets Fenrir on the plain of Vigrid at the last battle -- with the All-Father already gone down the wolf's throat. How does Vidarr kill Fenrir in Snorri's account?
answer: rips the wolf's mouth apart with his hands
choices: rips the wolf's mouth apart with his hands
drives Gungnir through the wolf's heart
hurls the wolf into the sea
beheads the wolf with a great axe
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 51. Vidarr plants his shod foot on Fenrir's lower jaw, grips the upper jaw with both hands, and tears the wolf's mouth apart, killing him. Odin's spear Gungnir is already lost inside the wolf; there is no beheading, no drowning. The specific act is a two-handed jaw-rending.  (Legend.)

question: When the gods first tried to bind Fenrir with Gleipnir the wolf was suspicious and demanded a pledge of good faith -- one god's hand placed in his jaws while the ribbon was tied. Only one god was willing to do it, and Fenrir bit the hand off at the wrist the moment he found he could not break loose. Which god lost his hand to Fenrir?
context: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning chapter 34. Tyr -- the same god who alone had fed Fenrir as a cub in Asgard -- placed his right hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge. When Fenrir found Gleipnir would not break he bit Tyr's hand off at the wrist, the place Snorri afterwards calls the wolf-joint. Heimdall the watchman, Bragi the poet, and Forseti the just-judge are other named Aesir but none of them made the pledge. Tyr is the specific hand-loser.  (Legend.)

question: The chief god of the Aesir in Norse myth is called the All-Father, lord of Asgard, master of poetry, war, and death. He is the father of Thor and the husband of Frigg. What is his name?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 20: Odin (Old Norse Odinn, English Woden) is the All-Father, chief of the Aesir. Baldr is his shining son slain by mistletoe; Heimdallr is the watchman at Bifrost; Njord is a Vanir god, father of Freyr and Freyja.  (Legend.)

question: In every picture the Vikings and their storytellers left behind, Odin is missing one part of himself -- something he traded away long before the sagas open, and it never comes back. What is Odin missing?
context: Odin is famously ONE-EYED, the eye left as a pledge in Mimir's well. Tyr is the god who lost a hand (bitten off by the wolf Fenrir); Fionn mac Cumhaill lost a fingertip on the Salmon of Knowledge in the Irish tradition; no major Norse god loses an ear.  (Legend.)

question: Beneath one of the three great roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil there is a well of water that grants wisdom to whoever drinks. It is guarded by an old and knowing giant. What is the name of that well and its guardian?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 15: under one of Yggdrasil's three roots (the one running toward the frost-giants) lies Mimir's well, whose water gives wisdom. Urd's well is under a DIFFERENT root and is where the three Norns shape fate. Hvergelmir is the roaring spring under the third root, in Niflheim. Byrgir is a well from a different myth (Bil and Hjuki).  (Legend.)

question: Beyond the plain nickname One-Eye, Odin gains a whole net of hidden-identity names from his wanderings in disguise. One of them, given as the title of a whole Poetic Edda poem, means the Masked One. Which Odin-name is that?
context: Grimnismal (Poetic Edda) takes its title from Grimnir, 'the Masked One' or 'the Hooded One' -- one of Odin's many aliases when he goes among mortals in disguise. Bolverk (the Ill-Worker) is the name he uses stealing the Mead of Poetry from the giant Suttung; Hangatyr (God of the Hanged) comes from his self-hanging on Yggdrasil; Har (the High) is his throne-name in the Havamal.  (Legend.)

question: The seeress in the Voluspa also says who drinks from the well every single morning from the pledge Odin left in it. Mimir does not drink plain water -- she names the drink specifically. What does Mimir drink from the well each morning?
context: Voluspa 28-29: 'Well I know, Odin, where you hid your eye -- in Mimir's famous well; Mimir drinks mead every morning from the Father of the Slain's pledge.' Mead (fermented honey drink) is the sacred liquor of the Norse gods generally -- see also the Mead of Poetry that Odin later steals from the giant Suttung, and the mead that the goat Heidrun's udder pours in Valhalla for the einherjar.  (Legend.)

question: Odin had already paid one eye at Mimir's well for a taste of wisdom, but he was still hungry for a deeper knowledge -- the magical marks that shape fate itself, the ones gods and men still carve on stone and wood. What is the Norse name for those magical marks?
context: The RUNES are the Old Norse writing system (Elder Futhark, Younger Futhark), and in the myths they are also the raw shapes of fate that gods, elves, dwarves, and men learn from Odin. The sagas are the long Icelandic prose stories written down centuries later; the Eddas are the two main mythological compilations (Poetic and Prose); the galdr are the spoken magic-songs (Odin learns nine of THOSE at the same time as the runes, but they are different from the runes themselves).  (Legend.)

question: Odin does not find the runes in a book or receive them from a friend. To win them he goes to the great ash at the middle of the nine worlds and uses it in a way no god had used it before -- as his own gallows. What is the name of that great ash?
context: Yggdrasil is the great ash tree at the center of Norse cosmology, with three roots and nine worlds strung through its branches. Laeradr is the tree that stands over the roof of Valhalla, browsed by the goat Heidrun and the stag Eikthyrnir; Mimameidr ('Mimi's tree') is a tree named in Fjolsvinnsmal, often identified with Yggdrasil but named separately; Hoddmimir's holt is the wood where the two human survivors of Ragnarok, Lif and Lifthrasir, hide out the end of the world.  (Legend.)

question: Odin climbs the tree and, without any hand but his own, hangs himself from a branch by the neck. He then wounds himself in the side with his own weapon, so the sacrifice is complete. What weapon does Odin use to wound himself on Yggdrasil?
context: Havamal 138: Odin is 'wounded with a spear' -- his own spear Gungnir (made by the sons of Ivaldi, the same dwarf-team who lost the wager to Sindri and Brokkr in the Mjolnir story). Odin is not a swordsman in the myths; his weapon is always the spear.  (Legend.)

question: On the ninth night the ordeal breaks. Odin does one loud, physical thing at the very moment he seizes the runes and then falls back down from the tree. What does he do at the moment of the seizing?
context: Havamal 139: on the ninth night Odin looked down, screamed out, and took up the runes -- then fell back from the tree. The scream is the release: the pain of nine nights and a spear-wound crashing at once into knowledge. There is no laughter, no prayer, no hymn in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: The name of the world-tree, Yggdrasil, is not a random compound. It literally means 'the horse of X' -- and the X is one of Odin's own many nicknames. Whose horse is Yggdrasil?
context: Ygg is one of Odin's names -- it means 'the Terrible' or 'the Awesome'. 'Horse of the hanged' is an Old Norse kenning for GALLOWS, and because Odin hangs himself from this tree, the tree becomes 'Ygg's horse' -- Ygg's gallows. So the very NAME of the world-tree carries this story inside it. Grimnir ('the Masked One'), Bolverk ('the Evil-Doer', the alias he uses in the Mead of Poetry theft), and Har ('the High One', the name that titles the Havamal itself) are all real Odin-names -- but the tree's name specifically embeds Ygg.  (Legend.)

question: The Havamal is a long Old Norse poem, and Odin himself is the speaker of much of it -- including this whole self-hanging passage. The title translates as 'Sayings of the ___', and the blank is one of Odin's plainest nicknames. What does 'Havamal' mean?
context: Havamal = 'Sayings of Har', and Har ('the High') is Odin's throne-name. Gangleri ('the Wanderer') is another Odin-name he uses when he travels in disguise (see the Grimnismal frame). Hangatyr ('God of the Hanged') and various wolf-related names are also his, but the poem's title takes the 'High One' name specifically.  (Legend.)

question: After Odin has the runes he does not keep them to himself. The Runatal names four different kinds of being who receive the runes from him and use them ever after. Which four groups get the runes?
answer: the Aesir, the elves, the dwarves, and mortal men
choices: the Aesir, the elves, the dwarves, and mortal men
the Aesir, the Vanir, the giants, and mortal men
the einherjar, the Valkyries, the Norns, and the trolls
the light-elves, the dark-elves, the frost-giants, and the fire-giants
context: Havamal 143 lists the four groups who receive the runes: the Aesir (Odin among them), the elves (through Dain the elf), the dwarves (through Dvalin the dwarf), and mortal men (through Odin himself, called Odroerir here). The Vanir and giants are notably NOT named as recipients -- the giants especially have their own separate wisdom-lore, and the runes come to gods and mortals through Odin's ordeal alone.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories, one of the gods is often described walking the roads of Midgard disguised as an old man in a broad hat pulled down low, a grey-blue cloak, and a walking staff. He has only one eye, having traded the other long ago for a drink from Mimir's well. Which god is the wanderer in these tales?
context: The one-eyed wanderer in the broad hat is Odin, All-Father of the Aesir. Thor is red-bearded and rides a goat-cart, never disguises himself as an old man. Freyr is the Vanir god of harvests. Heimdall is the golden guardian of the Bifrost bridge -- he stays at his post.  (Legend.)

question: In the Grimnismal, a stranger in a broad hat and dark cloak arrives at the hall of King Geirroth of the Goths. The king suspects him of being a spy or a wizard and demands his name. The stranger refuses. Geirroth orders him seized and tortured to force him to speak. What form of torture does Geirroth use on the captive?
answer: seated between two roaring fires for eight nights
choices: seated between two roaring fires for eight nights
hung upside-down from a rafter for a day
tied to a stake and lashed at dawn
sealed alive in a barrel of brine
context: Geirroth sets the captive on a bench between two fires and leaves him there for eight nights, hoping thirst and heat will loosen his tongue. This is the setup for the entire Grimnismal -- the captive stays silent for eight days and then, on the ninth, begins to speak. In some translations the count is 'eight nights and into the ninth day'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse folklore Odin does not ride the winter sky alone. He rides at the head of a ghostly procession -- riders, hounds, and the restless dead -- on his most famous mount. Which horse carries Odin through the sky in the Wild Hunt?
context: Sleipnir is Odin's eight-legged horse, born of Loki (who became a mare) and the giant stallion Svadilfari. Gullfaxi ('Golden-Mane') belonged to the giant Hrungnir and later to Thor's son Magni. Grani was Sigurd the dragonslayer's horse. Skinfaxi ('Shining-Mane') pulls the chariot of Day across the sky.  (Legend.)

question: In Scandinavia the ghostly winter ride of the dead across the sky is not called the Wild Hunt -- it has an older native name meaning 'the Terrifying Ride', still used in Norwegian villages a thousand years after the conversion to Christianity. What is the Old Norse / Norwegian name for the Wild Hunt?
context: Oskoreia (also spelled Oskorei, Oskorreid) means 'the Terrifying Ride' or 'the Thundering Host'. Another Norwegian name is Odensjakt, 'Odin's Hunt'. In German it is Das Wutende Heer, 'the Furious Army' (from Wodan, Odin's German name), and Die Wilde Jagd, 'the Wild Hunt', which the English name translates. The wrong choices are real Norse terms but different things: the Einherjar are Odin's chosen warriors in Valhalla waiting for Ragnarok, the Ragnarok is the doom of the gods itself, and the Landvaettir are the land-spirits who guard the ground.  (Legend.)

question: In the Fenian tale, Fionn's poet-son is carried away over the sea by a woman of the Sidhe to live on a distant island paradise from which few mortals ever return. What is the Irish name of that island?
context: Tir na nOg means 'the Land of the Young': no one there grows old, the trees are always in flower and fruit at once, and no sickness comes. Emain Ablach, Mag Mell ('the plain of delight'), and Ynys Wydryn ('the isle of glass') are three other real Celtic Otherworld names, all cognate with Avalon in Arthurian legend. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/

question: One morning as the Fianna hunted on the shore of a lake in Kerry, a woman rode up out of the sea on a white horse whose hooves never broke the surface of the waves. She named herself as the daughter of the sea-god Manannan mac Lir. What was her name?
context: Niamh Chinn Oir means 'Niamh of the Golden Head' (her hair fell to the horse's flank). Sadhbh is Oisin's own mother; Grainne is the woman Diarmuid runs away with; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife (Ulster Cycle). Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: In the tale of Oisin, Niamh's white horse carried the two of them off the sand at Loch Lein, out over the sea itself without breaking the surface of the water. In which direction did they ride to reach the Land of the Young?
context: In Irish tradition the Otherworld is always west, across the sea: the same direction where the ancient Irish believed the sun went to die each night. This is why later medieval Irish voyage-tales, the immrama, always sail west toward the islands of the blessed. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: The white horse that carried Oisin and Niamh over the sea to Tir na nOg is named in the tale. What was that horse's name?
choices: Liath Macha of the Grey Battle
context: Embarr (sometimes spelled Enbarr, meaning 'water-foam') belonged to the sea-god Manannan mac Lir before being lent to his daughter Niamh. Sleipnir is Odin's horse (Norse pillar); Pegasus is Bellerophon's (Greek pillar); Liath Macha is Cu Chulainn's chariot-horse from the Ulster Cycle. Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: Oisin lived in Tir na nOg with Niamh and their children for what felt to him like only a short stretch of years. How many years did he think had passed there before the homesickness for Ireland grew unbearable?
context: In the Otherworld the time seemed to be only three years to Oisin. The bitter joke of the tale is that three years in Tir na nOg were three hundred years in Ireland: the whole Fianna had been dead for centuries while he lived what he thought was a short married idyll. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: When Oisin asked leave to ride back to Ireland and visit his father Fionn and the old Fianna, Niamh let him take the white horse but gave him one strict warning about what he must never let happen while he was there. What did she warn him?
answer: That his feet must never touch Irish soil
choices: That his feet must never touch Irish soil
That he must never look back over his shoulder
That he must never speak his own name aloud
That he must never eat any food grown on land
context: The warning is a fatal condition: as long as he stayed on horseback the Otherworld's timelessness would hold him, but the moment he touched Irish ground the three hundred years he had missed would fall on him. Compare Orpheus's warning not to look back at Eurydice, a Greek-pillar tale of the same shape. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: Riding through Ireland on the white horse, Oisin found the country changed beyond recognition, Fionn centuries dead and the Fianna a legend not living men. Then he saw a group of men by the roadside working at something that was too heavy for them, and stopped to help. What were the men trying to do?
choices: Push a cart out of the mud
context: The detail is one of the sharpest in the tale: three hundred years on, the men of Ireland are so much smaller and weaker than the Fianna were that a group of them together cannot budge a boulder Oisin can lean down from the saddle and move with one hand. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: Leaning down from the saddle to help the men move the stone, Oisin's fatal moment comes not from a spear or from an enemy but from one small piece of tack that snaps under him. What breaks and sends him to the ground?
context: The saddle-girth is the strap that runs under the horse's belly and holds the saddle on. When it broke, saddle and rider both slid sideways to the ground. The whole three hundred years poured into him the instant his foot touched the soil. Source: https://irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/oisin-in-tir-na-nog/  (Legend.)

question: In the frame-story of the Middle Irish text Acallam na Senorach, 'The Colloquy of the Ancients', a wandering Christian saint finds the aged Oisin by the roadside and questions him for months about the old pagan days of the Fianna. Which saint hears out the whole Fenian Cycle from Oisin's mouth?
context: The Acallam na Senorach (c. 1200) uses Patrick as the sympathetic Christian listener to whom the last surviving pagan Fenian dictates the old warrior-tales before dying. Every other saint listed is a real early Irish saint. The device gave medieval Christian Ireland a way of preserving the pagan legends. Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/

question: The moment Oisin's saddle-girth snapped and he crashed to the ground beside the stone, the white horse that Niamh had lent him for the journey did not stay by his side. What did the horse do?
answer: Galloped riderless back over the waves to Tir na nOg
choices: Galloped riderless back over the waves to Tir na nOg
Reared up and vanished into a sea-mist
Was struck to stone where it stood beside him
Threw itself into the nearest river and drowned
context: Embarr of the Flowing Mane, Manannan mac Lir's own sea-horse, turned back the way it had come and ran west across the water to the Land of the Young, leaving Oisin ancient and blind by the Irish road. W. B. Yeats later reshaped the whole tale into his long poem The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), drawing on Michael Comyn's Laoi Oisin ar Thir na nOg (c. 1750). Source: https://godsandmonsters.info/oisin/  (Legend.)

question: On the Sunday before he was killed, Jesus arrived at the villages just outside Jerusalem and stopped. He sent two disciples ahead into the next town to find and bring back one particular animal, tied up near a door -- not a warhorse. Which animal did he send them for?
context: Mark 11:2 KJV: 'Go your way into the village over against you: and as soon as ye be entered into it, ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat; loose him, and bring him.' The choice of a donkey rather than a horse is the whole point of the scene -- a king coming in peace, not conquest. If any owner challenged them, the disciples were told to say 'The Lord hath need of him' (Mark 11:3).

question: Mark 11:2 drops one small specific detail about the exact colt Jesus asked for -- spelled out in six words. What does Mark note about the colt?
answer: No one had ever ridden it
choices: No one had ever ridden it
It had been born that spring
context: Mark 11:2 KJV: 'a colt tied, whereon never man sat.' The Old Testament required a similar untouched-ness for animals used in rites (see the red heifer in Numbers 19:2, or the cart for the Ark in 1 Samuel 6:7 -- 'a new cart, and take two milch kine, on which there hath come no yoke'). Nothing about colour, age, or tack is emphasised.

question: As Jesus rode past, the crowds shouted a single Hebrew word over and over. Matthew 21:9 records the full cry -- 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord' -- but the shout before that is the one everyone remembers. What was it?
context: Matthew 21:9 KJV: 'Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.' Hosanna comes from Psalm 118:25 KJV, 'Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD' -- literally 'save, please.' By New Testament times it had drifted from prayer into acclamation. Hallelujah means 'praise the Lord'; Selah is an untranslated musical direction from the Psalms; Amen means 'so be it.' All four are real preserved-Hebrew words in scripture -- only Hosanna belongs to this scene.

question: The whole scene echoes an old prophetic line from Zechariah 9:9. Fill in the blank: 'Behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; ______, and riding upon an ass.'
context: Zechariah 9:9 KJV in full. 'Lowly' means humble, close to the ground -- the opposite of a general on a war-horse. Zechariah wrote in the sixth or fifth century BC; by Jesus's time this verse was one of the standard messianic passages. Note the parallelism: JUST, HAVING SALVATION, LOWLY. Riding an ass rather than a horse was the deliberate sign of a king coming in peace rather than conquest.

question: Straight from the celebration on the road, Jesus went into the outer courts of the Temple and found a marketplace -- money-changers making a profit on the temple-tax exchange rate, dealers selling animals for sacrifice. John 2:15 says he did not just yell at them. He fashioned a specific object and used it to drive them out. What object did he make?
context: John 2:15 KJV: 'And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overturned the tables.' A scourge is a whip -- knotted together from small cords. This is the single most physically confrontational act of the ministry -- Jesus took the time to braid a whip before starting. Only John's gospel records the whip; the synoptics have the same scene without the cord detail.

question: As Jesus overturned the money-changers' tables in the temple courts, he shouted an accusation stitched together from two Old Testament lines -- one about what the temple was SUPPOSED to be (from Isaiah 56), one about what it had BECOME (from Jeremiah 7). Matthew 21:13 KJV records the full sentence. Fill in the second half: 'My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a ______.'
context: Matthew 21:13 KJV in full. The 'den of thieves' is the exact phrase from Jeremiah 7:11: 'Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?' A den is a robbers' hideout -- Jesus is not just calling them cheats, he is calling the temple a hideout for cheats. Mark 11:18 says the chief priests heard about the scene and 'sought how they might destroy him.'

question: The four gospels agree that Jesus drove the merchants out of the Temple -- but they do NOT agree on WHEN. Three of them place the scene in the very last week of Jesus's life, just after the entry on the donkey. The fourth places the exact same scene at the OPENING of the ministry, three years earlier. Which gospel is the odd one out?
context: John 2:13-17 places the cleansing at the start of the ministry -- the same chapter as the wedding at Cana; the synoptic gospels (Matthew 21, Mark 11, Luke 19) place it in Holy Week. Some readers reconcile the difference by proposing Jesus did it twice; others treat the timing as an artistic choice by John, who arranges his gospel by theme more than chronology. The bank states the divergence honestly rather than picking a side.

question: Prometheus, the wise Titan who had stolen fire for mortals, warned his younger brother never to accept a gift sent down from Zeus, foreseeing that any such gift would carry a hidden curse. What was the name of the foolish brother who ignored the warning and took Pandora as his bride?
context: Epimetheus ('Afterthought' in Greek) accepts Pandora and remembers his brother's warning only afterwards. All four choices are Titans of the same family: Menoetius was a brother of Prometheus struck down by Zeus in the Titanomachy, Iapetus was their father, Atlas was another brother, condemned to hold up the sky. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days 83-89; Wikipedia, 'Epimetheus'.  (Legend.)

question: Alone in the house of her new husband, Pandora is overcome by curiosity about the sealed vessel she has brought with her. She lifts the lid. What happens the moment the lid comes off?
answer: every evil swarms out and scatters over the world
choices: every evil swarms out and scatters over the world
the vessel bursts into an unquenchable flame
the vessel sinks silently into the earth
she is turned into stone where she stands
context: In Works and Days 94-99 the evils -- sickness, old age, hard labour, envy, war, hunger -- fly out of the jar as a swarm and can never be gathered back in. From that day on, mortals live with them. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days 94-99.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod's line about the ONE thing that stayed inside Pandora's jar has been debated since antiquity, because he never explains WHICH way the reader should take it. Two readings of that final line have been argued for over two thousand years. What is the great dispute over what remained inside the jar?
answer: whether it is trapped away from mortals or saved for them
choices: whether it is trapped away from mortals or saved for them
whether the Greek word means Hope or Fear
whether it is a goddess or an abstract quality
whether Zeus put it there or Pandora did
context: One reading: Hope is imprisoned in the jar, so mortals go through life with only the evils that flew out. The other reading: Hope is safe in the jar, kept for mortals to draw on. Hesiod does not say. Both readings have serious defenders. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pandora'; 'Pandora's box'.

question: The saint whose feast day fills the streets of Dublin, Boston, and New York on 17 March every year -- Patrick, patron saint of Ireland -- was born around 385 CE into a Roman-Christian family. His father Calpurnius was a local Roman magistrate and Christian deacon, and his grandfather Potitus had been a priest. In which country did that Roman-Christian family live?
context: Patrick calls his childhood home Bannavem Taburniae, a Romano-British estate whose exact location is unknown; most scholars place it in western Britain, perhaps modern Cumbria or Wales. The point matters: Ireland's patron saint was a foreigner, taken there as a slave. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick was still a boy at home in his father's British villa when a band of Irish pirates raided the coast, seized him, and shipped him across the Irish Sea to be sold as a slave. He tells this himself in his autobiography, and even gives his exact age at capture. How old was he when the Irish took him?
context: Patrick's own Confessio names the age. He is one of the very few Christian saints for whom we have such a precise personal biography in his own hand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick tells in his own words how long his Irish captivity lasted -- long enough to change him from a careless Roman-British teenager, who had barely paid attention to his family's Christian faith, into a man who prayed a hundred times a day on a bare hillside. How many years was Patrick a slave in Ireland before he escaped?
context: The Confessio is explicit on the count of six years. The prayer habit he formed in those years -- 'a hundred prayers by day and nearly as many at night' (Confessio 16) -- is what he credits with his conversion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: One night on the Irish hillside a voice came to Patrick in a dream. It told him his fasting had been well done and that he would soon go home to his own country. Then a second voice, later in the night, spoke a single short line that sent him walking straight out of slavery. What was the second voice's line?
choices: 'The angels of God go with you.'
context: Both dream-lines are recorded in the Confessio. Patrick took them literally, left his master's flock, and walked to the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick escaped his slavery by walking about two hundred miles to a port on the Irish coast, then talked his way onto an outbound ship. The ship was carrying an Irish export bound for the Continent. What was on board with Patrick?
context: The great Irish hounds were sought after in Rome and Gaul as war-dogs and hunting-dogs; a shipload of them was a serious cargo. The Confessio does not say the captain believed Patrick's story -- only that he took him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: One of the most famous 'facts' about Patrick -- that he drove the snakes out of Ireland with his crozier -- is not history at all. Ireland has had no snakes since the last ice age, tens of thousands of years before any Patrick. Even so, the snake-driving story was written down for the first time in a specific medieval Life of Patrick. In which century was the snakes story first written down?
context: The story first appears in Jocelyn of Furness's Life of Patrick, written around 1185 -- about 700 years after Patrick himself. Patrick's own writings never mention snakes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.  (Legend.)

question: After Patrick escaped Ireland and got home to Britain, he did not settle down. He crossed to Gaul, trained in theology (perhaps at Auxerre or the island monastery of Lerins), and then made a decision in the 430s or 440s CE that shaped every year of the rest of his life. What did Patrick decide to do in the 430s?
answer: Go back to Ireland as a missionary bishop
choices: Go back to Ireland as a missionary bishop
Stay in Gaul as a teacher at Auxerre
Retire to a hermit cave on the Loire
context: This is the moral centre of Patrick's story: he VOLUNTARILY RETURNED to the country of his enslavement, was ordained bishop, and spent decades preaching among the pagan Irish kings and druids -- never leaving again. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick left two documents in his own Latin hand -- the earliest personal writings that survive from Ireland's whole history. One is a fierce open letter of excommunication against a Christian British warlord who had raided the Irish coast and massacred Patrick's newly-baptised converts, selling the survivors as slaves. The other is Patrick's autobiography. What is the name of Patrick's autobiography?
context: 'Confessio' is Latin for 'declaration' or 'testimony' (not 'confession' in the modern sense). Vita Patricii is the title of the LATER Lives written by others; Peregrinatio means 'pilgrimage'; Lorica means 'breastplate' -- the name of a famous later prayer wrongly attributed to Patrick. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick's autobiography, the earliest personal document from Ireland's history, opens with an astonishing sentence -- the way a great missionary bishop, decades after founding a whole Christian church in Ireland, chose to introduce himself to posterity. How does Patrick open the book?
answer: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful.'
choices: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful.'
'I, Patrick, bishop and apostle to the Irish, greet you.'
'Blessed are you who read these words in the peace of the Lord.'
'By the grace of God I have brought the Gospel to the ends of the earth.'
context: The full opening: 'I am Patrick, a sinner, most unlearned, the least of all the faithful, and utterly despised by many.' The self-deprecation is not false modesty -- Patrick genuinely believed his shepherd-slave years had made him a rustic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessio_of_Saint_Patrick.

question: Patrick's other surviving document -- his Letter to Coroticus -- is aimed at a Christian British warlord who had crossed the sea, fallen on one of Patrick's newly-baptised Irish villages, and shipped off many of the new Christian converts to be sold as slaves in Britain. Patrick, himself once a slave in Ireland, does something in the letter that a fifth-century missionary bishop had no obvious right to do to a warlord in another country. What does Patrick's letter DO to Coroticus and his soldiers?
choices: It petitions the Pope in Rome to try them
It curses their descendants to the third generation
It offers them absolution if they will free the slaves
context: The Letter to Coroticus is one of the earliest surviving Christian denunciations of slave-trading by Christians. Patrick declares Coroticus's soldiers cut off from the Christian community until they repent and free the Irish captives -- an astonishing use of episcopal authority across a national border in the fifth century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick.

question: A slave girl followed the apostle Paul and his companion Silas through the streets of the Macedonian city of Philippi for days, shouting after them. Acts says she was possessed by a spirit of a specific kind. What kind of spirit?
context: Acts 16:16 -- the girl 'brought her masters much gain by soothsaying'. Divination meant she was used as a fortune-teller. When Paul finally turned and commanded the spirit out of her, her owners lost their income and dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates.

question: After the slave girl's owners lost their fortune-telling income, they hauled Paul and Silas before the Philippian magistrates. The magistrates ordered the two men stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison, where the jailer fastened their feet in a specific device. What device were their feet fastened in?
context: Acts 16:24 -- the jailer 'thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks'. Roman stocks pinned the ankles wide apart in a beam, an agonizing position after a public flogging.

question: Late that night, bruised and locked in the stocks in the inner prison at Philippi, Paul and Silas did something the other prisoners noticed. According to Acts 16:25, what were the two of them doing at midnight?
context: Acts 16:25 (KJV): 'And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.' The other captives listened from their own cells while the two beaten men sang.

question: As the jailer stood in the ruined doorway with his sword drawn, ready to fall on it, a voice from inside the darkened prison stopped his hand. Paul shouted a single sentence out of the black. What did Paul cry out?
answer: Do thyself no harm: for we are all here
choices: Do thyself no harm: for we are all here
Peace be with thee: the LORD is at hand
Fear not: the angels have delivered us
Stay thy hand: we come out unbound
context: Acts 16:28 (KJV): 'But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.' Not one prisoner had used the open doors to bolt.

question: After Paul's shout, the shaken jailer called for a light, ran into the inner prison, fell trembling at the two apostles' feet, and then took them out to his own house. Before dawn, before daylight ever reached Philippi, he did two things: he cleaned the beating-wounds on his prisoners, and he brought his whole family through the same ritual he had just accepted. What was that ritual?
context: Acts 16:33 -- 'And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and all his, straightway.'

question: Earlier in the same chapter of Acts, before the fortune-telling girl and the earthquake, Paul preached on a riverbank outside Philippi to a group of women who had gathered there to pray. One of them was a wealthy merchant from Thyatira, and she became the first person on European soil recorded in Acts as baptised. What did that first European convert sell for a living?
context: Acts 16:14 -- 'a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira'. Thyatira was famous for its purple-dye trade; Lydia's baptism and hospitality at Philippi came just before the events of the jail.

question: Paul reaches Athens alone, waiting for Silas and Timothy to catch up. He walks the streets of the city, and one sight above all others stirs him up. What does Paul see everywhere in Athens that troubles him?
answer: Statues and altars to countless gods on every corner
choices: Statues and altars to countless gods on every corner
Roman soldiers dragging Jewish believers to prison
Beggars starving outside the marble temples
Slaves being sold in the marketplace
context: Acts 17:16 KJV: 'his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.' Athens was the philosophical and religious capital of the Greek world, thick with shrines. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: In the Athenian marketplace Paul is soon met by philosophers from two of the city's most famous schools. They dismiss him as a 'babbler' and a 'setter forth of strange gods.' Which two philosophical schools does Acts 17 name as the ones that confront Paul?
context: Acts 17:18: 'Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him.' Epicureans followed Epicurus (pleasure as absence of pain); Stoics followed Zeno (virtue and reason). https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Standing on Mars' Hill, Paul opens his sermon with a compliment. He tells the Athenian philosophers that walking through their city he had seen many altars, and one in particular caught his eye - an altar with a strange inscription cut into it. What does Paul say the altar was inscribed to?
choices: To the god of the earth
To the god of the sea
context: Acts 17:23: 'I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.' Athenians built such altars as insurance against overlooking any deity. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Paul is a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia - the same province that produced a famous poet named Aratus. On Mars' Hill Paul quotes Aratus back to the Athenian philosophers, treating a line of Greek verse as a bridge to his own message. Which line from Aratus does Paul quote?
answer: For we are also his offspring
choices: For we are also his offspring
No man steps in the same river twice
Great is Diana of the Ephesians
context: Acts 17:28: 'as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.' The line comes from the Phenomena of Aratus of Soli, a Stoic-flavored poem about the heavens - and Aratus, like Paul, was from Cilicia. Distractors: Heraclitus's river fragment, Homer's Odyssey dawn-formula, and Acts 19's Ephesus riot cry - all real quotes, wrong scenes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: Paul's sermon on Mars' Hill quotes not one but two Greek poets in a single sentence. Alongside the line from Aratus, he offers another verse - 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' - a line traditionally credited to a poet-sage of six hundred years earlier. Whom does this second line traditionally come from?
context: Acts 17:28: 'For in him we live, and move, and have our being.' The line is traditionally attributed to Epimenides, the same Cretan sage credited with the plague-story behind the very altar 'to the unknown god' that Paul had quoted moments before. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: For most of the sermon on Mars' Hill the Athenian philosophers listen politely. But when Paul reaches one particular claim - one that Greek philosophy could not swallow - the audience breaks apart, some mocking, some saying 'we will hear thee again of this matter.' Which claim of Paul's split the Areopagus in two?
answer: That the dead would rise again in bodily form
choices: That the dead would rise again in bodily form
That the temples of Athens must all be torn down
That the emperor in Rome was a false god
That the Jewish Law bound Greeks as well as Jews
context: Acts 17:32: 'when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.' For an Athenian philosopher, the soul might survive - but a body coming back was absurd. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Acts names only two Athenian converts by name after Paul's sermon - a rare specificity for such a thin missionary haul. One is a man, and one is a woman named alongside him. Which pair does Acts 17:34 record?
answer: Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris
choices: Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris
Aquila the tentmaker and his wife Priscilla
Crispus the ruler and a woman named Lydia
Justus the god-fearer and a woman named Phoebe
context: Acts 17:34: 'certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris.' Dionysius sat as a member of the Areopagus council itself; later church tradition made him first bishop of Athens. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/17.htm

question: Paul's Athens visit ends with only a handful of converts - one of his thinnest missionary results anywhere in Acts. From Athens he moves straight on to the next Greek city down the isthmus, a boisterous port where his mission will finally take deep root and where he will stay a year and a half. To which city does Paul go next?
context: Acts 18:1-11: after Athens Paul went to Corinth, met the tentmaker couple Aquila and Priscilla, and 'continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.' Athens was the philosophical showpiece; Corinth was the churn where the mission took hold. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areopagus_sermon

question: Paul, arrested in Jerusalem, has been held for two years in Roman custody at the city that served as the Roman governor's headquarters in Judea. In which city is Paul being held when he appears before Festus and Agrippa?
context: Acts 23:33-35, 25:1-6. Caesarea Maritima was Herod the Great's showpiece harbor city and the seat of the Roman procurator in Judea. Paul had been sent there under armed escort after a plot against him in Jerusalem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: The Roman governor at Caesarea who inherits Paul's case from his predecessor Felix is a newly arrived official from Rome. Paul will speak before him and appeal to Caesar in his court. What is this governor's name?
context: Acts 24:27-25:1: Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judea around AD 59. Pilate had been governor a generation earlier under Tiberius; Sergius Paulus was proconsul of Cyprus in Acts 13; Claudius Lysias was the tribune who arrested Paul in Jerusalem. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: Standing in the audience-hall in bonds, Paul retells to Agrippa the story of his own conversion on the road to Damascus, and quotes the line he says Jesus spoke to him out of the light. What line does Paul say Jesus spoke to him on the road (Acts 26:14)?
answer: It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks
choices: It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks
context: Acts 26:14 KJV. 'Pricks' translates the Greek kentra - the sharp goads a farmer used to prod an ox; kicking back against them only wounded the ox. The image was already a Greek proverb (Euripides uses it). https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: As Paul is defending himself before Agrippa in the courtroom at Caesarea, the Roman governor Festus loses composure and interrupts him with a shout from the bench. What does Festus shout at Paul in Acts 26:24?
answer: Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad
choices: Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad
If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend
Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth
Away with such a fellow from the earth: he is not fit to live
context: Acts 26:24 KJV. The distractors are real KJV lines shouted at other men: John 19:12 (the Jerusalem crowd against Pilate over Jesus); Acts 19:25 (Demetrius the silversmith rousing Ephesus against Paul); Acts 22:22 (the Jerusalem mob against Paul from the barracks steps). https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: After Festus's outburst, Paul answers him calmly - denies the charge of madness, calls his speech 'the words of truth and soberness,' and then swings past Festus to press Agrippa directly. Paul says the king already knows about these events, for 'this thing was not done in ___.' Acts 26:26 finishes the line with what phrase?
context: Acts 26:26 KJV: 'for this thing was not done in a corner.' The phrase became proverbial in English for a public deed no one can pretend not to have heard about. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: Paul, still turned toward Agrippa in the audience-hall, presses the king harder: 'King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest.' Agrippa answers with one line that has echoed in English ever since. What does Agrippa say to Paul (Acts 26:28)?
answer: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
choices: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
Behold the man, I find no fault in him
What I have written, I have written
Great is thy faith, be it unto thee even as thou wilt
context: Acts 26:28 KJV. The other three are famous Pilate lines and one from Jesus - none are Agrippa. The 'almost' is the point: kept in the room by the King James version and by every English speaker who has ever used the phrase since. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: To Agrippa's 'almost thou persuadest me,' Paul answers gracefully - he wishes not only the king but everyone hearing him were as he is, 'both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these ___.' What word closes Paul's reply in Acts 26:29?
context: Acts 26:29 KJV: 'I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.' Paul is standing before the king in literal chains and calls attention to them as he closes. https://biblehub.com/kjv/acts/26.htm

question: After the hearing at Caesarea ends and the king, the governor, and Bernice have withdrawn, Agrippa turns to Festus with a rueful verdict: 'This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not ___.' What legal move had Paul already made (Acts 26:32)?
context: Acts 26:32 KJV: 'This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar.' A Roman citizen's appeal (provocatio ad Caesarem) transferred the case out of provincial jurisdiction; Festus was now legally obliged to send Paul to Rome. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herod_Agrippa_II

question: The book of Acts does not describe Paul's death. It ends instead with Paul at Rome, under a light form of house arrest -- in his own rented house, receiving all who came, preaching freely. For how long, per Acts 28:30, did this arrangement last?
answer: Two whole years in his own hired house
choices: Two whole years in his own hired house
Six months in his own hired house
Five whole years in his own hired house
Through one winter in his own hired house
context: Acts 28:30-31 KJV: 'And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, preaching the kingdom of God.' Acts ends here abruptly, without recording his death. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: Christian tradition, unanimous from the earliest sources, holds that Paul was executed at Rome sometime between AD 64 and AD 67, in the same wave of persecutions in which Peter was crucified. Under which Roman emperor does tradition say Paul was put to death?
context: Traditional dates for Paul's death fall between AD 64 and AD 67, within Nero's reign (AD 54-68). Domitian's persecution came a generation later; Diocletian's was in AD 303-311; Trajan wrote to Pliny about Christians around AD 112. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: During his arrest at Jerusalem, Paul was about to be flogged when he turned to the centurion holding him and asked, 'Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is uncondemned?' -- then named a status of his that stopped the flogging cold and later, at Rome, would entitle him to a quicker execution than Peter's crucifixion. What did Paul tell the centurion he was?
choices: A Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin
context: Paul's Roman citizenship (Acts 22:25-29) entitled him to trial in Rome and to decapitation (a citizen's death) rather than crucifixion (reserved for slaves and non-citizens). Paul was also a Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), a disciple of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) -- but none of those statuses stopped a Roman flogging. https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: Around the year 200, a church father pairs the two apostle-deaths in a single sentence in his work Prescription Against Heretics: Peter's passion likened to Jesus's, Paul's death likened to John the Baptist's beheading. Which church father wrote this line?
context: Tertullian of Carthage, Prescription Against Heretics 36, c. AD 200: 'Rome, where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's, where Paul is crowned by the death of John' -- John meaning John the Baptist, who was also beheaded (by Herod Antipas). https://seanmcdowell.org/blog/was-paul-beheaded-in-rome

question: Tradition places Paul's beheading outside Rome along the Via Ostiensis at a spring-site later called Tre Fontane (the three fountains). Today the ancient site is held and cared for by one particular contemplative monastic order. Which order of monks holds Tre Fontane today?
context: The Tre Fontane abbey is held today by the Trappists -- formally the Cistercian Order of the Strict Observance, a reformed branch of the Benedictines known for silence and manual labor. Benedictines of Monte Cassino, Franciscans of Assisi, and Dominicans of Bologna are all real orders with famous mother-houses elsewhere. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tre_Fontane_Abbey

question: Tradition holds that Peter and Paul both died at Rome under Nero and were buried in the two great apostle-tomb churches of the city -- Peter under St. Peter's at the Vatican, Paul under St. Paul Outside the Walls on the Via Ostiensis. The Roman church keeps a single feast day for the two of them together, remembered as the founding apostles of Rome. On which date is the feast of Saints Peter and Paul kept?
context: The Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul falls on 29 June, remembering the two founding apostles of the Roman church. 25 December is Christmas; 15 August is the feast of the Assumption of Mary; 1 November is All Saints' Day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tre_Fontane_Abbey

question: The suitors are dead in the hall of Ithaca; Odysseus has been bathed and dressed in fine clothes and Athena has made him beautiful again. But the woman who has waited for him longer than most people wait for anything comes down to the hall and will not so much as speak to him. She sits opposite him at the fire and just stares. How long has she been waiting?
context: Ten years of Trojan War, ten years of Odysseus's wandering home. Penelope has held Ithaca and Telemachus and the household together the whole time, and has been fooled by beggars claiming news of her husband more times than she can count. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: The woman by the fire will not speak. Their now-grown son, watching this stranger come home to a mother who will not embrace him, loses patience with her and rebukes her for it. What is the son's name?
context: Telemachus is the son Odysseus left in the cradle twenty years earlier and has just fought beside in the hall to kill the suitors. Orestes is Agamemnon's son (wrong family); Antinous was the leader of the dead suitors; Eumaeus is the loyal swineherd, not a son. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Telemachus accuses his mother of a heart harder than the stranger she will not welcome home. Penelope answers the boy calmly and turns to one particular member of the household to give an order about the bed. To whom in the household does she turn?
context: Eurycleia is Odysseus's own childhood nurse and the senior woman of the palace; she is the natural person to give a bed-making order to. Actoris was Penelope's dowry-attendant (Od. 23.228), Melantho a disloyal serving-girl, Eumaeus the loyal swineherd. The rest of the room is about to hear something very strange. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope turns to Eurycleia and gives an order that stops the room cold: take a certain heavy piece of furniture out of the private bridal chamber where it has always stood, and set it up somewhere else in the house. Which piece of furniture has she just publicly ordered moved?
context: The order is a deliberate trap. A household can move any loom or throne or table. But there is exactly one object in the palace that no living person could move without cutting it apart, and Penelope has just publicly ordered it moved, with fleeces on top so the stranger can sleep alone (Odyssey 23.177-180). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: When Penelope publicly orders their marriage-bed carried out of the bridal chamber, Odysseus flares up. He begins, 'What man has moved it? No mortal could do it, not the strongest man alive, unless a god came down and shifted it.' Then he explains why. When he first built the bridal chamber for his marriage, there was a living thing already growing on the spot, and he built the whole room around it. What was growing on the spot?
context: Homer is very specific (Odyssey 23.183-204): a shoot of olive, still living, that Odysseus made the center of the chamber. The choice of tree matters because the olive is sacred to Athena, the goddess who has helped Odysseus through the whole poem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: In telling Penelope why no one could have moved their marriage-bed, Odysseus explains its construction. He built the walls of the bridal chamber around a young olive tree growing on the spot and roofed the room over. What did he do to the tree so it could serve as the pedestal of the bed?
answer: cut it off at bedpost height and used the still-rooted stump
choices: cut it off at bedpost height and used the still-rooted stump
felled it, hollowed the trunk, and stood it back on the same spot as a post
uprooted it, seasoned the wood, and reset it as a corner post
left the tree whole and hung the bed from its living branches
context: The whole point of the bed is that its main pedestal is not a piece of furniture standing on the floor: it is a living tree, still rooted in the ground under the bedroom, its trunk cut to bedpost height and smoothed. The bed is literally rooted to the ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Because the pedestal of the bed is a tree still rooted in the ground under the room, no one could have moved that bed to another chamber without cutting the trunk apart. And no one in the world knows that private detail except Odysseus himself, and one other person. Whom else?
context: This is exactly why Penelope's move-the-bed order was a trap. Only her real husband, who built the bed, could know the secret; a false beggar with a good tongue could not. She has just used the one detail no impostor could possibly know to be sure of him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: The moment Odysseus names the secret of the olive-rooted bed, Penelope breaks. She runs to him and throws her arms around his neck (Odyssey 23.209-224). What does she confess in the same breath about why she was so cold to him at the fire?
answer: she feared a man would come to her with a lying story and take her
choices: she feared a man would come to her with a lying story and take her
she feared the gods would punish her for a hasty welcome
she feared her son would call her weak for believing quickly
she feared the suitors' kin would return before dawn
context: It is the single most human line in the whole recognition scene: twenty years of impostors and beggars have taught her not to trust a good story. Only the private construction of the bed is a fact no impostor could possibly have. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penelope.  (Legend.)

question: Homer, having brought husband and wife together, gives them the single most beautiful simile in the whole Odyssey for their reunion (Odyssey 23.233-240). He compares her joy at seeing him to the joy of what group of people, at seeing what?
choices: long-lost soldiers seeing their city walls
bound captives seeing the door swing open
starving traders seeing a granary opened
context: The simile inverts everything: Homer has spent a whole poem shipwrecking Odysseus, and now uses the swimmer-sighting-land image to describe how the wife feels seeing her husband. 'She could not let go of him.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: So that husband and wife can lie in the bed rooted in the olive tree and talk through the whole night, one of the gods bends the natural order for them. She stretches out the darkness itself. Which goddess does Homer credit for holding back the morning?
context: Athena delays the dawn so Odysseus and Penelope can talk all night. It is a small quiet miracle, and it fits: the tree that holds up their bed is sacred to Athena too, so this whole reunion happens inside the goddess's care. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: The bed is only one of several recognition tokens by which the returning Odysseus is finally known. Earlier that same evening, when the old nurse washes the stranger's feet, she gasps: she has recognized him by an old boyhood scar. Where on his body was the scar?
choices: on the sole of his foot
context: The scar on Odysseus's thigh was cut by a boar's tusk when he was a boy hunting with his grandfather Autolycus on Mount Parnassus. Eurycleia had nursed him then; her hands know the scar the moment she touches it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey.  (Legend.)

question: Fifty days after Passover, about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus were shut in a single room in Jerusalem, sitting together in one place. Which of the twelve, standing up with the other apostles, would that morning step out to preach to the crowd in the street?
context: Peter stood up with the eleven and became the voice of the group (Acts 2:14). The other three are all real apostles, but the sermon on the day of Pentecost is Peter's.

question: Before the wind and the fire came, the followers of Jesus had spent days together in the same shut room in Jerusalem, praying. In what part of a Jerusalem house does the Book of Acts place them during those days of waiting?
context: Acts 1:13 places the eleven and Jesus's family in an upper room in Jerusalem, and Acts 2:1-2 puts the whole company 'in one place' when the sound filled 'all the house where they were sitting'. The other three are plausible domestic spaces but not the one Acts names.

question: The room in Jerusalem was still and shut. Suddenly a great noise came from heaven and filled the whole house where the hundred and twenty were sitting. What did the sound of that noise resemble, according to the Book of Acts?
context: 'And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting' (Acts 2:2). The other three are all sounds from other scripture scenes (Sinai, Elijah's chariot, the ram's horn), used honestly as distractors.
