question: Right after the sound filled the house, something appeared and settled on every person in the room, one to each. What did each of the hundred and twenty see resting on the head of every other?
answer: a small flame like a tongue of fire
choices: a small flame like a tongue of fire
a white dove with olive branch
a bright cloud like at Sinai
context: 'And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them' (Acts 2:3). The dove is Jesus's baptism, the cloud is Sinai and Tabor, the laurel crown is Roman -- all wrong for this scene.

question: Not everyone in the street was amazed. Some in the crowd mocked the speakers and had a ready explanation for the strange behaviour. What accusation did the mockers throw at the hundred and twenty?
answer: These men are full of new wine
choices: These men are full of new wine
These men are possessed by demons
These men are prophets of Baal
These men are drunk on strong myrrh
context: 'Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine' (Acts 2:13). Peter would answer this exact charge in the next verse.

question: Standing up with the eleven, Peter answered the 'new wine' charge with a very specific point about the time of day. What hour did Peter tell the crowd it actually was?
answer: The third hour of the day, about nine in the morning
choices: The third hour of the day, about nine in the morning
The sixth hour of the day, about noon
The ninth hour of the day, about three in the afternoon
The eleventh hour of the day, near sunset
context: 'For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day' (Acts 2:15). The Jewish daytime hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour was about nine in the morning -- much too early for the accusation to make sense.

question: Peter had stood up 'with the eleven' at Pentecost -- eleven, not twelve, because Judas Iscariot was dead. In Acts 1 the group had cast lots to fill the empty seat before the day of Pentecost came. Who had been chosen by lot to make the number twelve again?
context: 'And the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles' (Acts 1:26). Barnabas, Stephen, and Silas all become prominent later in Acts, but none was chosen to replace Judas.

question: A country boy is raised alone in the wilds of Wales by his widowed mother. She keeps him deliberately ignorant of what knights are and what knighthood means -- because her husband and her elder sons were all killed as knights, and she cannot bear to lose him the same way. This boy will grow up to become the hero of the earliest Grail romance in any language. What is his name?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceval,_the_Story_of_the_Grail. Perceval (Welsh Peredur, German Parzival) is the country-bred fool who grows into the Grail knight. Lancelot is Arthur's greatest knight, raised by the Lady of the Lake. Gawain is Arthur's nephew. Tristan is the hero of the Cornish love-story parallel to Arthur.  (Legend.)

question: One day the boy is playing in the Welsh forest when he sees five men riding through the trees in a way he has never seen a man before -- clad head to foot in shining metal, mounted on great warhorses, their armour blazing in the sun. Not knowing what he is looking at, he falls on his knees. What does Perceval, seeing five knights for the first time in his life, believe them to be?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceval,_the_Story_of_the_Grail. Perceval kneels because his mother has taught him only two things: pray to God when you see God's servants, and never harm a stranger. The shining armour convinces him he is looking at heavenly beings. Kings, giants, and demons are the other kinds of stranger a Welsh boy might imagine but he chooses angels.  (Legend.)

question: After his knighting at Camelot, Perceval spends time with an older knight named Gornemant of Gorhaut, who takes him in and teaches him what a courtly knight owes his host and his lord. Gornemant gives him one particular piece of courtesy-advice that Perceval takes so seriously it will one day cost him the Grail. What did Gornemant teach Perceval NOT to do?
choices: speak of his mother in company
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://mcgoodwin.net/pages/otherbooks/ct_perceval.html. Gornemant tells Perceval that a proper knight does not chatter or pry -- silence at a stranger's table is a courtesy. The lesson is well-meant. When Perceval sees the great procession at the Fisher King's castle, he remembers Gornemant and holds his tongue. The rule Gornemant gave him is what ruins the world.  (Legend.)

question: As Perceval sits at supper with the wounded king a procession passes silently through the hall from one door to the other. At the head of it a young man carries a plain white lance -- and Perceval sees that from the very tip of it, though there is no one wounded near, a single drop falls, and another, and another, constantly, all through the meal. What is falling from the tip of the lance in the procession?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceval,_the_Story_of_the_Grail. The bleeding lance is the second wonder of the Grail procession alongside the graal itself. Later Grail writers identify it as the Lance of Longinus that pierced Jesus's side at the crucifixion; Chretien's original does not name its origin, only its wound.  (Legend.)

question: Behind the two candelabra walks a maiden holding an object set with jewels that gives off so great a light the candles pale beside it. Chretien de Troyes calls this object in his Old French a graal -- a word later Grail writers will make into the chalice of the Last Supper, but which in Chretien's own tongue means something quite different and everyday. What kind of vessel is a graal in Chretien's Old French sense?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail. In Chretien the graal is a jewelled platter that gives out a great light -- it is not yet a cup and not yet identified with the Last Supper. The identification of the Grail with the chalice used at the Last Supper is the addition of Robert de Boron in his Joseph d'Arimathie (c.1200) about twenty years later. The whole 'Holy Grail as cup' idea is a second-generation invention.

question: Perceval watches the procession pass. He is astonished by the bleeding lance, and by the maiden with the graal, and by the second maiden with a silver platter behind her. He wants to ask his host what any of it means. But he remembers Gornemant's rule and he holds his tongue and eats his supper in silence. What is the specific question about the graal that Perceval fails to ask?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://urthona.com/literature/the-unanswered-question-chretien-de-troyes-and-the-first-story-of-the-grail/. The unasked question is 'whom does the Grail serve?' -- and had he asked it, the wounded Fisher King (whom the Grail was in fact serving) would have been healed. The question is one of compassion, not curiosity; that is why it heals. When Perceval swallows the question to be polite, he swallows the whole cure.  (Legend.)

question: In the morning Perceval wakes to find the great castle utterly empty -- no servants, no host, no maidens, no wounded king. He puts on his armour alone, mounts his horse, and rides out over the drawbridge. As he passes it, the drawbridge does something behind him. He rides on into the forest and meets a weeping woman, who tells him what he has done. What does the drawbridge of the Fisher King's castle do the moment Perceval crosses it?
context: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval, le Conte du Graal (c.1181-90); https://mcgoodwin.net/pages/otherbooks/ct_perceval.html. The drawbridge slaps up so sharply behind him that his horse just clears it. In the forest a maiden tells Perceval that had he asked the question, the wounded king would have been healed and his kingdom (the Waste Land) restored; his silence has doomed both to remain as they are. The chance has been given once and refused.  (Legend.)

question: Chretien de Troyes never finishes the story. He dies around 1191 with Perceval's return to the Fisher King unwritten, and the poem breaks off in mid-adventure. A generation later a knight named Wolfram von Eschenbach takes up the tale and writes the return to the Grail castle and the healing of the Fisher King as a great verse romance in his own tongue. What is the title of Wolfram's completed version of the story?
context: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival (c.1210); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival. Wolfram's Parzival is a Middle High German verse romance that gives Perceval's return to the Grail castle and the healing of the Fisher King. Perlesvaus is a related but separate anonymous French Grail romance (c.1200-10). Le Morte d'Arthur is Malory's fifteenth-century English prose gathering of the whole cycle. Roman de Brut is Wace's Norman-French verse history of Arthur, without the Grail.

question: The story of Perceval also survives in an older Welsh telling that seems to preserve a version of the tale from before Chretien wrote it up in French verse. In the Welsh romance the country boy is called Peredur, and when he comes to the mysterious hall the procession he sees has no graal in it at all -- instead of a serving-dish full of light, the young women carry something that belongs to an older vengeance-tale, not a Grail-quest. In the Welsh Peredur son of Efrawg, what do the maidens carry through the hall?
answer: a severed head on a platter
choices: a severed head on a platter
a golden chalice full of wine
an ivory horn of a unicorn
context: Peredur son of Efrawg, in the Mabinogion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peredur_son_of_Efrawg. The Welsh Peredur has NO Grail question -- Peredur sees the head of a murdered kinsman on the platter and is meant later to avenge him. The Welsh version is probably a survival of an older Celtic vengeance-tale that Chretien Christianises into the Grail question. The Grail cycle grows out of the Welsh severed-head bowl.  (Legend.)

question: Perpetua's own diary begins with a detail that made her arrest particularly brutal: at the moment the guards took her, she was in the middle of a very ordinary daily task that any young mother in Carthage would be doing. When the soldiers came for her, what was she doing with her baby?
answer: Nursing her infant son at her breast
choices: Nursing her infant son at her breast
Bathing the baby in a copper basin
Wrapping the baby in swaddling cloths
context: Perpetua's baby son was still nursing when she was arrested; her family were pagan and her father brought the baby to the prison to try to break her will. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: A second woman was locked up with Perpetua in the Carthage prison -- a woman remembered together with Perpetua in the calendar to this day. Who was Felicity?
answer: An enslaved woman, eight months pregnant
choices: An enslaved woman, eight months pregnant
A young Roman matron in early pregnancy
A slave girl of the household, mute from birth
context: Felicitas (Felicity) is a slave; Perpetua is a noblewoman. The Passion carefully insists on their equality as Christians and their equal courage. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: Perpetua's family were pagans, and her old pagan father came to the prison over and over, weeping, kissing her hands, throwing himself at her feet, and finally holding her nursing baby out to her. He was begging her to do one specific thing that would end the whole trial and let her go home to her son. What was he begging her to do?
choices: Deny that she was ever baptised
Escape with him out of the prison
Curse the name of Jesus in public
context: Roman law allowed accused Christians to go free if they would offer even a pinch of incense to the emperor's statue or the state gods. Perpetua refused three times, in front of her father and finally in front of the governor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity.

question: Perpetua wrote that at the FOOT of that same golden ladder crouched a huge creature there to frighten off anyone trying to climb. Her teacher Saturus went up first and called down: 'Perpetua, I am waiting for you, but take care that it does not bite you.' In the name of Jesus, she answered, it would not bite her -- and she stepped onto its HEAD as her first rung upward. What creature was at the foot of the ladder?
choices: A lion with a bloody mane
context: Perpetua explicitly echoes Genesis 3 -- the woman stepping on the serpent's head. Some manuscripts call the creature a dragon. Passion 4. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.  (Legend.)

question: Eight months pregnant and terrified she would be spared the arena for being a mother, Felicity prayed to go into labour early -- and the whole prison prayed with her. She gave birth to a daughter two days ahead of time, in visible pain. A jailer standing by mocked her, saying that if she cried out like this in childbirth what would she do in front of the beasts? What did Felicity answer him?
answer: 'Now it is I who suffer; but there another will suffer in me, because I too shall suffer for him.'
choices: 'Now it is I who suffer; but there another will suffer in me, because I too shall suffer for him.'
'What you see now is nothing; wait until you see me stand alone against the beasts of the arena.'
'Take my child away from me at once, so that I may enter the sand as light as any of the men.'
'Save your mockery for the day when you yourself stand before the God whose people you strike.'
context: Passion 15. Under Roman law a pregnant woman could not be executed; Felicity was afraid of being reprieved on that ground and separated from the group. Her newborn daughter was smuggled out to a Christian family in the city. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: On the day of the games -- staged to celebrate the birthday of the emperor Septimius Severus's son Geta -- the men of the group were sent to be killed by a boar, a bear and a leopard. The two women were stripped, hung in nets, and sent out against one particular animal that the arena managers deliberately chose so that its sex would match the sex of the victims. What animal did they send against Perpetua and Felicity?
context: A young cow deliberately maddened for the arena. The crowd was so disgusted by the sight of the two half-naked women (one just having given birth) being tossed by a cow that they demanded the women be dressed and brought back in tunics before the fight went on. Passion 20. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: After the heifer had tossed Perpetua and her tunic was torn open, she stood up in the sand, calmly fixed her clothing to cover her legs, then asked for a pin and pinned her loose HAIR back up. She did this in the middle of the arena, in front of the whole crowd, for one very specific reason of Roman public custom. Why did Perpetua pin her hair back up?
answer: Because loose hair was the sign of mourning, and this was not a day for mourning
choices: Because loose hair was the sign of mourning, and this was not a day for mourning
Because loose hair was forbidden to freeborn Roman women in public
Because loose hair would be grabbed by the beast on the next charge
Because loose hair was the badge of a slave in Carthage
context: Passion 20. In the Roman world a woman with loose, unbound hair was in mourning. Perpetua deliberately would not let the crowd see her mourning her own death; she was going to it as to a wedding. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.

question: The day before the games Perpetua had a final vision that she wrote down carefully. In it she found herself in the arena, but her body had CHANGED -- she was no longer a nursing mother but stripped and turned into a man. She was made to wrestle a formidable adversary; she threw him and trod on his head, and understood only afterward that her real fight was not with beasts but with the devil. Who did Perpetua wrestle in that final vision?
choices: A veiled woman all in white
context: Passion 10. Egyptian wrestlers were famous champions in the Roman world; the vision-figure represents the devil in the shape of the toughest opponent Perpetua could imagine. Her victory over him becomes her spiritual reading of the martyrdom to come. Source: newadvent.org/fathers/0324.htm.  (Legend.)

question: A prophecy had warned Acrisius, king of Argos, that his own grandson would kill him. So he locked his daughter Danae inside a tower of bronze. What form did Zeus take to reach her through the tower roof?
context: The child born from that visit was Perseus. Zeus took the form of a swan for Leda and a bull for Europa; the tower story specifically has the shower of gold. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.1.  (Legend.)

question: When Acrisius learned that his daughter Danae had borne a son to Zeus, he could not risk killing them outright. What did he do with mother and baby instead?
answer: Sealed them in a wooden chest and cast them out to sea
choices: Sealed them in a wooden chest and cast them out to sea
Sold them as slaves to a foreign merchant
Sent them into exile by mule caravan
Handed them over to the priestesses of Hera
context: The chest washed up on the small Aegean island of Seriphos, where a kind fisherman drew it from the surf and took Danae and her baby in.  (Legend.)

question: The chest bearing Danae and her infant son drifted to a small Aegean island, where a kind fisherman pulled it from the surf. What was the fisherman's name?
context: Dictys raised Perseus as if he were his own. His brother Polydectes was the local king, and later became Perseus's enemy.  (Legend.)

question: The king of Seriphos wanted Danae for himself and wanted her grown son out of the way. He announced a pretend wedding and asked every guest for a specific gift. What did he demand from each guest?
context: The king was Polydectes, brother of Dictys. Perseus had no horse to give, and Polydectes used that shortfall to trap him.  (Legend.)

question: Cornered at the wedding-feast with no horse to offer, young Perseus made a wild boast about what he would bring King Polydectes instead. What did he promise to bring?
context: Polydectes leaped on the promise and held Perseus to it, expecting the boy to die trying. The other three are the quests of Jason and Heracles.  (Legend.)

question: Along with Athena, another god equipped Perseus for the Gorgon-quest by lending him a curved sickle-shaped sword called the harpe. Which god was it?
context: The same Greek word 'harpe' names the sickle Cronus used to unman Ouranos in Hesiod's Theogony.  (Legend.)

question: Athena told Perseus the way to the Gorgons was known only to three grey-haired witches called the Graeae. What did the three sisters share between them, passing it back and forth?
answer: A single eye and a single tooth
choices: A single eye and a single tooth
A single wing and a single claw
A single mirror and a single comb
A single flame and a single ember
context: Perseus snatched the eye mid-pass and refused to give it back until the sisters told him where to find the nymphs who guarded his equipment.  (Legend.)

question: In Greek myth three sisters live at the edge of the world; snakes writhe on their heads for hair, boar-tusks jut from their mouths, and any traveller who looks at their faces turns to stone. Perseus is sent to bring back one head. What is the family name of these three snake-haired sisters?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 270-283, names them Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa, daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and the sea-monster Ceto. The Harpies are winged snatchers, the Erinyes (Furies) are avengers, and the Graeae are the three grey-sisters who share a single eye.  (Legend.)

question: In Ovid's telling, a beautiful mortal priestess served in Athena's temple until the sea-god Poseidon assaulted her there; Athena, offended, transformed her hair into snakes and her face into a horror that turned any onlooker to stone. Which figure carries this Ovidian backstory?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.794-803. Arachne is turned into a spider for boasting at weaving; Callisto is turned into a bear by a jealous Hera; Andromeda is Perseus's later bride, chained to a rock for her mother's boast.  (Legend.)

question: Perseus needs a container that will hold Medusa's severed head without letting its stone-turning power leak out on him or on innocent bystanders during the long flight home. The nymphs give him a special bag for exactly this job. What is this bag called?
context: The kibisis is named in Hesiod's Shield of Heracles and in Apollodorus 2.4 as Perseus's Gorgon-head bag. The harpe is his curved sword; the aegis is Athena's shield-cloak; the labarum is the much later Christian standard of Constantine.  (Legend.)

question: In the Gorgons' cave Perseus strikes off Medusa's head with a single blow of his curved sword. In that instant something impossible happens at the wound: two beings leap out from the open neck, both fathered earlier by Poseidon. Which pair springs out?
choices: the Chimera and the Nemean Lion
context: Hesiod, Theogony 280-283. Pegasus is the winged horse later ridden by Bellerophon against the Chimera; Chrysaor is a warrior born already fully armed, whose name means 'he who has a golden sword'.  (Legend.)

question: Chrysaor, the warrior-brother of Pegasus born fully armed from Medusa's severed neck, grows up and himself fathers one of the great monsters Heracles must fight. Which of Heracles's twelve labors puts him face to face with Chrysaor's son?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 287-294. Chrysaor's son is Geryon, the three-bodied giant of Erytheia whose cattle Heracles is sent to steal for his tenth labor. The twelfth labor is Cerberus, the ninth is Hippolyta's girdle, and the sixth is driving off the Stymphalian birds.  (Legend.)

question: The Gorgon-head passes out of Perseus's hands at the end of the story. He gives it as a trophy to the goddess who first lent him the polished shield. For the rest of Greek art and myth the head shows up staring out from the middle of one specific piece of Athena's gear. Which piece?
context: Apollodorus 2.4. The Gorgoneion at the heart of Athena's aegis is how the goddess is depicted for the rest of Greek art and myth; Zeus's aegis carries the same face. The Palladium is the wooden Athena-statue guarded at Troy; her helmet-crest and spear-shaft carry no Gorgoneion in the tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Two of Jesus's twelve apostles walked up together to the great Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer, as they did every day. Peter was one of the pair. Which apostle went up the Temple steps at his side that afternoon?
context: 'Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer' (Acts 3:1). John, the son of Zebedee, is Peter's constant companion in the opening chapters of Acts. Andrew (Peter's brother), Philip, and Matthew are real apostles but not the one at the Temple that day.

question: At one Temple entrance in Jerusalem a certain man was carried and set down every day so he could beg alms from the pilgrims going in to pray. He had been unable to walk from birth. By what glowing epithet does the Book of Acts name this Temple gate?
context: 'A certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful' (Acts 3:2). Tradition identifies it with the Nicanor Gate of the Second Temple, said to be made of Corinthian bronze that shone like gold.

question: Peter and John reached the Temple at the hour of the second daily incense offering -- what Acts calls the ninth hour. Which time on our clock was the ninth hour?
context: 'Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour' (Acts 3:1). The ninth hour was roughly three in the afternoon -- the time of the second daily Temple sacrifice and its accompanying incense offering.

question: When the beggar looked up expecting money, Peter answered with a line the Church has quoted ever since. What was the line Peter spoke to him?
answer: Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: rise up and walk
choices: Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: rise up and walk
Take up thy bed and thy purse: rise, walk out from this gate of the Temple
Be it unto thee according to thy faith: rise up, take thy bed and go home
Thy sins are forgiven thee: rise up, take thy bed and walk into the Temple
context: Full line: 'Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk' (Acts 3:6). The other three are woven from real gospel healing lines (Mark 2:9, Matt 9:29, Mark 2:5) -- all plausible commands, none of them Peter's at the Beautiful Gate.

question: Peter did not wait for a reply. He reached out, took hold of the beggar to raise him, and immediately the man's feet and ankle bones received strength. Which hand did Peter take him by, according to Acts 3:7?
context: 'And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength' (Acts 3:7). In the ancient world the right hand carried the sense of power and covenant, and Acts records the detail specifically.

question: A grown man who had never in his life stood on his own feet was suddenly upright at the Beautiful Gate. He did not just walk. According to Acts 3:8, what other three-word thing did the healed beggar do as he went into the Temple with Peter and John?
answer: walking, and leaping, and praising God
choices: walking, and leaping, and praising God
kneeling, and weeping, and blessing God
shouting, and running, and calling on God
singing, and dancing, and glorifying God
context: 'And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God' (Acts 3:8). The Acts writer piles the three participles on purpose -- a grown man who has never walked, jumping.

question: The people saw the man who had begged every day at the Beautiful Gate now leaping into the Temple, and they crowded to Peter and John. Peter took the moment to preach a second time about Jesus. Where in the Temple courts did he stand to preach on this occasion?
context: 'And as the lame man which was healed held Peter and John, all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering' (Acts 3:11). Solomon's Porch was a covered colonnade along the east side of the Temple's outer court.

question: Peter's Beautiful Gate sermon was still drawing crowds at Solomon's Porch when the priests, the Sadducees, and the captain of the Temple guard broke in on the apostles. According to Acts 4, what did they do with Peter and John?
answer: held them in custody until the next day
choices: held them in custody until the next day
drove them out of the city before sundown
brought them at once before Herod the king
beat them with rods and released them
context: 'And they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide' (Acts 4:3). The priests, the captain of the Temple, and the Sadducees interrupted the sermon (Acts 4:1) and held the apostles overnight before hauling them before the council the next morning.

question: By the end of his life, tradition places the fisherman apostle Peter far from Galilee, leading the small Christian community in a great Mediterranean city where he was said to have been executed under Nero. In what city did Peter spend his last years, according to that tradition?
context: Early Church tradition (Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Irenaeus) places Peter's final ministry at Rome. Antioch, Alexandria, and Corinth were the other great early-Church cities but the tradition of Peter's death is tied specifically to Rome.  (Legend.)

question: The letter called 1 Peter closes with a greeting from 'the church that is at' a certain city. Peter names the city with a coded Old Testament name that ancient readers understood as pointing to Rome. Which name did he use?
context: 'The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you' (1 Peter 5:13). Most ancient interpreters read 'Babylon' here as a code word for Rome -- the great persecuting capital, like the Babylon of the Old Testament.

question: On the evening of the eighteenth of July, in the year sixty-four, a fire broke out in the shops by the Circus Maximus in Rome and raged for over a week, destroying most of the city. Which emperor was reigning when Rome burned?
context: The Great Fire of Rome began 18-19 July AD 64, under Nero. Tacitus (Annals 15.38-44) records that it burned for six days, was quenched, then broke out again for three more. Claudius, Domitian, and Trajan are all real first-century emperors but none was on the throne in AD 64.

question: After Rome burned, the emperor was himself widely suspected of ordering the fire to clear ground for his palace. To deflect the anger of the mob, he pinned the blame on a small unpopular sect and made a public spectacle of hunting them down. Which group did the emperor blame for the fire?
context: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 -- a hostile pagan source -- records that Nero blamed the fire on 'a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace' and had them arrested in large numbers.

question: Tacitus, no friend of the Christians, records the killings that followed the fire with disgust at the cruelty of the show. In the arena, some of the condemned were driven out before a crowd hungry for a beast-hunt. What does Tacitus specifically record was done to them there?
answer: They were torn to pieces by hunting dogs
choices: They were torn to pieces by hunting dogs
They were mauled by African bears
They were gored by wild bulls
They were hunted down by leopards
context: 'Besides being put to death they were made to serve as objects of amusement; they were clothed in the hides of beasts and torn to pieces by dogs' (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Others in the same passage were nailed to crosses or set on fire as living torches to light the imperial gardens -- an extraordinarily hostile witness confirming the cruelty of the persecution. Bears, bulls, and leopards were all real arena beasts elsewhere, but Tacitus names dogs.

question: The church father Origen, quoted by the historian Eusebius in Church History Book 3, records that Peter did not die on an ordinary cross. He asked the soldiers to hang him in an unusual posture, at his own request. In what position was Peter crucified, according to that tradition?
answer: nailed head downward, feet in the air
choices: nailed head downward, feet in the air
arms wrapped around a T-shaped cross
back to the wood, feet nailed apart
tied by the wrists to an X-shaped cross
context: Origen (early third century), preserved in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.1: Peter 'was crucified with his head downwards, as he himself had desired to suffer'. The X-shaped cross is the tradition of Peter's brother Andrew; the T-cross and the standard Latin cross are other real forms.  (Legend.)

question: Peter's execution is traditionally placed not in the main forum but in the emperor's own racecourse, a private stadium at the foot of a hill where the spectacle crowd could watch. On which hill was Nero's private circus, and Peter's cross with it?
context: Nero's private circus stood at the base of the Vatican Hill, well outside the sacred pomerium. The Palatine (imperial palaces), Capitoline (Jupiter's temple), and Aventine are all real hills of Rome, but the circus of Nero was at the Vatican -- which is why the basilica of Peter would later rise on that same slope.  (Legend.)

question: On the twenty-sixth of June in nineteen sixty-eight, a Pope stood in Rome and announced that bones excavated from under the high altar of St Peter's Basilica, in the ruins of a first-century burial chamber, were in the Vatican's view very likely those of the apostle himself. Which pope made that announcement?
context: Pope Paul VI announced on 26 June 1968 that the bones (of a strongly built man aged sixty to seventy, first century, wrapped in imperial purple with gold thread) were in the Vatican's view 'identified in a way that we consider convincing' as Peter's. Pius XII had begun the excavations; Paul VI reported the result.

question: In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I began persecuting the Jerusalem church and had the very first of the twelve apostles put to death with a sword. Which apostle did Herod kill?
context: Acts 12:2 -- 'And he killed James the brother of John with the sword.' This James (son of Zebedee) is the first of the Twelve to be martyred. Stephen the deacon is the first Christian martyr overall but not one of the Twelve; Judas dies earlier in Acts 1; Thomas's death is only in later tradition.

question: After killing the apostle James, Herod arrested Peter during the Jewish feast of Unleavened Bread and threw him into prison. Inside the cell, where was Peter sleeping when the story picks up?
choices: Hanging by his wrists in a stone pit
Locked in a wooden cage on the roof
context: Acts 12:6 -- Peter was 'sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains,' with keepers before the door as well. He was guarded by four squads of four soldiers each -- sixteen men in total.

question: Acts 12 gives an exact count of Peter's guard: Herod handed him over to squads of soldiers called quaternions, with a fresh squad rotating through each night-watch. How many soldiers were in a single quaternion?
context: Acts 12:4 -- Herod 'delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers to keep him.' A quaternion is a squad of four; four quaternions across the four watches of the night makes sixteen men guarding a single prisoner.

question: The night before Peter's trial, a bright light shone in the prison and an angel of the Lord stood over him. The angel had to strike Peter on the side to wake him and then said, 'Arise up quickly.' At that command, what happened next inside the cell?
answer: His chains fell off his hands
choices: His chains fell off his hands
The two guards turned to stone
The ceiling split open above him
A white dove landed on his shoulder
context: Acts 12:7 -- 'And his chains fell off from his hands.' The guards on either side stay asleep through the whole escape; the ceiling and the dove details are not in the text.

question: Following the angel, Peter walked past the first guard and the second guard and came to the last barrier between him and the city -- a heavy iron gate. According to Acts 12, what did this gate do as they approached?
choices: The angel struck it with a rod
Peter spoke a psalm and it split in half
context: Acts 12:10 -- the iron gate 'opened to them of his own accord.' They walked out, went down one street, and then the angel departed and Peter realized he was not seeing a vision.

question: Free in the city, Peter went straight to a house where the disciples were up late praying for him. Acts names it as the house of Mary, and identifies her by her son. Whose mother was she?
context: Acts 12:12 -- 'the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark.' This is the same John Mark traditionally credited with writing the Gospel of Mark and who later traveled with Barnabas and Paul.

question: A young servant girl came to answer Peter's knock at the gate. She recognized his voice through the door but was so overjoyed she ran back inside without letting him in, leaving Peter standing out in the street knocking. What was the servant girl's name?
context: Acts 12:13-14 -- 'a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda.' Dorcas is the seamstress raised by Peter in Acts 9; Priscilla is the tentmaker with Aquila; Lydia is the seller of purple in Acts 16.

question: When Rhoda burst in and swore Peter was standing at the gate, the disciples -- who had been praying for exactly this -- did not believe her. First they said she was out of her mind. Then, when she kept insisting, what did they conclude instead?
choices: It must be a Roman trick
context: Acts 12:15 -- 'Then said they, It is his angel.' The scene is the great comic beat of Acts: the church prays all night for Peter's release, gets exactly what it asked for, and refuses to open the door. All the while Peter is still outside knocking.

question: When morning came and Peter could not be found in his cell, Herod interrogated the keepers who had guarded him. What did Herod order done to Peter's guards?
choices: Sent them to the arena to face lions
context: Acts 12:19 -- Herod 'examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death.' Under Roman practice a soldier who lost a prisoner suffered the prisoner's sentence, so execution was the standard answer; slavery, the arena, and exile belonged to other punishments in other stories.

question: Not long after Peter's escape, Herod Agrippa sat on his royal throne at Caesarea and made a speech. Josephus adds that he wore a silver robe that flashed in the morning sun. The crowd shouted flattery at him. Which cry did the crowd make that Herod refused to correct?
answer: It is the voice of a god and not of a man
choices: It is the voice of a god and not of a man
Long live the son of David
Blessed is he who rides the eagle
context: Acts 12:22 -- 'And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.' Because Herod did not give God the glory, verse 23 says the angel of the Lord struck him and 'he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.'

question: The night Jesus is arrested and taken to the high priest's house for questioning, one of his closest disciples follows the arresting party 'afar off' and slips into the courtyard. The servants and guards there have kindled a fire against the cold, and he stands among them warming his hands. Which of the twelve is this disciple?
context: John 18:15-18 (KJV). Peter follows the arresting party into the high priest Caiaphas's courtyard. Andrew was Peter's brother; Thomas is the doubter of the Upper Room; Philip is the disciple who asks 'shew us the Father'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial_of_Peter.

question: Earlier that same night, at the last supper, Jesus had turned to Peter with a specific and painful warning: before a farmyard sound is heard a certain number of times, Peter would deny him three times. What sound did Jesus name?
context: Mark 14:30 (KJV): 'Verily I say unto thee, that this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Peter had answered, 'though I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise.' Source: Mark 14:30-31 (KJV).

question: John's gospel specifies the exact kind of fire the servants and officers had kindled in the courtyard where Peter warmed his hands -- a small detail he uses only twice in the whole New Testament. What kind of fire was it?
context: John 18:18 (KJV): 'the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves.' The Greek word anthrakia -- 'charcoal fire' -- appears only twice in the whole New Testament, both times in John. Source: John 18:18 (KJV).

question: In Mark's gospel, the first person to look hard at Peter across the firelight stares and says 'thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth'. Who is this first accuser?
answer: A servant-girl of the high priest
choices: A servant-girl of the high priest
A soldier of the Temple guard
context: Mark 14:66-67 (KJV): 'there cometh one of the maids of the high priest: And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him, and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth.' The gospel underlines the humiliation -- the great disciple is broken by the challenge of a serving-maid. Source: Mark 14:66-67 (KJV).

question: Peter denies the servant-girl, then a second challenger, and then a third. At the third accusation the bystanders say what has been giving him away in the firelight all along -- a specific mark on him that a Jerusalem crowd could pick out at once. What was it?
context: Matthew 26:73 (KJV): 'and after a while came unto him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee.' Mark 14:70: 'thou art a Galilaean, and thy speech agreeth thereto.' Galilean speech to a Judean ear was as distinctive as a country twang in a capital city. Source: Matthew 26:73; Mark 14:70 (KJV).

question: By the third accusation Peter is frantic to convince the bystanders he has nothing to do with the man on trial inside. Matthew records what he does next in one sharp phrase, ending with 'I know not the man'. What does Matthew say Peter did at the third denial?
answer: Began to curse and to swear
choices: Began to curse and to swear
context: Matthew 26:74 (KJV): 'Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.' The cursing here is not obscenity -- it is Peter calling down oaths on himself to prove he does not know Jesus. Source: Matthew 26:74 (KJV).

question: Peter has just denied Jesus for the third time, cursing and swearing that he does not know the man. The cock crows -- and one gospel adds a single line that is not in the others, the moment that breaks Peter open. In LUKE's gospel alone, what does Jesus do at that instant?
answer: Turns and looks upon Peter across the courtyard
choices: Turns and looks upon Peter across the courtyard
Cries out Peter's name from the hall
Sends John out to find Peter
Falls silent in front of his accusers
context: Luke 22:61 (KJV): 'And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord... And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.' Only Luke gives us the crossed gaze. Source: Luke 22:61-62 (KJV).

question: John's gospel is careful about a small, specific detail that no other gospel mentions -- the KIND of fire Peter stood warming himself at during the denials. That same word is used only twice in the whole New Testament, and both times in John. Where in John's gospel is the SECOND appearance?
answer: On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, where the risen Jesus cooks fish for the disciples
choices: On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, where the risen Jesus cooks fish for the disciples
By the tomb where Mary Magdalene mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener
In the locked upper room where the risen Jesus shows Thomas his hands
At the pool of Bethesda where Jesus heals the man who cannot walk
context: John 21:9 (KJV): 'they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.' At this second charcoal fire the risen Jesus asks Peter three times -- one for each denial -- 'lovest thou me?', and each time Peter answers 'yea, Lord'. Two charcoal fires, three denials answered by three affirmations: John's writer built the parallel on purpose. Source: John 21:9-17 (KJV).

question: The day after John the Baptist first pointed him out at the Jordan, Jesus met a young man from Bethsaida -- the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew -- and called him with two words: 'Follow me.' Which of the Twelve was this?
context: John 1:43-44 KJV: 'The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me. Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.'

question: Just after being called by Jesus, Philip ran to find a friend and told him excitedly, 'We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write -- Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.' What was the friend's name in John's gospel?
context: John 1:45 KJV. John's gospel alone gives this recruiting scene, and John is the only gospel that uses the name Nathanael.

question: Philip did not argue with his friend's Nazareth jibe. Instead he gave a three-word invitation that has become one of the most-quoted lines in the whole gospel of John. What did Philip say?
context: John 1:46 KJV. The phrase is often preached as a model of quiet witness -- no dispute, no proof, just an invitation to look.

question: As the sceptical friend walked up, Jesus greeted him with a compliment from across the way: 'Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no...' -- what?
context: John 1:47 KJV. 'Guile' means deceit or cunning -- Jesus is calling him a straightforward, honest man. Given his blunt Nazareth remark a moment before, the reader has just seen the trait for themselves.

question: Startled that this stranger seemed to know him, Nathanael asked, 'Whence knowest thou me?' Jesus answered that he had seen him before Philip ever fetched him -- in a particular spot. Where does Jesus say he saw Nathanael?
context: John 1:48 KJV: 'Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.' The fig tree in Jewish tradition was a place of study and prayer -- 'every man under his vine and under his fig tree' (Micah 4:4).

question: Three of the four gospels never mention Nathanael by name at all -- but they do list a disciple always paired with Philip in the roll of the Twelve, whom later Christian tradition identifies as the same man. What is Nathanael's name in Matthew, Mark, and Luke?
context: Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14. 'Bartholomew' is a patronymic -- Bar-Tolmai, 'son of Talmai' -- a family name rather than a given one, which is why tradition reads Nathanael Bar-Tolmai as a single man with a first name plus a surname.  (Legend.)

question: The Roman governor's opening question at the trial cuts straight to the political charge: 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' Jesus does not deny it. Mark 15:2 (KJV) records his answer in three words. Which reply is it?
context: Mark 15:2 KJV: 'And Pilate asked him, Art thou the King of the Jews? And he answering said unto him, Thou sayest it.' The phrase throws the assertion back on the questioner -- neither a full yes nor a denial. Matthew 27:11 and Luke 23:3 have almost the same exchange. 'I am he' is Jesus's line at the arrest in the garden (John 18:5-6). 'So it is written' and 'Blessed art thou' are other gospel phrases.

question: Only John's gospel adds a further exchange between the governor and the accused: Jesus says he came to bear witness to the truth. The governor throws back one three-word question -- and, John 18:38 (KJV) says, walks straight out of the room without waiting for an answer. What did he ask?
context: John 18:38 KJV: 'Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews.' A Roman governor tossing off a philosophy-final question at the accused and then leaving before the answer has kept commentators busy for two thousand years -- some hear a sneer, some hear a genuine question. Only John records it.

question: Going back out to the crowd waiting in the courtyard, the governor makes a public verdict on the accused. John 18:38 (KJV) has him say: 'I find in him no ______ at all.' Which word does the KJV use?
context: John 18:38 KJV: 'And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault at all.' Luke 23:4 has the same phrase. The remarkable thing about the Passion narrative is that Rome, the executing power, records itself as having found no case -- and killed him anyway. 'Sin' would be a religious rather than legal category; 'guilt' and 'wrong' are near-synonyms the KJV does not use here.

question: It was a Passover custom for the governor to release one prisoner as a goodwill gesture. He offers the crowd a choice: Jesus, or a man Mark 15:7 says had killed someone in an uprising. Which prisoner did the crowd shout for instead?
context: Matthew 27:20-21 and John 18:40 KJV. Barabbas is called 'a robber' in John and one who 'had committed murder in the insurrection' in Mark 15:7. The Passover-release custom is otherwise unattested outside the gospels. Judas Iscariot is the disciple who betrayed Jesus; Simon Magus is a magician in Acts 8; Ananias is a name that turns up in Acts 5 and Acts 9 -- none of them belong in this scene.

question: The soldiers take Jesus into the courtyard, strip him, throw a coloured robe on him, put a reed in his right hand as a mock sceptre, and kneel in front of him shouting 'Hail, King of the Jews' (Matthew 27:27-30). They also plait something and press it onto his head. What did they weave and jam onto his brow?
context: Matthew 27:29 and John 19:2 KJV. The specific plant is not named in the gospels -- Middle Eastern candidates include Ziziphus spina-christi (jujube). A laurel wreath was the Roman victor's crown, so the mockery is precise: a real king would get laurel, this 'king' gets thorns. Matthew's soldiers use a scarlet robe (27:28); Mark 15:17 and John 19:2 have purple. Both were royal colours in the ancient world -- the gospels do not blend the two, so quote one at a time.

question: For centuries Pontius Pilate was known only from the gospels, and some scholars doubted he had held a real Roman office at all. In June 1961, Italian archaeologists excavating the Roman theatre at Caesarea Maritima on the Mediterranean coast dug up a battered limestone slab with a Latin inscription that ended the argument -- it named Pilate and a specific title. What Latin title did the stone give him?
context: The Pilate Stone reads, in its damaged Latin: '[...]S TIBERIEUM / [...]PONTIUS PILATUS / [...]PRAEFECTUS IUDAEAE' -- Pilate as prefect of Judea, dedicating a building (a Tiberieum) to the emperor Tiberius. Later Roman writers sometimes called him 'procurator', but that title only came into use for such officials after AD 41 -- so the stone quietly corrects the ancient historians. Consuls headed the Roman state; a legatus was a senatorial commander; a quaestor was a junior finance official.

question: A very old bishop is dragged out of a farmhouse outside Smyrna on the west coast of Asia Minor, an elderly disciple of the apostle John from the generation before. He is brought back to the city to face the Roman proconsul in the stadium. What is this bishop's name?
context: Polycarp is the elderly bishop of Smyrna (modern Izmir). Irenaeus, who knew him personally as a boy, says Polycarp had been a disciple of the apostle John. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarp.

question: The proconsul asks the old bishop Polycarp for one simple thing to save his life: burn a pinch of incense to Caesar and say 'Caesar is Lord'. What does Polycarp do?
choices: He does it and repents later
He says he needs a night to think
context: Polycarp refuses the incense-test and gives his famous answer about serving Christ for eighty-six years (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: The proconsul in the stadium at Smyrna orders the old bishop Polycarp to save himself with one pinch of incense to Caesar. Polycarp answers by counting the years he has served Christ. What number of years does he give?
context: 'Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury; how then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9). The traditional reading is that Polycarp is counting from his baptism as a baby -- the last living link to the apostles. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: The proconsul at Smyrna tries to frighten the old bishop into recanting by warning him he will burn alive. Polycarp answers that the proconsul's fire is nothing next to another one. Which other fire does he name?
answer: The fire of the judgment to come
choices: The fire of the judgment to come
The fire that will end the wicked age
The fire that already burns in his heart
The fire that fell on Sodom and Gomorrah
context: 'Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished' -- and he warns of the fire of judgment to come (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: The crowd in the stadium at Smyrna has voted for fire, and Jews and pagans alike run out into the streets to build the pyre. Where does the Letter of the Church of Smyrna say they run to gather the wood?
choices: The gates of the pagan temples
The docks and the fishing boats
context: The letter says the crowd fetched wood 'out of the workshops and the baths' -- the trades and public buildings of the city -- to build the fire. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.

question: When the executioners at Smyrna move to nail the old bishop Polycarp to the stake, he stops them with a strange request. What does he ask them to do?
answer: Leave him unbound at the stake
choices: Leave him unbound at the stake
Leave him kneeling instead of standing
Leave him with his outer cloak on
context: 'Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me to remain in the pyre unmoved without the security of your nails' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 13). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: The pyre is lit around the old bishop of Smyrna and, according to the letter the Church of Smyrna writes about that day, the flames do something odd -- they refuse to touch him. What shape does the letter say the fire takes around him?
answer: An arch, like a ship's sail full of wind
choices: An arch, like a ship's sail full of wind
A tall column reaching to the clouds
A crown of flame above his head
A circle around him like a wall
context: 'The fire, shaping itself into the form of an arch, like the sail of a ship when filled with the wind, made a wall round about the body of the martyr' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 15). Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: The fire in the stadium at Smyrna will not consume Polycarp, so the proconsul orders someone up onto the pyre to finish him. Who is sent up, and with what weapon?
choices: A young archer with a bow
The chief priest with a knife
context: 'They commanded an executioner to go near and pierce him through with a dagger' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 16). The Greek word is 'confector', the arena finisher. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: When the executioner strikes the death-blow on the pyre in the stadium at Smyrna, the letter the Church of Smyrna writes reports a marvel at that moment. What does it say came out of Polycarp along with a great quantity of blood?
context: 'And on his doing this, there came forth a dove, and a great quantity of blood, so that the fire was extinguished' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 16). This detail is the earliest surviving example of the dove-at-martyrdom motif in Christian literature. Source: earlychristianwritings.com/text/martyrdompolycarp-roberts.html.  (Legend.)

question: One Olympian is lord of the sea, of horses, and of earthquakes; his wife is the sea-nymph Amphitrite, and he would become the losing challenger in the great Athens contest. Which Olympian is he?
context: Homer, Iliad 15.187-193, has Poseidon himself explain the three-way division of the world with his brothers Zeus (sky) and Hades (underworld). Apollo is the god of light and prophecy; Hermes the messenger; Ares the god of war. None of them holds the sea.  (Legend.)

question: The Cyclopes forged three great weapons during the war against the Titans -- Zeus's thunderbolt, Hades's helm, and Poseidon's own signature weapon, still called in Greek by the same name as the ordinary fishing spear of the coasts. What was Poseidon's weapon?
context: The Cyclopes forged the trident during the war against the Titans, at the same time as Zeus's thunderbolt and Hades's helm. The caduceus is Hermes's herald staff; the aegis is Athena's goatskin shield with the Gorgon face; the labrys is the Cretan double-axe. The Hellenistic poet Leonidas of Tarentum wrote of a real fisherman dedicating 'his sharp trident weapon of Poseidon' among his gear.  (Legend.)

question: A new city was rising on the rock of the Acropolis and had no patron god yet. Two Olympians claimed it -- Poseidon of the sea, and the grey-eyed goddess of wisdom and the loom, born fully armoured from Zeus's own forehead. Which goddess was Poseidon's rival?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Athena won the contest and the city took her name -- Athens. Artemis is the huntress; Hera is Zeus's queen (patron of Argos); Demeter is the grain-goddess (patron of Eleusis).  (Legend.)

question: For his gift in the Athens contest, Poseidon strode to the top of the Acropolis rock and struck it hard with his three-pronged spear. Something gushed up out of the wound in the stone -- and Pausanias, walking the Acropolis centuries later, was still shown the very spot inside the Erechtheion. What did Pausanias (1.26.5) say Poseidon's strike had left in the rock?
choices: a well of clear fresh water
a print of a horse's hoof
a print of a giant hand
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.26.5, and Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Pausanias also notes a trident-mark shown in the rock beside the well. Some alternate versions of the myth do have a horse spring from the strike (Poseidon's sacred animal), but the artefact still shown to travellers on the Acropolis was the sea-water well.  (Legend.)

question: Athena's turn in the contest came after Poseidon's strike. She planted a living thing right on the rock of the Acropolis beside where Poseidon had struck -- a sapling that Pausanias (1.27) says was still shown to travellers centuries later as the oldest of its kind in all Attica. What did Athena plant?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1; Pausanias 1.27. The laurel belongs to Apollo (Daphne turning into one to escape him); the pomegranate belongs to Persephone in the Hades story; the fig is sacred to Dionysus. Athena's tree defined Attica's industry -- olive oil filled the amphoras awarded to victors in the Panathenaic games.  (Legend.)

question: In the version told by Pseudo-Apollodorus, the judge of the Athens contest was not the Olympians or the townspeople but a very early king of Athens himself. Which of these Athenian kings did Apollodorus name as the judge?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1. Kekrops was the earliest of the Athenian kings -- a snake-legged autochthon (born from the soil). Erechtheus is the king the Erechtheion is named for. Aegeus is the father of Theseus (his name gave the Aegean Sea). Theseus is the hero-king of the Minotaur story.  (Legend.)

question: The traveller Pausanias, walking through the Erechtheion on the Acropolis in the 2nd century AD, was shown the salt well Poseidon had made. He records one strange thing the local guides claimed: when a particular wind blew, the well made a sound. What sound, according to Pausanias 1.26.5, did the salt well make in the south wind?
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.26.5. Pausanias also notes that the outline of a trident was shown in the rock beside the well as further evidence of Poseidon's strike. The horse's-cry is a red herring -- the horse was Poseidon's sacred creature, but the sound reported at the well was of waves.  (Legend.)

question: Poseidon and Athena had a SECOND, less famous quarrel over another city -- the seaside town of Troezen. This time Zeus stepped in as judge. Rather than pick one god, Zeus gave a different verdict. What did Zeus rule about Troezen?
answer: that Poseidon and Athena would share the city jointly
choices: that Poseidon and Athena would share the city jointly
that neither god would ever be worshipped there
that Athena must give her olive to Poseidon
that the town must be renamed for a mortal king
context: Pausanias 2.30.6. The Troezenians afterwards worshipped both -- Athena as Polias and Sthenias, Poseidon as King -- and the ancient coins of Troezen show a trident and Athena's head together on the same coin.  (Legend.)

question: In 480 BCE the Persian army of Xerxes sacked the Acropolis and burned every temple on it, including Athena's sacred olive tree. The historian Herodotus reports what the Athenians said happened at the burnt stump on the very next day. What did Herodotus (Histories 8.55) report at the stump?
answer: a fresh shoot a cubit long had sprouted from it
choices: a fresh shoot a cubit long had sprouted from it
a spring of clear water had burst out beneath it
an owl had come and perched on it at dawn
a laurel wreath had been laid on it in the night
context: Herodotus, Histories 8.55. The Athenians read the overnight sprout as a sign from Athena that the city herself would rise again -- and shortly afterwards the Greek fleet won at Salamis. Herodotus reports it plainly as fact, not as legend.

question: The three eldest sons of Cronus each carried a signature weapon forged for them by the same craftsmen during the war against the Titans -- Zeus took the thunderbolt, Poseidon took the trident, and Hades took the third. What did Hades receive at the same forging?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 501-506, and Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.2.1. The Cyclopes forged all three at once. Hades's helm (the 'cap of Aidos') was later borrowed by Perseus for the killing of Medusa and by Athena in the Iliad to hide from Ares -- an invisibility-cap in the oldest layer of Greek myth.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, the greatest warrior of Troy is killed in single combat before the walls of the city. His father, the aged king watching from those walls, is left with a son's body he cannot recover. Who is that aged king of Troy?
context: Priam, king of Troy, watches from the walls as Achilles kills Hector in single combat and then drags the body behind his chariot around the city. The whole Iliad turns on this loss. (Iliad Book 24; ageofheroes.org, litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: In the Iliad, the aged king of Troy watches from the walls as his greatest son is killed. Which Greek warrior killed the Trojan prince Hector in single combat?
context: Achilles kills Hector before the walls of Troy in Iliad Book 22, and then drags the body behind his chariot in sight of Hector's parents. Twelve days later Hector still lies un-buried in the Greek camp. (Iliad Book 22-24.)  (Legend.)

question: For twelve days after his son's death, King Priam has watched the Greek camp from the walls of Troy, unable to bury Hector. Zeus decides this cannot stand and sends a goddess-messenger to Priam with an order to go himself, alone at night, into the enemy camp to beg for the body. Which goddess does Zeus send with that order?
context: Zeus sends Iris, the rainbow messenger of the gods, down to Priam with orders to go alone at night with ransom to Achilles's tent. Iris is his usual messenger between Olympus and mortals in the Iliad. (Iliad 24; litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: The aged King Priam sets out at night in a wagon loaded with treasure to cross the plain into the Greek camp. He does not go alone -- a god, disguised as a young Myrmidon warrior, walks beside him and guides him past the sentries into Achilles's tent. Which god escorts him in that disguise?
context: Hermes, guide of souls and messenger, appears to Priam in the shape of a young Myrmidon warrior and leads him past the Greek sentries. It is the only time in the Iliad a god guides a mortal in body-shape rather than only in voice. (Iliad 24; pressbooks.pub/iliad.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam enters Achilles's tent unannounced at midnight, an old man alone before the young warrior he has come to beg. Before he speaks, he does something that will be remembered as the most astonishing act of a suppliant in the Iliad. What does Priam DO with his lips?
answer: He puts them to the hands of Achilles
choices: He puts them to the hands of Achilles
He puts them to the sword of Achilles
He puts them to the altar in the tent
He puts them to the forehead of Achilles
context: Priam clasps Achilles's knees in the ritual gesture of the suppliant and puts his lips to 'the terrible, man-slaughtering hands' -- the hands of the man who killed Hector. He tells Achilles he has endured what no man on earth has ever endured. (Iliad 24.503-506; litcharts.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam's speech breaks Achilles. The young warrior does not answer at first -- instead he weeps, and the two enemies sit together in the tent and cry, each for his own dead. Priam weeps for Hector. Achilles weeps for his own father AND for one other person he has lost. For whom does Achilles weep along with Peleus?
context: Achilles weeps for Peleus, whom he will never see again, and for Patroclus, the friend whose death drove him back into the war and made him kill Hector. Then he raises the old king up from his knees. (Iliad 24.507-516.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam asks Achilles for time to bury Hector properly -- a truce in which no Greek will attack Troy while the funeral is held. Achilles grants the request. How many days of truce does he give for the funeral of Hector?
context: The truce is eleven days total -- nine to gather wood for the pyre, one to burn the body, and one for the burial mound. It is one of the very few pauses in the whole war. (Iliad 24; americanliterature.com.)  (Legend.)

question: The Iliad is a poem that opens on the word 'wrath' and runs for roughly 15,000 lines about killing -- Greek killing Trojan, Trojan killing Greek. What is the final line of the whole poem?
answer: 'And so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses.'
choices: 'And so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses.'
'And so Achilles laid his friend upon the pyre.'
'And they raised a mound above the son of Priam.'
'And the ships of the Greeks lay silent on the shore.'
context: The Iliad ends not on Achilles, not on victory, not on Troy falling -- but on the burial of the enemy prince Achilles killed. It is one of the most famous endings in Western literature. (Iliad 24.804.)  (Legend.)

question: Priam does not enter Achilles's tent empty-handed. Zeus's order is that he go with a wagon of ransom worthy of a king's son. Homer names the contents in detail -- cloaks, tunics, cauldrons, tripods, and a weight of the most precious metal. HOW MANY talents of gold does Priam bring in the wagon?
context: The ransom is twelve robes, twelve cloaks, twelve blankets, twelve tunics, ten talents of gold, two shining tripods, four cauldrons, and a great cup given to Priam by the Thracians. (Iliad 24.229-235.)  (Legend.)

question: After the meal in the tent, Achilles gazes across at Priam and speaks about how the old king appears to him. What does Achilles say Priam LOOKS like?
choices: He looks like a king of old
He looks like the shade of a hero
He looks like his son Hector
context: Achilles marvels at how god-like Priam still appears even in his grief; Priam in turn marvels at how god-like Achilles is. They share a meal and sleep, enemies for one night at peace. (Iliad 24.629-634.)  (Legend.)

question: In the great war of the Titans against the Olympians, most Titans lost and were hurled down into Tartarus for good. Prometheus is different from his fellow Titans -- he keeps his freedom afterwards because of the side he chose in the war. Which side did Prometheus fight on?
answer: the side of Zeus and the Olympians
choices: the side of Zeus and the Olympians
the side of Cronus and the older Titans
he stayed neutral and fought for neither side
he fought first for one side and then the other
context: Hesiod, Theogony (and later mythographers). Prometheus's foresight told him the Olympians would win, so he broke with his own kind. That original alliance is what makes his LATER punishment by Zeus so sharp -- Zeus is punishing a former friend, not an old enemy.  (Legend.)

question: At a place called Mecone in Sikyon, Prometheus was asked to divide a great sacrificial ox into two portions -- one for the gods and one for mortals -- so Zeus could choose which the gods would keep forever. Prometheus made two piles. In the pile he wanted Zeus to pick, he hid the OX BONES underneath a beautiful covering. What did he cover the bones with?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 535-560. The other pile hid the meat and offal inside the ugly ox-stomach. Zeus, offered the choice, picked the fat-covered pile -- and from that day mortals kept the meat at every sacrifice while the gods received only the burnt fat and bones as smoke on the altar.  (Legend.)

question: After the trick at Mecone, Zeus took a specific gift away from mortals as their punishment. Prometheus would later have to slip back up to Olympus and STEAL that gift back for humans -- and be punished eternally for it. What did Prometheus steal?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 561-569. Wine belongs to a different god's story (Dionysus, who brings the vine to mortals later). Sleep and speech were never withdrawn -- they were never gifts anyone could grant or take away.  (Legend.)

question: To smuggle the stolen spark down from Olympus to earth without Zeus seeing, Prometheus hid it inside a hollow plant-stem -- a plant Greek peasants really did use to carry live embers from one hearth to another. What plant-stem did he carry the fire in, according to Hesiod (Theogony 565-569)?
context: The Greek word is 'narthex' -- the giant fennel, Ferula communis. Its dry white pith really does smoulder invisibly for hours, and Greek villagers used a fennel-stalk to carry embers from hearth to hearth well into modern times. The story matches an actual practice.  (Legend.)

question: As FURTHER punishment on mortals for accepting the stolen fire, Zeus had Hephaestus fashion the very first woman, PANDORA, and sent her down to Prometheus's foolish brother Epimetheus, who took her against Prometheus's warning. Pandora carried a specific object down with her that would loose all the evils on the world. What did Pandora bring?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 90-105. The Greek word is 'pithos' -- a large storage jar. It became 'Pandora's BOX' in English only when the 16th-century humanist Erasmus mistranslated pithos as pyxis ('box'). The spindle belongs to Klotho of the Fates; the mirror to Aphrodite; the horn (the cornucopia) belongs to the Amalthea nursing-goat story.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus's punishment on Prometheus himself was to have him chained to a bare wind-battered crag on a specific mountain-range so remote no other god would visit -- to hang there alone in the cold for generations. Which mountain-range did Zeus chain him to?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 521-525, and Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound. The Caucasus stood at the far eastern edge of the Greek-known world, where the sun was said to come up. Mount Ida is where Zeus was hidden as a baby (Cretan Ida) and where the Judgment of Paris took place (Trojan Ida). Mount Etna is where the giant Typhon was buried under the volcano. Mount Parnassus is Apollo's mountain, above Delphi.  (Legend.)

question: Prometheus was not left at the crag forever. Generations later a passing hero came through the Caucasus, saw the eagle at the crag, drew his bow, and shot the bird dead with an arrow -- then persuaded Zeus to leave Prometheus freed. Which hero shot the eagle?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 526-534. Perseus was the killer of Medusa (with Hades's helm). Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Cretan labyrinth. Bellerophon killed the Chimera from the back of Pegasus. Heracles was the arrow-shooter -- the same one who later killed the Nemean lion, the Hydra, and Geryon.  (Legend.)

question: In Aeschylus's play Prometheus Bound, Prometheus holds a SECRET that Zeus badly wants: the identity of the woman by whom Zeus is fated to father a son greater than himself. Prometheus refuses to name her until Zeus agrees to free him. Which woman was the secret name?
context: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound (with the lost sequel Prometheus Unbound). Warned by the secret, Zeus stopped pursuing Thetis and had her married off to the mortal Peleus instead -- and their son was Achilles, the greatest of the Greeks at Troy. Danae was the mother of Perseus by Zeus. Rhea was Zeus's own mother. Leto was mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse Volsunga Saga, an old king dies in battle when his sword shatters against a stranger's spear -- and he tells his young wife to keep the pieces for their unborn son. What is the name of this shattered sword that will one day be reforged?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 11-12; 15. Gram is the great sword of the Volsung line -- pulled out of the tree Barnstokk by King Sigmund, shattered against Odin's spear, and reforged for Sigurd. Tyrfing is the cursed dwarf-sword of the Hervarar saga. Skofnung is the sword of the legendary Danish king Hrolf Kraki. Hrunting is the sword Unferth lends to Beowulf for the fight with Grendel's mother. All four are named hero-swords of the Germanic legend-cycle -- Gram is the specific reforged one.

question: The young hero who will inherit Gram grows up to become the greatest hero of the Norse legend-cycle -- the same hero the Germans call Siegfried, whose story Wagner set to music. What is the Norse name of Siegfried?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 13-15. Sigurd (Old Norse) is Siegfried (German). Sigmund is Sigurd's father, the shattered-sword king. Sinfjotli is Sigmund's son by his own sister Signy, and Signy is Sigmund's twin sister. All four are Volsungs -- the specific dragon-slayer of the next generation is Sigurd.  (Legend.)

question: In his last battle King Sigmund is winning easily until an old man in a hooded cloak with a broad-brimmed hat steps out of the battle-line and blocks his next stroke with the weapon he carries. What is the weapon that this old stranger uses to shatter Gram?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 11. The old man in the hooded cloak with a broad-brimmed hat is Odin himself in his wanderer's disguise, and the spear he carries is Gungnir -- the same spear he will one day take to Ragnarok. Sigmund's sword shatters against it. Sigmund has been Odin's favourite for a lifetime; the moment Odin turns up on the battlefield with the spear is the moment Sigmund knows the god's favour is spent.  (Legend.)

question: In the smithy at King Hjalprek's court, Sigurd is fostered by an old and cunning smith who has a secret purpose in raising him: a brother of his own who long ago transformed into a dragon and now guards a cursed hoard, and whom the smith wants Sigurd to kill. What is the name of Sigurd's foster-father?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 14; Reginsmal prose introduction. Regin is the smith-brother of the dragon Fafnir and the foster-father of Sigurd. Andvari is the dwarf whose gold-hoard Regin and Fafnir stole in the first place (the cursed treasure). Alberich is the Nibelung dwarf of Wagner's opera -- an adjacent figure in the German retellings, but the Norse foster-father is Regin. Wayland is the great smith of another Germanic saga (Volundarkvida).  (Legend.)

question: In the smithy, before Sigurd ever asks for his father's broken pieces, his foster-father makes him not one but two brand-new swords. Sigurd swings each new sword once against the smithy's anvil to test it. What happens each time?
answer: the sword shatters at the first blow
choices: the sword shatters at the first blow
the blade sticks fast in the iron
the blade bends into a curve
the sword rings out with a clear note
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 15. Regin makes Sigurd two brand-new swords in turn; each shatters against the anvil on the first swing. Only after those two failures does Sigurd go to his mother Hjordis and ask for the pieces of Gram.  (Legend.)

question: After the two brand-new swords shatter against the anvil, Sigurd goes to his mother and asks her for the shards of the sword his father died holding. What is the name of Sigurd's mother, who gives him the pieces of Gram?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 12 and 15. Hjordis is Sigmund's young wife, who caught the shards on the battlefield and carried them with her when she remarried. Signy is Sigmund's sister and mother of Sinfjotli. Grimhild is the queen of the Nibelungs who later gives Sigurd a drink of forgetfulness. Brynhild is the valkyrie he will one day awaken -- his fated love. Hjordis is the specific keeper of the shards.  (Legend.)

question: The old smith takes the shards of the dead king's sword, melts them down, and hammers the metal out into a single new blade. When Sigurd swings the reforged blade against the smithy's anvil, what happens to the anvil?
answer: it is cloven in two down to its foundations
choices: it is cloven in two down to its foundations
it rings with a note heard for a league
it glows red without being heated
it splits into three equal pieces
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 15. The reforged Gram cleaves the anvil clean in two, down to the foundations -- exactly the reverse of the two brand-new swords that shattered against the same anvil earlier. The anvil-cleaving is a Germanic story-motif for 'this sword is not like the others'; Beowulf's sword Naegling gets a similar test in its own poem.  (Legend.)

question: Centuries after the Volsunga Saga was set down, a German composer retold the reforging of the shattered sword as the climax of Act I of the middle opera of his four-opera cycle -- but he gave the sword a different name. What did Wagner call the reforged sword in his Ring cycle?
context: Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Act I (Der Ring des Nibelungen). Wagner renamed Gram as Nothung ('need-sword') and made the reforging-scene one of the most famous moments in the whole Ring cycle -- Siegfried hammers the shards on the anvil while singing 'Nothung! Nothung!' Balmung is what Siegfried's sword is called in the earlier Middle High German Nibelungenlied. Grimming and Wittestein are named swords in still-other German heroic poems. Wagner's name for it is Nothung.  (Legend.)

question: In Tolkien's Lord of the Rings, the broken king's-sword of Elendil is reforged for Aragorn on the eve of the war -- a scene Tolkien openly borrowed from the reforging of Gram for Sigurd. What is the name Tolkien gives to the reforged blade?
context: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Return of the King; Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-Earth. Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon and read the Volsunga Saga in the original. Narsil is the earlier name of the same blade -- the sword of Elendil that broke under him at the fall of Sauron and lay in shards for three thousand years; when it is remade for Aragorn it is renamed Anduril, 'Flame of the West.' Glamdring is the elf-sword Gandalf carries. Sting is the short-sword Bilbo (and later Frodo) carries. Anduril is Tolkien's deliberate homage to Gram reforged.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood and his band of outlaws famously live hidden in the trees of one great English forest, in the county of Nottingham in the middle of the country. In WHICH forest is the greenwood band hidden?
context: Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire is the ballad-home of the Merry Men (with an alternate northern haunt at Barnsdale in Yorkshire). The New Forest was William the Conqueror's Hampshire hunting reserve; the Forest of Arden is Shakespeare's setting in As You Like It; Epping Forest lies east of London. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.  (Legend.)

question: So as not to be seen by foresters and the Sheriff's men when they move under the trees, Robin and the Merry Men all dress in a distinctive dyed woollen cloth, named for the English town whose weavers produced it. What COLOUR of cloth is the band's uniform?
context: 'Lincoln green' was a woollen cloth dyed with woad and weld in the city of Lincoln -- famous enough that Chaucer and the ballads name it.
