Kendal green (a duller cloth) also existed but is a different tradition. The other three colour-names here are invented for parity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.  (Legend.)

question: Robin Hood's signature WEAPON in the ballads is the same weapon that had won two of the most famous English victories of the previous century -- Crecy in 1346 and Agincourt in 1415. What weapon does Robin carry across his back in the medieval ballads?
context: The English longbow -- yew, six feet long, drawn with a 100-pound pull -- was the folk-hero weapon of Robin's own generation of readers. At Crecy and Agincourt English longbowmen shattered the French armoured cavalry; every English yeoman by law had to practice at the butts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: In the earliest surviving Robin Hood ballads the Merry Men are a much smaller band than the modern films show. Only THREE named companions of Robin appear in those earliest texts: Little John, Much the Miller's Son, and one third figure. Which of these named Robin-Hood characters IS in the earliest fifteenth-century ballads as the third companion?
context: The three named early Merry Men are Little John, Much the Miller's Son, and Will Scarlet (spelled 'Scathelock' or 'Scarlok' in the fifteenth-century texts). Friar Tuck, Alan-a-Dale, and Maid Marian all join the tradition later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.  (Legend.)

question: Two figures everyone thinks of as part of Robin's core company are ABSENT from the earliest medieval ballads -- both arrived in the legend LATER, through May Day village games and stage plays before working their way into the printed story. WHICH two later joined the band?
context: Maid Marian entered the tradition through the May Day games (originally as the queen of the May with a separate character called Robin), and Friar Tuck entered through Tudor stage plays; neither appears in the fifteenth-century ballads. Little John, Will Scarlet, Alan-a-Dale and Much the Miller ARE in the ballads. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: The single most famous phrase attached to Robin Hood today is NOT in any of the medieval ballads at all -- it is a much LATER paraphrase from an eighteenth-century collection by Joseph Ritson (1795) and Howard Pyle's children's novel of 1883. Which slogan is the later invention?
answer: robs from the rich and gives to the poor
choices: robs from the rich and gives to the poor
steals from Norman and shares with Saxon
takes from the king and gives to the church
spoils the tax-man and clothes the widow
context: The 'rich-to-poor' formula is a Ritson / Howard Pyle nineteenth-century summary; the medieval ballads themselves show Robin lending money to distressed knights (Sir Richard at the Lee) and helping impoverished yeomen -- charity WITHIN his own class, not modern redistribution. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: The Gest of Robyn Hode (Child 117), the great fifteenth-century poem, actually names the king in Robin's England only vaguely as 'Edward' -- some scholars argue Edward III. The now-familiar setting of Robin in the reign of RICHARD THE LIONHEART, opposed by an evil Prince John, is not in the medieval ballads at all -- it is a NOVELIST'S invention. Which novel by Sir Walter Scott first grafted the Richard / Prince John frame onto the Robin Hood story?
context: Sir Walter Scott's 1819 novel IVANHOE placed the Robin Hood story in the reign of Richard I (returning from crusade) with Prince John as villain; every twentieth-century film uses that Scott frame. Waverley (1814), Kenilworth (1821), and The Talisman (1825) are other Scott novels, all real, none of them the Robin one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood.

question: A Gest of Robyn Hode -- the great fifteenth-century Robin poem, roughly 1,824 lines of ballad verse -- is not one continuous story but is broken by the poet into a specific number of long sections. What NAME does the Gest give to its sections?
context: The Gest is divided into EIGHT FYTTES (an old English word for a division of a long poem, related to 'fit' as in 'fitting together'). 'Canto' is Italian, from Dante and Ariosto; 'geste' is the whole-poem genre-name (as in 'chanson de geste'); 'chanson' is French for song. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Gest_of_Robyn_Hode.

question: Old and worn out from a life in the greenwood, Robin Hood falls ill with a fever and rides to a Yorkshire nunnery for the standard medieval remedy against fever, the routine cure prescribed in monasteries and by barber-surgeons for centuries. What is that treatment?
context: Bleeding, or phlebotomy, was the routine medieval remedy for fevers and many other ailments -- practiced in monasteries and by barber-surgeons for centuries. Purging (forced vomiting or laxatives) and leeching (using leeches, a related bleeding-method) also existed. Trepanning is drilling a hole in the skull -- a real but different medieval surgery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: The Yorkshire nunnery where Robin goes to be bled is a Cistercian house dedicated to the Virgin Mary and Saint James, founded in 1155 near Brighouse. In the ballads the killing-place always goes by one name. What is the priory called?
context: Kirklees Priory was a small Cistercian nunnery in West Yorkshire near Brighouse. Nostell, Bolton, and Monk Bretton are all real, well-known Yorkshire priories of the same medieval era -- but only Kirklees carries the Robin Hood tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirklees_Priory.  (Legend.)

question: Robin's second-in-command has been left waiting outside the priory walls. Growing too weak to shout, Robin lifts an old signal and sounds it three times, each blast fainter than the last. What SIGNAL does the dying Robin use to bring his lieutenant running?
context: In the B-text of Child Ballad 120 the failing horn-blasts -- three of them, each weaker -- carry from the upper window of the priory to Little John waiting outside; John hears the weakness in the call, knows something is wrong, and forces his way in. A boar-horn, a shepherd's pipe, and a shawm are all real medieval blown signals used honestly as adjacent-but-wrong distractors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Hearing the failing horn, Robin's second-in-command breaks the locks and finds him bleeding out on the bed. This same lieutenant is Robin's oldest companion, a huge man who first met him on a narrow bridge over a forest stream and fought him to a draw with quarterstaves. WHO is this lieutenant?
context: The quarterstaff-bridge meeting is one of the most famous scenes in the ballads: Little John (called 'Little' in ironic contrast to his size) knocks Robin off the bridge, they laugh, and John joins the band. He is the one who forces the priory door at the death-scene. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Standing over his dying master, the lieutenant begs one furious favour: leave to take Robin's men, ride back to the priory, and put its buildings to the torch in revenge. Robin refuses, giving one clear reason. What REASON does he give for forbidding the revenge?
answer: he has never harmed a woman in all his life
choices: he has never harmed a woman in all his life
the church would set a curse on any who burned it
the nuns had done nothing wrong, only their head
the fire would spread to the poor cottages nearby
context: In the ballad Robin says, in effect, that he has never harmed a woman in all his life 'nor man in woman's company' -- and forbids Little John to burn the priory even in revenge for his own murder. The moral point is heavy: even at the moment of his killing, Robin holds to his own rule. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Refusing revenge, Robin instead makes his lieutenant a strange last request. He asks for his BOW and a single arrow, has himself lifted to the priory window, and looses one final shot out into the park. What does Robin ask his lieutenant to do WITH THAT ARROW after it falls?
answer: dig his grave wherever the arrow lands
choices: dig his grave wherever the arrow lands
carry the arrow back to Sherwood as a token
return it point-first to the prioress
hang it above the altar of the priory chapel
context: This is the great ballad-image of Robin's death: the last arrow shot from the sickbed marks the outlaw's own grave. Little John finds it in Kirklees Park and buries Robin there, as Robin had asked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: Robin's last instructions do not stop with the grave-site: he also asks that certain of his belongings be laid in the grave WITH his body, each in a particular place. WHICH arrangement of his gear does the ballad prescribe?
answer: his sword at his head, his arrows at his feet, his bow at his side
choices: his sword at his head, his arrows at his feet, his bow at his side
his cap on his chest, his horn on his shoulder, his knife in his hand
his cloak spread over him and his belt around his waist
his boots at the foot of the grave and his gloves under his head
context: The ballad specifies the burial-arrangement almost as a warrior-code: sword at his head, arrows (with the bow at his side) at his feet, and (in some versions) a green sod under his head. It reads like the burial of a yeoman-hero out of Old English tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Death.  (Legend.)

question: The ballad describes only where the arrow fell; but a real stone slab in West Yorkshire, in the park attached to the ruined priory, has been shown to visitors as Robin's grave for centuries. WHY is the inscription on that slab today almost impossible to read?
answer: souvenir hunters have chipped away pieces over the generations
choices: souvenir hunters have chipped away pieces over the generations
the priory monks scoured it clean at the Dissolution
Victorian railway-builders resurfaced it as a paving-stone
a fire in the eighteenth century blackened and cracked the face
context: The alleged grave in Kirklees Park has been pointed out as Robin's since at least the seventeenth century; visitors and pilgrims have chipped fragments from it for so many generations that the inscription is now almost gone. The slab itself is protected today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirklees_Priory.

question: Charlemagne's army is marching home from a long campaign in Spain and must cross the Pyrenees mountains through a narrow gorge that only a small unit can hold at a time. The pass where they cross gives its name to the whole disaster. WHAT is the pass called?
context: Roncesvalles (French Roncevaux) is a real pass through the western Pyrenees between Spain and France. The Brenner is in the Alps; the Khyber is between Afghanistan and Pakistan; Thermopylae is in Greece -- all famous narrow passes of history, all wrong for this story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.

question: Roland's rearguard is one of a wider group of Charlemagne's most trusted paladins, a fixed number of them who ride with the emperor as his closest companions. What NUMBER of these paladins does the chanson name?
context: The chanson gives Charlemagne twelve peers (douze pairs) -- Roland, Oliver, Turpin the Archbishop, Ganelon before his fall, and eight others. The number twelve echoes Christ's twelve apostles and the twelve knights of Arthur's later Round Table tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: The ambush at the pass is not bad luck; it is arranged from inside the Frankish army by one of Charlemagne's own barons, who has sold the rearguard's position and marching-time to the pagan enemy. In the chanson this traitor is Roland's own stepfather. WHAT is the traitor's name?
context: Ganelon is Roland's stepfather in the chanson. Nominated by Roland himself as messenger to King Marsile of Zaragoza, Ganelon takes it as a mortal insult and sells the rearguard's location for revenge. Pinabel is Ganelon's champion at the trial after the disaster; Baligant is a later Saracen emir; Blancandrin is Marsile's own envoy -- all real chanson figures, all wrong here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Trapped in the pass by a Saracen host outnumbering them a hundred to one, Roland's best friend and fellow peer begs him three times to sound his great horn and call the emperor's army back before it is too late. WHO is the friend at Roland's shoulder pleading with him?
context: Oliver, Roland's sworn brother-in-arms, is the voice of prudence in the chanson: he sees the odds, counts the Saracens from a hilltop, and begs Roland three times to blow the horn while there is still time. Turpin the Archbishop is a third peer on the field; Ogier the Dane and Naimon are other paladins of Charlemagne -- all real, wrong here. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: When Roland at last sounds the horn, he blows it with such fury that a specific injury happens to his own body from the effort. What HAPPENS to him as he blows?
answer: the veins in his temples burst
choices: the veins in his temples burst
his throat tears open and bleeds
the sword-cut in his side reopens
his eyes fill with blood and he goes blind
context: The chanson makes the horn-blast a physical martyrdom: Roland winds Olifant so hard that the veins in his temples burst and blood runs down his face -- but Charlemagne, thirty leagues away, hears it and turns his army back. The dying king's nephew has broken his own body to bring the news, and it is still too late. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: Alongside Olifant Roland fights with a named sword whose golden hilt, in the chanson, holds three sacred relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil, and hair of Saint Denis. What is the sword called?
context: Durendal is Roland's sword in the chanson, said to be unbreakable and to hold the three relics named. Excalibur is Arthur's sword; Joyeuse is Charlemagne's own sword; Tizona is one of the Cid's two named swords -- all real named blades of Western legend, all wrong for Roland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.

question: Even the archbishop of Charlemagne's court rides in the rearguard, a fighting bishop who cuts down dozens of the enemy with his own hand before falling at Roland's side. WHAT is the fighting archbishop's name?
context: Archbishop Turpin is one of the twelve peers, a warrior-bishop who fights and dies beside Roland; both are found on the field by Charlemagne after the pass. Anselm of Canterbury, Adalhard of Corbie, and Alcuin of York are all real medieval churchmen, but not the fighting archbishop of the chanson. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Roland.  (Legend.)

question: A famine in the days of the judges drove a man of Bethlehem to leave Israel with his wife Naomi and their two sons. To what neighboring country did the family go to wait out the hunger?
context: Ruth 1:1-2 KJV. Elimelech, Naomi, Mahlon, and Chilion cross the Dead Sea into Moab. Egypt, Edom, and Philistia are all real neighbors of Israel that a starving family could have fled to, but the text names Moab.

question: On the road back to Bethlehem, Naomi told her two daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' houses. Orpah kissed her and turned back to Moab; the other clung to Naomi and swore what famous pledge?
answer: 'Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.'
choices: 'Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.'
'Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.'
'Entreat me not to weep, for the Lord hath given, and the Lord hath taken away.'
'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want, though I walk in the shadow.'
context: Ruth 1:16 KJV, spoken by Ruth to Naomi. The other three are real famous verses -- Mary's answer to Gabriel (Luke 1:38), a mash of Job 1:21, and Psalm 23 -- but none is Ruth's pledge.

question: Coming home to Bethlehem, Naomi told the women who greeted her not to call her Naomi (which means 'pleasant') any more. What bitter new name did she ask them to use instead?
context: Ruth 1:20 KJV: 'Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.' Mara is Hebrew for 'bitter.' Hagar, Rahab, and Zilpah are all real Old Testament women, but none is the name Naomi chose.

question: Naomi and Ruth reach Bethlehem at the very beginning of the year's first grain harvest, and Ruth goes out to glean the corners of the fields left for the poor. Which grain was ripening in the fields she went to?
context: Ruth 1:22 and 2:23 KJV. Barley ripens in Israel in April, weeks before wheat -- so it is the first harvest a hungry widow can glean. Rye and millet were not the staple grains of ancient Israel.

question: Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech, noticed Ruth gleaning in his field and gave a secret order to his young men so she could gather far more grain than a stranger normally could. What did he tell them to do?
answer: Let handfuls fall on purpose for her out of the sheaves
choices: Let handfuls fall on purpose for her out of the sheaves
Deliver a full sack of grain to Naomi's door each evening
Bar the other gleaners from the field until she had finished
Weigh her grain double at the threshing floor scale
context: Ruth 2:16 KJV. Boaz's instruction disguises open charity as ordinary carelessness so Ruth is not shamed. The other options are the kinds of favors a rich landowner could grant, but only the dropped handfuls are in the text.

question: Following Naomi's counsel, Ruth washed and anointed herself, went at night to the threshingfloor where Boaz slept by his heap of corn, and lay down at his feet. At dawn Boaz sent her home with what in her veil?
choices: A silver ring set with carnelian
A written pledge sealed with his signet
A lamb from his own flock
context: Ruth 3:15 KJV. The six measures are both a betrothal gift and a public sign to Naomi that Boaz means to act. Signets, silver, and livestock are all real Iron Age wedding tokens, but the text specifies barley.

question: At the city gate of Bethlehem, a nearer kinsman refused to redeem Elimelech's field, so the sale to Boaz went through. The custom in Israel to seal such a deal in front of the elders was for one man to give the other what?
answer: His sandal, plucked off his foot
choices: His sandal, plucked off his foot
A cut lock of his own hair
A red cord tied around the wrist
A cup of wine poured on the ground
context: Ruth 4:7-8 KJV: 'a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel.' Boaz then buys the field and marries Ruth; their son Obed becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17).

question: An angel appeared to the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah and told her the son she would bear must be a Nazarite from the womb, sworn to God his whole life. What single thing was forbidden ever to touch his head?
context: Judges 13:5 KJV: 'no razor shall come upon his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb.' The son is Samson; his strength lies in his uncut hair. Anointing oil and crowns did later touch the heads of Israel's kings and priests, but never Samson's.

question: Walking down to Timnath to see the Philistine woman he wanted to marry, Samson was attacked in the vineyards by a young roaring lion. He killed it with nothing at all in his hands -- and later, going back to the carcass, he found what unlikely thing inside it?
answer: A swarm of bees and honey
choices: A swarm of bees and honey
context: Judges 14:5-9 KJV. Samson eats the honey and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from. The hidden find becomes the seed of his wedding riddle in the next rung.

question: Handed over to a Philistine army by his own people of Judah, Samson snapped the new ropes on his arms 'as flax burnt with fire' and picked up the first weapon he could find on the ground. Using what did he then slay a thousand men?
choices: The broken axle of a chariot
context: Judges 15:15-17 KJV. Samson cries, 'With the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps ... have I slain a thousand men,' and names the place Ramath-lehi ('Jawbone Hill'). The stone from a brook is David's weapon against Goliath (1 Samuel 17); the others are plausible battlefield finds.

question: Samson later loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, and the five lords of the Philistines came secretly to her to buy the secret of his strength. What was the name of the woman they paid?
context: Judges 16:4-5 KJV. Each of the five Philistine lords promised her eleven hundred pieces of silver. Jezebel, Bathsheba, and Michal are all real biblical women who married powerful men, but none is Samson's betrayer.

question: Three times Samson lied to Delilah about the secret of his strength, and three times she tried the trick while he slept. What did he tell her the third time?
answer: That she must weave his seven locks into the web of her loom
choices: That she must weave his seven locks into the web of her loom
That she must bind him with seven fresh green withs
That she must bind him with new ropes never used before
That she must pour wine upon his hair as he slept
context: Judges 16:13-14 KJV. Delilah wove his hair into the loom and fastened it with the pin; Samson woke and 'went away with the pin of the beam, and with the web.' The first two lies -- seven green withs and new ropes -- were his earlier answers (Judges 16:7, 16:11); the wine detail is invented. Only after this third lie did he finally tell her about the razor.

question: Blinded and set to grind at the mill in Gaza, Samson was led into the great temple to be mocked at a feast for the Philistines' god. Whose temple was it -- the god the lords were sacrificing to that day?
context: Judges 16:23 KJV: 'the lords of the Philistines gathered them together for to offer a great sacrifice unto Dagon their god.' Baal, Moloch, and Chemosh are real gods of Israel's other neighbors (Canaanites, Ammonites, Moabites), not the Philistines.

question: Before he was born, the prophet Samuel was promised to God by his mother -- a barren woman who wept and prayed at the temple of Shiloh until the priest Eli mistook her silent moving lips for drunkenness. What is Samuel's mother's name?
context: 1 Samuel 1:9-20 KJV. Hannah vows that if given a son she will give him to the LORD; Samuel is that son. Sarah was Abraham's wife (barren till Isaac); Rebekah was Isaac's wife (barren till the twins); Ruth was David's great-grandmother. All four are honest OT women.

question: The tall young Benjaminite whom Samuel privately anoints as Israel's first king meets the prophet by pure accident: Saul is out on a long errand for his father Kish, hunting for something valuable that has wandered off. What is Saul looking for when he stumbles onto Samuel?
context: 1 Samuel 9:3-19 KJV -- 'the asses of Kish Saul's father were lost.' Saul and his servant search for days; they end up in Samuel's town asking the seer where the donkeys have gone, and instead Saul is anointed king.

question: When Samuel meets the tall young Saul, he takes him aside privately, pours something over his head, and kisses him -- the secret sign that Saul is chosen as Israel's first king. What does Samuel pour on Saul's head?
context: 1 Samuel 10:1 KJV -- 'Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him.' The kiss and the oil together are the private anointing before the public choice at Mizpah.

question: At the public assembly at Mizpah, the lot falls on Saul to be king -- but when they call the tall Benjaminite forward, he is nowhere to be found. Where has the future king hidden himself?
context: 1 Samuel 10:22-23 KJV -- 'Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff.' They fetch him out and he stands head and shoulders above every man there. The reluctant giant king.

question: When Samuel is told to leave Saul's court and go anoint the next king, he travels to a small town south of Jerusalem, to the house of a shepherd-farmer with many sons. Whose house does Samuel enter to find the next king?
context: 1 Samuel 16:1-5 KJV -- 'fill thine horn with oil, and go, I will send thee to Jesse the Bethlehemite.' Boaz is David's great-grandfather (from Ruth); Obed is David's grandfather; Eli is the priest who raised Samuel. Honest OT-family distractors.

question: Samuel sees Jesse's oldest son Eliab -- tall, handsome, the kind of man who LOOKS like a king -- and thinks he has found the LORD's pick. But the word comes to Samuel: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the _____. What is the missing word?
context: 1 Samuel 16:7 KJV verbatim -- 'the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.' Perhaps the most quoted line in the whole Old Testament about how God chooses.

question: Seven of Jesse's sons pass before Samuel at Bethlehem and the LORD chooses none of them. Samuel asks if there is another; there is -- the YOUNGEST, out of the house entirely, doing a job the family did not think worth calling him in from. What is David doing when they finally send for him?
answer: keeping the sheep in the pasture
choices: hunting a lion in the hills
keeping the sheep in the pasture
context: 1 Samuel 16:11 KJV -- 'There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep.' When David is brought in he is 'ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to' (v.12).

question: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the greatest teacher of arms in the world is not a druid or a king but a warrior-woman who runs a martial school on a stormy island off the coast of Alba. She takes the boy-hero Cu Chulainn as her pupil. What is her name?
context: Scathach's name comes from Old Irish scath, meaning 'shadow' or 'phantom' -- 'the Shadowy One'. Medb is the warrior-queen of Connacht (Ulster Cycle, but an opponent, not a teacher); Deirdre 'of the Sorrows' is a tragic beauty of the same cycle; the Morrigan is the war-goddess who watches over battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Scathach the warrior-woman keeps her school at a fortress called Dun Scaith ('the Fortress of Shadows'), traditionally set on one particular island off the west coast of Scotland. On which island did later tradition place her stronghold?
context: The ruins called Dun Sgathaich near Tarskavaig on the Sleat peninsula of Skye mark the mythological site. The folk-etymology holds that the Isle of Skye (an t-Eilean Sgitheanach in Scots Gaelic) takes its own name from Scathach. Iona is the monastery-island of Columba; Man is the sea-god Manannan's island; Anglesey (Ynys Mon) is a druid-heartland in Welsh tradition. Source: https://spookyscotland.net/scathach/  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn crosses the sea to Alba to seek out Scathach because Forgall Manach, the father of the girl he wishes to marry, has set an impossible bride-price: no man can have his daughter's hand who has not first studied at the Fortress of Shadows. Which girl did Cu Chulainn wish to marry?
context: The story is told in Tochmarc Emire ('The Wooing of Emer'), one of the great foretales to the Tain. Grainne is the Fianna beauty who runs off with Diarmuid; Niamh carries Oisin to Tir na nOg; Deirdre is a doomed Ulster-Cycle heroine. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochmarc_Emire  (Legend.)

question: To reach Scathach's fortress Cu Chulainn must first cross a bridge that only its rightful students can pass -- step onto one end and the middle rises up and pitches the walker off. What single leap does Cu Chulainn use to cross it in one bound?
context: The salmon-leap (leim in bratain) is Scathach's signature technique: a running vault long enough to clear a bridge or a warrior's raised shield. Cu Chulainn will use it again years later at the Ford against Ferdiad. The chariot-wheel feat (roth-cles), the pole-vault for siege warfare, and the apple-feat (ubhall-cleas) are also real cles-feats Scathach teaches at her school -- but the bridge is crossed by the salmon-leap. Source: https://spookyscotland.net/scathach/  (Legend.)

question: Inside Scathach's fortress Cu Chulainn is not the only star pupil. He trains alongside another young warrior who will one day become his sworn foster-brother in arms -- the two of them eating from the same dish and sleeping with their shields interlocked. What is the other pupil's name?
context: Ferdiad is Cu Chulainn's dearest friend from their year at Scathach's school. Years later in the Tain the two will meet on opposite sides at the Ford -- three days of single combat that ends with Cu Chulainn killing Ferdiad and weeping over him. Conall Cernach is a fellow Ulster champion but trained elsewhere; Fionn and Oisin are heroes of the later Fenian Cycle, not the Ulster Cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Scathach has one rival warrior-woman who wars against her in Alba -- described in the tale as the most dangerous fighter in the world, and in some versions Scathach's own sister. Cu Chulainn is sent out to fight her in single combat. What is her name?
context: Aife and Scathach are named as daughters of Ard-Greimne of Lethra. Uathach is a warrior-woman of the same tale but not the rival. Fand is a sea-fairy of a different Cu Chulainn tale (The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn); Boudicca is a real historical Briton, not myth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Facing Aife in single combat and evenly matched, Cu Chulainn wins by shouting a lie -- claiming that the one thing Aife prizes most in all the world has just been destroyed in front of her. What does he shout has fallen off a cliff?
context: In the moment her head whips round to look, Cu Chulainn seizes her by the throat and pins her. He spares her life on the condition that she call off her enmity with Scathach and bear him a son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: The son Cu Chulainn fathers on Aife at the end of that duel grows up in Alba without ever meeting his father. Years later he sails alone to Ireland and challenges the champions of Ulster; Cu Chulainn is sent to face him and kills him in single combat, only recognising him as his own son when it is too late. What is the son's name?
context: Connla comes to Ireland at age seven under a geis (a magical taboo) that forbids him to name himself. The tale of Aided Oenfhir Aife ('The Death of Aife's Only Son') is one of the most heartbreaking in the Ulster Cycle -- a Sohrab-and-Rustum tale a thousand years before Firdausi. Cormac, Lugaid, and Amergin are all real Ulster-Cycle names, none of them Aife's son. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: Scathach's daughter is the one who first lets Cu Chulainn through the fortress gate; she takes him as a lover, and Cu Chulainn breaks her fingers by accident when he grabs the cup she offers him too hard. What is Scathach's daughter's name?
context: Uathach ('the Spectral One' -- her name echoes her mother's Shadow-name) hands Cu Chulainn the welcoming cup on his first day; his warrior's grip crushes her fingers. Emer is his betrothed back in Ireland; Sadhbh is Fionn's doe-wife in the later Fenian Cycle; Blathnat is a queen of a different Ulster tale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: At the end of the year and a day of training, Scathach gives Cu Chulainn a parting gift -- one deadly weapon she teaches to no other pupil, cast with the foot rather than the hand. Which spear does she place in his hand?
context: The Gae Bolg -- 'belly-spear' or 'notched spear' -- opens into barbs on entering the body and cannot be removed without cutting away the surrounding flesh. Cu Chulainn will use it to kill his foster-brother Ferdiad at the Ford in the Tain. Lugh's spear (the Areadbhar) is one of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha De Danann; the Luin of Celtchar is a flaming spear of another Ulster champion; Gungnir is Odin's Norse spear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sc%C3%A1thach  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Odyssey, the witch Circe warns Odysseus about a sea-passage where two monsters wait on facing cliffs -- one a six-headed cave-monster, one a whirlpool -- so no ship can avoid both. What is the famous NAME-PAIR for these two monsters?
choices: The Sirens and the Wandering Rocks
context: Circe warns Odysseus about the twin cliff-monsters Scylla and Charybdis, guarding a narrow strait where no ship can avoid both. (Odyssey 12; mythweb.com.)  (Legend.)

question: On one of the two cliffs of the strait crouches a monster with a woman's upper body sunk into a cave; her lower body is a mass of writhing necks. What is her name?
context: Scylla lives on one cliff of the strait. From her cave she reaches down with her many necks to snatch sailors off passing ships. (Odyssey 12; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: On the OPPOSITE cliff of the same strait -- 'within a bowshot' of Scylla, Homer says -- lurks a very different kind of horror, one that swallows and vomits three times each day. What is her name?
context: Charybdis is a monstrous whirlpool on the cliff opposite Scylla. Three times a day she swallows the sea and three times spits it up; no ship caught in her draw survives. (Odyssey 12; poetryintranslation.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Homer is very specific about the shape of the cliff-monster Scylla. She has twelve flailing feet, three rows of teeth in each mouth, and a fixed number of long serpent-necks each ending in a savage head. HOW MANY heads does she have?
context: Scylla has six long necks each with a dog-fanged head, three rows of teeth per mouth, and twelve legs. (Odyssey 12; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Circe puts the choice to Odysseus honestly: he cannot avoid both monsters, so he must pick which cliff to hug. She tells him to steer CLOSER to Scylla -- because Charybdis would swallow the whole ship, but Scylla will only take a fixed toll. HOW MANY of his crewmen will Scylla take as they pass?
context: Circe tells Odysseus to sail close to Scylla and lose six men -- one per head -- because Charybdis would take the whole ship. She explicitly forbids him to fight, because fighting will only cost him six more. (Odyssey 12; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey.)  (Legend.)

question: As Odysseus's ship passes under Scylla's cliff, her heads dart down and snatch his crewmen one after another. Odysseus later says that of everything he saw on his ten years of wandering -- the Cyclops, the Sirens, the land of the dead -- this was the most pitiful sight of all. WHAT does he say the dying men do as they are lifted up out of reach?
context: Odysseus: 'They called on my name, and I saw them lifted, and lifted still -- this was the most pitiful thing my eyes have seen of all my wanderings.' (Odyssey 12.245-259, Lattimore.)  (Legend.)

question: Before the passage, Circe warns Odysseus about Scylla in strange detail. Despite her monstrous size and the three rows of teeth in each mouth, her VOICE is not what you would expect. What does Circe say Scylla's voice sounds like?
context: Circe warns that Scylla's voice is 'no bigger than a newborn puppy's yelp' -- a tiny yipping sound coming from a giant monster. It is one of Homer's most unsettling details. (Odyssey 12; poetryintranslation.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus makes a hard captain's decision as they approach the strait. He knows six of his men are certain to die when they pass Scylla's cliff. He deliberately does NOT tell them what is waiting -- for what reason?
answer: He fears they will drop the oars and hide
choices: He fears they will drop the oars and hide
He fears they will mutiny and turn back
He fears they will attack Scylla with spears
He fears they will pray for the wrong god
context: Odysseus says plainly that he kept Scylla secret because if the men knew, they would drop the oars and huddle in the hold -- and then the ship, unrowed, would drift straight into Charybdis instead. (Odyssey 12; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Long after the Scylla passage, Odysseus loses his last ship and last crewmen far from the strait, and clings alone to a piece of wreckage. The current sweeps him BACK through the very same strait -- alone this time. He saves himself by grabbing a tree growing out of the cliff over Charybdis's mouth and hanging there like a bat, waiting for the whirlpool to vomit his raft back up. WHAT kind of tree does he cling to?
context: After the disaster on Thrinacia and the loss of his last ship, Odysseus is swept back through the strait alone and clings to a wild fig tree over Charybdis, hanging 'like a bat' until she spits his raft back up so he can drop onto it. One of the most vivid single images in the poem. (Odyssey 12.431-446.)  (Legend.)

question: The strait Homer describes at the edge of the known world was identified by later Greek and Roman writers -- Thucydides, Virgil, Pliny -- with a real narrow passage of water. WHICH real strait did they name as the home of Scylla and Charybdis?
context: Later tradition places Scylla on the Italian cliff and Charybdis on the Sicilian side of the Strait of Messina; the modern Italian town of Scilla in Calabria takes its name from the monster. (westportlibrary.libguides.com/scylla.)

question: A young officer in the emperor Diocletian's Praetorian Guard has been visiting fellow soldiers in the cells to encourage them; he is a secret Christian, and he is denounced. Diocletian orders him executed. What is this officer's name?
context: Sebastian was captain of the Praetorian Guard under Diocletian; traditional dates are c. 286-288 CE. Ambrose already knows his name by the end of the 4th century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.

question: Tied to a post and shot at close range by his own archers, Sebastian is left, in the Passio's famous line, 'as full of arrows' as what?
answer: An urchin is full of pricks
choices: An urchin is full of pricks
A grove is full of leaves
A quiver is full of shafts
A shield is full of dents
context: 'Sagittis obsitum ut ericium' in the 5th-century Passio -- 'as full of arrows as an urchin (hedgehog) is full of pricks'. The image became a stock phrase in medieval hagiography. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: That night, after the archers have gone, a Christian widow named Irene comes out to the post with a lamp to collect what she thinks is a corpse for burial. What does she find when she gets there?
context: The Passio says the widow Irene, whom it calls the widow of the martyr Castulus, came at night to bury Sebastian and found him still breathing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: As soon as Sebastian can walk again, he does something no one expects: he goes back and ambushes the emperor Diocletian in public. Where does he confront him?
answer: On the steps of the imperial palace
choices: On the steps of the imperial palace
In the middle of a chariot race
At a banquet with the senate
context: The Passio has Sebastian post himself on the palace stairs to ambush the emperor with a public speech accusing him of cruelty to the Christians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: Diocletian is astonished that the officer he had shot full of arrows is standing on his palace steps giving speeches. He orders Sebastian killed a second time. This time he does not use archers. What weapon does the second execution use?
context: The second sentence is death by cudgels in the Hippodrome. Sebastian's whole story turns on the reveal that the arrows are NOT what killed him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: After the second execution, Diocletian orders Sebastian's body dumped somewhere Christians will never be able to bury it. Where is the corpse thrown?
choices: Into the Tiber under the bridges
Onto the pyre of a criminal
Down a mineshaft outside the walls
context: The Cloaca Maxima was Rome's great main sewer, running under the Forum out to the Tiber -- meant as a final indignity, and to keep the body from becoming a relic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: The legend says a Roman Christian woman, guided by a dream, found the body in the sewer and buried it in a catacomb on the Appian Way where the Basilica of San Sebastiano now stands. What is her name?
context: The Passio names Lucina as the woman who recovered the body from the Cloaca Maxima after seeing Sebastian in a dream. All four choices are named early Roman Christian women martyrs or matrons. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.  (Legend.)

question: In medieval Europe Sebastian became the great patron saint invoked against ONE specific disaster. Which one, and why him?
answer: Plague, because he survived arrows and plague-strike was pictured as arrows
choices: Plague, because he survived arrows and plague-strike was pictured as arrows
Shipwreck, because the sewer washed him to the Tiber and the sea
Famine, because his body was thrown away like refuse
House fires, because his executioners burned the post
context: Ancient and medieval thought pictured pestilence as 'the arrows of the gods' or 'the arrows of God'. A saint who had famously survived a hail of arrows was the natural intercessor when plague hit a town. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sebastian.

question: The greatest hero of the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth is not born under the name he dies under. As a boy at Dun Dealgan (modern Dundalk) he is called something else -- a nephew of King Conchobar mac Nessa, born to Conchobar's sister Deichtine. What is his boyhood name?
context: The boy Setanta will earn a new name later in a single afternoon at a smith's gate. Fionn, Oisin, and Diarmuid are the great heroes of the LATER Fenian Cycle, a different tradition; Setanta belongs to the earlier Ulster Cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: One evening the boy Setanta comes late along the road to a feast, walking alone. The feast is at the house of a craftsman named Culann, one of the most honoured men in Ulster. What is Culann's trade?
context: Culann the smith is one of the great craftsmen of Ulster; his forge would have made the weapons of the king's warband. His name lives in Cu Chulainn's own -- 'the Hound of Culann' -- for what happens at his gate that night. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: King Conchobar has forgotten to warn the smith that another guest is coming behind him, and the smith has already loosed his savage guard-beast to protect the forge for the night. What kind of animal is chained at the smith's gate?
context: Culann's dog was an enormous chained war-hound, bred to kill wolves and men; it took three chains to hold him and it was said no other dog in Ireland could match him. Boars belong to the tale of Diarmuid; the bulls belong to the Cattle Raid; the black horse is Cu Chulainn's later chariot-horse, the Liath Macha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: The chained war-hound at Culann's gate is loosed and charges the boy Setanta as he walks up the road. He has no sword, no spear, and no shield -- only what he carried from his afternoon's play with the boys of Emain Macha. What is in his hands?
context: The boy had been playing iomain -- hurling, the old Irish stick-and-ball game, still played today. His hurley (camán) and small hard leather ball (sliotar) are all he has when the hound comes. David has the sling in the Bible (Christian pillar). Source: https://www.irelandsmythsandlegends.com/the-story-of-setanta

question: As the war-hound leaps for his throat, the boy Setanta strikes the small hard leather ball with the full swing of his stick. What does the ball do to the hound?
answer: Kills it, driven down its throat
choices: Kills it, driven down its throat
Puts out both its yellow eyes
Turns it aside from his gate
context: In the tale the ball goes down the throat with such force that in some versions it passes right through the dog. In others he then seizes the beast by the hind legs and dashes its head against a standing stone. Either way the hound is dead at his feet before the men at the feast come running out. Source: https://www.irelandsmythsandlegends.com/the-story-of-setanta

question: The smith Culann steps out of his house, sees the dead beast, and grieves aloud -- the hound was his living defence, and no pup of the same stock can be trained to replace it in less than a year. The boy, still standing at the gate, makes him a serious offer. What does Setanta offer to do?
answer: Guard the smith's house himself in the hound's place
choices: Guard the smith's house himself in the hound's place
Pay the smith the price of the hound in cattle
Fight a champion in single combat to earn the smith's forgiveness
Bring the smith the head of a wolf as recompense
context: The boy kneels and offers to sit at the smith's gate every night in the hound's place until a new pup of the same line can be reared. This offer -- a boy taking on a war-dog's watch -- is what changes his name forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culann  (Legend.)

question: That same afternoon, before the incident at the gate, Cathbad the druid had been teaching his pupils outside Emain Macha and let fall a prophecy about any boy who took up arms as a warrior for the first time on that particular date. What twin fate did Cathbad foretell for such a boy?
answer: A short life but lasting fame
choices: A short life but lasting fame
A long reign and a peaceful death
A wandering exile and a hidden grave
A cursed madness and a silent tongue
context: The same paired-fate formula appears in Achilles's mother's prophecy in the Iliad (Greek pillar). In both traditions the hero KNOWS the deal and takes it anyway: fame for years, not years for the man. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: The tale of the hound of Culann is not a standalone story: it sits embedded as an inset inside a larger saga, told by exiled Ulstermen in the enemy queen's camp who are trying to explain to her exactly who this one boy is who has been stopping her army single-handed. Inside which saga is the Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn nested?
choices: The Cattle Raid of Fraech (Tain Bo Fraich)
The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel (Togail Bruidne Da Derga)
context: The Macgnimrada Con Culaind ('The Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn') is a set of inset tales that Fergus mac Roich, exiled from Ulster, narrates to Medb of Connacht inside the Tain Bo Cuailnge -- the great cattle-raid epic. The other three are all real Ulster-Cycle tales, but the Boyhood Deeds sit specifically inside the Tain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: In the Ulster tradition Cu Chulainn has two fathers -- one mortal, one divine, a pattern the Irish repeat again and again for their great heroes. His mortal father is Sualtaim mac Roich, husband of Deichtine. Which of the gods is named as his divine father?
context: Lugh 'Long-Arm' (Lamhfhada) is the master-of-all-arts of the Tuatha De Danann and later comes down onto the battlefield to fight beside Cu Chulainn in the Tain. The Dagda is Lugh's father-in-law and lord of the cauldron; Manannan is the sea-god (father of Niamh); Nuada is the earlier king of the Tuatha with the silver arm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%BA_Chulainn  (Legend.)

question: While the ship lay at Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete, Paul warned the centurion Julius not to sail on any further that season. Two men on board overruled Paul's warning and pushed the ship back out to sea. Which two men were they?
answer: The master and owner of the ship
choices: The master and owner of the ship
The sailing master and the ship's scribe
The two senior sailors of the crew
context: Acts 27:11 -- 'the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.' It is a working-sailor argument about the season, not a religious dispute; the master and owner win, and the storm proves Paul right within days.

question: That midnight the sailors dropped a plumb-line and got twenty fathoms, then a little further fifteen. Terrified the ship would strike rocks in the dark, they dropped four heavy anchors and prayed for the day. From which part of the ship did they let those four anchors down?
context: Acts 27:29 -- 'they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day.' Anchoring from the stern (the back) is unusual -- most ships anchor by the bow -- but it kept the ship pointed toward the beach so they could run her ashore when day came.

question: That night, with the anchors holding and the ship pitching in the dark, Acts pauses to give the exact count of everyone on board -- prisoners, crew, and passengers together. How many souls were on the ship?
context: Acts 27:37 -- 'we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls.' Verse 44 adds that every one of the 276 made it to shore alive, some by swimming, some clinging to broken planks.

question: The wreck cast all 276 survivors ashore in the rain on a small Mediterranean island. The locals lit a bonfire on the beach for them and showed the shivering strangers unusual kindness. Acts names the island by its ancient name, Melita. By what name do we know it today?
context: Acts 28:1 -- 'they knew that the island was called Melita,' which is the ancient name for Malta. Crete is where the storm began; Cyprus and Rhodes lie further east along the earlier part of Paul's journey.

question: As Paul was gathering an armful of driftwood for the fire on the beach, a snake driven out by the heat lunged from the sticks and fastened onto him. Where on his body did the viper strike?
context: Acts 28:3 -- 'there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.' The islanders stood watching, waiting for him to swell up or drop dead; when Paul shook the snake off into the fire and felt nothing, they changed their minds and said he was a god.

question: The leading man of Malta -- a Roman citizen who owned lands near the beach -- took the survivors in for three days and lodged them courteously. His elderly father lay sick with fever and dysentery, and Paul went in, prayed, and laid hands on him. What was the chief man's name?
context: Acts 28:7-8 -- 'the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius.' Sergius Paulus is the proconsul of Cyprus in Acts 13; Gallio is the proconsul of Achaia in Acts 18; Cornelius is the centurion of Caesarea in Acts 10.

question: After the Castor-and-Pollux ship left Malta, Acts names three ports the ship touched before Paul reached Rome. The first was a great harbor where they laid over for three days before sailing on to Rhegium and Puteoli. Which port was it?
context: Acts 28:12-13 -- 'And landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days. And from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium... and the next day to Puteoli.' Messina, Catania, and Panormus (modern Palermo) are all real Sicilian ports of the ancient world, but Acts names Syracuse.

question: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god has a wife who lives with him in Asgard and is famous among the gods for one particular beauty. Poets say no woman in the nine worlds has ever had hair like hers -- long and thick and golden, falling all the way to the ground. What is the name of Thor's wife?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 31 and Skaldskaparmal 43: Sif is Thor's wife and is named for her extraordinary golden hair. Frigg is Odin's wife and queen of Asgard. Freyja is the Vanir goddess of love. Idunn is the goddess who keeps the golden apples of youth. Sif is also the mother of the god Ullr, the archer and skier of Asgard.  (Legend.)

question: Loki the trickster comes upon Thor's wife one afternoon while she is fast asleep in her chamber. For no reason but mischief, he takes out a knife and does something to her that will start a whole chain of trouble in Asgard. What does Loki do to Sif while she is sleeping?
answer: shears her golden hair to the scalp
choices: shears her golden hair to the scalp
steals a ring off her finger
cuts the strap of her golden girdle
carves a rune on her forehead
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki simply cuts off all Sif's famous hair, leaving her scalp bare. Snorri gives no motive beyond mischief -- this is one of the purest examples of Loki being cruel because he can. The other three options are inventions built out of other Norse objects (golden rings, girdles, runes) that have nothing to do with this scene.  (Legend.)

question: When Thor comes home and finds his wife bald, he seizes Loki and threatens him with a specific violence unless Loki makes it right. What does Thor threaten to do to Loki?
answer: break every bone in his body
choices: break every bone in his body
hang him from the branches of Yggdrasil
throw him into the sea for Jormungandr
sew his lips shut with an awl
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Thor threatens to break every bone in Loki's body unless Loki makes it right. The other three options are not what Thor threatens in this scene.  (Legend.)

question: The Sons of Ivaldi do not only make Sif a new fall of golden hair for Loki to carry home. In the same fire in the same workshop, they make two more marvels that Loki takes back to Asgard -- both of which end up as the signature possessions of other named gods. What are the two other treasures the Sons of Ivaldi make in the same session?
answer: the ship Skidbladnir and the spear Gungnir
choices: the ship Skidbladnir and the spear Gungnir
the hammer Mjolnir and the ring Draupnir
the sword Gram and the necklace Brisingamen
the boar Gullinbursti and the horse Sleipnir
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: the Sons of Ivaldi make three treasures in one session -- Sif's golden hair, Freyr's folding ship Skidbladnir, and Odin's spear Gungnir. Mjolnir, Draupnir and Gullinbursti are made by the OTHER pair of dwarves, Brokkr and Sindri, in the wager that comes next. Gram is Sigurd's dragon-slaying sword. Brisingamen is Freyja's necklace. Sleipnir is Loki's own eight-legged son.  (Legend.)

question: On his way back out of the dwarf-halls with the three treasures, Loki cannot resist making a boast to two other dwarf smiths he passes -- the boast that the Sons of Ivaldi are the finest smiths in all the worlds. Those two other dwarves take it as a challenge, and the second wager begins. Which two dwarf-brothers does Loki's boast provoke into the second contest?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr and Sindri (Sindri is sometimes called Eitri) take Loki's boast as a wager and set to work on three more treasures -- the boar Gullinbursti, the arm-ring Draupnir, and the hammer Mjolnir. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder Kvasir. Baugi and Suttung are giants in the Mead of Poetry story. Nordri and Sudri are two of the four sky-holding dwarves.  (Legend.)

question: Because of this story, Norse court-poets afterwards used a fixed poetic name-substitute -- a kenning -- for one particular thing, based on Sif's replacement hair. Whenever a skaldic poet wanted to refer to that thing indirectly, they would call it 'the hair of Sif'. What did the kenning 'the hair of Sif' mean in Norse poetry?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 39: the standard list of kennings for gold includes 'Sif's hair', because Sif's replacement hair was spun of real gold that grew on her head. 'Wheat at harvest' is the older grain-goddess reading some modern scholars give of Sif herself, but the kenning is for gold. Norse poets loved this kind of story-derived name -- 'Kvasir's blood' for poetry, 'the sea-king's ride' for a ship, 'Odin's storm' for a battle.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse Volsunga Saga a young hero armed with his reforged father-sword is sent by his foster-father to kill a dragon coiled around a cursed hoard of gold on the moor called Gnitaheid. What is the name of this Norse dragon?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 14 and 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. Fafnir is the dragon on Gnitaheid, once a man and the brother of the smith Regin. Nidhoggr is the dragon that gnaws the root of Yggdrasil in the underworld. Jormungandr is the Midgard-serpent that circles the world. Grendel is the man-shaped monster of Beowulf, not a dragon. Fafnir is the specific dragon Sigurd kills.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir is not a beast that has always been a dragon. He is described in the Volsunga Saga as being, in his earlier life, one particular kind of creature -- until greed drove him to transform himself. What was Fafnir before he became a dragon?
context: Volsunga Saga chapters 14 and 18. Fafnir was a man -- specifically the son of Hreidmar and the brother of Regin the smith and Otr the otter-shaped shape-shifter. When the family got the cursed hoard of Andvari's gold as compensation for Otr's killing, Fafnir killed his father, took all of the gold, and used a magic Helm of Awe to transform himself into a dragon so he could guard it alone. He is one of a small handful of dragons in world mythology who used to be human.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir the dragon has one battlefield weakness. His hide is so hard that no blade can pierce his back or his flanks -- and Regin tells Sigurd this before sending him out. Which part of Fafnir is soft enough for a sword to go into?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. Only the underside of Fafnir's belly is unarmoured -- everywhere else his hide turns the blade. This is why the strategy has to be a strike from BELOW as the dragon passes overhead. Smaug in Tolkien -- whose weak underbelly is famously exposed by a single missing scale -- was directly borrowed from Fafnir.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd's foster-father has one plan for how his young charge is to kill Fafnir. Regin tells Sigurd to go to the dragon's game-trail before dawn and prepare one specific ambush for when Fafnir crawls out to the water. What is Regin's plan?
answer: dig a pit in the trail and stab upward as the dragon passes over
choices: dig a pit in the trail and stab upward as the dragon passes over
drop a great stone from a cliff onto the dragon's spine
loose a burning arrow between the dragon's eyes at dawn
pour boiling oil down the mouth of the dragon's lair overnight
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal prose introduction. The Norse dragon-killing method is the pit-and-upward-thrust -- Regin's plan is that Sigurd hide in a trench cut into the game-trail and drive the blade UP as the dragon's soft belly passes over his head. It has entered European folklore as the standard way to kill any large monster from below.  (Legend.)

question: While Sigurd is digging his pit on the trail, an old stranger appears -- one-eyed, in a wanderer's cloak -- and gives him a critical piece of advice that Regin left out. What does the old wanderer tell Sigurd to add to Regin's plan?
answer: dig extra pits alongside to catch the blood
choices: dig extra pits alongside to catch the blood
smear the sword with poison before the strike
wait for the second dawn instead of the first
call the dragon by his mortal name to freeze him
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18. The one-eyed stranger is Odin himself. He warns Sigurd that a single pit will fill with the dragon's blood as Fafnir bleeds out overhead, and Sigurd would drown before he could climb out. The side-channels drain the flood away. This is one of a whole series of moments in the Volsunga Saga where Odin quietly intervenes in the Volsung line -- putting Gram in the tree at Signy's wedding, shattering it against Sigmund at the end, and now this.  (Legend.)

question: The dawn comes and the dragon crawls out of his lair towards the water. The earth trembles as he goes, and one particular thing rolls out ahead of him along the trail -- one of Fafnir's dragon-weapons even before his teeth or his hide. What rolls out in front of Fafnir as he approaches the pit?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18; Fafnismal 1. Fafnir's breath is described as poisonous -- rolling before him along the trail like a mist. The Norse do not always draw a hard line between snake-poison and dragon-fire; Fafnir is one of the venom-breathing dragons. Jormungandr the world-serpent kills Thor with the same kind of venom nine steps after Thor kills him.  (Legend.)

question: As the dragon crawls directly over the pit, Sigurd drives the reforged sword upward to the hilt into Fafnir's one weak place. What is the name of the sword Sigurd uses to kill Fafnir?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 18. Gram is the reforged sword of Sigurd's father Sigmund. Hrunting is the sword Unferth lends Beowulf in the fight with Grendel's mother. Durendal is Roland's sword at Roncesvalles -- an adjacent named blade from the Christian pillar. Tyrfing is the cursed dwarf-sword of the Hervarar saga. Gram is the specific sword that kills Fafnir.  (Legend.)

question: Norse dragons do not simply die. They know all things at their death, and they use their last breath to speak with the man who has killed them. What is the name of the Poetic Edda poem that records the whole dying-speech of the dragon on Gnitaheid?
context: Poetic Edda (Codex Regius); Carolyne Larrington translation. Fafnismal ('the sayings of Fafnir') is a dialogue-poem in which most of the verses are the dragon's dying words to Sigurd. Reginsmal ('the sayings of Regin') comes just before it in the manuscript and covers the smith's back-story. Sigrdrifumal is the awakening of the valkyrie Sigrdrifa. Vafthrudnismal is Odin's wisdom-contest with a different giant. The specific dying-speech poem is Fafnismal.  (Legend.)

question: The dying dragon warns Sigurd of something very concrete about the treasure he has just won -- a warning that turns out to be exactly correct across the rest of the Volsunga Saga. What does Fafnir warn Sigurd about the gold?
answer: the cursed hoard will destroy him too
choices: the cursed hoard will destroy him too
the gold must be thrown back into the river
the ring in the hoard commands nine armies
the hoard belongs by right to the giants
context: Fafnismal stanzas 8-10 and 20-22. Fafnir tells Sigurd that Andvari's gold has destroyed everyone who has held it, and it will destroy him too. Every remaining chapter of the Volsunga Saga proves him right -- from Regin's plot to Brynhild's suicide to Sigurd's own murder in bed to the final destruction of the Nibelungs. The other three choices are plausible dragon-warnings from adjacent stories, but the specific Fafnismal warning is the curse-on-all-who-hold-it.  (Legend.)

question: Fafnir gives Sigurd a SECOND warning as he dies, one that Sigurd will act on within the hour -- not about the treasure itself, but about the man who sent him here in the first place. What does Fafnir warn Sigurd about Regin?
answer: his own brother will betray him for the gold
choices: his own brother will betray him for the gold
his old master has poisoned the sword-hilt
his foster-father is really a giant in disguise
his true father was killed by Regin long ago
context: Fafnismal stanzas 22 and 31; Volsunga Saga chapter 19. Fafnir tells Sigurd that Regin -- Fafnir's own brother -- means to kill him for the hoard. In the very next chapter Sigurd tastes the dragon's blood, understands the speech of birds, and hears two nuthatches confirm exactly the same warning; he then beheads Regin with Gram before Regin can strike first. This is the moment the young hero shifts from foster-son to independent man.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse Volsunga Saga the young hero has just killed the dragon on Gnitaheid. His foster-father Regin sits down beside him, cuts one specific organ out of the dragon, and hands it to Sigurd with orders to cook it over the open fire while Regin lies down to sleep in the grass. Which organ does Regin cut out and give Sigurd to roast?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. Regin drinks the dragon's blood himself, cuts out Fafnir's heart, and tells Sigurd to cook it on a spit for him -- claiming he wants to eat it for the wisdom that comes with it. Then Regin lies down in the grass, exhausted, and falls asleep. In Norse dragon-lore the heart is the seat of the dragon's knowledge; the other organs carry no such magic.  (Legend.)

question: The dragon's heart is roasting on a spit over the fire. Sigurd wants to check if it is cooked through, so he pokes it with one finger to test the meat. The blood inside is boiling hot and it scalds him. Which finger does Sigurd burn?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. The scalded THUMB is a fixed detail of the story -- it is the thumb Sigurd tests with, and the thumb he then sticks in his mouth to cool it. The exact detail matters because the direct Celtic cousin of this story is Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Salmon of Knowledge, where Fionn burns his THUMB on the roasting salmon-skin and sucks it and gains all wisdom -- the same anatomical detail in a completely independent tradition.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd's thumb is scalded by the boiling dragon-blood. Without thinking he does the thing anyone does when they burn a finger -- he sticks the burned thumb in his mouth to cool it. The instant the dragon's blood touches his tongue a new power comes over him. What does Sigurd suddenly discover he can do?
choices: grow to twice a man's height
call fire from an open hand
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal prose after stanza 31. Dragon-blood confers the language of birds -- one of the oldest Germanic story-shapes, appearing in folktale all across northern Europe. Sigurd hears the chirping in the trees above his head resolve into voices talking about him. This is the folkloric-magic center of the whole saga, and the pivot to everything that follows.  (Legend.)

question: In the branches above the fire on Gnitaheid a small flock of birds is chattering about the young man on the ground. The first bird looks down at Sigurd tending the roasting heart and remarks that he would be a wiser lord if he did one specific thing with the heart on the spit -- instead of handing it over to sleeping Regin as ordered. What does the first bird say Sigurd should do?
choices: throw the heart into the river
bury the heart in the hoard
context: Fafnismal stanza 32. The whole point of the dragon-heart in Norse dragon-lore is that whoever eats it gains its wisdom. Regin claimed the heart for himself and Sigurd is dutifully cooking it for his foster-father, but the birds see the danger: the wisdom is going to the wrong man. Their first counsel is the simple one -- eat it yourself.  (Legend.)

question: The birds' chatter above Sigurd's head turns from advice to warning. They tell him something specific about the man lying asleep in the grass beside him -- his foster-father, the smith who reforged Sigurd's sword and taught him the pit-and-thrust that just killed the dragon. What do the birds tell Sigurd that Regin is planning?
answer: to kill Sigurd for the treasure
choices: to kill Sigurd for the treasure
to lie to Sigurd about the sword
to marry Sigurd's mother by force
to sell Sigurd to the giants
context: Fafnismal stanzas 33-37; Volsunga Saga chapter 19. This is the piece of news that turns the whole saga. Regin has been a father-figure to Sigurd since childhood -- reforged Gram out of the shards of Sigmund's sword, sent him out to Gnitaheid, taught him the pit-plan. He is also the dragon's brother, and now that Fafnir is dead the whole cursed hoard passes by rights to Regin -- if Sigurd is out of the way. The dying Fafnir had already warned Sigurd of exactly this; the birds are the second warning, and the one Sigurd finally acts on.  (Legend.)

question: Sigurd has heard the birds. He has heard the dying dragon. Regin lies asleep in the grass a few paces from the fire. Sigurd draws the sword Gram, walks over to his foster-father, and does one specific thing to him. What does Sigurd do to Regin?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal stanzas 39-40. Sigurd beheads Regin with a single stroke of Gram before Regin can wake up and strike first. The moment marks the young hero's shift from foster-son to independent man -- from taking orders from a tutor to acting on his own judgment. It is also the first killing Sigurd does without a tutor's plan, and the first killing that is unambiguously HIS choice.  (Legend.)

question: The chattering birds in the trees have one more piece of news for Sigurd. They tell him about a person he must go find -- someone lying asleep on a mountain called Hindarfjall, ringed by a wall of flame, waiting for a hero brave enough to ride through the fire and wake her. What kind of person is asleep on Hindarfjall?
context: Fafnismal stanzas 42-44. The sleeping figure is the Valkyrie who will be named Brynhild -- the birds send Sigurd toward her and the next act of the saga opens with him riding through the ring of fire. Valkyries in Norse myth are the choosers of the slain who serve Odin. A Norn is one of the three fates at the well of Urd. Giantesses and elf-queens are separate categories. The birds specifically name a Valkyrie.  (Legend.)

question: The gossiping voices in the branches above Sigurd's fire are not just any birds -- the Poetic Edda calls them igda, and the Volsunga Saga's prose paraphrase names them a specific little woodland bird that hops head-down along tree-trunks. What kind of bird does the Volsunga Saga say is chattering above Sigurd's head about Regin's plot?
context: Fafnismal stanzas 32-38; Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Bellows and Larrington translations. The Old Norse word igda in Fafnismal is one of the puzzles of the Poetic Edda -- Henry Adams Bellows translated it as nuthatches, Carolyne Larrington as tits, and some scholars simply as chattering birds. The Volsunga Saga's prose paraphrase of the scene commits to nuthatches, the small blue-and-buff woodland bird famous for creeping down tree-trunks head-first. Wrens, finches, and thrushes are all real woodland birds of northern Europe, but they are not the ones named in Sigurd's dragon-slaying scene.  (Legend.)

question: From the day he kills the dragon and beheads Regin, Sigurd carries a battle-name the skalds use for him for the rest of his life -- and for the rest of Norse and Germanic legend after him. Which byname does Sigurd earn on Gnitaheid?
context: Volsunga Saga chapter 19; Fafnismal title tradition. Fafnisbani means Fafnir's-Bane, slayer of Fafnir -- the standard skaldic epithet for Sigurd from this day on. Fenrisbani (Fenrir's-Bane) is a possible kenning for Vidar, who kills Fenrir at Ragnarok, not for Sigurd. Volsungr just means son of the Volsung line -- his family name, not his earned byname. Gramgjafi (giver of Gram) is not a standard epithet. Fafnisbani is the specific dragon-slaying byname.  (Legend.)

question: The scene of the hero cooking magic food, burning his finger, sticking it in his mouth, and gaining supernatural wisdom is not unique to Sigurd and the dragon's heart. Another young hero in Celtic tradition burns his thumb on a magical fish roasting on a spit, sucks the thumb, and gains all the wisdom of the world. Who is the Celtic hero who burns his thumb on a magic fish?
context: Fenian Cycle, the Boyhood Deeds of Fionn. The fish is the Salmon of Knowledge, caught in the river Boyne by the poet Finnegas after seven years' waiting; young Fionn is set to cook it, burns his thumb on the crackling skin, sticks the thumb in his mouth, and from that day on gains all knowledge whenever he bites his thumb. Cuchulainn is the Ulster hero of the Tain, no salmon story. Lugh is the many-skilled god of the Tuatha De Danann. Diarmuid is the Fenian who dies on the boar of Ben Bulben. The salmon-and-thumb story belongs to Fionn. The Sigurd-and-Fionn parallel is one of comparative mythology's most striking cousin-motifs -- two totally separate traditions, the same magic story-shape.  (Legend.)

question: A Syrian shepherd boy joins a monastery near Antioch, but his fasts and self-denial are so extreme that the other monks ask him to leave. He moves out to a stone hut alone. What is his name?
context: Simeon (c. 390-459 CE) was born in Sis in Cilicia in northern Syria, the son of a shepherd. His fellow monks near Antioch found his austerities beyond bearing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Crowds of pilgrims will not leave the Syrian hermit Simeon alone at ground level, so he tries something no Christian ascetic has ever done before: he moves his home OFF the ground. Where does he move it to?
answer: The top of a stone pillar
choices: The top of a stone pillar
A cave in the cliff face
The dead branches of a huge tree
A raft moored in the middle of a lake
context: The Greek word for pillar is 'stylos', from which comes 'stylite'. Simeon is the first Christian stylite. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Simeon lives up on his pillar but he does not just sit in silence -- the crowds gather below him every day to hear him. How does he feed himself up there, with no way to come down?
answer: Bread and water are hauled up in a basket on a rope
choices: Bread and water are hauled up in a basket on a rope
A servant climbs up each morning with a hot meal
He grows herbs in a wooden trough beside him
He is fed by ravens sent by an angel
context: Simeon's disciples tied bread and water to a rope and his followers hauled the basket up to the platform. From the top he preached twice a day to the crowd below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: The platform on top of Simeon's last pillar was tiny -- about one square metre, with a low balustrade around the edge. Given that space, how did he sleep at night?
choices: Curled tight in a hollow bowl
In a hammock strung across the pillar
Wrapped to the base of a wooden cross
context: There was not enough room on the platform to lie down. He slept standing, tied to a post fixed to the pillar so he would not fall while asleep. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: Simeon lived on top of that pillar for a very long time before he finally died on it in 459 CE. About how many years did he spend up there?
context: The traditional figure from Theodoret and later sources is thirty-seven years on the pillar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: One of the reasons we know so much about Simeon is that a nearby bishop wrote his life story WHILE HE WAS STILL ALIVE on the pillar -- a rare thing for a saint's Life. Who was that bishop?
context: Theodoret devoted a chapter of his 'Religious History' to Simeon while the ascetic was still on the pillar. He had visited him in person. All four distractors are real Greek-Christian bishops of the 4th-5th centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: After Simeon died on the pillar, the emperor Zeno built an enormous cruciform pilgrimage church around the shrunken stump of the pillar itself. What is that church called?
context: 'Qalat Simaan' means 'the fortress of Simeon' in Arabic. Built by Zeno in the 470s-490s around the shrunken stump of Simeon's pillar in northern Syria, it was for centuries one of the largest churches in Christendom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_Stylites.

question: On the walk out of the city toward the execution ground, Jesus is too exhausted to carry the crossbeam alone. The Roman soldiers grab a random bystander from the crowd and force him to shoulder it. Mark 15:21 (KJV) names the man in one phrase. Who was pulled from the crowd?
context: Mark 15:21 KJV: 'they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to bear his cross.' Joseph of Arimathea is the rich man who later gives Jesus his tomb (Matthew 27:57). Nicodemus is the Pharisee who visits Jesus by night (John 3:1). Cleopas is one of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:18). All four are real named figures from the Passion week -- only one gets grabbed to carry the cross.

question: Mark alone lists the two sons of the man who carried the cross, as if his first readers would recognise them. One is named Alexander. What is the other son's name?
context: Mark 15:21 KJV: 'the father of Alexander and Rufus.' Paul greets a 'Rufus, chosen in the Lord' in Romans 16:13, and church tradition has long guessed it is the same Rufus. Titus was a Greek convert Paul mentored; Silas was Paul's travelling companion after Barnabas; Barnabas was Paul's first missionary partner, and 'son of encouragement' in Acts 4:36. All four are real early-church names -- only one is the son of the man from Cyrene.

question: The execution ground outside the city was known by an Aramaic name whose literal meaning is 'the place of a skull' -- probably from the shape of the low hill. Mark 15:22 (KJV) gives it. What was the place called?
context: Mark 15:22 KJV: 'And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, The place of a skull.' The Latin for skull is 'calvaria' -- the source of the English name Calvary. Gethsemane is the olive grove where Jesus was arrested (Mark 14:32). Gabbatha is the pavement where Pilate sat to judge (John 19:13). Gehenna is a valley south of Jerusalem used as a byword for hell. All four sound alike, only one is the skull-place.

question: Pilate has a title-board fixed above Jesus's head on the cross reading 'JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS'. John 19:20 (KJV) notes the board was written in three languages so any traveller could read it. Which three?
context: John 19:19-20 KJV. Hebrew for the local Jewish population, Greek as the trade language of the eastern empire, Latin as the language of Rome. Only John records the trilingual detail. Egyptian and Persian belonged to other empires; Syriac (a form of Aramaic) is close to what Jesus and his neighbours actually spoke, but the gospel names Hebrew, not Syriac.

question: Christian crucifixes across Europe often carry a small plaque above the figure's head with four Latin letters, the initials of the sentence Pilate had nailed to the cross above Jesus. What are the four letters?
context: The Latin sentence was 'Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum' -- 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.' Latin uses I where English uses J, so IESUS begins with I. IHS is a different Christian monogram, from the Greek spelling of Jesus (I-H-S = IHSOUS). XPS is another Greek Christogram, from CHRIST (X-P from Greek chi-rho). SPQR is the Roman civic motto, Senatus Populusque Romanus. All four are real historic acronyms -- only one is the cross-sign.

question: The gospels together record seven sayings of Jesus from the cross, drawn from four different books. No single gospel has all seven. Only one saying is preserved in more than one gospel -- it appears in both Matthew and Mark, in the original Aramaic. Which cry is it?
answer: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
choices: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Into thy hands I commend my spirit
context: Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 KJV: 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?' (Matthew) / 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?' (Mark). It is the opening line of Psalm 22 -- an entire psalm the crucified man is quoting by its first words, the ancient way of naming a text.
