'It is finished' is John 19:30; 'Father, forgive them' is Luke 23:34; 'Into thy hands I commend my spirit' is Luke 23:46. All real cross-sayings, only one is preserved in Aramaic and shared by two evangelists.

question: The final saying in John 19:30 is translated into English as 'It is finished' -- but in the underlying gospel Greek it is a single word, the perfect-tense form of the verb 'to finish' or 'to fulfil'. Merchants used it to mean 'paid in full'. What is the Greek word?
context: John 19:30 in Greek: 'tetelestai'. Papyrus tax receipts from the same century use the word to mean 'paid off, account closed'. Maranatha is Aramaic 'Our Lord, come' (1 Corinthians 16:22). Kyrios is Greek for 'Lord'. Sabaoth is Hebrew 'armies/hosts', as in the Sanctus. All four are famous preserved-in-original-language words from scripture -- only one is the last word from the cross.

question: Jesus's Aramaic cry from the cross -- 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' -- is not a saying he invented in the moment. It is the opening line, quoted verbatim, of a much older Hebrew poem in the Jewish scriptures. Which text?
context: Psalm 22:1 KJV: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' In ancient Jewish practice, quoting the opening of a text was a way of pointing to the whole -- Psalm 22 goes on to describe hands and feet pierced and garments divided by lot, which is why the gospels weave the psalm's language through the crucifixion scene. Psalm 23 is 'The Lord is my shepherd'; Psalm 51 is David's confession after Bathsheba; Psalm 137 is 'By the rivers of Babylon'.

question: At the foot of the cross stood a Roman officer commanding the execution detail. Watching how Jesus dies, this officer -- a man of the executing power, not a follower -- says the line Mark 15:39 (KJV) preserves as the first human recognition in Mark's gospel: 'Truly this man was the Son of God.' What was his rank?
context: Mark 15:39 KJV. A centurion commanded roughly a hundred men -- the standard Roman infantry officer, and the man who would have run this kind of detail. The gospels never name him, but medieval Christian tradition later called him Longinus (apparently from Greek longche, 'spear', because of a separate legend that he was the soldier who pierced Jesus's side in John 19:34). A tribune outranked him; a legate commanded a whole legion; a decurion commanded cavalry. Only the centurion belongs at this cross.

question: Every gospel list of the Twelve Apostles ends the same way: two names paired together. The very last is Judas Iscariot, the betrayer. The second-to-last is a Simon -- not Peter, a different one -- carrying a one-word tag that would eventually become his standard name. Which Simon is this?
context: Matthew 10:4, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, and Acts 1:13 all name him Simon the Zealot (Greek Zelotes, from the Aramaic qanai, 'zealous'). Simon Magus is the sorcerer of Acts 8; Simon of Cyrene was the man pressed into carrying Jesus's cross; 'Simon Bar-Jonah' is Peter's given name (Jesus renames him Cephas / Peter, 'the Rock').

question: The apostle named just before Simon the Zealot in the lists is another Judas -- Judas son of James, called by a SECOND name in Matthew and Mark so no one confuses him with the betrayer. That second name, later Latinised as 'Jude', is what the Western church still uses for him. What is that second name?
context: Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18 list him as Thaddaeus (also Lebbaeus in some manuscripts); later Latin usage flattens Thaddaeus to Jude (as in Saint Jude). Barnabas was Paul's traveling companion; Barabbas was the criminal released at Passover; Bartimaeus was the blind beggar Jesus healed at Jericho.

question: The name Simon carried -- 'Zealot' -- was not just a personality label. It matched a real militant faction whose whole program was armed rebellion against the foreign power occupying the Holy Land in Simon's own lifetime. Which power were the Zealots fighting?
context: The Zealots were a militant Jewish party who wanted armed rebellion against Roman rule; Josephus (Jewish War) tracks them through the great revolt of AD 66-70 that ended with the destruction of the Temple. Whether Simon actually belonged to the party or was just personally zealous, the tag placed a former militant among former fishermen. The Seleucids were the earlier Greek overlords beaten back by the Maccabees; the Hasmonean priest-kings ruled between Seleucids and Rome; Herod's dynasty were Roman client-kings, not the occupying power itself.

question: The ancient historian Eusebius (Church History 1.13) tells a story he says he found in a royal archive: a local king had heard of Jesus's healings, written him a letter, and been promised a disciple would come after Jesus's death to heal him of his disease. The disciple sent was Thaddaeus. Which king was he sent to?
context: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 1.13, preserves the correspondence between Jesus and King Abgar V of Edessa (a small kingdom in what is now southeastern Turkey); Thaddaeus (called Addai in Syriac tradition) is sent after the resurrection and heals him. Herod Agrippa I ruled in Judea in the same century; Antiochus IV of Commagene was a Roman client-king on the Euphrates; Tigranes ruled Armenia -- all real small-kingdom rulers of the era, none tied to the Abgar legend.

question: Western medieval tradition sends Simon and Thaddaeus travelling together as missionaries, and they die together in the same country -- put to death for their preaching by the local priests. In which country does that joint martyrdom take place?
context: The 'Passion of Simon and Jude', a Western medieval Passion narrative, sends them together into Persia (some sources say Suanir) where both are killed. Britain is traditionally linked to Joseph of Arimathea; Ethiopia to Matthew (Matthew the Evangelist's traditional field); Spain to James the Greater, whose shrine is at Santiago de Compostela.  (Legend.)

question: In Roman Catholic devotion Thaddaeus is now known as Saint Jude -- and he has become the patron of one very specific kind of prayer. The reason is embarrassing: for centuries almost no one prayed to him at all, because his name was too close to another apostle's, so people worried they were addressing the wrong Judas. What is Saint Jude now the patron of?
context: Because 'Jude' (Judas son of James) was so easily confused with Judas Iscariot the betrayer, few Christians for centuries invoked him -- so tradition made him especially glad to help anyone who did. He became the patron of lost causes. Safe sea travel is Christopher (or Nicholas); students traditionally invoke Joseph of Cupertino or Thomas Aquinas; finding a spouse is Anthony of Padua (also lost objects).

question: Three months out of Egypt the Hebrews pitched their camp before the mountain where Moses would climb up to meet God. What was the name of that mountain?
context: Exodus 19:1-2 KJV. Ararat is where Noah's ark landed, Carmel is where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, and Nebo is where Moses would later die looking into Canaan -- all real mountains in the Bible, but the giving of the Law was at Sinai.

question: On the third morning the mountain quaked greatly, wrapped in a thick cloud with thunders and lightnings. Above all the noise one supernatural sound grew louder and louder until Moses spoke and God answered him. What was that sound?
answer: The voice of a trumpet exceeding loud
choices: The voice of a trumpet exceeding loud
The roaring of a great fire
The crashing of stone upon stone
context: Exodus 19:16, 19 KJV: 'and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud ... And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice.'

question: Moses climbed alone into the cloud on the mountain, and God spoke ten commandments to him for the people. Which of these was the very first?
answer: 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me.'
choices: 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me.'
'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.'
context: Exodus 20:3 KJV. The other three commandments are all real and part of the same Ten (Exodus 20:8, 12, 13), but the command against other gods stands at the head of the list.

question: Moses stayed on the mountaintop with God, without bread or water. How long was he up there before he came down with the tablets?
context: Exodus 34:28 KJV. The same 'forty days' shape returns with Noah's flood, Elijah's flight to Horeb, and Jesus in the wilderness. Three days and nights is Jonah in the fish; seven days is the flood-wait to send out the raven.

question: At the end of the forty days God handed Moses two tables of stone. The text says the writing on them was not carved by any craftsman, but was made how?
answer: Written with the finger of God
choices: Written with the finger of God
Burned in by lightning from heaven
Etched by the tip of a serpent's tooth
Cut by an angel with a diamond stylus
context: Exodus 31:18 KJV: 'two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God.' The other options fit the awe of the scene but the specific phrase in the text is the finger of God itself.

question: Down below, the people grew tired of waiting for Moses and pressed Aaron to make them gods to go before them. What did Aaron ask them to bring him as the raw metal for a molten idol?
answer: The golden earrings out of their ears
choices: The golden earrings out of their ears
The bronze mirrors of their women
The silver chains from their firstborn sons
The iron rings from their tent poles
context: Exodus 32:2-4 KJV. Aaron collects the earrings, melts them, and shapes a molten calf; the bronze mirrors of the women are a real biblical donation but for the tabernacle laver later (Exodus 38:8), not the calf.

question: Moses came down carrying the two stone tables and saw the golden calf and the people dancing before it. His anger burned so hot that he did what to the tablets at the foot of the mountain?
answer: Cast them out of his hands and broke them
choices: Cast them out of his hands and broke them
Buried them beneath a heap of stones
Hurled them into the fire of the calf
Carried them back up to the mountaintop
context: Exodus 32:19 KJV: 'and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount.' God will later command Moses to hew two new tables 'like unto the first' (Exodus 34:1) and rewrite them.

question: Moses did not stop at breaking the tablets. He took the calf itself and burned it in the fire, then ground the metal to fine powder and scattered it on the water of the camp. Then he made the children of Israel do what with that water?
choices: Pour it over the altar as an offering
Carry it to the far side of the camp
context: Exodus 32:20 KJV: 'and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it.' A punishment few readers remember -- the idol they had bowed to went down their own throats.

question: In Book 6 of the Iliad Homer gives Sisyphus a nickname that fits the whole story to come -- he was, Homer says flat out, this thing above all other mortals. What does Homer call Sisyphus?
context: Homer, Iliad 6.153. Swift-footed is Achilles's epithet; strongest is Heracles's; fairest suits a Ganymede or a Paris. Sisyphus's specific gift is cunning -- and every episode in his story (tricking Zeus, tricking Death, tricking Persephone) is a demonstration of it.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus, told on by Sisyphus, was furious at being informed on by a mortal. Zeus's response was to send a personified god down to Corinth to fetch Sisyphus to the underworld in chains. Which god did Zeus send to fetch him?
context: Thanatos is 'Death' personified in Greek myth -- his job is to fetch mortals down to Hades. Hermes was the guide of souls once they were already in transit. Hypnos is 'Sleep', Thanatos's brother, a different figure. Charon is the ferryman on the river Styx, not a god who came to fetch anyone.  (Legend.)

question: When Thanatos arrived at Corinth with his chains, Sisyphus asked him for a small favour first: to DEMONSTRATE how the chains worked. Thanatos put them on to show him -- and Sisyphus locked them. Where did the cunning king then stash the bound god of Death?
context: The myth is remembered for the sheer domesticity of it -- Death himself, chained up in an ordinary Corinthian cupboard. It is that ridiculous image (a household piece of furniture holding the god of death) that made the story famous.  (Legend.)

question: The crisis of no one being able to die eventually forced a specific Olympian to march down to Corinth in fury, free Thanatos from the cupboard, and hand Sisyphus over. Which of the Olympians came down and released Death?
context: Ares is the god of war -- and with no soldier dying in his battles any more, his whole business had been ruined. Apollo is the god of prophecy and archery; Hephaestus the smith; Dionysus the god of wine. None of them had a personal grievance, but Ares had every reason.  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus lived to a very old age on earth before he was finally dragged back to Hades. This time it was no personified Death that came for him -- Zeus sent a different Olympian, one of the twelve, to fetch the old king down by force. Which god finally brought Sisyphus in?
context: Hermes is 'psychopompos' -- the guide of the dead down into Hades, part of his broader role as the messenger of the gods. It took him personally, not Thanatos, to bring the old trickster in at last. Poseidon is lord of the sea; Apollo is Hermes's older half-brother; Ares had already been down once to release Death.  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus's eternal punishment is the most famous image in Greek underworld art -- endlessly rolling a great boulder up a hill, only to have it turn at the crest and roll back down again. In Homer's Odyssey 11 the poet gives the stone itself a single unforgettable adjective as it rolls back to the plain. What does Homer call the boulder?
context: Homer, Odyssey 11.593-600: 'planting his feet, straining hard, with hands and feet he pressed the huge stone toward the crest; but just as he was about to heave it over the top, the boulder's weight would turn it back, and down again to the plain the shameless thing would roll.' The stone carries the moral weight of Sisyphus's tricks -- Homer calls it shameless, as if the rock itself were in on the punishment.  (Legend.)

question: In 1942, the French writer Albert Camus wrote a famous essay that took Sisyphus's endless task as an image for the human condition itself, and closed with a single startling sentence about how to picture him. What is the last line of Camus's 'The Myth of Sisyphus'?
choices: the stone is heavier than any man knows
the gods forget nothing and forgive nothing
the hill will one day end and the stone will rest
context: Camus, 'Le Mythe de Sisyphe' (1942). Camus argues that the struggle itself, if faced honestly, fills a human heart -- and so we should picture Sisyphus content at the bottom of the hill, walking back down to his stone. The other three lines are invented.

question: Among the Norse gods, one of the Vanir who came to live in Asgard is the god of harvest, sunshine, and good weather -- the god the farmers of Sweden and Norway prayed to for a peaceful year and a good crop. He owns a golden boar and a magic ship. What is the name of this god?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 24: Freyr is the god of harvest, sunshine and peaceful weather, and the most-worshipped of the Vanir in Viking-age Sweden. Njord is Freyr's father, the sea-god who governs the winds and the tides. Tyr is the one-handed war-god. Bragi is the god of skaldic poetry. Freyr's father Njord came to Asgard as a hostage after the Aesir-Vanir war and Freyr came with him.  (Legend.)

question: One of Freyr's greatest possessions is a ship the dwarves made for him -- a ship that Snorri calls 'the best of all ships and the most skillfully made'. What is the name of Freyr's ship?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: Skidbladnir is Freyr's ship, praised by Snorri as 'the best of ships'. Naglfar is the dark counterpart -- the ship of dead men's nails that will carry the giants to Ragnarok. Ringhorn is the funeral ship of Baldr, launched with his body on it. Sessrumnir is Freyja's great hall in Folkvangr, whose name ('seat-roomer') is also listed in the Norse ship-catalogues among the named vessels of the gods.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri names the dwarf-craftsmen who forged Freyr's ship for him in Svartalfheim. It is the same family who spun out Sif's replacement hair of real gold in the previous errand. Which dwarf-family made Freyr's ship?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 35 and 43: the Sons of Ivaldi are the three dwarf-brothers who made three treasures in one workshop session -- Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship, and Odin's spear Gungnir. Brokkr and Sindri are the OTHER dwarf-smiths who make Mjolnir, Draupnir, and Gullinbursti in the second wager. Fjalar and Galar are the dwarves who murder Kvasir. Nordri and Sudri are two of the four sky-holding dwarves.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri says Freyr's ship is roomy enough to hold one particular company, in full war-gear with their weapons at their sides. Who is Skidbladnir large enough to carry?
answer: all the gods of Asgard together
choices: all the gods of Asgard together
all the einherjar of Valhalla in full number
all the giants of Jotunheim in one host
all the dwarves of Svartalfheim in full number
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: Skidbladnir is big enough to carry all the Aesir at once, in full war-gear with their weapons. Valhalla's einherjar (Odin's dead heroes) number in the hundreds of thousands and no ship in the nine worlds carries them. There is no Norse story of a giant-army or a full dwarf-host sailing in Skidbladnir. The wonder of Skidbladnir is that it fits every god in Asgard AND folds into a pocket afterwards.  (Legend.)

question: For all its size, Skidbladnir has one property no other ship in the Norse stories has -- a property that means Freyr can carry it around when he is not sailing. Once the voyage is over, what can Freyr do with Skidbladnir?
answer: fold it up like a cloth and put it in a pouch
choices: fold it up like a cloth and put it in a pouch
shrink it down to the size of a walnut and swallow it
leave it to sail itself home to Asgard
turn it into a wooden staff that never breaks
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43 and Skaldskaparmal 35: because it is 'assembled from thin pieces of wood' (which is what the name Skidbladnir means), the ship can be folded flat like a cloth and slipped into a pouch small enough to carry in a pocket. Mjolnir is the item that shrinks small enough to fit inside a shirt, not Skidbladnir. The other two options are inventions.  (Legend.)

question: Skidbladnir has a third marvellous property beside its size and its foldability -- a property that concerns what happens the instant Freyr raises the sail. The ship needs no oars. What happens as soon as Skidbladnir's sail goes up?
answer: a fair wind blows straight to Freyr's destination
choices: a fair wind blows straight to Freyr's destination
the sun rises to guide it by day and stars by night
the sea rises beneath the hull and carries it forward
the ship moves faster than any horse in Asgard
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43: as soon as the sail is raised Skidbladnir catches a fair wind blowing straight to wherever Freyr wants to go. There is no need to row, and the ship cannot be becalmed. This is the property that makes Skidbladnir most enviable to seafaring Norse audiences -- a wind on demand.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr's other great treasure from the same errand -- also made in Svartalfheim in the second wager by the dwarves Brokkr and Sindri -- is a live animal with a coat of gold that can pull a chariot through the air and across the sea, and whose gleaming hide lights up the darkest night. What creature is this second Freyr-treasure?
context: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal 35 and Gylfaginning 49: the boar is called Gullinbursti ('golden-bristled') or Slidrugtanni. Its glowing bristles light the darkest place. It pulls Freyr's chariot. Freyr rides it to Baldr's funeral. The Norse were pig-farmers and warriors -- for them the boar was a fitting mount for a harvest-god who was also a battle-god. The other three animals are not Freyr's mounts.  (Legend.)

question: Skidbladnir has a dark opposite named in the same stanza of the Poetic Edda's Grimnismal -- another ship, held not by any god but by the people of the fire-giant Surt, growing steadily larger year by year toward a launch at the end of the world. It is built out of one substance in particular. What is the doom-ship of the giants built from?
answer: the untrimmed nails of the dead
choices: the untrimmed nails of the dead
the timbers of Yggdrasil the world-tree
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 43 and 51 and Poetic Edda, Voluspa 50: the doom-ship is Naglfar, built from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead. Snorri says that is why the old Norse custom was to trim a corpse's nails before burial -- so as not to hand any more wood to the ship that will bring the giants to Ragnarok. In the Grimnismal stanza the two ships stand together: 'Skidbladnir the best of ships is built for shining Freyr; but of ships Naglfar is the greatest, which Muspell's people own.'  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth Odin the All-Father rides a great grey horse that can carry him between all the worlds, even down into the land of the dead. Snorri says this horse is stranger than any other horse ever born because of one feature of its body. What does Odin's horse have that no other horse has?
context: Gylfaginning 15: Snorri calls Odin's grey stallion the best of all horses, and says he has eight legs. Wings on horses belong to Greek myth (Pegasus). A single horn belongs to the medieval unicorn tradition. A mane of fire is a modern invention.  (Legend.)

question: In the Prose Edda the greatest of all horses is a grey stallion with eight legs, ridden by the chief of the Norse gods. What is the name of this eight-legged horse?
context: Gylfaginning 15: the horse is Sleipnir. Grani is the horse of the hero Sigurd (and, in the Volsunga saga, said to come from Sleipnir's own line). Gullfaxi is the golden-maned stallion Thor takes from the giant Hrungnir. Hrimfaxi is the horse of Night, whose bit-foam becomes the morning dew.  (Legend.)

question: Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir was not born of two horses. His father was an ordinary stallion, but his mother was one of the gods, who had shape-shifted for the night into a beautiful mare. Which god was Sleipnir's mother?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Loki turned himself into a mare during the affair of the Master Builder of Asgard, and later gave birth to Sleipnir. Odin becomes Sleipnir's rider, not his parent. Heimdall was born of nine mothers (waves of the sea). Freyr owns Skidbladnir and the boar Gullinbursti but is not linked to this birth.  (Legend.)

question: Loki is famous for changing his shape whenever he needs to escape or trick someone. He appears in the sagas as a mare running past a stallion, as a salmon caught in his own net, as an old woman named Thokk who refuses to weep for Baldr, and as one more small biting creature in the smithy of Brokkr. What small creature did Loki turn into to sting the dwarf at the bellows?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki became a gadfly (fluga) to bite Brokkr while Sindri forged Mjolnir. Norse tradition names four shape-changes for him -- mare, salmon, old-woman Thokk, and fly -- not hornet or spider or beetle.  (Legend.)

question: In the story of the Wall of Asgard, a giant craftsman comes to build the gods' rampart in one winter, and he insists on being allowed to use his own stallion to haul the stones. His stallion turns out to be so strong that the wall is nearly finished on time -- until Loki, in mare-form, lures him off. What is the name of this stone-hauling stallion?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder's stallion is Svadilfari, and Snorri says the horse hauled twice as much stone as the builder himself. Grani is Sigurd's horse. Blodughofi (Bloody-Hoof) belongs to Freyr. Falhofnir is one of the horses of the Aesir listed in Grimnismal.  (Legend.)

question: When Baldr the Shining was killed, the god Hermod volunteered to ride down to the underworld and beg the queen of the dead for Baldr's return. He borrowed Odin's horse Sleipnir and rode nine nights down dark valleys until he reached the iron gate of Hel's hall. What did Sleipnir do at the gate?
choices: kicked it down with his hooves
refused to go a step further
context: Gylfaginning 49: Hermod rode Sleipnir nine nights down through dark valleys to Hel, and at the gate Sleipnir leapt so hard and high that he came nowhere near it -- clearing it in a single bound. Kicking down Hel's gate, passing through as mist, and refusing to go further are not part of the story.  (Legend.)

question: The Master Builder of Asgard offered to raise the gods' wall in a single winter, and he named an outrageous price if he finished on time: the goddess Freyja as bride, plus the sun and the moon out of the sky. When the wall was nearly done and the Aesir realised he would win, they threatened one of their own with death unless he sabotaged the work himself. Which god had talked them into the bargain in the first place?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Loki had persuaded the Aesir to accept the bargain, so when the builder was on track to win Freyja, the sun and the moon, the gods threatened Loki with death unless he stopped the work. He did -- by shape-shifting into a mare and luring away Svadilfari. Thor kills the builder once the disguise breaks. Heimdall and Tyr are not part of this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Sleipnir's line did not end with Odin. The great hero Sigurd, dragon-slayer of the Volsung cycle, is said in the Volsunga saga to ride a horse whose bloodline runs back to Odin's own eight-legged mount. What is the name of Sigurd's horse?
context: Volsunga saga: Grani, the horse Sigurd rides through the ring of flames to Brynhild, is descended from Sleipnir's own line. Gullfaxi is the giant Hrungnir's golden-maned stallion, later given to Thor's son Magni. Blodughofi (Bloody-Hoof) belongs to Freyr. Falhofnir is one of the Aesir's horses in Grimnismal.  (Legend.)

question: In the Poetic Edda poem Sigrdrifumal, the valkyrie Sigrdrifa lists the great places where magical runes have been carved: on Bragi's tongue, on the ear of a bear, on the sledge's strap-bands -- and on one particular part of Odin's horse. On what part of Sleipnir does the poem say the runes are carved?
context: Sigrdrifumal 15 (Poetic Edda): runes were carved on Sleipnir's teeth, on the bear's paw, on Bragi's tongue, on the wolf's claws, on the eagle's beak, and on the sledge's strap-bands, so that magic would be borne into the world in all these places.  (Legend.)

question: On the Baltic island of Gotland stands a carved picture-stone from the eighth century -- older than any surviving manuscript of the Eddas. In its upper panel a rider arrives at a hall to be greeted by a woman with a drinking horn, and the mount he rides on has eight legs. What is the name of the Gotland stone that carries this scene?
context: The Tjangvide picture-stone (Gotland, c. 700-800 CE) is read as showing Odin arriving at Valhalla on Sleipnir -- the earliest surviving image of the eight-legged horse. Ramsund and Hylestad carry the Sigurd-and-Fafnir cycle. Altuna carries Thor fishing for Jormungand.

question: The young king Solomon, son of David, went up to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice, and that night God appeared to him in a dream with a startling offer: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Instead of long life or riches, what one thing did Solomon ask for?
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:9: 'Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad.' The reply pleased God, who then granted wisdom, and long life and riches on top.

question: Two women came before King Solomon fighting over one living baby. Each swore she was the mother; the other's own child had died in the night. To settle the case, Solomon called out for one particular object to be brought in. What did he order brought in?
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:24-25: 'And the king said, Bring me a sword. And they brought a sword before the king. And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.' Scales and elders and seals were the ordinary tools of justice, but Solomon needed something sharper.

question: When Solomon ordered his soldier to divide the living baby in two with a sword, one of the two women broke immediately and gave up her claim. What exactly did she cry out to the king?
answer: O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it
choices: O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it
O my lord, take him and raise him as thine own son
O my lord, take my life instead of the child's
O my lord, spare us and send the other away
context: KJV 1 Kings 3:26: 'Then spake the woman whose the living child was unto the king ... and she said, O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it.' Solomon then reversed the order and gave the child back to her, knowing she was the true mother.

question: In his fourth year as king, Solomon began to build the Temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah. The whole project took seven years. During that time one common sound of a construction site was never heard on the temple mount. What sound was missing?
answer: no iron tool struck the stone
choices: no iron tool struck the stone
no cry of a foreign labourer
no chariot wheel on the stones
no trumpet of the morning watch
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:7: 'neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.' The stones were dressed at the quarry and lifted into place already finished, so the site itself was silent.

question: At the porch of the finished Temple Solomon set up two great pillars of cast bronze, one on the right hand and one on the left, and he named each of them. What names did he give the two bronze pillars?
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:21: 'And he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz.' The other pairs are real biblical names -- Peleg and Joktan the sons of Eber, Nadab and Abihu the sons of Aaron, Zadok and Abiathar the two high priests in David's court -- but the pillars carried Jachin and Boaz.

question: In the courtyard of the Temple stood a huge round basin of cast bronze that the Bible calls 'the molten sea', ten cubits from brim to brim and five cubits high. What supported it off the ground?
choices: four bronze lions crouching at the corners
a single bronze pillar rising from the pavement
the shoulders of two carved bronze cherubim
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:25: 'It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east.' The molten sea held water for the priests' washing.

question: Beyond the veil of Solomon's Temple, in the windowless inner chamber, stood two enormous carved figures ten cubits tall. Their wings were stretched so wide that wingtip touched wall on either side and wingtip met wingtip in the middle of the room. Of what wood were those two figures carved?
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:23, 27: 'within the oracle he made two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high ... the wing of the one touched the one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall.' The tabernacle furniture was acacia; the roofs and paneling were cedar; the flooring was cypress.

question: The Queen of Sheba saw Solomon's palace, his food, the seating of his servants, his cupbearers, and 'his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD.' At that sight, according to 1 Kings 10, what happened to her?
answer: there was no more spirit in her
choices: there was no more spirit in her
she fell prostrate on the marble floor
she tore her royal garment in wonder
she wept and offered him her crown
context: KJV 1 Kings 10:4-5. The phrase captures a breath-taken astonishment -- the queen goes silent. She then names it aloud in the next rung.

question: When the Queen of Sheba recovered her voice at Solomon's court, she spoke the words that became her most famous line. She said that back home she had heard great things about him, but seeing them for herself, what did she say about the report?
answer: the half was not told me
choices: the half was not told me
not one word of it was true
the king's fame is greater than his house
such wisdom belongs only to the LORD
context: KJV 1 Kings 10:7: 'Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.'

question: The old age of King Solomon is the tragedy at the end of his story. 1 Kings 11 gives precise numbers for the two ranks of women in his household and blames them for turning his heart to foreign gods. What are those two numbers?
context: KJV 1 Kings 11:3: 'And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.' He built shrines to Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Milcom of the Ammonites in his old age -- the moral of the arc for the biblical author.

question: In the Holy Place of Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem stood a lampstand of pure hammered gold with a central shaft and six arms coming out its sides -- three on one side, three on the other -- carrying seven lamps in all. By what name is that seven-lamped golden lampstand known?
context: KJV Exodus 25:31-32: 'And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold ... six branches shall come out of the sides of it; three branches of the candlestick out of the one side, and three branches of the candlestick out of the other side.' The whole was to be beaten from one talent of pure gold (Ex 25:39). A thurible is a censer, a labarum was Constantine's battle standard, a monstrance is a vessel for the consecrated host.

question: On the golden table opposite the menorah, twelve loaves of bread were arranged in two rows of six -- one loaf for each of the twelve tribes of Israel -- kept always before the LORD and replaced every sabbath. What was this weekly bread called?
context: KJV Leviticus 24:5-6: 'thou shalt take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes ... thou shalt set them in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD.' The paschal lamb was the Passover meat; a wave offering was a portion lifted and waved; a drink offering was poured wine.

question: Every sabbath the priests removed the twelve loaves of showbread from the golden table and set out fresh ones. What became of the loaves that were taken away?
answer: Aaron's sons ate them in the holy place
choices: Aaron's sons ate them in the holy place
they were burned whole on the bronze altar
they were buried outside the camp
they were sent home to the twelve tribes
context: KJV Leviticus 24:9: 'it shall be Aaron's and his sons; and they shall eat it in the holy place: for it is most holy unto him of the offerings of the LORD made by fire by a perpetual statute.' The bread was too holy to burn or bury and was reserved for the priesthood alone.

question: The pure gold of the menorah was not smooth: each of the six branches carried a row of cups shaped like the blossoms of one particular flowering tree, with a knop and a flower between each cup. Whose blossom did those cups imitate?
context: KJV Exodus 25:33: 'Three bowls made like unto almonds, with a knop and a flower in one branch; and three bowls made like almonds in the other branch, with a knop and a flower.' Almond blossoms are the first to open each spring in the hills of Judea. Olive and fig and cedar are all sacred trees in the Old Testament but the menorah's cups copy the almond.

question: Beyond the veil of Solomon's Temple, in the windowless inner room called the Holy of Holies, stood two enormous carved figures ten cubits tall -- about fifteen feet -- their wingtips stretched so wide they touched the walls on either side and met in the middle of the chamber. Out of what wood were those two giant figures carved?
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:23: 'And within the oracle he made two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high.' 1 Kings 6:27 has their wings touching the walls on either side. The ark itself and the wilderness tabernacle furniture were of acacia (shittim) wood; the Temple's paneling and roof were cedar; cypress boards its floors.

question: Beyond the great seven-lamped menorah in the Holy Place, Solomon set out extra lampstands of pure gold ranged along the front of the oracle. How were those additional golden lampstands arranged before the oracle?
answer: five on the right side and five on the left
choices: five on the right side and five on the left
seven on the right side and seven on the left
three on the right side and three on the left
twelve in a single row across the front
context: KJV 1 Kings 7:49: 'And the candlesticks of pure gold, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the oracle.' Beyond the single seven-lamped menorah of Moses's pattern, Solomon added ten more lampstands framing the entrance to the Holy of Holies. Seven is the menorah's own lamp-count; twelve matches the tribes and the showbread loaves; three matches the branches per side of the menorah -- all near-misses, but 1 Kings names five and five.

question: When the priests opened the ark of the covenant in Solomon's day, what did they find inside?
answer: the two tables of stone from Horeb
choices: the two tables of stone from Horeb
the golden pot of manna from the wilderness
the rod of Aaron that had budded
the brazen serpent of Moses on its pole
context: KJV 1 Kings 8:9: 'There was nothing in the ark save the two tables of stone, which Moses put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the children of Israel.' A golden pot of manna and Aaron's budding rod are named in Hebrews 9:4 as tabernacle relics but 1 Kings makes a point of saying they were not in the ark by Solomon's day; the brazen serpent Nehushtan was set up on a pole in the wilderness (Numbers 21).

question: The ark had its own lid, called the mercy seat, made all of pure gold. Two smaller cherubim of hammered gold rose from that lid, of one piece with the seat itself. How were those two small cherubim positioned relative to each other?
answer: facing each other with wings spread over the seat
choices: facing each other with wings spread over the seat
back to back with wings folded down at their sides
kneeling with faces turned down to the floor
standing side by side facing out from the ark
context: KJV Exodus 25:20: 'And the cherubims shall stretch forth their wings on high, covering the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces shall look one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubims be.' The great olive-wood pair inside the oracle stood tall over the whole ark; the two small golden ones were part of the mercy seat itself.

question: 1 Kings 6:7 records something striking about how Solomon's Temple went up: throughout the seven years of building, a certain sound was never heard on the temple mount. What sound was that?
answer: no hammer or axe or any iron tool
choices: no hammer or axe or any iron tool
no bleating of the sacrificial flocks
no voice of a woman or a child
context: KJV 1 Kings 6:7: 'And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.' The stones were dressed at the quarry and lifted into place already finished. Trumpets and singers filled the courts at the dedication itself.

question: At the dedication of the finished Temple, the priests brought the ark to its place and came out, and a cloud filled the house so that they could not stand to minister. Solomon then spoke words about a house he had built. What did he say the house was for?
answer: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever
choices: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever
a shelter for the poor and the widow
a schoolhouse for the sons of the prophets
a memorial of the wars of David my father
context: KJV 1 Kings 8:13: 'I have surely built thee an house to dwell in, a settled place for thee to abide in for ever.' The Temple was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's captain Nebuzaradan in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9); Solomon's 'for ever' became one of the great questions of Jewish tradition ever after.

question: In the early Jerusalem church, the apostles were overwhelmed and picked seven men to handle the daily food distribution to the widows so they themselves could keep preaching. Acts names the very first of those seven -- a man 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost.' Who was he?
context: Acts 6:5 lists the seven, and Stephen is named first. Barnabas is the encourager who later travels with Paul; Timothy and Silas are Paul's later companions; none of them are among the original seven servants of the tables.

question: The role Stephen and the six others were chosen for -- to wait on tables so the apostles could give themselves to prayer and preaching -- became the model for a permanent office in the early Christian church. Which office grew out of this scene?
context: Acts 6:1-6 is traditionally read as the founding of the diaconate. Bishops (overseers) and elders are named later in Acts; the office of pope develops much later as the bishop of Rome; prophet is a spiritual gift, not an ordained office.

question: They dragged Stephen before the same council in Jerusalem that had condemned Jesus a few years earlier -- the body of 71 elders and priests that judged religious cases under the high priest. Which body tried Stephen?
choices: The council of the seventy elders
context: Acts 6:12 -- they 'brought him to the council,' the Sanhedrin, the same body that had tried Jesus. The Great Assembly (Knesset HaGedolah) was an earlier post-exilic body that had ceased centuries before; 'the council of the seventy elders' echoes Moses's seventy in Numbers 11 but is not the trial court of Acts; the high priest had no separate private tribunal apart from the Sanhedrin he presided over.

question: As Stephen stood before the Sanhedrin waiting to answer, everyone on the council stared at him. Acts 6:15 records what they saw when they looked at him -- one of the strangest single lines in the whole book. What did Stephen's face look like?
choices: The face of a small child
context: Acts 6:15 -- 'all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.' The verse gives no interpretation; it just reports what the council saw.

question: In answer to the blasphemy charges, Stephen preached the longest sermon in Acts -- a rapid retelling of the whole story of Israel. Where in the biblical story did Stephen begin his sermon?
context: Acts 7:2 -- 'The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran.' Stephen begins with Abraham and marches through Joseph, Moses, Joshua, David, and Solomon before turning on the council.

question: Stephen's speech ended with a hammer blow: he charged the council with the same crime as their fathers, always resisting the Holy Ghost. In two words he named them stiffnecked and something else -- the sharpest insult he could throw at Jerusalem's religious court. What was the second word?
context: Acts 7:51 -- 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost.' For a Jewish council whose very identity rested on the covenant of circumcision, calling them 'uncircumcised' was the most cutting reversal possible. The other three are all real biblical rebukes used elsewhere by the prophets and by Jesus, but none is what Stephen said here.

question: As the council's fury boiled over, Stephen looked up steadfastly into heaven and reported the vision he saw. Acts records his exact words. Who did Stephen say he saw standing at the right hand of God?
context: Acts 7:56 -- 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.' 'Son of man' is Jesus's own favorite title for himself in the gospels; it is the claim that pushed the council past rage into action.

question: The council members could not stand to hear Stephen's vision. Before running at him with one accord to drag him out of the city, Acts records one physical thing every one of them did with their hands. What did they do?
context: Acts 7:57 -- 'Then they cried out with a loud voice, and stopped their ears, and ran upon him with one accord.' Tearing robes is what the high priest did at Jesus's trial; the other two gestures are not in this scene.

question: Under the law of Moses, the witnesses in a stoning had to throw the first stones. As they prepared to hurl them at Stephen, the witnesses stripped off their outer cloaks and piled them at the feet of a young man watching the execution. Acts names that young man for the very first time here. Who was he?
context: Acts 7:58 -- 'and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul.' This is Saul of Tarsus -- the future apostle Paul -- on stage for the first time in the New Testament, guarding the coats at the killing of the first Christian martyr.

question: Immediately after Stephen's death, Acts 8:1 makes two observations about what followed. The first is about Saul, the young man who had been guarding the cloaks. What does the verse say about Saul?
answer: He was consenting to Stephen's death
choices: He was consenting to Stephen's death
He wept and asked for baptism
He was cursed with sudden blindness
context: Acts 8:1 -- 'And Saul was consenting unto his death.' Blindness comes later, on the road to Damascus in Acts 9. The same verse also reports a great persecution that scattered the church out of Jerusalem into Judea and Samaria -- which becomes the engine of the whole missionary spread of Acts.

question: In the Norse cosmos hung on the branches of the world-tree Yggdrasil, one of the nine worlds sits at the FAR SOUTHERN edge, older than Asgard and older than the gods themselves. It is one of the two primal worlds that existed before creation. Which world is the southern primal one?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 4 and 8. Muspelheim (also written Muspell) is the fiery southern world. Niflheim is its opposite -- the world of ice in the north -- the OTHER primal world. Jotunheim is the land of the giants. Svartalfheim is the underground realm of the dwarves. The two primal worlds are Muspelheim in the south and Niflheim in the north; the meeting of their fire and ice in the great void Ginnungagap is where creation begins.  (Legend.)

question: Freyr charges Surtr on the plain of Vigrid, but he has to fight the fire-giant without his usual weapon. Long before Ragnarok Freyr had given his famous magic sword -- a sword that fought all by itself against giants -- to his messenger Skirnir. Why did Freyr give the sword away?
answer: as bride-price for the giantess Gerdr
choices: as bride-price for the giantess Gerdr
as a fee to the dwarves who forged Mjolnir
as ransom for his sister Freyja
as payment for the horse Blodughofi
context: Skirnismal; Snorri, Gylfaginning 37 and 51. Freyr saw the beautiful giantess Gerdr from Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf, fell instantly in love, and sent his servant Skirnir to woo her. Skirnir named his fee -- Freyr's magic self-swinging sword and his horse -- and Freyr paid without hesitation. The whole point of the story is that Freyr dies at Ragnarok BECAUSE HE WAS IN LOVE. The moral of the Norse: never give away your sword, even for a wife.  (Legend.)

question: Sword-less on the plain of Vigrid, Freyr meets Surtr's flaming blade with a much humbler weapon in his hand -- the same weapon he had once used to kill the giant Beli. What does Freyr fight Surtr with at Ragnarok?
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 37 and 51. Freyr's antler-weapon is one of the great melancholy details of Ragnarok -- the fertility-god of the sunshine going to meet the fire-giant with nothing more than a piece of a deer's horn. Snorri notes that Freyr had earlier killed the giant Beli with the antler alone, so it is not a joke weapon; but against Surtr's flaming sword it is not enough, and Freyr falls.  (Legend.)

question: Of all the great Aesir and Vanir who die at Ragnarok, Freyr has the specific distinction of being one particular one. Which is he?
answer: the first great god to fall
choices: the first great god to fall
the last great god to fall
the only god who leaves no body
the only god slain by his own weapon
context: Snorri, Gylfaginning 51; Voluspa 53. Freyr falls first at Ragnarok -- before Odin is swallowed by Fenrir, before Thor kills Jormungandr and staggers nine steps and dies, before Tyr and Garmr end each other. The love-story that dropped his sword makes him also the first casualty of the last battle. But the fourth choice -- Freyr slain by his own weapon -- is a real motif from later tradition too: Surtr uses Freyr's own sword against him in some versions, so the fourth distractor is a live-and-plausible alternative.  (Legend.)

question: Icelanders living on top of active volcanoes kept the memory of the southern fire-giant alive in the very names they gave their mountains. What have Iceland's volcanoes sometimes been called?
context: Icelandic folk-tradition; the lava-cave Surtshellir on Iceland is a documented site named for Surtr, and the 1963 eruption that created the new Icelandic island Surtsey was named for the same fire-giant. Icelanders living on top of active volcanoes never entirely forgot the being at the southern edge of the world with the burning sword.  (Legend.)

question: Tantalus, a mortal king in Anatolia, was for a time such a favourite of the gods that he was invited to eat at their table on Olympus. In the darkest version of his myth, he killed one of his own children, made a stew of him, and served the boy up at a feast to test whether the gods would notice. Which of his sons did he cook?
context: Named in Apollodorus and dramatised across the Greek tragedians. Wikipedia: Tantalus, Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: Ixion, king of the Lapiths in Thessaly, invited his own father-in-law to a feast, walked him through the hall, and shoved him into a hidden pit of red-hot coals. The Greek poets remembered it as the first mortal kin-murder ever committed. Which father-in-law did Ixion push into the pit?
context: Pindar and Apollodorus name Deioneus (father of Ixion's wife Dia) as the victim; Ixion is remembered as the founding kin-slayer of Greek myth. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: The English verb 'tantalise' comes straight from Tantalus's punishment in the Odyssey, Book 11. He stands in a pool of water up to his chin, with a branch of ripe fruit hanging just above his head. What happens whenever he stoops down to drink from the pool?
answer: the water drains from the pool
choices: the water drains from the pool
the fruit falls into his mouth
a stone rolls onto his back
context: Odyssey 11.582-592: whenever Tantalus stoops the water drains away, and whenever he reaches the branch lifts out of reach. The verb 'tantalise' means to torment with the sight of something desired but kept out of reach. Wikipedia: Tantalus.  (Legend.)

question: When Tantalus served the stew of his own son at a feast on Olympus, most of the gods sensed the trick at once and refused to touch it, but one goddess was absent-minded that day and swallowed a piece before she realised what she was eating. Which goddess ate a piece?
context: Demeter was mourning her daughter Persephone at the time and ate absent-mindedly; her share was a piece of the boy's shoulder. Wikipedia: Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: A king of Argos in one of the darkest wedding-tales in Greek myth had fifty daughters and forced them all to marry the fifty sons of his brother Aegyptus. On the wedding night he handed each daughter a dagger and ordered her to kill her new husband in bed. Which king gave the fifty daggers?
context: The daughters were called the Danaids after their father Danaus. Apollodorus 2.1.4; Wikipedia: Danaids.  (Legend.)

question: After the gods discovered that Tantalus had cooked his son Pelops for their feast, the boy was pieced back together and brought back to life, but a piece of his shoulder had already been swallowed and was gone. The gods gave him a replacement shoulder-blade made of a special material. What material?
context: The ivory shoulder-blade of Pelops was said to have been carried by the Greeks to Troy centuries later. Hephaestus was credited with the craftsmanship. Wikipedia: Pelops.  (Legend.)

question: One of the fifty brides in the Argos wedding-tale refused her father's order and let her husband Lynceus live; she is the only exception in the massacre, and she is the reason Perseus later has any ancestors at all. What was her name?
context: Hypermnestra and Lynceus survived; their descendants included Perseus and thence Heracles. Aeschylus dramatised her in the lost Danaid trilogy. Wikipedia: Danaids.  (Legend.)

question: After Ixion had killed his own father-in-law, no mortal king would purify him, so Zeus generously took him up to Olympus as a guest. Ixion repaid this hospitality by reaching for Hera. Zeus was suspicious and moulded a phantom in his wife's shape out of cloud as a trap; Ixion embraced the cloud, and from that coupling was born the ancestor of a whole monstrous race. Which race?
context: Pindar, Pythian 2.21-48, gives the cloud-Hera (later named Nephele) and the birth of Centauros, ancestor of the Centaur race by the Magnesian mares. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: Every eternal punishment in Tartarus fits the crime: Tantalus who abused the gods' hospitality at their table gets reaching-food, and the Danaid brides who spilled blood in the bridal bed get carrying water. Ixion, for reaching for Hera at Zeus's own table, is bound to a single object that is his emblem forever after in Greek art. What is that object?
context: The burning wheel of Ixion, sometimes turning through the sky and sometimes deep in Tartarus, is his fixed emblem in ancient and later art. Wikipedia: Ixion.  (Legend.)

question: In 1515 a merchant family in the walled Castilian city of Avila welcomed a daughter, Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada. She would grow up to reform a whole religious order and become the first woman named a Doctor of the Catholic Church. Which order did she reform, first as a member of it and then as founder of a strict new branch?
context: Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Avila at age 20 and, forty-seven years later, had founded a whole new reformed wing of the order -- the Discalced Carmelites. The Franciscans trace back to Francis of Assisi, the Dominicans to Dominic de Guzman, the Benedictines to Benedict of Nursia -- all real medieval orders, none of them Teresa's.

question: At age 20 Teresa entered a Carmelite convent in Avila where the nuns kept their own servants, received visitors freely in the parlour, and travelled to family estates -- a comfortable, worldly house named for one of the great Christian feasts. She lived there mediocrely for twenty-five years before her prayer life caught fire. What was the name of the convent?
context: The Carmelite convent of the Incarnation still stands in Avila. Ascension, Visitation, and Annunciation are all real convent-naming feasts (the Visitation is even a whole female religious order founded by Francis de Sales), but Teresa's first house was the Incarnation.

question: About age forty, Teresa was walking through the convent when a statue in a corner caught her eye and stopped her cold -- it showed Christ during the flogging before Pilate, wounded and bound. She wept at her own tepidity of the last twenty-five years, and from that day her prayer life deepened rapidly into intense mystical experiences. What did she call that turning-point in her Autobiography?
context: 'Second' because she had already been a professed nun for twenty-five years; the moment in front of the wounded-Christ statue is described in her Autobiography ch. 9. 'Final vows' happened decades earlier; 'jubilee year' is a Roman canonical term for a fifty-year celebration; 'golden hour' is a modern trauma-medicine phrase, not Teresian vocabulary.

question: As her prayer deepened, Teresa began having ecstasies so intense that other nuns had to hold her body down; they reported she was literally lifted off the ground. Her most famous single vision, recorded in chapter 29 of her Autobiography, shows an angel holding a long golden spear tipped with a little fire, thrusting it several times through her heart. What Latin-derived name did Teresa give this experience?
context: From Latin 'trans' + 'verberare', to strike through -- the name for the piercing itself. The other three are real spiritual-writing terms (illumination for divine light, consolation for felt sweetness, conflagration for the fire of love in later mystics), but Teresa's own word for the spear-through-the-heart vision is Transverberation.

question: Pressed by confessors to write down her experiences for discernment, Teresa produced her masterwork in 1577, describing the soul as a crystal castle made of many rooms; the soul journeys through the rooms in stages of prayer until it reaches the innermost one, where union with God happens. How many rooms -- 'mansions' -- does she say the castle has?
context: Seven mansions (moradas) in the Castillo Interior (Interior Castle), each a deeper stage of prayer. The other numbers are famous elsewhere (three persons of the Trinity, twelve apostles, forty days in the wilderness); they are not Teresa's schema.

question: In A Gest of Robyn Hode (Child Ballad 117), the Sheriff of Nottingham announces a great archery contest in the town square, hoping Robin Hood will not be able to resist trying to win it. The prize is a single object every yeoman covets. What is the prize?
context: The prize in the Sheriff's contest is a silver arrow. Silver-arrow archery contests were a real English town tradition and continued in some towns down to the eighteenth century -- the ballad is drawing on a genuine sporting custom. Source: World Archery, Legend of Robin Hood; A Gest of Robyn Hode.

question: In the medieval ballad A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin comes to the Sheriff's contest in disguise and wins by shooting nearest the mark. The famous scene of Robin's second shot splitting the shaft of his rival's arrow -- the one already in the bullseye -- does not appear in any medieval ballad at all. In which nineteenth-century novel is that scene first written?
context: Sir Walter Scott wrote the arrow-splitting shot into Ivanhoe, published December 1819 (dated 1820), chapter 13. All four choices are real Scott novels, but only Ivanhoe carries the Robin Hood arrow scene. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: In Sir Walter Scott's 1819 Robin Hood novel, a mysterious yeoman archer in Lincoln green appears at a great English tournament and out-shoots the finest bowmen in the field. The reader only gradually realises he is Robin Hood in disguise. What name does the yeoman give in the novel?
context: Scott calls the disguised Robin 'Locksley' at the Ashby tournament, borrowing an older tradition (a c.1600 prose Life of Robin Hood names Locksley as Robin's birthplace). Wilfred, Athelstane, and Cedric are other main characters in Ivanhoe. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: At the tournament in Scott's novel, the disguised Robin Hood faces a rival archer -- the reigning champion of the field, a proud bowman whose grandfather is said to have shot at the Battle of Hastings. Robin splits this man's arrow down the shaft. What is the rival's name?
context: In Ivanhoe chapter 13, Locksley splits the arrow of Hubert, whose grandfather shot at Hastings. Splitting the arrow only ties the contest; Locksley then wins the tiebreaker with a second, harder shot at a still slenderer target. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: The Robin Hood scholar Thomas Ohlgren argues that the whole arrow-splitting tradition arose from a simple misreading of the earliest ballads. In A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin's most impressive contest shot was not an arrow at all -- it was splitting a slender target set up in front of the butts. What was that slender target?
context: In the medieval ballads Robin split a 'wand' -- a slim willow stick planted upright in front of the target. As colored targets came into fashion and readers forgot what a 'wand' was, later retellers substituted an opponent's arrow. All four choices are plausible slender targets, but the ballads specify willow. Source: Slate, Can you really split an arrow with an arrow?; A Gest of Robyn Hode.

question: Modern competition archers occasionally shoot so tight a group that a second arrow lodges inside the hollow shaft of the first arrow already in the target. The shot is vanishingly rare -- Mythbusters only reproduced it with hollow bamboo arrows -- and has its own nickname. What do archers call it?
context: Archers universally call the trick shot 'a Robin Hood', in tribute to Scott's Ivanhoe scene. Genuine Robin Hoods happen every so often at modern indoor competitions and ruin the front arrow -- most clubs charge a fee to celebrate them. Source: TV Tropes, Splitting the Arrow; Slate on Merida and the Robin Hood shot.

question: In Scott's Robin Hood novel, the archery contest where the disguised outlaw splits his rival's arrow takes place at a great tournament in the English Midlands, presided over by Prince John while King Richard is absent on Crusade. The tournament grounds are a real place still standing today, ruined but visitable. Where does the tournament take place?
context: Scott sets the tournament at Ashby-de-la-Zouche in Leicestershire, whose castle keep still stands in ruin. Kenilworth, Warwick, and Nottingham are all real English tournament-era castles Scott might have chosen; he picked Ashby. Source: Wikipedia, Ivanhoe.

question: Because Sir Walter Scott's novel was one of the most-read books of the nineteenth century, the arrow-splitting scene became the iconic Robin Hood moment for the twentieth century. In 1938 a major Hollywood studio filmed The Adventures of Robin Hood, and its leading man became the face every later Robin Hood answers to. Who was that leading man?
context: Errol Flynn's The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) became the template every later Robin Hood movie followed. Douglas Fairbanks had played Robin Hood in a silent 1922 film; Costner (1991) and Elwes (1993) came much later. Source: Slate, Can you really split an arrow with an arrow?; TV Tropes, Splitting the Arrow.

question: King Arthur is dying after his last battle against Mordred at Camlann. He gives his most trusted surviving knight one last order: take Excalibur down to the water and throw it in. Which knight did Arthur send with the sword?
context: Sir Bedivere is Arthur's cupbearer and, by Malory Book XXI, the last living knight at his side. In the older Welsh tradition he is 'Bedwyr' and one of Arthur's earliest companions. Gawain has died earlier of a head-wound. Kay, Arthur's foster-brother, is long gone. Lucan the Butler is present at the last battle but dies of his wounds before Excalibur is returned.  (Legend.)

question: The barge is not empty. It carries three queens and their attendants, all draped in one particular colour of hood, weeping as they wait. What colour do the ladies wear?
context: Malory Book XXI ch.6: 'a little barge with many fair ladies in it, and among them all was a queen, and all they had black hoods, and all they wept and shrieked when they saw King Arthur'. Black is the mourning colour of the whole scene. White is the colour of the Grail knights; scarlet of the martyr; green of the fairy Otherworld -- all wrong for this cortege.  (Legend.)

question: The queens lift Arthur into the barge and lay him down in a very particular way. How is Arthur laid?
answer: with his head in a queen's lap
choices: with his head in a queen's lap
seated upon a throne of oak
chained to a mast of iron
context: Malory Book XXI ch.6: 'they set them down, and in one of their laps King Arthur laid his head'. It's a pieta-like image, deliberately gentle. A throne would be a coronation; a cloak-wrapping a battle-death; a chained mast a captive's death -- none fit this scene.  (Legend.)

question: The name Avalon comes from an older Welsh word, afal. In modern English what does afal mean?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae Book XI (c.1136) explains 'Insula Avallonis' from Welsh 'afal' (apple) -- hence Ynys Afallon, the Isle of Apples. Apples are the fruit of the Otherworld across Celtic mythology, also seen in the Irish Emain Ablach ('Emain of Apples'). Mist, mound, and swan all suit Otherworld islands in other traditions, but Avalon's name is specifically the apple-word.  (Legend.)

question: The morning after the barge leaves, Bedivere wanders inland weeping and comes upon a hermit in a valley beside a fresh mound of earth. The hermit tells him that at midnight a company of black-hooded ladies came to his door bearing a body -- and that he has just finished a solemn task for them. What had the hermit just done?
choices: burned the body on a pyre
dressed the body in mail for a war-grave
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7. The hermit does not know whose body it is -- the ladies came at midnight, gave him the body, and paid him with a hundred bezants to bury it. Embalming with spices belongs to Egyptian and biblical burials (Joseph, Jesus); a pyre would be pagan Norse or Greek, not Christian British; a war-grave in mail belongs to a battlefield death like Beowulf's. The whole point of the scene is that Arthur's death is uncertain -- a grave is dug, but no name is given.  (Legend.)

question: Malory refuses to say plainly whether the buried body was Arthur's. In one of the most famous passages in the whole book he writes: 'yet some men say... that King Arthur is not dead, but'. How does the sentence continue?
choices: he walks with the Round Table
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7, near-verbatim: 'yet some men say in many parts of England that King Arthur is not dead, but had by the will of our Lord Jesu into another place; and men say that he shall come again, and he shall win the holy cross'. Malory refuses to give a verdict. The three wrong choices are made-up flourishes; Malory's line is specifically about RETURN, not undersea sleep or star-fire.  (Legend.)

question: According to Malory a Latin epitaph was carved on Arthur's supposed tomb, four short words that sum up the whole legend of a king who died-but-did-not-die. It reads 'Hic iacet Arthurus, rex quondam rexque futurus.' What do those last four Latin words mean in English?
choices: the king who died at Camlann
the king who healed the wound
the king of the round table
context: Malory Book XXI ch.7. 'Rex quondam' = 'king in time past'; 'rexque futurus' = 'and king to come'. The line closes the whole Morte d'Arthur and gave T.H. White the title of his 1958 novel 'The Once and Future King'. The three wrong choices describe Arthur but do not translate the Latin.  (Legend.)

question: In 1191, seven years after their abbey was gutted by fire and while they were desperate to raise money to rebuild, the monks of Glastonbury Abbey announced they had DUG UP a very famous grave in their cemetery -- a lead cross with a Latin inscription and a giant coffin below. Whose grave did they claim to have found?
context: The Glastonbury monks' 1191 discovery of a lead cross reading 'Here lies buried the famous King Arthur on the Isle of Avalon' is regarded by modern historians as a pious forgery -- perfectly timed to bring pilgrims and coin after the 1184 fire. The same abbey also promoted the legend that Joseph of Arimathea had come to Glastonbury with the Grail -- two miracles, both marketable. Patrick's burial is claimed at Downpatrick in Ireland. Merlin's grave has no such tourist site.

question: In the book of Genesis, God tests Abraham with a terrible command: take your only son, the one whom you love, and offer him as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you. Which son does God name?
context: Genesis 22:2. Isaac is the son of Abraham and Sarah, the child of the covenant. Ishmael is Abraham's older son by Hagar. Jacob and Esau are Isaac's own twin sons, born a generation later.

question: Abraham rises early the next morning, saddles his donkey, and takes two young men with him. He prepares one thing above all else and loads it on the donkey for the burnt offering God has demanded on the mountain. What?
context: Genesis 22:3. Abraham himself cleaves the wood for the fire before setting out on the three-day journey to the land of Moriah.

question: On the third day Abraham sees the place afar off. He orders the two young men to wait below with the donkey, and he and Isaac climb on alone. As they start up the slope, what does Abraham lay upon his son to carry?
answer: The wood for the burnt offering
choices: The wood for the burnt offering
The fire in a clay pot
A skin of water for the altar
context: Genesis 22:6. Abraham himself keeps the fire and the knife in his own hands; the wood he lays on Isaac's shoulders. Christian readers later heard an echo of another son carrying his own wood up a hill.

question: As they climb together, Isaac notices something is missing. He turns to his father and says: 'Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the ...?' Fill in Isaac's question.
choices: Goat for the altar of incense
context: Genesis 22:7. Abraham answers, 'My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.' Doves, bullocks, and goats are all real offerings elsewhere in the Torah, but the lamb is the answer Isaac's question demands.

question: On the mountaintop Abraham builds an altar, arranges the wood, and binds his son. He lays Isaac on the altar upon the wood and stretches out his hand. What does he take up in that hand?
context: Genesis 22:10. The KJV word is 'knife.' It is what the angel of the LORD, calling from heaven at the last instant, tells Abraham to 'lay not thine hand upon the lad.'

question: The angel of the LORD calls out of heaven and stops the killing at the last instant. Abraham lifts his eyes and sees an animal caught behind him in a thicket by its horns. What animal has taken his son's place on the altar?
context: Genesis 22:13. Not a lamb (the very word Isaac had asked for), not a goat, not a bullock. A ram, an adult male sheep, caught by its curled horns in the thicket. The horns are what let it be found.

question: Abraham names the mountaintop so the deliverance will be remembered. He calls it JEHOVAH-JIREH. What does that Hebrew name mean in English?
context: Genesis 22:14. Jehovah-jireh literally means 'the LORD will see' or 'the LORD will provide.' Jehovah-nissi (banner) is what Moses names an altar after defeating Amalek; Jehovah-shalom (peace) is Gideon's altar; 'the LORD is my shepherd' is David's psalm.

question: Only one gospel gives any scene from Jesus's childhood after the Nativity. Luke tells how his parents took him with them to Jerusalem for a great feast they attended every year. Which feast?
context: Luke 2:41 KJV: 'Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.' Passover was one of the three pilgrim feasts Jewish families travelled to Jerusalem to keep.

question: Luke's scene of Jesus lost in Jerusalem gives one small detail about his age at the time -- the only such detail the gospels record between the manger and his adult ministry. How old was he?
context: Luke 2:42 KJV: 'And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem after the custom of the feast.' Between this scene and Jesus's baptism as an adult, the gospels record nothing else -- the so-called 'hidden years.'

question: As the caravan of pilgrims left Jerusalem after the Passover, Mary and Joseph did not notice Jesus was missing. They had supposed he was walking with kinsmen and acquaintances. How long did they travel before they realised he was gone?
context: Luke 2:44 KJV: 'they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.' Pilgrim caravans travelled as extended clans, so a twelve-year-old walking with cousins would not have been noticed.

question: Having turned back to Jerusalem to look for their son, Mary and Joseph searched the city before at last finding him. According to Luke, how long did the search take?
context: Luke 2:46 KJV: 'And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.' The 'three days' echo has been noted by commentators alongside the later three days in the tomb.

question: Finding the boy at last, Mary spoke first -- a mother's half-scolding line to a child who had frightened her for days. Luke gives the words exactly. How does she begin?
answer: Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?
choices: Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?
Child, thou art weary; come home with us now
Rejoice, for that which was lost is found again
How camest thou hither, when we bade thee stay?
context: Luke 2:48 KJV: 'Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing.' It is the only line the gospels give Mary in the whole scene -- direct, wounded, a mother's voice.

question: Jesus's answer to Mary in the Temple is the first line of speech any gospel records from him. He begins 'How is it that ye sought me?' -- and then finishes the thought in one line. How does the sentence end?
answer: wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
choices: wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
know ye not that a prophet is without honour, save in his own country?
hath not the Lord chosen the weak things of the world?
have ye not read what David did, when he was hungered?
context: Luke 2:49 KJV. 'Wist' is old English for 'knew.' These are the first recorded words of Jesus in any of the four gospels -- a twelve-year-old's answer to his frightened mother, setting up in one line the tension between his household and his mission; the reply also tells them where they should have looked for him.

question: Years after fleeing Egypt, Moses is now a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law. He leads the sheep to the backside of the desert and comes to the mountain of God. What is the name of Moses's father-in-law, whose flock he keeps in Midian?
context: Exodus 3:1. Jethro is the priest of Midian who took Moses in after Moses killed the Egyptian and fled. Laban is Jacob's uncle in Haran; Bethuel is Rebekah's father in Genesis; Potiphar is Joseph's Egyptian master, from an earlier generation.

question: As Moses walks near the mountain of God, he sees a bush on fire at the roadside. He looks longer, and he sees something impossible about the fire. What is impossible about the way this bush burns?
answer: The bush is not being burned up
choices: The bush is not being burned up
The flames give off no heat at all
The bush is dripping honey from its branches
context: Exodus 3:2-3. The bush 'burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.' Moses says, 'I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.' That impossibility is what draws him close enough for God to speak.

question: When Moses turns to look at the burning bush, God calls to him from within the flames, twice by name: 'Moses, Moses.' God's first command tells Moses the place he has walked into is holy. What must Moses do at once?
answer: Take his sandals off his feet
choices: Take his sandals off his feet
Cover his face with his cloak
Bow down flat on the ground
context: Exodus 3:5. 'Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.' Moses also hides his face, but that comes after the shoes and is not a command.

question: God tells Moses he has heard the cry of the Hebrews in Egypt and Moses must go and bring them out. But Moses asks a nervous question: when the Hebrews demand to know who sent him, what name should he give? God gives Moses a strange four-word name for himself. What is it?
context: Exodus 3:14. 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.' 'Ancient of Days' is from Daniel's vision; 'Alpha and Omega' is from Revelation; 'Lord of Hosts' is a later prophetic title. Only 'I AM THAT I AM' comes from the bush.

question: Moses doubts the Hebrews will believe him, so God gives him a sign to prove himself. God tells Moses to cast the staff in his hand down onto the ground. When Moses does, the staff instantly changes into a living creature so frightening Moses runs from it. What does the staff become?
context: Exodus 4:2-4. When Moses takes it back by the tail it becomes a rod again in his hand. Aaron later performs the same trick before Pharaoh, and the Egyptian magicians match it, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs. Frogs, locusts, and Nile crocodiles all belong to the Egypt frame Moses is being sent into, but the staff becomes a serpent.

question: Even after both signs, Moses tries to talk his way out of the mission. He tells God the honest reason he cannot lead: he cannot speak well. In his own words he is 'not eloquent ... but slow of speech, and of a slow ---'. Fill in the last word of Moses's excuse.
context: Exodus 4:10. 'I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.' Jewish tradition later reads this as a stutter Moses had from childhood; that stutter is why the next rung matters so much.

question: God's anger kindles at Moses's protest that he is slow of tongue, but instead of firing him God appoints someone to be Moses's spokesman: an older brother who can speak well and is already on his way from Egypt to meet him. Who is Moses's brother, the mouthpiece?
context: Exodus 4:14-16. Aaron is Moses's older brother; God says Aaron 'can speak well' and 'shall be thy spokesman unto the people.' Caleb, Hur, and Joshua are all real Exodus-era men (Hur helps hold up Moses's arms at Rephidim; Joshua is Moses's captain in battle; Caleb is one of the twelve spies), but none of them is Moses's brother.

question: Two prophets had warned Odysseus that the animals grazing on the island of Thrinacia must never be touched. Seven great herds and seven great flocks lived there, and they never bred and never died -- they belonged to one of the gods. Which god?
context: In Homer's Odyssey (Book 12), Thrinacia is the island of Helios, the sun who sees everything from his chariot in the sky. Both Circe on Aeaea and the shade of Tiresias in Hades had warned Odysseus: do not touch a single beast on that island. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.127-141.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus wanted to sail past the island of the sun god's herds, but his exhausted crew begged to beach for the night. His stubborn second-in-command overruled him and insisted they land. Who was this second-in-command?
context: Eurylochus is Odysseus's lieutenant throughout the Odyssey and repeatedly the crew's mouthpiece against his captain -- earlier he refused to enter Circe's palace, and here he overrules Odysseus about beaching on Thrinacia. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.279-294.  (Legend.)
