question: Before he let his men beach on Thrinacia, Odysseus made every crewman swear a solemn oath. What did they swear to do?
answer: Eat only the ship's own stores and touch nothing on the island
choices: Eat only the ship's own stores and touch nothing on the island
Sail again at first light no matter the weather
Never again drink wine on the voyage
Kill no living creature until they reached Ithaca
context: Odysseus knew the danger and made his men swear on it. But when the winds pinned them for a month and the stores ran out, the oath fell apart. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.298-304.  (Legend.)

question: The herds on Thrinacia never bred and never died. Every one of them was tended by two divine sisters, the daughters of the sun god. What were their names?
context: Phaethusa and Lampetie -- their names mean 'the shining' and 'the radiant' -- were the daughters of Helios by the nymph Neaera, and they lived on Thrinacia caring for the deathless herds. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.131-133.  (Legend.)

question: The foul winds pinned Odysseus's ship on Thrinacia and the ship's stores gave out. For how long were the crew trapped and starving before they finally broke their oath?
context: A full month of contrary winds -- long enough for the stores to run out and for the crew's fish-and-bird foraging to fail. Odysseus went off alone to pray for deliverance, and while he was asleep Eurylochus led the slaughter. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.325-330.  (Legend.)

question: While Odysseus slept off in a sheltered spot after praying to the gods for a way home, his second-in-command told the starving crew that any death was better than starving to death. What did the crew then do?
answer: Slaughtered the deathless cattle of the god
choices: Slaughtered the deathless cattle of the god
Set fire to their own ship for warmth
Ate their captain's share of the last stores
Sacrificed the youngest crewman to the sea
context: Eurylochus argued they could build the god a great temple back on Ithaca and be forgiven. They killed the best of the herd and roasted the meat -- and Odysseus woke to the smell of it. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.339-365.  (Legend.)

question: One of the two shining daughters ran straight to her father the sun god and told him what the crew had done. He immediately threatened Zeus with an extraordinary punishment against the whole world if the killers were not repaid. What did he threaten to do?
answer: Leave the sky and go down and shine among the dead
choices: Leave the sky and go down and shine among the dead
Burn every crop on the whole earth to ash
Never again let a wind blow across the sea
Drag the moon down out of the night sky
context: One of the most striking single lines in Homer -- Helios threatens to abandon the world of the living and shine for the dead in Hades if his cattle are not avenged. Zeus, alarmed, promises the thunderbolt. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.382-383.  (Legend.)

question: The wind turned fair. The guilty crew put out to sea. Once they were well out from the island, the storm hit. First a black cloud, then a great gust that snapped the mast (the falling mast killed the pilot at the tiller), and then -- what?
answer: A thunderbolt split the ship in two
choices: A thunderbolt split the ship in two
A whirlwind lifted the ship and dashed it back down
A hailstone the size of a boulder broke the hull
The sky turned black and a rain of fire fell on the deck
context: Zeus's promised thunderbolt strikes as soon as the ship clears the island. Every man of the crew drowns; Odysseus, who ate none of the cattle, is the only survivor. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.403-417.  (Legend.)

question: The current on Odysseus's makeshift raft swept him nine days across the sea to a wooded island where a nymph took him in -- and kept him there for seven long years before she would let him go. What was the nymph's name?
context: The island was Ogygia, and the nymph was Calypso, daughter of Atlas. She wanted Odysseus for her husband and only released him after seven years, when Athena persuaded Zeus to send Hermes with the order. Source: Homer, Odyssey 7.244-266 and 5.13-42.  (Legend.)

question: The whole plot of the epic is set in motion by an argument in one very specific place -- not a battlefield, not a throne-room, not a druid's grove. Where are the king and queen when the quarrel begins?
answer: In their royal bed at Cruachan
choices: In their royal bed at Cruachan
On the walls of Emain Macha
By the ford at Ath Fhirdiad
context: The opening scene is famous in world literature as the Pillow-Talk -- an entire war epic launched from a marital argument in bed. Cruachan (modern Rathcroghan in Co. Roscommon) was the royal seat of the kingdom of Connacht. Source: https://mythopedia.com/library/tain-bo-cuailnge-dunn-1914/1-the-pillow-talk/  (Legend.)

question: The queen who lies in the royal bed at Cruachan quarrelling with her husband is not a wife who fights from behind a curtain. She rides her own chariot, kills in single combat, and drives the war herself while her husband largely keeps to her shadow. What is her name?
context: Medb (anglicised Maeve) of Connacht is one of the great warrior-queens of world myth -- her name is glossed 'she who intoxicates' and is cognate with the English word 'mead'. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife (Ulster side); Deirdre is a tragic beauty; Grainne belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Source: https://irishmyths.com/myths/cattle-raid-cooley-tain-bo-cuailnge/  (Legend.)

question: The king who lies beside Medb in the bed at Cruachan is her husband, king of the same province of Connacht. What is his name?
context: Ailill mac Mata is Medb's husband and consort-king; the Tain repeatedly makes clear that in this marriage Medb is the driving will. Conchobar mac Nessa is the king of ULSTER, the enemy in this war; Fergus mac Roich is an exiled Ulsterman who fights on Medb's side; Cormac is a later high-king of Ireland. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: Lying awake in the royal bed, Medb and Ailill do a strange thing: they compare their possessions item by item -- gold, servants, weapons, jewellery, flocks, herds. To Medb's fury, the count comes out exactly equal on every single count except for one particular kind of possession. What is the one thing on which they are not equal?
context: Ailill has one bull in his herds so magnificent that Medb has no equal to it -- and this is the fact she cannot bear. The whole war of the Tain will be a woman's determination to match a single animal her husband owns. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: The great bull that gives Ailill his advantage over Medb was NOT bought in from another kingdom. He was originally born in Medb's own herd. Why, according to the tale, did he leave her herd for Ailill's?
answer: He refused to be owned by a woman
choices: He refused to be owned by a woman
He was traded away in a game of fidchell
He was stolen by raiders from Munster
He was frightened off by a druid's curse
context: The bull's own defection is the sharpest twist of the pillow-talk: the animal himself judged that a queen was not a fit owner, and walked into the king's pasture. For Medb, sovereignty over Connacht was inseparable from being able to match her husband's wealth exactly. Fidchell is a real early-Irish board game. Source: https://loraobrien.ie/tain-bo-cuailgne-cattle-raid-of-cooley-a-beginners-guide/  (Legend.)

question: Daire mac Fiachna agrees to lease the Brown Bull for a year for a fair price, and Medb's men are welcomed to a feast in his hall. The deal falls apart because of a single moment during that feast. What ruins Medb's negotiation?
answer: Her messengers boast, drunk, that they would take the bull by force if refused
choices: Her messengers boast, drunk, that they would take the bull by force if refused
Her messengers demand the bull outright as a tribute rather than a lease
Her messengers insult Daire's wife at the feast-table
Her messengers offer Daire half the going price and no more
context: Daire overhears the drunken boast, understands that Medb was never going to leave without the bull one way or another, and formally withdraws his consent. In doing so he gives Medb the pretext for war she needed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: Refused the Brown Bull by Daire mac Fiachna, Medb does not send a second embassy. She raises an army instead -- an army drawn from all the great territorial divisions of Ireland, welded together against Ulster alone. From how many of the provinces of Ireland is Medb's army raised?
context: Medb raises the army of the four provinces -- Connacht, Munster, Leinster, and even a body of exiled Ulstermen -- against Ulster itself. Ireland was traditionally divided into four kingdoms with a symbolic fifth (Meath) at the centre. Twelve is the Round Table number (Arthurian pillar); seven is the number of Ulster kings-in-training at Emain Macha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A1in_B%C3%B3_C%C3%BAailnge  (Legend.)

question: The great war of the Tain ends not with the death of Medb, not with the fall of Ulster, but with the two prize bulls of the epic meeting on the field of Cruachan itself -- fighting each other along the same route the raid had taken. Which bull wins the final duel?
answer: The Donn Cuailnge kills the Finnbennach
choices: The Donn Cuailnge kills the Finnbennach
The Finnbennach kills the Donn Cuailnge
Both bulls die at the same instant
Both bulls turn and refuse to fight
context: The Brown of Cooley gores the White-Horned to death and scatters pieces of him across the map of Ireland -- and then, exhausted, drops dead himself. The epic ends with both prize bulls dead in the mud and Medb no richer than the night of the pillow-talk. Source: https://irishmyths.com/myths/cattle-raid-cooley-tain-bo-cuailnge/  (Legend.)

question: In the Ulster Cycle a sharp-tongued poet is so hated for his mischief that when he throws a great feast the warriors will only agree to come if he sits apart in a separate raised gallery, so his poison-verses cannot reach them across the hall. Who is this Ulster poet?
context: Bricriu mac Carbada is the hospitaller (briugu) and troublemaker of Ulster, known for a satirist's tongue so vicious that his mere presence at the hearth started fights. The tale of the feast is called Fled Bricrenn ('Bricriu's Feast'). Sencha mac Ailella is Ulster's chief judge and peacemaker; Amairgen mac Ecit is Conall Cernach's father, another Ulster poet; Ferghus mac Roich is the exiled king. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricriu.  (Legend.)

question: The three Ulster champions who each believe they have been promised the Champion's Portion at Bricriu's feast are the greatest three warriors of the province. Cu Chulainn is one, and Conall Cernach is another. Who is the third?
context: Loegaire Buadach ('Loegaire the Victorious') is the third of the top-rank Ulster champions and the first to take up the beheading challenge later in the tale. Cet mac Magach is a Connacht champion; Fer Diad is Cu Chulainn's foster-brother from Connacht; Laeg mac Riangabra is Cu Chulainn's charioteer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The dispute over the Champion's Portion cannot be settled. Contests of arms are held, kings are asked to judge, Cu Chulainn is repeatedly named the winner -- but the other two refuse the verdict. Then one night a great stranger enters the hall of Emain Macha and offers a strange bargain to the champions. What appearance does the stranger take?
answer: a huge rough herdsman (bachlach) with an axe
choices: a huge rough herdsman (bachlach) with an axe
an armoured Fomorian captain from the sea
a druid of the Dagda in white robes
a giant of the Fir Bolg in bronze mail
context: The Irish word bachlach means 'churl' or 'lout'; in the tale the shape-shifter chooses the form of a rough herdsman with a great axe -- the most unassuming shape possible, which makes the beheading trick land harder. The Fomorians are a race of old sea-enemies of the Tuatha De; the Fir Bolg are the pre-Tuatha rulers of Ireland; a druid would judge, not challenge with an axe. Source: oxfordreference.com Bachlach entry; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The first champion to accept the bargain strikes at the giant with the axe and takes his head clean off in one blow. The next moment is what makes the tale unforgettable and gives the whole story-motif its name in medieval studies. What does the beheaded stranger do?
answer: picks up his own head, tucks it under his arm, and walks out of the hall
choices: picks up his own head, tucks it under his arm, and walks out of the hall
grows a new head from the stump on the spot
vanishes into a mist and leaves the axe standing upright in the floor
turns into a raven and flies out through the smoke-hole
context: The picked-up-head is the visual signature of what medievalists call the 'beheading game': proof that the challenger is otherworldly and the bargain will fall due. He returns the next morning, head restored, to collect the return blow. Six centuries later Sir Gawain and the Green Knight uses exactly the same beat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beheading_game; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The giant returns to Emain Macha the next morning to collect the return blow. The champion who beheaded him the night before -- and had sworn to offer his own neck in the morning -- refuses the bargain and slips away. Which of the three champions was the first to flee?
context: Loegaire is the first to try the challenge and the first to break his word; Conall takes the same bargain on the second night and likewise flees when the giant comes back with the axe. Only Cu Chulainn will keep faith. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: On the third night one champion takes the axe and beheads the giant herdsman, watches him carry his head out of the hall, and next morning WHEN THE GIANT RETURNS keeps his word -- stretches his own neck on the block without flinching and waits for the blow. Which of the three great Ulster champions is this?
context: The whole tale points at this moment: Cu Chulainn alone honours the exchange. Conall and Loegaire had both fled at first light. Fer Diad is not one of the three great Ulster champions -- he is Cu Chulainn's Connacht foster-brother, who will later fight him at the ford in the Tain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: With Cu Chulainn's neck stretched on the block, the giant lifts the axe and swings three times. On the third stroke he lets the blade fall -- but he has TURNED IT IN HIS HAND so it does no wound. What part of the axe does he strike Cu Chulainn's neck with?
answer: the flat or blunt back of the blade
choices: the flat or blunt back of the blade
the wooden handle just above the head
the leather thong lashing the head to the shaft
the pommel-stone at the butt of the shaft
context: The turned axe is the mercy that pays out the bargain: Cu Chulainn keeps his word, the giant keeps his (a blow, not a killing), and honour is preserved on both sides. The 14th-century Sir Gawain and the Green Knight uses the same three-swing structure at the Green Chapel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gawain_and_the_Green_Knight; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fled_Bricrenn.  (Legend.)

question: The beheading-bargain from Fled Bricrenn passes down through French Arthurian romance and eventually gives an English poet his opening scene: on Christmas Day at Camelot a huge green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's hall carrying a holly-branch in one hand and a great axe in the other, and offers the same bargain the bachlach offered in Ulster -- strike me tonight, take yours in a year. What is this romance called?
answer: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
choices: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
context: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (late 14th century, by the anonymous 'Gawain-poet') opens with exactly the green-knight-with-holly scene: the same beheading bargain, the same year-and-a-day delay, and at the end the same three-swing axe-blow that Cu Roi gave Cu Chulainn. Pearl and Patience are two other alliterative poems in the same manuscript by the same anonymous poet; the Alliterative Morte Arthure is a separate 14th-century Arthurian poem, but has no beheading-game. Fled Bricrenn is the ancestor, likely transmitted through Chretien de Troyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beheading_game.  (Legend.)

question: The mischief-maker who set the whole quarrel in motion does not survive his own cycle for long. In the closing hour of the Tain Bo Cuailnge, when the great cattle-raid ends at Cruachan and the fighting is over, Bricriu -- who has come out to watch the sport he was so fond of stirring in others -- meets his end. How does Bricriu mac Carbada die?
answer: trampled to death between the two great bulls of the Tain
choices: trampled to death between the two great bulls of the Tain
poisoned by his own wife at the feasting-table
beheaded by Cu Roi mac Daire in a return match
starved after being locked into his own raised gallery
context: The Brown Bull of Cooley and the White-Horned Bull of Ai fight to the death at Cruachan at the end of the Tain, and Bricriu is caught between them and trampled. The Ulster tradition treats it as poetic justice for a life of stirring fights. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricriu.  (Legend.)

question: In Irish myth a Tuatha De figure named Lir lost his first wife and married her sister to be a mother to his four small children. The new stepmother grew jealous of how much Lir loved the children and, striking them with a druid's rod on the edge of a lake, turned all four of them into something. Into what shape did the stepmother turn Lir's four children?
context: This is the opening of Oidheadh Chlainne Lir ('The Fate of the Children of Lir'), one of the great tragic tales of medieval Ireland. Aoife, the second wife, transforms the four children at Loch Dairbhreach (Lake Derravaragh) in modern County Westmeath. Swans in Irish myth are almost always a shape of the enchanted or the mourning; this story is why the Irish will not shoot a swan to this day.  (Legend.)

question: The daughter of Lir was the eldest of the four children and would spend nine hundred years as a swan protecting her three brothers. She is one of the most beloved figures in Irish myth, and the Oisin Kelly bronze in the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin shows her rising in swan-shape with her brothers beside her. What is the name of Lir's daughter?
context: Fionnuala is the eldest child of Lir and Aoibh, sister to Aodh, Fiacra, and Conn. Deirdre is the sorrow-figure of the Ulster cycle (the Children of Uisneach). Etain is the swan-maiden of Tochmarc Etaine, a different tale. Grainne is the woman who elopes with Diarmuid in the Fionn cycle.  (Legend.)

question: Lir's first wife had died bearing their children, and to comfort him and mother the little ones he married her sister. She started as a good stepmother, but jealousy of the children's place in Lir's heart grew in her until she took them out to the lake with a druid's rod. What is the name of the jealous stepmother-sister?
context: Aoife (EE-fa) is the sister of Lir's dead first wife Aoibh. Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne, mother of Aengus. Medb is the queen of Connacht in the Ulster cycle Tain. Sadhbh is Fionn mac Cumhaill's deer-wife, mother of Oisin -- also a shape-shifting story, but a different one.  (Legend.)

question: The druid's rod took away the children's human shape, but Aoife's power could not reach two other things -- two human gifts that stayed inside the swan-bodies for the whole length of the curse, so that Lir himself could still recognise his own children when he found them on the water. Which two human gifts did the four keep as swans?
context: In every telling of Oidheadh Chlainne Lir the four kept human speech and human reason inside the swan-shape -- Fionnuala could still tell her father Lir what Aoife had done, and the four could still sing plaintive songs that were said to be the sweetest in Ireland. Only the bodies were changed.  (Legend.)

question: The curse Aoife laid on the four children was not one wandering exile but a set number of them, and it lasted an enormous stretch of time -- so long that all who had known the children as children were dead many times over before it ended. How long in total did Aoife's curse last?
context: The curse lasted nine hundred years in total, divided into three periods of three hundred: first on the peaceful Lake Derravaragh in Westmeath; then on the cold Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland; then on the wild Atlantic off the Isle of Inishglora in the west. Only after all nine centuries would the conditions of the curse's ending come together.  (Legend.)

question: The second three-hundred-year exile was the hardest of the three. The four had to leave the calm lake in Westmeath and beat their wings out over a narrow northern channel notorious for its storms and freezing spray -- the middle exile of the curse, and the one the tale lingers on longest. What is the name of that middle sea-exile?
context: Sruth na Maoile, the Sea of Moyle, is the narrow strait between the north-east coast of Antrim and the Mull of Kintyre in Scotland -- notorious for hard weather, and the specific water the tale names for the second exile. The North Channel is a broader modern name for waters overlapping that area. The Minch is off the Scottish Hebrides. The Irish Sea is the wider basin south of it. The middle exile is always specifically the Moyle.  (Legend.)

question: On the Sea of Moyle the four suffered three centuries of cold and storm, and the eldest child did one thing for the three younger ones every hard night that has kept her the emblem of Irish sisterhood ever since. What did Fionnuala do for her three brothers on the freezing Moyle?
answer: sheltered them beneath her wings against the spray
choices: sheltered them beneath her wings against the spray
sang the psalms she remembered from Lir's hall
led them south each night to warmer water
wove a nest of driftwood to hold them together
context: In every version of the tale Fionnuala, the eldest, wraps her three brothers under her outstretched wings on the black nights of the Moyle, warming them against the freezing sea-spray. That single image -- the sister sheltering her brothers -- is the emotional heart of the tale and the reason the Oisin Kelly sculpture stands in the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin as an emblem of Irish sisterly and national protection.  (Legend.)

question: The curse was not left open-ended. Aoife set two very specific conditions -- both had to come true in the same hour before the swan-shape would fall away. Which pair of conditions did Aoife lay for the curse to break?
answer: a woman of the south marries a man of the north, and Christian bells ring over Ireland
choices: a woman of the south marries a man of the north, and Christian bells ring over Ireland
the moon is full over the sea three nights running, and a swan is killed by an eagle
a druid drinks from the well of Segais, and a stag is seen at dawn beside it
the High King is crowned on the Tara stone, and a raven speaks aloud in his hall
context: The two conditions in the Aoife-curse: a woman of the south (Munster) must marry a man of the north (Connacht), and the bells of Christianity must sound across Ireland. Both come true at once when the hermit Mochaomhog rings his monastery-bells on the western island of Inishglora and news comes of the Munster-Connacht royal marriage. The curse breaks in the same hour.  (Legend.)

question: When at last the bells of a hermit rang out on Inishglora and the curse broke, the four swans changed back into human shape on the shore. What kind of human bodies stood there in the moment the feathers fell away?
answer: ancient shrunken bodies, lean and bony
choices: ancient shrunken bodies, lean and bony
young adults just as Lir had first known them
little children the same age Aoife had cursed
shining figures of light without weight
context: The transformation back into human shape ages them all nine centuries in an instant: the swans' feathers fall off to reveal three lean, bony old men and one old woman. Mochaomhog baptises them in that last hour, and they die and are buried together, Fionnuala in the middle with her three brothers under her arms as she had sheltered them on the Sea of Moyle.  (Legend.)

question: Medieval Irish storytellers grouped 'The Fate of the Children of Lir' with 'The Fate of the Children of Uisneach' (Deirdre) and 'The Fate of the Children of Tuireann' as a fixed set of three, and every Irish schoolchild for a century has learned the trio by that name. What did the medieval Irish call that set of three?
choices: the Three Laments of the Bards
context: Tri Truaighe na Scealaigheachta -- the Three Sorrows of Storytelling -- is the medieval Irish grouping of the three great tragic tales: Lir, Uisneach (Deirdre), and Tuireann. The other three choices are plausible-sounding invented Irish groupings of the same emotional register; the real fixed traditional name is 'the Three Sorrows of Storytelling'.

question: The Cantar de Mio Cid tells us that the Cid rings the city and settles his men in for a long, patient blockade. The poem states plainly how many months the warband penned the city in before it was starved into surrender: 'Know that for how many months he penned them there, before at last they were forced to yield.' Fill in the poem's number.
context: The poem: 'Know that for nine months he penned them there. When the tenth arrived, they were forced to yield.' (Historically the siege lasted longer, from October 1092 to June 1094; the poem compresses it to nine.) Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part III (poetryintranslation.com).  (Legend.)

question: All the years the Cid was in exile, campaigning across the frontier, his wife and two young daughters did not travel with him. The poem says he left them safe at a Castilian monastery just outside Burgos, where they waited out the war. Which monastery kept the Cid's family?
context: San Pedro de Cardena, a Benedictine monastery just outside Burgos, sheltered Jimena and the daughters through the exile. The Cid himself was originally buried there before his tomb was moved to Burgos Cathedral. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Parts I and III; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.  (Legend.)

question: In the Cantar de Mio Cid, the Cid's wife is a great lady of Castile. Through all the years of exile she has kept the family together at a Castilian monastery while her husband fights his way across Iberia. What is her name in the poem?
context: Dona Jimena Diaz was the historical Cid's real wife; the poem keeps her name. Urraca was Alfonso VI's daughter and later queen; Berenguela and Leonor are later Castilian queens. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The Cid brings Dona Jimena and their two daughters up onto the highest battlement of the alcazar of Valencia. The girls stand there, staring out at the roofs of the city and the sea beyond, in the scene that gives the poem its middle cantar its most tender image. In the Cantar de Mio Cid, what are the two daughters' names?
context: The poem names them Dona Elvira and Dona Sol -- though the historical Cid's real daughters were called Cristina and Maria. The poet changed the names, and the poem's names are the ones that survived in Spanish story. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part IV; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.  (Legend.)

question: The Cid has just broken the Moroccan relief army on the plain outside Valencia. The captured horses and gold from the enemy camp will make every one of his men rich for life. In the poem, the Cid picks the finest of his own share of the horses and sends them across Castile as a gift to the very king who had once exiled him, King Alfonso VI. How many horses does the poem have him send?
context: The poem: 'And lead a full two hundred to King Alfonso.' This gift is the pivot of the poem's second cantar -- the beginning of the Cid's reconciliation with the king who banished him. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Part IV.  (Legend.)

question: King Alfonso VI, softened by the Cid's gift and by the Cid's growing fame, arranges a match for the Cid's two daughters. He weds them to two young men of a great house Alfonso favored -- a match the Cid himself is uneasy about, but which the king insists upon. The wedding is celebrated at the church of Santa Maria in Valencia, with feasting that lasts fifteen days. Whom does the poem have the daughters married to?
context: The Infantes (princes) of Carrion, Fernando and Diego, are the villains of the third cantar -- the marriage ends in the outrage at the oak-wood of Corpes, where they beat the daughters and abandon them, and the Cid takes his vengeance in the king's court. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid Parts III-IV.  (Legend.)

question: The great warrior-hero of medieval Castile, Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, is remembered across Spain by a shorter title given him by his Muslim opponents, an Arabic word meaning lord or master. What TITLE is he known by in every song and chronicle?
context: 'Cid' comes from Arabic 'sayyid' meaning lord -- a title of respect his Muslim opponents used, which stuck to him permanently in the Castilian tradition. Caudillo (leader), alcalde (mayor), and adelantado (frontier governor) are all real Spanish titles, but not his. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The Cid spent his last years ruling a great port city on the east coast of Spain that he had captured from Muslim hands and now held as his own principality. What CITY did the Cid hold at the end of his life?
context: The Cid captured Valencia from its Muslim ruler in 1094 and ruled it as an independent principality until his death in 1099. Toledo had already fallen to King Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085; Cordoba and Granada remained in Muslim hands for centuries longer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The Cid dies in his eastern-coast palace on 10 July 1099, worn out by decades of border-warfare -- but at that same moment a great enemy army is camped outside the walls of his city, threatening to take it back the moment the news of his death gets out. Which North African Berber empire is besieging him?
context: The Almoravids -- a Berber dynasty from what is now Morocco and Mauritania -- had crossed into Spain in 1086 and were the great new threat to Christian and independent principalities alike. The Almohads came a generation later; the Umayyads were the earlier caliphs of Cordoba; the Nasrids were the last Muslim dynasty of Granada. All real, only the Almoravids fit 1099. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The city inside its walls has one great hope of holding out: nobody outside must learn that the Cid is dead, or morale will collapse. The person who takes charge of the deception is the Cid's own WIFE, a Castilian noblewoman who has stood by him through his years of exile. What is HER NAME?
context: Dona Jimena Diaz, a noblewoman of Asturias, was the Cid's wife; she took over the defence of Valencia in the days after his death. Urraca, Berenguela, and Constanza are all real names of medieval Castilian and Leonese queens or noblewomen -- adjacent, wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: The Cid's warhorse in the legend is one of the most famous named horses in all of Western tradition, praised in the Cantar de Mio Cid as a horse without equal. What is the Cid's horse called?
context: Babieca is the Cid's warhorse in the Cantar and every later chronicle. Bucephalus was Alexander the Great's warhorse; Sleipnir was Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse myth; Veillantif was Roland's horse in the Song of Roland -- all real named steeds of Western legend. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babieca.

question: History records that Jimena held Valencia for about three years after the Cid's death. In 1102, what did she do?
answer: she abandoned the city and carried her husband's body west to Castile
choices: she abandoned the city and carried her husband's body west to Castile
she was killed on the walls in a final Almoravid assault on the palace
she surrendered the city to King Alfonso the Sixth as a Christian fief
she turned the palace into a fortified nunnery and stayed to defend it
context: History records that Jimena held Valencia until 1102 and then, unable to hold on longer against the Almoravids, evacuated the city (burning it as she left, according to some chronicles) and carried her husband's body west to Castile. The legendary phantom-charge belongs to story, not to what really happened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cid.

question: In the Ulster Cycle a supernatural woman comes to live secretly with a widowed farmer named Crunniuc, blesses his household with prosperity, and asks only that he never boast about her to strangers. Which figure of Irish myth is this woman?
context: Macha is a supernatural woman of Ulster, variously called a goddess of the land or one of the three Morrigna sisters, who comes to live in secret with the widower Crunniuc mac Agnomain. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of a different Ulster tale; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife; Brigid is a Tuatha De goddess of the flame. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: Macha is forced to run the foot-race against the royal chariot-team. What happens as she crosses the finish line?
answer: she collapses in labour and delivers twins on the field
choices: she collapses in labour and delivers twins on the field
she is trampled under the hooves of the king's team
she runs on past the line and out of Ulster forever
she throws herself on the king's spear in front of the crowd
context: Macha wins the race and, in the same breath, delivers twins on the ground -- a boy named Fir ('True') and a girl named Fial ('Modest'). The double birth in front of the whole assembly is the moment that gives Emain Macha its name: 'the twins of Macha.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: As she lies on the ground bleeding, Macha calls down a curse on every fighting man of Ulster within hearing. In the hour of the province's greatest need, she says, they shall be laid on their beds and suffer a particular sharp pain. What pain is it?
answer: the pangs of a woman in labour
choices: the pangs of a woman in labour
the fever that comes with the plague of the crows
the palsy that seizes the sword-hand of the perjurer
the thirst that no water in Ireland can slake
context: The Ulstermen must feel the same labour-pain Macha herself has just felt -- for five days and four nights (or five nights and four days, versions vary) whenever the province is invaded, and the curse binds nine generations. It is a wholly unique motif in world myth. Source: storyarchaeology.com/noinden-ulad-the-story-of-macha; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: Generations later, Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, driving her army across the border to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley. The Ulster fighting-men -- king, princes, and champions alike -- are helpless. Why can none of them fight?
answer: they are all bedridden by the curse Macha laid on their forefathers
choices: they are all bedridden by the curse Macha laid on their forefathers
they are away at a great feast in Emain Macha and cannot be recalled
they are bound by an oath of peace with Connacht that Conchobar refuses to break
they have all been paralysed by a druid of Medb's court in advance of the war
context: Macha's curse is the mythic pre-condition of the Tain: at the hour of Ulster's greatest need the whole fighting force is on its back in labour-pain, for nine generations, for five days and four nights at a stretch. It is what makes Cu Chulainn's one-man defence necessary and honourable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: One Ulster warrior alone is spared the curse and free to fight while every other man of the province lies in bed. He goes down to the border-fords single-handed and holds Medb's whole invading army back for weeks. Which warrior is this?
context: Cu Chulainn is immune to Macha's curse -- in one version because he is only a boy of seventeen and has not come of fighting age with the men of Ulster, in another because he is half-divine as the son of the god Lugh. His single-handed defence of the fords is the central drama of the Tain. Conall, Loegaire, and the exiled Ferghus are all fully-grown Ulster champions -- all laid low by the curse. Source: storyarchaeology.com/noinden-ulad-the-story-of-macha.  (Legend.)

question: Macha's curse does not fall on the Ulstermen all at once and forever. It falls in bouts, each of a particular length, every time an army marches on the province. How long is a single bout of the debility said to last?
choices: one full turning of the moon
context: Each bout of noinden Ulad lasts five days and four nights (or, in some manuscripts, five nights and four days -- the compilers disagree), and the curse binds nine generations of Ulster fighting-men. That the debility comes in short, sharp bouts -- and not as a permanent blight -- is what lets the province survive at all. Source: storyarchaeology.com/noinden-ulad-the-story-of-macha.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Odyssey, sailing home from Troy, Odysseus and twelve of his crew land on an island of huge shepherd giants and walk into the cave of one of them, hoping for a guest-gift. What is the name of the man-eating giant whose cave they enter?
context: Polyphemus is a Cyclops, a huge one-eyed shepherd giant. His cave is the setting for the most famous single episode of the Odyssey. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus and his men are trapped inside Polyphemus's cave when the giant comes home and rolls something across the mouth so that no ordinary man can move it. What does he roll across the cave mouth?
context: Polyphemus seals the cave with a massive stone that no ordinary man could shift. Odysseus and his crew cannot simply kill the giant in his sleep, because then they would never be able to move the stone. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Polyphemus is a giant with only ONE of a feature the crew have two of, and that single feature is the target of Odysseus's whole plan. Which single feature does he have only ONE of?
context: Cyclopes are one-eyed giants. Blinding that single eye is the crux of Odysseus's escape plan -- with the giant blind, the crew can slip past him when he opens the cave. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Trapped in the cave and watching the giant eat crewmen two at a time, Odysseus and his surviving men work in secret while Polyphemus is out with his flocks. They take the giant's own great staff and sharpen it into a huge pointed weapon, hardening its point in the fire. From WHAT wood is this staff made?
context: The staff is olive-wood, the sacred tree of Athena. Odysseus and his men shape and fire-harden the point, then hide it, waiting for the giant to fall asleep. (Odyssey 9; cliffsnotes.com.)  (Legend.)

question: That evening Polyphemus comes home and eats two more crewmen. Odysseus, hiding the fire-hardened stake, offers him a skin of very strong wine to drink. The drunk giant, pleased, asks the guest's name so he can offer a proper guest-gift in return. WHAT name does Odysseus give?
context: Odysseus says: 'Outis is my name; my mother, my father, my friends call me Outis.' 'Outis' is Greek for 'Nobody.' The giant, pleased, promises: 'I will eat Nobody last, after all his friends.' (Odyssey 9.366-367; Wikipedia: Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: The giant drinks the wine and passes out. Odysseus and four picked men take the sharpened olive stake, heat its point until it glows red in the fire, and drive it into the giant's eye. Homer compares the way they work the burning stake to a shipwright doing WHAT with a beam?
context: Homer writes that they turn the burning stake in the giant's eye 'as a shipwright bores a beam with a drill' -- one of the most famous similes in the Odyssey. (Odyssey 9.383-388; theoi.com.)  (Legend.)

question: Polyphemus roars in agony from the burning stake. The other Cyclopes on the island come running to the mouth of the cave and shout in: 'Polyphemus, who is hurting you?' Because of the name Odysseus gave, Polyphemus's shouted answer makes the neighbors turn around and leave. WHAT do they conclude is happening to him?
context: The wounded giant screams 'Nobody is killing me!' The other Cyclopes hear 'no man' and conclude it must be a sickness sent by Zeus that no mortal can help with -- so they leave. (Odyssey 9; Wikipedia: Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: In the morning the blinded giant rolls back the stone to let his flock out to pasture, and sits at the cave mouth checking each ram with his hands as it passes, to make sure no man rides out. Odysseus has already outsmarted this. HOW have he and his men escaped past the giant's hands?
answer: Tied to the bellies of the rams
choices: Tied to the bellies of the rams
Rolled up in the giant's own fleece cloaks
Standing on the shoulders of the biggest sheep
context: Odysseus lashes each surviving man to the belly of one of the giant's rams -- and clings himself to the belly of the biggest ram. The blind Polyphemus feels only wool on the backs of the animals as the flock passes. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: Once safely back on the ship and pulling away from the shore, Odysseus does ONE thing that he will regret for the next ten years of wandering. He cannot help himself -- he shouts something back across the water to the blinded giant on the cliff. WHAT does he shout?
choices: A curse on the whole island
context: Odysseus taunts the blinded Polyphemus by shouting his true name across the water -- his one great mistake. Now the giant knows exactly whom to curse. (Odyssey 9; sparknotes.com/lit/odyssey.)  (Legend.)

question: Knowing at last the true name of the man who blinded him, Polyphemus lifts his hands and prays to his own FATHER -- a powerful Olympian who will hear him -- to punish Odysseus. WHICH god is Polyphemus's father?
context: Polyphemus is a son of Poseidon, god of the sea, and a sea-nymph. That parentage is why his curse has real weight over the whole Odyssey -- Odysseus is at sea, in Poseidon's domain, for another ten years. (Odyssey 9; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outis.)  (Legend.)

question: Polyphemus's prayer to his father is very specific. He does not ask that Odysseus die on the way home. He asks TWO conditions that shape the rest of the Odyssey. WHAT does he pray Odysseus's homecoming will be like?
context: Polyphemus prays that Odysseus either never reach home, or if he must, that he reach it LATE and ALONE and find his house in trouble. Poseidon hears, and that prayer is the reason the Odyssey lasts ten years and Odysseus arrives home without a single crewman left. (Odyssey 9; readtheodyssey.org.)  (Legend.)

question: The Greek word 'Cyclops' is a compound of two Greek roots -- kyklo- meaning 'circle' plus another root meaning one part of the body. What does the word literally MEAN in Greek?
context: 'Cyclops' comes from kyklo- ('circle', 'round') plus -ops ('eye') -- so 'round-eye'. The one great circular eye is the defining feature. (cliffsnotes.com.)

question: In Irish myth a huge, red-bearded, big-bellied god in a hooded cloak is the chief of the Tuatha De Danann. His people call him 'good' -- not because he is kindly, but because he is skilled at every craft: war, magic, poetry, husbandry, cooking. Which of these chief-gods is he?
context: The Dagda is the father-figure of the Tuatha De Danann -- his name means 'the good god' in the sense of 'good at everything.' Nuada Silver-Arm is the first king of the Tuatha De but loses the throne through his wound; Lugh Lamhfhada is Nuada's grandson, master of every art; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god who later divides the fairy mounds among the Tuatha De. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda carries a great weapon so heavy that eight men together cannot lift it. He has to drag it behind him across the ground, and it leaves a furrow like a boundary-ditch through the earth wherever he walks. What Irish name do the tales give this dragged weapon?
context: Lorg Mor means simply 'the great staff' in Old Irish. The Gae Bolg is Cuchulainn's belly-spear; the Claiomh Solais is the Sword of Light belonging to Nuada; the Gai Assail is Lugh's victory-spear -- three other famous Irish weapons, each from its own ladder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda; worldhistory.org/The_Dagda/.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda owns a great cauldron, brought from the northern city of Murias, and no company of warriors ever leaves it hungry. Every man draws out as much food as his hunger calls for, and the more the cauldron is emptied the more it fills. What is this cauldron called in Irish?
context: Coire Ansic means 'the un-dry cauldron' in Old Irish. The Cauldrons of Ceridwen, Bran, and Annwn all belong to the WELSH branch of Celtic tradition -- honest distractors from a sister tradition, but not the Dagda's Irish cauldron. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda owns a magic harp that will answer to no voice but his. After the Second Battle of Moytura the Fomorians steal it and carry it away to their feast-hall, hanging it on the wall. The Dagda walks in among the drinking Fomorians, calls the harp aloud by its two secret names, and the harp tears itself off the wall. What happens as it flies through the hall to his hand?
answer: It kills nine Fomorians on its flight
choices: It kills nine Fomorians on its flight
It sings the Fomorians dead where they sit
It turns to gold in mid-air
It calls fire down onto the roof-beams
context: The scene is Cath Maige Tuired sec 162. The Dagda calls 'Come Daur Da Bla, come Coir Cetharchair' and the harp answers, killing nine Fomorians as it flies past them. Only then does he play its three great strains. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: Once the Dagda has his harp back in his hand, he sits down among the beaten Fomorians and plays THREE great strains on it. The first is the Goltrai, the weeping strain -- no man hearing it can hold back tears. The third is the Suantrai, the sleeping strain -- everyone in earshot falls into a deep sleep. What is the middle strain, the second one, called?
context: The three great strains of the Dagda's harp are Goltrai (weeping), Geantrai (laughing), and Suantrai (sleeping) -- fixed in Irish tradition as the Three Noble Strains of harp music down to the modern day. The other three names in the list are inventions on the same pattern. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uaithne.  (Legend.)

question: In Cath Maige Tuired the Fomorians decide to humiliate the Dagda through his own hunger. They dig a great pit in the ground and pour into it eighty gallons of new milk, an equal weight of meal and fat, and whole herds of sheep, pigs, and goats boiled together. Then the Fomorian king Indech tells the Dagda he will be killed unless he eats every last drop. He picks up the ladle they set beside the pit. How big is this ladle?
answer: Big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it
choices: Big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it
Big enough to carry the head of an ox in one scoop
Big enough to bail a small boat with
Big enough to serve nine warriors at once
context: The line is preserved verbatim from Cath Maige Tuired sec 89: the ladle 'was big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it.' The Dagda eats the whole pit, and afterwards his belly is 'as big as a house cauldron' and the Fomorians laugh at him. The rude humour of the scene was kept intact by the Christian monk-copyists. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda has a great hall in Ireland that he holds until his son Aengus tricks him out of it. Aengus comes to his father and asks for the hall 'for a day and a night'; when the Dagda agrees, Aengus turns the Old Irish phrase against him -- claiming it can also mean 'day and night forever.' Where is the Dagda's hall that Aengus takes from him?
answer: Bru na Boinne on the river Boyne
choices: Bru na Boinne on the river Boyne
Tara, the seat of the High Kings
the Hill of Uisneach in the midlands
context: Bru na Boinne ('the mansion of the Boyne') is the Newgrange passage-tomb complex on the north bank of the Boyne -- older than the Egyptian pyramids, and whose great chamber lights up at dawn on the winter solstice each year. Tara is the political seat, Emain Macha is the Ulster capital of the Red Branch, Uisneach is the mythic centre-point of Ireland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The Dagda's harp is called Uaithne, but it will not fly to his hand unless he addresses it by BOTH of its two secret bynames, which are written down in Cath Maige Tuired. One name is Coir Cetharchair, 'Four-Angled Music.' What is the other?
answer: Daur Da Bla, 'Oak of Two Meadows'
choices: Daur Da Bla, 'Oak of Two Meadows'
context: The two names are preserved together in Cath Maige Tuired sec 162: Daur Da Bla and Coir Cetharchair. The wood-and-tree distractors are inventions on Irish-sounding patterns -- yew, hazel, and Nuada's harp all live elsewhere in Irish tradition but none is the Dagda's harp-name. The 'four-angled' name is thought to describe the frame's shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uaithne.  (Legend.)

question: The night before the Second Battle of Moytura, the Dagda meets a woman washing bloody armour at a ford on the river Unius. It is the feast of Samhain, when the walls between worlds grow thin, and the washer-at-the-ford is a sign of death for the men whose armour she scrubs. She lies with the Dagda at the ford, and in return promises him the destruction of the Fomorian king. Which of the Tuatha De is she?
choices: Danu, mother of the Tuatha De
context: The tryst at the ford of the Unius on Samhain is one of the most famous scenes of Irish myth. The washer-at-the-ford scrubbing the armour of doomed men is the Morrigan's signature image. Brigid is the Dagda's daughter, goddess of the flame at Kildare; Danu is the ancestress the whole Tuatha De are named for; Aine is a sun-and-sovereignty goddess of Munster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: After eating the Fomorians' mocking porridge and walking away with a belly 'as big as a house cauldron', the Dagda meets a young woman on the shore of Traigh Eabha. She satirises him in verse, blocks his way by turning into obstacles, and demands he carry her on his back. She turns out to be the daughter of an enemy king -- and the Dagda's later coupling with her is preserved in the same saga. Whose daughter is she?
answer: the daughter of the Fomorian king Indech
choices: the daughter of the Fomorian king Indech
the daughter of the Fir Bolg king Eochaid
the daughter of the Milesian druid Amergin
the daughter of the Ulster king Conchobar
context: Indech mac De Domnann is the Fomorian king who served the porridge, and it is his daughter the Dagda meets on the shore afterwards -- a wonderfully rude scene kept intact by the medieval monks. Eochaid, Amergin, and Conchobar belong to other cycles of Irish tradition. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: Before he was the apostle Paul, Saul of Tarsus was on the road hunting Christians. He carried official letters from the high priest in Jerusalem authorising him to arrest any followers of Jesus he could find in the synagogues of one particular city and drag them back in chains. To what city was Saul travelling that day?
context: Acts 9:1-2 (KJV): 'And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest, and desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem.' Damascus at the time held a substantial Jewish community; hunting Christ-followers there was Saul's next planned raid.

question: Saul of Tarsus was almost at Damascus, at midday, when 'suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven'. What did the light do to Saul in that instant?
answer: It knocked him to the ground
choices: It knocked him to the ground
It set his cloak on fire
It made his horse rear up and bolt
It froze him where he stood
context: Acts 9:3-4 (KJV): 'And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him...' The horse everyone remembers from paintings (Caravaggio, Michelangelo) is nowhere in the text -- Acts just says Saul fell.

question: Saul lay stunned on the Damascus road under a light from heaven. A voice called him twice by name and spoke to him. What did the voice say?
choices: 'Saul, Saul, thy sins be forgiven thee'
context: Acts 9:4 (KJV). The double name -- 'Saul, Saul' -- is a biblical marker of direct divine address (compare 'Abraham, Abraham', 'Moses, Moses', 'Samuel, Samuel'). The point is startling: the voice does not accuse Saul of persecuting the disciples; it says Saul is persecuting the speaker himself.

question: Under the light on the Damascus road, Saul called back into the sky: 'Who art thou, Lord?' Whom did the voice name itself as?
context: Acts 9:5 (KJV): 'And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.' For a Pharisee hunting a heretical sect, hearing that the crucified rabbi is not only alive but identifying himself with the hunted is the whole hinge of the story.

question: After the light on the road, Saul stood up and opened his eyes and could not see. His companions had to lead him by the hand into Damascus. For how long did the blindness last, during which he neither ate nor drank?
context: Acts 9:8-9 (KJV): 'And Saul arose from the earth; and when his eyes were opened, he saw no man: but they led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. And he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink.' The three-day-in-darkness beat deliberately echoes Jonah in the fish and Jesus in the tomb.

question: A disciple in Damascus named Ananias received a vision telling him to go find the blinded Saul at the house of a man named Judas. The vision gave him the actual street name to look for. What was the street called?
context: Acts 9:11 (KJV): 'Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth.' The Via Recta ran east-west across Roman Damascus; a stretch of it is still walkable in the old city today.

question: Ananias objected: this Saul was the man jailing Christians. But he went anyway, entered the house, and laid hands on the blinded man. How did Ananias greet Saul as he did so?
context: Acts 9:17 (KJV): 'And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.' 'Brother' -- from the disciple whose friends Saul had come to arrest -- is the first word of Christian welcome Saul ever hears.

question: When Ananias laid hands on the blinded Saul in the house on Straight Street, the sight returned instantly, and Acts describes something visible dropping away from his eyes at that moment. What did the text say fell?
context: Acts 9:18 (KJV): 'And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.' The Greek word (lepides) is the ordinary word for fish-scales. The literal image is the point: Saul's spiritual blindness comes off like a fish being cleaned.

question: The moment Saul could see again, he was baptised, and he did not go into hiding. Immediately he began preaching in the synagogues of Damascus -- the very synagogues he had come to raid. What was the message of his very first sermons?
answer: that Jesus is the Son of God
choices: that Jesus is the Son of God
that the Temple in Jerusalem would fall
that the Gentiles need not be circumcised
that the end of the world was at hand
context: Acts 9:20 (KJV): 'And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.' The reversal is total: the man sent to arrest the sect now stands in the same synagogue pulpits proclaiming its central claim.

question: Saul's preaching enraged the Damascus Jews, who set watchmen at the city gates day and night to kill him. To smuggle him out, the disciples took him up onto the city wall at night and lowered him down the outside. What did they lower him in?
context: Acts 9:25 (KJV): 'Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket.' The Greek word (spuris) is the big woven hamper used for grain or dung -- the same word used for the seven baskets left over after Jesus fed the four thousand. The dignity of the future apostle to the Gentiles starts with being lowered down a wall in a farm hamper.

question: Years later, writing to the Corinthians about his hardships, Paul boasts of the humiliating Damascus escape in his own words: 'through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands.' Which ruler's officer does Paul name as the one who had been trying to seize him?
context: 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 (KJV): 'In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands.' Aretas IV of Nabataea controlled Damascus in the mid-30s AD. Paul lists this escape at the bottom of a boast-list of beatings and shipwrecks, deliberately closing on the least heroic image he can find.

question: Paul retold his Damascus-road story three times in Acts. In the version he told years later before King Agrippa, the voice from heaven added one extra line beyond 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?' -- a farmer's saying that only shows up in this retelling. Which King James line did the voice add in the Agrippa version?
answer: 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks'
choices: 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks'
'my yoke is easy and my burden is light'
'the harvest is plenteous, but the labourers are few'
'thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder'
context: Acts 26:14 (KJV): 'And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.' A prick (or goad) was the pointed iron on the ploughman's stick used to steer an ox; a stubborn ox that kicked back only drove the iron in deeper. The extra line only appears in the Agrippa retelling.

question: The Ulster Cycle names one hero above all -- a young warrior of twenty-seven trained on the Isle of Shadow, master of the belly-spear, and the only Ulsterman who fights on when the rest of the province lies helpless under a curse. He dies at the end of the cycle's death-tale, the Aided Con Culainn. Who is this hero?
context: Conchobar and Fergus are kings of Ulster in the same cycle; Fionn belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: In the Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn'), the fatal war-band that closes in on the hero is drawn together by one western queen -- the same ruler whose great cattle-raid he had wrecked years before, and who has been waiting for revenge. Which queen raises the war-band?
context: Medb of Connacht had lost her champion Ferdiad and much of her army in the Tain Bo Cuailnge; she draws the sons of every man Cu Chulainn ever killed into one war-band. Emer is Cu Chulainn's own wife; Deirdre is from the Sons of Uisliu tale; Grainne belongs to the Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: The war-band Medb raises against Cu Chulainn has three factions, each with a personal reason to want the hero dead. One is a son avenging his father Cu Roi; another is Erc, avenging his father Cairbre Nia Fer. The third faction is not a warrior at all but the sorcerous grown offspring of a wizard Cu Chulainn had killed, working magic against him from the day they were born. Who is the third group?
choices: the Fomorian survivors of Mag Tuired
context: Cu Chulainn had killed the wizard Cailitin; his widow bore posthumous children specifically trained in sorcery for revenge. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn goes to his last fight already broken by a single trick the children of Cailitin have set for him on the road. An old crone by the wayside offers him a hospitality-meal, and by the ancient rule against refusing a host, he cannot say no. Under his geasa (personal taboos) he had sworn never to eat one meat in particular. What meat does the crone put in front of him?
context: His name means 'the Hound of Culann' -- eating dog is his forbidden meat. Refusing hospitality is equally forbidden, so the crone traps him coming and going. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: In the fight itself Lugaid mac Con Roi has three magical spears, and a prophecy attached to each: each spear will fell a king. The first spear does not kill Cu Chulainn. It kills 'the king of chariot-drivers' -- Cu Chulainn's own charioteer, the man who has ridden with him since the boyhood-deeds. What is the charioteer's name?
context: Loeg had floated the Gae Bolg down the ford for Cu Chulainn in the fight with Ferdiad; the first of Lugaid's three prophesied spears takes him now. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: The stone Cu Chulainn ties himself to is a real granite pillar, about ten feet tall, that still stands today in a field in County Louth -- the field was long known locally as 'the Field of Slaughter'. What is the stone called?
context: Clochafarmore stands in Rathiddy Townland near Knockbridge, County Louth. The Lia Fail is the coronation stone at Tara; the Blarney Stone is in Cork; the Turoe Stone is a decorated La Tene pillar in Galway. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Voices from the Dawn.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn, tied upright and dying, keeps his sword in his hand. Medb's warriors stand off at a distance and will not come near him. For days they wait for the sign that he is truly dead -- the arrival of a specific bird on his shoulder, associated all through his life with the war-goddess who had offered herself to him and been refused. Which bird finally lands?
context: The raven is the Morrigan, the war-goddess in bird-form; her landing to drink his blood is the confirmation his enemies have been waiting for. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: With the raven on the shoulder confirming the death, the leader of the war-band finally dares approach the standing corpse and cut off the head. The dying hero's sword falls from his hand as the blade comes down and takes a specific price from the killer. Who is the killer, and what does he lose?
answer: Lugaid mac Con Roi -- he loses his own hand
choices: Lugaid mac Con Roi -- he loses his own hand
Erc mac Cairpre -- he loses his shield-arm
Cet mac Matach -- he loses his sword-arm
Ailill mac Mata -- he loses his chariot-horse
context: The falling sword severs Lugaid's hand -- one final blow from a corpse. Wikipedia: Lugaid mac Con Roi.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's foster-brother tracks down the one-handed Lugaid to avenge the killing. To keep the fight fair he ties one of his own hands into his belt and fights Lugaid one-handed too. Even so he cannot finish it until his own horse takes a bite out of Lugaid's side. Who is the avenger?
context: Conall's fair-fight code -- matching Lugaid's missing hand -- is a standing image in the Ulster Cycle; the horse's bite is his own warhorse Dub-Sainglend. Wikipedia: Lugaid mac Con Roi.  (Legend.)

question: The single image of Cu Chulainn tied upright to a stone with a raven on his shoulder became the memorial image of modern Irish independence -- a bronze of this exact scene, modelled from life by an Irish sculptor in 1911-12, was installed by order of Eamon de Valera as the official public memorial to one specific rising. In which building was the statue installed, and for which rising?
answer: in Dublin's General Post Office, for the 1916 Easter Rising
choices: in Dublin's General Post Office, for the 1916 Easter Rising
in Kilmainham Gaol, for the 1798 Rebellion
in Dublin Castle, for the 1867 Fenian Rising
in Trinity College, for the 1803 Emmet Rising
context: Oliver Sheppard's 'The Death of Cuchulain' was unveiled at the GPO in Easter Week 1935 as the official memorial to the 1916 Rising -- the GPO having been the rebels' headquarters. Wikipedia: Oliver Sheppard.

question: Fresh from the fall of Jericho, Joshua sends about three thousand men against the small city of Ai and expects an easy second win. The men are routed and Joshua 7:5 counts the Israelite dead by exact number. How many men die at Ai?
context: Joshua 7:5 KJV: 'And the men of Ai smote of them about thirty and six men.' Six hundred belongs to Samson's slaughter with the jawbone; seventy is a common biblical count (the seventy elders, the seventy nations); twelve hundred is a plausible battle-loss but not the number Joshua 7 records. The thirty-six is famously SMALL -- and that is the sting.

question: Told by God that Israel has sinned and someone has taken of the accursed thing from Jericho, Joshua brings all the tribes near by lot -- then families, households, and man by man -- until the lot falls on one specific person. Who does the lot fall on?
context: Joshua 7:18 KJV: 'and Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.' Nadab is Aaron's son consumed by fire for offering strange incense; Korah leads the wilderness rebellion swallowed by the earth; Zimri son of Salu is pierced by Phinehas at Peor -- all three real biblical judgement-stories on other men.

question: Confessing before Joshua, Achan lists the three items he stole from the ruins of Jericho and hid under the earth in the midst of his tent: a goodly WHAT, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight?
context: Joshua 7:21 KJV: 'When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight... I coveted them, and took them.' Persian robes, Egyptian mantles, and Philistine cloaks all appear elsewhere in the Bible as spoil-types, but Achan's specific loot is Babylonish -- a name that would have meant 'foreign luxury from far Mesopotamia' to the hearer.

question: The second time Israel attacks Ai, Joshua hides an ambush of thirty thousand men behind the city, then draws the defenders out with a feigned flight. At the crucial moment God gives him a signal to trigger the ambush: 'Stretch out the WHAT that is in thy hand toward Ai' (Joshua 8:18)?
context: Joshua 8:18 KJV: 'Stretch out the spear that is in thy hand toward Ai; for I will give it into thine hand. And Joshua stretched out the spear that he had in his hand toward the city.' Moses's stretched-out staff parts the Red Sea and defeats Amalek at Rephidim, and Aaron's rod buds in the tabernacle -- both are real staff-signals in scripture, but at Ai the sign is Joshua's spear.

question: Years after Ai, defending the men of Gibeon against five Amorite kings, Joshua speaks to God in front of all Israel and asks for something no one had ever asked. He commands: 'Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of ____' (Joshua 10:12). Which valley does he name for the moon?
context: Joshua 10:12 KJV: 'Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.' Elah is where David meets Goliath; Sorek is where Samson meets Delilah; Kidron is the brook Jesus crosses to Gethsemane -- all real biblical valleys, all wrong for this scene. Ajalon is the paired half of the sun-and-moon verse and the half people always forget.

question: Joshua 10:13 pauses after the sun-and-moon miracle to cite a source book for the verse -- an outside record now lost. Which book does Joshua 10:13 name as its source for the sun standing still?
choices: the book of the Wars of the LORD
the book of the Chronicles of the Kings
context: Joshua 10:13 KJV: 'Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven.' The book of Jasher ('the Upright') is quoted twice in scripture (also 2 Samuel 1:18 for David's lament for Saul and Jonathan) and is now lost. The book of the Wars of the LORD is cited in Numbers 21; Chronicles-of-the-Kings is cited throughout Kings; Enoch is a later apocryphal book quoted in Jude.

question: A witch had kept Odysseus and his crew as her guests for a year, and when he finally asked to sail home to Ithaca she told him he could not go straight there -- first he had to sail to the edge of the world and speak with the dead. Which witch gave him these instructions?
context: Circe, who had turned Odysseus's men into pigs and then become his lover for a year on the island of Aeaea, gives him the sailing directions for the Halls of Hades: cross the river Ocean to the western edge of the world. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.487-540.  (Legend.)

question: At the edge of the underworld Odysseus dug a small pit and poured a mixture into it as an offering to the dead. What did the mixture contain?
answer: Milk with honey, then wine, then water
choices: Milk with honey, then wine, then water
context: The pit is a libation-trench: sweet milk with honey first, then sweet wine, then plain water, and sprinkled barley on top. Only after the libations does Odysseus cut the throats of the sacrifice animals into the same trench. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.24-28.  (Legend.)

question: Over the pit Odysseus cut the throats of two animals so their blood would pool in the trench. He had chosen them very carefully by their color. What kind of animals were they?
answer: A black ram and a black ewe
choices: A black ram and a black ewe
A pure white bull and a pure white heifer
A red rooster and a white dove
context: Black victims were the standard offering for the powers of the underworld, as white victims were for the sky gods. Circe herself had picked out this pair from her own flocks. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.571-574 and 11.34-36.  (Legend.)

question: The shades of the dead crowded around the trench, and Odysseus had to drive them back with his sword. Homer's dead have lost most of what they were in life, and until they had drunk the blood from the pit there was one thing no shade could do. What could no shade do until it had drunk from the pit?
context: Homer's underworld is a place of witless shades who drift without memory or voice; the black blood restores just enough of the living power to hold a conversation. It is the reason Odysseus can even question Tiresias. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.34-50.  (Legend.)

question: The very first shade to reach the pit had died only a day or two before. He was the youngest crewman, and he had drunkenly fallen off the roof of Circe's palace and broken his neck the night before they sailed. What was his name?
context: Elpenor is the youngest and least warlike of the crew; his body was left unburied in the rush to leave Aeaea. His shade begs Odysseus to sail back and bury him properly. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10.552-560 and 11.51-83.  (Legend.)

question: The unburied crewman begged Odysseus to sail back to Circe's island and give his body a proper burial. He also asked that one particular object be planted upright on the beach as his grave-marker. What object?
context: The oar as grave-marker becomes a small poem inside the epic: the tool a rower spent his life pulling, planted upright over him in the sand. Odysseus does go back and does this. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.71-78 and 12.8-15.  (Legend.)

question: The blind seer told Odysseus that even after he reached home he must one day take an oar and walk inland from Ithaca until he came to a country where the people had never seen the sea. He would know he had arrived when a stranger, seeing the oar on his shoulder, mistook it for what?
context: A winnowing fan is the shovel-shaped tool a farmer uses to toss threshed grain into the air so the wind carries off the chaff. When someone that far inland saw Odysseus's oar and called it a winnowing fan, he was to plant the oar there and sacrifice a ram, a bull and a boar to Poseidon -- and the sea god's anger would end. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.121-137.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus tried to embrace one of the shades at the pit -- a woman he had loved, dead since he sailed for Troy -- but she was only a shade and his arms met nothing. How many times did he try to hold her before he understood?
context: Three times he lunged forward to hold his mother Anticleia, and each time -- in the famous simile -- his arms passed through her 'like a shadow, or like a dream' (Lattimore). Anticleia, daughter of Autolycus, told her son she had died of grief waiting for his return. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.204-208 and 11.152-224.  (Legend.)

question: The shade of the greatest warrior of the Iliad, king now over all the dead, drank the blood and spoke to Odysseus. He said he would rather be alive in the meanest work on earth than hold that crown. What was the work he named?
answer: A hired hand of a landless man
choices: A hired hand of a landless man
A galley slave on a merchant's oar
A shepherd on a barren mountain
context: The line is Odyssey 11.489-491, in Lattimore's translation: 'I would rather follow the plow as thrall to another man, one with no land allotted him and not much to live on, than be a king over all the perished dead.' Achilles, who chose glory over long life in the Iliad, now saying he chose wrong. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.489-491.  (Legend.)

question: Another great Greek warrior's shade came to the pit and refused to drink or even speak. Odysseus called out and tried to make peace, but the shade only turned his back and walked away in silence. Which shade?
context: Ajax son of Telamon had lost the vote for Achilles's armor to Odysseus, and it had driven him mad and then to suicide -- he was still angry in death. His dignified silence at the pit is one of the most famous moments in Greek literature. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: In the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth a roving warrior-band lives in the wild forests of Ireland by season, sworn to defend the High King against foreign invaders in war and to hunt and feast in peace. Who leads this warrior-band?
context: Fionn mac Cumhaill (anglicised Finn McCool) leads the Clann Baiscne of Leinster, the elite branch of the Fianna, in rivalry with Goll mac Morna's Clann Morna of Connacht. Cu Chulainn is the hero of the earlier Ulster Cycle -- a different tradition. Nuada Silver-Arm is a Tuatha De Danann king; Conaire Mor is a High King from the Ulster-period tale Togail Bruidne Da Derga. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fianna.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn mac Cumhaill's warrior-band takes its name from the Old Irish word for a small band of hunter-warriors. The same word gives 19th-century Irish nationalists their name a thousand years later. What is the band called in Irish?
context: The Fianna are the warrior-hunter bands of Gaelic Ireland; the 19th-century Fenian Brotherhood of Irish republicans took the name deliberately, borrowing the ancient association with sworn warrior loyalty. The Aos Si are the fairy-folk; the Tuatha De Danann are the old gods; the Fomorians are the sea-born enemies of the gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fianna.  (Legend.)

question: The Fianna are not the king's regular soldiers. They live outside the ordinary property and marriage rules of tuath (clan) life. According to Geoffrey Keating's 17th-century account, they spend half the year in the wild hunting for their meat -- from Beltane (roughly May) until which other festival?
context: The Fianna are seasonal: from Beltane to Samhain (about May to November) they must live in the wild by hunting; from Samhain to Beltane they are quartered on the nobility. Lughnasadh is the harvest festival of Lugh; Imbolc marks the start of spring; the Newgrange solstice is Neolithic (millennia older than the Fianna). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fianna.  (Legend.)

question: The next entry-test is physical and brutal. The candidate is placed in a hole in the ground so deep it comes to the fold of his belt. He is given only two implements to defend himself. What are they?
answer: a shield and a fore-arm's length of hazel stick
choices: a shield and a fore-arm's length of hazel stick
a bronze sword and a leather sling
an iron helm and a wooden club
a spear and a woollen cloak
context: The pit-test forces the candidate to defend himself from the waist up while nine warriors cast spears at him. The hazel stick is not a weapon of offence -- it is a length just long enough to beat aside a hurled spear. Hazel is a symbolic wood in Irish tradition, associated with the Fianna's own hero Fionn (who burned his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge cooked over hazel-wood). Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: As the candidate stands buried to the belt in the pit with his shield and hazel stick, a number of warriors line up at some distance and hurl their spears at him all at once. If even one spear touches him, he fails. How many warriors, and from what distance?
answer: nine warriors from nine furrows' width away
choices: nine warriors from nine furrows' width away
three warriors from three ridges away
seven warriors from a single bow-shot
twelve warriors from the length of a chariot-run
context: Silva Gadelica gives the numbers: 'nine warriors, having nine spears, with a ten furrows' width betwixt them and him' -- the sources vary between nine and ten furrows, but nine warriors is fixed. Nine is a recurring sacred number in Irish story (the nine hazels of Segais, the nine daughters of Manannan). Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: The Fianna do not test for brute strength alone. In one running-trial the candidate is sent through a thick forest at full speed pursued by a war-band. Four small details of his person and gear were checked at the end of the run -- any one of them ruined would fail him. Which of these was one of the four?
answer: not a plait of his hair might come loose in the branches
choices: not a plait of his hair might come loose in the branches
not a fleck of mud might spatter his shield-boss
not a tuft of moss might cling to his cloak-hem
not a smear of sap might mark his bow-stave
context: The braided-hair test measures poise, silence, and control at speed: a runner who bulls through the wood loses his plaits in the branches and fails. The same trial also disqualifies him if he cracks a dry stick underfoot, if his weapons quiver in his hand, or if he is caught or wounded -- four tests inside one run. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)
