question: In the same forest run the candidate must also handle the branches themselves. He is required to leap any bough level with his brow, and to do one other thing without slowing his pace. What?
answer: stoop under any bough level with his knee
choices: stoop under any bough level with his knee
shatter any branch level with his ribs
sing a stave of poetry between each stride
unstring and restring his bow one-handed
context: Silva Gadelica lists it in a single breath: 'he jumped a stick level with his brow, and stooped to pass under one even with his knee.' The pair is not choose-one; both had to be performed, mid-run, without any drop in speed. The other choices are invented parallels for testing shape. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: Still in the forest run, at full pursuit, the candidate is required to perform one more feat that separates the Fianna from ordinary warriors: without breaking stride he must attend to his own injury. What must he do?
answer: pluck a thorn from his own foot without slowing
choices: pluck a thorn from his own foot without slowing
bind a bleeding wrist one-handed while running
shake the pine-needles out of his eyes without looking down
swap the shield to the wounded arm on the run
context: The thorn-in-the-foot test is the strangest and best-remembered detail of the Fianna tests: a runner in a Gaelic forest picks up thorns constantly, and the candidate must reach down at full speed, extract the thorn cleanly, and never lose a step. All three distractors are shaped from the same run but are not the sourced trial. Source: psychemedia.github.io/finn-resources/entry-tests.html.  (Legend.)

question: The full corpus of Fenian tales survives largely because two aged veterans of the Fianna outlive their band and, in the frame of a 12th-century text called the Colloquy of the Ancients, recite the old stories to a churchman newly arrived in Ireland. One of the two narrators is Fionn's own son, the poet Oisin. Who is the other -- Fionn's kinsman, remembered as the swift-footed of the Fianna?
context: Caoilte mac Ronain co-narrates the Acallam na Senorach ('Colloquy of the Ancients,' c. 1200) with Oisin -- the longest surviving work of medieval Irish literature at some 8,000 lines. Diarmuid dies young at the boar-hunt of Ben Bulben; Oscar is Oisin's own son and dies at the Battle of Gabhra; Goll mac Morna is the leader of the rival Connacht Fianna, not Fionn's kinsman. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acallam_na_Sen%C3%B3rach.  (Legend.)

question: The churchman who listens to Oisin and Caoilte's tales in the Colloquy of the Ancients is portrayed with unexpected warmth. He is not shown as hostile to the old ways; he weeps at the passing of the Fianna, and gives orders that Caoilte's stories be written down and preserved. Which Irish saint is this listener?
context: The Acallam na Senorach frames Oisin and Caoilte as pagan warrior-survivors telling Patrick the old tales place by place across Ireland. Columba is the 6th-century founder of Iona; Kevin is the 6th-century hermit of the Wicklow mountains; Malachy is the 12th-century reformer of the Irish church. Patrick is the traditional 5th-century missionary and the only Irish saint the compiler could plausibly frame as contemporary with the last Fianna survivors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acallam_na_Sen%C3%B3rach.  (Legend.)

question: The Lebor Gabala Erenn, the Irish Book of Invasions, lists six waves of settlers who came to Ireland one after another. Right before the Tuatha De Danann arrived, one older people held the whole island. Which people held Ireland in the wave just before the Tuatha De Danann?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the Fir Bolg are the fourth wave (after Cessair, Partholon, and Nemed), followed by the Tuatha De Danann as the fifth. The Milesians come sixth. The Fomorians are the monstrous sea-raiders, not a settler-wave. Danaans is a Greek term.  (Legend.)

question: The Fir Bolg were not a fresh people out of nowhere. They were descendants of an earlier wave of settlers who had been almost wiped out by Fomorian raids, reduced to a handful of survivors who fled the island. Whose descendants were the Fir Bolg?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: after Fomorian raids reduced the people of Nemed to a handful, the survivors scattered; the group that went to Greece became the Fir Bolg and returned. Partholon's people had died of plague long before. Cessair's people all drowned in the Flood. The Fomorians are the sea-raider enemies, not ancestors.  (Legend.)

question: Some scholars think the name 'Fir Bolg' does not really mean 'men of bags' at all, but is instead cognate with the name of a well-known Continental Celtic tribe -- the tribe that later gave its name to the modern country of Belgium. Which Continental Celtic tribe do these scholars link the Fir Bolg to?
context: One scholarly proposal reads 'Bolg' as cognate with Belgae, the Continental Celtic confederation Caesar fought in Gaul and whose name survives in Belgium. The Helvetii were the Swiss-plateau Celts. The Iceni were Boudica's tribe in Britain. The Averni (Arverni) were Vercingetorix's people in central Gaul.

question: The Lebor Gabala tells a folk-story to explain the odd name 'bag-men'. The Nemedian survivors ended up enslaved in a foreign land far to the south, forced by their masters to haul heavy leather sacks up bare rocky hillsides day after day. What did the sacks hold?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the enslaved Nemedians were made to carry leather bags of earth up onto bare rocky hillsides to build soil for the crops of their masters. When they escaped they used the very same bags to stitch hide-boats and sailed home to Ireland. Hence 'men of bags'.  (Legend.)

question: The Book of Invasions names the foreign country where the Fir Bolg were enslaved and made to haul the earth-bags. It is the same country to which many of the scattered Nemedians had fled after the Fomorian raids. In which land were the Fir Bolg supposedly enslaved?
context: Lebor Gabala Erenn: the Nemedian survivors went to Greece and were enslaved there for many generations before returning to Ireland as the Fir Bolg. Spain is where the Milesians (the sixth wave) are said to have come from. Egypt and Britain do not figure in this part of the tale.  (Legend.)

question: Once the Fir Bolg reached Ireland, their king Slainge mac Dela and his brothers made the country's most lasting division. They cut the whole island into a set number of provinces, called coigeda, one for each brother. Into how many provinces did the Fir Bolg divide Ireland?
context: The Fir Bolg divided Ireland into five coigeda ('fifths' -- the Irish word 'cuig' still means five today): Ulster, Leinster, Munster, Connacht, and Mide (the sacred centre). Modern Ireland has four provinces because Mide was gradually absorbed into Leinster in the medieval period.  (Legend.)

question: Of the five Fir Bolg provinces, four still exist by name today -- Ulster in the north, Leinster in the east, Munster in the south, and Connacht in the west. The fifth was the sacred one at the centre of the island, absorbed into Leinster in the Middle Ages. What was the fifth Fir Bolg province called?
context: Mide (modern Meath) was the sacred central fifth, where the High King's seat at Tara stood. Tara is a hill within Mide, not a province. Brega and Uisneach are smaller sacred sites in the region, not the province itself. Meath survives in Ireland today as a county, not a province.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann arrived in Ireland concealed in dark clouds, and the two peoples met in a great battle on a plain in what is now County Mayo. In this battle the Fir Bolg champion Sreng, in a single sword-stroke, cut off the right hand of the Tuatha king Nuada. What is that battle called?
context: The First Battle of Moytura (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga) was fought at Cong in County Mayo, where Sreng struck off Nuada's hand. Clontarf (1014) is history, not myth. The Second Battle of Moytura is later, against the Fomorians. Ventry is a battle of the Fianna cycle.  (Legend.)

question: The Fir Bolg lost the First Battle of Moytura, but the victorious Tuatha De Danann treated the defeated survivors with respect and offered them a single one of the five provinces to keep as their own for ever. To this day many families of that province proudly claim Fir Bolg ancestry. Which province did the Tuatha grant the Fir Bolg to keep?
context: The surviving Fir Bolg were granted their pick of the five provinces and chose Connacht, the west. In later legend many Connacht families proudly claim Fir Bolg ancestry -- the Fir Bolg do not vanish; they retreat west and quietly persist. Per the Lebor Gabala, Connacht had already been assigned to the brother Genann in the original fivefold division.

question: In the great Ulster-cycle epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the western queen who leads the cattle-raid against Cuchulainn rules from a huge earthen fortress in Roscommon -- the ancient royal seat that had belonged to the Fir Bolg when Connacht was their province. Which Connacht queen rules from that old Fir Bolg royal seat at Cruachan?
context: Queen Medb (Maeve) of Connacht rules from Cruachan / Rath Croghan in Roscommon, on the site of the old Fir Bolg capital. Deirdre is the tragic heroine of the Sons of Uisnech. Macha is an earlier goddess-queen of Ulster. Emer is Cuchulainn's wife, not a Connacht queen.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek poet Hesiod wrote a long poem to his brother Perses, who had cheated him out of his share of their father's inheritance. Buried inside that poem is a myth of how the world grew worse across a series of ages, one after another, each race of mortals worse than the last. How many ages of mortals does Hesiod count in the myth?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 106-201. Hesiod counts five ages: Gold, Silver, Bronze, the Age of Heroes, and Iron. Four are named for metals; the Age of Heroes breaks the metal pattern. Centuries later Ovid compressed the schema down to four (dropping the Heroes); the biblical Book of Daniel 2.31-45 has a four-metal decline too, in Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod's first age of mortals lived like gods -- no toil, no old age, no winter, feasting all their lives in perpetual spring. Which god was king of heaven in this happiest first age?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 109-120. The first age was under Cronus, before Zeus overthrew him. Uranus is even earlier, the primal sky castrated by Cronus. Hades has always been king of the dead, never of heaven. When the golden race died out they did not go to Hades but became daimones -- benevolent spirits watching over the living.  (Legend.)

question: The second age was named for a different metal, and its mortals had a strange lifespan: they lived a hundred years as little children under their mothers, and only a short foolish adulthood before dying. For what metal was this second age named?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 127-142. The Silver race refused to sacrifice to the gods, and Zeus (now king in place of Cronus) buried them beneath the earth in anger at their impiety. The pattern of the metals -- gold, silver, and then bronze -- is a sequence of decline, each race worse than the last.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod says the third race, the Bronze Age race, had bronze weapons and bronze armour and bronze tools -- and one other thing made of bronze that no later people had. What else did the Bronze Age race have made of bronze?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 143-155. The bronze race even lived in bronze houses -- 'there was no black iron yet' in the world, Hesiod says. They were terrible warriors born from ash-trees, and destroyed themselves by their own violence, going down nameless into the dark house of Hades.  (Legend.)

question: When the heroes died, some went down to Hades, but Hesiod says the best of them were sent instead to a place at the edge of the world Ocean, where the fields give grain three times a year and Cronus is king again. What is Hesiod's name for that place?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 166-173. The Isles of the Blessed lie at the edge of Ocean; there Cronus (dethroned by Zeus) reigns quietly and the earth yields three harvests a year. The Fields of Aaru are the Egyptian afterlife; Persephone rules the shades in Hades; the Halls of Bragi (or Valhalla) are Norse. Later Greeks called the same place the Elysian Fields.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod says he lives in the FIFTH and worst age -- his own present -- and he wishes he had died before it or been born after it. His fifth age is named for a hard, dull metal that was still new in his day. For what metal is Hesiod's fifth age named?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 174-179. Iron is the fifth age, our own. Steel as a distinct alloy is not named by Hesiod; clay is Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue in the biblical Book of Daniel; ash is the material of the Bronze race, born from ash-trees. Iron for Hesiod is the metal of toil and grief -- workaday, useful, ordinary, without splendour.  (Legend.)

question: Hesiod ends the myth with a picture of the end of the Iron Age. Two goddesses -- one the personification of shame that holds a person back from wrong, the other of righteous indignation that falls upon a wrong-doer -- wrap their faces in white robes and leave the earth for Olympus. What are the names of these two departing goddesses?
context: Hesiod, Works and Days 197-201. Aidos is reverence-that-restrains from within; Nemesis is righteous indignation from without. Themis and Dike are the older law and justice; Hera and Hebe are queen of gods and cupbearer; Iris and Nike are messenger and victory. When Aidos and Nemesis go, Hesiod says, mortals have no defence at all against evil.  (Legend.)

question: Centuries after Hesiod, the Roman poet Ovid retold the ages of the world in the opening book of the Metamorphoses -- a straight fall from paradise to violence -- and left one of Hesiod's five ages out of the sequence entirely. Which age did Ovid leave out?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-150. Ovid kept the four metal ages -- gold, silver, bronze, iron -- but dropped Hesiod's inserted Age of Heroes, since he was telling a straight decline from paradise to violence. The biblical Book of Daniel 2.31-45 also has four (Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue: gold head, silver breast, bronze belly, iron legs with feet of iron and clay). Only Hesiod has five.

question: Before any of the six waves of settlers arrived in Ireland, a dark race already lived on the rocky islands and coasts and made war on every incoming people -- the primordial enemies of Partholon, Nemed, and finally the Tuatha De Danann. What are they called?
context: The Fomorians (Old Irish Fomoire) are Ireland's ancient monstrous race in the Book of Invasions. The Fir Bolg are the fourth wave of settlers (defeated by the Tuatha De at the First Battle of Moytura); the Milesians are the human sixth wave who displace the Tuatha De; 'the Danaans' is another name for the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: The Book of Invasions describes the Fomorians as MISSHAPEN sea-monster people. In the most common description a Fomorian warrior has only one of each of three body parts a whole man would have two of. Which three?
answer: one eye, one arm, one leg
choices: one eye, one arm, one leg
one hand, one foot, one ear
one shoulder, one hip, one knee
one lip, one nostril, one tooth
context: Wikipedia and Book of Invasions tradition: many Fomorians in the primary tales have one eye, one arm, and one leg -- a mirror-image of the Irish blemish-taboo that put Nuada off the throne when he lost a single hand. Some Fomorians are also given human bodies with goat heads.  (Legend.)

question: Under the Fomorian chief Conand, who ruled from his tower on Tory Island, the third wave of Irish settlers (the people of Nemed) were forced to hand over a crushing tribute every year on the eve of Samhain (November 1). What fraction of their children and grain did they have to give?
context: The Book of Invasions and the Conand-mythology tradition: the Nemedians paid two-thirds of their children, grain, and cattle to Conand's Tower on Tory Island every Samhain. The tribute is the mythic charter for Samhain as the sinister half of the Celtic year. One-half, one-tenth, and nine-tenths are the wrong fractions.  (Legend.)

question: The Nemedians eventually rose against Conand's tribute, stormed his tower on Tory Island, and were nearly wiped out in the counter-attack -- only a tiny remnant survived the Fomorian reprisal to leave Ireland. How many Nemedian survivors are named in tradition?
context: The Book of Invasions: after the storming of Conand's Tower and the Fomorian counter-attack, only thirty Nemedians survived, and they fled Ireland in different directions -- the ancestors, in tradition, of the Fir Bolg and (through Britain) of the Tuatha De themselves.  (Legend.)

question: Two of the greatest Tuatha De heroes were themselves HALF-FOMORIAN by blood -- born from a mixed union between Tuatha and Fomorian. Bres, the deposed king, was one. Which other famous Tuatha De hero also had a Fomorian mother (Ethniu, Balor's daughter)?
context: Lugh's father Cian was Tuatha De and his mother Ethniu was Balor of the Evil Eye's daughter, locked in the crystal tower on Tory Island. So the young champion who kills Balor at Moytura is killing his own grandfather. Bres, the Dagda, Ogma, and Nuada are all full Tuatha De by ancestry -- only Bres and Lugh have the mixed line.  (Legend.)

question: The pattern of the Tuatha De vs the Fomorians -- a younger race of order-bringing gods overthrowing an older wilder race they must fight and eventually die against -- has close cousins in other pillars of Western myth. In NORSE myth, which race plays the Fomorian role against the Aesir?
context: The Jotnar (frost-giants and fire-giants of Jotunheim, Muspelheim, and elsewhere) are the Norse structural parallel to the Fomorians -- an older, wilder race the Aesir must fight and eventually die against at Ragnarok. The Vanir are a second god-family the Aesir reconciled with; the Einherjar are Odin's dead warrior host in Valhalla; the Alfar are the elves.  (Legend.)

question: The war between the Tuatha De and the Fomorians ended in one climactic battle in County Sligo where Lugh killed his grandfather Balor with a sling-stone and the Fomorian host was broken and driven into the sea forever. Which battle?
context: Cath Maige Tuired ('the battle of the plain of pillars') is the great mythological showdown that ends the Fomorian threat. The FIRST Battle of Moytura was Tuatha De vs Fir Bolg (where Nuada lost his hand). The Battle of Tailtiu is where the Tuatha De later fall to the Milesians; the Battle of the Boyne (1690) and Clontarf (1014) are historical Irish battles, not mythic.  (Legend.)

question: Traditional Aran Islanders credited the Fomorians with raising the great stone forts that still stand on the sea-cliffs of the largest Aran island -- rings of drystone wall on the very edge of the ocean, hundreds of feet above the waves. Which fort is the most famous of these Fomorian-attributed ruins?
context: Dun Aengus (Dun Aonghasa) on Inishmore in the Aran Islands is a semicircle of drystone rampart on a cliff-edge 300 feet above the Atlantic; local tradition assigns it to the Fomorians, though archaeology dates it to the Iron Age. Dun Aluinne is an inland ringfort; the Cashel of the Kings is the seat of the kings of Munster; the Grianan of Aileach is a hilltop ringfort near Derry.  (Legend.)

question: When the Tuatha De Danann arrived in Ireland, the tales say they brought a sacred set of magical objects with them -- one from each of the northern cities of learning where their druid-teachers had trained them. In every medieval Irish source the set is counted exactly the same way. How many treasures do they bring?
context: The Four Treasures are one of the great numbered sets of Western myth, alongside the Norse dwarves' six treasures and the twelve Instruments of the Passion. Four is the ritual number of Irish myth -- four cities (Falias, Gorias, Findias, Murias), four teachers, four objects, and later four virtues of kingship attached to them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The Lia Fail on the Hill of Tara is not just a monument -- in the old tales it is a test. When a claimant to the High Kingship of Ireland stands upon it, the stone will do one particular thing if the claimant is the rightful king. If he is a pretender, silence. What does the stone do for the true king?
answer: It cries out with a loud shriek
choices: It cries out with a loud shriek
It splits in two beneath his feet
It gives off a warm golden glow
It sinks a hand's breadth into the ground
context: The Lia Fail's shriek beneath the rightful king is the founding motif of Irish sacred kingship: sovereignty is not chosen but recognised. The same motif is echoed in the Arthurian Sword in the Stone, and (say Scots tradition) survives in the coronation stone taken to Scone and later to Westminster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lia_F%C3%A1il.  (Legend.)

question: One of the Four Treasures is a weapon so hungry for battle that it burns red-hot from its own thirst. Between fights, its wielder must plunge it into a cauldron of dark blood -- or milk -- to still it and cool it. It has never been beaten in any battle it was carried into, and no cast of it has ever missed. To whom does this weapon belong?
context: The Spear of Lugh is also called Gai Assail or Slea Bua ('the victory spear'), and it is the weapon Lugh will use to kill his grandfather Balor of the Evil Eye at the Second Battle of Moytura. Nuada owns the Sword of Light, the Dagda owns the club Lorg Mor and the cauldron, and Manannan owns his own sword Fragarach -- all real Tuatha De weapons, but none matches the never-missing thirsty spear. Source: morgynbard.com/post/the-gift-of-the-four-treasures.  (Legend.)

question: Lugh's spear -- the one that burned red-hot from its own thirst and had to be quenched between fights in a cauldron of blood or milk -- was brought to Ireland from one of the four northern otherworld cities where the Tuatha De trained. From which city did the Spear come?
context: The four cities are always listed in the same order in the medieval sources, each paired to one treasure: Falias (stone), Gorias (spear), Findias (sword), Murias (cauldron). Kids will guess the spear-and-sword pair swapped; the primary text keeps spear at Gorias and sword at Findias. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The Cauldron of the Dagda carries ONE promise attached to it in the medieval sources -- a fixed formula preserved in Cath Maige Tuired and the Lebor Gabala Erenn. What does the formula say?
answer: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied
choices: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied
No man who ate from it could ever be poisoned
No warrior who tasted it could be killed by iron
No woman who tasted it could bear a mortal child
context: The formula, straight from Lebor Gabala Erenn and Cath Maige Tuired, is that no company ever leaves the cauldron unsatisfied. The other three would have been fine legendary powers, but none of them is the promise the sources carry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.

question: Each of the four northern cities the Tuatha De studied in had its own druid-teacher, and the medieval sources preserve all four teacher-names. Morfessa taught in Falias, Uiscias taught in Findias, Semias taught in Murias. Who taught in the city of Gorias, the city that gave up the Spear?
context: The four teachers in the medieval formula: Morfessa, Esras, Uiscias, Semias -- obscure druid-masters whose names are preserved only in this one glossed passage. Amergin is the Milesian druid, Cathbad is Conchobar's druid in the Ulster Cycle, Mog Ruith is the great blind sorcerer of Munster -- three real druid-names of Irish tradition, but from other cycles. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Treasures_of_the_Tuatha_D%C3%A9_Danann.  (Legend.)

question: The 'stone that cries out under the true king' motif on the Hill of Tara did not stay in Ireland. Scottish tradition holds that a stone said to be the Lia Fail was carried east to be used at the coronation of Scottish kings, and later carried again to England by Edward I to sit beneath the coronation chair of English monarchs at Westminster. What is this stone called in English?
context: The Stone of Scone (also called the Stone of Destiny) was taken by Edward I in 1296 and set beneath the wooden coronation chair at Westminster Abbey, where it stayed until 1996. Scots and Irish scholars have disputed for a thousand years whether it is really the Lia Fail. The Blarney Stone (Cork) is a real kissing-luck stone; the Kingston Coronation Stone is the real Anglo-Saxon coronation stone at Kingston-upon-Thames where seven Saxon kings were crowned; the Turoe Stone is a real La Tene decorated stone in County Galway -- three real famous stones of Britain and Ireland, each with a different purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_of_Scone.

question: The Four Treasures do not just appear in a stray gloss -- they are named together in the opening passage of one of the two great Mythological-Cycle sagas of Ireland, the saga that also carries the porridge scene, the harp scene, and the killing of Balor. Which saga opens with the four cities and their treasures?
answer: Cath Maige Tuired ('The Second Battle of Moytura')
choices: Cath Maige Tuired ('The Second Battle of Moytura')
the Tain Bo Cuailnge ('The Cattle Raid of Cooley')
Togail Bruidne Da Derga ('The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel')
the Acallam na Senorach ('Colloquy of the Ancients')
context: Cath Maige Tuired opens with the four cities and their gifts; the Tain is the Ulster Cycle war-epic (Cuchulainn's world); Togail Bruidne Da Derga is the tragic-king tale of Conaire Mor; the Acallam na Senorach is the huge Fionn-cycle framing dialogue between Oisin and St Patrick. Source: celt.ucc.ie/published/T300010.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the hero Cu Chulainn carries one signature weapon that Queen Medb's warriors dread above every sword he owns -- a spear given to him by his teacher on the Isle of Shadow, and the weapon he saves for the fights he is losing. What is the name of Cu Chulainn's signature spear?
context: Birgha is Fionn mac Cumhaill's spear in the Fenian Cycle; Areadbhar is Lugh's spear in later Tuatha De Danann lists; the Gae Assail is another spear-name in the same Tuatha tradition. The Gae Bolg is Cu Chulainn's alone. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Before he could carry the Gae Bolg, Cu Chulainn spent years on the Isle of Shadow (Alba) being trained in every warrior's feat by a female fighting-master who tutored heroes from across the Irish world. Who trained him and gave him the spear?
context: Scathach ('the Shadowy One') ran a school for heroes on Alba; Cu Chulainn and his foster-brother Ferdiad both studied with her, but Scathach taught the Gae Bolg feat to Cu Chulainn alone. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg, Ferdiad.  (Legend.)

question: The Gae Bolg is not thrown from the hand like an ordinary spear. Scathach's rule is strict: the caster must stand in the current of a ford, and the charioteer floats the shaft down the stream on the water so the warrior can catch it -- not with his hand, but with a specific part of his body. From what part of the body is the Gae Bolg cast?
answer: from between the toes of the foot
choices: from between the toes of the foot
from the shoulder in an underhand hurl
from the crook of the elbow
from the mouth as a warcry-launch
context: The Gae Bolg is caught between the toes as it floats past and kicked up at the enemy -- a technique some scholars suspect began as spear-fishing. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: The horror of the Gae Bolg is not the throw. It is what the spear does the moment its tip breaks the enemy's skin. The point enters like an ordinary javelin, one small wound -- and then, inside the body, it changes. What does the Gae Bolg do once it is inside the wound?
answer: it opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb
choices: it opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb
it bursts into a cold blue flame
it splits the enemy's shadow from his body
it calls its twin spear across the battlefield to strike
context: The medieval text says the spear enters as a single wound but opens into thirty barbs inside the flesh, filling every limb and joint. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Once the Gae Bolg has opened inside a body, the barbs make ordinary extraction impossible. Any warrior who tries to pull the spear back out through the entry wound only hooks the barbs deeper. In the Tain Bo Cuailnge, how is the Gae Bolg actually retrieved from the corpse?
answer: the flesh has to be cut open around it
choices: the flesh has to be cut open around it
it dissolves out of the wound after a day
the wielder whistles it back through the air
it must be pulled by two horses at once
context: In the Tain, Cu Chulainn's charioteer has to come forward after the killing of Ferdiad and cut the body open to take the Gae Bolg back -- the extraction kills the enemy a second time. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: During the great cattle-raid of Cooley, Queen Medb of Connacht wants Cu Chulainn dead, but she cannot beat him with an ordinary champion. So she uses bribes, shame, and her daughter Findabair to ply an Irish champion with drink and force him to fight Cu Chulainn at the ford. Which warrior does Medb push into the ford?
context: Ferdiad was Cu Chulainn's foster-brother -- they had trained together under Scathach and were equal in every feat but two. Wikipedia: Ferdiad.  (Legend.)

question: Ferdiad and Cu Chulainn had studied under Scathach on the Isle of Shadow, drilled identically in every feat but two. Cu Chulainn's exclusive was the Gae Bolg. Ferdiad's matching exclusive was a bodily gift Scathach never gave Cu Chulainn -- the one thing that let Ferdiad hold the ford against him for three days. What was Ferdiad's exclusive advantage?
answer: his horn-skin that ordinary weapons could not pierce
choices: his horn-skin that ordinary weapons could not pierce
his ability to fight in the warp-spasm ristrad
his geis against striking a foster-brother
his chariot-team that could not be outrun
context: The Tain says the two foster-brothers were equal in all martial feats save two: Cu Chulainn alone knew the Gae Bolg, and Ferdiad alone had impenetrable horn-skin. It is why every ordinary weapon Cu Chulainn tried in the ford failed and why the Gae Bolg had to come out. Wikipedia: Ferdiad, Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: On the last day of the ford-duel, Ferdiad has beaten every ordinary weapon Cu Chulainn has and Cu Chulainn is losing. He calls out to his charioteer for the one weapon he has been holding back. In the water of the ford, standing mid-current, who is the charioteer that floats the Gae Bolg down the stream to him?
context: Loeg is Cu Chulainn's lifelong charioteer; he floats the Gae Bolg down the current in the ford and later has to cut Ferdiad open to take the spear back out. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.  (Legend.)

question: Standing over the body he has just killed with the Gae Bolg, Cu Chulainn breaks into a long formal lament for the foster-brother Medb's war has forced him to destroy. In the Tain, the first line of his lament is 'Ah, Ferdiad, betrayed to death. / Our last meeting, oh, how sad!' What is the third line of that opening?
choices: 'The gods have set us at swords.'
context: The lament turns the whole ford-episode from a victory into a wound -- Cu Chulainn is broken by having killed the brother Scathach's fosterage bound to him. Wikipedia: Ferdiad.  (Legend.)

question: The 'bolg' element in the spear's name has never been settled by Old Irish scholarship. The medieval glossators offer at least three competing readings that keep resurfacing in modern editions of the Tain. Which reading is NOT one of the traditional Old Irish glosses for 'bolg' in 'Gae Bolg'?
context: 'Bag' (a bag-full of barbs), 'notch or gap', and 'belly' are the recurring medieval glosses; Eric Hamp reconstructs Proto-Celtic for 'spear of mortal pain'. The sea-monster-bone origin -- the beast of Coinchend -- is a modern addition by Lady Gregory in her 1902 'Cuchulain of Muirthemne', not a medieval gloss. Wikipedia: Gae Bulg.

question: In the Ulster Cycle a druid may lay a magical prohibition on a hero at birth or on any warrior later in life -- a single act the man must never do, on pain of ruin. Every hero has his own personalised set of these prohibitions, and cleverness in setting one against another is how enemies in the Irish tales bring a great warrior down. What is the Irish word for such a prohibition?
context: Plural geasa (roughly 'gaysh' / 'gaysha'). Fian = a warrior-band (compare fianna); fidchell = the Irish board game; filid = a poet. Wikipedia: Geis.  (Legend.)

question: The champion of the Ulster Cycle takes his hero-name as a boy after killing the guard-dog of a smith and offering to serve as its replacement until a new hound can be raised. From then on he is called by a name that means 'the Hound' of that smith. Who is the hero?
context: The smith was Culann; the name Cu Chulainn is literally 'the Hound of Culann'. Wikipedia: Cu Chulainn.  (Legend.)

question: In the Aided Con Culainn ('The Death of Cu Chulainn') the war-band closing in on the hero is joined by a set of sorcerous siblings -- posthumous children of a wizard Cu Chulainn had killed years before, raised specifically by their mother to be trained in the magic that could undo him. Which family?
context: Cailitin's widow bore his children after his death and trained them in sorcery for revenge. The sons of Uisliu belong to Deirdre's tale; the children of Lir were turned into swans; the Dagda's daughters are from a different cycle. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn.  (Legend.)

question: Riding to his last battle Cu Chulainn passes an open fire at the roadside where three old crones -- each blind in the left eye -- are cooking a piece of meat and call him over to share it. Both the fire and the spits the meat turns on are cut from the same sacred tree, the wood the old Irish tales most often name for druidic work and protection against ill. What wood is it?
context: The Aided Con Culainn specifies the crones' fire is of rowan sticks and their spits are of rowan -- rowan (caorthann) is the Irish tree of druidic power. Ash is Yggdrasil in the Norse tradition; oak is the druids' great tree but not the wood keyed in this tale; hazel is Fionn's Salmon-of-Knowledge tree. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Seven Miles of Steel Thistles blog.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn accepts the meal from the three crones and takes the piece of roast meat in one hand. From that moment the strength drains out of the arm that held it, and out of the whole side of his body served by that arm. It is the side he will need most against the war-band waiting for him. Which side goes dead?
answer: his left side, from shoulder to fingertip
choices: his left side, from shoulder to fingertip
his right side, from shoulder to fingertip
context: He took the meat in his left hand; the whole left side goes. He also puts the bone down on his left thigh and the thigh is struck through too. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Steel Thistles.  (Legend.)

question: The Irish idea of a personalised, druid-laid magical prohibition has cousins in the other great heroic cultures. In Greek epic the corresponding word means an impersonal share of destiny apportioned to a mortal by the gods -- the same word used for Achilles's choice between a short glorious life and a long dim one. What is the Greek word?
context: Norse wyrd is the parallel in that tradition. Arete = excellence; hubris = overreach; kleos = fame. Wikipedia: Moira; Geis.

question: Not every Irish hero brought down by his prohibitions belongs to the Ulster Cycle. The High King who dies in the tale Togail Bruidne Da Derga ('The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel') has an unusually long list of geasa -- and on a single unlucky night a chain of unavoidable acts breaks EVERY ONE of them before he reaches the hostel where he will die. Who is the king?
context: Togail Bruidne Da Derga is one of the great tragic sagas of the Mythological Cycle. Cormac mac Airt is a later High King associated with wisdom-tales; Nuada is a Tuatha De Danann king; Diarmait mac Cerbaill is a historical-legendary king. Wikipedia: Togail Bruidne Da Derga.

question: The Fenian Cycle has its own famous geis-tale: a young warrior of the Fianna is placed under a compulsion he cannot refuse when a princess named Grainne, on the night of her betrothal-feast to Fionn mac Cumhaill, corners him and lays her geis upon him to run away with her instead. Which warrior does she trap?
context: The tale is Toraiocht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne, 'The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne'. Oisin is Fionn's son; Caoilte is Fionn's runner; Goll is Fionn's rival. Wikipedia: Toraiocht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne.  (Legend.)

question: The Aided Con Culainn survives in an Old Irish version preserved in a specific twelfth-century manuscript compiled at a Cistercian abbey in County Laois -- the same great codex that preserves much of the Ulster Cycle, the Fenian Cycle, and one of the two main recensions of the Tain Bo Cuailnge. Which manuscript?
context: Lebor Laignech, compiled c.1160 at Terryglass/Oughaval. The Book of Kells is a gospel-book; Ballymote is a later (14th c.) codex; the Cathach is a 6th-c. psalter. Wikipedia: Aided Con Culainn; Book of Leinster.

question: On the north coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland, some 40,000 hexagonal stone columns march down out of the cliff and into the sea in a broad, flat pavement wide enough to walk on. Tourists have visited it since the 17th century, and UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1986. What is this famous stretch of basalt columns called?
context: The Irish name is Clochan an Aifir. Geologically the columns are the top of a 60-million-year-old cooled lava flow. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.

question: In the folk-legend attached to the Antrim basalt columns, the pavement is not a lava flow at all -- it is the work of a single builder who tore up rocks and set them one against another all the way across the sea toward Scotland, so he could walk over dry-shod and fight a rival on the other shore. Which Irish hero does the folk-tale name as the builder?
context: Cu Chulainn is the hero of the Ulster Cycle; Lugh is a Tuatha De Danann warrior; Conall Cernach is a foster-brother of Cu Chulainn. In the folk-tale of the causeway Fionn is treated as a full-sized giant, which drifts from the manuscript Fenian Cycle where he is a human-scale chief of the Fianna. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: In the folk-tale of the Antrim basalt columns, the reason Fionn mac Cumhaill builds his causeway across the sea in the first place is that a rival on the other shore has been shouting insults across the water for months, and Fionn wants to settle it in person. Where does the rival live, and what is his name?
answer: in Scotland -- his name is Benandonner
choices: in Scotland -- his name is Benandonner
in Wales -- his name is Bran the Blessed
in the Isle of Man -- his name is Manannan mac Lir
in Norway -- his name is Ymir
context: Benandonner (the Red Man) shouts across the North Channel; Fionn accepts the challenge and starts building. Bran the Blessed is Welsh; Manannan is Irish; Ymir is Norse. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn mac Cumhaill has torn up rocks and built his causeway most of the way across the North Channel when he catches sight of his Scottish rival up close for the first time. He stops in mid-crossing, looks properly, and runs. What has he just realised?
answer: the rival is far bigger than he is
choices: the rival is far bigger than he is
the rival has been dead for a year
the rival's causeway is finished first
the rival is his own long-lost brother
context: Fionn had assumed he was the bigger giant; halfway across he sees the size of Benandonner and turns for home to think. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: Fionn has run home to Ireland with the Scottish giant close behind him, and he has no plan and no time. His clever wife -- usually named Oonagh, though some tellings call her Sadhbh -- takes charge, tells him to lie still and not speak a word, and prepares the household to greet the rival at the door. Under what identity is she going to pass Fionn off?
answer: her infant son sleeping in the cradle
choices: her infant son sleeping in the cradle
the family's dog-boy tending the hearth
a dead uncle laid out for the wake
a deaf servant sweeping the floor
context: The whole trick turns on the giant thinking he is looking at a baby. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: When Benandonner arrives at Fionn's door roaring for a fight, Fionn's wife greets him politely, says Fionn is out hunting, and sets the Scottish giant down for tea and fresh loaves while he waits. The loaves she serves him are not ordinary bread -- she has baked something hard inside each one that makes the giant crunch and grimace, and lets her boast about how tough the men of the house must be. What has she baked into the loaves?
context: In the folk-tale these are iron griddles or 'bakestones' baked right into the bread -- the whole point is that if the men here eat bread this hard, the father must be enormous. Cited in Irish Central and Irish Road Trip retellings.  (Legend.)

question: Benandonner, sitting in Fionn's kitchen with his teeth ringing from the griddle-bread, finally notices the enormous 'baby' asleep in the cradle by the fire. He stares. He does the arithmetic. Then he panics and runs. What arithmetic did he just do that sends him bolting for the door?
answer: if the baby is this size, the father must be monstrous
choices: if the baby is this size, the father must be monstrous
if the baby is this loud, the neighbours will come
if the baby is this hungry, the food will not last
if the baby is this ugly, the mother must be his match
context: That inference -- father-must-be-worse -- is the whole hinge of the trick. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: Benandonner has fled back onto the causeway toward Scotland with Fionn (he thinks) about to come out of the house after him. He does not just run. As he runs he does something specific to the stone pavement under his feet, and it is this action that the folk-tale uses to explain a real fact about the modern basalt columns. What does Benandonner do to the causeway as he flees?
answer: he tears up the stones behind him as he goes
choices: he tears up the stones behind him as he goes
he sinks the middle spans under the sea
he sets fire to the wooden pilings
he calls a storm down to wash it away
context: The tearing-up is the folk-tale's answer to why the real basalt formation survives only at the two ends of the crossing and not in the middle. Wikipedia: Giant's Causeway.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus answers the lawyer's question with a story. He sets it on a specific road: a man travelling downhill 'from Jerusalem to _______' when he is jumped by bandits and left half dead. What is the destination city in Luke 10:30?
context: Luke 10:30 KJV: 'A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves.' The word 'down' is literal -- Jerusalem sits at about 2,300 feet above sea level and Jericho at about 1,300 feet below, so the road drops more than 3,000 feet in some seventeen miles of desert. Bethany is a village of the same descent but only two miles from Jerusalem; Emmaus is the town of the post-resurrection walk (Luke 24); Nazareth is Jesus's home village up in Galilee, in the wrong direction entirely.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus sets his parable on a real seventeen-mile road, notorious in his day for bandit ambushes -- narrow, twisting through desert canyons, riddled with caves. The road drops from Jerusalem down to Jericho -- but by how much in elevation over those seventeen miles?
context: Jerusalem sits at roughly 2,300 feet above sea level; Jericho, near the Dead Sea, lies about 1,300 feet below -- so the road drops around 3,300 to 3,600 feet in about seventeen miles of desert wadis. The steep descent, isolated terrain, and cliffside caves made it a bandit-country classic. In Arabic the pass carried the name tal`at ed-damm, 'Ascent of Blood', from its ambush reputation; Jerome, writing from Bethlehem in the fourth century, notes the same.

question: Two respectable travellers come along the road before help arrives. The first is a temple priest, who 'passed by on the other side' (Luke 10:31). Luke 10:32 (KJV) names the second traveller, also heading away from the temple. Who was he?
context: Luke 10:32 KJV: 'And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side.' The Levites were the tribe of Israel set apart for temple service under the priesthood. The point of the pairing is that Jesus is naming the two most respectable religious figures of the day -- the men most trained in the law that the lawyer just quoted -- as the ones who refuse to help. Pharisees, scribes, and temple guards all appear elsewhere in the gospels but are not in this parable.  (Legend.)

question: The third traveller stops. He belongs to a group Jesus's Jewish audience despised so deeply that the lawyer, hearing the story, will refuse even to speak the group's name aloud at the end. Luke 10:33 (KJV) names them. Who were they?
context: Luke 10:33 KJV. The Samaritans kept the first five books of Moses but rejected Jerusalem as the true worship-place, holding to Mount Gerizim instead. John Hyrcanus destroyed their Gerizim temple in 109 BCE; a few decades later, at Passover around 8 CE, Josephus (Antiquities 18.29-30) says some Samaritans crept into the Jerusalem Temple courts at night and scattered human bones, desecrating the sanctuary. Sadducees, Idumeans, and Herodians were other first-century Judean factions, but they are not the group at the centre of this parable.  (Legend.)

question: After bandaging the wounded man's cuts, the Samaritan does one more inconvenient thing before the inn. Luke 10:34 (KJV) names in three plain words what he set the man upon -- giving up his own transport to do it. What did he put the wounded man on?
context: Luke 10:34 KJV: 'and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.' 'Beast' in KJV translates the Greek 'ktenos' -- a generic word for a mount, most likely a donkey or a mule; the gospel does not name the species, but the point is that it was his and he gave it up. Carrying on his back would be Christ-on-the-shoulders imagery from a different parable (Luke 15:5, the lost sheep); a cloak on the ground is the Palm Sunday scene; the parable does not use a cart.  (Legend.)

question: In the morning, before leaving, the Samaritan hands the innkeeper coins to cover the wounded man's care. Luke 10:35 in KJV calls the payment 'two pence' -- but 'pence' translates a specific coin-name behind the KJV English. What coin does the Greek text name?
context: The KJV 'penny/pence' consistently renders the Greek denarion -- the standard Roman silver piece, roughly a labourer's daily wage. Two denarii were roughly two days' wages -- enough for perhaps a week or two of room and board at a modest inn. The drachma was a Greek silver coin; the shekel was Jewish temple currency; the talent was an enormous unit (about 6,000 denarii), the weight-based sum in the parable of the talents (Matthew 25). The Samaritan does not pay a fortune. He pays enough to start, and promises more.  (Legend.)

question: The Samaritan does not just leave money and go -- he adds a promise that is the sharpest detail in the whole parable. Luke 10:35 (KJV) has him tell the innkeeper: 'Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will _____'. Which word closes the promise?
context: Luke 10:35 KJV in full: 'Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.' The wounded man now has an open account at the inn, with a stranger's word for the balance -- unlimited care, guaranteed by a Samaritan the innkeeper will have to trust to come back at all. In the ancient world, before signed contracts or banks, the plain future-tense 'I will repay thee' between two strangers was the whole guarantee. The other choices soften it into a reward, a restitution, or paperwork.  (Legend.)

question: At the end of the parable, Jesus turns the question back at the lawyer -- 'Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?' The lawyer, apparently unable to say the word 'Samaritan' aloud, answers with a phrase Luke 10:37 (KJV) records. What did he say?
answer: He that shewed mercy on him
choices: He that shewed mercy on him
context: Luke 10:37 KJV. Jesus's reply is even shorter -- 'Go, and do thou likewise.' The lawyer's refusal to name the Samaritan is the quiet punchline: even having heard the story, he can only describe the hero by his action, not his people. The parable does not overturn Leviticus 19:18 ('love thy neighbour as thyself'); it enlarges the definition of neighbour until it includes the man on the other side of every antagonism.  (Legend.)

question: In the Gospels a wealthy follower of Jesus goes to Pilate after the crucifixion, asks for the body, and buries it in his own new-cut rock tomb. What was this man's name?
context: Matthew 27:57-60; Mark 15:43-46; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich member of the Sanhedrin and secret disciple, wraps Jesus in linen and lays him in his own tomb. Simon of Cyrene is the man forced to carry the cross. Nicodemus helps with the burial spices but not the tomb. Lazarus is the friend Jesus raised at Bethany.

question: Medieval French romances turned the Grail into the cup Jesus lifted at a Passover meal in an upper room in Jerusalem, the night before he was arrested. Which meal from the Gospels is this?
choices: the Feeding of the Five Thousand
context: The Grail-as-cup identification (Robert de Boron, c.1200) points back to the Last Supper -- the Passover meal in the upper room, source of the Christian Eucharist. Cana is where Jesus turned water into wine; the Feeding of the Five Thousand is the loaves-and-fishes miracle; the Feast of Tabernacles is a Jewish harvest festival.

question: A French poet writing around the year 1200 was the first to turn the mysterious 'graal' of Chretien's Perceval into a Christian relic: the very cup from the Last Supper. Which poet made this identification?
context: Robert de Boron's verse Joseph d'Arimathie (c.1200) fused the Grail with the Eucharist cup for the first time. Chretien de Troyes wrote the earlier Perceval (c.1181-90) where the graal is only a serving-dish. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (c.1210) made it a stone from heaven instead. Thomas Malory, writing much later in the 1400s, took the cup version and put it into English.  (Legend.)

question: In Robert de Boron's poem the same cup from the upper-room supper turns up again at the crucifixion, held by Joseph of Arimathea below the cross. Joseph uses it to catch what the Roman soldier Longinus draws out with a lance-thrust into Jesus's side. What does the cup collect?
context: In Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie, Joseph catches the blood flowing from Jesus's side after the soldier's lance-thrust. The cup thus carries both the memory of the Last Supper wine and actual drops of blood -- twice hallowed. The shroud is Joseph's linen cloth, wrapping the body. The crown of thorns is a separate relic given to the mocking soldiers. Frankincense is one of the Magi's birth-gifts, not part of this scene.  (Legend.)

question: In Robert de Boron's tale Joseph is thrown into prison right after the crucifixion. According to the legend, how many years did he sit in that cell before he was set free by the Emperor Vespasian?
context: The legend places Joseph in prison for exactly forty-two years, fed each day by a wafer laid in the cup by a dove and by daily visits from the risen Jesus who taught him the 'secrets of the Grail'. Vespasian, later Roman emperor, hears of him and releases him. Seven, twelve, and a hundred are all round biblical numbers but not the one this story uses.

question: Released from the Roman prison, Joseph of Arimathea gathers his family and companions and sails west with the cup, eventually landing in a distant kingdom where he founds its first Christian community. In which land does the legend place his landing?
context: The Joseph-to-Britain journey is 12th-century French legend, first written down by Robert de Boron and expanded in the Vulgate Estoire del Saint Graal (c.1220). Egypt is where the Holy Family flees from Herod (a different story). Spain is where the apostle James is buried by legend (Santiago). Armenia was the first officially Christian kingdom historically, but not part of the Grail story.

question: In the west of England, on a hill outside a small town, Joseph is said to have thrust his walking staff into the ground -- and by morning the staff had taken root and grown into a flowering thorn tree. In which town does the legend place his staff?
context: The tree, called the Glastonbury Thorn, grew on Wearyall Hill until it was chopped down by Puritan soldiers in the 17th century; a successor stood there until it was vandalised in 2010, but cuttings survive. Canterbury is Becket's cathedral. Winchester is Alfred's royal city. Tintagel is Arthur's Cornish birthplace.  (Legend.)

question: The Glastonbury Thorn is not just legend -- the abbey really did grow a hawthorn that flowered TWICE a year, once in spring and once in a very particular season the Christian world already treated as holy. When does the second flowering come?
context: The tree, botanically Crataegus monogyna 'Biflora', really is a rare cultivar that blooms in midwinter as well as in spring -- the Christmas bloom is the source of the miracle-claim. To this day a flowering sprig from a surviving specimen is sent to the British monarch every Christmas. Easter, midsummer, and harvest all have Christian feasts but not the Glastonbury Thorn story.

question: Not every medieval poet agreed the Grail was a cup. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (c.1210) tells a totally different origin: Wolfram's Grail gives off a light so bright the candles pale, and no one who has seen it can die within the week. In Wolfram's version, what is the Grail?
choices: a mirror sent by the moon
context: Wolfram calls his Grail 'lapsit exillis', usually read as garbled Latin for 'the stone that fell from heaven'. It gives off a light so bright the candles pale, and no one who has seen it can die within the week. Robert de Boron's cup-version was more popular in later English romance (Malory follows the cup); Wolfram's stone-version inspired Wagner's opera Parsifal.  (Legend.)

question: In the Grail cycle the cup is passed down Joseph's descendants -- a line of wounded kings who guard it at the castle of Corbenic. Each of them is crippled by the Dolorous Stroke and waits generation after generation for a destined knight to arrive and ask the right question that will heal the wound. What is this line of guardians called?
context: The Fisher King line, keepers of the Grail at Corbenic, waits generation after generation for the destined knight who will ask the right question and end the wound. Unable to walk from the groin-wound, each king spends his days in a small boat on the castle lake with a rod in his hand -- the source of the name. Galahad finally achieves the healing in Malory Book XVII. Nazarites are Old Testament vow-keepers (Samson). 'Marys of the Sea' is a separate Provencal Grail-adjacent legend of Mary Magdalene landing in France. The Knights Templar were a real 12th-century order later fictionally attached to the Grail story.

question: The medieval abbey that promoted the Joseph-of-Arimathea legend was also the same abbey that made another very famous 'discovery' in the year 1191, right after a fire had burned down their treasury. What did the Glastonbury monks claim to have dug up in 1191?
context: In 1191, seven years after the great fire of 1184 gutted the abbey, the monks announced they had unearthed a lead cross reading 'Here lies buried the famous King Arthur on the Isle of Avalon' alongside a giant coffin. Modern historians treat it as a pious forgery to attract pilgrims and rebuilding funds -- both the Arthur claim and the Joseph claim served the abbey's income. The True Cross was 'found' by Helena, mother of Constantine. Saint Peter's bones are at the Vatican. The Ark has never been claimed by a Western monastery.

question: The first thing to enter the supper hall in Chretien's procession is a young man carrying a weapon. It looks like an ordinary spear except for one uncanny detail -- from its tip, without stopping, a single drop keeps falling and running down the bearer's hand. What is falling from the tip?
context: Chretien's opening image: 'a lance whose point was as pure white as snow, and from the point a drop of blood ran down the shaft'. The bleeding lance is one of the strangest images in medieval literature -- centuries of readers have argued what it means. Wax would drip from a candle; oil from a lamp; dew from a plant -- none from a spear-point.  (Legend.)

question: After the lance-bearer and the two candelabrum-boys come two maidens. The first bears the graal itself -- Chretien describes it as a wide shallow serving-dish of pure gold, set with precious stones, giving off a light so bright the candles pale. What does the second maiden carry?
context: Chretien's Old French: 'un tailleoir d'argent' -- a silver carving-platter. The four elements of the procession are lance, candelabra, graal, platter. Wolfram's Parzival gives a different set. The horn belongs to Roland's story (Olifant); a crown or cloak would suit a coronation, not the Grail procession.  (Legend.)

question: In the later Vulgate Queste and in Malory the bleeding relic carried in the Grail procession is identified with a real object from the Passion story, said to still bleed because it once tasted holy blood. Which Passion relic is it?
context: The Christianising of Chretien's original: the anonymous bleeding relic becomes the Lance of Longinus, the Roman soldier's spear that pierced Jesus's side at the crucifixion. Malory keeps this identification. The Sword of Peter is the one Peter drew in Gethsemane to cut off Malchus's ear. The Nails and the Reed are separate Passion relics.  (Legend.)

question: Perceval, warned by his tutor Gornemant never to ask idle questions of a host, watches the shining dish and the bleeding lance pass and stays silent all through supper. When he wakes the next morning at the Grail Castle, what does he find?
answer: the castle empty and every soul gone
choices: the castle empty and every soul gone
the Fisher King healed and standing tall
the Grail waiting on his pillow at last
the maidens returning to explain each relic
context: Perceval's silence at the Grail is the great failure of Chretien's poem. He wakes to an abandoned castle -- the Fisher King, the maidens, the procession, all vanished -- and rides out to find the surrounding land still waste. The moral, that courtesy misapplied can be worse than boldness, runs through the whole Grail cycle. Chretien died before finishing the poem, and other writers took up the ending.  (Legend.)

question: The Fisher King's wound has a specific origin story. Long before Perceval's visit, a knight named Sir Balin was cornered inside a chapel at Corbenic, snatched the very Lance of Longinus off its wall, and drove it through the king's thighs. What name did later writers give this catastrophic blow?
context: The Dolorous Stroke, developed in the Vulgate Cycle and the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin, is the founding wound of the whole Grail geography. Balin acts in self-defence but the misuse of the holy lance breaks everything around him. Camlann is Arthur's final battle where Mordred deals HIS death-wound; Uther is Arthur's father with a different death; the Stroke of Mordred blurs those.  (Legend.)

question: In Chretien's original text there is one exact wording Perceval was supposed to speak as the shining dish passed him at supper. Every later Grail poet quotes it. What was the question Perceval failed to ask?
choices: What kingdom does the king rule?
Who wounded the king in the chapel?
context: Chretien's phrasing has echoed down eight centuries: the point is not to ask WHAT it is, but WHOM it feeds -- because inside the Grail Castle, unseen, the Grail is carrying a single wafer to the Fisher King's aged father, who has lived on that wafer for years. Perceval's silence keeps him from ever learning this. Later versions add the alternate 'What ails you, king?', but the served-whom question is Chretien's original.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory Book XVII three knights of the Round Table achieve the Grail together -- Perceval, Bors, and one third -- but only ONE of them goes on to touch the Fisher King's wound with blood from the Lance and heal both king and Waste Land. Which knight heals the king?
context: Malory Book XVII ch.21: Galahad, purest of the three, is the one who anoints the Fisher King's thighs with drops from the Lance -- king is healed, Waste Land restored. Lancelot is Galahad's father but too stained by his love for Guinevere to complete the quest. Gawain fails early. Kay never comes near the Grail. Galahad dies shortly after in ecstasy at the sight of the uncovered cup.  (Legend.)

question: At Antioch, some men who had come down from Judea started teaching the Gentile converts that they could not be saved unless they underwent one particular rite of the law of Moses. Which requirement did those Judea men try to impose on Gentile Christians?
context: Acts 15:1 (KJV): 'And certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.' The demand set off the first great argument inside the Christian church.

question: The Antioch church could not settle the Gentile-circumcision fight themselves, so they sent two of their leading missionaries up to Jerusalem to put the question to the apostles and elders in person. Which two men did Antioch send?
context: Acts 15:2 (KJV): '...they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.' Paul and Barnabas had just finished their first missionary journey together and were the two men who had actually been baptising Gentiles in the field.

question: At the Jerusalem council, Peter stood up to argue against forcing the Mosaic law on Gentile converts. He said requiring the whole law would put on the disciples' necks a burden that even the ancestors of Israel had never been able to bear. What single word did Peter use for that burden?
context: Acts 15:10 (KJV): 'Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?' The yoke image is the ox-harness of Jewish tradition -- the ordinary Talmudic phrase for accepting the Law was 'to take the yoke of the commandments upon oneself'.

question: The decisive verdict at the Jerusalem council was not delivered by Peter or by Paul. It was given by another figure -- the man who by then led the Jerusalem church, and who by tradition was the brother of Jesus. Who gave the final ruling?
context: Acts 15:13-19 (KJV): 'And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me... Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God.' The James in question is not one of the Twelve but James the Just, brother of Jesus, who ran the Jerusalem congregation and later wrote the epistle.

question: James ruled that Gentile converts did NOT have to be circumcised. Instead, the council decree named only four things Gentiles must abstain from -- three food-and-blood rules and one sexual rule. Which of these was on the King James list of four?
context: Acts 15:20 (KJV): '...that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood.' A strangled animal has not had its blood drained; the ban lines up with the older Noahide category. The four together: idol-meat, blood, things strangled, fornication.

question: The Jerusalem council did not just send its verdict back to Antioch by messenger. It wrote a formal letter -- the earliest surviving Christian church document. What extraordinary opening phrase did the letter use to introduce its own decision?
answer: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us'
choices: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us'
'in the name of the Father and of the Son'
context: Acts 15:28 (KJV): 'For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.' The phrase gave later church councils their formula for issuing binding decrees; nothing quite like it had been written before.

question: The council did not trust the letter to Paul and Barnabas alone -- Antioch might suspect the missionaries of softening the wording in their own favour. So the Jerusalem apostles sent two of their own men back with the letter as witnesses. One of them was called Judas Barsabas. Who was the other?
context: Acts 15:22 (KJV): '...to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren.' Silas -- the same Silas who will shortly become Paul's next travelling partner -- first appears here as a Jerusalem witness to the decree.

question: Not long after the council, Paul proposed to Barnabas that they revisit the churches they had planted together. Barnabas agreed but insisted on bringing a young man who had abandoned them mid-mission the first time out, at a place called Perga. Which young companion did Barnabas insist on bringing?
context: Acts 15:37-38 (KJV): 'And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work.' John Mark was Barnabas's cousin (Colossians 4:10), which was probably why Barnabas kept defending him.

question: Paul refused. Barnabas refused to budge. Acts describes the argument between the two greatest missionaries of the early church as being 'so sharp' that they split their partnership on the spot. After the break, Barnabas took the young man in dispute and sailed off. To which island did Barnabas sail?
context: Acts 15:39 (KJV): 'And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus.' Cyprus was Barnabas's own homeland (Acts 4:36) and the first stop on the earlier joint journey with Paul.

question: After the split, Barnabas took the ship west to Cyprus with John Mark. Paul stayed on the mainland and set out with his own new partner in the opposite direction, travelling overland to strengthen the churches. Through which two connected regions did Paul travel on that overland route?
context: Acts 15:40-41 (KJV): 'And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God. And he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.' Cilicia was Paul's own home province -- Tarsus, his birthplace, sat in Cilicia. He was walking home before going west.

question: In the story that kicks off the Trojan War, a young Trojan prince named Paris is tending sheep when three goddesses come to him for judgment. On which mountain overlooking the Troad is Paris living?
context: Paris had been exposed as an infant and raised by a herdsman on Mount Ida, which overlooks Troy; the three goddesses came to him there. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paris (mythology)' and 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Paris was not raised as a Trojan prince at all -- his mother Hecuba was told to expose him at birth because of a terrible dream she had while pregnant. What did Hecuba dream she would give birth to?
answer: A flaming torch that burned the city
choices: A flaming torch that burned the city
A silver wolf that ate the sheep
A great serpent that swallowed the sun
A black bull that gored the king
context: The seer Aesacus read the dream as prophecy of Troy's ruin, so the baby was left on Mount Ida to die. He was rescued and raised as a shepherd. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: The trouble began at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. One goddess had not been invited, and in revenge she rolled a golden apple into the hall inscribed with just two words that set three goddesses fighting. Who was the uninvited goddess?
context: The apple's inscription read 'to the fairest', and Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus refused to pick a winner among the three goddesses himself, so he sent one of the Olympians down to Mount Ida to bring them to the shepherd Paris for judgment. Which Olympian did Zeus send?
context: Hermes as psychopomp and messenger was the natural choice; each goddess then offered Paris a private bribe on the mountainside. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Athena, standing beside Hera on the mountainside, made her own offer to Paris. What did she promise him?
answer: Wisdom and unmatched skill in war
choices: Wisdom and unmatched skill in war
A shield no spear could pierce
The most beautiful woman in the world
A ship that could sail the sky
context: Athena offered what she herself embodies -- craft and battle-wisdom, so no mortal would defeat him. Paris turned it down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Aphrodite made the last offer on the mountainside: not power, not wisdom, but a person -- the most beautiful mortal woman alive, promised to Paris as his wife. Who was the woman she promised him?
answer: Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta
choices: Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta
Andromache, wife of Hector of Troy
Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon of Mycenae
Penelope, wife of Odysseus of Ithaca
context: Aphrodite offered the woman -- and the woman was already married. Paris chose her, and choosing her started the war. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Helen, the woman Aphrodite had promised, was no ordinary mortal -- her father was Zeus himself, who had visited her mother Leda in a strange disguise. What form did Zeus take when he came to Leda?
context: Leda bore Helen (and her siblings) after Zeus visited her as a swan; some versions say Helen hatched from an egg. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Paris sailed to Sparta and was received as an honored guest by King Menelaus. Then the king was called away and left Paris alone in his palace with Helen. Where had Menelaus gone, that left his wife unguarded?
answer: To Crete for his grandfather's funeral
choices: To Crete for his grandfather's funeral
To Delphi to consult the oracle
To Athens to fight beside Theseus
To Egypt to buy horses for Sparta
context: Menelaus went to Crete to bury his grandfather Catreus, leaving Helen in Paris's company. Paris carried her home to Troy while he was away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: The two goddesses Paris rejected on Mount Ida -- Hera and Athena -- never forgave the insult, and both fought against Troy for the whole war. In Iliad Book 5, Athena even guides a mortal Greek warrior to charge and wound Aphrodite herself in battle. Which warrior did Athena aim at the goddess?
context: In Iliad 5 Diomedes, urged on by Athena, cuts Aphrodite's hand with his spear as she tries to shield her son Aeneas; the wound was the goddesses' revenge for the judgment. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: Homer's Iliad only glances at the judgment scene -- one brief passage in Book 24 calls it the folly that came home. The full story of the three goddesses and the bribes is preserved instead in a lost epic poem of the Trojan cycle. What is the name of that lost cyclic epic?
context: The Kypria (also spelled Cypria) told the events leading up to the Iliad, including the judgment; it survives only in summaries and fragments. Apollodorus and Ovid's Heroides 16 also preserve the scene. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.

question: Jesus and the Twelve gather in an upper room in Jerusalem to eat the Passover. Partway through the meal, Jesus tells them that one of the people eating with him will betray him. As they go around the table, the disciples each begin to ask the same short, worried question. What question?
context: Mark 14:18-19; Matthew 26:22. Each disciple in turn asks whether he himself is the traitor -- none of them yet knows it is Judas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: At the same meal, Jesus takes a loaf, blesses it, breaks it into pieces, and hands the pieces around the table. As he does, he speaks one short sentence over the bread that Christians have repeated at their central rite for two thousand years. What did he say?
choices: 'Take, eat: this is the bread of heaven.'
'Take, eat: this is the bread of life.'
'Take, eat: this is my flesh, given for you.'
context: Matthew 26:26. The full line: 'And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat: this is my body.' The other three lines are echoes and paraphrases from later liturgy and from John 6, but Matthew's Last Supper wording is this one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: After the bread, Jesus lifts the cup of wine, gives thanks, and passes it around. He tells the Twelve that what is in the cup is his blood, and he attaches a specific purpose to it -- what the blood is 'shed for'. What purpose does he name?
context: Matthew 26:28: 'For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.' 'Remission' here means forgiveness -- the wiping-away of sins. The other three phrases are real biblical themes tied to different scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: In the garden, Jesus takes Peter, James and John a stone's throw further off and asks them to keep watch while he prays. Falling on his face, he asks his Father for one thing 'if it be possible' -- and then, having asked, submits. What does he ask for?
answer: that this cup pass from him
choices: that this cup pass from him
that the temple veil be spared
context: Matthew 26:39: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.' The 'cup' is the suffering of the crucifixion; the image echoes the cup he passed around a few hours earlier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agony_in_the_Garden.

question: Three times Jesus goes back to check on Peter, James and John while he is praying. Three times he finds them fast asleep. The first time, he wakes Peter with a short, wounded question -- how long he could not stay awake with him. How long?
context: Matthew 26:40: 'What, could ye not watch with me one hour?' The other choices are all real Gospel-era ways of marking time overnight, but the line Jesus uses is the plain 'one hour'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agony_in_the_Garden.

question: Judas walks into the garden with a band of soldiers and Temple police. He has told them in advance how to know which man to seize -- a small, ordinary greeting that in this setting becomes a signal. What is the signal Judas told them to look for?
context: Matthew 26:48: 'Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast.' Judas then walks up and greets Jesus with 'Hail, master' and kisses him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_of_Judas.

question: When the soldiers move in, Peter panics, pulls out a sword, and swings. He slices off the ear of the high priest's servant -- John's Gospel is the only one of the four that gives the servant's name. Whose ear?
context: John 18:10 -- and Luke 22:50 adds that it was specifically the man's right ear. Luke alone then reports that Jesus touched the wound and healed it, his last recorded healing before the resurrection. The other three are all real biblical servants keyed to their masters: Onesimus is the runaway servant returned in Paul's letter to Philemon; Gehazi is the prophet Elisha's servant in 2 Kings; Doeg is King Saul's chief herdsman. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malchus.

question: Jesus turns on Peter and tells him to put the weapon away, wrapping the rebuke in one short line that has echoed through every argument about violence and self-defence since. He says: 'they that take the sword shall...' -- what?
context: Matthew 26:52. In the same breath Jesus tells Peter he could summon twelve legions of angels if he wished -- and does not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_of_Judas.

question: Leonardo da Vinci's 'Last Supper' (1495-98), painted on the refectory wall of a Milan convent, does not show the bread and cup being lifted. Leonardo picked an earlier moment in the meal -- the instant a single line from Jesus sends a shockwave down both sides of the long table. Which moment?
answer: Jesus saying, 'one of you shall betray me'
choices: Jesus saying, 'one of you shall betray me'
Jesus rising to lead them to the garden
context: The twelve apostles react in four clusters of three -- shock, denial, questioning, calculation -- while Judas alone leans back with the money-bag. All four listed moments happen at the Last Supper in the Gospels; Leonardo picked the betrayal-announcement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Supper.

question: Jesus opens a short parable in Luke 15 with a shepherd who has a hundred sheep and finds that one has strayed. What does the shepherd do with the ninety-nine he still has?
answer: Leaves them in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost
choices: Leaves them in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost
Pens them safely in the fold and then goes home for the night
Sends a hired hand out after the missing one and stays himself
Calls his neighbours to help him watch the flock overnight
context: Luke 15:4 KJV: 'What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?' Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: Jesus tells a second little parable right after the lost sheep: a woman loses one small silver coin. How many coins did she have altogether before she lost the one?
context: Luke 15:8 KJV: 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' The coins were drachmas -- Greek silver, each about a day's wages. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: The shepherd in Luke 15 finds his one lost sheep out in the wilderness. Jesus describes exactly how he brings the animal back home again.
