answer: He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home himself
choices: He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home himself
He ties a rope round its neck and leads it back with his staff
He whistles for his sheepdog to drive it back to the fold
He signals for the other shepherds to help him drive it home
context: Luke 15:5 KJV: 'And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.' The image of a young man carrying a live lamb across his neck became the very first common picture of Jesus in Christian art. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: The woman in Luke 15 has lost one of her ten pieces of silver somewhere inside her house. Jesus names the two very ordinary things she does to hunt for it.
answer: Lights a candle and sweeps the house
choices: Lights a candle and sweeps the house
Wakes her husband and searches the storeroom
Turns out her chest and shakes out the bedding
Sends her servant girl outside to check the courtyard
context: Luke 15:8 KJV: '...doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' Village houses in first-century Galilee had small windows and packed-earth floors -- a coin in the dust really did need a lamp and a broom. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: The shepherd in Luke 15 gets home with the sheep on his shoulders and calls his friends and neighbours together. Jesus gives the exact words he says to them.
answer: 'Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost'
choices: 'Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost'
'Blessed be the Lord; he hath restored what was taken from me'
'Come, my friends, and eat with me; my flock is whole again'
'Give thanks to God, who hath spared the least of these'
context: Luke 15:6 KJV. Two verses later the woman with the coin says almost the same line -- 'Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost' (Luke 15:9). The near-identical wording deliberately pairs the two scenes. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: The picture Jesus paints in Luke 15 of a young man walking home with a sheep draped across his shoulders became the very first common image of Jesus in Christian art. It was painted around AD 200 -- more than a century before Constantine -- on the ceiling of a burial chamber in Rome. In which Roman burial complex is that earliest painting?
context: The 'Good Shepherd' fresco sits on the domed ceiling of the Cubiculum of the Veiled Woman in the Catacomb of Priscilla, on the Via Salaria in Rome, around AD 200. The pose deliberately echoes the older Greek statue-type of Hermes Kriophoros, Hermes the ram-bearer -- a shape a Roman viewer would already recognise. Source: Bible Odyssey, 'The Good Shepherd in the Catacomb of Priscilla'.

question: Jesus does not tell the twin parables of the lost sheep and the lost coin out of nowhere. Luke 15:2 gives the specific complaint he is answering, spoken by the Pharisees and scribes as they watched him at supper.
answer: 'This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them'
choices: 'This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them'
'By what authority doest thou these things?'
'Master, we would see a sign from thee'
'Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?'
context: Luke 15:2 KJV. The whole of Luke 15 -- lost sheep, lost coin, and the longer Prodigal Son that follows -- is Jesus's reply to that single murmured line. The ratio of loss tightens as he goes: one in a hundred, then one in ten, then one in two. Source: KJV Luke 15.

question: After Achilles was killed at Troy, his god-forged armor was to be awarded to the Greek warrior who most deserved it. Two men were the contenders: the clever Odysseus, and the strongest fighter left in the whole Greek camp -- the man who had carried Achilles's body off the battlefield. Who was the other contender?
context: Ajax the Great, son of Telamon and king of Salamis, was the strongest Greek warrior left after Achilles fell. In the fight around Achilles's corpse it was Ajax who carried the body off while Odysseus covered his back. Source: Sophocles, Ajax, prologue; Little Iliad tradition.  (Legend.)

question: The two Greek contenders for Achilles's armor had very different strengths. The son of Telamon was the strongest fighter. His rival won the armor instead. What did his rival win by?
context: The armor of Achilles went to Odysseus for the persuasive speech he made. Ajax, who had physically saved the body, got nothing but the shame of having been beaten by words. Source: Sophocles, Ajax, prologue; Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: Publicly shamed in front of the whole Greek army, Ajax took up his sword that night to kill the three men he blamed for his humiliation. Which three did he set out to murder?
choices: Nestor, Ajax the Lesser and Teucer
context: Agamemnon and Menelaus (the two Atreid kings who had allowed the vote) and Odysseus (who had won it) -- the three Greek chieftains Ajax held responsible for his disgrace. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 41-65.  (Legend.)

question: As Ajax crept toward the tents to murder his enemies, a goddess intervened -- twisting his sight in the darkness so he could not tell friend from beast. Which goddess turned his madness on the camp herds?
context: Athena, patron of clever Odysseus throughout the Iliad and Odyssey, twists Ajax's sight in the darkness so he cannot tell friend from beast. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 51-65 and 91-117.  (Legend.)

question: The madness the goddess cast on Ajax made him see the wrong targets in the dark. Instead of the Greek chieftains he had gone out to kill, what did he actually slaughter that night?
choices: A group of captive Trojan women
The horses of the Greek chariots
context: Ajax butchered the flocks and herds of the Greek camp, killing them one by one and believing each animal was one of the generals he blamed. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 51-65 and 231-244.  (Legend.)

question: In the middle of his slaughter, Ajax dragged one especially large animal back to his tent, tied it to a post, and began whipping it with a cord -- because in his madness he believed he had captured his most-hated enemy alive. Which animal did he tie to the tent-post, and whom did he think he was whipping?
answer: A ram, thinking it was Odysseus
choices: A ram, thinking it was Odysseus
A bull, thinking it was Agamemnon
A stallion, thinking it was Menelaus
A boar, thinking it was Diomedes
context: The huge ram bound to the tent-post is the play's central emblem of Ajax's madness -- the strongest warrior in the army beating a sheep and mocking it as if it were the man who beat him with words. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 231-244 and 297-330.  (Legend.)

question: At dawn the goddess lifted the madness. Ajax stood among the carcasses with his hands wet, the bound ram still bawling behind him, and understood what he had done. In the play by Sophocles, two figures came in from the tent and found him weeping. Who were they?
answer: His concubine Tecmessa and their small son
choices: His concubine Tecmessa and their small son
His half-brother Teucer and a herald
The prophet Calchas and a priest of Apollo
His father Telamon and his mother
context: Tecmessa is a captive war-prize turned Ajax's partner; the child is their infant son Eurysaces. Their entrance is the most tender scene in the tragedy -- a father in ruin and a small boy who does not yet understand. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 201-347.  (Legend.)

question: The small boy at his father's feet in Sophocles's play was Ajax's only son -- named by his father for the piece of war-gear that made Ajax famous: his tower-shield of seven ox-hides with a bronze layer on top. What was the boy's name?
context: Eurysaces, from Greek eurys (broad) + sakos (shield) -- 'Broad-Shield' -- named for his father's tower-shield, the seven ox-hides with a bronze layer on top that Homer describes in Iliad 7.219-220. He grew up under Teucer's protection after the play. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 574-577.  (Legend.)

question: The two Atreid kings, still furious about Ajax's murder plot, tried to leave his body unburied on the beach as carrion for dogs and birds. One of Ajax's own men had to stand up to them and fight for his right to a proper burial -- his half-brother, a famous archer of the Greek army. What was the half-brother's name?
context: Teucer, son of Telamon by a captive Trojan princess, was Ajax's half-brother and the greatest archer in the Greek army. Odysseus himself finally shamed Agamemnon into allowing the burial -- one of the great acts of magnanimity in Greek literature. Source: Sophocles, Ajax 1047-1420.  (Legend.)

question: Years later, in Odyssey 11, Odysseus meets Ajax's shade in the underworld and tries to make peace -- to say that no one, not even Odysseus himself, had wished this on him. How does Ajax's shade answer?
answer: He says nothing and walks away in silence
choices: He says nothing and walks away in silence
He weeps and forgives Odysseus at last
He curses Odysseus by every god of the dead
He asks Odysseus to look after young Eurysaces
context: One of the most famous moments of dignified fury in Western literature: even in death Ajax will not speak to the man who beat him with words. Homer says the shade 'went off into the darkness of Erebus with the other souls of the perished dead'. Source: Homer, Odyssey 11.541-565.  (Legend.)

question: Matthew's Gospel opens its Nativity with strangers walking into Jerusalem from a long way east. They go straight to the palace and ask the question that terrifies King Herod -- where is the newborn king of the Jews? They explain how they knew to come at all. What have they seen?
context: Matthew 2:2: 'Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.' The pillar of fire is from the Exodus, the moon-to-blood from Revelation, and the white bird echoes Jesus's later baptism dove. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: The visitors from the east arrive at the child's house, kneel down, and open their travel-treasures at his feet. They give three gifts -- the same trio that Christmas carols have listed ever since. Which trio?
context: Matthew 2:11. Frankincense is a fragrant resin burned as incense; myrrh is a bitter resin used to embalm the dead -- which is why the myrrh gift has always struck readers as an odd present for a newborn. The other three trios are all real ancient trade goods along the same caravan routes, but none of them are the magi's gifts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: Christmas cards, carols, and school plays all show three crowned kings following the star. Matthew's Gospel calls the visitors from the east something quite different, and never once puts a crown on them. What does Matthew call them?
context: The Greek is magoi -- a class of Persian priest-astrologers, students of the stars. The 'three kings' upgrade is medieval, read back into Matthew from Old Testament lines about foreign rulers bringing tribute. Prophets, scribes and shepherds all appear elsewhere in the Nativity story; the magi are their own category. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.

question: Before the wise men leave Jerusalem, Herod pulls them aside and gives them a private instruction. Come back this way, he says, and tell me exactly where the child is. He gives them a friendly reason for asking -- a reason that turns out to be a straight-faced lie. What reason did he give?
answer: 'that I may come and worship him also'
choices: 'that I may come and worship him also'
'that I may send him gifts of my own'
'that I may bless his mother and father'
'that I may guard him against my enemies'
context: Matthew 2:8. Warned in a dream not to trust him, the magi go home 'another way' and never report back -- which is what triggers what happens next in Bethlehem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: When Herod works out that the wise men have slipped past him and vanished, he does not chase them. Instead he sends soldiers into a small town six miles south of Jerusalem with an order that would let no rival grow up. Whom did he order killed?
answer: every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under
choices: every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under
every firstborn son in the district of Judea
every priest of the temple who had greeted the magi
every foreign traveller camped outside the walls
context: Matthew 2:16. Christians have kept a feast for these children -- the Holy Innocents -- since at least the second century, marked in the Western church on 28 December, four days after Christmas. The killing of the firstborn is Exodus 12; a temple purge and a foreigner sweep both fit Herod's paranoid style but are not the Matthew story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Joseph does not wait for Herod's soldiers. Warned in a dream by an angel, he gets Mary and the baby up in the middle of the night and flees the country -- the scene painters have drawn a thousand times, a woman on a donkey with a baby and a man on foot walking beside. Where did they flee to?
context: Matthew 2:13-14. Egypt was the classic hiding-place for a Jewish family in trouble -- a Roman province, but outside Herod's reach, with a large existing Jewish community. Matthew is also quietly echoing the older story of Israel itself coming out of Egypt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: After the family has been in Egypt long enough for Herod to die, Joseph is told in another dream that it is safe to go back. He starts to head home to Bethlehem, but hears news that changes the route -- Herod's cruel son Archelaus is now the ruler of Judea. So Joseph veers north and settles the family in a small town in Galilee. Which town?
context: Matthew 2:22-23. All four are real Galilean towns Jesus knew: Capernaum will become his adult base of ministry, Bethsaida is the home of Peter and Andrew, and Cana is the site of the wedding-water-into-wine -- but the boyhood home in Matthew is Nazareth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Four days after Christmas, Western churches mark a feast for the little boys Herod's soldiers killed at Bethlehem when they could not find Jesus. Christians have kept it since at least the second century, tucked deep inside the Christmas season. What is this feast called?
answer: the Feast of the Holy Innocents
choices: the Feast of the Holy Innocents
context: The Feast of the Holy Innocents falls on 28 December in the Western church. The Feast of the Circumcision is 1 January (eight days after Christmas, as Jewish law required); the Feast of the Presentation is 2 February, when Mary brings the baby to the Temple; the Feast of Stephen is 26 December -- the 'Good King Wenceslas' feast, for the first Christian martyr. All four are real feasts of the Christmas cycle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Innocents.

question: Long after Matthew was written, Christian tradition settled on three names for the wise men -- one African, one Asian, one European in the medieval imagination. Two of the names are Caspar and Melchior. What is the third?
context: The trio Caspar-Melchior-Balthasar is fixed by the sixth century -- see the Ravenna mosaic at Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, where the three are shown in procession with their names lettered above them. Bartholomew is one of the Twelve, Barabbas the prisoner released at the Passion, and Barnabas the missionary companion of Paul -- all real New Testament figures, none of them a magus. Source: christianiconography.info/Edited%20in%202013/Italy/sApolNuovoLeftNave.magi.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_Magi.  (Legend.)

question: In the Prose Edda a stranger arrives at the hall of the Norse gods and offers to build them a great stone rampart -- one that no giant will ever be able to break through. Around which stronghold does the stranger offer to build his wall?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the stranger offers to build a rampart around Asgard, the home of the Aesir. Valhalla is Odin's hall inside Asgard, not the outer boundary. Midgard is the world of humans. Jotunheim is where the giants live -- what the wall is supposed to keep OUT.  (Legend.)

question: The stranger who offered to build the wall around Asgard would not name any price in gold or silver. Instead he asked for one of the Aesir's own goddesses as his wife -- a shocking payment the gods almost refused outright. Which goddess did the builder demand as his bride?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder demanded Freyja the goddess of love. Frigg is Odin's wife. Sif is Thor's wife (the same Sif whose golden hair Loki cut off). Idunn keeps the apples of youth. On top of the goddess, the builder also demanded the sun and the moon.  (Legend.)

question: The stranger's demand for Freyja alone was staggering, but he added a second and a third thing to his price -- two more prizes he would take home if he finished the wall on time. Alongside Freyja as his bride, what else did the builder ask for?
choices: the sacred spear and the ship
the golden apples and the mead
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder demanded Freyja, plus the sun and the moon out of the sky. The spear Gungnir and the ship Skidbladnir are dwarf-forged gifts to the gods, not up for wager. Idunn's apples of youth and the Mead of Poetry are other treasures. Yggdrasil the world-tree and Mimir's well are cosmological features, not gifts to give.  (Legend.)

question: The Aesir were about to refuse the builder's shocking bargain when one of the gods argued them into taking it -- with the sly twist that the builder must do all the work single-handed, in one winter, or lose everything. Which of the gods talked the Aesir into the deal?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Loki talked the reluctant Aesir into accepting on the impossible-sounding terms. Odin presides but does not push the bargain. Thor is away in the east fighting trolls when the deal is struck. Heimdall watches Bifrost, not the bargaining table.  (Legend.)

question: The builder agreed to the one-winter, no-helper terms on a single condition -- he must be allowed to use his own animal to haul the stones. Snorri says this beast turned out to do more of the wall-work than the builder himself did. What kind of animal did the builder bring with him?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder brought Svadilfari, a stallion whose stone-hauling did more work than his master. Oxen haul stones in many myths (Rome's plough, Ireland's cattle-raid) but not this one. Freyr's Gullinbursti is a boar, from the Brokkr wager. Bears do not appear in this tale.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri tells us how close the builder was to winning. Working through winter with only his stallion, he had raised walls so high the giants could not have broken them, and only one part of the fortification was still unfinished when the deadline was almost on him. What was left to build with three days to go?
context: Gylfaginning 42: with three days before the first day of summer, only the gateway (the doorway through the wall) remained. Snorri does not describe watchtowers, a keep, or a well inside Asgard's outer wall; those are medieval castle features.  (Legend.)

question: Seeing they were about to lose their goddess and the light of the sky, the Aesir did not politely renegotiate -- they turned on one of their own and threatened him with death unless he sabotaged the wall himself. Which god did the Aesir threaten to kill if he did not stop the builder?
context: Gylfaginning 42: because Loki was the one who had pushed the deal through, the Aesir threatened him with death unless he wrecked it. Odin is the chief but does not receive the threat. Baldr is the shining son, not yet dead in this story. Freyr is Freyja's brother and would be a victim, not a saboteur.  (Legend.)

question: When the sun rose and the wall stood unfinished, the builder saw he had been cheated of Freyja and the sky and flew into a rage -- and in his fury his disguise fell away. Snorri says he had never been the ordinary craftsman he pretended to be. What was the builder truly?
context: Gylfaginning 42: the builder was a hrimthurs, a frost-giant, in disguise. The dwarves live in Svartalfheim and forge (Brokkr, Sindri, the Sons of Ivaldi). Elves have their own realm (Alfheim) but do not appear in this bargain. Sorcerers are not a Norse category the tale uses.  (Legend.)

question: The moment the builder revealed himself as a frost-giant, the Aesir said an oath to a giant in disguise was worth less than the sun and the moon. One of the gods walked up to the raging builder and settled the whole matter with a single blow. Which god struck the killing blow?
context: Gylfaginning 42: Thor had been away in the east fighting trolls and came home just in time; he paid the builder with a single hammer-blow that shattered his skull and sent him 'down to Niflhel.' Odin does not do the killing. Tyr fights Garm at Ragnarok. Vidar avenges Odin against Fenrir. Only Thor is the wall-story's executioner.  (Legend.)

question: In the medieval Book of Invasions, six waves of settlers reach Ireland in turn -- Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and one last people. This sixth and final wave sails in from Iberia and becomes the ancestors of the modern Irish Gaels. What is this last people called?
context: The Milesians -- sons of Mil Espaine, 'Mil of Spain' -- are the sixth and final wave in Lebor Gabala Erenn. The Fomorians are the sea-born enemies of the gods; the Aos Si are the fairy folk (in fact the Tuatha De renamed); the Fianna are the roving warrior-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill, centuries later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: As the Milesians marched inland from the coast, three queens of the Tuatha De Danann came out to meet them, one after another. Each queen made the Milesian druid Amergin swear that Ireland would be named after her -- and Amergin promised each in turn. THREE queens. The three sisters are Eriu, Fodla, and one more. Who is she?
context: The three land-goddesses are Eriu, Banba, and Fodla -- all three still survive as poetic names for Ireland in Irish literature, but Eriu's name became Eire in daily speech. Brigid, Danu, and the Morrigan are three other great Tuatha De goddesses, each with her own domain (flame, ancestry, war) and her own ladder. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: When the Milesian ships came in sight of the Irish shore, the druids of the Tuatha De Danann worked their fiercest magic. A great storm blew up from the land against the invaders, howling out over the waves. How far back out to sea did the magic wind drive the Milesian fleet?
context: 'Nine waves' is the ritual formula in the sources -- the exact distance beyond which the Tuatha De's magic could not reach. Once the Milesians were driven the nine waves out, only Amergin's counter-magic could bring them back. Nine is the great ritual number in Celtic and Norse myth alike. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: The chief druid and poet of the Milesians was the man who out-magicked the Tuatha De's wind and sang the Milesians onto the Irish shore. His epithet meant 'White-Kneed', and his name is preserved in the Book of Invasions and the Book of Leinster. Who was he?
context: Amergin Gluingel ('white-kneed Amergin') is the founding poet of Irish tradition -- the man whose verse ends the age of the gods and opens the age of the Gaels. Cathbad is Conchobar's druid in the Ulster Cycle; Mog Ruith is the great blind sorcerer of Munster; Tuan mac Cairill is the ancient shape-changing witness who lived through all six invasions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amergin_Gl%C3%BAingel.  (Legend.)

question: Once Amergin's first poem had calmed the magic wind and the Milesian ships had come safely back to shore, Amergin stepped out onto the beach and chanted a second poem to claim the land itself. That second poem opens: 'I am a wind on the sea, I am a wave of the ocean, I am the roar of the sea, I am a stag of...' How many tines does the stag of the poem carry on its antlers?
context: 'I am a stag of seven tines' is the fixed formula in every surviving translation of the Song of Amergin. A tine is a point of an antler; seven tines is a magnificent, mature stag. Nine is the ritual number of the wind; three and twelve are the other ritual numbers of Irish myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Amergin.  (Legend.)

question: Amergin's landing-song rolls out a long chain of images -- the poet claiming himself into every part of the Irish natural world. One line names a fish famous in later Irish myth as the fish of wisdom (the same fish that will burn Fionn mac Cumhaill's thumb centuries later). In which watery place does Amergin say he is that fish?
context: 'I am a salmon in a pool' is the fixed line in the surviving translations. The salmon-of-wisdom motif runs all through Irish tradition -- the same fish appears in the Fenian Cycle as the Salmon of Knowledge that Fionn cooks and accidentally tastes, gaining all wisdom. The Song of Amergin is one of the oldest surviving pieces of writing in the Irish language, preserved in the Lebor Gabala Erenn and copied into the Book of Leinster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Amergin.  (Legend.)

question: The Milesians won the war against the Tuatha De Danann in battle -- but the sons of Mil were wise enough to know they had been fighting gods. They offered a settlement instead. The Milesians would keep one part of Ireland; the Tuatha De would keep another part. How was Ireland divided?
answer: Milesians take the surface, Tuatha De take the underground
choices: Milesians take the surface, Tuatha De take the underground
Milesians take the south, Tuatha De take the north
Milesians take the coasts, Tuatha De take the mountains
Milesians take the summer, Tuatha De take the winter
context: The famous division: the Milesians (the modern Irish) hold the visible land, sea, and sky; the Tuatha De hold every hollow-hill, fairy-fort, and sidhe mound beneath the ground. This is how the old gods became the fairy folk who live under Ireland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: In old Irish myth a dark-winged bird was known to settle on shield-rims and spear-points as an army lined up for battle -- and whichever side she chose was the side about to die. The Tuatha De Danann called this bird-shape one of their goddesses in the shape she liked best. Which goddess flies over the battlefield as a crow?
context: The Morrigan is the war-and-prophecy goddess of the Tuatha De Danann; her most famous shape is the crow (badb) settling on the doomed side of a fight. Brigid is the goddess of poetry, flame, and healing; Danu is the mother-goddess whose name is in Tuatha De Danann itself; Aine is a summer sun-goddess of Munster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan.  (Legend.)

question: In the Book of Invasions the Morrigan is not one goddess but a trio -- three war-sisters, daughters of Ernmas, together known as 'the Morrigan.' One is Badb, the Scald-Crow battle-hag. One is Anand (sometimes called Nemain, 'Frenzy'). The third has her name still stamped on the ancient royal seat of Ulster and on the modern city of Armagh. Who is she?
context: Macha is the horse-and-sovereignty sister; EMAIN MACHA (Navan Fort, the seat of the Ulster kings) and ARD MACHA ('Macha's Height,' modern Armagh) both bear her name. Brigid, Boann (the goddess of the River Boyne), and Etain are all other great Tuatha De women. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macha.  (Legend.)

question: The old Irish new year fell on the night of November 1, when farmers brought their cattle down from summer pasture and the barrier between the mortal world and the Otherworld was said to thin. It is the same night the Morrigan chose for her most famous meeting at the ford before Moytura, and its distant descendant is what English speakers now call Halloween. What is the Irish name of that night?
context: SAMHAIN (November 1) is the ancestor of modern Halloween -- one of the four quarter-festivals of the Irish year. Bealtaine (May 1) opens summer; Lughnasadh (August 1) is the harvest festival of Lugh; Imbolc (February 1) is the spring festival of Brigid. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhain.  (Legend.)

question: On the eve of Samhain, in the days before the Tuatha De's great fight with the Fomorians, the chief-god of the Tuatha De came down to a stream in what is now County Sligo looking for the Morrigan. He found her straddling the water -- one foot on the north bank, one foot on the south, washing herself at the water. Which of the Tuatha De met her there?
context: The Dagda -- 'the Good God' -- is the chief of the Tuatha De and the Morrigan's partner in the sacred-marriage tryst that seals the Tuatha De's war-alliance with the goddess of the land. Lugh is the war-leader, Nuada the deposed king, Ogma the champion. Source: Cath Maige Tuired section 84; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dagda.  (Legend.)

question: The stream where the Dagda met the Morrigan straddling the water was the ford on one particular river, in Corann near modern Riverstown -- and the ford-tryst on Samhain has been fixed there in the sagas ever since. On which river is that ford?
context: The Unius flows through Corann in County Sligo; the Morrigan's ford is on it, near Riverstown. The Boyne is the river of Newgrange (Aengus's mound); the Shannon is the longest river in Ireland; the Liffey runs through Dublin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Morrigan; Cath Maige Tuired section 84.  (Legend.)

question: In return for lying with the Dagda at the ford, the Morrigan pledged she would go alone against the Fomorian king before the battle and cripple him from within. In the words of Cath Maige Tuired she promised to take from him 'the blood of his heart and the kidneys of his valour.' Which Fomorian king did she name?
context: Indech mac De Domnann is the Fomorian king the Morrigan promises to un-man; the pledge is preserved verbatim in Cath Maige Tuired section 84. Balor is the one-eyed champion killed by Lugh; Bres is the half-Fomorian king the Tuatha De once tried and deposed; Elatha is Bres's father. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired section 84.  (Legend.)

question: The wailing woman of later Irish folklore -- the ghostly figure heard keening outside a house on the night the head of the family is about to die -- is the folk descendant of the Morrigan's Washer-at-the-Ford face. In Ireland she has her own name, and hearing her cry at your door is the warning nobody wants. What is she called?
context: BEAN-SIDHE means 'woman of the sidhe' (fairy-mound), anglicised as BANSHEE -- the folk-shadow of the Washer at the Ford, an aos si woman heard keening for a coming death. The Puca is a shape-changing sidhe trickster; the Leanan-Sidhe is a fairy-lover; the Cailleach is the old woman of winter. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee.  (Legend.)

question: In the fight itself the Morrigan stood above the battlefield and chanted a rousing rosc that broke the Fomorian nerve, and after the Fomorian king Balor was killed she chanted a second poem -- one that celebrated the victory and then rolled straight on into a dark prophecy of the world's end: 'summer without blossoms, cattle will be without milk, women without modesty, men without valour...' At the end of which battle did she chant that prophecy?
context: The prophecy is preserved in Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167 at the close of the SECOND battle of Moytura (Tuatha De vs Fomorians). The First Battle of Moytura was the Tuatha De against the Fir Bolg. The Cattle Raid of Cooley is Cuchulainn's saga. The Battle of Ventry is a Fenian-cycle tale. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167.  (Legend.)

question: The Morrigan's closing rosc at Moytura -- 'I shall not see a world which will be dear to me...' -- rolls straight from a battle-cry into a foretelling that stands beside two other famous Western poems in the same shape: the Norse Voluspa (Odin questioning the seeress) and one book of the Christian Bible whose visions of beasts, seals, and a final battle have haunted Western art ever since. Which book is that?
context: REVELATION (the Apocalypse of John) closes the New Testament with the final-days vision -- the Western Christian counterpart to the Morrigan's rosc and to the Voluspa. Daniel and Isaiah contain famous apocalyptic passages of their own; Genesis is the opening book of origins. Source: celt.ucc.ie Cath Maige Tuired sections 166-167; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation.  (Legend.)

question: In the Tain Bo Cuailnge the Morrigan comes to Cu Chulainn at the ford in her most beautiful young-woman shape, in the middle of the war he is holding off alone. She offers him two things together, one of them a gift no goddess offers lightly. What does she offer?
answer: her love and her aid in the fighting
choices: her love and her aid in the fighting
a magic spear and a golden shield
a chariot and a team of horses
a cauldron of healing and a druid's cloak
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge (Recension I, ed. O'Rahilly 1976): the Morrigan appears to Cu Chulainn as a beautiful young woman in royal dress and offers herself and her supernatural help against the army of Connacht. Lugh's spear, chariots and cauldrons belong to other Irish myths.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn does not recognise the goddess at the ford. He is in the middle of holding the border alone and cannot afford a distraction, so he refuses her plainly. How does the Morrigan answer his refusal?
answer: she promises to oppose him in the fights to come
choices: she promises to oppose him in the fights to come
she rides away in silence and never returns
she laughs and offers him a second chance the next day
she strikes him blind with a look
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge: when the young warrior turns her down (he does not know she is a goddess), the Morrigan tells him that if he will not have her love he will have her hate -- she will hinder him herself in his next fights. The Tain then delivers exactly that in three animal-shape scenes.  (Legend.)

question: After the last of the fights Cu Chulainn passes an old woman at the roadside who is lame in one leg, blind in one eye, and has one arm crushed -- the exact three wounds he has just given the eel, the heifer, and the wolf. Whatever she is doing, when he takes her hospitality and blesses her three times, each blessing heals one of those wounds. What is she doing?
answer: milking a cow and offering him three drinks
choices: milking a cow and offering him three drinks
spinning wool and asking him to hold the thread
washing bloody clothes in a stream
carrying firewood and asking him to lift the bundle
context: Tain Bo Cuailnge: the old woman is the Morrigan in disguise, and she is milking a cow at the roadside. Cu Chulainn is thirsty and asks for a drink; she gives him three, and after each one he blesses her -- and each blessing heals one of the wounds he has just inflicted. Washing bloody clothes at a ford is Badb's Washer-at-the-Ford omen, a related but different scene; spinning and firewood belong elsewhere.  (Legend.)

question: Long before the Ulster Cycle the Morrigan already had a job among the older gods. At the second Battle of Moytura, the Cath Maige Tuired, she does something in the middle of the fight that turns the whole battle for the Tuatha De Danann against the Fomorians. What does she do?
answer: chants a poem that breaks the Fomorian line
choices: chants a poem that breaks the Fomorian line
throws Balor's own eye back at him
wakes the dead of the Tuatha De for one more charge
opens the earth beneath the Fomorian king
context: Cath Maige Tuired (the second Battle of Moytura): the Morrigan promises the Dagda on Samhain eve that she will aid the Tuatha De against the Fomorians, and during the battle she chants a poem -- 'kings rise up to the battle' -- and the Fomorians break and are driven into the sea. Balor's eye is put out by Lugh's sling-stone (a different rung); the dead are not raised; the earth-opening motif is not part of this fight.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories the whole cosmos hangs from one great being that has three roots -- one reaching to the frost-giants, one to Hel, and one to the gods -- and nine worlds strung through its branches. Under a hall by a well at its second root live the three fate-women who choose the life of every child born. What is the name of that great world-holder?
context: Yggdrasil is the great ash at the center of Norse cosmology, with three roots and nine worlds strung through its branches. Laerad is the tree that stands over Valhalla, from whose leaves the goat Heidrun grazes; Glasir is the golden-leaved grove that stands before Valhalla's doors; Barnstokkr is the apple-tree that grows through the hall of the Volsungs, where Odin drove in the sword Sigmund alone could pull free.  (Legend.)

question: Beside the second root of the world-tree Yggdrasil stands a well of water so holy that anything dipped in it comes out white as an eggshell's inner film. Beside the well is a hall, and out of the hall each dawn come three maidens with a knife and a stave of ash-wood, on which they carve. What are the three carving-maidens called in Norse myth?
context: The Norns come out of their hall beside the well of Urd and carve on wood, setting the fate of every being in the nine worlds. The Valkyries are the choosers-of-the-slain who carry fallen warriors up to Valhalla. The Disir are a broader class of protective female spirits, tied to family lines. The Idisi are the Old High German equivalent, mentioned in the Merseburg Charms -- close cousins but a different name.  (Legend.)

question: In Voluspa 20 the three fate-women of Norse myth are named -- and their names are just three Old Norse words for three ordinary things a Norse-speaker used every day. The three words together mean 'Was', 'Being', and 'Shall-Be'. What are the three names?
context: Urd = 'was / has-become' (past); Verdandi = 'becoming / that-which-is' (present participle); Skuld = 'shall-be / debt-owed-to-the-future' (future). Frigg / Freyja / Sif are three Aesir goddesses. Modi / Magni / Vidar are three sons of the gods who survive Ragnarok. Nott / Dag / Sol are Night, Day, and Sun.  (Legend.)

question: Voluspa 20 says the three Norns come out of their hall beside the well and set the life of every child born into the nine worlds -- and once they have done it, no god (not even Odin) can undo the doom. How do the Norns SET a child's fate?
answer: they carve runes on a stave of ash
choices: they carve runes on a stave of ash
they weave a thread on a great loom and cut it at death
they spit into the well and read the ripples
they whisper a secret name over the cradle
context: Voluspa 20: the three Norns 'scored' -- they carve the runes that decide fate onto wood. Once cut, the rune stands: no god, not even Odin, can un-carve it. The loom-and-thread image is real too, but it belongs to the Greek Moirai and later medieval retellings; the older Poetic-Edda picture is knife-on-wood. Spitting-into-a-well is the mead-of-poetry story, not a fate-rite. Whispering a name is Anglo-Saxon nam-giefu, not Norse.  (Legend.)

question: The Voluspa is not told in the poet's own voice -- it is spoken by a single female figure who claims she has personally SEEN the three Norns at their well and watched them carve the fate of the world, including its ending at Ragnarok. What kind of speaker is the Voluspa's narrator?
context: The Voluspa (literally 'the volva's prophecy') is spoken by a volva, a seeress, who claims first-hand sight of the Norns at Urdarbrunnr. Her testimony -- what she saw them carve -- is the frame for the whole poem, up through Ragnarok. A skald is a court-poet who composes praise-verse for kings. A godi is a chieftain-priest who ran temple sacrifices. A thul is a reciter of wisdom-verse (Odin is called Fimbulthul, 'great thul', in Havamal).  (Legend.)

question: The Old Norse word for FATE is not one of the god-names but a special ancient noun meaning literally 'ancient-law' or 'primal-layer'. Voluspa 20 says this thing was laid down by the three Norns before the Aesir came into their power -- meaning even Odin acts inside a story someone else has already written. What is the Norse word for fate itself?
context: Orlog (Old Norse orlog / urlag) literally means 'primal-law' or 'that-which-was-laid-down-first' (or- 'ancient' + log 'law, layer'). It is above the gods; even Odin acts inside it. Urdr is the eldest Norn's own name (and 'that which was'). Skop means 'shaping / doom-shape' -- what fate does to a person. Aldr means 'lifespan / age' -- how long a person lives, not fate itself.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus was teaching inside a house in Capernaum, and the crowd was packed so tight around the door that no one else could squeeze in. Four men arrived carrying a paralysed friend on his sleeping mat -- they needed to get him to Jesus. Blocked at the door, the four found another way in. Where did they take their friend to reach him?
choices: Around to a side courtyard opening
context: Mark 2:1-4. First-century Galilean houses had flat roofs made of wooden beams overlaid with thatch and packed mud -- soft enough to dig through, sturdy enough to walk on. The stairs to the roof were usually on the outside of the house.

question: After the exchange with the scribes, Jesus turned back to the paralysed man on the mat and gave him a short three-part command -- get up, do something with your bed, and go home. He proved his point by healing the man in front of the whole crowded room. What was the middle instruction Jesus gave about the bed?
choices: Leave thy bed for the poor
Burn thy bed in the fire
Sell thy bed at the market
context: Mark 2:11 -- 'Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house'. The man immediately rose, picked up his mat, and walked out through the crowd (Mark 2:12); this was the proof-in-action for the scribes.

question: Later in Mark, Jesus is leaving the city of Jericho on the road. A blind beggar is sitting by the roadside, hears that Jesus is passing, and starts shouting for help. Mark is the only gospel that gives this beggar a NAME -- and then explains what it means. What is the name Mark gives him?
context: Mark 10:46 places Bartimaeus by the roadside as Jesus leaves Jericho. Zacchaeus was a tax collector Jesus met in Jericho going the OTHER direction (Luke 19); Lazarus was raised from the dead in Bethany; Malchus was the servant whose ear Peter cut off in Gethsemane.

question: The beggar's name in Aramaic is BAR-Timaeus, which is why the gospel takes the trouble to translate it. The Aramaic prefix BAR- is a family word: it names the same relationship the Hebrew prefix BEN- names in a name like Benjamin, and the same relationship the Gaelic prefix MAC- names in a name like MacDonald. What relationship do all three of these prefixes name?
context: Bar in Aramaic, ben in Hebrew, and mac in Gaelic all mean 'son of'. Bartimaeus = son of Timaeus; Benjamin = son of the right hand; MacDonald = son of Donald. Mark 10:46 spells the meaning out for Greek-speaking readers who didn't know Aramaic.

question: The blind beggar shouted 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' as Jesus passed. The crowd told him to be quiet -- he was making a scene. What did the beggar do next?
answer: Shouted the same words even louder
choices: Grabbed at the cloaks of the passers-by around him
Shouted the same words even louder
Called out the names of the disciples one by one
Begged a bystander to lead him closer to Jesus
context: Mark 10:48 -- 'many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me'. This persistence is what Mark uses to show his faith: he refuses to be shushed. It is only after this second, louder cry that Jesus stops and calls for him.

question: When Jesus finally stopped and called the blind beggar over, the man did something with an item of clothing that a beggar in first-century Jericho would probably have owned nothing more valuable than -- and then ran to Jesus. Mark records the action deliberately. What did the beggar do with his cloak?
answer: Threw it off into the road
choices: Threw it off into the road
Tore it up as a sign of grief
context: Mark 10:50 -- 'And he, casting away his garment, rose, and came to Jesus.' For a beggar the outer cloak served as coat by day and blanket by night; discarding it before he could see was the risk of a man expecting to be healed.

question: Jesus asked the blind beggar a single question before healing him -- a question the gospel highlights because the answer sounds so obvious. What did Jesus ask him?
answer: What wilt thou that I should do unto thee
choices: Believest thou that I am able to do this
What wilt thou that I should do unto thee
Who do men say that I am
context: Mark 10:51. All four are REAL questions Jesus asks in the gospels ('wilt thou be made whole' to the paralytic at Bethesda in John 5, 'believest thou' to the blind men in Matthew 9, 'who do men say' to the disciples at Caesarea Philippi in Mark 8). The Bartimaeus question is the one that makes the beggar name his desire out loud.

question: When the woman with the twelve-year haemorrhage came forward trembling and admitted she was the one who had touched Jesus's cloak in the crowd, Jesus did not scold her. Instead he gave her a single line that Mark records word for word -- the same line he later says to Bartimaeus about how he was healed. What did Jesus tell her had made her whole?
context: Mark 5:34 -- 'Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace'. Jesus uses the exact same phrase to Bartimaeus at Mark 10:52: 'thy faith hath made thee whole'. In both scenes it is the person's trust, not the physical touch or the shouted words, that Jesus names as the healer.

question: As the Hebrews march out of Egypt, Moses does not lead them alone. God goes before them in a visible sign that changes shape with the time of day: a tall column of one thing during the day and a tall column of another thing at night. What are the two forms of the guiding column?
answer: Cloud by day and fire by night
choices: Cloud by day and fire by night
Smoke by day and ash by night
Rain by day and lightning by night
Mist by day and moonlight by night
context: Exodus 13:21. The pillar is one continuous presence; only its appearance changes with the hour. Later at the sea it moves from before them to behind them and stands between the two camps overnight.

question: Pharaoh's heart hardens again after the Hebrews leave and he decides to bring them back by force. Exodus says he takes six hundred CHOSEN ones of a specific Egyptian war-craft, with a captain over every one. Six hundred of what does Pharaoh muster?
context: Exodus 14:7. 'Six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots of Egypt, and captains over every one of them.' Egyptian chariots of the New Kingdom were fast, light, two-wheeled, carrying a driver and an archer.

question: When the Hebrews see the Egyptian chariots bearing down and the water at their backs, they turn on Moses with a bitter, sarcastic question. In the King James wording, they cry: 'Because there were no --- in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?' Fill in the missing word.
context: Exodus 14:11. Egypt was famous for its tombs (the pyramids and rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings). The Hebrews' sneer is that Egypt had plenty of graves; Moses did not need to drag them to the desert to bury them.

question: Moses answers the panic with a famous three-verb command in the King James text. He tells the Hebrews to do exactly three things while God fights for them. What are the three things?
answer: Fear not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD
choices: Fear not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD
Kneel, cry out, and wait for the LORD to answer
Trust, obey, and follow the pillar of cloud
Draw your swords, form up, and charge the sea
context: Exodus 14:13. Moses forbids both flight and combat: the Hebrews are to hold their line and watch. In the next verse he adds, 'The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.'

question: That night Moses stretches his rod over the water and God drives the sea back. The wind that does the driving is named twice in the King James verse: God sends it 'all that night' and it blows from one specific direction. From what direction does the wind blow?
context: Exodus 14:21. 'The LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land.' The east wind is a recurring instrument of God's judgment in the prophets (Jonah, Hosea, Ezekiel).

question: The Egyptian chariots follow the Hebrews down into the seabed, and God stops them by ruining one part of the chariots so they cannot drive properly. What breaks on the Egyptian chariots?
context: Exodus 14:25. 'And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily; so that the Egyptians said, Let us flee from the face of Israel; for the LORD fighteth for them.' The chariots bog down; Moses then stretches out his hand again and the water returns.

question: Jesus opens one of his most famous parables with a plain, one-line setup: 'A certain man had two sons' (Luke 15:11). The younger boy walks up to his father one morning with a demand that would have shocked every listener at the time. What does he ask for?
choices: the deed to the family land
context: Luke 15:12: 'Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me.' In first-century terms this is close to telling his father, 'I wish you were already dead' -- a son normally only asks for his portion after the funeral. A blessing over the herd (Isaac to Jacob), a deed to land (Naboth's vineyard), and a dowry chest all belong to other Bible scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: With his share of the money in hand, the younger son leaves home for 'a far country'. Luke sums up what happens to the money there in one memorable phrase that gets quoted whenever the parable is retold. What does the boy do with the money?
choices: buries it in a field for safekeeping
lends it to strangers at interest
pays it into the local temple
context: Luke 15:13: 'wasted his substance with riotous living.' The Greek behind 'riotous' means unrestrained, dissolute -- the kind of spending that leaves no trace. Burying money in a field is what the third servant does in Jesus's Parable of the Talents; lending at interest and paying into the temple both figure in other Gospel scenes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: Once his money is gone, a famine hits the country he has moved to. Broke, hungry, and unable to go home, the son hires himself out to a local farmer for the lowest job available in that world -- a job a young Jewish man would have found humiliating on top of miserable. What is the job?
context: Luke 15:15. Pigs are unclean animals in the Mosaic law -- the equivalent of hiring yourself out to shovel something ritually filthy every day. That is Jesus's point: rock bottom for a Jewish audience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: Standing in the pig-pen, Luke says the son 'came to himself' -- he snaps out of it. He decides to go home and rehearses a short, humble speech to say to his father. The first line names two audiences he has wronged. What does the speech begin with?
answer: 'I have sinned against heaven, and before thee'
choices: 'I have sinned against heaven, and before thee'
'I have wasted thy silver and my name'
'I have shamed thy house and my mother's memory'
'I have broken every commandment given to Moses'
context: Luke 15:18-19, continued: 'and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.' The boy has planned it out -- but as it turns out, he never gets to finish the speech. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The son begins his rehearsed apology -- 'Father, I have sinned...' -- but before he can finish, his father is already shouting orders to the servants. Three specific things are to be brought out and put on the returning boy at once, before the boy can say another word. Which three?
answer: the best robe, a ring, and shoes
choices: the best robe, a ring, and shoes
a crown, a rod, and a golden chain
linen bands, oil, and a lamp
context: Luke 15:22. Each token means something specific: the robe is the honoured guest's mantle, the ring carries the father's seal (authority over the household), and shoes mark him as a free son and not a barefoot slave. Sackcloth and ashes are mourning wear (Job, Nineveh); linen bands and oil are burial gear (Lazarus). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: In the same breath, still holding his son, the father cuts him off mid-apology and shouts an order to the servants to kill one specific animal at once for a welcome-home feast. Which animal?
context: Luke 15:23: 'And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry.' The 'fatted calf' was a young beast penned apart from the herd and grain-fed for the biggest occasion the family would ever mark -- the household's showpiece meat. The Passover lamb, the two turtledoves (poor family's temple offering), and the ram of consecration (Aaron's priesthood, Exodus 29) are all real biblical animals sacrificed for particular occasions -- but the parable's feast animal is the calf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The elder brother has been out working in the fields all this time. He comes home, hears music and dancing, refuses to go inside, and starts listing his own long years of service to his father. In the middle of the rant, he complains that his father has never once given HIM a young animal to roast for a party with his friends -- a much smaller beast than the one being killed inside. What smaller animal does he name?
context: Luke 15:29: 'yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends' -- a kid, a young goat, the everyday party meat, versus the fatted calf being killed for his brother. The elder brother's fury is exact and petty: 'you never gave me even the cheap one.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: Luke sets this parable inside a group of three that Jesus tells one after another in Luke 15 -- three stories, each about something valuable being lost and then found. The Prodigal Son is the third. What are the other two?
answer: a lost sheep and a lost coin
choices: a lost sheep and a lost coin
a lost ring and a lost letter
a lost donkey and a lost cloak
a lost bride and a lost harp
context: Luke 15:3-7 (a shepherd leaves 99 sheep to find one that has wandered off), Luke 15:8-10 (a woman sweeps the whole house for one lost silver coin from her string of ten), and Luke 15:11-32 (the Lost Son). Together the three parables form Luke's 'lost-and-found' set. The other lost-object pairings in the choices are not from Jesus's parables. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The father goes out to the sulking elder brother and answers the whole complaint in one line that the parable turns on. He tells him everything the father has is already his -- but they had to celebrate, because his brother had been counted as one thing and now was another. In what pair does he put it?
answer: was dead, and is alive again
choices: was dead, and is alive again
was in shadow, and is in light
context: Luke 15:32. The father repeats a version of the same line from earlier in the scene: 'this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.' The other three pairs are all real Gospel formulas -- blind-now-sees is John 9, shadow-and-light is the Isaiah quotation over Galilee, silenced-and-speaks is Zechariah after John the Baptist's birth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodigal_Son.

question: The Tain Bo Cuailnge describes a physical transformation that comes over its young champion when he loses himself in combat: his body reshapes into something no longer human. Later Irish literature holds this passage as the signature battle-image of the whole tradition. Which hero undergoes it?
context: Fionn belongs to the later Fenian Cycle and never undergoes ristrad; Beowulf and Sigurd are heroes of other traditions listed here as adjacent distractors. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's battle-transformation has a specific Old Irish name -- a single word the Tain uses whenever the change comes on him. English translators have rendered it 'the warp-spasm' or 'the distortion'. What is the Old Irish word?
context: Also spelled riastradh. Geis = a magical prohibition; imbas = poetic inspiration; dinnshenchas = the lore of place-names. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: Above the twisted body the Tain describes something rising straight from the crown of Cu Chulainn's head -- a column, described as taller than the mast of a ship, made either of dark blood or black smoke, visible from a distance to every warrior on the field. The Irish call it the LON LAITH. What is that in English?
context: Lon laith, sometimes 'warrior's moon'. A single black column above the crown -- his mark on any battlefield. Mythical Archives; Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: The Tain gives one specific detail about Cu Chulainn's eyes in the ristrad that has become one of the most-quoted images in Irish literature. One eye retreats -- so deep the text says a wild crane could not probe it out. The other eye does the opposite. What does the other eye do?
answer: it bulges out onto his cheek
choices: it bulges out onto his cheek
it turns red as a hot coal
it closes and does not open
context: One eye in, one eye out. One of the most reprinted passages in early Irish literature. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: From Cu Chulainn's mouth in the ristrad the Tain gives one more sensory detail: his lower jaw strikes the upper 'a lion-killing blow' and out come objects as large as a ram's fleece each. What comes out?
context: The image is of the hero literally spitting fire the size of ram-fleeces. Wikipedia: Riastrad.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's boyhood deeds close with a scene of practical horror: he comes back to Emain Macha from his first raid still in the ristrad, and the men of Ulster are so afraid he will slaughter them all that they will not open the gates. Conchobar's queen Mugain leads the women of the fort out to the plain. What do they do to shame him out of the frenzy?
answer: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
choices: they walk out to meet him naked, baring their breasts
they set fire to their own hair in front of him
they lay their infant sons at his feet
they sing his mother's death-lament together
context: Mugain leads the women out; Cu Chulainn covers his face at the sight -- the shame breaks the frenzy long enough for the warriors to seize him. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain Recension I).  (Legend.)

question: With the boy Cu Chulainn's face covered from the women, the warriors seize him and plunge him into a series of vats of cold water to cool the ristrad off him. The Tain reports what happens to each. FIRST vat: the water bursts the wooden staves. SECOND vat: the water boils with bubbles the size of a fist. What happens in the THIRD vat?
answer: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
choices: the water heats only to a comfortable bath
the water freezes solid around him
the water is thrown out untouched
context: First bursts, second boils, third tempers -- and the boy is himself again. Mugain then puts a blue mantle and silver brooch on him and seats him at Conchobar's knee. Cuchulainn's Boyish Deeds (Tain).  (Legend.)

question: The ristrad passage in the Tain is one of the longest sustained physical descriptions in early Irish literature -- a set-piece Old Irish scribes clearly relished. In which of the great medieval Irish codices does the fullest surviving version of the Tain (Recension II) appear?
choices: the Annals of the Four Masters
context: Lebor Laignech, c.1160. The Book of Kells is a gospel-book; the Cathach is a 6th-c. psalter; the Annals are 17th-c. history. Recension I is in the Lebor na hUidre. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

question: Scholars set the ristrad beside a related Norse battle-state -- a frenzy of certain of Odin's warriors, said to fight in a trance without pain of wound or fire, and to remember nothing of it after. What is the Norse word for that state?
context: 'Going berserk'. Scholars note the ristrad is more monstrous and more visually elaborate than berserkergangr -- a physical melting into a fighting-shape, not merely a fury. Wergild = blood-price; einherjar = Odin's chosen dead in Valhalla; seidhr = Norse magic. Wikipedia: Berserker; Riastrad.

question: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, King Arthur has a great round wooden table set up at Camelot where his chosen knights sit as equals, none at the head. On what high feast day of the year do these knights all ride in to Camelot to renew their vows together?
context: Pentecost falls fifty days after Easter and was the high feast of the Round Table year in Malory. The knights gathered, feasted, and renewed the oath together; scribes recorded what each had done in the year past. Malory's Book III opens the pattern. Christmas and Easter were the two greatest feasts of the church year but did not have this special Round Table meaning; All Hallows (November 1) was a solemn feast for the dead, not for oath-renewal.  (Legend.)

question: The chosen knights of King Arthur sit as equals at his great round table at Camelot. Malory says that at the high feast the fellowship of the Round Table was always kept full, at about how many seated knights in all?
context: Malory gives 150 as the count of the fellowship of the Round Table at its full strength (Book III). Twelve is the number of apostles in the Christian pillar and of the Peers of France in the Roland tradition; forty is a number of days (the flood, the wilderness); three hundred is closer to the personal retinue of a great earl.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory, each seat around the Round Table bore the name of the knight who was to sit there, written in gold letters that appeared of themselves. One seat was called the Siege Perilous and was left empty because anyone unworthy who sat in it would die. For what one knight was that seat reserved by Merlin's prophecy?
context: Galahad, Lancelot's pure son by Elaine, was the only knight who could safely sit in the Siege Perilous; his coming was foretold from the making of the table. Lancelot was the greatest in arms but flawed by his love for the queen. Gawain was Arthur's chief nephew and a great knight but hot-tempered. Kay was the seneschal, sharp-tongued and not of the highest chivalry.  (Legend.)

question: At the high feast at Camelot, the fellowship of the Round Table renewed their vows together each year. In Malory's oath, the knights swore never to commit outrage or murder, always to flee treason, always to help ladies and widows, and never to take up battle in a wrongful quarrel. What else did the oath command about a defeated enemy?
answer: always to give mercy to any who asked mercy
choices: always to give mercy to any who asked mercy
always to hang defeated foes as a warning to others
always to hold captured knights for ransom
always to demand a public confession before sparing life
context: The mercy clause is the heart of the Pentecostal Oath: to spare any beaten foe who called for mercy, upon pain of forfeiture of his lordship and worship as an Arthurian knight. Hanging defeated foes was the crime of Malory's villains, such as the Red Knight of the Red Launds who had hanged nearly forty. Ransom was normal in real medieval war but was not written into the Round Table oath. Public confession is not there either.  (Legend.)

question: In Malory's Book XX, the fellowship of the Round Table is broken not by an outside army but from within. What accusation, brought before Arthur by Agravaine and Mordred, forced the king to condemn Queen Guinevere to the pyre and set the fellowship at war with itself?
answer: that she had lain with Sir Lancelot
choices: that she had lain with Sir Lancelot
that she had plotted with Morgan le Fay to poison the king
that she had taken the treasury of Camelot in secret to Benoic
that she had been born the daughter of a witch
context: Agravaine and Mordred trapped Lancelot in the queen's chamber and forced the accusation into the open; by his own laws Arthur had to condemn her to burn. Morgan le Fay's poisoning schemes belong to earlier books and did not touch the queen. The Benoic treasury and witch-birth accusations are inventions and do not appear in Malory.  (Legend.)

question: While Arthur was across the sea in France, laying siege to Lancelot in the castle of Joyous Gard, one member of the Round Table seized the throne of Britain in Arthur's absence, forced a crown on his own head, and tried to marry Queen Guinevere. Arthur turned back to fight him at the last battle of Camlann, where both were mortally wounded and the fellowship destroyed. Who was the usurper?
context: In Malory, Mordred is Arthur's own son by his half-sister Morgause, and himself a knight of the Round Table. Camlann killed nearly every knight on both sides. Agravaine was already dead before Camlann, killed with Colgrevaunce in the ambush of Lancelot. Palamedes was the Saracen knight of the Grail cycle; Meliagrance was the earlier abductor of Guinevere killed by Lancelot.  (Legend.)

question: After Camlann, only one knight of the Round Table remained with the dying Arthur on the shore. Arthur ordered him to throw Excalibur back into the water; a hand rose from the lake to catch it, and Arthur was carried away in a black barge to Avalon. Malory closes the book with the Latin epitaph said to be written on Arthur's tomb: what does it say?
answer: Here lies Arthur, the once and future king
choices: Here lies Arthur, the once and future king
Here lies the last of the Britons
Here rests the flower of chivalry
Here sleeps the sword that broke
context: Malory ends: 'HIC IACET ARTHURUS, REX QUONDAM REXQUE FUTURUS.' The 'once and future' promise is the tradition that Arthur is not truly dead but will return in Britain's greatest need; T.H. White's 'The Once and Future King' (1958) takes its title straight from this epitaph. The other three are invented for the choices.  (Legend.)

question: The Greek warriors who had hidden in the belly of the wooden horse climbed down at nightfall, opened a gate in the wall of Troy from within, and let the Greek army pour back into the city. What did the Greeks then do to the city itself?
context: The night the wooden horse trick pays off. The city is torched and the royal family destroyed one by one -- the dark counterweight to the cleverness of the horse. Sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2 and the Iliou Persis summary in Proclus.  (Legend.)

question: As Troy burned, the old king Priam pulled on his armour and ran to a family altar in his own courtyard for sanctuary. Who was the Greek warrior who ran him down and killed him at that altar?
context: Neoptolemus (also called Pyrrhus) came to Troy as a teenager, after Achilles was already dead. He becomes the face of the sack. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558.  (Legend.)

question: In Virgil's Aeneid, before Neoptolemus killed Priam himself, he first killed another son of Priam right in front of the old king to make him watch. Which son of Priam did Neoptolemus cut down at his father's feet?
context: Polites ran wounded through the palace and died at his father's feet. Priam then threw a spear at Neoptolemus that harmlessly bounced off the shield, and Neoptolemus dragged him to the altar and cut his throat. Deiphobus (who married Helen after Paris died) and Helenus (the prophet-son) also survived into the last night of Troy. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558.  (Legend.)

question: Cassandra was clinging to the wooden cult image inside a temple on the citadel of Troy. Which goddess's temple was it?
context: The temple was Athena's, which is why the sacrilege about to happen matters so much: Athena had helped the Greeks the whole ten years and is about to switch sides. Source: Iliou Persis summary; Euripides, Trojan Women prologue.  (Legend.)

question: A Greek warrior tore Cassandra away from the temple statue so violently that the wooden image of the goddess was dislodged and toppled. Which Greek warrior committed this sacrilege at Athena's altar?
answer: Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus of Locris
choices: Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus of Locris
context: There are two Ajaxes in the Greek army and children mix them up: Ajax the Great (Ajax son of Telamon) killed himself in a rage before Troy fell, after the armour of the dead Achilles was awarded to Odysseus instead of to him. Ajax the Lesser (son of Oileus) is the one at Athena's altar. Source: Iliou Persis summary; Odyssey 4.499-511.  (Legend.)

question: Hector's baby son had been a problem for the victorious Greeks: if he grew up, he would come back and avenge his father. In Euripides's play Trojan Women, what do the Greeks do to the child?
answer: They throw him from the walls of Troy
choices: They throw him from the walls of Troy
They cut his throat over Achilles's tomb
They drown him in the harbor of Troy
They bury him alive in the palace foundations
context: In Trojan Women, the herald Talthybius tells Andromache that the Greek council, at Odysseus's urging, has decided the child cannot be allowed to live. Source: Euripides, Trojan Women 719-739.  (Legend.)

question: In Euripides's Trojan Women, after Astyanax's body was carried back into ruined Troy, his grandmother Hecuba washed the child and laid him out for burial on a single object saved from his dead father. What object served as his bier?
choices: The topmost tile of the citadel
context: The shield that had covered Hector in battle now covers the child in the grave -- one of the most piercing images in Greek tragedy. Source: Euripides, Trojan Women 1133-1206.  (Legend.)

question: After Troy fell, the surviving royal women of Troy were parcelled out to the Greek captains as slaves. Which Greek captain took Cassandra as his prize?
context: Agamemnon and Cassandra were both cut down in the bath at Mycenae by his wife Clytemnestra (with Aegisthus) -- the opening scene of Aeschylus's Oresteia. Source: Aeschylus, Agamemnon; Odyssey 11.405-434.  (Legend.)

question: Priam's youngest daughter Polyxena was singled out by Neoptolemus after the sack of Troy. What did Neoptolemus do to her?
choices: Burned her alive on Achilles's pyre
Buried her beside Achilles in his tomb
Gave her as slave to Odysseus
context: The ghost of Achilles had demanded a bride from the Trojan spoils, and Neoptolemus carried out the demand on his father's behalf. Polyxena is the Trojan counterpart to Iphigenia, the girl sacrificed by the Greeks before the war began. In Euripides's Hecuba she asks to die standing, refusing to be treated as a slave. Source: Euripides, Hecuba; Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.  (Legend.)

question: Athenian audiences watched Euripides stage Trojan Women in 415 BCE, the year after Athens had massacred the men of a small island and enslaved its women. The play's grief-drenched sympathy for the losing side reads as protest. Which island's fate the year before is the background?
context: The Melian Dialogue in Thucydides 5 records Athens's ultimatum to Melos in 416 BCE: submit or be destroyed. When Melos refused, Athens killed the men and enslaved the women and children. Trojan Women premiered the following spring. Source: Thucydides 5.84-116; Euripides, Trojan Women (415 BCE).

question: In Matthew's gospel Jesus climbs a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, and before he begins his longest single teaching he takes a very specific posture -- the posture a rabbi always used when teaching students. What did Jesus do?
context: Matthew 5:1 -- 'seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him'. A rabbi taught SITTING; the audience stood or sat lower. This is why the whole discourse is called the Sermon on the Mount.

question: The very first Beatitude promises the KINGDOM OF HEAVEN. Which of these groups did Jesus say it belongs to?
context: Matthew 5:3 -- 'Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven'. Each of the other three groups also gets a promise: the pure in heart shall see God, the peacemakers shall be called children of God, those who mourn shall be comforted.

question: Jesus tells the crowd on the hillside they are the SALT of the earth. In the very next line he gives them a second image and pairs it with a picture -- something built high up that everyone can see for miles. What does he say cannot be hid?
answer: A city set on a hill
choices: A lamp lit on a hilltop
A city set on a hill
context: Matthew 5:14 -- 'Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.' The pairing (salt + light) is the point; the city is the picture Jesus uses to make the light-image concrete.

question: Halfway through the Sermon on the Mount Jesus teaches his disciples a short prayer that Christians would go on repeating for two thousand years. It has SEVEN petitions and it begins with a direct address. What are the opening words in the King James wording?
answer: Our Father which art in heaven
choices: Blessed be the name of God forever
Our Father which art in heaven
Hear O Israel the Lord our God
Almighty God unto whom all hearts
context: Matthew 6:9-13 -- 'After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done...' This is the Lord's Prayer.

question: To argue that God will provide for his followers, Jesus points to a flower growing wild and says even Solomon, the richest king of Israel, in all his glory was never dressed as well as one of these. Which flowering plant does he tell them to consider?
context: Matthew 6:28-29 -- 'Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.'

question: One line near the end of the sermon has been called the Golden Rule for centuries -- a single instruction that Jesus said sums up 'the law and the prophets'. Which of these is the Golden Rule?
answer: Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them
choices: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another
Do good to them that hate you, and pray for them that despitefully use you
context: Matthew 7:12. All four choices are real ethical teachings -- the first is the older 'silver rule' Rabbi Hillel gave, the third is from Paul in Romans 13:8, the fourth is from Jesus earlier in the same sermon at Matthew 5:44. The POSITIVE form 'do unto others' is what makes the Golden Rule distinctive.

question: The Sermon on the Mount closes with a parable about TWO BUILDERS. One puts his house on solid ROCK and it stands; the other builds on a different foundation, and when the rain descended and the floods came and the winds blew, Jesus says 'great was the fall of it'. What did the foolish man build his house on?
context: Matthew 7:24-27. The wise man's house on the rock stands; the foolish man's house on the sand collapses when the rain, floods and winds beat on it. This is the very last image before the sermon ends.

question: Luke's gospel preserves a shorter parallel to the Sermon on the Mount, and the setting is different -- Luke has Jesus come down and stand on a level place, not on a mountain, which is why Luke's version is called the Sermon on the PLAIN. Luke also matches each of his four blessings with a paired line delivered in the same rhythm, opening with a single sharp English word. What word opens each of Luke's four paired lines?
context: Luke 6:17-26 -- often called the Sermon on the Plain because Luke has Jesus come down and stand 'in the plain' (a level place). Luke gives four blessings (poor, hungry, weeping, hated) each answered by a matching 'Woe unto you' (rich, full, laughing, well-spoken-of).

question: In the ballads of Robin Hood, one royal officer sends his men into Sherwood again and again to catch Robin and hang the outlaws from the walls of his stone castle. Which town is that castle in?
context: The Sheriff of Nottingham is Robin Hood's chief enemy across the whole cycle. Robin's greenwood may be Barnsdale or Sherwood depending on the ballad, but the Sheriff is always tied to Nottingham. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Monk.  (Legend.)

question: A monk who had been robbed by Robin Hood spots him kneeling at prayer inside a Nottingham church and runs out to fetch the one man in the town powerful enough to put Robin in chains. What is that man's title?
context: In Robin Hood and the Monk (Child 119, earliest surviving Robin Hood ballad, c.1450) the monk fetches the Sheriff, who captures Robin in the church. Little John and Much the Miller's Son later rescue him. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and the Monk.  (Legend.)

question: The office of sheriff in England is older than the Robin Hood ballads by centuries. The word itself is a squashed-together Old English title -- two words for 'shire' and for the king's officer in it. What is that older Old English word the modern 'sheriff' comes from?
context: 'Sheriff' is a worn-down form of Old English 'scir-gerefa' -- shire-reeve, the king's reeve (officer) over a shire. Thanes were noble landholders, wardens and marshals were later Norman-French titles. Source: Wikipedia, Sheriff of Nottingham (position).

question: A medieval English sheriff owed the king's Exchequer a fixed sum each year from his shire -- and anything he could collect above that sum, he kept for himself. This arrangement had its own name in medieval finance. What was the practice called?
context: Sheriffs 'farmed' their shires -- paid a set farm (firma) to the Exchequer and pocketed everything squeezed above it. Gleaning was picking up leftover grain, reeving was general officer-work, tithing was the church tenth. Tax-farming is what made the office one of the most hated in the shires and gave rise to the Sheriff of Nottingham as a story-villain. Source: Wikipedia, Sheriff of Nottingham (position).

question: In A Gest of Robyn Hode, the Sheriff of Nottingham proclaims a grand contest at Nottingham as a trap to lure Robin out of hiding. Robin comes in disguise and wins it. What kind of contest is it?
context: In Fytte 5 of A Gest of Robyn Hode the Sheriff offers a prize arrow of gold and silver; Robin wins the shoot, is ambushed, Little John is wounded, and they take refuge at Sir Richard at the Lee's castle. Source: Wikipedia, A Gest of Robyn Hode.  (Legend.)

question: The oldest Robin Hood ballads -- A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin Hood and the Monk, Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne -- put the Sheriff of Nottingham on the page over and over. But in those ballads, one thing about him is missing. What is missing?
context: The Sheriff is only 'the Sheriff' or 'the high Sheriff of Nottingham' in the earliest ballads -- no first name, no family name, no coat of arms. His villainy is his office. Later Victorian retellings invented names ('Sir Reginald', 'Sir Guy') that are not in the medieval texts. Source: Robbins Library, The Sheriff.  (Legend.)
