question: In Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne (Child 118), Robin kills the bounty-hunter Guy and puts on Guy's distinctive cloak -- a strange, shaggy garment cut from an animal's skin. What kind of skin is Guy's cloak made of?
context: In Child 118, Guy of Gisborne wears a distinctive horse-hide cloak. After Robin kills Guy, he dons the horse-hide, disfigures Guy's face with his own bow-tip to hide the corpse's identity, and blows Guy's horn to signal a false victory to the Sheriff. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne.  (Legend.)

question: One real man was High Sheriff of Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire in the years of King John. His brutality -- protection payments squeezed from Nottingham, wrongful seizures, threats of arson against those who would not pay -- was so notorious he was named by name in the 1215 Magna Carta, in a clause ordering him and his kin expelled from royal office. What was his name?
context: Philip Marc, a Touraine-born supporter of King John, held Nottingham from 1208. Clause 50 of Magna Carta orders him, his brothers, and his nephew Geoffrey removed from office and out of England -- one of very few individuals singled out by name in the charter. He is probably the closest historical model behind the ballad villain. Source: Wikipedia, Philip Marc.

question: Achilles's dearest companion Patroclus had gone into battle wearing Achilles's own armour, and had been killed and stripped of it. Achilles now had nothing to fight in. Who had killed Patroclus and taken the armour?
context: Iliad 16 -- Patroclus, wearing Achilles's armour to scare the Trojans, is killed by Hector and stripped. Achilles's rage at this drives the rest of the poem. Source: Homer, Iliad 16.  (Legend.)

question: Achilles could not fight without armour, so his mother went to a god's forge to beg a new set for him. Who was Achilles's mother?
context: Thetis, one of the Nereids, married the mortal Peleus and bore Achilles. She spends the Iliad interceding for her son. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.  (Legend.)

question: Thetis went to the forge of the smith of the Olympian gods, the crippled god who hammered out divine armour, thunderbolts, and winged sandals for the other gods. Which god was she visiting?
context: Hephaestus was the smith of Olympus; the Romans called him Vulcan. He also forged Zeus's thunderbolts, Poseidon's trident, and Hermes's winged sandals. Source: Homer, Iliad 18; Hephaestus in Hesiod, Theogony.  (Legend.)

question: The very centre of the shield showed the whole cosmos: earth, sky, sea, the sun, the full moon, and a set of named constellations Homer catalogues one by one -- the Pleiades, the Hyades, mighty Orion, and one more that Homer says men also call 'the Wain'. What is that last one?
context: 'The Bear, whom men also call the Wain' -- Iliad 18.487-489, Lattimore's translation. The Wain (wagon) is the old English name for the same constellation Americans call the Big Dipper. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.483-489.  (Legend.)

question: Around the outer rim of the shield Hephaestus laid the great world-encircling river that Homer names as the boundary of everything. What is the river's name?
context: Okeanos (Ocean) was, for Homer, not the sea but a river that circled the flat disc of the world. Styx and Acheron are rivers of the underworld; Eridanos is a river of the far north. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.607-608.  (Legend.)

question: Farther out from the cosmic centre Hephaestus inlaid two cities. One was a city at peace, with a bridal procession by torchlight winding through the streets and elders judging a quarrel in the market. What was the other city's condition?
context: The two-cities scene is Iliad 18.490-540. The besieged city has an ambush laid at the river outside its walls -- a snapshot of war to answer the snapshot of peace. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.509-540.  (Legend.)

question: On one of the pastoral panels of the shield, Hephaestus inlaid a fight among the herds: two predators had brought down an ox from the herd of oxen, and the herdsmen and their dogs could not drive them off. What two predators were shown?
context: Iliad 18.573-586. The lions are gorging on the ox's black blood; the men and dogs stand back. Homer's world had lions, though they had gone extinct in Greece by classical times. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.573-586.  (Legend.)

question: The last scene before the outer river was a great dancing-floor where young men and young women danced hand in hand. Homer compares it to a legendary dancing-floor built long ago at a palace where a certain famous princess once danced. Which princess?
context: Iliad 18.590-592 -- the dancing-floor Daedalus built at Knossos for Ariadne (Minos's daughter, later the giver of the thread that saves Theseus in the Labyrinth). Source: Homer, Iliad 18.590-606.  (Legend.)

question: Years after finishing the twelve labors, Heracles marries a Calydonian princess, the sister of Meleager who once led the great boar-hunt. She is the wife who will unwittingly bring about his death by trusting a dying centaur's lie. What is her name?
context: Sophocles's Trachiniae and Apollodorus 2.7 name Deianira as Heracles's Calydonian wife. Megara was his first wife, whom he killed in his madness; Alcmene is his mortal mother; Iole is the captive girl whose arrival triggers the tragedy.  (Legend.)

question: In midstream Nessus bolts for the far bank with Deianira on his back. Heracles turns, draws his great bow, and drops the centaur with a single shot from long range. The arrow he uses is the same kind that once left the centaur Chiron in incurable pain. What is on its tip?
choices: starlight from the forges of Hephaestus
sap from the golden apples of the Hesperides
context: Apollodorus 2.5.2 and 2.7.6. Heracles kept the arrows he dipped in the Hydra's blood after killing it at Lerna; the same poison had already crippled Chiron and Pholus, and will finally kill Heracles himself.  (Legend.)

question: Dying on the bank, Nessus calls Deianira close and tells her a parting lie. He says to soak up some of the blood pouring from his wound and hide it in a jar; smeared later on any of her husband's clothes, he promises, it will act like a certain kind of magic she should keep in reserve. What does Nessus claim the blood is?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 570-587. The blood is really soaked in Hydra-venom from the arrow just fired; Nessus knows perfectly well he has handed her a delayed murder-weapon disguised as a love-charm.  (Legend.)

question: Years after the river-crossing Heracles sacks a city and brings home a captive princess. Deianira, sitting at home, watches the young woman arrive and fears her husband is about to leave her for a younger bride. Panicking, she remembers the dying centaur's advice. What is the captive girl's name?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae. Iole, daughter of King Eurytus of Oechalia, is the fresh bride who triggers Deianira's panic. Omphale is the Lydian queen Heracles once served in women's clothing; Auge and Chalciope are other Heracles-women from earlier episodes.  (Legend.)

question: Deianira's soaked gift reaches Heracles at his sacrifice on Cape Cenaeum in Euboea. He puts it on for the ritual, and as his body warms the cloth something horrific begins. He panics and tears at the shirt to rip it off. What comes off with the cloth?
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 1046-1075. The Hydra-venom in the soaked blood, activated by body-heat, fuses the fabric to Heracles's skin and eats through muscle; when he rips at the shirt his own flesh tears away with it, and in his agony he uproots trees on the mountainside.  (Legend.)

question: Learning from a messenger that her jar of 'love-charm' was really Hydra-poison and that she has just killed her own husband, Deianira does not wait for his return. What does she do in that same hour?
choices: she flees to a temple for sanctuary
she runs to warn her son Hyllus
she throws the empty jar into the sea
context: Sophocles, Trachiniae 812-946. Deianira takes her own life the moment she understands what she has done; in Sophocles she uses a sword on her marriage-bed. The horror of the play is that she is innocent of intent -- she meant only to keep her husband.  (Legend.)

question: Knowing no cure exists for Hydra-poison, the burning Heracles has his companions carry him up a mountain, orders a great pyre of oak logs built, and lies down on it to end his agony. What is the mountain called?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.229-272; Sophocles's Trachiniae ends with Heracles carried toward Oeta. Ida is Zeus's Cretan mountain; Pelion is the mountain of Chiron's cave; Cithaeron is where the infant Heracles was said to have strangled the twin lions.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles orders his companions to set fire to the great pyre and end him. Every one of them refuses in horror. Finally one man agrees -- but only in exchange for Heracles's bow and the last of the Hydra-poisoned arrows. Which companion strikes the flame?
context: Sophocles's Philoctetes. Iolaus is Heracles's chariot-nephew who cauterised the Hydra-stumps; Hylas is his young companion carried off by nymphs at a spring; Theseus is the Athenian hero of another cycle. Philoctetes is specifically the one who lights the pyre and earns the bow.  (Legend.)

question: A Greek oracle warns that Troy cannot be taken until Heracles's bow is brought to the war, and Philoctetes -- carrying the very bow he was given for lighting the pyre -- eventually shoots one of King Priam's sons dead outside the walls. Which Trojan prince does he kill with that bow?
context: Sophocles's Philoctetes and the Little Iliad. The oracle's condition is that Troy cannot fall without Heracles's bow. Hector is killed earlier by Achilles; Aeneas escapes the city and founds the Roman line; Deiphobus, another son of Priam, is killed later at the sack. Paris is the prince whose theft of Helen began the war, and Philoctetes with Heracles's bow shoots him down.  (Legend.)

question: As the pyre on Mount Oeta burns, the mortal part of Heracles is consumed and only his Zeus-half is carried up to Olympus. There Hera at last reconciles with the stepson she has hounded his whole life and gives him her own daughter as bride. Which daughter of Hera does Heracles marry on Olympus?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.229-272. Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera, is cup-bearer of the gods until she marries the deified Heracles. Eileithyia is Hera's daughter of childbirth (the goddess who delayed Heracles's own birth); Enyo is a war-goddess sometimes called Hera's daughter; Angelos is an obscure daughter of Hera in local tradition.  (Legend.)

question: After the Tuatha De Danann went underground into the hollow hills, later Irish tradition stopped calling them 'the Tuatha De' at all -- they became a new folk under a new name, the beings that English-speakers now just call 'the fairies' or 'the Good Folk.' Which of these is that Irish name?
context: AOS SI (pronounced roughly ees-shee, literally 'folk of the mounds') is the Irish name for the fairy folk -- the Tuatha De Danann in retreat underground. The Fianna are the roving warrior-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill; the Fir Bolg are the fourth wave in the Book of Invasions; the Sons of Mil are the Milesians (the modern Irish) themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aos_Si.  (Legend.)

question: One night of the year the barrier between the sidhe mounds and the world above is said to open, so that the aos si walk out and the ghosts of the dead walk in. Modern Ireland has inherited that same night, and much of the world now keeps its distant descendant on the eve of it as HALLOWEEN. Which old Irish festival is this?
context: SAMHAIN (November 1) is the direct ancestor of Halloween -- the night the sidhe open. Bealtaine (May 1) opens summer; Lughnasadh (August 1) is the harvest festival; Imbolc (February 1) is spring's opening. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhain.  (Legend.)

question: Once the settlement with the Milesians was struck, one of the Tuatha De took charge of dividing up the underground kingdom, handing out one mound to each of his fellow gods -- and then raised a magical mist called the FETH FIADA over the whole country to hide the aos si from mortal eyes. Which of the Tuatha De did this?
context: Manannan mac Lir ('son of the sea') is the Tuatha De sea-god who links the visible world to the Otherworld across the water; he assigned the mounds and raised the FETH FIADA (as in Altram Tige Da Medar, the Fosterage of the House of the Two Vessels). Lugh Lamhfhada is the long-armed spear-god, Nuada Silver-Arm is the first Tuatha De king, Ogma is the champion who invented the ogham script -- all Tuatha De heroes but not the divider. Source: irishmyths.com/2025/08/27/god-map-fairy-mounds-tuath-de-danann.  (Legend.)

question: In the story of Oisin the son of Fionn mac Cumhaill, Oisin rides off with the Otherworld princess Niamh and spends what he thinks is one long happy stay in the Land of Youth. When he finally rides back and his foot touches Irish soil again, he turns instantly into a withered old man and dies -- because he has been away for centuries, not weeks. How long, by the count of the story, had Oisin actually been gone?
context: Oisin is gone THREE HUNDRED YEARS while it feels to him like a short stay; the classic 'time-in-fairyland' story. Time in the sidhe mounds and Tir na nOg does not run at the same rate as time above ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oisin.  (Legend.)

question: One species of tree -- especially a solitary specimen standing alone in the middle of a field, unattached to any hedge or wood -- is sacred to the aos si in Irish folk-tradition, and farmers to this day will plough carefully around it rather than cut it down. Which tree is it?
context: The lone HAWTHORN (whitethorn) is the classic fairy-tree; to cut one down is to invite the aos si's wrath. Yew is the graveyard tree of Ireland; rowan is planted against fairy mischief (a protection, not a mound); ash is one of the sacred five 'guardian trees' but not the specifically-fairy tree. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aos_Si; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorn.  (Legend.)

question: In 1999 the route of a brand-new motorway in County Clare was actually altered around a single small hawthorn -- because the Irish folklorist Eddie Lenihan told the papers it was a rendezvous-point for the Kerry aos si on their way to fight the Connacht aos si, and the construction workers refused to touch it. The story made the international news and the tree still stands. What was the tree at?
context: The LATOON FAIRY BUSH in County Clare -- a lone whitethorn on the route of the new M18 -- was spared in May 1999 after Lenihan's letter to the Irish Times went viral (CNN, BBC, New York Times all picked it up). Tara is the High Kings' hill in Meath; Skellig is the monastic sea-crag in Kerry; Uisneach is the mythic centre of Ireland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latoon_fairy_bush.

question: In the city of Ephesus, Paul rented out a lecture hall and taught in it daily for two full years. Acts names the local Ephesian schoolmaster who owned the hall. What was the hall-owner's name?
context: Acts 19:9-10 (KJV): '...disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus. And this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus.' The Greek name tyrannos originally meant a ruler who had seized power outside the constitution -- it is the root of the English word 'tyrant'. The schoolmaster himself is just the person whose lecture-room Paul rented daily for two years.

question: Ephesus was famous across the Greek world as the home of a temple to a goddess -- a temple so large it counted as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Which goddess did the great Ephesian temple honour?
context: Acts 19:27 (KJV) calls her 'the great goddess Diana' -- the Latin name the King James translators used for Artemis. The Ephesian version of the goddess was pictured with rows of what look like breasts, eggs, or dates across her chest; the temple was the biggest structure in the Greek world of its day, and one of the Seven Wonders alongside the pyramids, the Hanging Gardens, the Lighthouse at Alexandria, and others.

question: So many Ephesians converted under Paul's teaching that owners of magic spellbooks hauled their scrolls into the market square and set them on fire in public. Acts records the shocking value of the burnt-book pile in coins. What was the counted value of the books they burned?
context: Acts 19:19 (KJV): 'Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.' If those pieces were drachmas (a day's wages), the burnt library was worth about 137 years of a labourer's pay.

question: Ephesus had a booming souvenir trade tied to its great temple: craftsmen hammered out tiny metal models of the temple facade -- pocket-sized versions of the shrine, sold to pilgrims. From what metal did the Ephesus craftsmen chiefly make those shrines?
context: Acts 19:24 (KJV): 'For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen.' Small terracotta and metal facade-models have been dug up around the Ephesus site by modern archaeologists, matching the Acts description.

question: One of the Ephesian craftsmen called all the fellow workers of his trade together and gave a warning speech: this man Paul was turning people away from idols not just in Ephesus but throughout all Asia, and their whole livelihood was in danger of being set at nought. Who was the craftsman who called the meeting?
context: Acts 19:24-27 (KJV). Demetrius is careful to mix commercial self-interest with civic-religious pride: he warns that Paul is not only shrinking their profits but 'the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed'. The playbook of a threatened guild has not changed in two thousand years.

question: The mob rushed to the great open-air stone theatre of Ephesus, and dragged two of Paul's travelling companions in with them. Both men were from Macedonia; one was named Aristarchus. What was the name of the other companion the crowd seized?
context: Acts 19:29 (KJV): 'And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.' The Ephesus theatre still stands today, cut into the slope of Mount Pion, with about sixty rows of seats and room for around 25,000 people. A visitor can sit where the crowd sat.

question: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus is sailing home from Troy when he is warned about a stretch of sea where women sing so beautifully that any sailor who hears them steers his ship onto the rocks. What are these singing women called?
context: The Sirens sat on a meadow-shore heaped with the bones of dead sailors their song had drawn to death. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12; Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Circe, the enchantress on the island of Aeaea, warned Odysseus about the Sirens before he sailed -- but first she had done something remarkable to his crew that Odysseus had had to reverse. What had Circe done to Odysseus's men?
choices: Put them to sleep for a year
context: Circe transformed Odysseus's landing party into swine with a touch of her wand; Odysseus, protected by the herb moly, forced her to change them back before she then hosted him and warned him of the Sirens ahead. Source: Homer, Odyssey 10 and 12; Wikipedia, 'Circe'.  (Legend.)

question: Circe told Odysseus that no man could hear the song and steer, so his crew had to be deafened. She told him to soften a lump of one specific substance in the sun and press it into every sailor's ears. What did she tell him to use?
context: Odysseus kneaded a great lump of beeswax warm in his hands and stopped every crewman's ears one by one, so they could not hear the Sirens at all. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.170-180; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus himself wanted to HEAR the song and live. Circe told him there was only one way: he could listen, but only if his crew did one specific thing to him before the ship reached the singers. What did the crew have to do to Odysseus?
answer: Bind him standing upright to the mast
choices: Bind him standing upright to the mast
Chain him inside the hold below decks
Blindfold him and lash his hands
Lock him inside a wooden chest
context: Circe's rule was that Odysseus could listen only if he was bound hand and foot to the ship's mast, unable to steer or leap overboard. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: When Odysseus gave his crew their orders, he warned them: if he begged to be released while the song was playing, they must NOT let him go. What was his exact standing order to the crew?
choices: Row on and ignore all his signals
Turn the ship out to open sea
context: Odysseus told them that begging would be a sign of the song's power, not a real command; if he pleaded to be released, the crew was to bind him TIGHTER. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.160-165; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: The Sirens' song in Homer is not about love or seduction at all -- what they promise the passing sailor is very different. In the Odyssey, what do the Sirens offer to tell Odysseus if he will come ashore to them?
answer: All that comes to pass on the fertile earth
choices: All that comes to pass on the fertile earth
The road home to Ithaca in three days
The song that raises the dead from Hades
The name of the god who cursed his voyage
context: The Sirens promise KNOWLEDGE -- omniscient understanding of everything that happens on the earth, and of all the Greeks and Trojans suffered at Troy. It is a lure aimed at Odysseus's cleverness. Source: Homer, Odyssey 12.184-191.  (Legend.)

question: As the ship glided past the meadow of bones and the song swelled, Odysseus struggled against his ropes and threw his eyebrows up as a signal to be freed. Two crewmen stood up and did the opposite -- they came over and tightened his bonds. What are the two names Homer gives us?
context: Homer names Perimedes and Eurylochus as the two crewmen who obeyed the standing order and bound their captain tighter to the mast (Odyssey 12.195-200). Source: Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Homer's Odyssey never gives the Sirens names on the shore. Later Greek writers standardized the count at three and gave them names. What are the three names later Greeks gave the Sirens?
context: Homer counts only two Sirens and never names them. Post-Homeric Greek tradition fixed the count at three and named them Parthenope, Ligeia, and Leucosia. The distractor triads are the three Fates, the three Furies, and the three Graces. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: Modern pictures show the Sirens as mermaids -- women with fish tails from the waist down. But the very earliest Greek vase-paintings show them with a completely different body. What did the earliest Greek artists give the Sirens instead of fish tails?
context: Early Greek vase-painting portrays the Sirens as bird-bodied creatures with human heads. The fish-tailed mermaid form is a medieval and Renaissance development. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: The English language still carries this Homeric scene as an everyday idiom. If someone today says a proposal is a 'siren song', what do they mean by that phrase?
choices: A warning cry before a battle
A promise from a dying friend
A tune sung only by children
context: 'Siren song' names anything alluring that leads the follower to ruin -- the phrase comes straight from Odysseus's episode with the Sirens. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siren (mythology)'.

question: A medieval Irish book compiled in the 11th century, the Lebor Gabala Erenn ('the Book of the Taking of Ireland'), gives the island an origin story in successive waves of settlers, one after another, each taking the land from the last. How many waves does the book count?
context: The book is the LEBOR GABALA ERENN, and it counts six waves: Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and the Milesians. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebor_Gabala_Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: The medieval Irish 'Book of Invasions' opens with a first wave of settlers led by a granddaughter of Noah. She set sail with fifty women and only three men and reached Ireland forty days before the Flood, hoping to outrun the water. What was her name?
context: CESSAIR is the leader of the first wave in the Book of Invasions -- fifty women, three men, one ship, forty days before the Flood. Every one of the fifty women is named in the manuscripts. Eriu is the Tuatha De queen whose name became Eire; Danu is the mother-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann; Boann is the goddess of the River Boyne. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessair.  (Legend.)

question: The Flood swallowed everyone in Cessair's fleet except a single man -- her own husband. He alone survived, according to the tale, by shape-shifting for the whole year of the Flood into one particular animal (and later lived on through all the other invasions as the eye-witness of Irish history). What did he shape-shift into first?
context: FINTAN MAC BOCHRA turned into a SALMON to survive the Flood -- the same salmon-of-wisdom motif that runs through Irish story into the Fenian Cycle. He later took the shapes of an eagle and a hawk (and finally a man again) to live on as witness through every wave of the six. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fintan_mac_Bochra.  (Legend.)

question: The Book of Invasions gives Cessair's husband a proper name he keeps through his many centuries of shape-shifting. It is a name Irish tradition returns to again and again as 'the witness of all Ireland.' Which of these is it?
context: FINTAN MAC BOCHRA is Cessair's husband who lives through all six invasions. Tuan mac Cairill is a parallel shape-changing witness from the wave of Partholon (with the same job); Mog Ruith is the great blind druid of Munster; Amergin Gluingel is the Milesian poet -- the man of the sixth wave, not the first. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fintan_mac_Bochra.  (Legend.)

question: The second wave of invaders reached Ireland roughly three hundred years after the Flood, led by a man whose name the medieval scribes give as Partholon. His people cleared new plains for farming and brought in the first cattle. Then, all in one week, they were wiped out to a man -- leaving only one shape-changing survivor, Tuan mac Cairill, to witness what came next. What killed them?
context: Partholon's people are wiped out by a PLAGUE in one week, leaving only Tuan mac Cairill as a shape-changing sole survivor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partholon.  (Legend.)

question: The fourth wave in the Book of Invasions carries a strange name in Irish -- FIR BOLG, which the medieval scribes explain with a legend: this people had been slaves overseas, forced by their masters to carry the raw material for building-work in leather bags on their backs, until they escaped and sailed home. Which material were they carrying?
context: 'FIR BOLG' means 'men of bags' -- the legend is that in Greece they were forced to carry earth in leather bags to fill in rocky ground before they broke free and returned to Ireland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fir_Bolg.

question: When the Fir Bolg reached Ireland their five chieftains carved the island up into five kingdoms, and the names of four of those five are still on the map today as Ulster, Leinster, Munster, and Connacht. The fifth was the sacred middle kingdom that gave its name to a modern county still called by its Irish form. Which is that fifth province?
context: MIDE ('the middle') is the fifth province of the Fir Bolg carve-up, surviving as the modern county name MEATH (an anglicisation of Mide). Ossory, Breifne, and Thomond are all real Irish sub-kingdoms of later medieval Ireland but not one of the original five provinces. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meath; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fir_Bolg.  (Legend.)

question: The fifth wave of the Book of Invasions -- the WAVE OF THE GODS, the Tuatha De Danann -- rolled in over Ireland in dark clouds of fog and beat the Fir Bolg in a great fight. That fight is one of the two great Battles of Moytura. Which one was it?
context: The FIRST Battle of Moytura (Cath Maige Tuired Cunga) was Tuatha De against the Fir Bolg. The SECOND Battle of Moytura, later, was Tuatha De against the Fomorians. Clontarf (1014) is a historical battle -- Brian Boru against the Vikings. The Battle of Ventry is a Fenian-cycle tale of Fionn mac Cumhaill. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cath_Maige_Tuired.  (Legend.)

question: The sixth wave in the Book of Invasions -- the wave that STAYED, the wave the modern Irish descend from -- is named after its leader, whose own name doubles as an epithet: MIL of somewhere. From which land does Mil, the founder of the sixth wave, take his name?
context: MIL ESPAINE -- 'Mil of SPAIN' -- gives his name to the MILESIANS, the sixth wave. The medieval Irish schools placed the launching-point in Iberia (specifically Galicia in the north-west). Egypt, Greece, and Sicily are all launching-points for other, earlier waves in the same book (Partholon's people, for instance, are said to pass through Sicily and Greece). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milesians_(Irish).  (Legend.)

question: The druid-poet of the Milesians, the man who sang the invaders onto Irish soil with a claiming-poem the Book of Invasions preserves in full, carries an unusual epithet in the manuscripts -- a nickname referring to a part of his own body. What does his epithet 'Gluingel' actually mean?
context: AMERGIN GLUINGEL -- 'White-Kneed Amergin' -- is the founding poet of Irish tradition. 'Silver-Armed' is Nuada (Nuada Airgetlam) of the Tuatha De; 'Swift-Footed' is a Homeric epithet (Achilles); 'Sharp-Eyed' is a general Celtic hero-epithet but not Amergin's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amergin_Gluingel.  (Legend.)

question: The Book of Invasions is a work of medieval CHRISTIAN-IRISH SYNCRETISM -- an anonymous monk-compiler in the 11th century trying to fit Ireland's older pagan cosmology, gods and all, into a wider world-history he already believed in. Which biblical framing is he trying to fit the whole thing inside?
context: The compiler works from a GENESIS-and-FLOOD frame -- which is exactly why the first wave is a granddaughter of Noah trying to outrun the deluge. The whole scheme is designed to give Ireland an origin story to rival Rome and Israel. Exodus, the fall of Jerusalem, and Revelation are all later biblical events. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebor_Gabala_Erenn.  (Legend.)

question: Jesus pushes a boat out from the shore of the Sea of Galilee, sits down in it while the crowd stands on the beach, and opens a parable with a single farmer image. What is the farmer doing?
choices: Threshing wheat on a stone floor
Digging a well beside his field
context: Matthew 13:3 KJV: 'Behold, a sower went forth to sow.' The parable of the Sower opens Matthew 13 -- a chapter-long teaching Jesus delivers seated in a boat, using seven parables in a row. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: In the parable of the Sower, some seed falls on the beaten footpath running alongside the field. Jesus names what happens to that seed almost at once.
answer: The birds come and eat it up
choices: The birds come and eat it up
The rain washes it into the ditch
The oxen tread it into the dust
The wind blows it back into the sack
context: Matthew 13:4 KJV: 'And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up.' The 'way side' is the packed footpath at the edge of a Galilean field where seed could not sink in. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: In the parable of the Sower, seed falls on stony ground where there is only a thin layer of soil over the rock. Jesus says it springs up quickly -- and then something goes wrong.
answer: It withers in the sun because it has no root
choices: It withers in the sun because it has no root
It is trampled flat by the shepherd's flock
The stones grow warm and scorch the young shoot
The seed cracks apart before it can send up a stalk
context: Matthew 13:5-6 KJV: '...forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: In the parable of the Sower, the seed that falls on GOOD ground finally bears fruit. Jesus gives three specific numbers for how much it yields, listed in one order in Matthew and the reverse order in Mark. In Matthew 13:8 the numbers are given in this order:
context: Matthew 13:8 KJV: 'But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.' Mark 4:8 reverses the order to ascending -- thirty, sixty, hundred. Source: KJV Matthew 13, Mark 4.

question: Most of Jesus's parables are left standing without explanation, but the Sower is one of the very few he DECODES afterward for his disciples. In Matthew 13:22 he names one thing that acts like the thorns and chokes the seed of the word.
answer: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
choices: The care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches
The false teaching of the elders and the scribes
The pride of learning and the boast of knowledge
The hunger and the thirst and the labour of the field
context: Matthew 13:22 KJV: 'He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.' The Sower is one of the very few parables Jesus explains rung by rung. Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: In the same chapter as the Sower, Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to the smallest of seeds, one a Galilean farmer could barely see between his fingers. Which seed does he name?
context: Matthew 13:31-32 KJV: 'The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.' Source: KJV Matthew 13.

question: The 'grain of mustard seed' in Matthew 13 is not just rhetoric -- botanists identify it as the black mustard of Galilee, Brassica nigra, whose seed measures only about one to two millimetres across. In good Galilean soil, how tall can that same plant grow in a single season?
context: Black mustard (Brassica nigra) really does grow eight to ten feet tall in the fertile soil of the Levant in a single growing season, forming a woody bush -- large enough for small birds to perch and shelter in. It is botanically an herbaceous annual, not a true tree, so Jesus's 'becometh a tree' is rhetorical scale, but the plant is genuinely dramatic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustard_seed ; biologyinsights.com/how-big-is-a-mustard-seed-tree.

question: Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record the same seed-parables, but ONE seed parable is found only in Mark and nowhere else. In it a farmer scatters seed and then 'sleepeth, and riseth night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how' (Mark 4:26-27). What is that Mark-only parable called?
context: Mark 4:26-29 is the only parable unique to Mark's gospel. Its picture of the stages of growth -- 'first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear' -- shows a farmer who cannot force the growth, only wait and reap. Source: KJV Mark 4 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Growing_Seed.

question: The disciples Peter, Andrew, James and John worked as commercial fishermen on the shore of one specific lake -- the same lake where Jesus later slept through a violent storm in the stern of their boat, and where on another night he walked out across the waves to reach them. Which lake?
context: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long. It sits some 210 metres below sea level, which is one reason the temperature contrast with the ring of hills around it drives such abrupt storms. The disciples Peter, Andrew, James and John were commercial fishermen from its shore.

question: While the wind and waves were nearly swamping the boat and the disciples were fighting to keep it afloat, Jesus was in the stern of the boat -- and Mark keeps one small homely detail about him that Matthew and Luke both drop. What was Jesus doing?
choices: Bailing out water with the others
context: Mark 4:38 -- 'he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow'. Only Mark keeps the pillow detail -- Matthew and Luke both say 'asleep' but drop the cushion. It is one of the small vivid touches that tradition says Peter (Mark's source) remembered from the actual boat.

question: The disciples, sure the boat was going down, shook Jesus awake with one panicked question -- Mark preserves the exact wording. What did they say to him?
answer: Master, carest thou not that we perish
choices: Lord, if it be thou, save us
Master, carest thou not that we perish
Peace be still, we are undone
Have mercy on us, son of David
context: Mark 4:38. All four choices are real gospel lines -- 'Lord, if it be thou' is Peter on the water in Matthew 14, 'peace be still' is what Jesus SAYS a moment later, and 'son of David, have mercy' is Bartimaeus in Mark 10. The reproach ('carest thou NOT') is the mark of this specific scene.

question: On a later crossing of the same lake, the disciples were alone in the boat at night, rowing against a headwind, when they saw a figure approaching them ACROSS THE WATER. Their first reaction was not joy or recognition -- they were terrified. What did they think the figure was?
context: Matthew 14:26 -- 'they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear'. Mark 6:49 uses the same word (phantasma). Jesus called back at once: 'Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.'

question: Matthew's gospel adds a scene the other gospels leave out -- ONE of the disciples in the boat called back to the figure walking on the water and asked to be told to come out onto the water too. Which disciple did this?
context: Matthew 14:28 -- 'Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water'. Only Matthew records this. Mark and John both cut straight from Jesus reassuring the disciples to Jesus getting into the boat and the wind dropping.

question: Peter actually climbed out of the boat and took several steps on the water toward Jesus. Then something specific broke his concentration and he began to sink -- Matthew names it exactly. What did Peter notice that made him afraid?
choices: The waves against the far shore
context: Matthew 14:30 -- 'when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me'. Matthew is careful: it isn't the WATER that scared Peter (he was already walking on it), it's the wind he suddenly noticed.

question: When Jesus caught the sinking Peter and lifted him back to standing on the water, he gave him a two-part sentence -- one nickname and one question. The nickname was tender-ironic ('O thou of little faith'), and then Jesus asked him a single question about what had just happened. What did Jesus ask?
context: Matthew 14:31 -- 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?' The other three are real Jesus/Paul lines -- 'why hast thou forsaken me' is the cry from the cross (Matthew 27:46), 'believest thou this' is to Martha at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:26), 'who did hinder you' is Paul to the Galatians (Galatians 5:7).

question: The walking-on-water scene comes directly after a specific miracle earlier the same evening -- one that all four gospels record and that gave Jesus a reason to dismiss the disciples and go up the mountain alone to pray. Which miracle happened just hours before he walked across the lake to the boat?
answer: The feeding of the five thousand
choices: The feeding of the five thousand
context: Matthew 14:13-33; Mark 6:30-52; John 6:1-21. Every gospel places the walking-on-water on the crossing right after the feeding -- Jesus dismissed the fed crowd (about 5,000 men fed with five loaves and two fish), sent the disciples over the lake, and stayed alone on the mountain until the fourth watch of the night, when he came to them across the water.

question: Odysseus finally reached home in Ithaca after twenty years, but did not walk into his own hall as the king. He wanted first to see who had been eating his stores. What disguise did he choose?
context: Athena disguises Odysseus so he can walk the palace unrecognised and count his enemies. Source: Homer, Odyssey 13.397-403; 17.  (Legend.)

question: For years, a mob of young noblemen had been feasting daily in Odysseus's hall, pressing his wife Penelope to remarry. They had not all come from Ithaca -- they had sailed in from the neighbouring islands too. How many islands in all did these suitors come from?
context: Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and Ithaca itself -- 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, 12 from Ithaca, 108 in all. Source: Homer, Odyssey 16.245-253.  (Legend.)

question: The Odyssey gives an exact count of the young noblemen eating in Odysseus's hall. How many suitors were there in all?
context: 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, 12 from Ithaca -- the number matters because Odysseus, his son, and two servants have to kill every one of them. Source: Homer, Odyssey 16.245-253.  (Legend.)

question: To hold the suitors off for three years, Penelope had promised to choose one of them the moment she finished weaving a burial shroud -- and every night she quietly undid what she had woven that day. Whose burial shroud was she pretending to weave?
context: Odysseus's aged father Laertes was still alive, living on a small farm outside town; Penelope claimed she owed him the shroud out of duty. A palace maid named Melantho eventually betrayed the trick. Source: Homer, Odyssey 2.93-110; 19.137-156.  (Legend.)

question: Penelope finally announced a contest: whoever could string Odysseus's own great old bow and shoot one arrow through a line of iron axe-heads would be her new husband. How many axe-heads did the arrow have to pass through?
context: Twelve is a specific and famously puzzling number -- Homer describes the axes lined up in a straight row and Odysseus sending one arrow through all the sockets. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.75-79; 21.420-423.  (Legend.)

question: The great bow that lay unstrung in the palace storeroom the whole time Odysseus was away had been given to him as a young man by a guest-friend, long before the war at Troy. Which friend, whose name the Odyssey names carefully, had made him that gift?
context: Iphitus and the young Odysseus had exchanged guest-gifts -- Iphitus giving the great bow, Odysseus giving a sword and spear. The bow was too precious to carry to Troy and had waited in the storeroom for the whole span of the Iliad plus the whole span of the Odyssey. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.11-41.  (Legend.)

question: The suitors tried the bow one by one. They even softened its horn at the fire and oiled it, but not one of them could bend it enough to slip the string on. Then the disguised beggar in the corner quietly asked to try. Who in the hall commanded that the stranger be given the bow?
context: Telemachus was in on the plan. He commands the servants to hand the bow across and tells his mother to go to her chamber -- the men will handle what comes next. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.343-358.  (Legend.)

question: The old beggar took the bow and, Homer writes, strung it as easily 'as when a man skilled in the lyre easily stretches a string to a new peg.' He plucked it once and it sang like a bird. Then he shot one arrow clean through all twelve axe-head sockets. What did he do NEXT, before the suitors could react?
answer: Threw off the rags and leapt onto the great threshold of the hall
choices: Threw off the rags and leapt onto the great threshold of the hall
Called for a herald to announce his true name
Turned the bow on Penelope to test her loyalty
Ran to the palace gate to bar it against the town
context: 'Now for another mark,' he says -- Odyssey 22.5-6, Fagles's translation. From the raised stone threshold he has a clear line of fire over the whole hall. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.1-8.  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus and Telemachus were only two men against more than a hundred. Two loyal household slaves helped them bar the doors of the great hall and kill the suitors from the shadows. What were the two loyal servants' jobs on Odysseus's farm?
context: Eumaeus the swineherd (whose hut had been Odysseus's first shelter on Ithaca) and Philoetius the cowherd. Both had proved their loyalty when Odysseus tested them. Source: Homer, Odyssey 21.188-244; 22.  (Legend.)

question: One of Odysseus's own household staff, the goatherd Melanthius, was a traitor -- he had kicked the disguised beggar in the road and had been feeding the suitors the best of the herd. During the fight, he was caught trying to sneak a fresh load of weapons and armour to the surviving suitors. What did Odysseus's men do to him?
answer: Hoisted him up from the beams of the storeroom
choices: Hoisted him up from the beams of the storeroom
Threw him from the palace roof
Sold him overseas the next morning
context: Eumaeus and Philoetius bind his feet and hands behind him and haul him up to the rafters on a rope, to leave him hanging until the fight is over. Homer's later description of his end -- nose and ears cut off, hands and feet chopped -- is one of the grimmest passages in the poem. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.187-193; 22.474-477.  (Legend.)

question: After all the suitors were dead, Telemachus turned to a second reckoning inside the palace. Twelve of the household maids had gone willingly to the suitors' beds during Odysseus's twenty-year absence. Odysseus told his son to kill them cleanly with the sword; Telemachus refused that and did something else. What did Telemachus do to the twelve maids?
answer: Hanged them from a ship's cable in the courtyard
choices: Hanged them from a ship's cable in the courtyard
Sold them into slavery in Egypt
Sent them into exile on Zacynthus
Bricked them into the storeroom walls
context: Odyssey 22.457-473. Homer's simile is brutal: they hang 'like doves caught in a net.' The ancient Greeks called this whole massacre -- suitors and maids together -- the Mnesterophonia, 'the suitor-slaying'. Source: Homer, Odyssey 22.437-473.  (Legend.)

question: Uther Pendragon, King of Britain, has died leaving no acknowledged heir, and the barons are ready to fight each other for the crown. In Malory Book I, one adviser goes to the Archbishop of Canterbury and tells him to summon every lord in the land to London by Christmas, so that God can show a sign who should be the rightful king. Who is that adviser?
context: Malory Book I ch.5. Merlin is the counsellor at every hinge of the early Arthur story. Sir Ector will turn out to be Arthur's foster-father. Sir Bedivere is the knight who will one day return the sword to the lake. Sir Kay is Ector's son and Arthur's foster-brother.  (Legend.)

question: The great lords of Britain have gathered in London for the feast, praying in the church for a sign of who should be king. When they come out, a great square block of marble has appeared in the yard beside the church, and set on top of it is a steel anvil with a fair sword driven through the anvil into the block. Around the blade, plain to see, are letters written in what colour?
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'letters there were written in gold about the sword.' Silver, black and blood-red letters do not appear on the sword; Malory names the letters gold and only gold.  (Legend.)

question: The letters written in gold around the sword in the churchyard tell everyone exactly what the sword means. Malory gives the inscription almost word for word from Caxton's 1485 print. What do the gold letters say the puller of this sword shall be?
answer: rightwise king born of all England
choices: rightwise king born of all England
chosen champion of the Round Table
servant to the Archbishop of Canterbury
sworn defender of the Holy Grail
context: Malory Book I ch.5, near-verbatim Caxton 1485: 'Whoso pulleth out this sword of this stone and anvil is rightwise king born of all England.' The Round Table, the Archbishop's service and the Grail defence are all real later Arthurian ideas but not what the inscription promises.  (Legend.)

question: Every great baron and knight in England comes to the churchyard on Christmas morning and takes his turn trying to pull the sword out of the stone. In Malory, what happens when they pull?
answer: not one of them can move the sword
choices: not one of them can move the sword
the sword cuts every hand that touches it
the stone sinks into the ground when they touch it
the sword shatters at the first strong pull
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'not one of them all might stir the sword nor move it.' The sword hurts no hand, the stone stays put, and the sword does not break in this scene -- it will break much later in Arthur's own hand.  (Legend.)

question: On New Year's Day the barons hold a great joust in a field near the churchyard to keep the young knights busy. A young squire named Arthur rides in the retinue of his elder foster-brother, a knight who has just realised he has left his own weapon behind at the inn. Arthur is sent back for it and finds the inn locked and empty. Whose forgotten weapon has Arthur ridden home to fetch?
context: Malory Book I ch.5: Kay is Sir Ector's own son and Arthur's foster-brother. Pellinore is a real Malory king who meets Arthur later, but is not his foster-brother. Bedivere is a later Round Table knight. Ulfius rode with Uther the night Arthur was conceived, not this scene.  (Legend.)

question: Finding the inn locked, the young squire Arthur will not return to his foster-brother empty-handed. He remembers the sword he saw stuck in the stone in the churchyard, rides there alone, and takes hold of it. What does the sword do when Arthur puts his hand to it?
choices: it burns his palm and holds fast
it names him aloud in a great voice
it will not move until he prays
context: Malory Book I ch.5: Arthur 'pulled it out of the stone lightly and fiercely.' No burning hand, no speaking sword, no prayer -- Malory's Arthur simply lifts it out as if the stone had never held it.  (Legend.)

question: When Sir Kay sees the drawn sword in Arthur's hand he knows at once what it is, and hurries with it to his father Sir Ector, claiming to be the rightful king himself. Ector does not believe him and questions him hard. In Malory, what does Kay finally admit?
answer: that his young brother Arthur brought him the sword
choices: that his young brother Arthur brought him the sword
that a stranger on the road handed it to him
that he pulled a copy the Archbishop had made
that Merlin had put it into his hand
context: Malory Book I ch.5: pressed by Ector, Kay confesses his younger foster-brother Arthur drew and brought the sword. The other three stories -- a road stranger, a copy, a gift from Merlin -- appear nowhere in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Sir Ector takes Arthur back to the churchyard and makes the boy set the sword into the anvil again and pull it out a second time, to be sure. Ector himself tries, and cannot move it. Sir Kay tries, and cannot move it. Arthur draws it out again as easily as before. What do Ector and Kay do the instant Arthur holds the drawn sword?
choices: they seize him and lock him in the church
they ride at once for the coast
they hide the sword under the altar
context: Malory Book I ch.5: Ector and Kay kneel before Arthur, and Ector tells him that Uther Pendragon was Arthur's true father and that he, Ector, is only his foster-father. Weeping, Arthur begs Ector to remain his father in his heart.  (Legend.)

question: The great barons refuse to accept the Christmas result and demand the sword-test be held again. In Malory the same test is set at three of the great feasts of the Christian year -- Candlemas, Easter, and finally the feast at which the commons at last cry that Arthur shall be king and put in no more delay. What is that third and final feast?
context: Malory Book I ch.5-7: Candlemas, Easter and Pentecost mark the three delayed tests. At Pentecost the commons cry 'we will have Arthur unto our king, we will put him no more in delay.' Michaelmas, All Hallows and Epiphany are real medieval feasts but not this sequence.  (Legend.)

question: To keep the sword from being stolen or moved between the failed attempts of the great lords, the Archbishop of Canterbury sets a guard on it day and night in the churchyard. In Malory, how large is this guard?
context: Malory Book I ch.5: 'the Archbishop ordained ten knights, men of good fame, that they should watch the sword.' Three bishops, a hundred squires and a lone hermit do not appear in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Not long after Arthur is crowned, the sword he drew from the stone shatters in his own hand in single combat with a strong king he has ridden out to meet in Malory Book I ch.25. Merlin then leads Arthur to a lake, where a hand rises from the water holding a second and greater blade -- the sword every child now names 'Excalibur.' Whose sword-stroke breaks Arthur's first sword in that fight?
context: Malory Book I ch.25: Pellinore, whom Arthur meets at a fountain, breaks the stone-sword clean in two. Merlin then takes Arthur to the lake and Excalibur is given by the Lady of the Lake. Lot, Ryence and Mark are real Malory kings but not the sword-breaker here.  (Legend.)

question: The sword-in-the-stone scene that everyone knows was not always part of Arthur's story. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's earlier Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136) there is no stone, no anvil, no test -- Arthur is simply crowned as Uther's son as soon as his father dies. At what age does Geoffrey's Arthur take the crown in that older version?
context: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136): Arthur is crowned at fifteen, with no sword-test. The stone-and-anvil episode was invented by the French poet Robert de Boron in his Merlin (c.1200), and that later version is what Malory follows.

question: In a parable Jesus tells in Matthew 25, a rich man is about to leave on a long journey. He calls three of his servants, hands each of them some of his money to look after while he is gone, and departs. How much does he give the first servant, the second, and the third?
answer: Five talents, then two talents, then one talent
choices: Five talents, then two talents, then one talent
Three talents, then three talents, then three talents
Ten talents, then five talents, then one talent
Two talents, then two talents, then two talents
context: Matthew 25:15 KJV: 'And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.' Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: In the parable, the first two servants take the money the master has left them and trade with it -- doubling what they were given. The third servant, afraid of the master, does something very different with his share.
answer: He digs a hole in the ground and buries it
choices: He digs a hole in the ground and buries it
He lends it out to moneychangers for interest
He gives it away to beggars in the marketplace
He hides it inside a hollow beam in the roof
context: Matthew 25:18 KJV: 'But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money.' Later in the same parable the master rebukes him precisely because he did not even lend it to the exchangers to earn interest (Matthew 25:27). Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: The scolded servant confesses he buried the money because he was afraid of his master. What does the master order done with the one buried talent he took back?
answer: Given to the servant who now has ten talents
choices: Given to the servant who now has ten talents
Thrown into the fire so no one could use it
Divided equally between the two other servants
Kept in the master's own strongbox from then on
context: Matthew 25:28 KJV: 'Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents.' The line that follows -- 'unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance' -- has been quoted for two thousand years as the Matthew Effect. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: Right before the talents parable, Jesus tells another parable in Matthew 25 comparing the kingdom of heaven to ten young women who go out at night with their lamps to meet a bridegroom. Five of them are called wise; the other five are called something specific.
context: Matthew 25:2 KJV: 'And five of them were wise, and five were foolish.' The wise five brought extra oil in vessels alongside their lamps; the foolish five brought only what was already in the wick. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: The wedding party in Matthew 25 is delayed, and all ten of the women fall asleep waiting. Then a shout goes up and startles them all awake. At what hour of the night does the shout come, according to Matthew 25:6?
choices: At the first watch, just after sundown
At cockcrow, near the third watch
At dawn, as the sky was reddening
context: Matthew 25:6 KJV: 'And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.' The midnight timing is why the wise women's SPARE oil matters -- the ordinary wick oil has burned all evening and is running low just as the bridegroom finally arrives. Source: KJV Matthew 25.

question: In the Ten Virgins parable, the foolish five run out to buy oil for their dying lamps and while they are gone the bridegroom arrives. The door is shut. When they finally get back and pound on it, crying 'Lord, Lord, open to us,' what answer comes back from inside?
context: Matthew 25:12 KJV: 'But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.' It is the parable's punchline -- the door already shut, the answer as flat as the shut door itself. Bonus: the English word 'talent' meaning a natural ability came out of the OTHER parable in this same chapter -- Old English 'talent' meant only a weight of silver; the sense of a gift entrusted for use developed by the mid-1400s from medieval preaching on Matthew 25. Source: KJV Matthew 25 ; etymonline.com/word/talent.

question: After Moses's first demand, Pharaoh's punishment is to make the Hebrews' work harder. The overseers still demand the same number of bricks a day but no longer give the slaves one thing they had been given for free. What must the Hebrews now gather themselves in the fields?
context: Exodus 5:7-8. Pharaoh says, 'Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick, as heretofore: let them go and gather straw for themselves.' Source: Wikipedia, Plagues of Egypt.

question: The second plague sends creatures swarming up out of the Nile into the houses of Egypt, into the bedchambers, and into the wooden troughs where the bread is being kneaded. What creatures?
context: Exodus 8:3. The frogs come up and 'cover the land of Egypt,' entering ovens, bedrooms, and kneading-troughs before Pharaoh begs Moses to remove them. Source: Wikipedia, Plagues of Egypt.

question: During the sixth plague, the affliction is so severe that Pharaoh's court magicians (Jannes and Jambres, by tradition) cannot even stand in front of Moses. Their bodies are covered in the same thing every Egyptian's is. What is the sixth plague?
context: Exodus 9:11 KJV: 'And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians.' The magicians match plagues 1 and 2 with their enchantments, fail at 3, and are physically laid low by 6. Source: Wikipedia, Jannes and Jambres.

question: To be spared the death of the firstborn, each Hebrew family kills a lamb at twilight and paints its blood on the lintel and the two side posts of the door. The paintbrush they are told to use is a bunch of one specific plant, dipped in the blood in the basin (Exodus 12:22). What plant?
context: Exodus 12:22 KJV: 'And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood.' Hyssop returns at the crucifixion in John 19:29, sponge of vinegar lifted on a hyssop stalk. Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: The Hebrews eat the Passover lamb roast with fire, dressed to leave that very hour: loins girded, shoes on their feet, staff in their hand. Two other foods are served with the lamb, named in the same verse (Exodus 12:8). What two?
context: Exodus 12:8, 11 KJV: 'they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it... with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand.' The unleavened bread and the bitter herbs (maror) are still eaten every Passover seder today. Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: In the night the firstborn die, Pharaoh cries out for Moses to leave, and the Hebrews carry their raw dough on their SHOULDERS because there is no time to leaven it (Exodus 12:34). What single word does the King James Bible use for what they did to the Egyptians on the way out, taking jewels of silver and gold and raiment?
context: Exodus 12:35-36 KJV: 'they borrowed of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment... and they spoiled the Egyptians.' Pharaoh's summons that same night: 'Rise up, and get you forth from among my people' (Exodus 12:31). Source: Bible Gateway, Exodus 12 KJV.

question: The rooster of Jotunheim -- the land of the giants -- sits in a dark forest and crows to muster the giants' army against the gods. His Old Norse name means 'hider' or 'deceiver'. What is the name of the giants' rooster?
context: Voluspa stanza 42. Fjalar the rooster is one of Voluspa's eerier names -- a bird whose crowing HIDES the safety of the old world and DECEIVES no one about what is coming. Vidofnir is a completely different named rooster who sits atop the tree Mimameidr in the poem Fjolsvinnsmal -- not the Ragnarok rooster. Salgofnir ('hall-crower') is the rooster that wakes the einherjar of Valhalla in some skaldic verse -- again NOT the Jotunheim doom-rooster. Vindsvalr ('cold-wind') is the father of Winter in Vafthrudnismal -- a wintry-sounding Norse name that would fit a doom-rooster but is not one. Fjalar is the specific gallows-wood rooster. There is a completely separate Fjalar in Norse myth -- the murderous dwarf who killed the wise Kvasir to make the Mead of Poetry -- but the two Fjalars are unrelated; the name is simply reused.  (Legend.)

question: The rooster of the underworld halls of Hel is the strangest of the three. He has NO NAME in the Voluspa at all -- he is only described by his color, a single Old Norse adjective. What color is Hel's rooster?
context: Voluspa stanza 43. Sotraudr (sot 'soot' + raudr 'red') -- 'soot-red' -- is the whole description we get of the Hel rooster. He has no proper name, only that color. The nameless-ness is part of the horror: the roosters of Asgard and Jotunheim have names because their worlds have names; the dead in Hel have no such dignity, and neither does their bird.  (Legend.)

question: Norse myth has TWO different figures named Fjalar. One is the Jotunheim rooster of Voluspa. The OTHER Fjalar is a very different creature from a very different story -- he and his brother Galar murdered the wise being Kvasir and brewed his blood into the Mead of Poetry. What kind of creature is the other Fjalar?
context: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal (the Mead of Poetry story) vs. Voluspa 42. The dwarves Fjalar and Galar killed Kvasir -- the wisest being ever made, born from the gods' spit -- and drained his blood into three vessels, mixed it with honey, and brewed the Mead of Poetry that gives anyone who drinks it the gift of verse. The dwarf-Fjalar and the rooster-Fjalar are completely unrelated; the Norse simply reused the name, the way English reuses 'John'. Scholars flag this kind of name-reuse as evidence that Norse myth was assembled from many local traditions, not written by one hand.  (Legend.)

question: In Scandinavian folk-tradition long after the conversion to Christianity, one particular kind of rooster crowing at an unusual hour was still considered very bad luck -- an echo of the three doom-cocks of Voluspa a thousand years later. What color of rooster was thought unlucky when it crowed at an odd hour?
context: Scandinavian folk-belief. A black rooster crowing at midnight or another wrong hour kept its association with the underworld cock of Hel long after the Christianisation of Iceland and Scandinavia. The image of doom announced by a bird-cry survives in bits of the folk-tradition even now.  (Legend.)

question: Before Zeus and the Olympians ruled the world, the throne belonged to an older generation of gods. Their king was Cronus, and his brothers and sisters shared power with him. Cronus was one of twelve of these older gods, born of Gaia and Ouranos, and it is by their group name that they are always remembered. What are they called?
context: Named in Hesiod's Theogony 133-138. Cronus was the youngest of the twelve. Wikipedia: Cronus, Titans.  (Legend.)

question: The Titan king Cronus lived in dread of a prophecy that one of his own children would grow up to overthrow him. Each time his wife Rhea gave birth, he took the newborn from her arms and did one terrible thing to keep the prophecy from coming true. What did Cronus do to each of his newborn children?
answer: swallowed the newborn on the spot
choices: swallowed the newborn on the spot
cast the newborn into the sea
chained the newborn to a rock
burned the newborn on an altar
context: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon all went down one after another. Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: Rhea, sick of watching Cronus swallow her babies, hid her sixth pregnancy and gave birth in a hidden cave on a great island in the Mediterranean. This is the island where Zeus was born and raised in secret. Which island is it?
context: The cave is set on Mount Ida (or Mount Dikte in other versions). Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: When Rhea gave birth in the Cretan cave, she had to hand SOMETHING to Cronus for him to swallow so he would think the baby was gone. She wrapped an ordinary object in the baby's swaddling-clothes and gave him that instead. What did Cronus actually swallow that day?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 485. The stone bundle is one of the most famous single images in Greek myth. Wikipedia: Cronus.  (Legend.)

question: The baby Zeus in his Cretan cave still cried like any newborn, and Cronus was a listening god. Around the mouth of the cave a band of young warrior-spirits danced continually and clashed their spears against their bronze shields to drown out the crying. What were these dancing warrior-spirits called?
context: The armed dance of the Kouretes was still performed at festivals of Zeus on Crete centuries later. Wikipedia: Amalthea.  (Legend.)

question: The war Zeus and his freed brothers and sisters then fought against Cronus and the other Titans lasted a long time before either side broke through. Hesiod gives it a memorable duration that has stuck as a fixed number in later poetry. How long did the Titanomachy last?
context: The ten-year Titanomachy is a deliberate poetic mirror of the ten-year Trojan War. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: The one-eyed giant smiths Zeus freed from Tartarus repaid the three brothers by forging each of them a signature weapon or gift. Zeus was given the thunderbolt and Poseidon the trident. What did the Cyclopes forge for Hades?
context: The Cap of Hades (or Cap of Darkness) let its wearer become unseen. Perseus later borrowed it to sneak up on the sleeping Medusa. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: Once the Titans were locked away in Tartarus behind bronze gates, Zeus and his two brothers had to divide the world between them. They did not fight over it and they did not let anyone else assign it; they used one simple method to decide who ruled the sky, who ruled the sea, and who ruled the underworld. How did the three brothers decide the split?
context: Iliad 15.187-193, where Poseidon tells the story: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld, and all three shared earth and Olympus. Wikipedia: Titanomachy.  (Legend.)

question: The gospels say Jesus led a small group of his closest disciples up a high mountain, apart, to witness a strange vision-scene later called the Transfiguration. How many disciples did he take with him?
context: Peter, James, and John -- the same 'inner three' Jesus later takes deeper into the garden at Gethsemane and into the room where he raises Jairus's daughter (Matthew 17:1; Mark 5:37; Mark 14:33).

question: As the three disciples watched on the mountaintop, Jesus was transfigured before them. Matthew describes his face shining like the sun. What does Matthew say happened to his clothing?
answer: It became white as the light
choices: It became white as the light
It became white as fresh snow
context: Matthew 17:2 KJV: 'his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.' The three distractors are also real biblical light-imagery -- Mark 9:3 compares the garments to snow, Daniel 7:9 describes the Ancient of Days with 'garment white as snow' and hair 'like the pure wool', and Revelation 1:15 gives Christ's feet 'like unto fine brass' -- but Matthew's specific line here is 'white as the light'.

question: Peter, James, and John watched Jesus shine like the sun on the mountaintop and then saw two figures from centuries before -- famous names from the Hebrew Bible -- appear beside him and talk with him. Who were the two visitors?
context: Matthew 17:3; Mark 9:4; Luke 9:30. Moses represents the Law and Elijah the prophets -- the two great Hebrew traditions standing together with Jesus.

question: As Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed the mountaintop and a voice came out of the cloud. Matthew records exactly what the voice said. What were the words?
answer: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him
choices: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him
Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona: flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee
Fear not: for I am with thee, and will bless thee
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock
context: Matthew 17:5 KJV. The same voice from heaven spoke almost identical words at Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:17) -- but on the mountain 'hear ye him' is added, a direct command to the three disciples.

question: The Eastern Orthodox Church keeps the feast of the Transfiguration every year on 6 August, and traditionally, on that day, the first fruits of one particular harvest are brought to the church to be blessed. Which fruit?
context: In Orthodox practice the first grapes of the harvest are brought to be blessed at the Transfiguration liturgy on 6 August -- tying the mountaintop light-scene to the yearly turning of the vineyards. In some regional traditions apples or other early fruit are blessed instead where grapes do not yet ripen; grapes are the classical Byzantine custom.

question: After ten years of siege the Greeks still could not break the walls of Troy, so one of their leaders proposed a trick to get inside without a battle. Which Greek hero came up with the plan?
context: Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, proposed the trick after force had failed for ten years. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: Under Odysseus's direction, the Greek craftsman Epeios built a huge hollow wooden thing, big enough to hide picked warriors inside its belly. In the shape of what animal was Epeios's hollow gift built?
context: Epeios built the enormous wooden horse with the help of the goddess Athena; the shape gave the whole story its name. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: Epeios cut an inscription into the horse's flank so the Trojans would read it as an innocent gift. The inscription named it as an offering to one particular goddess -- the same goddess who had helped Epeios build it. Which goddess was named on the inscription?
context: The inscription dedicated the horse to Athena as if the Greeks had left it behind as a peace-offering for a safe journey home. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: For the trick to work, the Greek army had to look as though it had given up and sailed away. But the ships never went home -- they hid just out of sight of the Trojan beach, behind a small island nearby. What is the name of that island where the Greek fleet hid?
context: The Greek fleet hid behind Tenedos, an island just off the Trojan coast, waiting for the signal from inside the walls. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: When the Trojans found the horse standing on the empty beach, one man was deeply suspicious -- a priest of Apollo, who ran up and hurled his spear at the wooden flank so hard that the whole hollow thing BOOMED. What is the name of this priest?
context: Laocoon, priest of Apollo, threw his spear and heard the boom -- yet the Trojans refused to believe him. Source: Wikipedia, 'Laocoon'.  (Legend.)

question: A single Greek was dragged in front of King Priam in tears, claiming he had been left behind on the beach because his own side had wanted to kill him. He swore the horse was a peace-offering to Athena, and Priam took pity and cut him loose. What is the weeping prisoner's name?
context: Sinon was the planted liar -- his tears convinced Priam to spare him and drag the horse inside. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The moment of the priest's death is frozen in one of the most famous surviving works of ancient sculpture -- a marble group of a bearded man and two boys wrestling the coils. Where is this ancient sculpture kept today?
context: The Laocoon Group was unearthed in a Roman vineyard in 1506 and is now displayed in the Vatican Museums; Pliny credited three Rhodian sculptors -- Agesander, Athenodoros, and Polydorus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Laocoon'.

question: That night, once the Trojans had feasted and fallen asleep, the weeping prisoner Sinon lit a beacon on the wall to signal the fleet hidden behind the island. The men inside the horse then came down onto the street below by one specific means. How did the Greeks get out of the horse?
answer: By a rope-ladder from a trapdoor in the belly
choices: By a rope-ladder from a trapdoor in the belly
By hacking the horse apart from inside with axes
By waiting for slaves to open a hatch in the back
By sliding down the tail through a hidden gap
context: The picked warriors came down a rope-ladder through a trapdoor cut into the horse's belly, opened the city gates, and let the returning army in. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: The wooden-horse story is not in the Iliad at all -- the Iliad ends before the city falls. Instead the fullest ancient telling is put into the mouth of a Trojan survivor, an eyewitness, in a much later Latin epic. Which epic tells the horse story at length in the survivor's own voice?
context: In Aeneid Book 2, Aeneas himself tells Dido the story of the horse and the fall of the city. Homer's Odyssey Book 8 has a shorter version sung by the bard Demodocus. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.

question: One of the strangest scenes involving the horse comes from Odyssey Book 4. Helen -- now inside the walls of Troy -- was said to walk around the horse at night imitating one specific set of voices, trying to get the men hidden inside to call back. Whose voices did Helen imitate?
answer: The voices of their wives back home
choices: The voices of their wives back home
The voices of their own commanders
context: In Odyssey 4.271-289, Helen called out to the hidden men in the exact voices of each man's wife; Odysseus had to physically hold his hand over each man's mouth to keep them silent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trojan Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: Irish myth tells of a supernatural people who arrived in Ireland long before the modern Irish, and who are the closest thing Irish tradition has to a family of gods. Their name literally means 'the people of the goddess so-and-so' -- carrying the name of one particular mother-goddess. Which goddess do the Tuatha De Danann carry the name of?
context: Danu (also called Anu) is the mother-goddess whose name the Tuatha De Danann ('the people of the goddess Danu') carry. Almost no story about Danu herself survives -- she is a name behind a name. Brigid is the poetry-and-smithcraft goddess inside the Tuatha De Danann. Macha is one of the three faces of the Morrigan. Aine is a summer sun-goddess of Munster. Source: Irish Myths, 'Who Are the Tuatha De Danann?' -- https://irishmyths.com/2023/11/15/tuatha-de-danann/  (Legend.)

question: The god-people of Danu arrived in Ireland by sea, but the Lebor Gabala Erenn says the sky went black for three days as they came, so that watchers on the shore could not see the sun. What was the source of the darkness that hid the sun for those three days?
answer: the smoke of their own ships burning on the beach
choices: the smoke of their own ships burning on the beach
a storm the Fomorians raised to stop them landing
a plague of ravens the Morrigan sent before them
a cloud of ash from a mountain in the north
context: The moment the Tuatha De Danann stepped ashore they set fire to every vessel that had carried them, so that they could never think of retreating. The smoke of the burning ships was what darkened the sky for three days. Source: Celtic Life International, 'The Tuatha de Danann'; Book of Invasions redaction on the fifth invasion.  (Legend.)

question: Before the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland they were trained in four cities in the north of the world, and from each city they brought one great treasure. One treasure was a great stone that would cry out under the foot of the true king of Ireland -- it stood at Tara and later gave its name to the hill. From which of the four northern cities did that crying stone come?
context: The Stone of Fal (Lia Fail) came from Falias, one of the four northern cities where the Tuatha De Danann trained. It stood at Tara and cried out under the foot of the rightful king. The other three cities each gave a different treasure: Gorias gave the Spear of Lugh, Findias gave the Sword of Nuada, and Murias gave the Cauldron of the Dagda. Source: Wikipedia, 'Four Treasures of the Tuatha De Danann'.  (Legend.)

question: The first king of the Tuatha De Danann in Ireland lost his hand fighting the Fir Bolg at the First Battle of Moytura, and by the old Irish law a mutilated man could not sit as king. His brothers made him a new hand out of one metal, and he was restored to the throne and given a new name from it. Out of what did his brothers make the hand that gave him his royal name?
context: Nuada lost his hand at the First Battle of Moytura against the Fir Bolg. Dian Cecht the healer-god crafted him a working hand of silver, and from that day he was called Nuada Airgetlam -- Nuada of the SILVER HAND. Later Miach, Dian Cecht's son, grew him a hand of living flesh, and Dian Cecht killed his own son in jealousy. Source: Timeless Myths, 'Celtic Gods and Goddesses'.  (Legend.)
