question: The chief god of the Tuatha De Danann has an epithet that simply calls him 'the good god' -- not 'good' in a moral sense but 'good AT everything'. He is a huge bearded figure who wields a great club (one end kills, the other end heals) and owns a bottomless cauldron of plenty. Which of the Tuatha bears the epithet 'the good god'?
context: The Dagda -- 'good god' in the sense of 'competent at every art' -- is chief of the Tuatha De Danann and owner of both the bottomless cauldron of Murias and the double-ended club. Lugh is the young sun-god and master of all arts, but the 'good god' epithet is not his. Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god who later assigns the fairy-mounds. Aengus is the god of love, and in one story tricks the Dagda out of his hall at Bru na Boinne. Source: Mythopedia, 'Dagda'.  (Legend.)

question: The Tuatha De Danann were themselves eventually overthrown in Ireland by the sixth and last wave of settlers in the Book of Invasions -- a people led by the poet Amergin, who calmed the sea with his verse so his people could land. What was that final wave called in the Book of Invasions?
context: The Milesians (the 'sons of Mil'), led by the poet Amergin, were the sixth and final wave in the Book of Invasions. They are the ancestors of the historical Gaels of Ireland. The Fomorians were the monstrous sea-people the Tuatha had already beaten at the Second Battle of Moytura. The Nemedians and the followers of Partholon were earlier waves, all wiped out before the Tuatha arrived. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tuatha De Danann'.  (Legend.)

question: When the Milesians beat the Tuatha De Danann, the poet Amergin was asked to divide Ireland between the two peoples. He divided it cleverly -- and by his division the Tuatha did not die, but were driven into a country that overlaps ours in space. What was the Tuatha De Danann's share of Ireland after Amergin's division?
answer: everything underground -- the halls beneath the hills
choices: everything underground -- the halls beneath the hills
everything to the west of the river Shannon
everything covered by the sea at high tide
everything inside the walls of the royal forts
context: Amergin gave the Milesians the portion of Ireland ABOVE ground and gave the Tuatha De Danann the portion BELOW ground. The god-people did not perish; they retreated INTO the hills and became the people who live inside the fairy-mounds. Source: Myth and Folklore Wiki; godsandmonsters.info, 'Sidhe'.  (Legend.)

question: After the god-people were driven underground, one of the Tuatha took charge of distributing them among the grassy mounds of Ireland -- he gave Aengus the mound at Newgrange, gave Midir the mound of Bri Leith, and raised a magical mist called the feth fiada to hide the mounds from human eyes. Which of the Tuatha divided the mounds among the others?
context: Manannan mac Lir, the sea-god, is said to have led the Tuatha into the sidhe (SHEE) mounds after the Milesian conquest and given each god a mound. He is also credited with raising the feth fiada, the magical mist that hides the mounds from human sight. Nuada by then had died at the Second Battle of Moytura. Lugh returned to the Otherworld with him. Dian Cecht is the healer, not the divider of mounds. Source: Wikipedia, 'Manannan mac Lir'.  (Legend.)

question: After their defeat the Tuatha De Danann were called by a new Irish name, taken from the earth-mounds they now lived inside -- Aos Si, meaning 'people of the mounds'. That name becomes in English the name for one particular kind of Irish supernatural being of a thousand later stories. Into what did the Tuatha De Danann turn, in later Irish tradition?
context: The Aos Si ('people of the mounds', pronounced roughly ees shee) are the god-people in retreat -- and this is the origin of Ireland's fairy-folk. When later stories talk of the sidhe or the good people or the gentry of the hills, they are talking about the diminished Tuatha De Danann. The leprechaun is a solitary shoemaker-sprite, the pooka a shape-shifting trickster of the roads, and the banshee a wailing death-herald -- all Irish supernatural beings, but none of them the Aos Si themselves. Source: godsandmonsters.info, 'Sidhe'; Sharon Wray, 'A Brief History of the Aos si'.  (Legend.)

question: The war-goddess of the Tuatha De Danann is a shape-changing figure who appears as a crow or a raven above battlefields, offers prophecy of doom, and later tries to seduce Cuchulainn before his last stand. What is her name?
context: The Morrigan ('great queen' or 'phantom queen') is the war-goddess and prophet of doom of the Tuatha De Danann, and is often described as a trio (with Badb and Macha, or Badb and Nemain). Brigid is the goddess of poetry, healing, and smithcraft. Danu is the silent mother-goddess. Etain is the heroine of the tale of Midir and Etain, not a war-goddess. Source: Timeless Myths, 'Celtic Gods and Goddesses'.  (Legend.)

question: The whole war of the Tain Bo Cuailnge is fought for ONE thing. The queen of Connacht discovers that her husband Ailill owns a magnificent white-horned bull she has no equal for in her own herd -- so she raises an army and marches on Ulster to steal a rival bull to match it. Who is the queen?
context: The pillow-talk of Medb and Ailill counting their possessions opens the Tain; the great bull is the one thing on which Ailill outmatches her. Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife; Deirdre is from a different Ulster tale; Grainne belongs to the later Fenian Cycle. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: Ailill's great bull of Connacht is named for its most striking feature. The Old Irish name means simply 'the White-Horned'. What is it called?
context: Finn = 'white/fair', bennach = 'horned'. Donn Cuailnge is the OTHER bull, from Ulster (the next rung). Liath Macha is Cu Chulainn's grey horse; Enbarr is Manannan's horse. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: The two bulls are the last shape of a much older enmity. The tale De Chophur in da Muccida ('The Quarrel of the Two Pig-Keepers') tells how a pair of supernatural swineherds -- Friuch and Rucht -- transformed through many shapes fighting each other. Their final change before the bulls was into two of the same tiny thing, swallowed by two cows and reborn. What were they?
context: The cows that drank the worms then gave birth to Donn Cuailnge and Finnbennach. The Tain war is the LAST stage of this quarrel. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge; De Chophur in da Muccida.  (Legend.)

question: Cu Chulainn's single-handed defence of the ford collapses only when the men of Ulster finally rally, and even then Medb's raiders manage the one thing the whole war was FOR: they drive the brown bull off into Connacht. They bring him back to the royal seat of Medb and Ailill, where the two king-bulls are put in a single enclosure. What is the name of that royal seat?
context: Cruachan (modern Rathcroghan, County Roscommon) is Medb and Ailill's capital. Emain Macha is the seat of Conchobar and the Ulstermen; Tara is the High King's seat; Dun Aengus is a stone fort on Inishmore. Wikipedia: Rathcroghan.  (Legend.)

question: The moment the two king-bulls see each other in the pen at Cruachan they attack, and the whole assembly comes out to watch. The fight does not stay at Cruachan. Instead it rages across the whole of Ireland, tearing up ground, bellowing so no one sleeps. How long does the combat last?
answer: a full day and a full night
choices: a full day and a full night
the seven nights of a wake
context: Recension I closes with this all-Ireland running battle from noon to noon. The 'three summers and three winters' echoes older Indo-European fight-formulas but is not this text. Wikipedia: Tain Bo Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: In the morning the brown bull of Ulster emerges the winner. As he runs home to Cooley he carries something on his horns: what is left of Finnbennach, torn apart in the night. Along the way he drops pieces of the losing bull, and the tale claims that the Irish landscape itself keeps the memory -- each piece falling gives a landmark its name. Modern Athlone, on the river Shannon, is said in this tradition to be named for one such fallen piece. Which piece?
context: Ath Luain = 'Ford of the Loin'; the Old Irish luan is the loin or thigh, and the school-lore collection at Dúchas.ie preserves the tradition that the bull's loin-bone dropped there. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge; Dúchas.ie schools collection, Christian Brothers, Athlone.  (Legend.)

question: When the winning bull finally reaches his home country, he stops. He sets his back against a hill, gives a great bellow -- and does not walk away from the victory. What kills him?
choices: Medb's men catch up and spear him
the Morrigan takes him in raven-form
context: The exertion, the fury, the grief for a rival -- the story leaves the exact cause unsettled; the heart simply bursts. Wikipedia: Donn Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: Medb's greatest personal cost in the Tain was her own foster-brother and champion, a warrior trained beside Cu Chulainn under the warrior-woman Scathach on the Isle of Skye. She goaded him with gifts and shame to fight Cu Chulainn at the ford; on the third day Cu Chulainn killed him with the belly-spear Gae Bolg. Who was he?
context: Ferdiad and Cu Chulainn were foster-brothers trained together by Scathach; Medb's demand that Ferdiad fight him is one of the Tain's most-quoted set-pieces, and Cu Chulainn weeps over his body afterward. Loegaire Buadach and Conall Cernach are Ulster champions; Cet mac Matach is a Connacht warrior from a different tale. Wikipedia: Ferdiad; Tain Bo Cuailnge.  (Legend.)

question: In the Prose Edda Loki once cut off the golden hair of Thor's wife as a prank, and to save his own life he went down to the dwarf-quarter to have new hair made. Loki's habit of bragging landed him in a much bigger scrape while he was there. What did Loki wager against the dwarves' craftsmanship?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki bet his own head that no other dwarves could match the Sons of Ivaldi. Odin gives an eye at Mimir's well. Tyr loses a hand in the wolf Fenrir's mouth. Bragi speaks with a rune-carved tongue but does not wager it. Loki is the head-wagerer.  (Legend.)

question: Loki's boast about the Sons of Ivaldi was overheard in the smithy of a dwarf who refused to let his own brother be called second-best. That dwarf and his brother would soon accept the head-wager and forge three treasures of their own. What is the name of the dwarf-brother who took Loki's bet?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Brokkr took the wager on his brother's behalf. Alviss is the all-wise dwarf whom Thor keeps talking until sunrise turns him to stone. Andvari owns the cursed gold ring of the Volsung cycle. Regin fosters Sigurd and urges him to kill Fafnir. Only Brokkr bets against Loki.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr did not do the smithing himself. He worked alongside his brother, the master craftsman who stood at the anvil with the hammer, while Brokkr worked the bellows to keep the fire at just the right heat. What is the name of Brokkr's smith-brother?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Sindri (also called Eitri) is the master smith and Brokkr the bellows-worker. Ivaldi is the FATHER of the rival dwarves who made Sif's hair, Skidbladnir, and Gungnir. Dvalinn is a dwarf-name that appears in Volundarkvida and Havamal. Fjalar (with Galar) murdered Kvasir for the Mead of Poetry.  (Legend.)

question: Loki knew that if the fire at Sindri's forge faltered for a single moment the metal would spoil. To try to spoil it he shape-shifted into a small biting thing and attacked the dwarf at the bellows. Snorri names Loki's new form as a stinging insect -- what insect did Loki become?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki became a fly (fluga, sometimes translated 'gadfly'). Wasps and mosquitoes and moths do not appear in the tale. Loki's other famous shape-changes are the mare who bore Sleipnir, the salmon caught in his own net, and the old woman Thokk who refused to weep for Baldr.  (Legend.)

question: The first treasure Sindri drew from the forge was a living animal that could run through air and water and light up the sky around it. Loki's fly bit Brokkr's hand while this piece was being made, but Brokkr never broke rhythm. What was Sindri's first treasure?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: the first treasure was Gullinbursti, the golden-bristled boar, given to Freyr -- his bristles lit the air around him and he ran across sea and sky. Fenrir the wolf is a child of Loki and Angrboda, not a dwarf-forged treasure. Tanngrisnir is one of the goats that pulls Thor's chariot. Jormungandr the world-serpent circles Midgard.  (Legend.)

question: The second treasure to come out of the forge was a small piece of gold that would drop eight new copies of itself off its own body every ninth night, making its wearer richer forever. Loki's fly bit Brokkr's neck this time, but Brokkr kept pumping the bellows and the piece came out perfect. What is Sindri's second treasure called?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Draupnir the golden arm-ring drips eight new rings of equal weight every ninth night, and passes to Odin. Andvaranaut is the cursed ring of the Volsung cycle. Sviagris is the pig-ring of the Swedish kings. Brisingamen is Freyja's famous neck-piece, not a ring at all.  (Legend.)

question: On the third and hardest treasure Loki gave up on Brokkr's hands and neck and struck the dwarf's face directly, biting him hard enough that blood flowed and he had to raise one hand for the space of a heartbeat to wipe it. Where did the fly bite Brokkr this final time?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: the third bite was on the eyelid; blood ran into Brokkr's eye and he lifted a hand to wipe it, breaking the bellows-rhythm for one moment. The lip, ear, and forehead do not appear in Snorri's version. That one flinch would have consequences.  (Legend.)

question: Because Brokkr lifted his hand from the bellows for a single instant while making the third treasure, the piece came out of the forge with one defect that no amount of hammering could fix. Thor took it up anyway -- but he could never wield it the way a great warrior wields a normal weapon. What was wrong with the third treasure when it came off the anvil?
answer: the handle was too short to grip in two hands
choices: the handle was too short to grip in two hands
one face was cast from ordinary iron
the head was too heavy to swing at all
one side of the head was left unhardened
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Mjolnir came out with a haft so short that Thor could only manage it one-handed, and needed the iron gauntlets Jarngreipr (and the belt Megingjord) to wield it at full strength. The other defects are plausible smith-faults but not the one Snorri names.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr and Sindri carried all six treasures -- the three from the Sons of Ivaldi and their own three -- up to Asgard, where the gods themselves would judge which pair had won the wager. Which three gods sat as judges of the treasures?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Odin, Thor, and Freyr are the judges, one for each pair of Ivaldi/Sindri gifts (Odin gets Gungnir/Draupnir, Thor gets Sif's hair and Mjolnir, Freyr gets Skidbladnir and Gullinbursti). The other combinations are real gods but not the judging panel.  (Legend.)

question: Brokkr had won the wager, and by the terms of the bet Loki's head belonged to him. Loki dodged death by pointing to one word in the bargain -- he had bet a body-part, but not the joint that connected it to the rest of him. In fury Brokkr let the head stand but silenced Loki's boasting mouth for a while. What did Brokkr do to Loki?
context: Skaldskaparmal 43: Loki argued that the neck was not part of the head he had wagered, so Brokkr could not behead him. In frustration Brokkr sewed Loki's lips shut with awl and thong to silence his boasting -- until Loki tore the stitches out. Cutting the tongue, iron gags, and branding do not appear in the tale.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth, a mortal king of the Myrmidons in Phthia married a sea-nymph in a wedding on Mount Pelion; every Olympian god came. From that marriage was born the greatest warrior of the Trojan War. Who was their son?
context: The mortal king was Peleus; the sea-nymph was Thetis. Their son Achilles was the central figure of Homer's Iliad. Peleus won Thetis by holding onto her tightly through every one of her sea-shape transformations, as the sea-god Proteus had instructed him. Source: Wikipedia, 'Peleus'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth of the wedding of Peleus and Thetis on Mount Pelion, every god and goddess was invited except one. Which goddess was left off the guest list?
context: Eris's name means simply 'Strife'. The other three are real Greek goddesses honestly used as distractors -- Nemesis in particular is a goddess of divine payback, but Nemesis was NOT the one snubbed at the wedding. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth of the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, Eris was insulted at being uninvited. She rolled a single object into the middle of the banquet hall, and the whole Trojan War, in the myth's own logic, began with it. What did she roll into the hall?
context: The apple was inscribed with a single Greek word -- KALLISTEI, 'for the fairest' (or 'to the most beautiful'). Later Greek and Roman writers called it 'the Apple of Discord'. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Apple of Discord' and 'Eris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: Eris's golden apple, rolled into the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, was inscribed with a single Greek word. What did that word mean?
context: The Greek is 'tei kallistei' -- 'to the most beautiful' or 'for the fairest'. The Latin sources render it 'formosissima'. It was designed to force a beauty contest among the goddesses at the feast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Apple of Discord'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth of the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, three goddesses reached for the golden apple at once, each claiming it was meant for her. Two of them were Athena and Aphrodite. Who was the third?
context: Hera was queen of the gods and wife of Zeus. Athena was gray-eyed goddess of wisdom and war-craft; Aphrodite was goddess of love and desire. All four distractors are real Olympian goddesses -- Artemis, Demeter, and Persephone are honestly wrong here. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth, three goddesses were fighting over the golden apple at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. Zeus refused to judge the quarrel himself and instead sent one specific messenger god down to fetch a mortal judge from Mount Ida. Which god did Zeus send?
context: Hermes, the wing-sandalled messenger of the Olympians, was Zeus's usual errand-runner between gods and mortals. Iris was a real divine messenger too (she carried word for Hera), but the Judgement of Paris myth names Hermes as the one who led the three goddesses down to Mount Ida. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth, Zeus sent Hermes to fetch a mortal to decide the quarrel over the golden apple. Hermes went to the slopes of Mount Ida in the Troad, where the chosen judge was tending sheep. Who was that young herdsman?
answer: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy
choices: Paris, son of Priam king of Troy
Ganymede of the house of Tros
context: Paris had been exposed at birth because of a prophecy that he would bring ruin to Troy, and he was raised as a herdsman on Mount Ida. All four distractors are real Trojan-cycle figures used honestly -- Aeneas, Ganymede, and Tithonus are all really tied to Troy's royal house. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth, each of the three goddesses tried to bribe the young Paris on Mount Ida for the golden apple. Hera offered kingship, Athena offered wisdom and war-craft; Aphrodite offered him one specific mortal woman -- the wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Who was she?
context: Helen of Sparta -- soon to be Helen of Troy -- was called the most beautiful woman in the world. Paris accepted Aphrodite's offer, took Helen back to Troy, and the Greek kings sailed after them. The distractors are all real Trojan-cycle women: Clytemnestra was Helen's sister and wife of Agamemnon; Andromache was Hector's wife; Cassandra was Paris's own sister, the prophetess no one believed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Judgement of Paris'.  (Legend.)

question: In the prose summary of the lost Greek poem the Kypria, which begins the whole Trojan War cycle, Zeus himself was said to have deliberately arranged the discord at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. What was the reason the Kypria gave for his doing so?
answer: The earth was overburdened with too many mortals
choices: The earth was overburdened with too many mortals
The Fates had ordered him to end the age of heroes
Prometheus had warned him a great hero would soon rise
Hera had begged him for revenge on the Trojans
context: The Kypria (a lost early poem of the Epic Cycle, preserved only in a prose summary) says Zeus arranged the discord because the earth was groaning under too many mortals; the Trojan War was his way to thin their numbers. This makes Eris's apple part of a divine plan, not a random insult. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eris (mythology)'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Greek myth, Peleus wanted the sea-nymph Thetis for a wife, but she kept turning into different shapes to escape him. The sea-god Proteus told Peleus one thing he had to do. What did Proteus tell him?
answer: Hold onto her tightly until she stopped
choices: Hold onto her tightly until she stopped
Speak her true name three times
Cut a lock of her hair with a bronze knife
Bind her wrists with a rope of kelp
context: Thetis turned into fire, water, a lion, and a serpent trying to escape him, but Peleus held on until she gave in. Later Greek and Roman art shows him gripping her through all the transformations. Source: Wikipedia, 'Peleus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Norse myth Ragnarok is the doom of the gods -- Odin swallowed by the wolf, Thor down beside the world-serpent, Surt burning the whole world with fire, and the sea rising to cover every land. But the Voluspa, the great seeress-poem of the Poetic Edda, does NOT stop there. In stanza 59 the seeress lifts her voice and says she sees something happen a second time. What does she see?
answer: a new earth rise from the sea, green anew
choices: a new earth rise from the sea, green anew
a great feast set in Valhalla
the ships of the dead sail out again
the giants build a hall on the ash
context: Voluspa 59 in the Poetic Edda: 'She sees rise up a second time earth from the ocean, green anew.' After Surt's fire and the drowning of the world, a new green earth surfaces from the flood -- the surprise of Norse eschatology is that the ending is also a beginning. The other three choices are real Norse motifs (Valhalla-feasting, Naglfar the ship of the dead, giants and their halls) but none is the second-rising of stanza 59.  (Legend.)

question: Not everyone dies at Ragnarok. Two HUMANS hide themselves away from Surt's fire and live through the end of the world. From the two of them, all of the humans of the new green earth will descend. What is the man called?
context: Vafthrudnismal 45 and Snorri's Gylfaginning 53. The Old Norse name Lif means simply 'life, the life of the body.' Ask is the FIRST man of Norse myth (carved from an ash tree by Odin, Vili, and Ve at the beginning of the world) -- not the survivor at the end. Bor is Odin's father, one of the primordial line. Bergelmir is the frost-giant who survived the FIRST flood (of Ymir's blood) at the world's beginning, not Ragnarok. The two Ragnarok-survivor humans are Lif and Lifthrasir.  (Legend.)

question: For as long as they are hidden away in the wood, Lif and Lifthrasir have no bread and no meat -- they eat none of the food of Midgard. Vafthrudnismal 45 tells you what they DO live on while the world burns. What do the two survivors drink for food inside the wood?
choices: the milk of a hidden cow
context: Vafthrudnismal 45. Their sustenance is morgindoggvar -- the morning dew. The image is that after the fire and the flood, the very first food of the new humanity is the drops that gather at dawn on the leaves of Yggdrasil itself. Audhumla the cow feeds the frost-giant Ymir at the world's BEGINNING, not its end; sap and hoarded honey belong to other Norse strands.  (Legend.)

question: In Voluspa 61 the surviving gods gather together on a grassy plain and sit down in the grass to talk of Odin's runes and of the world-serpent. This is the SAME plain where the Aesir first held their meetings in the world's youth -- so their end brings them back to where they started. What is this grassy plain called?
context: Voluspa 61 (and Voluspa 7, at the world's dawn). Idavoll is where the Aesir first raised their halls and forges in the beginning; and it is where the small band of surviving gods -- Baldr, Hodr, Vidarr, Vali, Modi, Magni, and Honir -- meet again after the fire. Vigrid is the OTHER plain, the battlefield of Ragnarok itself. Folkvangr is Freyja's field; Glasir is the golden-leaved grove outside Valhalla.  (Legend.)

question: As the surviving gods sit talking on the grass of Idavoll, they reach down and find something in the grass that the Aesir had owned in the world's dawn and had lost somewhere in Asgard when the trouble started -- and here they are, on the fresh grass of the new world. What do the gods find lying in the grass at Idavoll?
context: Voluspa 61: 'In the grass shall the wondrous golden tables be found, which they possessed in ancient days.' In Old Norse, gullnar toflur -- the golden playing-pieces from the gods' board-game in the world's youth. It is one of the strangest and gentlest images in all of Norse myth: gods sitting in fresh grass after the end of the world, picking up the toys they had lost when they were young. Gungnir is Odin's spear (broken with him inside Fenrir's mouth at Ragnarok); Heimdall's Gjallarhorn has already been blown; Odroerir is the vat that held the Mead of Poetry, kept by Odin in Asgard. None of those three are found lying in the grass at Idavoll.  (Legend.)

question: Thor is dead beside the world-serpent, but he leaves TWO SONS behind, and both of them survive Ragnarok. Vafthrudnismal 51 says Vidarr and Vali will inhabit the temples of the gods when Surt's fire is slaked, and that Thor's two sons will inherit one very specific thing from their father. What do Thor's sons Modi and Magni inherit?
context: Vafthrudnismal 51: 'Modi and Magni shall Mjollnir possess.' The two brothers -- Modi ('the wrathful,' Thor's son by Sif) and Magni ('the strong,' Thor's son by the giantess Jarnsaxa) -- carry the hammer forward into the new world. Thor's iron gauntlets (Jarngreipr), his iron chariot pulled by the goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr, and his belt of strength (Megingjord) are Thor's other named gear; the poem singles out MJOLNIR as the sons' inheritance.  (Legend.)

question: In Voluspa 64 the seeress describes a hall she calls 'more beautiful than the sun, better than gold,' and she says the trustworthy troops shall dwell there and have joy for evermore. She gives this hall a specific name, standing on the new earth after Ragnarok. What is this hall called?
context: Voluspa 64: 'She sees a hall standing, more beautiful than the sun, better than gold, at Gimle -- there shall the trustworthy troops dwell, and joy shall have for evermore.' Voluspa 37 names two other post-Ragnarok halls in the same eschatological cluster: Brimir's beer-hall on Okolnir ('never-cold'), and Sindri's hall of red gold in the Nidafjoll mountains. All three stand on the new earth after Surt's fire; Gimle is the one the seeress calls more beautiful than the sun.  (Legend.)

question: The Voluspa does not end on the golden hall Gimle. Its very last stanza (66) darkens the peace one more time. Out from Nidafjoll ('Moon-wane Hills') the seeress sees a great dark dragon come flying up over the plain, and he is CARRYING SOMETHING in his wings. What is Nidhoggr the dragon carrying as he flies up in the poem's final image?
context: Voluspa 66: 'Then comes there the dark dragon flying, the glittering serpent, up from Nidafjoll -- he bears in his feathers dead bodies as he flies over the plain, and now the seeress sinks.' Nidhoggr ('Spite-striker'), the same dragon who gnaws at Yggdrasil's root through the whole poem, flies up carrying corpses in his wings, and that is the last thing the seeress sees before her prophecy ends. Scholars are split on whether it is a last dark note or a strange redemption -- but corpses in the wings is what she sees.  (Legend.)

question: Snorri Sturluson, in his thirteenth-century Prose Edda, retells most of the Voluspa's Ragnarok-ending in Gylfaginning 52-53. In Snorri's version too, the surviving gods gather on the plain of Idavoll and sit together in the grass. What is the FIRST specific subject Snorri says they talk about there, sitting on the grass?
answer: the runes and events of the past
choices: the runes and events of the past
the road up to the new hall
the ships that survived the flood
the fate of the missing Aesir
context: Gylfaginning 53. Snorri: the survivors 'come together and talk of things and remember their runes and speak of the events that had happened before, of the Midgard-Serpent and of the Fenris-Wolf.' In Snorri's telling the very first thing the new world does is REMEMBER -- the gods hand the memory of the old world down through their talk on the grass. It is what turns Ragnarok from an ending into a beginning.

question: In Homer's Iliad, Achilles quarrelled with Agamemnon, the commander of the Greek army at Troy. Agamemnon forced Achilles to give up a captive girl. What was her name?
context: Briseis was Achilles's war-prize, taken when he sacked her city of Lyrnessus. All four distractors are real women of the Trojan cycle used honestly: Cassandra was Priam's prophet-daughter, Andromache was Hector's wife, Iphigenia was Agamemnon's own daughter. Source: Wikipedia, 'Briseis'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, Achilles had one companion closer to him than any other -- a man raised with him as a boy in the house of Achilles's father Peleus. What was that companion's name?
context: Patroclus and Achilles were raised together as boys in the household of Achilles's father Peleus. Homer's word for their bond is 'hetairos' -- companion. All four distractors are real Greek heroes at Troy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, the very first word of the whole poem names what the whole story is about. Sing, goddess, the ______ of Achilles son of Peleus. What is the missing word?
context: The Greek word is 'menin' -- 'wrath' or 'rage'. Richmond Lattimore's translation opens: 'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus, and its devastation, which put pains thousandfold upon the Achaeans.' The Iliad is, from its first breath, a poem about anger. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, after Agamemnon seized Briseis from him, Achilles did not draw his sword against Agamemnon. He did something else -- a choice that shaped the whole rest of the poem. What did Achilles do?
answer: Refused to fight for the Greek army
choices: Refused to fight for the Greek army
Sailed home to Phthia that night
context: Achilles pulled his Myrmidons back to their tents and would not fight. His plan: let the Greeks lose without him, until Agamemnon learned what Achilles was worth. That withdrawal is what turns a personal quarrel into the disaster of the whole war. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, after Achilles refused to fight, his mother went up to Olympus and persuaded Zeus to let the Trojans push the Greeks back to their ships. Who was Achilles's divine mother?
context: Thetis was the sea-nymph Peleus had married; Achilles was her only surviving son. She went up to Zeus and begged him -- so that Agamemnon would learn how badly he needed her son. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad book 15, the Trojans pushed the Greeks all the way back to their beach and set fire to the very first ship. Who led the Trojan charge that got them to the ships?
context: Hector was the greatest of the Trojan warriors and Priam's eldest son. All four distractors are real Trojan captains used honestly -- Paris was Hector's brother, Aeneas the greatest ally, Sarpedon a Lycian ally and son of Zeus himself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, with the Greek ships burning, Patroclus begged Achilles for something. He was not begging for Achilles to fight -- he was begging for a loan. What did Patroclus ask to borrow?
context: Patroclus's plan was to wear Achilles's own armour into the fight so that the Trojans would think Achilles had returned and would run. Achilles agreed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, Achilles agreed to lend Patroclus his armour, but he gave one strict order. Push the Trojans back from the ships -- and then do what?
answer: Stop, and do not chase them to the walls of Troy
choices: Stop, and do not chase them to the walls of Troy
Wait for Achilles himself to arrive in battle
Bring back Hector's helmet as a token
Set fire to the Trojan camp in return
context: Achilles warned him plainly: drive them from the ships, then come back. Patroclus disobeyed. He pressed the Trojans all the way to the Scaean Gates of Troy itself -- and that was where he was killed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad book 16, Patroclus fell in his borrowed armour at the Scaean Gates of Troy. Three foes struck him one after another: a god struck him first and dazed him, a Trojan named Euphorbos speared him, and then Hector killed him. Which god was it who first struck Patroclus at the gate?
context: Homer writes that Apollo himself came down and struck Patroclus, dazing him and knocking the borrowed armour loose. Then Euphorbos speared him, and Hector delivered the killing blow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Patroclus'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad, when word of Patroclus's death was brought to Achilles, he collapsed on the ground and did one thing so violent that his mother heard it under the sea and rose to him. What did he do?
answer: Poured black ashes on his own hair
choices: Poured black ashes on his own hair
Broke his father's spear across his knee
Cut off his own long hair with a knife
Threw his golden shield into the sea
context: Achilles took the black ashes of the mourning fire and poured them over his golden hair, and he howled -- Homer says his mother Thetis heard it in her father's halls beneath the sea and came up to him. Antilochus had to hold his hands to keep him from cutting his own throat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: In Homer's Iliad after Patroclus was killed, Achilles swore an oath about what he would not do until Hector was dead by his hand. Three of these things Achilles refused -- which was NOT part of the oath?
answer: He would not sail home to Phthia
choices: He would not sail home to Phthia
context: Achilles swore he would neither eat, nor sleep, nor bury Patroclus's body, until Hector was dead by his hand. Sailing home was never part of the oath -- Achilles had already been told by Thetis that if he killed Hector, he himself would die soon after. He killed Hector anyway. Source: Wikipedia, 'Achilles'.  (Legend.)

question: The two sworn friends thought themselves worthy of daughters of Zeus. First they set out to help Theseus win his chosen wife -- a girl still a child, whom Theseus carried off and left with his mother Aethra in Attica. Whom did the two heroes carry off for Theseus?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 31: Theseus carried off Helen -- the future Helen of Troy -- while she was still a child and left her with his mother Aethra in Attica. Persephone was Hades's wife (and would be Pirithous's fatal target next); Ariadne is the Cretan princess who gave Theseus the thread through the Labyrinth; Iphigenia is Agamemnon's daughter.  (Legend.)

question: Then it was Pirithous's turn to name a bride. He had lost his own first wife Hippodamia in the great brawl at his wedding-feast, and now he swore he would carry off a goddess -- one already married to another Olympian. Which goddess did Pirithous swear to carry off from her husband?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24; Diodorus Siculus 4.63: Pirithous set his sights on Persephone, wife of Hades and queen of the dead. Amphitrite is wife of Poseidon; Hera wife of Zeus; Aphrodite wife of Hephaestus (but lover of Ares) -- all married Olympian goddesses. Pirithous's first wife Hippodamia had been the woman a centaur tried to abduct at the wedding-feast, starting the great Lapith-vs-centaur brawl in Ovid's Metamorphoses 12.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus was bound by his own oath to help his friend take a wife, however wild Pirithous's choice. So he went down with him. Where did the two friends enter the underworld to begin their descent?
answer: through a cave at Cape Tainaron
choices: through a cave at Cape Tainaron
through the crater of Mount Etna
through a well at the oracle of Dodona
through the sea-gate of the Bosporus
context: Pausanias, Description of Greece 3.25.4; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: the descent was at Cape Tainaron on the southern tip of the Peloponnese, one of the ancient Greek entrances to Hades. Aeneas descends by Cumae in Italy in Virgil; Odysseus reaches the shore of the dead across Ocean.  (Legend.)

question: Hades, king of the underworld, did not meet the two friends with drawn weapons. He came out politely, welcomed them into his hall, and did one thing that seemed the kindest reception they could have hoped for. What did Hades do when Theseus and Pirithous arrived in his hall?
answer: offered them seats at his table
choices: offered them seats at his table
poured them cups of dark wine
sent for Persephone to greet them
led them to the fires of Tartarus
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: Hades welcomed the two friends and, on the pretence of a feast, invited them first to sit down. It was the trap.  (Legend.)

question: The moment Theseus and Pirithous sat down on the offered seats they discovered that the seats themselves were the trap. Their bodies grew fast to the stone and they could not rise from the table. By what name are these seats known in the story?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: the seats were the Chairs of Forgetfulness -- thronoi lethes in Greek -- and the two heroes grew into the stone and were held there. Their memories faded and they forgot why they had come. Apollodorus is the only ancient source that names the chairs explicitly this way. Diodorus 4.63 tells the trap without the name.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles gripped Theseus by the arm and tore him bodily off the Chair of Forgetfulness. So violent was the pull that some pieces of Theseus stayed behind on the stone. Athenians afterwards joked that this was why the men of Athens had a peculiar body-feature. Which part of Theseus did Heracles leave stuck to the chair?
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24; scholia on Aristophanes, Knights 1368: pieces of Theseus's thighs stayed on the stone, and Athenian men afterwards were said to have unusually narrow thighs because of it -- a comic folk-etymology from the Athenian comic stage.  (Legend.)

question: Heracles reached next for Pirithous, meaning to tear him free the same way. But the earth shook underfoot and Persephone herself forbade the rescue. Why was Pirithous refused release when Theseus had been allowed to go?
answer: Pirithous had planned the outrage against Persephone
choices: Pirithous had planned the outrage against Persephone
Pirithous had killed a suppliant in Hades
Pirithous had cursed Cerberus at the gate
context: Diodorus Siculus 4.63; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24: Persephone forbade Pirithous's release because he was the one who had conceived the plan to carry her off. Theseus had only come along in oath-loyalty to his friend. Pirithous is left stuck to the chair in Hades forever.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus made it back to the upper world, but his long absence had broken his kingship in Athens. In the end he was driven into exile on an Aegean island, where the local king pretended to receive him as a guest and then pushed him off a cliff to his death. On what island was Theseus murdered in exile?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 35: Theseus was killed on Scyros by King Lycomedes, who pushed him off a cliff. Naxos is where Theseus abandoned Ariadne; Delos is the sacred birth-island of Apollo and Artemis; Aegina is the island of Aeacus. Later the Athenian general Cimon recovered what were said to be Theseus's bones from Scyros in 475 BCE and brought them home to Athens.  (Legend.)

question: During the years Theseus was stuck in Hades, his stolen Spartan child-bride Helen sat in Attica in the keeping of his mother Aethra. Then two great warriors marched an army into Attica to recover their sister and take her home. Who were the brothers who invaded Attica to fetch Helen back?
context: Herodotus, Histories 9.73; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23: Helen's brothers Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, invaded Attica, freed Helen, and carried off Theseus's own mother Aethra as a captive-servant to Helen -- who was still with Helen years later in Homer's Iliad. Menelaus and Agamemnon are the Atreid brothers of the Trojan War; Ajax and Teucer are sons of Telamon.  (Legend.)

question: The Minotaur lived inside a great maze at Knossos on Crete, so cunningly designed that anyone who went in could never find the way out again. King Minos had it built by his own household craftsman. Who was the craftsman who designed the maze?
context: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.1.4; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15-19. Daedalus was an Athenian by birth who had fled to Crete after killing his nephew Perdix out of jealousy. Icarus is his own son; Hephaestus is the divine smith; Prometheus was the fire-bringer. The maze is called the LABYRINTH.  (Legend.)

question: When Theseus's ship sailed from Athens for Crete, it carried a black mourning sail. His father the king of Athens gave the pilot a second sail of a different colour, folded away in the hold, with strict orders: on the way back, if Theseus was alive, raise the second sail; if Theseus was dead, keep the black one flying. What colour was the second sail?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 17.4-5: Aegeus 'gave the pilot another sail, a white one, ordering him, if he returned with Theseus safe, to hoist the white sail, but otherwise to sail with the black one.'  (Legend.)

question: When Ariadne gave Theseus her ball of thread that would let him beat the maze, she told him one exact thing to do with it, so that the thread would actually guide him back out again -- a detail spelled out in Apollodorus's version of the tale. What did she tell him to do with the end of the thread as he stepped into the Labyrinth?
answer: Tie one end to the door of the Labyrinth and let the ball unwind as he walked in
choices: Tie one end to the door of the Labyrinth and let the ball unwind as he walked in
Hold the ball tightly in his fist and let it unspool as he pushed on through the passages
Tie one end firmly around his own wrist and cut it loose once the beast was dead
Trail the thread quietly behind him without touching it, letting it fall as he passed
context: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.9. Ariadne 'gave him a clue of thread' and told him to fasten one end to the door of the labyrinth as he entered, and to unwind it as he penetrated the maze. It is Ariadne's engineering, not just her love, that saves Theseus -- Theseus follows the taut thread back to the door and out. The English word 'clue' comes directly from this 'clew' of thread.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus sailed home from Crete with the fourteen freed Athenians and with Ariadne. On the island of Naxos he abandoned her asleep on the beach and sailed on without her. In one famous version of the tale, another god then came to Naxos, found her weeping, and took her as his own bride. Which god?
context: Diodorus 4.61; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.9. The wine-god Dionysus is said to have given Ariadne a golden crown as a wedding gift -- and when she died it was thrown into the sky as the constellation Corona Borealis (the Northern Crown).  (Legend.)

question: Sailing home to Athens after Naxos, grieving or distracted, Theseus broke the one promise he had made to his father before leaving. What had he forgotten to do?
answer: He forgot to raise the white sail in place of the black one
choices: He forgot to raise the white sail in place of the black one
He forgot to pour a libation of wine to Poseidon before setting off
He forgot to return the sword Ariadne had given him
He forgot to bury the Minotaur's body in the sea
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 22.1. This is the promise from rung 3 -- broken, and about to cost his father his life. Grief for Ariadne, in some tellings, is why the change of sail slipped his mind.  (Legend.)

question: Athens's tribute to King Minos was a fixed number of young men and an equal number of young women, sent to Crete every nine years to be fed to the Minotaur. How many youths were in each tribute-shipment, all told?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 15.1: 'they sent heralds and made their supplication and entered into an agreement to send him every nine years a tribute of seven youths and as many maidens.' Seven plus seven -- fourteen. Some later sources say every year instead of every nine years.  (Legend.)

question: In English, when we say 'I have a CLUE' or 'the detective was following a clue,' we are using a word whose older spelling was 'clew,' from Old English cliewen. From what famous mythic escape did the modern sense -- 'the thing that guides you out of a puzzle' -- come?
answer: Ariadne's thread guiding Theseus out of the Labyrinth
choices: Ariadne's thread guiding Theseus out of the Labyrinth
Odysseus escaping the Cyclops's cave beneath the belly of the ram
Perseus using Athena's mirrored shield to escape the gaze of Medusa
Orpheus climbing back from the Underworld with Eurydice behind him
context: OED and etymonline.com trace the sense-shift precisely to Ariadne's clew of thread; by the 17th century 'clue' had come to mean any hint that leads you out of a puzzle. Every time an English detective story uses the word, it is quietly retelling this myth.

question: After Theseus had escaped Crete, King Minos threw the craftsman who had designed the maze into prison for having helped Ariadne. To escape from Crete himself, the craftsman built two pairs of wings for himself and his son. What became of the son during their flight to freedom?
answer: Icarus flew too near the sun, whose heat melted the wax, and he fell into the sea
choices: Icarus flew too near the sun, whose heat melted the wax, and he fell into the sea
Icarus was struck by an arrow of Apollo who mistook him for a bird
Icarus was blown out to sea by a sudden storm and was never seen again
Icarus grew tired mid-flight and drowned before reaching the mainland
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-235; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.12. The stretch of sea where he fell is called the Icarian Sea to this day, off the island of Icaria. His father Daedalus flew on and landed safely in Sicily.  (Legend.)

question: The young hero Theseus grows up in the town of Troezen in his mother Aethra's household, not knowing his father. When he is old enough, Aethra leads him to a great boulder and tells him to lift it. Underneath lie two objects his absent father left as tokens years before. What two things does he find?
answer: a sword and a pair of sandals
choices: a sword and a pair of sandals
a bow and a quiver of arrows
a crown and a golden ring
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-4. The tokens belong to Aegeus, king of Athens; when Theseus reaches the city and lays them before Aegeus, the king recognises his son. Pausanias 2.32.7 records that the boulder was still shown to travellers in his day.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus's mother Aethra finally tells him the name of the man who left the sword and sandals under the boulder years ago. He sets out to find that father in a great walled city to the north. What is the father's name?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 3-6. Aegeus is king of Athens. In another tradition Theseus is also son of the god Poseidon on the same night, so he is treated as doubly-fathered. Laius is Oedipus's father at Thebes; Menelaus rules Sparta and is Helen's husband; Peleus is Achilles's father.  (Legend.)

question: Setting out from Troezen to find his father in Athens, Theseus refuses the safe short ship-passage. He insists on going the long way, on foot, on a road famous for bandits and monsters. Which route does he take?
answer: the overland road around the Saronic Gulf
choices: the overland road around the Saronic Gulf
the ridge above the vale of Tempe
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 6-7. The choice is deliberate: Theseus wants a career of his own before he arrives at his father's court. The stretch of coast between Troezen and Athens (the modern Isthmus of Corinth) was famous in myth for road-monsters.  (Legend.)

question: On the dangerous overland road Theseus meets six road-monsters in turn. He kills each of them by a single memorable rule that gives Greek storytellers their favourite kind of poetic justice. What is the rule?
answer: he kills each one by that killer's own method
choices: he kills each one by that killer's own method
he lets each one strike first and disarms them
he offers each one mercy and kills only those who refuse
he binds each one and hands them over to Aegeus
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8-11. The pattern is the point of the cycle: the club-bearer's club, the pine-bender's pines, the cliff-kicker's cliff, the wrestler's grip, and the bed-stretcher's bed each turn on their owner.  (Legend.)

question: The first road-monster at Epidaurus is a giant who bludgeons every traveller with a great brass club. Theseus wrests it away and beats the giant dead with his own weapon -- then keeps the club and carries it for the rest of his life as a trophy. What is this club-swinger called?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8. Periphetes is nicknamed Corynetes, 'the Club-Bearer'. Antaeus is the Libyan wrestler Heracles crushes; Cacus is the Aventine fire-thief; Talos is the bronze automaton of Crete -- all real Greek strongmen, none of them the Epidaurus bandit.  (Legend.)

question: The second bandit on the road bends two pine trees down to the ground, ties his victim's arms and legs each to a different bent trunk, then lets the trees spring back apart so the traveller is torn in half. Theseus ties HIM between his own two pines and lets go. What name is this pine-artist known by?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 8. Sinis is nicknamed Pityocamptes, 'the Pine-Bender'. Nessus is the centaur of the Deianira story; Amycus is the boxer of the Argonauts; Diomedes is the Thracian who feeds his mares on strangers.  (Legend.)

question: Between two of the bandits Theseus turns aside to kill a giant beast that has been terrorising farmers in the countryside near Corinth: not a bandit at all, but an animal gone monstrous, remembered by the ancient Greek name Crommyonian. What kind of animal does he kill on this detour?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 9. She is the Crommyonian Sow, sometimes named Phaea after the old woman who raised her. A many-headed serpent is Heracles's Hydra; a bronze-hooved bull recalls the Cretan Bull; a fire-breathing goat is part of the Chimera.  (Legend.)

question: On a narrow clifftop path above the sea Theseus finds a robber who has a favourite trick: he forces every passing traveller to kneel and wash his feet, and while they are kneeling he kicks them off the cliff into the water below. Theseus lets him take up his usual seat, then kicks HIM over the edge. What is this cliff-robber's name?
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 10. Sciron sits on the Sceironian Rocks on the road between Megara and Attica. Busiris is the Egyptian king who sacrifices foreign guests; Lityerses is the reaper-tyrant of Phrygia; Antaeus is Heracles's Libyan wrestler.  (Legend.)

question: The last and most famous bandit on the road runs a lonely roadside inn near Athens. He offers every traveller a bed for the night -- an iron one -- and then makes each guest fit it. Theseus ties HIM to the same bed and finishes him the same way. What is the innkeeper's fitting-trick?
answer: short guests get stretched, tall guests get chopped down
choices: short guests get stretched, tall guests get chopped down
guests get bound in chains until they starve to fit
guests get force-fed until they burst to fit
guests get frozen with cold iron until they shrink to fit
context: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 11. The innkeeper is Procrustes ('the Stretcher'), also called Damastes. The trick's mechanical honesty -- fit the person to the bed, never the bed to the person -- is why it survives as a proverb.  (Legend.)

question: The Athens innkeeper's iron-bed trick outlasted every other episode on Theseus's road-trip. It turned into a single English phrase that means 'a rigid framework forced on things that don't fit it', and every modern European language borrows a version of it. Which two-word phrase carries the tale into everyday speech?
context: The innkeeper is named Procrustes ('the Stretcher'). The phrase 'Procrustean bed' entered English via Latin and is used in statistics, editing, law, and philosophy for any standard imposed by amputation or stretching. The Gordian knot means an intractable problem cut through; the Trojan horse a deceptive gift; the Damoclean sword a hanging danger over privilege.

question: Freed at last, Thomas Aquinas went north to study under the greatest teacher in Europe. Because Thomas was huge, heavy, and almost silent in class, the other students mocked him with an animal nickname. What did they call him?
context: His teacher was Albertus Magnus, Albert the Great. Thomas's massive silence at the back of the hall convinced classmates he was slow-witted; they had no idea what was going on inside his head. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: When Albert the Great heard his own students at Cologne laughing at their huge, silent classmate Thomas Aquinas, Albert answered with a warning about the animal nickname they had given him. He said that one day this beast would do WHAT to the whole world?
choices: plough its fields to the sea
context: The line survives in several forms: 'You call him the Dumb Ox; I tell you that this Dumb Ox will one day fill the world with his bellowing.' Albert had spotted the theological giant hidden inside the heavy young Sicilian. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Around 1265 Thomas Aquinas began his enormous masterwork, structured as thousands of questions, each with objections, replies, and citations from the fathers, Aristotle, and the Muslim commentator Averroes. What is this unfinished work called?
context: He had already finished the Summa Contra Gentiles, aimed at non-Christian readers. The Summa Theologiae was meant as a full teaching guide for beginners in theology, and Thomas never lived to finish it. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: In the Summa Theologiae Thomas Aquinas cites Aristotle so constantly that he no longer bothers to name him, calling him only by a single title. What did Aquinas call Aristotle?
context: In parallel, Aquinas called the Muslim writer Averroes simply 'the Commentator' because his line-by-line reading of Aristotle was without rival. Both nicknames were casual medieval scholar-slang and treated as obvious. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: On December 6, 1273, the Feast of Saint Nicholas, Thomas Aquinas was celebrating Mass at the Dominican priory in Naples when something happened during the service that changed him forever. Witnesses said the Mass was interrupted by an unusually long WHAT?
context: From the moment of that long ecstasy Thomas laid down his pen and stopped adding to the great Summa Theologiae. He was working on the sacrament of Penance in Part III. He never wrote another article. Christian History Institute, 'I can write no more'.

question: When his companion Reginald of Piperno begged the silent Thomas Aquinas to take up the Summa again after the Naples Mass, Thomas gave a single reason. He told Reginald that everything he had ever written seemed to him like WHAT compared with what had been revealed to him?
context: Aquinas said, in effect: 'Reginald, I cannot; all that I have written seems like straw to me compared with what I have seen.' He never dictated another article of the Summa. Christian History Institute, 'I can write no more'.

question: A few months after laying down his pen, Thomas Aquinas set out for a great church council at Lyons. On the road he struck his head hard on a low branch, fell ill, and died on March 7, 1274, aged about forty-nine. At which abbey did he end his journey?
context: Fossanova, a Cistercian house on the road between Naples and Rome, took the sick Dominican in. He died there and was later canonized by Pope John XXII in 1323. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas'.

question: Thomas Becket and King Henry II of England were so close in the 1150s that they hunted, drank, and rode together like brothers, with Becket serving as the king's Chancellor. In 1162 the king rewarded his old drinking companion with a great church post, sure the old friend would keep the clergy in line for the crown. Which post did Becket receive?
context: Henry had already made Becket his Chancellor. He assumed the new archbishop would sign whatever the crown wanted. He was very wrong. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Once he was Archbishop, Thomas Becket shocked his old friend Henry II by turning strict churchman and blocking royal courts from trying priests and monks. Henry answered in 1164 with sixteen articles meant to bring the church under the crown, named after the palace where he issued them. What were they called?
context: The heart of the fight was 'criminous clerks': clergy accused of murder or theft, whom Henry wanted judged in the king's courts, not the bishops'. Becket refused to sign; the quarrel drove him into exile in France for nearly six years. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: The fullest eyewitness account of Thomas Becket's murder was written about ten years after the killing by a visiting monk from Cambridge who was standing beside Becket in the cathedral and was wounded in the arm defending him. What was that monk's name?
context: Grim's Vita S. Thomae, written around 1180, is the source for almost every famous detail: Becket's last words, the sword shattering on the pavement, the parting taunt of Hugh of Horsea. Wikipedia, 'Edward Grim'.

question: Taking King Henry II's Christmas outburst as an order, a small band of his household knights crossed the Channel and rode hard for Canterbury to deal with Thomas Becket. Their names are still remembered: Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and one more. Who was the fourth?
context: Le Breton would strike the last and most terrible blow of the four. All four knights were later exiled to the Holy Land as penitents by the pope for fourteen years. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Late on December 29, 1170, the four knights came for Thomas Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral itself. The monks tried to bar the doors of the church; Becket ordered them to open again. In which part of the great cathedral did the knights finally catch him?
context: Becket had come down from vespers. He refused to hide or run, telling the monks it was wrong to make a fortress out of the house of prayer. The eyewitness Edward Grim, a visiting monk from Cambridge, was standing beside him. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'; Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: Facing the four armed knights inside Canterbury Cathedral, Thomas Becket refused to run or draw a weapon. The wounded monk beside him wrote down Becket's answer word for word. For whose name and for what did Becket say he was ready to die?
answer: for the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church
choices: for the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church
for the name of King Henry and the peace of the realm
for the name of Rome and the honor of the pope
for the name of England and the safety of the monks
context: Grim's Vita S. Thomae records the exact line: 'For the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church I am ready to embrace death.' Becket made no move to defend himself. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: As Thomas Becket knelt inside Canterbury Cathedral, Richard le Breton struck the final blow with such force that the sword shattered against the stone pavement. According to the eyewitness monk Edward Grim, that same downward stroke did something terrible to Becket's head that showed the watchers he was dead on the spot. What did the blow do?
answer: sliced off the crown of his skull
choices: sliced off the crown of his skull
drove a nail into his temple
context: Grim writes that the blow 'shattered the sword on the stone pavement and separated the crown of Becket's head, which was large, from his skull.' A fragment of the broken sword-tip was preserved for centuries as a relic. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: After the four knights had finished, a cleric who had come with them, Hugh of Horsea, stepped over Thomas Becket's body in the cathedral, set his foot on the archbishop's neck, and used a sword for one final horror. What did he do?
answer: drove the sword-tip into his skull
choices: drove the sword-tip into his skull
carved a cross on his cheek
context: Grim records Hugh's parting taunt: 'Let us away, knights; this fellow will arise no more.' Within hours the monks were gathering the blood and brains into vessels as relics. Edward Grim, 'Vita S. Thomae' (c. 1180).

question: The monks of Canterbury undressed Thomas Becket's body to prepare it for burial and gasped: the fine outer robes of the murdered archbishop hid a secret garment of hidden penance, and it was crawling with vermin. What was it?
context: The old friend of the king had turned in private into a rough-cloth ascetic. Along with Grim's eyewitness murder, the shocking hair shirt convinced Rome: Pope Alexander III canonized Becket in 1173, barely two years after his death. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: In July 1174, King Henry II himself came to Canterbury to do public penance at Thomas Becket's tomb. He walked in as no king walks, submitting to something at the shrine that no earlier English king had endured in public. What did he submit to?
context: Every monk of the cathedral chapter struck the kneeling king with a rod. It was one of the most humbling scenes ever staged by a medieval king. Wikipedia, 'Thomas Becket'.

question: Thomas More, born in London in 1478, was a lawyer, a scholar, and a close friend of the Dutch humanist Erasmus. In 1516 he published a little Latin book describing an imaginary island of perfect politics. Its title was a word he had just coined from Greek roots meaning 'no place'. What was the word?
context: The Greek OU + TOPOS becomes Utopia, 'no place'. The joke in the name is that More's ideal island is nowhere real. The book gave English a word we still use every day. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: As the king's highest legal officer, Thomas More refused to back King Henry VIII's plan to divorce Catherine of Aragon and to declare himself Supreme Head of the Church of England. In 1532 More did something no one expected. What did he do?
answer: resigned his office and went home
choices: resigned his office and went home
led an army into the north
married a second wife in secret
context: More gave up the great seal and retired to his Chelsea house with his large learned family, hoping to be left alone. Henry would not leave him alone. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: At Thomas More's trial in Westminster Hall on July 1, 1535, the crucial evidence was a piece of perjury: a royal official swore that More had privately told him Parliament could not make the king head of the Church. Who was the perjurer?
context: More denied Rich's account under oath, calling him a liar to his face. The jury convicted More anyway, in about fifteen minutes. Rich, later Lord Rich, went on to a long and notorious career. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'; famous-trials.com, 'Trial of Sir Thomas More'.

question: On the morning of July 6, 1535, Thomas More was led out to Tower Hill in London for beheading. The wooden scaffold looked unsteady, so More made a wry remark to the officer at his elbow. What did he ask the officer?
answer: to see him safe up, and let him shift for himself coming down
choices: to see him safe up, and let him shift for himself coming down
to strike quickly, for his neck was but a little one
to lend him a strong arm as he was an old man
to say a Requiem Mass at St Paul's that afternoon
context: William Roper, More's son-in-law, records the words: 'I pray you, Master Lieutenant, see me safe up; and for my coming down let me shift for myself.' The joke was that More would be coming down as a corpse and would manage the descent one way or another. William Roper, 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557).

question: Kneeling at the block on Tower Hill, Thomas More stopped the executioner to arrange his own long beard carefully over the wood, out of the way of the axe. According to his son-in-law William Roper, what did More say as he did it?
answer: This hath not offended the King
choices: This hath not offended the King
Do thy work and fear not
context: It is the last recorded joke of a man famous for jokes. The beard, at least, was innocent of treason and should not lose its head. William Roper, 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557).

question: Just before the axe fell on Tower Hill, Thomas More spoke a final sentence that became one of the most quoted last words in English history: 'I die the King's good servant, but God's first.' The line survives because two independent sources wrote it down within weeks. One was his son-in-law William Roper's memoir. What was the other?
choices: the diary of the Spanish ambassador Eustace Chapuys
the Acts and Monuments of John Foxe
context: A newsletter sent from London to Paris that August carried a full account of the execution, including the last words, to readers on the Continent. Together with Roper's 'Life of Sir Thomas More' (c. 1557), it is why we can still quote the line today.

question: After Thomas More's beheading, his severed head was parboiled and stuck up on a pike on London Bridge, the standard treatment for traitors. About a month later his daughter Margaret Roper bribed the bridge-keeper and rescued it. What did the keeper's job usually involve doing with old heads?
choices: burying them in an unmarked pit
carting them out to the city gates
returning them to the Tower for storage
context: Margaret paid the keeper to give her father's head to her instead of into the river. It was a brave and dangerous thing to do; the Crown considered it treason to honour the traitor's remains. Wikipedia, 'Margaret Roper'.

question: Margaret Roper carried her father Thomas More's rescued head home from London Bridge and preserved it for the rest of her life. How did she keep it?
context: Margaret kept the head until her own death in 1544 at about thirty-nine. It eventually came to rest in the Roper family vault beneath St Dunstan's church in Canterbury, where visitors can still see the grate over the vault today. Wikipedia, 'Margaret Roper'.

question: One honest complication in the story of Thomas More: before his own trial he had spent his Chancellorship prosecuting people he considered heretics. Six of them were burned during his time in office. At which London execution ground?
context: Smithfield, just outside the London wall, was the burning-ground for heretics under the Tudors. More is remembered as a martyr for his own conscience, but as Lord Chancellor he sent Protestants to the fire for theirs. Wikipedia, 'Thomas More'.

question: One of the Twelve apostles is introduced in the Gospel of John by a Greek nickname that means 'the twin.' What is the nickname?
context: John 11:16 KJV: 'Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples...' Didymus is Greek for 'twin.' Boanerges ('sons of thunder') was James and John; Iscariot was Judas's byname; Cephas ('rock') was Simon Peter's.

question: Jesus decides to go back to Judea to raise Lazarus, even though enemies there have already tried to stone him. One apostle turns to the others and says grimly, 'Let us also go, that we may die with him.' Which apostle?
context: John 11:16 KJV. Thomas -- the same apostle later called 'Doubting' -- is the one who volunteers to walk into danger with Jesus here. Peter is the impulsive one at other moments, Andrew is the quiet brother, Philip asks about the loaves.

question: The English phrase 'a doubting Thomas' comes from a single scene in the Gospel of John. What in particular does Thomas say he must see or touch before he will believe Jesus is risen?
answer: The nail prints in the hands, and the wound in the side
choices: The nail prints in the hands, and the wound in the side
An angel rolling back the tomb stone
Jesus eating bread and fish before them
The empty grave-clothes folded in the tomb
context: John 20:25 KJV: 'Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.' The other options are all real post-resurrection details, but from different scenes.

question: Eight days after the first resurrection appearance, Jesus stands in the room and turns straight to the disciple who had refused to believe without proof. What does Jesus say to him first?
answer: Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands
choices: Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands
Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these
Get thee behind me, Satan, thou art an offence unto me
Whom seek ye? I am he: if therefore ye seek me, let these go
context: John 20:27 KJV: 'Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.' The other quotes are Jesus to Peter on the shore (John 21:15), Jesus to Peter about the cross (Matt 16:23), and Jesus in the garden at his arrest (John 18:7-8).

question: The Kerala tradition remembers that after landing on the Malabar coast about AD 52, the apostle Thomas founded a fixed number of churches along the shore, remembered together by the Malayalam name 'Ezharappallikal.' How many churches does the tradition count?
context: The Ezharappallikal are traditionally called 'the seven and a half churches' of Kerala -- seven full churches plus one small one -- attributed to Thomas's Malabar mission. Twelve is the number of apostles; forty is Jesus's wilderness days; three is a general biblical number.  (Legend.)

question: The tradition of the Saint Thomas Christians holds that after preaching along the coasts of India, the apostle Thomas was killed at Mylapore, on the east coast near modern Chennai. How does the tradition say he died?
answer: Stabbed with a spear while at prayer
choices: Stabbed with a spear while at prayer
Crucified upside-down at his own request
Beheaded by a Roman sword outside the city walls
Boiled alive in a cauldron of oil
context: The Mylapore tradition (San Thome, Chennai) holds Thomas was speared at prayer. The upside-down crucifixion belongs to Peter (Rome, tradition); beheading by Roman sword belongs to Paul (Ostian Way); the cauldron of oil belongs to John the Beloved (Rome, tradition -- who survived it).  (Legend.)

question: The Norse Midgard Serpent is the great sea-monster that wraps the whole world -- so long he holds his own tail in his teeth. He was one of three monstrous children Loki fathered on the giantess Angrboda; the other two are Hel, the death-goddess, and Fenrir, the wolf. What is the Midgard Serpent's own name?
context: Jormungandr is the world-encircling sea-serpent, the eternal enemy of Thor. Nidhogg is the dragon at Yggdrasil's third root, gnawing at the world-tree's root and chewing corpses in Hel. Garm is the great hound chained at the gates of Hel. Fafnir was a dwarf who turned into a dragon, killed by Sigurd the Volsung.  (Legend.)

question: Thor goes to visit the giant Hymir on an errand: the sea-god Aegir has agreed to host a feast for all the Aesir, but he needs a cauldron big enough to brew ale for every god at once, and Hymir owns the only cauldron that huge. Hymir agrees to lend it -- but on one condition. What does Hymir make Thor do first?
answer: row out to sea and help catch enough fish for supper
choices: row out to sea and help catch enough fish for supper
sing three drinking-songs before the whole hall
wrestle Hymir's champion in the yard for a day
drink from Hymir's great horn without a breath
context: Hymiskvida and Gylfaginning 48: Hymir agrees to the loan only if Thor helps him catch enough fish to feed the household that night. The three wrong choices are real motifs from other Thor-among-the-giants stories -- the horn-drinking is Utgardaloki's contest (where the horn turns out to be the sea itself), and wrestling and drinking-song feats belong to other giant-halls.  (Legend.)

question: Before the boat can go out Hymir tells Thor to fetch his own bait -- the giant will not spare any. Thor walks into Hymir's cattle-pasture, chooses the biggest black bull in the herd, and does one shocking thing to get his bait. What does Thor do to Hymir's biggest ox?
answer: rips its head off with his bare hands
choices: rips its head off with his bare hands
cuts a thick steak from its shoulder
chases it into the sea and drowns it
hurls Mjolnir at it and pulps the skull
context: Gylfaginning 48 and Hymiskvida: Thor walks up to the biggest black bull in the herd and tears the head off with his bare hands, then carries the head down to the boat as bait. Hymir, watching from the doorway, says nothing but goes very pale.  (Legend.)

question: The biggest black bull in Hymir's herd -- the one whose head Thor takes for fish-bait -- is not just any ox. He has a name meaning 'Sky-Bellower' or 'Heaven-Bellower', in Old Norse. What is the ox's name?
context: Himinhrjot means 'Heaven-Bellower' -- Old Norse himin ('sky, heaven') + hrjot- ('roarer, bellower'). Audhumla is the primeval cow who licked the ice to free the first god at the world's beginning. Sanngrid is a Valkyrie. Saehrimnir is the boar in Valhalla who is butchered every night and whole again every morning to feed the einherjar.  (Legend.)

question: Thor drops his baited hook into the deep, and the Midgard Serpent takes it. Thor braces his feet against the hull of the little boat to heave -- and puts so much of his god-strength into the pull that one shocking thing happens to the boat itself. What happens to the hull when Thor braces?
answer: his heels punch through the planks and he stands on the sea-floor
choices: his heels punch through the planks and he stands on the sea-floor
the boat splits down the middle and both men fall in
the mast snaps and drops across his shoulders
the oars break in his hands like dry twigs
context: Gylfaginning 48: Thor pulls so hard that his feet drive straight through the bottom of the boat, and he ends up bracing against the SEA-FLOOR itself as he heaves the serpent's head up out of the water. It is the most famous 'Thor's strength' image in the Prose Edda.  (Legend.)

question: This scene of Thor and Hymir fishing for the Serpent is not just written down in the Eddas -- it is one of the most-carved myth-scenes in Viking-age stone. A 10th-century cross-shaft fragment in an English churchyard shows Thor and Hymir sitting in a boat, an ox-head bait dangling on a line, and a serpent-mouth rising from the waves below. In which English county does this stone stand?
context: The Gosforth Fishing Stone was found in the churchyard of St Mary's, Gosforth, in Cumbria in March 1882 by C. A. Parker, while he was measuring the taller Gosforth Cross beside it. It is a fragment of what was probably a second cross-shaft, from the first half of the 10th century -- Anglo-Norse, from a Viking-settled region of England. The Ilkley Cross, Rothbury Cross, and Sutton Hoo are all real English early-medieval sites but do not carry this scene.

question: Thor and Jormungandr meet a second time -- and the second time will be their last. Voluspa 55 and 56 tell the end at Ragnarok, when every god fights his fated enemy. Thor kills the Midgard Serpent with Mjolnir -- but the Serpent has poisoned him. How far does Thor stagger before he dies of Jormungandr's venom?
context: Voluspa 55-56: Thor smites the Serpent, then 'steps nine paces from the coiled beast and falls'. Nine is the signature Norse number -- nine worlds, nine nights Odin hangs on the tree, nine paces for Thor. The number is not arbitrary. The Ragnarok scene ends the god-versus-monster contest that began in Hymir's boat: the same two opponents, the same god's hammer, but this time nobody cuts the line.  (Legend.)

question: Thor the thunder-god has met the world-serpent Jormungandr twice before their final meeting, and both times the fight ended without a winner. The FIRST time is at the hall of the giant-king Utgard-Loki. Thor is challenged to lift a huge grey CAT off the floor -- but the cat is really the world-serpent in disguise. How much of the cat does Thor manage to lift off the floor?
context: Gylfaginning 47. At Utgard-Loki's court Thor is tricked into an unwinnable challenge: the cat is Jormungandr in disguise and lifting the world-serpent off Midgard is impossible. Thor pours in every ounce of god-strength and manages exactly ONE paw off the floor. Utgard-Loki tells him afterwards that even that terrified the giants -- Thor came close to breaking the world in half by lifting the serpent that holds it.  (Legend.)

question: The SECOND time Thor and Jormungandr meet, Thor is out on the open sea in a small boat with the giant Hymir. Thor drops an ox-head over the side as bait, and the world-serpent takes it. When the serpent's head rises out of the water beside the boat, Hymir panics and does what?
answer: cuts the line with his knife
choices: cuts the line with his knife
drops his oar into the sea
screams a warding spell at the serpent
hurls the ox-head back at the serpent
context: Gylfaginning 48 and the Eddic poem Hymiskvida. Hymir sees the world-serpent's head come up out of the sea beside the boat, drops his knife on the line, and cuts Thor's catch loose. The serpent sinks back into the deep with Thor's ox-head bait still in his mouth -- and Thor swings Mjolnir at Hymir's head in fury, but the giant dives overboard and swims for shore. The score between god and serpent is left unfinished for ages.  (Legend.)

question: At Ragnarok the world-serpent releases his own tail out of his mouth for the first time in all the ages of the world, and he rises out of the ocean and comes ASHORE with the giants' host to meet the gods on a specific battlefield where the last battle is fought. What is the name of that battlefield?
context: Voluspa 55 and Gylfaginning 51. Vigrid is the great plain where the gods and the giants meet for the last battle at Ragnarok -- Snorri gives it a hundred leagues on every side.
