Bifrost is the rainbow-bridge that Surt and his fire-host shatter as they cross into Asgard. Idavoll is the meadow at the CENTER of Asgard where the surviving gods will meet again in the new world after Ragnarok. Folkvangr is Freyja's own field, where she takes half the battle-dead. As Jormungandr comes ashore he sprays so much venom that the sea itself is fouled before the two hosts even meet.  (Legend.)

question: On the plain of Vigrid, Thor and the world-serpent finally close for the third and last time. Thor swings the weapon Mjolnir at Jormungandr's head -- and this time he does what he has never been able to do before. What does Thor do to Jormungandr with the hammer?
choices: hurls him back into the sea
context: Voluspa 55-56 and Gylfaginning 51. Thor strikes with Mjolnir and CRUSHES the world-serpent's head -- the killing blow that the ox-head bait at sea and the cat-lift at Utgard-Loki both pointed toward. Binding, sea-return, and burning belong to other Norse fights (the wolf Fenrir was bound with the ribbon Gleipnir; Balder's body was set on the burning ship Hringhorni; nothing is 'thrown back into the sea' at Ragnarok because the sea itself has risen). The hammer to the head is the specific end.  (Legend.)

question: Voluspa 56 does not call Thor by his own name in the killing-of-Jormungandr stanza. It calls him by a MATRONYMIC -- 'the son of Hlodyn,' where Hlodyn is a name for Thor's mother, the goddess of one very specific thing. Hlodyn is a name for the goddess of WHAT?
context: Voluspa 56 in Bellows: 'Fares Hlodyn's son to fight the serpent.' Hlodyn (also Jord, also Fjorgyn) is Thor's mother, the goddess of the earth herself -- so at the moment Thor kills the serpent who wraps the earth, the poet calls him by his EARTH-mother's name. Nott (Night), Ran (sea), and Sif (Thor's wife, associated with grain and golden hair) are other Norse goddesses -- Hlodyn is specifically the earth.  (Legend.)

question: Thor kills the world-serpent, but at the moment the hammer comes down, the poison the serpent had already breathed on him is already in his body. He staggers forward and walks a specific and famous number of paces from the dead serpent before he falls to the ground dead. How many paces does Thor walk?
context: Gylfaginning 51: 'Nine paces will Fjorgyn's son [Thor] step, then fall to the earth dead, from the venom of the serpent.' Voluspa 56 says the same. The number is not incidental -- nine is one of Norse myth's sacred numbers (see the T5 rung on this ladder). The serpent's venom kills him, but only after he has walked away from the body he beat.  (Legend.)

question: Thor is dead beside the world-serpent, but he leaves TWO SONS behind, and both survive Ragnarok. Vafthrudnismal 51 names them and gives them one very specific thing to inherit from their father, so that his weapon will still be in the new world. Which two of Thor's sons carry Mjolnir into the new world?
context: Vafthrudnismal 51: 'Modi and Magni shall Mjollnir possess, when Vingnir is dead.' Modi is Thor's son by Sif (his name means 'the wrathful, the courageous'); Magni is Thor's son by the giantess Jarnsaxa (his name means 'the strong'). Vidarr and Vali are Odin's other sons, and they do survive Ragnarok too, but they inherit their father's HALLS, not Thor's hammer. Bragi and Hodr are gods but not Ragnarok inheritors. Njord and Freyr are Vanir gods and Freyr dies at Ragnarok to Surt.  (Legend.)

question: Nine paces is not a random number in this scene. Norse myth uses NINE for its most sacred images throughout the Eddas -- the number is deliberately woven through the whole tradition. Which of these is ALSO explicitly counted as nine?
answer: the worlds held up by Yggdrasil
choices: the worlds held up by Yggdrasil
the wolves that chase the sun
the ravens that fly around Odin
context: The world-tree Yggdrasil holds up NINE worlds -- Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim, Vanaheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Helheim. Odin also hangs on Yggdrasil for nine nights to win the runes; Draupnir the ring drops eight new gold rings every ninth night; Thor walks nine paces to die. Only TWO wolves chase the sun and moon (Skoll and Hati); only TWO ravens fly around Odin (Huginn and Muninn); Thor's hammer-strokes aren't counted. Nine is the number of the worlds.  (Legend.)

question: On the first night of the journey east, Thor and his companions find what looks like a huge empty hall and crawl inside to sleep. At dawn they discover the 'hall' was actually part of a giant's clothing, dropped in the road. What had they slept inside?
answer: the thumb of a giant's glove
choices: the thumb of a giant's glove
the hood of a giant's cloak
the toe of a giant's boot
the sleeve of a giant's shirt
context: Gylfaginning 45. The 'hall' was the empty thumb of the glove of the sleeping giant Skrymir, whose snoring shook the ground. The other three items are the sort of thing you might expect a giant to drop; the glove-thumb is the specific detail in Snorri's Prose Edda.  (Legend.)

question: Thor and his party finally reach Utgard, a castle so gigantic that the front gate is barred with bars taller than a man. They cannot open it. What do they do to get inside?
answer: slip in sideways between the bars
choices: slip in sideways between the bars
climb the wall on the north side
shout until a guard opens a side door
smash the lock off with Mjolnir
context: Gylfaginning 46. The bars of Utgard's gate are so widely spaced that even Thor and his companions can walk through them sideways. It is the first hint that this castle is not what it seems: the king inside is scaling everything up to make his guests feel small.  (Legend.)

question: At the feast in Utgard, the king Utgardaloki says no one may sit at his table who cannot do some feat. Loki brags he can out-eat any man alive. Two long troughs of meat are set out, and Loki is matched against a man called Logi. Loki eats his meat clean to the bones -- but he loses. What did Logi do?
answer: ate the meat, the bones, AND the trough
choices: ate the meat, the bones, AND the trough
swallowed his trough in a single gulp
finished before Loki had taken a bite
ate a second trough while Loki chewed
context: Gylfaginning 46. Logi chews trough and all -- because Logi, as Utgardaloki reveals the next morning, is Wildfire itself, and fire consumes everything it touches.  (Legend.)

question: The farm boy Thialfi, brought along on the journey because he can outrun any human, is challenged to a footrace against a boy called Hugi on the courtyard track. Three times they run; three times Thialfi loses so badly that by the time he crosses the finish line, Hugi is already doing something. What?
context: Gylfaginning 46. Hugi finishes so fast that he has time to turn round and jog back before Thialfi arrives. Hugi turns out to be Thought itself, and nothing in any world can outrun thought.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki turns to Thor and offers a drinking test: here is a horn, and here at his court any real man drains it in one swallow, or at worst two, or three at the most shameful. Thor puts his lips to the rim and pulls, and pulls, and pulls a third time -- and the level has barely dropped. Why can Thor not empty the horn?
answer: its far end opens into the sea
choices: its far end opens into the sea
a giant kept refilling it from behind
the mead grows back as fast as he drinks
the horn has no bottom at all
context: Gylfaginning 46-47. Utgardaloki reveals the trick the next morning: the horn was set with its lower end in the ocean.  (Legend.)

question: Humiliated by the horn, Thor demands another test. Utgardaloki points to a large grey cat curled on the flagstones and tells him to lift it off the floor. Thor stoops, gets his arm under its belly, and heaves with all his god-strength. What is the most he can manage?
answer: one paw comes off the floor
choices: one paw comes off the floor
the cat sits upright but does not rise
he raises the cat above his head
the cat purrs and does not move at all
context: Gylfaginning 46. The cat merely arches its back until one paw lifts; Thor cannot get more than that. What kind of creature the cat truly was, Utgardaloki will reveal the next morning outside the castle.  (Legend.)

question: Twice beaten and furious, Thor calls for a wrestling match against any man in Utgard's hall. Utgardaloki laughs and says no one there wants to fight the god at grips -- but perhaps his old nurse will oblige. The nurse hobbles out, and the harder Thor pulls, the firmer she stands. How does the wrestling end?
answer: Thor is brought down onto one knee
choices: Thor is brought down onto one knee
Thor is thrown flat on his back
Thor breaks free and storms out
the nurse tosses him across the hall
context: Gylfaginning 46. Utgardaloki calls the match. The old nurse's name is Elli, and Utgardaloki later says of her: 'none such has ever been, and none shall be, if he becomes so old as to abide her, that she shall not cause him to fall.' What Elli truly is he saves for the morning reveal.  (Legend.)

question: The morning after the contests, Utgardaloki walks Thor's party out of the castle and finally tells the truth about what each opponent really was. The grey cat Thor had nearly lifted was not a cat at all. What was the cat?
context: Gylfaginning 47. The 'cat' was the world-serpent that circles the earth; by lifting one paw Thor had lifted the serpent's coil out of the ocean, an almost impossible feat. Fenrir will fight Odin at Ragnarok; Nidhogg gnaws at Yggdrasil's third root; Garm guards the gates of Hel.  (Legend.)

question: In the same reveal outside the castle, Utgardaloki explains that Thor's three great pulls at the drinking horn were not wasted after all -- they had done something visible to the whole world. What did Thor's three swallows actually accomplish?
answer: they created the tides in the sea
choices: they created the tides in the sea
they drained the biggest fjord dry
they hollowed the sea-caves of Norway
they froze the northern sea for winter
context: Gylfaginning 47. The lower end of the horn opened into the ocean itself; Thor's three great swallows drew sea-level down so far that the whole ocean has ebbed and flowed ever since. It is Snorri's mythic origin of the tides.  (Legend.)

question: Utgardaloki then names the old nurse who had wrestled Thor to one knee, and admits it was the most astonishing feat of the visit -- because no living thing had ever come off that well against her. What did the nurse really personify?
context: Gylfaginning 47. The nurse Elli is Old Age herself. Utgardaloki tells Thor: no one has ever been who did not fall entirely to Elli in the end, if only he lived long enough to meet her; that Thor came down onto only one knee is a marvel. Elli appears in no other extant Norse source, only in this scene.  (Legend.)

question: The reveal ends the story, and Thor, incandescent, spins on his heel and lifts Mjolnir to smash Utgardaloki where he stands. But when the hammer comes up there is nothing to swing at. What has happened to Utgardaloki, his castle, and everything in it?
answer: they have all vanished; only empty plain remains
choices: they have all vanished; only empty plain remains
they have shrunk to the size of an anthill
they have been swallowed by the earth
they have been carried off in a fog-bank
context: Gylfaginning 47. The whole illusion drops: castle, king, horn, cat, nurse, hall -- gone. Thor stands with Mjolnir raised over an empty grass plain. Utgardaloki, the reader learns, was Skrymir on the road as well; the three deep valleys Thor had left in a mountainside during the journey were where the giant had slipped a mountain between himself and Mjolnir while pretending to sleep.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse stories one god does not ride a horse at all. He crosses the sky in a chariot pulled by two GOATS whose hooves strike sparks against the clouds. He is the red-bearded thunder-god with the hammer Mjolnir. Which god drives the goat-chariot?
context: Gylfaginning 21. Thor's chariot pulled by two goats is one of Snorri's most famous images. Odin rides the eight-legged horse Sleipnir; Freyr rides the golden boar Gullinbursti (or the ship Skidbladnir); Baldr has no famous mount.  (Legend.)

question: Thor's two chariot-goats are named Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr in the Prose Edda. Both names are built on the same Old Norse word for a body part the goats are famous for. Which body part do both goat-names name?
context: Gylfaginning 21. Both names carry the element tann- ('tooth'): Tanngrisnir means 'tooth-barer' or 'snarler', Tanngnjostr means 'tooth-grinder' or 'tooth-gnasher'. The teeth of the chariot-goats are front and centre in the name-pair.  (Legend.)

question: On a long road east into Jotunheim, Thor never runs out of meat for himself and his companions, no matter how many nights they camp in the wilderness. What does he do with his two chariot-goats each evening?
answer: slaughter and eat them, then wake them at dawn
choices: slaughter and eat them, then wake them at dawn
milk them for a river of ale each night
shear their wool into a fresh cloak each night
ride them one day and eat them the next
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor slaughters the goats, roasts and eats the meat, then blesses the hides at dawn with Mjolnir. Provided every bone has been laid whole on the hide, the goats stand up alive and ready to be harnessed again.  (Legend.)

question: The trick that resurrects Thor's eaten goats depends on one strict condition being kept overnight. If this condition is broken the goats still come back to life -- but they come back damaged. What is the condition?
answer: every bone must be laid whole on the hide
choices: every bone must be laid whole on the hide
no fire may touch the hide overnight
the goats' names must not be spoken
the meat must be finished before midnight
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor gives strict instructions before dinner: eat all the meat you like, but every single bone goes intact on the hide. What comes back in the morning is exactly what was laid on the hide the night before -- damaged bones make a damaged goat.  (Legend.)

question: One night, travelling east into Jotunheim with Loki, Thor stops at a poor farmhouse. The peasants have nothing to feed the god's party, so Thor solves the problem himself by slaughtering both his own goats and roasting the meat over the family's fire. Who does he then invite to share the meal?
choices: only Loki, apart from the others
the farmer alone at his own table
no one; the meat is for him
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor turns the empty farmhouse into a feast: he brings the meat, the family brings the hearth. He gives them the same strict warning he always gives -- eat what you like, but leave every bone whole on the hide.  (Legend.)

question: The farmer's son at that supper takes his knife to one of the goat's thigh-bones before laying it back on the hide with the rest. What does the boy do to the bone?
answer: splits it lengthwise to suck the marrow
choices: splits it lengthwise to suck the marrow
gnaws a notch off the end of it
snaps it in two across his knee
carves his initials along its side
context: Gylfaginning 44. The boy takes his knife to a thigh-bone and splits it lengthwise to get at the marrow inside, then lays the split halves back on the hide with the rest of the bones. He thinks nobody will notice.  (Legend.)

question: At dawn Thor walks out to the goat-hides, raises Mjolnir, and blesses them into life. Both goats stand up alive at the wave of the hammer. But one of them is not quite whole. What is wrong with the resurrected goat?
answer: it is lame in a hind leg
choices: it is lame in a hind leg
one of its horns has snapped off
it has lost the sight in one eye
it will not answer to its name
context: Gylfaginning 44. The split thigh-bone becomes a lame hind leg. The boy's midnight snack has broken a chariot-goat for good.  (Legend.)

question: Seeing the goat step down lame, Thor's face goes so dark that Snorri says his brows dropped low over his eyes and his knuckles turned white on Mjolnir. The whole farm family throws itself to the floor and offers to pay any price to save their lives. What price does Thor take?
answer: their two children as his servants forever
choices: their two children as his servants forever
every animal in the farm's stables
the farm and the fields it stands on
seven years of the farmer's own labour
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thor forgoes destroying the family and takes their son and daughter as bond-servants. The exchange is stark: one goat-leg for two lives.  (Legend.)

question: The two farm-children Thor takes into his service that morning are a brother and a sister. The BOY -- the one who split the bone -- will run at Thor's side across the giant-country and later run a losing race at Utgardaloki's court. What is the boy's name?
context: Gylfaginning 44. Thialfi becomes Thor's fastest human servant, famed as the swiftest runner among men. Bragi is the god of poetry; Ullr is a god of the bow and skis; Vidar is Odin's silent, avenging son.  (Legend.)

question: The girl Thor takes from the same farmhouse -- the sister of the boy who broke the goat-bone -- also enters the god's service that morning, and travels with the party into Jotunheim. What is the sister's name?
context: Gylfaginning 44. Roskva is named in the Prose Edda alongside her brother as the second of the two children given to Thor. Sif is Thor's own wife (of golden hair); Idunn keeps the apples of youth for the Aesir; Skadi is the giantess who married Njord after her father's death.  (Legend.)

question: The Prose Edda gives both of Thor's goats names built on the same tooth-word (tann-). Tanngnjostr means 'tooth-grinder'. What does the other name, Tanngrisnir, mean?
context: Gylfaginning 21. Tanngrisnir translates as 'tooth-barer' or 'snarler'; Tanngnjostr as 'tooth-grinder' or 'tooth-gnasher'. Both names put the goats' teeth front and centre, which fits creatures that pull the thunder-god's chariot through the sky.  (Legend.)

question: The same boy who split the goat-bone at the farmhouse later runs a footrace at Utgardaloki's court and is beaten so badly by an opponent called Hugi that the loss becomes legendary. What does Hugi secretly turn out to be, once Utgardaloki lifts the illusion?
context: Gylfaginning 46-47. Hugi is the personification of Thought; nothing in any world can outrun thought, and Thialfi's defeat is no shame. In the same reveal Loki's eating opponent Logi is unmasked as Wildfire, and the horn Thor could not drain has its far end in the sea.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse poem Thrymskvida, the thunder-god of the Aesir wakes one morning, gropes for the weapon he has always kept beside him, and finds only empty air. He shakes his beard so hard in fury that all Asgard hears it, and calls at once for Loki. What weapon has been stolen from the sleeping god?
context: Thrymskvida 1-2: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone. Gungnir is Odin's spear. Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Hervarar Saga. Gram is the sword Sigurd will one day reforge from his father's broken blade to kill Fafnir.  (Legend.)

question: Loki agrees to help Thor find the missing hammer, and goes to the goddess Freyja to borrow one of her treasures for the trip to Jotunheim. What does Loki borrow from Freyja to reach the land of the giants?
context: Thrymskvida 3-5: Freyja lends Loki her feather-cloak (fjadrhamr) and he flies in falcon shape to Jotunheim. All four items belong to Freyja -- her boar Hildisvini, her chariot drawn by cats, and her dwarf-forged necklace Brisingamen -- but Thrymskvida specifically names the falcon-cloak as what Loki borrows.  (Legend.)

question: The giant tells Loki that he will only give Mjolnir back if the Aesir send him Freyja as his bride. Meanwhile the hammer itself is safe -- Thrym has buried it far under the earth, deep enough that no god can just dig it up. How deep does the poem say Thrym buried Mjolnir?
context: Thrymskvida 8: Thrym boasts that Mjolnir is buried eight leagues (about eight miles) below the ground. The other depths are the sort of round numbers a listener might guess; the poem is exact about eight.  (Legend.)

question: Since Freyja will not go, the gods hold an assembly to plan another way. One of the Aesir proposes the plan that will actually work: dress Thor himself in a bride's clothes and send HIM to Jotunheim to marry Thrym. Which of the Aesir is said in Thrymskvida to propose the disguise?
context: Thrymskvida 15: Heimdall the watchman speaks up with the plan to disguise Thor. Odin is silent in this poem. Bragi is the god of poetry. Tyr will lose his hand in Fenrir's mouth. Heimdall alone proposes the bridal disguise.  (Legend.)

question: At the wedding-feast in Thrym's hall the veiled bride sits down at the table and, before anyone else has taken a bite, demolishes the food set for the whole wedding-party. The poet lists three separate things the bride eats and drinks alone -- a whole ox, a stack of salmon, and every vat of mead the giants can bring. How many salmon does the poem say the bride swallowed at the feast?
context: Thrymskvida 24: the bride ate one ox and eight salmon and all the dainties meant for the women, and drained three vats of mead. The poet loves the number eight in Thrymskvida -- eight leagues to the buried hammer earlier, eight salmon on the plate here.  (Legend.)

question: Thrym stares in astonishment at how much food the bride has just eaten. The 'maidservant' at the bride's side leans in and whispers a smooth lie in Thrym's ear to explain the appetite. What does Loki tell Thrym is the reason for the bride's hunger?
answer: she has fasted eight nights for eagerness
choices: she has fasted eight nights for eagerness
she has traveled eight days without food
brides of her people always eat before the vows
she is carrying an unborn heir and eats for two
context: Thrymskvida 26: Loki tells Thrym that Freyja was so eager for Jotunheim that she has not eaten for eight nights. The number matches Thrym's earlier boast that the hammer is buried eight leagues down; the poet loves the number eight in this poem.  (Legend.)

question: Thrym leans in for the wedding kiss and reaches to lift the bridal veil to see the face beneath. He gets one look and springs back the length of the hall in terror. What did Thrym see under the veil that terrified him?
context: Thrymskvida 27-28: Thrym recoils from Freyja's terrible eyes, which burn like fire. Loki covers again -- 'she has not slept for eight nights either, in her longing for Jotunheim.' The specific tell that gives Thor away in Thrym's own hall is his EYES, not his beard or his hands.  (Legend.)

question: In the old Cornish romance, a young knight of Lyonesse is sent by his uncle the King of Cornwall to sail to Ireland and bring back the Irish princess Iseult the Fair as a bride -- not for himself, but for his uncle. What is this young knight's name?
context: The Tristan legend survives from Beroul (c.1170) and Thomas of Britain (c.1175). Lancelot is Arthur's champion and Guinevere's lover in Chretien and Malory. Gawain is Arthur's nephew. Perceval is the Grail knight. Only Tristan sails to Ireland for a bride.

question: The King of Cornwall who sends Tristan to Ireland to fetch a bride is Tristan's own uncle -- Tristan is his nephew and his champion. In the legend the whole tragedy turns on the fact that Tristan owes this king his loyalty. What is the king's name?
context: King Mark of Cornwall, Tristan's uncle, is the wronged husband in the romance. Arthur is Britain's high king in the parallel cycle. Uther is Arthur's father, generations earlier. Ryence is a rival king in Malory's early books.  (Legend.)

question: Iseult's mother the Queen of Ireland brews something in a flask of gold on the day the ship sails and gives it to Iseult's maid Brangaine, telling her to serve it to the bride and groom on their wedding night in Cornwall. What is in the flask?
context: The queen's flask is a love potion meant for King Mark and his bride on their wedding night, so they will love one another forever. Sleeping draughts, salves and truth-serums are stock medieval story-devices but not what the queen sends.  (Legend.)

question: On the ship carrying Iseult from Ireland to Cornwall the summer weather is hot and the two young passengers are thirsty. Left alone below decks, they find the golden flask Brangaine has been guarding, uncap it, and drink from it together. What do they think they are drinking?
context: Tristan and Iseult mistake the flask for wine, share a cup, and are bound in love from that moment. Water, medicine and ale do not appear -- the mistake in the story is specifically wine.  (Legend.)

question: In Beroul's Anglo-Norman verse (c.1170) the potion does its work but its magic runs out after a set span. Thomas of Britain's later, courtly version says the potion binds Tristan and Iseult forever. In Beroul, how long do the potion's effects last before wearing off?
context: Beroul (c.1170) sets the potion's power at three years, after which the lovers can at last consider parting. Thomas of Britain and the courtly branch make the love last a lifetime. One hundred days, seven winters and a single moon are not attested spans.  (Legend.)

question: Iseult marries King Mark of Cornwall as arranged, but the potion holds; she and Tristan meet in secret again and again, and at last are discovered. To escape Mark's court the lovers flee together into a great forest and live rough there, sleeping in bowers of tree-boughs and eating venison Tristan hunts. What is this forest called?
context: The Forest of Morois is where Tristan and Iseult live in exile in Beroul and later versions. Broceliande is Merlin's enchanted wood in the Arthurian cycle. The Forest Perilous is a name for various dangerous woods. Camelot is a court, not a forest.  (Legend.)

question: Mark chooses to spare the sleeping lovers, but he leaves the hut with a small quiet signal that he was there. He does not touch either of them; he does not shout the camp awake. In Beroul, what does King Mark do before he slips back out into the trees?
answer: he swaps his own sword for Tristan's on the bed
choices: he swaps his own sword for Tristan's on the bed
he cuts a lock from Iseult's hair
he sets his crown at Tristan's feet
he stabs the hut's roof with an arrow
context: Beroul c.1170: Mark exchanges his own sword for Tristan's and his ring for Iseult's, so when they wake they will know he came, saw, and forbore. The lock of hair, the laid-down crown and the pierced roof do not appear in the passage.  (Legend.)

question: Years later, exiled from Cornwall, Tristan settles in Brittany and marries a second princess -- but he never loves her, and never forgets Iseult the Fair. The second wife shares Iseult the Fair's first name but carries a different epithet the legend never lets you forget. What is she called?
context: Iseult of the White Hands (Isolde of Brittany) marries Tristan in the Brittany section of Thomas of Britain and Malory Book XII. The Green Isle, Silent, and Lyonesse epithets are not attached to this second Iseult.  (Legend.)

question: Wounded and dying in Brittany, Tristan sends a messenger by ship for the ONLY healer who can save him -- Iseult the Fair, back in Cornwall. He tells the crew to raise sails of one colour on the return trip if she is coming, and sails of a different colour if she has refused him. Which colours does Tristan set for the two signals?
answer: white for yes, black for no
choices: white for yes, black for no
gold for yes, grey for no
red for yes, blue for no
green for yes, black for no
context: Thomas of Britain c.1175: white sails if Iseult the Fair comes, black sails if she refuses. This same white/black-sails device is directly borrowed from the Greek myth of Theseus's father Aegeus.  (Legend.)

question: The ship comes back over the water and Iseult the Fair is aboard, so the sails on the mast are white. Tristan's wife lies to him about the sails, telling him they are black. In the legend Tristan hears her words and, before Iseult the Fair can even step onto shore, he does one thing and one thing only. What does the dying Tristan do?
answer: he dies of grief on the spot
choices: he dies of grief on the spot
he calls for a priest and takes the sacrament
he curses his wife with his last breath
he crawls to the harbour to see for himself
context: Thomas of Britain c.1175: Tristan hears the lie and dies at once of grief; Iseult the Fair steps off the ship, finds him already dead, lies down beside him and dies of grief also. Sacrament, curse and crawl-to-harbour appear in no early version.  (Legend.)

question: The white-sail / black-sail signal Tristan sets from his sickbed did not begin with him. Centuries earlier a Greek hero sailed off to kill a monster and promised his old father he would change his ship's sails from black to white on the return if he lived -- forgot, kept the black sails up, and his watching father, seeing them, threw himself off the cliff. Which Greek hero's story is this?
context: Theseus sailed from Athens to Crete to kill the Minotaur; his father Aegeus, watching from the cliff, saw the black sails still up and drowned himself in the sea now called the Aegean. Perseus, Jason and Bellerophon are Greek heroes but not the sail story.  (Legend.)

question: In the Norse binding of the wolf Fenrir, one god steps forward and lays his hand in the wolf's jaws as a pledge of good faith, and loses it when the trick is sprung. Which god?
context: Snorri's Gylfaginning 34 names Tyr as the only god brave enough to make the pledge. When Fenrir realised the ribbon Gleipnir would not break, he bit off Tyr's right hand. Baldr is Odin's shining son killed by mistletoe; Bragi is the god of poetry; Forseti is the god of justice at Glitnir.  (Legend.)

question: The English weekday Tuesday takes its name from an Anglo-Saxon god. The Anglo-Saxon god behind Tuesday is the same figure the Norse called Tyr. What was his Anglo-Saxon name?
context: Old English Tiwesdaeg means Tiw's Day, later worn down to Tuesday. Woden is the Anglo-Saxon Odin (Wednesday). Thunor is Thor (Thursday). Frige is Frigg (Friday).

question: Snorri names a second Ragnarok pair who kill each other on the same field of Vigrid, apart from Tyr and Garmr. Which pair?
context: Snorri writes in Gylfaginning 51: Loki has battle with Heimdall, and each is the other's slayer. Heimdallr is the watchman of Bifrost with the Gjallarhorn; the two had an old grudge from the fight over Freyja's necklace. Thor's Ragnarok fight is with Jormungandr the world serpent; Odin's is with Fenrir the wolf; Vidar avenges Odin by killing Fenrir, and himself survives to see the new world.  (Legend.)

question: The Norse binding of Fenrir depended on a ribbon the dwarves of Nidavellir made from six impossible things: the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, the spit of a bird, the beard of a woman, and one more. What was the sixth?
answer: the sound of a cat's footsteps
choices: the sound of a cat's footsteps
context: Snorri's Gylfaginning 34 lists all six ingredients. The ribbon, called Gleipnir, was as soft as silk yet impossible to break. It was this ribbon Fenrir would not accept until Tyr laid his hand in the wolf's mouth as pledge.  (Legend.)

question: Long before Arthur is born, a king of Britain sits at a great banquet at his court and sees the beautiful wife of one of his own dukes. He falls violently in love with her on the spot -- and the whole legend of Arthur begins because of it. What is this king's name?
context: Malory Book I ch.1-2 and Geoffrey of Monmouth Historia Book VIII: Uther Pendragon is Arthur's father. Aurelius Ambrosius is Uther's elder brother who ruled before him. Vortigern is the earlier king who brought the Saxons in. Cadwallader is a much later Welsh king. Only Uther falls for Igraine.  (Legend.)

question: The woman King Uther Pendragon loves at the banquet is not free -- she is the wife of Gorlois, one of his own dukes. In the legend she is remembered as the mother of Arthur. What is her name?
context: Igraine (Igerna in Geoffrey) is Arthur's mother, wife of Gorlois of Cornwall. Guinevere is Arthur's own queen a generation later. Morgan le Fay is Igraine's daughter and Arthur's half-sister. Nimue is the enchantress who traps Merlin. Only Igraine is Arthur's mother.  (Legend.)

question: When Igraine's husband sees how the king looks at her, he does not stay at court to argue. He carries her away from the banquet that very night and shuts her up in his safest castle -- a stronghold on a great crag cut off from the mainland by sea on almost every side. What is this fortress called?
context: Tintagel on the Cornish coast is Gorlois's stronghold in Geoffrey Historia VIII.19 and in Malory; it is also a real 5th-6th c. archaeological site. Camelot is Arthur's own court city, later. Camlann is the field of Arthur's last battle. Astolat is the town of Elaine the Lily Maid.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin agrees to help Uther reach Igraine at Tintagel -- but sets a hard price. Merlin does not want gold, or land, or a favour at court. He wants ONE thing that will belong to Uther after that night, and Uther must swear an oath on it before Merlin will act. What does Merlin demand?
answer: the child Uther will father that night
choices: the child Uther will father that night
the crown itself when Uther is dead
context: Malory Book I ch.2: Merlin makes Uther swear that the child conceived that night shall be given to Merlin to be raised as he sees fit -- and that child is Arthur. The crown, Gorlois's head, and Tintagel are all things Uther could have offered but not what Merlin asks.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin does not stop at disguising the king. He also disguises the two knights who ride at Uther's side that night, changing them into the likenesses of Duke Gorlois's own two chief companions so the guards will not question them either. In Malory, one of these two changed knights is Sir Ulfius. Merlin himself takes the shape of the OTHER knight. Whose likeness does Merlin wear?
context: Malory Book I ch.2: Sir Ulfius rides as Sir Jordanus, and Merlin himself takes the shape of Sir Brastias, Gorlois's chief knight. Bedivere, Kay and Lucan are famous later Round Table knights but do not appear in the Tintagel-night trick.  (Legend.)

question: The disguise works: the guards at Tintagel open the gate, and the king in Gorlois's shape rides in and is welcomed by Igraine as her own husband home from war. That same night, miles away at his other castle of Dimilioc, the real Duke Gorlois leads a sortie out against the besieging army and is killed in the fighting. Word of his death does not reach Igraine until when?
context: Geoffrey Historia VIII.19: Gorlois falls in his sortie the same night; the messengers reach Tintagel at dawn. That is when Igraine begins to wonder how the man in her bed could have been her husband, since Gorlois was already dead. The other timings would collapse the whole story.  (Legend.)

question: Merlin holds Uther to his oath. When the baby Arthur is born, the mage carries him out of Tintagel by a secret postern and delivers him to a trusted knight and his wife, to be raised as their own son in secret and never told he is a king's child. In Malory, what is the name of the knight who becomes Arthur's foster-father?
context: Malory Book I ch.3: Arthur is delivered by Merlin to Sir Ector to be raised alongside Ector's own son Kay. Ulfius and Brastias were the two knights who rode with Uther and Merlin the disguise-night. Kay is Ector's son, Arthur's foster-brother, not the foster-father.  (Legend.)

question: The Tintagel shape-change story was first written down around 1136 by Geoffrey of Monmouth, and for centuries scholars dismissed the crag-castle as pure legend -- no real king ever held it. Then modern archaeologists dug the Tintagel headland and found the sub-Roman layer was NOT empty. They pulled out something that showed the site had been a high-status stronghold in the very century Uther and Arthur are set. What did they find in the dirt?
choices: a stone throne carved with a dragon
a hoard of Saxon silver coins
context: Excavations on the Tintagel headland uncovered large quantities of 5th-6th century imported pottery from the eastern Mediterranean -- amphorae for wine and oil, fine tablewares -- the sort of luxury goods only a high-status stronghold could pull in that far west. No Roman eagle, no dragon throne, no Saxon hoard have been found there. Geoffrey's Historia Regum Britanniae (c.1136) invented the shape-change scene, but he set it on a site that really was a big deal in the sub-Roman age.

question: Jesus, his mother Mary, and his disciples are guests at a village wedding in Galilee. Which small Galilean village does John's gospel name as the setting for this feast?
context: John 2:1-2. Nazareth is where Jesus grew up; Capernaum becomes his ministry base; Bethsaida is Peter and Andrew's hometown. The wedding is at Cana, a small village whose exact site scholars still debate.

question: At the wedding in Cana of Galilee, partway through the feast a small crisis strikes. Which practical thing runs out that Mary quietly points out to Jesus?
context: John 2:3. A village feast running dry of wine would have shamed the host family for a generation; Mary flags it to Jesus without ceremony.

question: When Mary tells Jesus the wine has run out at the wedding, he answers her with a question that begins 'Woman, what have I to do with thee?' and adds one more short line. What does he say?
answer: Mine hour is not yet come
choices: Mine hour is not yet come
context: John 2:4, King James Version. In John's gospel Jesus repeatedly puts off his 'hour' until the Passion; here he seems to push back, then acts anyway.

question: After Jesus tells her his hour has not yet come, Mary does not argue. Instead she turns to the servants at the wedding and gives them one short instruction. What does she tell them?
answer: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it
choices: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it
Fetch the master of the feast
Send for more from the village
context: John 2:5, King James Version. These are Mary's last recorded words in any gospel -- a full stop of trust before the first miracle.

question: Jesus points the servants at a set of six large jars standing nearby, set out for a Jewish household rite. What are those jars made of?
context: John 2:6. Under Jewish purification custom, stone vessels were considered easier to keep ritually clean than clay ones, so the household kept large stone jars ready for hand-washing and vessel-washing at feasts.

question: John says each of the six great jars at the wedding holds 'two or three firkins apiece' -- meaning roughly how much water each?
context: John 2:6. A firkin was about nine to ten gallons; six jars at the top end works out to well over a hundred and fifty gallons of wine for a village party -- an absurd, superabundant amount.

question: The servants fill the six great jars with water and draw some out. Jesus tells them to carry a cup to one particular person at the wedding first, to taste. Whom does he send it to?
context: John 2:8. The 'governor of the feast' was a kind of head steward who supervised the meal and its wine. He tastes the cup without any idea where it came from -- only the servants who drew it know.

question: The master of the feast tastes the cup, not knowing where the drink has come from. He calls the bridegroom over and pays him a compliment. What is the punchline of what he says?
answer: Thou hast kept the good wine until now
choices: Thou hast kept the good wine until now
Thou hast poured out the wine of gladness
A finer vintage I have not tasted in Galilee
This wine shames the vineyards of Judah
context: John 2:10, King James Version. The custom, he says, is to serve the good wine first and the cheap wine after the guests are past noticing -- the bridegroom, he thinks, has flipped the order. The bridegroom has done nothing at all. The other lines here are invented parallels, not scripture.

question: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has grown old. Fifty years after tearing off Grendel's arm in the Danish mead-hall Heorot, Beowulf has been the king of the Geats for a long time, ruling in peace. Then trouble comes to his own land -- a runaway slave stumbles into a barrow-mound on a headland and steals one bright thing from a hoard guarded by a sleeping monster. What does the slave steal from the hoard?
context: Beowulf 2214-2231. The fleeing slave picks up a single golden cup from the pile and creeps back out of the mound. When the monster wakes and counts his gold and finds the cup gone, he goes berserk. Every other detail is a real Anglo-Saxon treasure motif -- helmets, rings, and daggers all appear elsewhere in the poem -- but the specific stolen item is the cup.  (Legend.)

question: The monster in the barrow whose hoard was robbed of the golden cup wakes up furious. That very night he uncoils, flies out over the countryside of Geatland breathing fire, and burns down one specific building to the ground. What does the dragon burn down that first night?
context: Beowulf 2302-2323. The dragon burns Beowulf's own royal hall to the ground -- the poet marks it as the personal insult that drives Beowulf, now old, to arm one last time and ride out. The watchtower, the ships, and the forge all fit Migration-era Geatland, but the dragon's first burning is the king's hall.  (Legend.)

question: Beowulf rides to the barrow with a war-band. The poet names the count exactly, so the coming shame will land hard when most of them break. How many thanes does Beowulf take with him to the mound to fight the dragon?
context: Beowulf 2401-2405. He takes eleven thanes with him -- twelve fighters counting the king himself. The number is set up carefully so that the poet can later tell you EXACTLY how many run (ten) and exactly how many stay (one), and the arithmetic is the shame. Seven, thirteen, and nine are all common war-band counts in Old English and Norse verse, but this specific ride to the mound is eleven.  (Legend.)

question: At the barrow, Beowulf shouts a war-cry down into the mouth of the mound and the dragon comes rushing out breathing fire. Beowulf swings his old sword against the dragon's scaled head -- but the sword lets him down. In one of Beowulf's most-quoted lines, 'the blade failed him in the fight; his old iron was not fated to help him.' What is the name of Beowulf's own sword in the dragon-fight?
context: Beowulf 2679-2687. Naegling is Beowulf's own famous blade -- and it shatters in his grip when it bites too shallow on the dragon's scales. Hrunting was Unferth's sword, which had failed Beowulf earlier against Grendel's mother in the mere; the giant-forged wall-sword in that mere-cave was unnamed and melted in the monster's blood. Nothung and Balmung are the German sword-names from Wagner's Ring cycle and the Nibelungenlied for Sigurd's / Siegfried's sword, not Beowulf's.  (Legend.)

question: Once Beowulf's sword shatters, the dragon closes in and does one very specific thing that will kill the old king in the end. What does the dragon do?
answer: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
choices: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
lifts him into the air by the shield
context: Beowulf 2688-2705. The dragon sinks his fangs into Beowulf's neck -- and along with the bite comes the venom that will kill the king even after the dragon is dead. Everything else the dragon does in the poem (breathing fire, coiling on the hoard, flying with wings) is real, but the specific killing wound is the fanged bite to the throat.  (Legend.)

question: Of the eleven thanes Beowulf brought, ten turn and run into the woods when the flame comes. Only ONE thane -- a young kinsman of Beowulf who has never fought a battle before this day -- runs INTO the fire beside his falling king and helps him kill the dragon. What is the loyal thane's name?
context: Beowulf 2596-2601. Wiglaf, son of Weohstan, of the Waegmunding clan and Beowulf's own kinsman, is the one thane who does not flee. His Old English name means 'battle-remnant' or 'battle-heir' -- the one who stays behind after the others are gone. Hondscioh was the Geat Grendel devoured first in Heorot fifty years earlier; Aeschere was Hrothgar's counsellor, killed by Grendel's mother; Hygelac was Beowulf's own late king back in Geatland. The one who stays with Beowulf against the dragon is Wiglaf.  (Legend.)

question: Wiglaf drives his sword up into the dragon's softer lower body where the scales are thin, and the flames drop. Then Beowulf himself, dying from the throat-wound but still on his feet, draws a shorter weapon from his belt and finishes the dragon in one specific way. What does Beowulf do with his belt-knife?
answer: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
choices: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
drives it through the dragon's eye
buries it in the dragon's tongue
wedges it in the dragon's jaws
context: Beowulf 2699-2705. With Wiglaf's sword-thrust already inside the dragon, Beowulf pulls his war-knife and cuts the beast in two at the belly. The dragon dies between them. The eye-thrust belongs to Odysseus and Polyphemus in the Greek Odyssey; the tongue and the jaws are common dragon-slaying motifs but not Beowulf's move. The specific finish is the knife across the middle.  (Legend.)

question: Dying beside the dead dragon, Beowulf gives Wiglaf one specific request before the venom finishes him. What does the dying Beowulf ask Wiglaf to do?
answer: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
choices: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
raise a mound high on the headland
carry his ring-mail back to the queen
send word to the ten who fled
context: Beowulf 2743-2820. The old king asks Wiglaf to go into the barrow and bring out some of the dragon's hoarded gold so he can look on the treasure he won for his people before he dies. Wiglaf does it -- he carries out cups and standards and lays them at his king's feet, and Beowulf sees the gold and gives thanks and dies. The headland-mound is arranged by the Geats LATER, after his death; the ring-mail stays with the body; the ten cowards are dealt with by Wiglaf, not by Beowulf.  (Legend.)

question: Around Beowulf's finished burial-mound at Hronesnaess, a picked band of warriors -- 'brave in battle, sons of noblemen' -- ride round and round the mound singing dirges and reciting his praises. The poet gives their exact number. How many horsemen ride around the mound?
context: Beowulf 3169-3177. Twelve of the best Geat warriors ride round the mound, voicing their grief and speaking Beowulf's deeds aloud so the sound would rise. The circling-praise image is one of the most-copied endings in Old English studies. Seven, three, and twenty-four all appear in other Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse ceremonies but the number of horsemen at this specific mound is twelve.  (Legend.)

question: The very last word of the Beowulf poem -- lofgeornost -- is one of the most-quoted words in all of Old English literature. The full closing line calls Beowulf the mildest of the world's kings, the gentlest, the kindest to his people, and one thing more. The word lofgeornost means 'keenest for' what?
context: Beowulf 3182: 'lofgeornost' -- Old English lof ('praise, fame') + geornost ('most eager'). The line says Beowulf was 'of the world's kings the mildest of men and gentlest, kindest to his people, and keenest for praise.' Scholars still argue whether that final word is admiring (a hero's rightful hunger for lasting fame) or a small pointed criticism (a king who cared what people said of him too much); either way, praise is what the last word names, not gold or peace or wisdom.

question: Northumbria's royal household was itself split between the two customs: King Oswiu kept the Celtic date and his queen Eanfled kept the Roman date. Bede records what awkward result this produced in the same palace during the same weeks?
answer: The king feasted Easter while the queen still fasted Lent
choices: The king feasted Easter while the queen still fasted Lent
The king's household ate meat while the queen's household kept Lent fast
The queen's chaplain refused to share the vigil table with the king's
The two royal chapels lit the paschal candle a week apart
context: King Oswiu of Northumbria kept the Ionan Easter; his queen Eanfled, raised in Kent, kept the Roman date. Bede reports (Historia Ecclesiastica III.25) that in some years one royal faction was celebrating Easter while the other was still fasting Lent. The other three household frictions are the kind of thing a divided-calendar palace would face, but Bede's specific complaint is the feast-and-fast overlap. This mismatch is what pushed Oswiu to call the synod.

question: In 664 King Oswiu called a great church meeting to settle the Easter question. It was held on the North Sea cliffs at a double monastery run by a powerful Anglo-Saxon abbess who personally preferred the Celtic side but still hosted the debate. Who was that abbess?
context: The Synod of Whitby (664) was held at Streanaeshalch, Hilda's double monastery of monks and nuns. Hilda favored the Ionan tradition but presided as host. Etheldreda founded Ely; Aebbe ruled the double monastery at Coldingham; Hildelith later led Barking. All four are real 7th-century English abbesses -- only Hilda hosted Whitby.

question: At the meeting on the cliffs the Celtic side was argued by the bishop of Lindisfarne, an Irish monk who cited the tradition of Saint Columba and John the Evangelist. Who spoke for the Celtic Easter?
context: Colman, bishop of Lindisfarne, defended the Ionan 84-year Easter cycle. Cedd was present as a translator between Old English and Irish. Agilbert was the Frankish bishop on the Roman side. Cuthbert, the great Lindisfarne saint, came later and accepted the Roman decision.

question: Colman lost the Whitby debate but refused to change his practice. Rather than accept the Roman date and the Roman tonsure, he took his Irish monks and left the Northumbrian coast for good. What did he take with him as he sailed away?
answer: Some of the relics of Aidan
choices: Some of the relics of Aidan
The abbey's copy of the four Gospels
context: Bede reports that Colman carried away some of the relics of Aidan (his predecessor and founder of Lindisfarne) when he withdrew to Iona after 664. The other three items are plausible-sounding but not what Bede records.

question: In the Robin Hood ballads, Robin's outlaw band living in the forest with him has a famous nickname. What are they called together?
context: 'Merry Men' is the traditional name for Robin Hood's outlaw band. The earliest ballads name a core of them individually: Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son. Source: Wikipedia, Merry Men.  (Legend.)

question: When Robin Hood tries to cross a narrow log-bridge over a stream in Sherwood, a giant of a man refuses to step aside; the two fight with quarterstaves and Robin ends up in the water. Which of the Merry Men has just beaten Robin at his own game?
context: The log-bridge fight is the traditional first-meeting between Robin and Little John: Little John's staff knocks Robin into the stream, and the giant then joins the band. The earliest ballads name Robin's core companions as Little John, Will Scarlet, and Much the Miller's Son; later broadsides bring in Alan-a-Dale. Source: Wikipedia, Merry Men.  (Legend.)

question: One of Robin Hood's Merry Men in the earliest ballads is so small that a later ballad, Robin Hood and Queen Katherine, calls him 'Midge' instead of his usual name. Which of Robin's outlaws is this small companion?
context: Much the Miller's Son is one of Robin's three earliest ballad-companions (with Little John and Will Scarlet). In Robin Hood and Queen Katherine he is called Midge -- a name that suggests small stature and hints that Much was traditionally imagined as short. Source: Wikipedia, Much the Miller's Son.  (Legend.)

question: The Merry Men are famous in the ballads for wearing one shared woolen cloth, dyed in an English city that gave the color its name. Which color?
context: Lincoln green is the traditional woolen dye of the Merry Men, associated with the city of Lincoln. One member of the band is the exception -- he stands out in bright cloth of a different color, which is why he has the nickname he does. Source: Wikipedia, Will Scarlet.  (Legend.)

question: In the ballad Robin Hood and Allen a Dale, a young man is weeping under an oak in Sherwood. He tells Robin that his beloved is being forced to marry a rich old knight in the morning. What is the young man's trade?
context: Alan-a-Dale is a wandering minstrel who joins the Merry Men in Child 138. His beloved is being forced by her father to marry an old knight for money. Alan carries a lute or harp, which lets Robin's later disguise as a harper work. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and Allan-a-Dale.  (Legend.)

question: On the wedding morning in Robin Hood and Allen a Dale, Robin walks into the church dressed as a harper and stops the marriage. The bishop refuses to marry Alan and his sweetheart, saying consent must be asked. Robin puts the bishop's cloak on one of his outlaws, who asks the consent question over and over until it counts. Which outlaw takes the bishop's place?
context: In Child 138 Robin robes Little John in the bishop's cloak; Little John asks the consent question seven times (in mockery of the bishop's 'three times' rule) and marries Alan-a-Dale to his sweetheart on the spot. Source: Wikipedia, Robin Hood and Allan-a-Dale.  (Legend.)

question: Friar Tuck is one of the most beloved Merry Men in the modern imagination, but he is not present in the earliest fifteenth-century ballads at all. When he first shows up in the Robin Hood story, he comes in through a very different kind of performance. Which one?
context: Friar Tuck appears in a c.1475 play, Robyn Hod and the Shryff off Notyngham, and again in a 1560 May-games play. He probably comes into the Robin Hood tradition through the jovial-friar figure of English May-games and morris dances, not through the earliest ballads. Maid Marian arrives the same way, from the French Jeu de Robin et Marion and English May Day festivities. Source: Wikipedia, Friar Tuck.  (Legend.)

question: In the first quarter of the 1200s a Bavarian knight-poet sat down to retell, in Middle High German, an unfinished French Grail-poem by Chretien de Troyes. He turned it into an epic of about 25,000 rhymed lines that became the greatest German Arthurian romance. What was this Bavarian poet's name?
context: Wolfram von Eschenbach was a Bavarian knight who wrote around 1200-1210. Hartmann von Aue wrote Erec and Iwein; Gottfried von Strassburg wrote Tristan; Walther von der Vogelweide is the great Middle High German lyric poet. All four are real 13th-century German poets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.

question: Wolfram von Eschenbach's huge Middle High German epic follows one young Arthurian knight, born to a father named Gahmuret and a mother named Herzeloyde ('heart's sorrow'), from birth all the way to the kingship of the Grail. What is this hero's name, and the name of Wolfram's poem?
context: Parzival is Wolfram's version of the French hero Perceval. Erec and Iwein are the two Arthurian heroes Hartmann von Aue wrote about; Tristan is the hero of Gottfried von Strassburg's rival epic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.  (Legend.)

question: In Wolfram's Parzival the Grail-stone did not originate on earth. According to the hermit Trevrizent, who tells Parzival the true story, the stone was carried down out of heaven by a specific company of angels. Which angels were those?
answer: the ones who stayed neutral in Lucifer's war
choices: the ones who stayed neutral in Lucifer's war
the guardians of Eden's eastern gate
the seraphim around the throne of God
context: Wolfram's Grail is guarded by NEUTRAL angels -- a bold and strange invention, since medieval theology usually had NO neutral angels (Dante later flatly rejected the idea in Inferno III). It is one of the reasons Wolfram's poem was read as touched by heresy for centuries afterwards. Michael's host, the cherubim at Eden's gate (Genesis 3:24), and the seraphim around the throne (Isaiah 6) are all real biblical angelic groups, but none of them brought down the Grail in Wolfram. Source: premieretat.com/wolframs-parzival-the-esoteric-metaphysics-of-the-grail.  (Legend.)

question: Wolfram's Grail-stone gives whoever LOOKS on it whatever food and drink they most desire, and preserves their youth. But once a year a small white bird descends from heaven and lays a Communion wafer upon the stone, and that wafer renews its power. On what day of the year does this happen?
context: Good Friday is the day the church remembers the Crucifixion, and Wolfram places the wafer-descent there for that reason. Easter Sunday, Christmas Eve, and Pentecost are all major days of the church year and would be natural guesses, but Wolfram specifies Good Friday. The bird is a white dove. Source: swordandcup.substack.com/p/the-grails-secret-origin-and-sacred.  (Legend.)

question: The Grail-stone has a further miraculous property Wolfram invents that nothing in the French tradition has: from time to time writing appears on it by itself, and once someone has read the writing, it fades away. What is the writing?
answer: the names of new Grail Knights
choices: the names of new Grail Knights
the sins of the dying king
the year of the world's ending
the words of a hidden prayer
context: Whenever a new knight is to be summoned to serve the Grail, his name appears on the stone; once someone has read it, the writing vanishes. The stone effectively RECRUITS its own knights. Robert Eisler and other 20th-century scholars pointed to the parallel with the alchemists' philosopher's stone; others compare it to the Book of Life in Revelation. Source: premieretat.com/wolframs-parzival-the-esoteric-metaphysics-of-the-grail.  (Legend.)

question: Late in Wolfram's poem, Parzival at last returns to the Grail Castle and stands before the wounded Grail-King, his own uncle Anfortas. This time, unlike his first failed visit, he asks a single question -- and the question itself heals Anfortas and makes Parzival the new Grail-King. What does Parzival ask?
context: Compassion is the whole moral engine of Wolfram's version: the young Parzival's first failure was that, taught to be a courteous knight, he stayed silent about his host's obvious pain. Years later he finally asks the compassionate question -- and that is what wins the Grail. The Middle High German is 'oeheim, waz wirret dier?' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parzival.  (Legend.)

question: Wolfram opens his Parzival with a startling backstory the French tradition never had: the hero's father Gahmuret went east and married the black African queen Belacane of Zazamanc. Their son -- Parzival's older half-brother -- is born with skin patched black and white, said to look like a magpie or a written-on parchment. What is this half-brother's name?
context: Feirefiz means 'piebald son' (from Old French 'vaire fiz'). He is one of the most striking figures in medieval European literature -- a black-and-white African-European Grail-knight, presented by Wolfram with full dignity. Gawan is Wolfram's version of the Arthurian Gawain; Anfortas is the wounded Grail King; Trevrizent is Parzival's hermit uncle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feirefiz.  (Legend.)

question: In the closing pages of Parzival, Feirefiz is baptised, marries the Grail-bearer Repanse de Schoye, and takes her east. Wolfram then makes their son the founder of a famous half-legendary Christian kingdom in the far East, beyond the Muslim world -- a kingdom medieval Europe spent centuries trying to find. Who is Feirefiz's son said to be?
context: Prester John was a real medieval legend -- letters purporting to be from a great Christian king in India or Ethiopia circulated across Europe from the 1160s onward, and expeditions were actually sent to find him. Wolfram folds that legend into the Grail-story, tying the Grail lineage to the far East. Charlemagne, Saladin, and Baldwin of Jerusalem are real historical rulers of the crusading era, not sons of Feirefiz. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feirefiz.

question: At the centre of the Norse cosmos stands a single enormous tree whose branches spread above all the worlds and whose roots reach down to three separate wells. Voluspa calls it 'a tall tree, showered with shining loam.' What is the name of this world-tree?
context: Voluspa 19; Gylfaginning 15-16. Yggdrasil is the axis of the nine worlds. Laeradr is the tree said to stand over Valhalla (the one Heidrun the goat eats from); Mimameid ('Mimi's tree') is another mythic tree named in Fjolsvinnsmal; Barnstokkr is the great oak-trunk growing through King Volsung's hall in the Volsunga saga. All four are real named trees in Norse tradition -- Yggdrasil is the world-tree.  (Legend.)

question: Norse tradition is specific about what SPECIES of tree the world-tree is -- both Voluspa 19 and Gylfaginning 15 name it as one particular hardwood common in the northern forests. What kind of tree is the world-tree?
context: Voluspa 19 and Gylfaginning 15 both call the world-tree an ash. Zeus's sacred tree at Dodona was an oak; the yew was sacred to some Celtic sites; birch is the sacred tree of certain Siberian traditions. The Norse tree is an ash specifically.  (Legend.)

question: The name of the Norse world-tree literally means 'Odin's horse'. Odin also has the by-name 'Ygg', which means 'the Terrible'. Why is the tree called Odin's horse?
answer: it was his gallows the night he hanged himself for the runes
choices: it was his gallows the night he hanged himself for the runes
he tied his eight-legged horse to it every morning
he rides its branches down from Asgard to Midgard
its roots grew where his horse first pawed the earth
context: The kenning 'gallows' = 'horse of the hanged' is a common Old Norse metaphor: a hanged man 'rides' the gallows. Odin hanged himself on the world-tree for nine nights, pierced with his own spear, and won the runes; the tree became Ygg's-horse ever after.  (Legend.)

question: The Norns sit at the bottom of Yggdrasil beside one of the three great wells the tree's roots drink from. This is the well where the fates of gods and men are spoken. What is the Norns' well called?
context: Gylfaginning 15-16 and Voluspa 20. Urd's well feeds one of Yggdrasil's three roots and is where the three Norns -- Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld -- draw water to keep the tree alive. Mimir's well is where Odin traded his eye for wisdom; Hvergelmir bubbles up in cold Niflheim under the third root; Byrgir is the well from which Bil and Hjuki were fetching water when the moon-god Mani caught them up into the sky.  (Legend.)

question: Four HARTS -- male deer -- pace round the branches of Yggdrasil, cropping the leaves and bark. Grimnismal names all four in a single verse. What are the four harts of Yggdrasil called?
context: Grimnismal 33. The four hart-names all begin with D. Sleipnir/Grani/Gullfaxi/Hofvarpnir are famous horses (Odin's, Sigurd's, Gunnar's, Frigg's). Skoll/Hati/Fenrir/Garm are the four great wolves. Odin/Vili/Ve/Bor are Odin and his family.  (Legend.)

question: On the roof of Valhalla a she-goat named Heidrun stands eating leaves plucked from Yggdrasil's branches, and from her udder flows the endless supply of one particular drink for the warriors inside the hall. What comes from the udder of Heidrun?
context: Grimnismal 25. Heidrun the goat gives mead, not milk, and the mead never runs out; the Einherjar in Valhalla drink from it forever. The other three are the drinks a real Norse hall might have poured -- but the goat on Valhalla's roof pours only mead.  (Legend.)

question: Deep beneath the third root of Yggdrasil lies a serpent-dragon whose name means 'Malice-Striker'. Day and night he gnaws at the root, trying to bring the whole world-tree down. What is the dragon's name?
context: Grimnismal 32 and Gylfaginning 16. Nidhogg gnaws at the root and, in Voluspa, also chews the corpses of oath-breakers in Hel. Fafnir is the dwarf-turned-dragon killed by Sigurd for the ring-hoard; Jormungandr is the Midgard Serpent that circles the sea; Fenrir is the wolf of Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: A creature called 'Drill-Tooth' or 'Bore-Tooth' scurries up and down the trunk of Yggdrasil all day long, carrying insults between the eagle perched at the crown and the dragon gnawing at the root, keeping the quarrel between the two ends of the world-tree going. What is his name?
context: Grimnismal 32; Gylfaginning 16. Ratatoskr's name breaks down as rata- ('boring, gnawing') + -toskr ('tusk, tooth') -- and yes, he is a squirrel. Nagelfar is the ship built from dead men's nails that will sail at Ragnarok; Hraesvelg is the giant in eagle-shape whose wing-beats stir the winds of the world; Vidofnir is a golden cockerel that perches at the top of the mythic tree Mimameid in Fjolsvinnsmal.  (Legend.)

question: Vafthrudnismal 45 promises that after the fire of Ragnarok has swept the nine worlds, TWO humans -- one man and one woman -- will step out into the reborn earth to begin the human race again. What are the two survivors called?
context: Vafthrudnismal 45. Lif ('Life') and Lifthrasir ('Life-Yearner') are the two survivors who ride out the end inside the world-tree. Ask and Embla were the FIRST man and woman, carved from driftwood by Odin at the beginning; Sigurd and Brynhild are the doomed lovers of the Volsung cycle; Baldr and Nanna are the Aesir couple, Baldr slain before Ragnarok.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus rules the Olympian gods from the summit of Mount Olympus, and his signature weapon is a single flash-and-crash object that no other god wields. When kings and armies swore oaths, they swore by his weapon. What weapon is it?
context: The trident belongs to Poseidon, the caduceus to Hermes, and the golden bow to Apollo. Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Every Olympian god has a sacred bird that stands for him or her: Athena has the owl, Hera the peacock, and Aphrodite the dove. Zeus, the king of them all, has a bird that appears again and again on Greek and Roman standards and coins as his emblem. Which bird is Zeus's?
context: The eagle is Zeus's sacred bird throughout Greek myth and later Roman iconography (it later became the emblem of the Roman legions). Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus's thunderbolt was not something he made himself. It was forged for him during the great war of the gods, as a gift from three grateful giant smiths he had just freed from Tartarus, each named for what a thunderstorm sounds and looks like (Brontes, Steropes, Arges). What kind of monsters were these three smiths?
context: The three Elder Cyclopes: Brontes ('Thunder'), Steropes ('Lightning'), and Arges ('Bright'). Wikipedia: Zeus, Cyclopes.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus visited Leda, queen of Sparta, in a disguise so famous that Renaissance masters (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Correggio) painted the scene again and again on huge canvases. Their mortal daughter would grow up to be Helen of Troy. In what shape did Zeus come to Leda?
context: From the union came two eggs. From one hatched Helen of Troy and Pollux (Zeus's), and from the other Castor and Clytemnestra (Tyndareus's). Wikipedia: Leda.  (Legend.)

question: The Phoenician princess Europa was picking flowers on the beach at Tyre when a majestic white beast, gentle as a house pet, knelt beside her. She climbed on its back to play; it stood up, walked into the surf, and swam all the way to Crete, where it turned back into Zeus. In what shape did Zeus carry Europa off?
context: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875. On Crete she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon. Wikipedia: Europa.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus's oracle in the mountains of Epirus was one of the oldest in Greece, older than Delphi. Priests and priestesses stood beneath a single enormous sacred tree there and gave answers by listening to the sound of its leaves and branches. Which tree was Zeus's oracle-tree at Dodona?
context: The oak at Dodona was Zeus's alone. Compare Athena's olive at Athens, Apollo's laurel at Delphi. Wikipedia: Zeus.  (Legend.)

question: Zeus grew fond of a mortal boy famous for being the handsomest young man in the world, a prince of Troy who was up on the mountainside tending sheep. He sent his own eagle down to snatch the boy up alive into the sky and set him at the Olympian table to pour the gods' wine forever. What was the boy's name?
context: Ganymede replaced Hebe as cupbearer to the gods. The largest moon of Jupiter is named for him. Wikipedia: Ganymede.  (Legend.)

question: The Titan Prometheus tricked Zeus at Mecone by wrapping the bones and gristle of the sacrificed ox in shining fat and hiding the good meat inside the animal's stomach; Zeus (who could see the trick perfectly well) chose the fat-covered pile out of spite. In fury he denied mortals fire, so Prometheus stole fire from heaven and slipped it down to earth hidden inside an ordinary stalk. Inside what kind of stalk did Prometheus hide the stolen fire?
context: Hesiod, Theogony 521-616. Fennel stalks have a spongy pith that will hold a smouldering coal for a long time; Greeks travelling long distances really did carry fire this way. Wikipedia: Prometheus.  (Legend.)
